design_detail: Secondary analysis of the two-wave US National Epidemiologic Survey on Alcohol and Related Conditions (NESARC; Wave 1 2001-2002, Wave 2 2004-2005), using retrospective ages of onset to build discrete-time survival models of the transition from first use to DSM-IV dependence for four substances: nicotine, alcohol, cannabis and cocaine. Cumulative transition probabilities were estimated by the actuarial method overall and by racial and ethnic group, and predictors were estimated with univariable and stepwise multivariable discrete-time survival models with person-year as the unit of analysis.
can_establish: For US adults interviewed in both NESARC waves, the retrospectively reconstructed cumulative probability of meeting DSM-IV dependence criteria after first use of nicotine, alcohol, cannabis or cocaine, the time from first use to dependence, differences between racial and ethnic groups, and which measured characteristics predict that transition.
cannot_establish: Anything specific to methamphetamine or amphetamines: this paper analyses only nicotine, alcohol, cannabis and cocaine, and stimulants appear only inside a composite 'any other substance use disorder' covariate. It also cannot establish causal ordering for time-varying predictors measured once, cannot correct recall of ages of onset decades earlier, and does not cover institutionalized populations.

sample.recruitment: National probability sample of the US civilian non-institutionalized population aged 18 and over living in households and group quarters (college quarters, group homes, boarding houses, non-transient hotels), with oversampling of Black and Hispanic respondents and of adults aged 18 to 24. Analysis is restricted to the subsamples reporting lifetime use of each substance.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: Wave 2 respondents reporting lifetime use of the substance in question (first full cigarette; at least one alcoholic drink not counting sips; any cannabis use; any cocaine or crack use). Excluded by the survey frame: institutionalized people, and at Wave 2 those who had died (n=1403), were deported or physically or mentally impaired (n=781) or were on active military duty (n=950).
sample.demographics: Weighted use prevalences by group are given in Table 1 (for example cocaine use reported by 9.0% of men and 4.8% of women; 7.5% of White, 4.2% of Black, 6.0% of Hispanic, 3.4% of Native Hawaiian or other Pacific Islander and 10.4% of American Indian or Alaska Native respondents). Age, urbanicity, nativity, education, individual and family income, marital status and employment are tabulated for each substance.
sample.attrition: Of 43,093 Wave 1 respondents, 34,653 were re-interviewed at Wave 2 (80.4%, editors' calculation). Weights adjust for Wave 2 non-response; the authors report that after weighting there were no significant differences between Wave 2 respondents and the eligible target population on Wave 1 sociodemographics or on any lifetime substance, mood, anxiety or personality disorder.
sample.selection_effects: Survivor and participation bias: people who died, were institutionalized or were too impaired to be interviewed between waves are excluded, and the authors note that institutionalized people have higher rates of dependence, so transition probabilities are likely underestimated. Ages of onset for both use and dependence are recalled retrospectively, in some cases decades later, by people whose recall may be affected by the drug use being reported.

exposure.measurement: Self-report in the AUDADIS-IV structured diagnostic interview: age at first full cigarette, first alcoholic drink, first cannabis use and first cocaine or crack use. No biological verification. The authors cite test-retest reliability of kappa 0.54 to 0.91 for AUDADIS-IV substance use disorder diagnoses.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not analysed. The exposure is any lifetime use and its age of onset; quantity, frequency, route and continuity of use are not modelled. The authors list intermittent rather than continuous use as a limitation that makes the time from onset to dependence imprecise.
exposure.polysubstance: Handled as covariates: dependence on each of the other three index substances, and a composite 'any lifetime substance use disorder' covering the ten AUDADIS-IV classes (sedatives, tranquilizers, painkillers, stimulants, cannabis, cocaine or crack, hallucinogens, inhalants or solvents, heroin, other) plus alcohol and nicotine, excluding the substance under analysis. The paper reports that about half of people who used nicotine, a third of those who used alcohol, 80% of those who used cannabis and 93% of those who used cocaine had another substance use disorder (editors' calculation from Table 2).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: Within each substance, people who used it but had not (yet) become dependent, with person-years censored at the Wave 2 interview; and, for the racial and ethnic comparisons, White people who used it as the reference group.
comparison.matching: None. Adjustment by multivariable discrete-time survival models with stepwise selection by likelihood-ratio test, so the covariate set differs between substances (the cocaine model retains no age or sex term, for example).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Pre-use characteristics are largely unmeasured or measured only as lifetime diagnoses without dates, so most psychiatric covariates cannot be placed before or after the start of use. Education, marital status and mood, anxiety and other substance use disorders were entered as time-dependent; income could not be, which the authors name as a limitation for interpreting racial and ethnic differences.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Other substance use is adjusted for rather than excluded; comparison groups include people using other drugs.

outcomes.instruments: AUDADIS-IV (Wave 2 version) computer algorithms for DSM-IV dependence (3 or more of 7 criteria in a 12-month period) for each substance; DSM-IV mood, anxiety, psychotic, conduct and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorders and personality disorders, with reported test-retest reliability of kappa 0.40 to 0.77 and good to excellent convergent validity. Family history of substance use disorder among first-degree relatives and early onset (before age 14) were self-reported.
outcomes.validity_norms: Reliability and validity evidence is cited for the instrument; all outcomes are retrospective self-report, and dependence is DSM-IV, not DSM-5 use disorder, so the figures are not interchangeable with DSM-5 use-disorder prevalences.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Transition' is the appearance of DSM-IV dependence at any age after the age of first use, in person-year survival time. Cumulative probability is the actuarial estimate at 1 year, 10 years and lifetime (that is, the end of the observed curve, which the paper describes as the probability of becoming dependent 'at some time in their life').
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Four substances, each with lifetime and interval probabilities, five racial and ethnic strata with log-rank tests, and univariable and multivariable models over roughly 20 covariates; stepwise selection was used, which further inflates the chance of spurious retained predictors.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable; lay-interviewer structured interview with computer-generated diagnoses.

analysis.effect_sizes: Cumulative probability of transition to dependence: nicotine 67.5%, alcohol 22.7%, cocaine 20.9%, cannabis 8.9% lifetime; at one decade after first use, nicotine 15.6%, cocaine 14.8%, alcohol 11.0%, cannabis 5.9%; within the first year, about 2% for nicotine, alcohol and cannabis and 7.1% for cocaine. Median time from first use to dependence: nicotine about 27 years, alcohol 13, cannabis 5, cocaine 4. By racial and ethnic group (lifetime): nicotine 64.1% White, 70.7% Black, 64.7% Hispanic, 64.5% Native Hawaiian or other Pacific Islander, 85.1% American Indian or Alaska Native (log-rank 41.53, p<0.01); alcohol 22.6%, 21.4%, 26.7%, 16.9%, 29.0% (log-rank 47.16, p<0.01); cannabis 8.2%, 9.7%, 10.0%, 15.9%, 14.8% (log-rank 17.57, p<0.01); cocaine 16.8%, 35.9%, 20.5%, 20.3%, 22.5% (log-rank 30.40, p<0.01). Adjusted hazard ratios (Table 4) include, for cocaine dependence: Black versus White people who used cocaine 3.45 (2.2-5.3); mood disorder 2.58 (1.5-4.4); personality disorder 1.99 (1.4-2.9); alcohol dependence 2.56 (1.7-3.8); cannabis dependence 3.84 (1.8-8.2); onset before age 14, 0.34 (0.1-0.9). For cannabis dependence: male sex 1.44 (1.1-1.9); age 18 to 29 versus 45 and over 3.09 (1.9-4.9); mood disorder 2.69 (1.9-3.9); cocaine dependence 4.14 (2.3-7.6); onset before 14, 0.63 (0.5-0.9). For nicotine dependence: age 18 to 29, 15.78 (13.9-17.9); anxiety disorder 1.96 (1.8-2.2); alcohol dependence 2.35 (2.1-2.6). No confidence interval is given for any cumulative probability.
analysis.covariates: Sex, age group, race and ethnicity, urbanicity, nativity, education, individual and family income, marital status, employment, mood, anxiety, personality, conduct, psychotic and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorders, dependence on each of the other three substances, family history of substance use disorder and onset before age 14; education, marital status and mood, anxiety and other substance use disorders entered as time-dependent. Stepwise selection means the final models differ by substance.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Secondary analysis of an existing survey; no protocol or analysis plan referenced.
analysis.selective_reporting: Characteristics of the people who became dependent are in supplementary tables (not read). Stepwise selection leaves several covariates absent from some columns of Table 4 without the non-significant estimates being shown. No intervals are reported for the cumulative probabilities, which are the paper's most-cited numbers.
analysis.power: Not discussed. Precision varies greatly by cell: the cocaine dependence model rests on 376 cases, the cannabis model on 529, and some subgroup cells are very small (only 51 people who used cocaine reported first use before age 14, yet an adjusted hazard ratio of 0.34 for that variable is reported).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among US adults who had ever used each substance, the retrospectively estimated lifetime probability of DSM-IV dependence was 67.5% for nicotine, 22.7% for alcohol, 20.9% for cocaine and 8.9% for cannabis, with dependence appearing fastest after cocaine and cannabis use. Transition probabilities differed by racial and ethnic group, most sharply for cocaine (35.9% in Black versus 16.8% in White people who used cocaine). Psychiatric disorders, other substance dependence, family history and some sociodemographic factors predicted transition across substances. Early onset predicted transition in unadjusted models but reversed direction for cannabis and cocaine after adjustment.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The paper's conclusions stay close to its data. The relevant gap is one of scope rather than overreach: it is routinely cited for the conditional probability of dependence given use, and it provides no estimate for methamphetamine or any amphetamine. A further gap is that the discussion explains racial and ethnic differences in transition with mechanisms (acculturative stress, discrimination, social capital, genetics) that the study did not measure, while the authors themselves note that income could not be modelled over time; and lifetime cumulative probabilities from actuarial curves are presented without intervals, although they project beyond the observed follow-up of many respondents.

timeline.event: Anthony, Warner and Kessler estimate dependence given use from the National Comorbidity Survey, including an estimate for stimulants, which is the usual source for amphetamine-type figures
Wagner and Anthony estimate 12% to 13% alcohol, 8% cannabis and 15% to 16% cocaine dependence within a decade of first use (cited in this paper's introduction and discussion as the comparison).
This study: NESARC two-wave estimates for nicotine, alcohol, cannabis and cocaine.

replication.where_it_stands: The decade-level estimates agree closely with the earlier National Comorbidity Survey work for alcohol, cannabis and cocaine, which is a genuine replication across two independent national surveys with different instruments. For methamphetamine the question remains open in this literature: the encyclopedia's conditional-probability figure for amphetamine-type stimulants must come from another source (Anthony et al., 1994 for stimulants, or a NESARC analysis of the stimulant category), not from this paper.

funding.funder: Not reported in the PMC author manuscript: it contains no funding statement, acknowledgements or role-of-funding-source section. One author is at the Laboratory of Epidemiology and Biometry, Division of Intramural Clinical and Biological Research, National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (NIAAA), the agency that conducts NESARC, and is the corresponding author.
funding.declared_conflicts: Not reported in this version of the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Authors at the New York State Psychiatric Institute and Columbia University (Department of Psychiatry and Mailman School of Public Health), Hospital de la Santa Creu i Sant Pau (Barcelona) and NIAAA. The survey's custodian agency is represented among the authors.

what_would_settle_it: For the encyclopedia's purpose, an equivalent analysis of the NESARC or NSDUH stimulant and methamphetamine categories, with prospective or at least repeated measurement of use frequency and route, would give a conditional probability of dependence after first methamphetamine use; more generally, a prospective cohort followed from before first use would remove the recall and survivor bias in all of these retrospective estimates.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: National probability frame for US civilian non-institutionalized adults, with Black, Hispanic and young adults oversampled; institutionalized people, who have higher dependence rates, are excluded, as the authors note.
Multistage probability sample with design-based analysis (Taylor series linearization in SUDAAN) and Wave 2 weights.
Large overall, but the cocaine (376 dependence cases) and cannabis (529) models and several racial and ethnic cells are small; the cell for cocaine use before age 14 contains 51 people.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Tables 1 and 2 describe sociodemographic, psychiatric and substance-use characteristics for each substance subsample, although their row totals do not match the stated subsample sizes (see reporting issues).

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: 80.4% of Wave 1 respondents were re-interviewed (editors' calculation); weights adjust for non-response and the authors report no significant differences between respondents and the eligible target population on baseline measures.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: AUDADIS-IV with documented reliability and validity, but entirely self-report with no biological or record verification, and ages of onset are recalled retrospectively, in some cases across decades, by people whose recall may be affected by their drug use (a limitation the authors state).

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: The same structured instrument and computer algorithms for all respondents; dependence is DSM-IV throughout.

Actuarial survival estimation and discrete-time survival models with time-dependent covariates are appropriate for onset data, but cumulative probabilities are reported without confidence intervals, stepwise selection makes the models non-comparable across substances and inflates selection on chance, and no multiplicity adjustment is applied.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low rate managed
domains.note: Wave 2 retention is good and weighted, but the cumulative Wave 1 and Wave 2 response is lower than the retention figure alone suggests, and people who died or became too impaired between waves are necessarily excluded (survivor bias in a dependence-outcome analysis).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A well-conducted secondary analysis of a large national probability survey with a validated instrument and an appropriate survival framework. The limits on its numbers are structural rather than procedural: retrospective recall of ages of onset, exclusion of institutionalized and deceased people, lifetime cumulative probabilities projected without intervals, and stepwise model selection. For this encyclopedia the decisive point is not bias but scope: the paper contains no methamphetamine or amphetamine estimate, so it cannot support any claim about methamphetamine dependence liability.

key_findings.finding: The paper analyses only four substances, nicotine, alcohol, cannabis and cocaine. Methamphetamine and amphetamines are never an exposure or outcome; 'stimulants' appear only as one of the ten AUDADIS-IV classes making up a composite 'any other substance use disorder' covariate. No methamphetamine-specific conditional probability of dependence can be taken from this paper.
key_findings.locator: Title and Abstract; Methods › 2.3.1 Substance use and dependence; Table 2 footnote a
key_findings.note: Recorded explicitly because this reference is commonly cited for dependence-given-use figures across drugs.

key_findings.finding: Lifetime cumulative probability of transition from first use to DSM-IV dependence: nicotine 67.5%, alcohol 22.7%, cocaine 20.9%, cannabis 8.9%. No confidence intervals are given.

Cumulative probability of dependence one decade after first use: nicotine 15.6%, cocaine 14.8%, alcohol 11.0%, cannabis 5.9%. Within the first year of use: about 2% for nicotine, alcohol and cannabis, and 7.1% for cocaine.
Median time from first use to dependence: about 27 years for nicotine, 13 for alcohol, 5 for cannabis and 4 for cocaine.
key_findings.note: The subgroup medians in section 3.3.2 and 3.3.4 (8 years for alcohol and 2 years for cocaine among White people who used them, who are the largest group) do not sit easily with these overall values; see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Cocaine showed the largest racial and ethnic difference: lifetime transition to dependence in 35.9% of Black versus 16.8% of White, 20.5% of Hispanic, 20.3% of Native Hawaiian or other Pacific Islander and 22.5% of American Indian or Alaska Native people who used it (log-rank 30.40, p<0.01). In the adjusted model, Black people who used cocaine had a hazard ratio of 3.45 (95% CI 2.2 to 5.3) versus White people who used it.

Transition to nicotine dependence was highest among American Indian or Alaska Native people who used nicotine (85.1% versus 64.1% in White people who used it; log-rank 41.53, p<0.01); for alcohol the range was 16.9% (Native Hawaiian or other Pacific Islander) to 29.0% (American Indian or Alaska Native); for cannabis 8.2% (White) to 15.9% (Native Hawaiian or other Pacific Islander).

Psychiatric comorbidity predicted transition for every substance in adjusted models: mood disorder hazard ratios 1.62 (nicotine), 2.29 (alcohol), 2.69 (cannabis), 2.58 (cocaine); personality disorder 1.42, 1.64, 2.30, 1.99; anxiety disorder 1.96, 1.98, 2.31 (not retained for cocaine).

Dependence on another substance strongly predicted transition: for example cannabis dependence predicted cocaine dependence (hazard ratio 3.84, 1.8 to 8.2) and cocaine dependence predicted cannabis dependence (4.14, 2.3 to 7.6); alcohol dependence predicted nicotine (2.35), cannabis (2.55) and cocaine (2.56) dependence.

Early onset (before age 14) predicted transition in unadjusted models (cannabis 2.47, cocaine 1.65 non-significant, nicotine 1.29, alcohol 2.51) but reversed direction after adjustment for cannabis (0.63, 0.5 to 0.9) and cocaine (0.34, 0.1 to 0.9), while remaining positive for nicotine (1.13). The authors interpret this as early onset being a marker of concomitant psychiatric and substance comorbidity rather than a risk factor in itself.
key_findings.note: Only 51 people who used cocaine reported first use before age 14 (Table 2), so the adjusted estimate of 0.34 rests on a very small cell.

key_findings.finding: Co-occurring substance use disorders were the norm among people who used the illicit substances: about 51% of people who used nicotine, 31% of those who used alcohol, 81% of those who used cannabis and 93% of those who used cocaine had a substance use disorder involving another substance (editors' calculation from Table 2 counts; the discussion states one third, half, more than 80% and 90%).

Sample: 43,093 Wave 1 respondents, 34,653 re-interviewed at Wave 2 (80.4%, editors' calculation); analyses use the subsamples reporting lifetime use of each substance (stated as 15,918 nicotine, 28,907 alcohol, 7,389 cannabis, 2,259 cocaine), with DSM-IV diagnoses generated by AUDADIS-IV algorithms and all estimates weighted to the US population.
key_findings.locator: Methods › 2.1 Sample and procedures; 2.2 Data collection

key_findings.finding: Stated limitations: self-report without objective confirmation; recall bias increasing with the interval since the event and with drug-related cognitive impairment; intermittent rather than continuous use making the time from onset to dependence imprecise; exclusion of institutionalized people, who have higher dependence rates; and the impossibility of modelling income as a time-dependent covariate.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, last paragraph before the summary

reporting_issues.issue: The row totals in Table 1 do not match the subsample sizes stated in the abstract and methods. Every stratification in Table 1 sums to 16,053 for nicotine, 29,160 for alcohol, 7,409 for cannabis and 2,263 for cocaine, while the stated subsamples are 15,918, 28,907, 7,389 and 2,259 (arithmetic by the editors, consistent across gender, age, race, urbanicity, nativity, education and employment).
reporting_issues.consequence: The denominators of the descriptive table are internally consistent but differ from the analytic Ns by 135, 253, 20 and 4 people. The percentages quoted in the discussion for co-occurring substance use disorders reproduce the Table 1 denominators, so the larger figures appear to be the actual subsample sizes.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 2 the counts for 'any lifetime psychiatric disorder' are identical to those for 'any lifetime mood disorder' (for example 11,458 and 4,595 for nicotine; 4,573 and 2,836 for cannabis) while the accompanying percentages differ sharply (nicotine 27.4% versus 44.5% in the 'no' rows, cannabis 5.1% versus 17.7%).
reporting_issues.consequence: The two rows cannot both be right: the number of people with no psychiatric disorder of any kind cannot equal the number with no mood disorder. One set of counts or percentages has been mis-transcribed, so Table 2's psychiatric rows should not be quoted.

reporting_issues.issue: The number of dependence cases in Tables 3 and 4 (7,320 nicotine, 4,822 alcohol, 529 cannabis, 376 cocaine) is lower than the number of people with each lifetime dependence diagnosis in Table 2 (7,473, 4,869, 564, 398), with no explanation.
reporting_issues.consequence: Between 2% and 6% of dependence cases are missing from the survival models, presumably for missing onset ages; the exclusion is not described or characterized.

reporting_issues.issue: The overall median latency to dependence (13 years for alcohol, 4 for cocaine) is longer than the median reported for White people who used each substance, who are the largest group in each subsample (8 years for alcohol, 2 years for cocaine).
reporting_issues.consequence: An overall median should normally lie near that of the dominant group; either the overall and subgroup medians come from differently specified curves or one set is misreported. Latency figures should be cited with this caveat.

reporting_issues.issue: Section 3.1 states that 'rates of nicotine, alcohol, cannabis and alcohol use were higher among males', listing alcohol twice where cocaine is meant.
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical; the table shows the intended comparison.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 prints an individual-income cell for the nicotine subsample as '44.o' instead of 44.0.
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical only.

reporting_issues.issue: No confidence intervals are given for any cumulative transition probability, including the headline lifetime figures of 67.5%, 22.7%, 20.9% and 8.9%.
reporting_issues.consequence: The precision of the most-cited numbers in the paper cannot be assessed, and lifetime estimates from actuarial curves extrapolate beyond the follow-up observed for younger respondents.

reporting_issues.issue: Multivariable models were built by stepwise selection, so covariates appear in some substance columns of Table 4 and not others (the cocaine model retains neither sex nor age group), and the non-selected estimates are not shown.
reporting_issues.consequence: The paper's claim that predictors are shared across substances is partly an artefact of which variables survived selection in each model; the columns of Table 4 are not directly comparable.

reporting_issues.issue: The PMC author manuscript carries no funding statement, acknowledgements or conflict-of-interest declaration.
reporting_issues.consequence: Funding and interests cannot be recorded from this version; the published version or the journal page would be needed.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC3069146 (author manuscript; all sections, Tables 1 to 4 rendered as text, author affiliations and footnotes read; Figures 1 and 2, the survival curves, are images and their values were taken only from the text; supplementary tables 5 and 6 were not read)

editorial_corrections.reason: Language (METHODS §9): 25 replacements, no change of meaning, number or citation; list in data/verification/language-2026-10-16.json

design_detail: Narrative review of the clinical pharmacology of methamphetamine: chemistry and molecular mechanisms; pharmacokinetics by route (Table 1) and detection times (Table 2); acute effects identified in prospective studies (Table 3); and adverse effects (overdose, psychosis, cardiovascular complications, withdrawal, neurotoxicity, neuropsychological impairment, Parkinson's disease, sexual behaviour, teratogenic and other effects). Literature from a PubMed search (English, human studies, 1966–2007), reference lists, book chapters and monographs; no inclusion criteria, no appraisal of the cited studies and no quantitative synthesis. 183 references.
can_establish: What the cited literature up to 2007 reported about methamphetamine's pharmacokinetics, acute effects and adverse effects, and which primary studies those statements come from, as a map of sources to read.
cannot_establish: How often any adverse effect occurs among people who use methamphetamine or among those who present with toxicity (the figures are second-hand and mostly lack denominators), what predicts death, or whether the chronic harms described are caused by methamphetamine (the cited observational studies are not appraised).

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). PubMed search for methamphetamine, methylamphetamine or metamfetamine, limited to English-language human studies published 1966–2007: 447 articles, screened by hand; reference lists, book chapters and monographs from peak bodies added; inclusion decided by consensus between the two authors; mechanisms, chemistry and molecular pharmacology were not searched systematically (pp. 1085–1086, Methods).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Excluded on screening: preclinical studies, review articles superseded by more recent reviews, and papers the authors judged less relevant (p. 1085). No inclusion criteria stated.
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: Selection by the authors' judgment without stated criteria, from one database in English only. For acute toxicity the review relies on case reports (several of them amphetamine poisonings, from 1960 onward), a few emergency-department series and a treatment trial, and forensic series, which over-represent severe and fatal cases and give no population denominators.

exposure.measurement: Not applicable at review level. The cited laboratory studies used low-to-moderate oral, intranasal, smoked or intravenous doses as study conditions, with one high-dose intravenous study of 12 people, for whom the review says previous histories of psychosis should be considered, without giving a number (p. 1088); illicit amounts come from self-report, which the review notes has not been substantiated objectively (p. 1088).
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed for the toxicity and mortality evidence: the proportion of deaths with other drugs detected is not given.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: Not applicable (narrative review).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not discussed for the observational evidence on psychosis, cognition and Parkinson's disease, beyond previous psychosis among the high-dose study's participants (p. 1088) and family history of schizophrenia in persistent psychosis (p. 1091).

outcomes.instruments: Not applicable (they vary across the cited studies).
outcomes.operationalization: Overdose features are listed from case reports; frequencies of features in non-fatal presentations come from emergency-department series; causes of death come from case reports and forensic series.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (no statistical synthesis).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: As cited, without appraisal. Pharmacokinetics (p. 1087, Table 1): terminal plasma half-life about 10 hours across routes, with substantial individual variability (9.1 h intravenous, 12 h smoked, 9.1 h oral, 11 h intranasal); bioavailability 67–90% smoked, 67% oral, 79% intranasal. Acute toxicity (pp. 1088, 1091): among non-fatal presentations, agitation in about 20%, suicidal ideation in 6–12%, acute psychosis in 7–12%, rhabdomyolysis in up to 14% and seizures in 3–4%; an estimated 94 000 US emergency-department visits associated with recent methamphetamine use in 2005; proposed toxic (200–5000 µg/l) and fatal (above 10 000 µg/l) plasma concentrations overlap with reported deaths (as low as 90 µg/l) and survival (9460 µg/l). Psychosis (p. 1091): of 170 Japanese people with methamphetamine psychosis, 59% recovered within 30 days, 41% had symptoms beyond a month and 28% beyond 6 months of abstinence. Cardiomyopathy: a 3.7-fold increased risk (p. 1091). Parkinson's disease (p. 1093): one retrospective case–control study of amphetamines, an eightfold risk with a mean of 27 years between exposure and onset.
analysis.covariates: Not applicable.
analysis.selective_reporting: The cited studies are neither appraised nor described by design or size. The overdose section lists features without saying how often they occur; the emergency-department frequencies come without sample sizes. The Parkinson's disease argument rests on one case–control study of amphetamines and a dopamine-transporter threshold argument. The neurotoxicity section equates a baboon regimen with human illicit use by simple body-weight scaling, without an allometric or pharmacokinetic basis (p. 1092).
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: A broad summary of the literature to 2007, with pharmacokinetic values from controlled human studies and adverse-effect frequencies taken second-hand from small clinical series and case reports.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract links repeated use, through neurotoxicity, to prolonged psychiatric symptoms, cognitive impairment and an increased risk of Parkinson's disease (p. 1085); the body supports the Parkinson's link with one case–control study of amphetamines and an extrapolation from dopamine-transporter deficits that, by its own account, are below the level associated with Parkinsonian signs (p. 1093). The neurotoxicity section states as established that repeated exposure to amphetamines damages dopaminergic and serotonergic axons, mainly from animal work (p. 1092). The abstract does not mention the overdose syndrome. Within the toxicity section the statements are modest and follow the cited sources, but frequencies are given without denominators, and the forensic observation that many methamphetamine-related deaths result from accidents, suicide and homicide is not quantified.

timeline.event: This review: half-life about 10 hours; overdose features and frequencies from case reports, emergency-department and forensic series.
Review cites this review (its reference 16) for the methamphetamine half-life
Review gives about 10 hours for the methamphetamine half-life, citing this review

replication.where_it_stands: A widely reused reference review for pharmacokinetics. For acute toxicity it is a pointer to primary sources that are still to be read and carded before any frequency is cited: emergency-department series (Gray et al., 2007; Derlet et al., 1989), a treatment trial (Richards et al., 1997), case reports and forensic series of deaths (Inoue et al., 2006; Kalant and Kalant, 1975; Logan et al., 1998; Shaw, 1999; Zhu et al., 2000).

funding.funder: No funding statement for the review; the first author was supported by a Dora Lush Scholarship from the National Health and Medical Research Council of Australia (p. 1094, Acknowledgements).
funding.declared_conflicts: Declarations of interest: none (p. 1094).
funding.affiliations_note: Pharmacology and Anaesthesiology Unit, University of Western Australia; Division of Mental Health, St George's, University of London (p. 1085). None of the authors' own studies is cited. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the review.

what_would_settle_it: For acute toxicity: prospective emergency-department or poison-centre cohorts of people presenting after methamphetamine use, with toxicological confirmation, recording how often each feature occurs, the case fatality and the features at presentation that predict death, with denominators. For the chronic harms, the primary cohort and case–control studies the review cites, appraised directly.

domains.note: A documented PubMed search (terms, limits, 447 hits) and reference-list searching, but selection by the authors' judgment of relevance without stated criteria, one database, English only, and no systematic search for mechanisms.

No appraisal: case reports, emergency-department series, a treatment trial and animal studies are cited side by side, frequencies without denominators; some qualifications are given (the high-dose study's participants, the concentration ranges, self-reported illicit amounts).

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: None of the authors' own studies is cited.
Mechanisms in Table 3 are labelled possible, but human neurotoxicity and the Parkinson's disease risk are stated with more confidence than the cited evidence carries.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence on adverse effects (descriptions of severe cases against how often harms occur)
domains.note: The under-represented side is evidence on how often harms occur among people who use methamphetamine: the toxicity and chronic-harm sections rest on case reports and clinical samples. Recovery is mentioned (resolution of most psychoses, partial recovery of striatal markers with abstinence).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS §5.3). The review documents a search but selects without criteria and does not appraise what it cites; it qualifies some evidence carefully but not its statements on human neurotoxicity and Parkinson's disease. It may be cited for pharmacokinetic summaries traced to their primary studies and as a pointer to the primary toxicity literature; frequencies of toxic features are to be cited from the primary series, and a claim resting on this review alone stays at draft and says its figures are second-hand.

key_findings.finding: Search: PubMed, English-language human studies 1966–2007, 447 articles screened by hand; preclinical studies, superseded reviews and papers judged less relevant were excluded; reference lists, books and monographs added; inclusion by consensus of the two authors; mechanisms not searched systematically.

The terminal plasma half-life of methamphetamine is about 10 hours, similar across routes but with substantial individual variability; Table 1 gives 9.1 h (intravenous), 12 h (smoked), 9.1 h (oral, range 3–17) and 11 h (intranasal).
key_findings.locator: Clinical pharmacology › Clinical pharmacokinetics, 3rd paragraph; Table 1
key_findings.note: Table 1 values are mean ± standard error and/or range from single studies (references 33, 152, 153, 11, 30, 154, 32); see reporting issues on the intranasal row.

key_findings.finding: Based on case reports, the common features of methamphetamine overdose are agitation, dilated pupils, tachycardia, hypertension and rapid respiration; other features include shivering, dyspnoea, chest pain, hyperpyrexia and cardiac, hepatic or renal failure; coma and seizures are less frequent. An estimated 94 000 US emergency-department visits were associated with recent methamphetamine use in 2005.
key_findings.note: The sources for the features (references 29 and 44–51) are case reports, several of amphetamine poisoning, published from 1960 onward.

key_findings.finding: Non-fatal methamphetamine toxicity presents typically with tachycardia, hypertension and altered mental status: agitation in about 20% of cases, suicidal ideation in 6–12%, acute psychosis in 7–12%; rhabdomyolysis in up to 14% of presentations; seizures in 3–4%.
key_findings.note: No sample sizes or denominators are given. By the reference list, the sources are an evaluation of amphetamine-related emergency presentations (Gray et al., 2007), a trial of benzodiazepine against butyrophenone treatment of methamphetamine toxicity (Richards et al., 1997), 127 cases of amphetamine toxicity (Derlet et al., 1989) and a paper titled as a study of protection against d-amphetamine toxicity (Derlet et al., 1990), which may not be a clinical series; none has been read.

key_findings.finding: Case reports attribute methamphetamine-associated deaths most often to multiple congestion, pulmonary oedema or congestion, cerebrovascular haemorrhage, ventricular fibrillation, acute cardiac failure or hyperpyrexia, and others to septic injection or aspiration of vomit; several forensic studies suggest that a significant and possibly greater proportion of methamphetamine-related deaths arise from accidents, suicide and homicide.
key_findings.note: The causes of death rest on a single case report (Inoue et al., 2006) and a 1975 review of deaths in people who used amphetamines (Kalant and Kalant); the forensic series are from the USA, Taiwan and Japan (references 58–60). No proportions are given.

key_findings.finding: Proposed toxic (200–5000 µg/l) and fatal (above 10 000 µg/l) plasma concentrations are guides only: deaths have been reported at concentrations as low as 90 µg/l and survival at 9460 µg/l.
key_findings.locator: Adverse effects › Methamphetamine overdose, 4th paragraph (after Table 3)
key_findings.note: The PDF's text layer renders the unit µg/l as mg/l throughout; the printed pages show µg/l (checked on the rendered pp. 1087, 1088 and 1091).

key_findings.finding: Few systematic studies exist on cardiovascular complications, so most of the evidence comes from case studies: acute coronary syndrome, aortic dissection and sudden cardiac death; a 3.7-fold increased risk of cardiomyopathy; and, from population studies, a higher risk of haemorrhagic and ischaemic stroke.
Among 170 Japanese people with methamphetamine psychosis, 59% recovered within 30 days, 41% still had symptoms after a month and 28% after more than 6 months of abstinence.

The case for an increased Parkinson's disease risk rests on one retrospective case–control study (prolonged amphetamine use, an eightfold risk, a mean of 27 years between exposure and onset; reference 133), on the argument that Parkinsonian signs appear with striatal dopamine-transporter deficits of 47% or more, against 20–30% in people recently abstinent from methamphetamine, plus an age-related decline of about 4.5% per decade, and on one study (reference 105, Volkow et al., 2001) cited both for psychomotor dysfunction consistent with Parkinson's disease and for Parkinson-like disturbances in people whose dopaminergic damage was within the Parkinson range. The review also notes two studies (references 107 and 123: Johanson et al., 2006; Chang et al., 2002) that did not find such deficits despite neuronal pathology consistent with the disorder.

reporting_issues.issue: The review writes that dopamine-transporter deficits in recently abstinent people are typically 20–30% of normal levels, which taken literally means a 70–80% deficit; the argument (deficits below the 47% associated with Parkinsonian signs) requires reductions of 20–30%.
reporting_issues.consequence: A wording error that reverses the size of the deficit if quoted as printed.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 1 the intranasal half-life (11 ± 1 hours) carries footnote a, which the legend defines as a peak effect estimated from plots of subjective effect; and the intravenous time to peak concentration is printed as 6 ± 11 minutes, a standard error larger than the geometric mean it accompanies.
reporting_issues.consequence: Either the footnote is misplaced or the half-life was read from a plot; the intravenous value cannot be interpreted as printed. Neither value is used in a claim.

reporting_issues.issue: The text gives the intranasal time to peak plasma concentration as 4 hours (reference 35), while Table 1 gives 169 ± 8 minutes (reference 32); the two sources are not reconciled.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; cite the primary studies.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 3 the mechanism given for increased blood pressure reads as an increase in heart rate in pithed rats via α-adrenoceptors, apparently repeated from the heart-rate row.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor copy error in the mechanisms column.

reporting_issues.issue: Of the four sources cited for the features and frequencies of non-fatal presentations (references 52–55), two are titled as series of amphetamine-related presentations or amphetamine toxicity (Gray et al., 2007; Derlet et al., 1989), one as a study of protection against d-amphetamine toxicity (Derlet et al., 1990), which may not be a clinical series, and one as a treatment trial in methamphetamine toxicity (Richards et al., 1997).
reporting_issues.consequence: The frequencies may not describe people presenting with methamphetamine toxicity; to be checked in the primary papers before any is cited.

reporting_issues.issue: The review says population studies indicate that methamphetamine raises the risk of haemorrhagic and ischaemic stroke, citing references 50 and 78; reference 50 is a series of four cases and reference 78 is a population-based study of young adults hospitalized with amphetamine or cocaine diagnoses, so only one source is a population study and its exposure is not specific to methamphetamine. The 3.7-fold cardiomyopathy figure comes from a single study in young patients (reference 76).
reporting_issues.consequence: The stroke and cardiomyopathy statements (key finding 6) are stronger than their sources; reference 78 should be cited for stroke in people with amphetamine or cocaine diagnoses, not as methamphetamine-specific population evidence.

reporting_issues.issue: The review's statement that a fatal overdose has been reported after a single intravenous dose rests on one case report (reference 29), whose title describes a patient who died nine days after the injection.
reporting_issues.consequence: A single case with nine days of survival cannot be read as describing typical fatal exposures; the review gives no population data linking dose to death.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says psychosis can occur at the higher doses typically used by people who use illicit methamphetamine, as a fact, while the body says the self-reported illicit amounts behind this have not been substantiated objectively and the pharmacokinetics of illicit methamphetamine remain to be described, adding only that forensic plasma levels are consistent with them.
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract is more certain than the body about what people who use illicit methamphetamine actually take; the body's caveat should accompany any use of the abstract's statement.

design_detail: FDG-PET follow-up in the same drug-court programme as Volkow et al. (2001a–c). Five people with methamphetamine dependence scanned after short abstinence (mean 3 months) and again after protracted abstinence (mean 14 months); 8 more scanned once after at least 9 months; cross-sectional comparison with 11 non-using controls and with the 12 people scanned in short abstinence. Motor, memory and attention tests repeated in the 5 retested participants only.
can_establish: That in the 5 retested participants relative thalamic metabolism rose between scans while striatal metabolism did not change, and that striatal metabolism was lower than in controls in both short- and protracted-abstinence groups.
cannot_establish: That thalamic metabolism 'recovers' in people who stop using generally (5 selected completers; test statistics internally inconsistent); that thalamic change produced the test improvements (5 people, no retested controls for practice effects); or anything about amotivation or anhedonia (not measured).

sample.recruitment: Methamphetamine group enrolled in a California drug-court monitoring rehabilitation programme with weekly or biweekly drug screens and daily centre visits; controls by advertisement (p. 243).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: DSM-IV methamphetamine dependence; average use at least 0.25 g/day, 5 days a week, 2 years; at least 2 weeks' abstinence. Excluded: HIV seropositivity, comorbid neuropsychiatric disorder, medical illness, dependence on other drugs except nicotine (p. 243).
sample.demographics: Retested methamphetamine group: 3 women, 2 men, age 29 (SD 3). Methamphetamine group tested once: 6 women, 2 men, age 36 (SD 3). Controls: 7 women, 4 men, age 31 (SD 7). Short-abstinence group of 12: 7 women, 5 men, age 30 (SD 6) (p. 243). Education, IQ and smoking not reported.
sample.attrition: Of 12 people first scanned within 6 months of last use, only 5 stayed drug-free for 9 months and were rescanned; relapsers were excluded from follow-up (pp. 243, 247).
sample.selection_effects: The retested participants are those who stayed abstinent, a group shown in the companion DAT paper to have had higher baseline DAT and better test scores than dropouts (Volkow et al., 2001b, p. 9416). In this programme relapse meant a return to jail (p. 247).

exposure.measurement: Self-reported history; random urine screens within 2-week periods plus a pre-scan urine test (pp. 243, 247).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Inclusion threshold only (p. 243).
exposure.polysubstance: Dependence on other drugs except nicotine excluded; other use not quantified.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Retested: 3 months (SD 1.6) then 14 months (SD 2), i.e. 12–17 months. Once-only: 17 months (SD 10). Short-abstinence group: 64 days (SD 40) (pp. 242–243). The authors note intermittent use between random tests could have been missed (p. 247).

comparison.controls: 11 non-using volunteers recruited by advertisement, scanned once (p. 243).
comparison.matching: Described as age-matched; sex mix similar; education, IQ and smoking not reported.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No pre-use scan.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Excluded for drug abuse or dependence other than nicotine (p. 243).

outcomes.instruments: FDG-PET at rest; striatum, thalamus and occipital cortex (control region) by template regions of interest; relative measures = region/global; SPM99 (p. 243). Timed Gait, Grooved Pegboard, Rey AVLT (immediate, delayed, interference recall), Symbol Digit Modalities Test in the methamphetamine group only (p. 243).
outcomes.validity_norms: Test scores were compared neither with controls nor with norms.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Recovery' = within-person change in relative metabolism; 'functional significance' = correlation of metabolic change with test-score change in 5 people.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None for region-of-interest or correlation analyses; the authors say they limited the number of tests to avoid multiple comparisons (p. 247). SPM: voxel p<0.001 with cluster-level correction (p. 243).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported.

analysis.effect_sizes: Retested participants, short vs protracted: no change in global (42.6 vs 40.8 µmol/100 g/min) or absolute regional metabolism; relative thalamic metabolism +12% (SD 9%), reported as t=2.3, df=9, p<0.05; striatum +2.7% (SD 6.7%), occipital +0.4%, not significant (p. 244). Correlations of thalamic change with test change in the 5: Timed Gait r=0.88, Symbol Digit r=0.96, delayed recall r=0.98 (each df=3); Grooved Pegboard r=0.26 and immediate/interference recall r=0.32 not significant (p. 244; Figure 2, p. 245). Cross-sectional: relative caudate metabolism lower than controls (1.35, SD 0.06) after short (1.20, SD 0.10) and protracted abstinence (1.23, SD 0.09); putamen likewise; thalamus lower after short abstinence (1.11 vs 1.31, t=−5.3) but 'not different' after protracted abstinence (1.23 vs 1.31) (p. 244). Editors' calculation from the reported means and SDs: protracted-abstinence thalamus vs controls d≈−0.8, p≈0.05–0.07, so the thalamus did not return to control levels in any demonstrated sense. The protracted-abstinence group had higher thalamic metabolism than the short-abstinence group (t=−3.8, df=23) with no striatal difference (p. 245).
analysis.covariates: None.
analysis.selective_reporting: Test scores are reported only as correlations with metabolic change; their raw changes and practice effects are not reported.
analysis.power: Not reported; the authors note the small, possibly unrepresentative sample (p. 247).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 5 selected people abstinent from methamphetamine, thalamic metabolism relative to the whole brain rose and striatal metabolism did not change significantly; relative striatal metabolism stayed below controls in short and protracted abstinence. The paper reports that larger thalamic increases went with larger test-score gains on 3 of 5 measures, but its Figure 2 cannot be reconciled with the same people's test means in Volkow et al. (2001b) (reporting issue 3), so the direction of that relation is uncertain.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and discussion present thalamic 'recovery' as associated with improved motor and memory performance and therefore functionally significant (abstract; pp. 245–247), and suggest that lower accumbens metabolism could account for persistent amotivation and anhedonia (abstract; p. 246), which the study did not measure. The summary speaks of protracted abstinence and rehabilitation reversing some methamphetamine-induced alterations (p. 247), a causal reading the design cannot support. The test 'improvements' have no practice-effect control.

Critical review: no educational data, no normative comparison of cognitive scores
Review: thalamic change correlated with test improvement, but no procedure controlled for practice effects

replication.where_it_stands: A control-retested FDG study over the first month of abstinence (10 people who used methamphetamine, 12 controls) found larger increases in global metabolism in the methamphetamine group than in controls (Berman et al., summarized by Dean et al., 2013, p. 265); no study has repeated the 12-month thalamic finding.

funding.funder: US Department of Energy contract; National Institute on Drug Abuse grants; Office of National Drug Control Policy; NIH General Clinical Research Center grants (p. 247).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Same group and programme as Volkow et al. (2001a–c).

what_would_settle_it: Repeated imaging and testing over 12–24 months in all people entering treatment, including those who relapse, with non-using controls retested at the same intervals.

domains.note: Smoking, education and other drug use not reported or adjusted.
Abstinence monitored by random urine screens; intermittent use possible (p. 247).
Only those who stayed abstinent were followed; relapsers excluded.
Daily programme attendance, cognitive behaviour therapy, threat of jail.
7 of 12 not followed.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A 5-person selected follow-up with inconsistent statistics; the cross-sectional comparisons share the confounding of the parent study.

key_findings.finding: In 5 people rescanned at 12–17 months, relative (region-to-global) thalamic metabolism rose by 12% (SD 9%), while relative striatal (+2.7%) and occipital (+0.4%) metabolism showed no significant change; global metabolism (42.6 vs 40.8 µmol/100 g/min) and absolute regional metabolism, including the thalamus, did not change significantly.
key_findings.note: Reported as t=2.3, df=9; a paired test in 5 people has df=4 (p≈0.08 for t=2.3); the reported mean and SD imply t≈3.0, p≈0.04 (editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: Relative caudate and putamen metabolism were lower than in controls both after short and after protracted abstinence.
Relative thalamic metabolism was lower than controls after short abstinence (1.11 vs 1.31) and described as not different after protracted abstinence (1.23 vs 1.31).
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: d≈−0.8, p≈0.05–0.07; not evidence of return to control levels.

key_findings.finding: In the 5, thalamic change correlated with change on Timed Gait (r=0.88), Symbol Digit (r=0.96) and delayed recall (r=0.98), not with pegboard or immediate recall.
key_findings.note: The direction of these correlations is uncertain: read against the same five people's mean test scores in Volkow et al. (2001b, pp. 9415–9416), the plotted changes imply that larger thalamic increases went with smaller improvements (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Neuropsychological tests were given to the methamphetamine group only and limited to tests previously correlated with DAT.
Relapse in the programme meant a return to jail; urine tests were random within 2-week windows.

Absolute global metabolism did not differ significantly between the 11 controls (33.8, SD 7.4 µmol/100 g/min) and the methamphetamine group after short (38.5, SD 8.5) or protracted abstinence (37.3, SD 6.3).
key_findings.note: The short-abstinence participants are those of Volkow et al. (2001c), whose 14% global elevation was reported against a different control group of 21; the comparisons share participants and are not independent. Editors' calculation, short abstinence vs controls: d≈0.6 (95% CI about −0.25 to 1.42).

reporting_issues.issue: The paired comparison in 5 people is reported with df=9 (expected 4), and the test statistics do not match the reported means and SDs of the change: thalamus +12% (SD 9%) implies t≈3.0, not 2.3; striatum +2.7% (SD 6.7%) implies t≈0.9 with 5 people (the printed t=1.3 would need about 10 observations); occipital +0.4% (SD 9%) implies t≈0.1, not 1.2.
reporting_issues.consequence: The headline thalamic increase is borderline (p between about 0.04 and 0.08 depending on which reported number is right) and rests on 5 people.

reporting_issues.issue: The methods say the comparison with controls used 10 protracted-abstinence participants (the 5 retested plus 5 of the 8 tested once), but the reported degrees of freedom (df=22 with 11 controls) imply 13, and a later comparison uses N=13; why 3 participants were left out, or whether they were, is not explained. The short-abstinence group is likewise described as the 7 participants who did not stay abstinent (Introduction; Method, Subjects, p. 243) but analysed as the original 12 (Statistical Analysis; df=21), which include the 5 retested, so the unpaired short- versus protracted-abstinence comparison (12 vs 13, df=23, p. 245) counts the same 5 people in both groups.
reporting_issues.consequence: Group composition is unclear.

reporting_issues.issue: Amotivation and anhedonia are discussed as consequences of lower accumbens metabolism (abstract; p. 246) but were not measured.
reporting_issues.consequence: Speculation appears in the abstract's conclusions.

reporting_issues.issue: Figure 2 does not state the sign convention of its score changes, and they cannot be reconciled with the means reported for the same five people in Volkow et al. (2001b): there Timed Gait went from 10.0 to 8.6 s and delayed recall from 11.6 to 12.8 words, whereas the plotted changes average about +13% for Timed Gait and about −12% for delayed recall (editors' reading of the points).
reporting_issues.consequence: If the plotted values are earlier-minus-later changes (the reading consistent with Volkow et al., 2001b), the three significant correlations run opposite to the abstract: larger thalamic increases went with smaller improvements. If they are later-minus-earlier, most of the five got slower and recalled fewer words. Either way the abstract's link to improved performance is not supported as stated.

reporting_issues.issue: The tests are said to be those previously shown to correlate with DAT, but the Symbol Digit Modalities Test did not correlate with DAT in Volkow et al. (2001a, pp. 379–380) and was not among the tests retested in Volkow et al. (2001b).
reporting_issues.consequence: The stated basis for choosing the tests does not hold for one of the three tests that produced a significant correlation.

reporting_issues.issue: The nucleus accumbens decrease after protracted abstinence, which the abstract highlights, is reported only in the text from statistical parametric mapping; Figure 3 shows the short-abstinence comparison only, and no cluster size, coordinates or statistics are given for the protracted group.
reporting_issues.consequence: The accumbens finding after protracted abstinence, and the amotivation and anhedonia interpretation built on it, cannot be checked from the paper.
