design_detail: Systematic review with random-effects meta-analysis (PROSPERO CRD42017081893) of the association between use of amphetamines (methamphetamine and amphetamine pooled together; MDMA and other stimulants excluded) and five mental-health outcomes: psychosis, violence, suicidality, depression, anxiety. Two exposure contrasts were pooled: any use versus no use, and amphetamine use disorder versus no amphetamine use disorder. Unadjusted and adjusted odds ratios were pooled separately. 149 studies met the inclusion criteria; 59 contributed to meta-analyses.
can_establish: The average size and spread of the reported association between use of amphetamines and each mental-health outcome in the published literature up to May 2017, and how much that association shrinks when primary studies adjust for demographics, other substance use and premorbid risk.
cannot_establish: Causation or direction of effect (47 of 59 pooled studies are cross-sectional and the comparison is usually within substance-using samples); absolute risks (no rates are reported anywhere); dose-response or route-specific risk (the authors abandoned these analyses for lack of comparable data); whether methamphetamine differs from amphetamine (the two are pooled by design); and whether the literature is affected by publication bias (not assessed).

sample.recruitment: Database search (Medline, EMBASE, PsycINFO), May 2017; English-language peer-reviewed journal articles on humans from 1950. Participants in the pooled studies came mostly from criminal-justice, drug-treatment, psychiatric and other clinical or sentinel samples rather than from general populations; the authors state that most comparisons were made within substance-using samples (Results › Characteristics of included studies). Pooled participant counts per estimate range from 52 to 81,316 (Table 2).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: human cross-sectional, case-control, cohort studies and randomized trials examining any measure of use of amphetamines against psychosis (positive symptoms or psychotic disorders), violence (perpetration only), suicidality (ideation, attempts, completed suicide, excluding other self-harm), depression or anxiety; pharmaceutical and non-medical use; no age or clinical restriction. Excluded: non-English, non-human, no empirical data, wrong design, wrong exposure or outcome, no usable data; crossover trials (carryover), except pre-crossover data; MDMA and other stimulants.
sample.demographics: Of the 59 studies in the meta-analyses, 31 were from the USA, 10 Australia, 8 Southeast Asia, 6 Europe, 2 Canada, 1 Saudi Arabia, 1 South Africa; 47 cross-sectional, 11 cohort, 1 case-control. Table 1 gives each study's setting, percentage men (0 to 100) and mean or median age (15 to 51). The authors note that most evidence comes from high-income countries.
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level. Attrition within primary studies is not reported in Table 1 or the synthesis.
sample.selection_effects: Three databases, English only, no grey literature, no registry or reference-list searching reported; the search was run in May 2017 and the paper was published in October 2019, so about two years of literature is missing (only a separate PubMed search for reviews was run to July 2019). Pooled samples are heavily weighted to prisons, detention centres, emergency departments, psychiatric inpatient units and drug-treatment services, and the comparison group usually also used other drugs, which the authors say makes the estimates conservative relative to a general-population comparison.

exposure.measurement: Whatever each primary study used: self-report of any use, frequency measures, or a diagnosed amphetamine use disorder (diagnostic instruments vary; several studies used hospital or registry diagnoses). Methamphetamine and amphetamine were pooled deliberately because self-report rarely distinguishes them. The authors judged measurement of the exposure to be particularly poor in the violence studies (Results › Characteristics of included studies).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not synthesizable. The review planned four exposure categories (any use, use disorder, frequency of use, route of administration) and could pool only the first two: there were too few studies on route and too much heterogeneity in frequency measures (Methods › Data synthesis). The authors state in their limitations that it therefore remains unclear what level of use conveys risk, while most people who use amphetamines do so infrequently.
exposure.polysubstance: Handled only through whatever adjustment the primary studies made. 'Other substance use' is one of the three covariate families behind the adjusted estimates, and most comparisons were made within substance-using samples, so the implicit comparator often used other drugs. The authors state the unadjusted estimates are likely inflated by co-occurring risk factors and that the within-substance-using comparisons likely understate the contrast with the general population.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable; this is a review of observational associations and the timing of exposure relative to outcome is usually unknown (most studies are cross-sectional).

comparison.controls: People not using amphetamines (or without an amphetamine use disorder) within each primary study, most often drawn from the same substance-using or clinical sample.
comparison.matching: Not applicable at review level. Adjusted estimates come from primary-study models that adjusted for some combination of demographics, other substance use and premorbid risk; the review pooled these adjusted odds ratios across studies with different covariate sets.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: The authors name familial risk for psychosis, childhood trauma, perinatal factors, immigration and urbanicity as premorbid factors that were not controlled in the included studies; also socio-economic position and antisocial personality for violence.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Comparison groups in most pooled studies were themselves people who used other substances, which the authors state biases the pooled estimates downwards relative to a general-population comparison.

outcomes.instruments: Heterogeneous by design. Psychosis: symptom screens and scales (Brief Psychiatric Rating Scale, psychosis screens), clinical diagnoses, hospital admission or registry diagnoses of schizophrenia. Violence: self-reported violent acts, hostility scales (Brief Symptom Inventory, Conflict Tactics Scale, Opiate Treatment Index), criminal charges, re-offending records. Suicidality: ideation, attempts, completed suicide. Depression: symptom scales (CES-D, BDI, PHQ-9) or diagnostic interviews (SCID, MINI, CIDI, DIS). Anxiety: symptom screen or DSM-IV diagnosis (3 studies).
outcomes.validity_norms: Primary-study quality was scored with Joanna Briggs Institute critical-appraisal checklists for each design, converted to the percentage of applicable items endorsed. Average quality 68% for studies in the meta-analyses and 64% for all included studies; the lowest-quality pooled sets were violence (56 to 58%) and unadjusted suicidality (56 to 57%). Individual studies in Table 1 score as low as 13%.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Mental health outcome' was any clearly defined symptom, event, diagnosis or proxy (including hospital admission). The primary summary measure was the odds ratio; where a study did not report one, the reviewers built a 2x2 table and computed it. Studies with more than two exposure groups were collapsed (for example mild-to-moderate and severe dependence combined into one dependence category).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. 18 counts the primary pooled estimates in Table 2 (9 exposure-outcome cells, unadjusted and adjusted); the paper also reports at least 8 further pooled subgroup estimates in the text, described as post hoc.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Screening of titles and abstracts was done by one researcher; full-text review was by two independent reviewers with a third for unresolved conflicts; extraction and quality assessment were done by one reviewer and checked by a second.

analysis.effect_sizes: Random-effects (Stata metan, random) pooled odds ratios with 95% CIs, I-squared for heterogeneity; no tau-squared, no prediction intervals, no absolute rates, no meta-regression (too few studies). Any use versus no use: psychosis OR 2.0 (1.3 to 3.3), 7 studies, n=3436, I2=80%; adjusted 5.3 (3.4 to 8.3) from a single study with 1064 observations on 278 participants. Violence 2.2 (1.2 to 4.1), 10 studies, n=30,084, I2=95%; adjusted 1.4 (0.8 to 2.4), 6 studies, n=26,289, I2=25%. Suicidality 4.4 (2.4 to 8.2), 7 studies, n=19,703, I2=84%; adjusted 1.7 (1.0 to 2.9), 4 studies, n=7066, I2=77%. Depression 1.6 (1.1 to 2.2), 7 studies, n=19,526, I2=80%; adjusted 1.3 (1.2 to 1.4), 6 studies, n=2684, I2=0%. Anxiety: no data. Amphetamine use disorder versus none: psychosis 3.0 (1.9 to 4.8), 13 studies, n=81,316, I2=90%; adjusted 2.4 (1.6 to 3.5), 4 studies, n=7648, I2=35%. Violence 6.2 (3.1 to 12.3), 1 study, n=52. Suicidality 2.3 (1.8 to 2.9), 7 studies, n=23,302, I2=57%; adjusted 1.5 (1.3 to 1.8), 4 studies, n=21,753, I2=0%. Depression 1.2 (0.5 to 2.7), 6 studies, n=3584, I2=87%; adjusted 2.8 (0.6 to 11.8), 1 twin study. Anxiety 0.6 (0.2 to 1.8), 3 studies, n=1200, I2=66%. Post-hoc subgroups: psychotic symptoms, any use 2.7 (1.5 to 4.7), use disorder 4.3 (2.9 to 6.5); psychotic disorder, any use 1.3 (1.0 to 1.9), p=0.087, use disorder 2.3 (1.2 to 4.7), I2=93%; violent behaviour 3.7 (3.1 to 4.5), I2=34% versus violent offending 1.0 (0.4 to 2.7), I2=94%; suicide attempts 3.6 (2.2 to 5.9); suicidal ideation (use disorder) 2.2 (1.8 to 2.8); depression in general-population samples 2.0 (1.6 to 2.4), I2=11% versus substance-using samples 1.1 (0.7 to 1.7), I2=76%.
analysis.covariates: At review level, none: adjusted estimates were taken as reported by the primary studies and pooled. The covariate families recorded were demographics, other substance use and premorbid risk; which variables each study used is in a supplement that was not read. Pooling adjusted estimates from different models means the adjusted pooled odds ratios do not correspond to a single specified adjustment set.
analysis.preregistration_detail: PROSPERO CRD42017081893; PRISMA checklist in Supplement A. Planned analyses of frequency of use and route of administration were dropped for lack of comparable data, and subgroup analyses (symptoms vs disorder, behaviour vs offending, attempts vs ideation, population vs substance-using samples) are described in the paper as post hoc.
analysis.selective_reporting: The review is explicit about its post-hoc analyses and about the dropped exposure categories. Anxiety for any use could not be analysed. Absolute rates are never reported for any outcome. The 'Research in context' box says the literature search for reviews was updated to July 2019 while the main search dates from May 2017.
analysis.power: Not formally addressed. Several pooled cells rest on one study (adjusted psychosis for any use; violence for use disorder, n=52 exposed; adjusted depression for use disorder) or three (anxiety), so their intervals are study-specific rather than meta-analytic. The authors state the number of studies was too small for meta-regression or funnel plots.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Across mostly cross-sectional studies in mostly clinical and criminal-justice samples, any use of amphetamines was associated with about twice the odds of psychosis, 2.2 times the odds of violence, 4.4 times the odds of suicidality and 1.6 times the odds of depression; amphetamine use disorder with 3.0 times the odds of psychosis and 2.3 times the odds of suicidality. Adjustment for demographics, other substance use and premorbid risk reduced violence to a non-significant 1.4 (0.8 to 2.4), suicidality to 1.7 (1.0 to 2.9) and depression to 1.3 (1.2 to 1.4). Heterogeneity was high for most unadjusted estimates (I2 up to 95%). Associations were larger for psychotic symptoms than for diagnosed psychotic disorders, and for violent behaviour than for violent offending; the depression association was present in general-population samples (OR 2.0) and absent within substance-using samples (OR 1.1).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that methamphetamine use is "an important risk factor for poor mental health". Gaps: (1) the abstract's conclusion is about methamphetamine, while the analysis deliberately pooled methamphetamine with amphetamine and could not separate them; (2) 'risk factor' language rests on a body of evidence the authors themselves describe as mostly cross-sectional with unknown direction of effect, a point they make clearly in the discussion and limitations but not in the abstract; (3) the abstract reports the adjusted psychosis estimate for any use as part of a list without noting it comes from a single within-person study of people entering treatment; (4) no absolute risks are given anywhere, so an 'important risk factor' cannot be weighed against base rates; (5) the discussion states that the adjusted suicidality odds ratios were 1.4 and 1.5, while Table 2 and the abstract give 1.7 and 1.5. Against this, the discussion is notably restrained: it grades the evidence by outcome, calls the violence evidence poor-quality, and says the depression and suicidality associations may be generic to substance use.

timeline.event: Curran et al. systematic review of stimulant psychosis (cited in this review's introduction as background).
McKetin et al. prospective within-person cohort showing dose-related psychotic symptoms; contributes the single adjusted psychosis estimate for any use in this review (OR 5.3)
This review: the first meta-analysis of amphetamine use and mental-health outcomes, by the authors' own account.
Companion meta-analysis from an overlapping author group on mortality in people who use amphetamines

replication.where_it_stands: The only meta-analysis on this question identified by its authors, and still the standard reference for pooled mental-health associations. Its estimates should be read with its own caveats: a 2017 search, pooled methamphetamine and amphetamine, clinical and criminal-justice samples, unadjusted estimates inflated by confounding and adjusted estimates based on few studies. Primary studies central to the encyclopedia are inside the pooled estimates: McKetin et al. (2013), the review's only adjusted any-use psychosis estimate, and the California schizophrenia cohort of Callaghan, Cunningham and Allebeck (2012, American Journal of Psychiatry; the review's ref. 40), which is not the Parkinson's-disease study held as callaghan_2012. Claims must not cite them as independent support.

funding.funder: National Drug and Alcohol Research Centre, University of New South Wales; Curtin University; NHMRC; NIH. NDARC is supported by the Australian Government Department of Health; the senior author holds an NHMRC fellowship and an NIDA grant (R01DA1104470); the first author holds a Curtin Senior Research Fellowship. The paper states the funders had no role in design, analysis, writing or the decision to submit.
funding.declared_conflicts: Two authors have received investigator-initiated untied educational grants for studies of opioid medications from Indivior, Mundipharma and Seqirus. One author was a paid expert witness in a New Zealand Court of Appeal case on sentencing for methamphetamine-related offending and is an unpaid trustee of a non-profit treatment provider. Other authors declare nothing.
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from NDARC (UNSW), University of Queensland, Curtin University, University of Otago, Monash, University of Western Australia and NSW Health. Several authors are also authors of primary studies included in the meta-analyses (for example the 2013 cohort and the 2014 violence paper), so review authors appraised their own studies; data extraction and quality assessment were checked by a second reviewer but no procedure for this specific conflict is described.

what_would_settle_it: Prospective general-population cohorts with repeated within-person measurement of amphetamine use and of psychosis, depression, suicidality and violence, measuring premorbid risk (familial psychosis risk, childhood trauma, socio-economic position, antisocial traits) before exposure begins, reporting absolute incidence as well as relative odds, and distinguishing methamphetamine from amphetamine and dose and route; an individual-participant-data meta-analysis of existing cohorts would be the achievable near-term version.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population, exposure, comparator and five outcomes specified; designs specified.

PROSPERO CRD42017081893 and a PRISMA checklist; but planned exposure categories were dropped and subgroup analyses are described as post hoc, and the registered analysis plan was not compared with what was done in the paper itself.
Designs chosen as best suited to estimating risk, with the Cochrane design guide cited and crossover trials excluded for carryover.

Three databases with full strategies in a supplement and authors contacted for missing data, but English-language only without justification, no grey literature, no trial registries, no reference-list or forward citation searching, and a search two years older than publication.
Titles and abstracts were screened by a single researcher; only full-text review was duplicated.

Extraction with a structured template by one reviewer, checked by a second, with discrepancies resolved by discussion and if needed a third reviewer (2.5 Data extraction). Two reviewers thus reached consensus on the extracted data, which meets the item's first criterion; extraction was not independent and in duplicate.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Exclusion reasons were coded into seven categories and summarized in the PRISMA figure (an image), but no list of excluded full-text studies with reasons appears in the article; supplements were not read.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 1 gives country, recruitment years, setting, design, quality score, N and exposed N, sex and age, and outcome measure; exposure definitions, covariates and funding of primary studies are only in supplements.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: JBI checklists by design, checked by a second reviewer, with the main shortfalls named (failure to identify and control confounders; poor exposure measurement in violence studies), but collapsed into a single percentage score, which obscures which domains failed in which study.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Not reported.

Random-effects pooling (Stata metan, random), chosen to accommodate heterogeneity; adjusted odds ratios reported by the primary studies were pooled separately from unadjusted ones; no randomized trial entered the pools (2.7; 3.1; Table 2). The unadjusted pools combine crude 2×2 data without a stated reason beyond availability, but they are labelled unadjusted, reported beside the adjusted pools and called likely inflated by confounding by the authors (4.1, 3rd paragraph): judged met on balance, a close call. Other weaknesses not scored by this item: adjusted estimates come from models with different covariate sets, cross-sectional and cohort designs are combined, several cells rest on one study, and no tau-squared or prediction interval is given despite I2 up to 95%.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: Table 2 reports a meta-analysis-weighted average quality score for each pooled estimate, but no analysis examines how study quality affects the pooled estimates (no sensitivity analysis excluding low-quality studies, no stratification or meta-regression by quality). The separate adjusted pools show the effect of confounder adjustment across partly different sets of studies, not the effect of the assessed risk of bias.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: Each outcome is graded by level of evidence, the violence evidence is called poor-quality, and the discussion states that unadjusted estimates are likely inflated.

I2 is reported for every pool and heterogeneity is discussed (3.2; 4.1, 2nd paragraph); its sources were investigated with post hoc subgroup analyses that explain part of it (psychotic symptoms vs diagnosed disorder; violent behaviour, I2 34%, vs violent offending, I2 94%; suicide attempts vs ideation; for depression, general-population samples, I2 11%, vs substance-using samples, I2 76%); too few studies allowed no meta-regression.
Explicitly not assessed: the authors state there were too few studies for funnel plots.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding and author conflicts are declared; the paper does not flag that several authors wrote included primary studies.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: AMSTAR 2 scores two critical items as 'no' (no list of excluded studies with reasons; publication bias not investigated), which mechanically gives critically low confidence, with three further critical items (2, 4 and 9) only partially met and two (11 and 13) met. This is a judgment about how far the pooled numbers can be trusted as unbiased summaries, not about the paper's value: the review is registered, transparent, uses appropriate random-effects methods, grades its own evidence by outcome and states its limitations plainly. The practical consequences are that the pooled estimates may be inflated by unassessed small-study and publication effects, that the unadjusted estimates are confounded (as the authors say), and that heterogeneity of I2 up to 95% means a single pooled odds ratio describes no particular population.

key_findings.finding: 149 studies met the inclusion criteria (48 psychosis, 29 violence, 28 suicidality, 49 depression, 15 anxiety); 115 cross-sectional, 27 cohort, 4 case-control, 3 randomized trials. 59 studies entered the meta-analyses (19 psychosis, 12 violence, 15 suicidality, 16 depression, 3 anxiety), of which 47 were cross-sectional, 11 cohort and 1 case-control.
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.1 Characteristics of included studies, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Any use of amphetamines versus no use, pooled unadjusted odds ratios: psychosis 2.0 (95% CI 1.3 to 3.3), 7 studies, n=3436, I2=80%; violence 2.2 (1.2 to 4.1), 10 studies, n=30,084, I2=95%; suicidality 4.4 (2.4 to 8.2), 7 studies, n=19,703, I2=84%; depression 1.6 (1.1 to 2.2), 7 studies, n=19,526, I2=80%. No data for anxiety.

Any use of amphetamines, pooled adjusted odds ratios (for demographics, other substance use and premorbid risk): violence 1.4 (0.8 to 2.4), 6 studies, I2=25%, not significant; suicidality 1.7 (1.0 to 2.9), 4 studies, I2=77%; depression 1.3 (1.2 to 1.4), 6 studies, n=2684, I2=0%; psychosis 5.3 (3.4 to 8.3) from one study only.
key_findings.note: The adjusted psychosis estimate rests on a single prospective study (McKetin et al., 2013) with 1064 observations from 278 participants, and is larger than the unadjusted pooled estimate of 2.0 because it is a within-person dose-response analysis in people entering treatment, not a different adjustment of the same comparison.

key_findings.finding: Amphetamine use disorder versus none, pooled unadjusted odds ratios: psychosis 3.0 (1.9 to 4.8), 13 studies, n=81,316, I2=90%; suicidality 2.3 (1.8 to 2.9), 7 studies, n=23,302, I2=57%; depression 1.2 (0.5 to 2.7), 6 studies, I2=87%, not significant; anxiety 0.6 (0.2 to 1.8), 3 studies, not significant; violence 6.2 (3.1 to 12.3) from a single study.

Amphetamine use disorder, pooled adjusted odds ratios: psychosis 2.4 (1.6 to 3.5), 4 studies, I2=35%; suicidality 1.5 (1.3 to 1.8), 4 studies, n=21,753, I2=0%; depression 2.8 (0.6 to 11.8) from one twin study; no adjusted estimates for violence or anxiety.

Psychosis subgroups: the association was larger for psychotic symptoms (any use OR 2.7, 1.5 to 4.7, I2=80%; use disorder OR 4.3, 2.9 to 6.5, I2=47%) than for a diagnosed psychotic disorder (any use OR 1.3, 1.0 to 1.9, p=0.087, I2=0%; use disorder OR 2.3, 1.2 to 4.7, I2=93%).

Violence subgroups: unadjusted odds were raised and fairly consistent for violent behaviour (OR 3.7, 3.1 to 4.5, I2=34%) but null for violent offending (OR 1.0, 0.4 to 2.7, I2=94%). The weighted quality of the any-use violence pools was 56% (unadjusted) and 58% (adjusted), tied lowest with the unadjusted any-use suicidality pool (56%; use-disorder suicidality 57%), and the single use-disorder violence study scored 43%; the authors note poor measurement of amphetamine use in the violence studies.
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.4 Violence, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Results › 3.1, 2nd paragraph; Table 2

key_findings.finding: Suicidality subgroups: suicide attempts OR 3.6 (2.2 to 5.9), I2=46%, 6 studies; suicidal ideation in people with an amphetamine use disorder OR 2.2 (1.8 to 2.8), I2=22%, 5 studies. Only one included study examined completed suicide; in that drug-treatment follow-up, suicide deaths were higher than expected but not significantly raised relative to opioid use, and most cases involved premorbid risk.

Depression was associated with any use in general-population samples (OR 2.0, 1.6 to 2.4, I2=11%) but not within substance-using samples (OR 1.1, 0.7 to 1.7, I2=76%). The review notes that all but one of the supporting studies measured depressive symptoms rather than diagnosed major depression, whereas major depression was the outcome in every use-disorder study, and attributes the null association between amphetamine use disorder and depression to samples with high levels of other substance use or clinical conditions.

Primary-study quality (Joanna Briggs checklists, percentage of applicable items endorsed): average 68% for studies in the meta-analyses and 64% for all 149 included studies; the commonest shortfall was failure to identify and control confounders. Individual study scores in Table 1 range from 13% to 100%.

Planned analyses by frequency of use and by route of administration could not be done: too few studies on route and too heterogeneous measurement of frequency. The authors state it therefore remains unclear what level of use conveys risk, while most people who use amphetamines use infrequently.
key_findings.locator: Methods › 2.7 Data synthesis; Discussion › 4.2 Limitations of this review

key_findings.finding: Publication bias was not assessed (too few studies for funnel plots), no meta-regression was possible, and no prediction intervals or absolute rates are reported for any outcome.
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.1, 3rd paragraph; Discussion › 4.1 Limitations of the evidence; Table 2

key_findings.finding: The searches were run in May 2017 and limited to English-language peer-reviewed articles in Medline, EMBASE and PsycINFO from 1950; the paper was published in October 2019, and only a separate search for reviews was updated to 26 July 2019.
key_findings.locator: Methods › 2.2 Searches; Research in context › Evidence before this study

reporting_issues.issue: Section 3.5 states that after adjustment the suicidality odds ratios were 1.4 and 1.5, while Table 2 and the abstract give 1.7 (1.0 to 2.9) for any use and 1.5 (1.3 to 1.8) for use disorder.
reporting_issues.consequence: The adjusted suicidality estimate for any use appears in two versions; the table value (1.7, lower limit 1.0) should be used, and any claim about the adjusted association should note that its interval touches 1.0.

reporting_issues.issue: The reference list contains duplicate entries for the same studies, and Table 1 and Table 2 cite different numbers for them: McKetin 2013 is [29] in Table 1 and [105] in Table 2; McKetin 2014 is [47] and [106]; Sutherland 2015 is [57] and [107]; Capra 2015 is [61] and [108].
reporting_issues.consequence: A reader matching Table 2's reference lists against Table 1 will conclude that studies are missing from the pooled sets when they are present under a second number; it also makes the study counts hard to audit.

reporting_issues.issue: The adjusted suicidality analyses cite reference [109] (Walls et al., 2008), which does not appear anywhere in Table 1 among the studies in the meta-analyses.
reporting_issues.consequence: Table 1 is not a complete list of the studies contributing to the pooled estimates, so the table cannot be used to reconstruct the analyses.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 2 the participant count for the amphetamine-use-disorder violence estimate is given as n=52, which is the number of exposed people in Watanabe (2005); Table 1 gives that study's total as 1108 (52 exposed).
reporting_issues.consequence: The pooled estimate of 6.2 (3.1 to 12.3) appears to rest on 52 people when it is a single study of 1108 with 52 exposed; either way it is one study and should not be read as a meta-analytic result.

reporting_issues.issue: Section 3.3 contains an incomplete sentence: the hazard ratios for amphetamine use disorder relative to other substance use disorders in Callaghan et al. are introduced but the range itself is missing from the text.
reporting_issues.consequence: The comparison with other substances cannot be quantified from this review; the primary study must be read for those values.

reporting_issues.issue: The heading of section 3.7 reads '[80,81] Anxiety', with citation markers embedded in the heading, and references [80] and [81] (two depression studies) are not cited in the depression section text where they belong.
reporting_issues.consequence: Typesetting error; the two studies are listed in Table 1 under depression and amphetamine use disorder, so the pooled sets are unaffected.

reporting_issues.issue: The title of the article as rendered reads 'Mental health outcomes associated with of the use of amphetamines'.
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical error in the published title; no effect on content, but worth matching exactly when the reference record is built from Crossref.

reporting_issues.issue: Several pooled cells labelled as meta-analytic results in Table 2 contain a single study (adjusted psychosis for any use; violence for use disorder; adjusted depression for use disorder), and I2 is given as 'NA' for them.
reporting_issues.consequence: These are single-study estimates presented in a table of pooled estimates; the abstract lists the first of them among its headline odds ratios without saying so.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 lists Callaghan et al. (2012) with N 10,815,900 (36,162 exposed), but the 13-study use-disorder psychosis pool that includes it has n=81,316 in Table 2, and the other 12 studies in that pool sum to 13,243 in Table 1, which leaves about 68,000 for Callaghan et al. (editors' arithmetic); the comparison actually analysed for that study is not described in the main text.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Table 1 (Callaghan 2012 row); Table 2 (psychosis, use disorder)
reporting_issues.consequence: The pooled n cannot be reconciled from the article; the comparison used for the largest contributing study must be taken from Supplement E or the primary paper before the n is quoted.

reporting_issues.issue: The violent-offending subgroup cites reference [55], a 2018 typology of new psychoactive substance use in the general Australian population, among its five studies; the violent-offence study listed in Table 1, Sutherland et al. (2015), is [57] there and [107] in Table 2, so [55] appears to be a numbering error.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › 3.4 Violence, 3rd paragraph; Table 1; references 55, 57 and 107
reporting_issues.consequence: Another citation-numbering error of the kind in reporting issue 1; the subgroup's studies can still be identified from Table 1, but the reference numbers cannot be used as printed to audit it.

disagreements.resolution: Changed to 'yes'. Decided from 2.7, 3.1, Table 2 and 4.1 against the item's criteria for non-randomized studies (justified pooling, an appropriate weighted technique allowing for heterogeneity, adjusted estimates combined rather than raw data alone, randomized and non-randomized evidence kept apart): met on balance, because adjusted estimates were pooled and reported separately; the lack of a stated reason for also pooling crude data makes it a close call (see the note).

disagreements.resolution: Changed to 'no'. Decided from 2.6, 2.7, 3.1 and Table 2: 'yes' requires analyses of the possible impact of risk of bias on the summary estimates (the pools include studies of variable quality); a weighted average quality score describes the evidence but does not test its impact.

disagreements.first_pass: partial-yes: I2 reported throughout and heterogeneity discussed; post-hoc subgroups explain some of it (symptoms vs disorder, behaviour vs offending, population vs substance-using samples), but meta-regression was not possible.

disagreements.resolution: Changed to 'yes'. Decided from 3.2–3.6 and 4.1: 'yes' requires an investigation of the sources of heterogeneity and a discussion of its impact on the results; the post hoc subgroup analyses and the limitations section provide both, within the limits of the number of studies.

disagreements.first_pass: AMSTAR 2 scores two critical items as 'no' (no list of excluded studies with reasons; publication bias not investigated), which mechanically gives critically low confidence, with four further critical items only partially met. This is a judgment about how far the pooled numbers can be trusted as unbiased summaries, not about the paper's value: the review is registered, transparent, uses appropriate random-effects methods, grades its own evidence by outcome and states its limitations plainly. The practical consequences are that the pooled estimates may be inflated by unassessed small-study and publication effects, that the unadjusted estimates are confounded (as the authors say), and that heterogeneity of I2 up to 95% means a single pooled odds ratio describes no particular population.

disagreements.resolution: Overall recomputed with the AMSTAR 2 critical-item rule after items 6, 11, 12 and 14 were re-decided: critical items 7 and 15 are 'no' (two critical flaws), items 2, 4 and 9 'partial yes', items 11 and 13 'yes', so the overall stays critically low. Reasoning updated for the count of partly met critical items.

design_detail: PROSPERO-registered systematic review and meta-analysis restricted to studies that reported a period of abstinence: 31 cross-sectional studies (1008 abstinent people with methamphetamine abuse or dependence, 984 healthy controls). Tests grouped into Cattell-Horn-Carroll (CHC) broad abilities; random-effects pooling of Hedges' g with prediction intervals; adapted QUADAS-2 risk-of-bias assessment; meta-regression and sensitivity analyses.
can_establish: How large the average differences are between people abstinent from methamphetamine and controls by cognitive ability, how much they vary between studies (prediction intervals), and how sensitive they are to study quality and publication bias.
cannot_establish: Whether methamphetamine caused the differences (cross-sectional only; the authors say so, pp. 748–749), or the course of recovery within people.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (meta-analysis).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Methamphetamine as primary drug with a history of abuse or dependence; a reported abstinence period; healthy comparison group without stimulant abuse or dependence; valid and reliable cognitive tests; English. Excluded animal studies, case reports and commentaries (p. 742).
sample.demographics: Methamphetamine group: weighted age 33.4, education 12.3 years. Controls: age 34.8, education 13.9 years (p. 744; Table 1). Mean abstinence 128.8 days (SD 99.5) across 31 studies (Table 1, p. 744).
sample.selection_effects: 48% of studies did not match groups on education (p. 744). No study was rated at low risk of bias: removing 'unclear' studies would have removed all studies (p. 743). Participants retained in treatment-based samples may be healthier than dropouts (p. 749).

exposure.measurement: As in the primary studies; 15 studies did not report whether controls had urinalysis (p. 747).
exposure.polysubstance: Quantity of use, route, other drug use, personality and undiagnosed psychiatric conditions not reported in enough studies to analyse (p. 749).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Required to be reported; mean 128.8 days across studies (Table 1, p. 744).

comparison.controls: Healthy comparison participants in each study.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No premorbid ability measures; education used as a partial proxy, while noting it may underestimate premorbid ability in people who began use at school age (p. 748).

outcomes.instruments: Tests assigned to CHC broad abilities from published factor analyses by two independent raters (pp. 742–743): fluid reasoning, short-term working memory, learning efficiency, visual-spatial processing, comprehension knowledge, retrieval fluency, processing speed, reaction and decision speed, psychomotor speed.
outcomes.validity_norms: Group differences only.
outcomes.operationalization: Hedges' g, negative = methamphetamine group worse; tests within a study averaged per ability (p. 743).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Holm-Bonferroni within (and, as a secondary check, across) abilities for meta-regressions (pp. 743–744).

analysis.effect_sizes: Table 2 (p. 745), Hedges' g [95% CI; prediction interval]: fluid reasoning −0.02 [−0.46, 0.42; −2.04 to 1.45], 14 studies; short-term working memory −0.19 [−0.44, 0.06; −1.01 to 1.01], 12; learning efficiency −0.47 [−0.58, −0.37; −0.60 to −0.34], 17, I²=1%; visual-spatial processing −0.42 [−0.74, −0.11; −1.39 to 0.54], 5; comprehension knowledge −0.43 [−0.69, −0.18; −1.32 to 0.44], 12; retrieval fluency −0.32 [−0.59, −0.04; −1.18 to 0.54], 9; processing speed −0.28 [−0.52, −0.04; −1.34 to 0.78], 22; reaction and decision speed 0.00, 3 studies; psychomotor speed −0.35 [−0.65, −0.05; −1.30 to 0.60], 9. Publication bias: Egger significant for working memory (p=.05) and learning efficiency (p=.01); trim-and-fill: working memory −0.04 [−0.26, 0.18], learning efficiency −0.40 [−0.52, −0.28] (p. 745). Risk-of-bias subgroups: comprehension knowledge −0.67 in high-risk vs −0.09 in unclear-risk studies (Qbet=7.69, p=.006) (p. 745). Longer duration of use predicted larger fluid-reasoning differences (β=−0.16 per year, Holm p=.002), although fluid reasoning showed no average difference (pp. 744, 746).
analysis.covariates: Single meta-regressions for abilities with more than 10 data points.
analysis.preregistration_detail: PROSPERO CRD42018083598 (p. 742); deviations not discussed.
analysis.selective_reporting: Sensitivity results in the text and in Table 6 disagree (see reporting issues).
analysis.power: Limited for visual-spatial processing (5 studies) and reaction/decision speed (3).

interpretation_gap.results_show: People abstinent from methamphetamine score on average below controls on learning efficiency (robust: g −0.47, narrow prediction interval, little change after trim-and-fill) and, less consistently, on several other abilities whose prediction intervals all include zero; fluid reasoning, working memory and reaction speed show no reliable difference.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The conclusion that strong statements about impaired cognition in people abstinent from methamphetamine are premature (abstract; p. 749) matches the data. The discussion groups comprehension knowledge with abilities dependent on frontostriatal circuits (p. 746); comprehension knowledge (vocabulary-type crystallized knowledge) is the kind of measure used to estimate premorbid ability (for example, reading tests used to estimate IQ, Dean et al., 2013, p. 261), and here its group difference was confined to high-risk-of-bias studies (p. 745), which fits pre-existing or educational differences better than a drug effect.

timeline.event: Earlier meta-analysis without an abstinence requirement: medium average differences
Meta-analysis of 44 studies: moderate average differences, strong publication bias
Meta-analysis of 68 later studies: larger average differences with wide prediction intervals

replication.where_it_stands: Learning and verbal memory differences are the most consistent finding across all four meta-analyses; other domains vary between reviews.

funding.declared_conflicts: Not reported in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: University of Melbourne.

what_would_settle_it: Longitudinal cohorts with pre-use cognitive testing, or twin designs, with abstinence verified and controls matched on education and premorbid ability (pp. 748–749).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Provisional: AMSTAR 2 item 7 (a list of excluded studies with reasons, a critical item) can only be judged from a supplement not yet read. The strongest methods of the four meta-analyses (registration, prediction intervals, risk-of-bias sensitivity, publication-bias adjustment), lowered by single-person extraction, an ill-fitting risk-of-bias tool, unverified exclusion list, no funding statement, and internal inconsistencies in the sensitivity results.

key_findings.finding: 31 studies, 1008 people abstinent from methamphetamine and 984 controls; the methamphetamine group had 1.6 fewer years of education on average (12.3 vs 13.9).
key_findings.locator: Results, Study Selection and Characteristics; Table 1

key_findings.finding: Learning efficiency: g −0.47 (95% CI −0.58 to −0.37), prediction interval −0.60 to −0.34, I²=1%; −0.40 after trim-and-fill.
No reliable difference in fluid reasoning (g −0.02), short-term working memory (−0.19; −0.04 after trim-and-fill) or reaction and decision speed (0.00, 3 studies).
Prediction intervals include zero for every ability except learning efficiency.
No study was rated at low risk of bias; comprehension knowledge differed only in high-risk studies (−0.67 vs −0.09).

The authors conclude that strong statements about impaired cognition in people abstinent from methamphetamine are premature because cross-sectional designs cannot separate pre-existing differences from drug effects.

Length of abstinence significantly moderated the comprehension-knowledge difference (11 studies; Q model 27.58, p<.001; residual Q 7.70, p=.57), the only ability where it did, and survived Holm–Bonferroni correction within and across abilities; the coefficient is printed as −0.00 with its interval bounds in the wrong order, so its direction cannot be read.

key_findings.finding: In the primary analysis six of nine abilities had 95% CIs excluding zero (learning efficiency −0.47, visual-spatial −0.42, comprehension knowledge −0.43, retrieval fluency −0.32, processing speed −0.28, psychomotor speed −0.35); only learning efficiency also had a prediction interval excluding zero and stayed significant in both sensitivity analyses and after trim-and-fill.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says removing the four abuse-or-dependence studies did not change the results but that confidence intervals for six abilities, including learning efficiency, then overlapped zero; Table 6 shows learning efficiency still clearly negative (−0.45, −0.57 to −0.34).

reporting_issues.consequence: Sign or value error.

reporting_issues.issue: The text reports a 95% CI of −0.04 to 0.41 for reaction and decision speed, while Table 2 prints the estimate as 0.00 with no usable interval.
reporting_issues.consequence: That ability's estimate is unreliable (3 studies, 47 participants who used methamphetamine).

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 counts more participants (for example 1203 in the methamphetamine groups for age) than the 1008 stated in the text; the comprehension-knowledge abstinence coefficient is printed with interval bounds in the wrong order (0.0002, −0.0008).

reporting_issues.issue: The text says removing high-risk-of-bias studies did not change the results, while noting that the intervals for comprehension knowledge, fluid reasoning and visual-spatial processing then included zero; Table 6 also shows short-term working memory becoming significant (−0.28, −0.52 to −0.04), which the text does not mention.

design_detail: PROSPERO-registered systematic review and three-level meta-analysis with robust variance estimation of studies published May 2017–May 2025 (designed not to overlap Potvin et al., 2018): 68 independent studies, 242 effect sizes, 5244 people with methamphetamine use disorder and 3801 healthy controls, in 13 domains including self-reported impulsivity. Abstinence modelled by phase and by restricted cubic splines; GRADE certainty by domain.
can_establish: The average difference between people with methamphetamine use disorder and healthy controls in the 2017–2025 literature, its spread across settings (prediction intervals), and whether study samples tested at different abstinence durations differ on average.
cannot_establish: That methamphetamine caused the differences, that cognition does or does not recover within people (all comparisons are between different studies' samples), or clinical significance for individuals (prediction interval includes zero).

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (meta-analysis). Included studies' samples: 87.2% male; 36 'exclusive' use-disorder samples, 18 polysubstance, 14 with psychiatric comorbidity (p. 6).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Adults with DSM or ICD methamphetamine use disorder, including those with polysubstance use or psychiatric comorbidity; healthy controls without substance use disorders (nicotine and caffeine allowed); validated tests or self-report impulsivity; cross-sectional or baseline data; abstinence verified. Excluded: under 18; traumatic brain injury, stroke, epilepsy or HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder; testing within 48 hours of last use or without documented abstinence; non-English (p. 2).
sample.demographics: Education 9.94 vs 11.33 years; weighted mean duration of use 7.38 years; abstinence 4.2–971 days, weighted mean 248.2 days (p. 6).
sample.selection_effects: Only 10.3% of studies reported outcomes beyond 12 months of abstinence (p. 10); 51.5% of studies met the paper's quality threshold (p. 6).

exposure.measurement: As in the primary studies; abstinence verified by biological testing, clinical assessment or study protocol (p. 2).
exposure.polysubstance: Included by design to reflect treatment populations; compared as subgroups (p. 2).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: At least 48 hours; phases defined as under 1 month (described as the acute withdrawal phase), 1–12 months and over 12 months (p. 5).

comparison.controls: Healthy controls without substance use disorders other than nicotine or caffeine and without current neurological or psychiatric conditions (p. 2).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No premorbid ability; age, sex and education available only as study averages (p. 10).

outcomes.instruments: Performance tests and self-report impulsivity scales coded into 13 domains using MATRICS, the unity/diversity model of executive function and RDoC (p. 4).
outcomes.validity_norms: Group differences only.
outcomes.operationalization: Hedges' g, negative = methamphetamine group worse; overall estimate pools all 13 domains including self-reported impulsivity (pp. 1, 6).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Benjamini–Hochberg for omnibus domain and subgroup tests; spline trend tests unadjusted and labelled exploratory (p. 4).

analysis.effect_sizes: Overall g=−0.68 (95% CI −0.77 to −0.58), Q(241)=1379.6, I²=85.3% (35.7% between studies, 49.6% within), 95% prediction interval −1.58 to 0.22 (p. 6). By domain (Table 2, p. 7): visuospatial −1.09 (7 studies), shifting −0.86, self-reported impulsivity −0.86 (27), planning −0.82, verbal learning and memory −0.79 (17), processing speed −0.74, attention −0.67, visual learning and memory −0.64, verbal fluency −0.53, inhibitory control −0.50 (19), decision-making −0.50, working memory −0.45, social cognition −0.42 (12); domains did not differ significantly (F(12,140.1)=2.07, P=0.10) (p. 6). Abstinence phases: under 1 month −0.70 (15 studies), 1–12 months −0.63 (35), over 12 months −0.88 (7); F(2,14.9)=1.20, P=0.33 (p. 7). Splines: no trend for inhibitory control (17 studies, 7–265 days) or self-reported impulsivity (21, 23–280 days) (p. 7). Sex: higher proportion of men associated with smaller differences, β=0.518 (0.079–0.957), P=0.03 in the fully adjusted model (p. 6). Comorbidity subgroups did not differ (P=0.26), equivalence indeterminate (pp. 6–7). Publication bias: overall Egger P=0.32, trim-and-fill identified no missing studies (adjusted −0.65 vs −0.68); domain-level Egger P=0.005 (verbal learning and memory) and P<0.001 (working memory) (p. 7).
analysis.covariates: Age, sex and education (study level) in multivariable meta-regression (p. 4).
analysis.preregistration_detail: PROSPERO CRD420251004391 (p. 2); deviations not discussed in the main text.
analysis.selective_reporting: Domain-level publication-bias signals for verbal learning/memory and working memory are attributed to lower test reliability in smaller domains (p. 7), though these domains have 14–17 studies.
analysis.power: Abstinence and comorbidity comparisons acknowledged as underpowered (pp. 9–10).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Samples of people with methamphetamine use disorder scored on average two-thirds of a standard deviation below healthy controls, with very large heterogeneity and a prediction interval running from large deficits to none; samples tested at different abstinence durations did not differ significantly, with few studies beyond a year.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The conclusions describe the impairment as generalized and clinically significant and state that passive abstinence fails to restore cognitive function across short-, medium- and long-term windows (p. 10). Clinical significance is not shown by standardized group differences, the pooled 'neurocognitive' estimate includes questionnaire-measured impulsivity, and the abstinence result compares different samples rather than following people over time, as the paper itself says in the note to Figure 3 (p. 9); the long-term phase rests on 7 studies and the spline models on the first nine months (p. 10).

timeline.event: Earlier meta-analysis on the pre-2017 literature, which this review deliberately does not overlap
Abstinence-restricted meta-analysis with smaller differences

replication.where_it_stands: Published 2026; no commentary or replication yet. Its visuospatial finding contradicts the relative sparing reported by Potvin et al. (2018); its sex finding runs opposite to Scott et al. (2007).

funding.funder: National Science and Technology Major Projects for Science, Technology and Innovation 2030, China (2021ZD0202102) (p. 1).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors report no conflicts of interest (p. 1).
funding.affiliations_note: A large language model was used for language editing, according to the acknowledgments (p. 10). Extraction data available on request only (p. 1).

what_would_settle_it: Within-person longitudinal studies across 1–3 years of abstinence with retested controls and premorbid estimates; separating questionnaire impulsivity from performance measures in pooled estimates.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Provisional: AMSTAR 2 item 7 (a list of excluded studies with reasons, a critical item) can only be judged from a supplement not yet read. Methodologically the most advanced of the four meta-analyses. Confidence in its conclusions is limited less by its methods than by its interpretation: pooling questionnaire impulsivity into a cognitive estimate, causal and clinical language for cross-sectional group differences, and an upgrade for large effect in GRADE despite a plausible confounder (education 9.9 vs 11.3 years). All domains ended at very low certainty in its own GRADE.

key_findings.finding: 68 studies (2017–2025), 5244 in the methamphetamine groups and 3801 controls; overall g=−0.68 (95% CI −0.77 to −0.58) with a prediction interval of −1.58 to 0.22.
key_findings.locator: Results, Study Characteristics and Overall Cognitive Impairment; Abstract
key_findings.note: Page numbers are those of the online-first PDF.

key_findings.finding: The overall estimate pools 13 domains including self-reported impulsivity (g=−0.86, 27 studies), a questionnaire rather than a performance measure.
Domain estimates ranged from −0.42 (social cognition) to −1.09 (visuospatial, 7 studies); no significant differences between domains.
key_findings.note: The printed P=0.10 does not match the printed F(12, 140.1)=2.07, which gives p≈0.023 (editors' calculation; see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Samples tested under 1 month, 1–12 months and over 12 months abstinent did not differ (−0.70, −0.63, −0.88; P=0.33); only 7 studies over 12 months.
key_findings.note: Four of the 7 studies in the over-12-month stratum are large samples (326–567 people who used methamphetamine: Chen et al., 2022; Jiang et al., 2022; Jiang et al., 2025; Tian et al., 2022; Table 1, pp. 3–4), so that estimate rests heavily on a few cohorts; the authors attribute its larger size to sample selection (p. 7).

key_findings.finding: GRADE certainty was very low for all 13 domains.
Studies with more men showed smaller differences (β=0.518, P=0.03), an ecological association the authors warn against reading at the individual level.
The methamphetamine group had 9.94 vs controls' 11.33 years of education; education did not significantly moderate effects at the study level.

Domain-level Egger tests were significant for verbal learning and memory (P=0.005) and working memory (P<0.001) and below the paper's own P<0.10 criterion for shifting (P=0.055) and self-reported impulsivity (P=0.066); overall Egger P=0.32; trim-and-fill identified no missing studies (adjusted g −0.65 vs −0.68).
key_findings.locator: Sensitivity Analyses and Publication Bias; Table 2

reporting_issues.issue: The conclusion that passive abstinence fails to restore cognition (p. 10) contradicts the paper's own caution that its cross-sectional estimates should not be read as individual remission trajectories (Figure 3 note, p. 9).
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstinence finding means 'no detectable difference between samples', not 'no recovery'.

reporting_issues.issue: GRADE upgrading for large effect (|g|≥0.80) is applied to cross-sectional comparisons with an obvious candidate confounder (education).
reporting_issues.consequence: No effect on the final ratings (all very low), but the reasoning is not standard.

reporting_issues.issue: The between-domain omnibus test is printed as F(12, 140.1)=2.07, P=0.10, but the printed F and degrees of freedom give p≈0.023 (editors' calculation), whereas the comorbidity and abstinence-phase tests match their printed p-values; the paper applies Benjamini–Hochberg correction to the domain and comorbidity omnibus tests (p. 4) but does not say this value is adjusted.
reporting_issues.consequence: Even adjusted over those two tests the domain p would be about 0.045, so the statement that domains did not differ, and the reading of the impairment as generalized, may not hold.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 contains pairs of entries with near-identical sample characteristics that may be the same participants counted twice: Fitzpatrick et al. 2020 and 2021 (both 108 in the methamphetamine group and 50 controls, 81/38 men); Wang et al. 2024 and Zhou et al. 2024 (46/44 vs 45/43, the same mean ages 31.4/26 and education 11.5); Luo et al. 2024, S4 and S59 (102/51 vs 96/46, near-identical age, abstinence and years of use).
reporting_issues.consequence: If these overlap, the 68 independent studies overstate independence; this cannot be settled without the primary papers.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 marks planning and problem solving (Egger P=0.986) and inhibitory control (P=0.128) as downgraded for publication bias, although the footnote criterion is Egger P<0.10 and the text names four domains meeting it.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor: every domain ends at very low certainty either way, but the downgrading is not applied as stated.

design_detail: Cross-sectional FDG-PET study of regional brain glucose metabolism in the same 15 people with methamphetamine dependence as Volkow et al. (2001a), abstinent at least 2 weeks, and 21 non-using controls (18 of them also in the DAT study). Region-of-interest analysis (10 composite regions plus global) and statistical parametric mapping.
can_establish: That this methamphetamine group had higher whole-brain and parietal metabolism and lower relative thalamic and striatal metabolism than this control group at the time of scanning.
cannot_establish: That methamphetamine caused the differences (no pre-use scan; large differences in smoking and sex ratio between groups), what the higher metabolism means biologically (the gliosis interpretation is speculation, as the authors say), or any cognitive consequence (tests were given to the methamphetamine group only).

sample.recruitment: Methamphetamine group from several drug rehabilitation centres in the Los Angeles area; controls by local advertisement (p. 384).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: DSM-IV methamphetamine dependence; average use at least 0.5 g/day, 5 days a week, for at least 2 years; at least 2 weeks' abstinence (urine-confirmed). Excluded: HIV seropositivity, comorbid psychiatric or neurological illness, abnormal screening tests, addiction to drugs other than methamphetamine or nicotine, head trauma with loss of consciousness over 30 minutes (p. 384).
sample.demographics: Methamphetamine group: 6 men, 9 women, age 32 (SD 7). Controls: 15 men, 6 women, age 31 (SD 8) (p. 384). Women 60% vs 28% (p. 386). Smokers 73% vs 24% (p. 387). Education not reported.
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: Treatment-centre participants who used methamphetamine heavily against advertisement-recruited controls; sex ratio and smoking differ markedly; the authors also expect the methamphetamine group drank more alcohol and used more cannabis than controls (p. 387).

exposure.measurement: Self-reported history corroborated by physician evaluation; urine toxicology at entry and before scanning (p. 384).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Inclusion thresholds only in this paper (p. 384); detailed use history is tabulated in the companion DAT paper (Volkow et al., 2001a, Table 1).
exposure.polysubstance: Dependence on other drugs except nicotine excluded; the authors state the methamphetamine group probably consumed more alcohol and cannabis than controls (p. 387).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: 12 participants tested 2 weeks to 5 months after last use, 3 participants 11–35 months (p. 384). Outpatients; the authors note the reported time since last use cannot be confirmed with certainty (p. 387).

comparison.controls: 21 healthy volunteers by advertisement, no history of drug abuse or dependence (p. 384).
comparison.matching: Age similar; sex and smoking not matched; separate analyses by sex reported as consistent (p. 386).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No pre-use scan; no IQ or education reported in this paper.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Excluded for drug abuse; the authors acknowledge possible denial of drug use by controls and that HIV was not tested in controls (p. 387).

outcomes.instruments: FDG-PET (one 20-minute emission scan at rest, eyes open); 114 regions of interest combined into 10 composite regions and global metabolism; relative measures = region/global; SPM98 (p. 384).
outcomes.validity_norms: Neuropsychological battery (motor, attention, memory, mood, NART) given to the methamphetamine group only; no group or normative comparison (pp. 384, 387).
outcomes.operationalization: Group differences in absolute and relative regional metabolism; correlations within the methamphetamine group with test scores, years and dose of use, and days since last use.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Partial: threshold p<0.01 for regional comparisons, justified as midway between 0.05 and Bonferroni (p. 384); SPM at p<0.005 uncorrected with a cluster-size threshold of 250 pixels (p. 384). The 14% global difference (p<0.05) is reported as significant although it does not meet the paper's own p<0.01 threshold.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported.

analysis.effect_sizes: Global metabolism 38.4 (SD 8) vs 33.6 (SD 5) µmol/100 g/min, 14% higher in the methamphetamine group, t=2.2, df=34, p<0.05 (p. 384). Parietal cortex 20% higher (t=2.9, df=34, p<0.01; Figure 2). Frontal, temporal, occipital cortex and hippocampus 11–12% higher at p<0.05, described as not significant under the p<0.01 threshold (p. 384). Relative to global: parietal 5% higher; thalamus 17%, caudate 12%, putamen 6% lower (pp. 384–385; Figure 3); caudate difference larger than putamen (group × region F=4.8, df=1,34, p<0.05) (p. 385). Three participants abstinent at least 11 months: relative caudate metabolism 12% lower than controls (t=3.6, df=22, p<0.002) (p. 385). No metabolic measure correlated with days since last use; parietal relative metabolism correlated with Grooved Pegboard r=0.73 (df=14, p<0.003); whole-brain metabolism correlated with years of use r=−0.62 but not after covarying age (p. 385).
analysis.covariates: Age for one correlation; sex examined by stratification (p. 386); smoking not addressed analytically.
analysis.selective_reporting: Neuropsychological results are reported only as the correlations that reached significance.
analysis.power: Not reported.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Higher global and parietal and lower relative thalamic and striatal glucose metabolism in 15 people abstinent from methamphetamine than in 21 controls who differed in sex ratio and smoking.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The discussion and summary state that methamphetamine at the doses people take causes or induces long-lasting changes in brain metabolism (pp. 386–387) and that the findings should alert clinicians to a possible higher risk of neurodegenerative disease (p. 387). The limitations paragraph on the same page concedes the smoking imbalance, likely heavier alcohol and cannabis use in the methamphetamine group, uncertain abstinence dates, and that cognitive tests were done in the methamphetamine group only, so group differences in cognition cannot be determined (p. 387). The causal wording is not supported by the design; the hypermetabolism-as-gliosis reading is offered as speculation (pp. 386–387).

timeline.event: DAT study in the same methamphetamine group
Follow-up in the same programme: thalamic relative metabolism partly recovered; striatal did not
Critical review: higher absolute metabolism here was not replicated by London et al. (2004), who found no difference in global metabolism; the paper reports no cognitive results and no education data

replication.where_it_stands: The direction of whole-brain metabolic differences is not consistent across groups (Hart et al., 2012, p. 597). Lower relative striatal metabolism in people who use methamphetamine is more consistent but shares the same confounding by smoking and selection.

funding.funder: US Department of Energy contract (Brookhaven National Laboratory); National Institute on Drug Abuse grants; Office of National Drug Control Policy; NIH General Clinical Research Center grant (p. 388).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Same group and sample as Volkow et al. (2001a).

what_would_settle_it: Longitudinal imaging from before regular use, or comparison groups matched on smoking, sex and other drug use, with cognition measured in both groups against norms.

domains.note: Smoking 73% vs 24%; women 60% vs 28%; probable alcohol and cannabis differences; none adjusted.
Abstinence duration self-reported in outpatients (acknowledged p. 387).
Different recruitment sources for the two groups.
FDG-PET objective; uncorrected SPM threshold; blinding not reported.
Global difference reported as significant despite missing the stated threshold; cognitive results reported only as significant correlations.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Metabolic group differences are measured objectively but are confounded by smoking and sex at a scale that could plausibly produce them, and the multiple-comparison rule is applied inconsistently.

key_findings.finding: Whole-brain glucose metabolism was 14% higher in 15 people who used methamphetamine than in 21 controls (38.4 vs 33.6 µmol/100 g/min, t=2.2, df=34, p<0.05), most in the parietal cortex (20%).
key_findings.note: p<0.05 does not meet the paper's own p<0.01 threshold for multiple comparisons.

key_findings.finding: Relative to whole-brain metabolism, the methamphetamine group had lower metabolism in the thalamus (17%), caudate (12%) and putamen (6%), and higher in parietal cortex (5%).
Three participants abstinent 11–35 months also had 12% lower relative caudate metabolism than controls.
No metabolic measure correlated with days since last use; thalamic and striatal metabolism did not correlate with any test score.
key_findings.locator: Results, end of 2nd paragraph (days since last use) and 3rd paragraph (test scores), right column

key_findings.finding: Smokers were 73% of the methamphetamine group and 24% of controls; women 60% and 28%.
The authors state that neurocognitive tests were done only in the methamphetamine group, so it cannot be determined how much the groups differed.

In absolute values (Figure 2, editors' reading of the bars), the methamphetamine group's thalamic metabolism was about 4% lower than controls', caudate about equal and putamen about 8% higher; the lower relative thalamic and striatal values arise after dividing by a whole-brain value that was 14% higher in the methamphetamine group.

The authors liken the pattern (lower relative thalamic and striatal metabolism; DAT reductions of similar size in caudate and putamen in other studies) to atypical parkinsonism rather than idiopathic Parkinson's disease, which shows no change or higher striatal and thalamic metabolism and greater putamen than caudate DAT loss; no patients were studied.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 4th paragraph (left column into right column)

reporting_issues.issue: The 14% global metabolic difference (t=2.2, p<0.05) is presented as significant, but the methods set p<0.01 as the significance threshold for multiple comparisons, and other regions with similar t values (2.0–2.4) are described as not significant.
reporting_issues.consequence: The headline 'higher whole-brain metabolism' finding does not meet the paper's own criterion.

reporting_issues.issue: Correlations in 15 people who used methamphetamine are reported with df=14 (expected 13).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor.

reporting_issues.issue: The text gives 11–12% higher absolute metabolism in frontal, temporal and occipital cortex and hippocampus, but the Figure 2 bars indicate about 13%, 12%, 17% and 17% (editors' reading).
reporting_issues.consequence: The text understates the plotted occipital and hippocampal differences; bar readings are approximate.

reporting_issues.issue: The sex-stratified analysis is reported only in part (data not shown): higher whole-brain metabolism is given for the 9 women vs 6 control women but not for the 6 men vs 15 control men; putamen is reported for men only and parietal cortex for neither sex.
reporting_issues.consequence: The statement that results were consistent across sexes is only partly documented; whether the whole-brain elevation survives stratification by sex is not shown.

reporting_issues.issue: The longest abstinence among the three participants abstinent 11 months or more is given as 35 months here (p. 384) but as 36 months in the companion transporter paper on the same 15 people (Volkow et al., 2001a, p. 378).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; each paper's figure should be cited as printed.

design_detail: Systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis (Hedges' g) of case-control PET and SPECT studies comparing striatal dopamine measures (stimulant-induced dopamine release, dopamine transporter [DAT] availability, D2/3 receptor availability; VMAT2, dopamine synthesis and D1 described without pooling) between people who use cocaine or amphetamine/methamphetamine and healthy controls. Whole striatum only. Databases: PubMed, EMBASE and PsycINFO from inception to 14 May 2016 (Abstract › Data sources); search strings, selection flow and inclusion details are in a supplement. Language limits, grey literature and hand-searching are not stated in the main text. No protocol or registration is mentioned.
can_establish: That published case-control imaging studies, taken together, report lower striatal DAT availability and lower D2/3 receptor availability in people who use amphetamine-type stimulants than in controls, with the DAT difference the largest, and lower stimulant-induced dopamine release mainly in people who use cocaine.
cannot_establish: Whether the differences were caused by stimulant use, preceded it, reflect loss of terminals or regulation, or change with abstinence (every primary study is cross-sectional and the review ran no analysis by abstinence duration, smoking or other drug use), nor how trustworthy the primary studies are (their risk of bias was not assessed).

sample.recruitment: Primary studies identified by database search; recruitment of their participants not summarized in the main text (study characteristics are in the supplement, not read).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: studies of the striatal dopamine system in people who use cocaine or amphetamine/methamphetamine, with a control group, reporting means and SDs for both groups (Methods › Study selection). One cocaine DAT study was excluded because participants had HIV (Results › Dopamine transporter). Two cocaine DAT PET studies had overlapping samples (Results › Dopamine transporter). Duplicate screening and duplicate extraction are not described in the main text.
sample.demographics: Not summarized in the main text; extracted variables (age, sex, substance use, comorbid substance use, abstinence confirmation and duration, diagnosis, imaging method) are listed in Methods › Data extraction.
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: Only studies reporting group means and SDs were eligible. The amphetamine-type group mixes methamphetamine-dependent people with people who used dexamphetamine recreationally (two included studies by Schrantee and Schouw). The abstract states that in most of the review's 31 studies abstinence lasted 5 days to 3 weeks; the main text gives no abstinence for the 9 amphetamine-type DAT studies (refs 27–35), which include three of people abstinent for years on average (McCann et al., 1998, 2008; Johanson et al., 2006, as described by Hart et al., 2012), and the authors note marked differences even in studies of several months' abstinence (Discussion › Implications, 7th paragraph), so the amphetamine-type DAT estimate cannot be read as describing early abstinence. Possible sample overlap among studies from the same groups (two DAT studies by Volkow and colleagues, two by McCann and colleagues) is not discussed.

exposure.measurement: As defined in each primary study; the review extracted diagnosis, method of abstinence confirmation and duration of abstinence but does not report them in the main text.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not summarized in the main text.
exposure.polysubstance: Comorbid substance use was extracted but not analysed. The Limitations note that studies varied in nicotine and alcohol use and abstinence, and assert that such variation would obscure rather than account for the effects (Discussion › Limitations); no analysis supports this.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Majority of the review's 31 studies: 5 days to 3 weeks (Abstract › Results); not given for the 9 amphetamine-type DAT studies, which include three of people abstinent for years on average (McCann et al., 1998, 2008; Johanson et al., 2006). VMAT2 studies in people who used methamphetamine had mean abstinence of 2.6 days, 19 days and about 3 months (Results › Other dopaminergic measures). No analysis by abstinence duration.

comparison.controls: Healthy controls of the primary studies.
comparison.matching: Matching within primary studies not summarized or assessed.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No primary study had a pre-use measure; the review discusses a model in which lower dopamine markers precede use but cannot test it (Discussion, models paragraphs).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not summarized.

outcomes.instruments: Whole-striatum PET/SPECT indices: change in D2/3 binding after an amphetamine or methylphenidate challenge (dopamine release); DAT availability; D2/3 receptor availability; also VMAT2 availability, [18F]-DOPA uptake and D1 availability. Effect size Hedges' g, stimulant groups minus controls.
outcomes.validity_norms: The authors note D2/3 tracers do not separate D2 from D3 or high- from low-affinity states and are sensitive to endogenous dopamine; tracer interaction with methamphetamine may lower VMAT2 estimates in early abstinence (Discussion; Results › Other dopaminergic measures).
outcomes.operationalization: An alteration is a pooled standardized group difference with p<0.05.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; seven pooled analyses each at p<0.05 (two-tailed).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported. No risk-of-bias tool was applied to the primary studies (none mentioned in Methods).

analysis.effect_sizes: All pooled estimates (Hedges' g, random effects, whole striatum; Results). Dopamine release: all stimulants, 7 studies, 164 in the stimulant groups vs 139 controls, g=−0.84 (95% CI −1.08 to −0.60), p<0.001; cocaine only, 5 studies, g=−0.87 (−1.15 to −0.60), p<0.001; amphetamine-type, 2 studies, not pooled: SMD −1.05 (−1.76 to −0.34) and −0.40 (−1.11 to 0.32). DAT: all stimulants, 12 studies, 177 vs 191, g=−0.91 (−1.50 to −0.32), p<0.01; amphetamine-type, 9 studies, 108 vs 126, g=−1.47 (−1.83 to −1.10), p<0.001; cocaine not pooled (two SPECT studies in acute abstinence found higher DAT, two overlapping PET studies no difference). D2/3 receptors: all stimulants, 19 studies, 342 vs 321, g=−0.76 (−0.92 to −0.60), p<0.001; cocaine, 12 studies, g=−0.73 (−0.94 to −0.53), p<0.001; amphetamine-type, 7 studies, g=−0.81 (−1.12 to −0.49), p<0.001. Not pooled: [18F]-DOPA in people who use cocaine (1 study) 0.46 (−0.46 to 1.39); VMAT2 (4 studies) lower in the cocaine group at 2 weeks, g 1.6 (0.68 to 2.52), and in the methamphetamine group at 3 months, g 1.68 (0.86 to 2.5), but higher in two methamphetamine studies in early abstinence, g 1.16 (0.56 to 1.76); D1 (1 cocaine study) no difference. Heterogeneity: described as low except for DAT; I², τ² and prediction intervals are not given in the main text (supplement). Forest plots (Figures 1–3) are images and were not extracted.
analysis.covariates: None. The only moderator analysis is the split by drug class (study-level). No meta-regression on abstinence duration, smoking, alcohol, tracer or route; leave-one-out sensitivity analyses reported only in the supplement.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration mentioned in the main text.
analysis.selective_reporting: Publication bias assessed by funnel plots and regression tests, with results only in the supplement; the main text says only that the funnel plots show few large studies (Discussion › Limitations). No adjusted estimate. Sensitivity and heterogeneity results are also confined to the supplement.
analysis.power: Not reported. The amphetamine-type release question rests on 2 small studies; FDOPA, D1 and VMAT2 on 1–4 studies each.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Pooled case-control differences: lower striatal DAT (g −1.47 in the amphetamine-type groups, mostly early abstinence), lower D2/3 availability (g −0.81 amphetamine-type, −0.73 cocaine) and lower stimulant-induced release (pooled mainly from cocaine studies). VMAT2 findings in people who use methamphetamine go in both directions depending on abstinence. Primary studies were not appraised for risk of bias and no confounder or abstinence analysis was run.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that pre- and post-synaptic dopamine function is down-regulated in people who use stimulants, and the Conclusions call the evidence robust with large effect sizes and recommend restoring dopamine function as a treatment target (Abstract › Conclusion; Conclusions). Down-regulation names a mechanism the cross-sectional data cannot identify; the Discussion itself sets out adaptive, pre-existing and hybrid models and states the findings do not address the temporal relationship (Discussion, models paragraphs). The release finding is generalized to all stimulants though only two amphetamine-type studies exist. The Discussion calls g of −0.76 to −0.91 large to very large. Robustness is asserted without any risk-of-bias assessment, and the claim that confounding by nicotine or alcohol could only obscure the effects is not tested.

timeline.event: Earliest included amphetamine-type DAT study: 6 people abstinent from methamphetamine and 4 from methcathinone vs 10 controls (McCann et al., 1998; appraised in this batch).
Critical assessment of whether dopamine-marker reductions in people who use methamphetamine mean neuronal damage

replication.where_it_stands: The authors describe this as the first meta-analysis of these imaging findings (Discussion, 1st paragraph). The DAT reduction in the amphetamine-type groups is the most consistent pooled finding; its meaning (terminal loss, regulation or pre-existing difference) and its course with abstinence are not addressed by the pooled data.

Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A preregistered update with risk-of-bias appraisal of each imaging study, individual-participant or meta-regression analysis of DAT by abstinence duration, tobacco and other drug use, and separate pooling of VMAT2 by abstinence phase; ultimately, prospective imaging before and after the onset of regular use.
