risk_of_bias.reasoning: More than one critical flaw: no protocol, no risk-of-bias assessment of the primary studies and no account of it in the interpretation, pooling of unadjusted observational data (including opposite-direction cocaine DAT results in the combined estimate), and publication-bias results not discussed. Items 4, 5, 7 and 8 were judged from the main text only, because the supplement is a downloadable .docx that was not opened; the overall rating does not depend on them. Critically low confidence describes the review's methods, not the direction of the DAT finding, which is consistent across the amphetamine-type studies.

key_findings.finding: DAT availability in people who use amphetamine-type stimulants (9 studies, 108 vs 126 controls): g=−1.47 (95% CI −1.83 to −1.10), p<0.001.
key_findings.locator: Results › Dopamine transporter, 1st paragraph; Abstract › Results
key_findings.note: The nine pooled studies are cited as refs 27–35: Chou et al. (2007), Johanson et al. (2006), McCann et al. (2008), McCann et al. (1998), Schouw et al. (2013; people using dexamphetamine recreationally), Sekine et al. (2001), Volkow et al. (2001, J Neurosci, the recovery follow-up; encyclopedia volkow_2001b), Yuan et al. (2014) and Volkow et al. (2015). The 2001 American Journal of Psychiatry DAT study (encyclopedia volkow_2001a) is not in the reference list. Per-study values and abstinence are in the unread supplement.

key_findings.finding: DAT availability, all stimulants (12 studies: 3 cocaine, 9 amphetamine-type; 177 in the stimulant groups vs 191 controls): g=−0.91 (−1.50 to −0.32), p<0.01. Cocaine studies were inconsistent: two SPECT studies in acute abstinence (up to 4 days; mean 7 days) found higher DAT, two overlapping PET studies found no difference; one study excluded for HIV comorbidity.

D2/3 receptor availability: all stimulants, 19 studies, 342 in the stimulant groups vs 321 controls, g=−0.76 (−0.92 to −0.60); cocaine, 12 studies, g=−0.73 (−0.94 to −0.53); amphetamine-type, 7 studies, g=−0.81 (−1.12 to −0.49); all p<0.001.

Stimulant-induced dopamine release: all stimulants, 7 studies, 164 in the stimulant groups vs 139 controls, g=−0.84 (−1.08 to −0.60); cocaine only, 5 studies, g=−0.87 (−1.15 to −0.60); amphetamine-type stimulants only 2 studies, not pooled, SMD −1.05 (−1.76 to −0.34) and −0.40 (−1.11 to 0.32).

VMAT2 (not pooled, 4 studies): lower in the cocaine group at 2 weeks' abstinence (g 1.6, 0.68 to 2.52) and in the methamphetamine group after 3 months (g 1.68, 0.86 to 2.5); higher in two studies of people in early abstinence from methamphetamine (mean 2.6 and 19 days; g 1.16, 0.56 to 1.76). The authors note tracer binding may be underestimated in early abstinence because methamphetamine acts at the same VMAT2 site.
key_findings.note: Signs as printed: reductions and increases are both given as positive g; see reporting issues. The authors' caveat (residual methamphetamine at the tracer site could lead to underestimated VMAT2) runs opposite to the interpretation of the early-abstinence rise given by the group that ran those studies (less competition from depleted vesicular dopamine, so higher binding; as summarized by Kish et al., 2017, VMAT2 section).

key_findings.finding: Dopamine synthesis ([18F]-DOPA): one cocaine study, described as showing reduced synthesis capacity, effect size 0.46 (−0.46 to 1.39); no amphetamine-type study. D1 receptors: one cocaine study, no group difference.
In most of the 31 included studies abstinence lasted 5 days to 3 weeks (a description of the review as a whole; abstinence is not given per analysis in the main text).
Heterogeneity was described as low in all analyses except DAT; no I², τ² or prediction interval is printed in the main text. Funnel plots showed few large studies; test results are in the supplement.

The authors set out three models (adaptive down-regulation, pre-existing reductions, hybrid) and state that the data cannot address the temporal relation between dopamine changes and phase of addiction; they cite human DAT recovery with abstinence and the one post-mortem study (reduced DAT without neuron loss) against neuron loss, and two registry studies of Parkinson's disease risk in its favour.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Implications for understanding stimulant misuse and dependence, 3rd–8th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The 31 studies and 519 in the stimulant groups vs 512 controls in the abstract equal the D2/3 set (19 studies, 342/321) plus the DAT set (12 studies, 177/191); the release studies (refs 16–22) are a subset of the D2/3 set; one VMAT2 study (Johanson et al., 2006, ref 28) is counted through the DAT set, while the other three VMAT2 studies (refs 50–52), the DOPA study (ref 49) and the D1 study (ref 53) are outside the count (editors' arithmetic).

The authors note marked dopaminergic differences even in studies with several months of abstinence and, citing one study (Volkow et al., 2015, ref 35), state that dopamine receptor density and dopamine release remained lower after about 9 months of abstinence, while DAT recovers with detoxification (citing reviews and the same study).
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Implications for understanding stimulant misuse and dependence, 3rd and 7th paragraphs
key_findings.note: Second-hand, from one study by a co-author's group; check Volkow et al. (2015) before use.

editorial_corrections.reason: Language (METHODS §9): 28 replacements, no change of meaning, number or citation; list in data/verification/language-2026-10-16b.json

design_detail: PET study with the VMAT2 ligand (+)[11C]dihydrotetrabenazine ((+)[11C]DTBZ), whose binding at tracer doses rises when vesicular dopamine is low. Cross-sectional comparison at a first scan (mean 2.6 days after last use) between 28 people who used methamphetamine, 9 people who used cocaine and 22 controls, plus a short prospective follow-up: a second scan about a week later in those who stayed abstinent (17 methamphetamine, 8 cocaine, 9 controls). Binding potential (BPND) by simplified reference-tissue model with occipital reference, in limbic, associative and sensorimotor striatum and whole striatum, with a voxelwise analysis.
can_establish: That striatal (+)[11C]DTBZ binding was higher in people actively using methamphetamine, scanned a few days after last use, than in controls or in people who used cocaine, that it tracked recency and frequency of recent use, and that in the subgroup who stayed abstinent about ten days it was no longer distinguishable from controls.
cannot_establish: That vesicular dopamine itself was measured (binding is an indirect, competition-based index and VMAT2 protein could also change), that use caused the difference (no pre-use scan; groups differ in education, IQ, depression, smoking and cannabis), that the follow-up shows recovery in people who use methamphetamine generally (only those who stayed abstinent were rescanned, and they already had lower binding at scan 1), or that the methamphetamine group was cognitively impaired relative to controls (group comparisons appear only in the supplement and are described as slight).

sample.recruitment: Self-referred in response to a web advertisement; non-treatment-seeking, actively using participants; all compensated for their time. Data from 12 of the 22 controls were taken from the authors' earlier 2008 study; all participants who used drugs were new recruits (Materials and Methods › Subjects).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Aged 19–45, no significant medical condition or head trauma. Controls: no current or past DSM-IV Axis I disorder (SCID), no abuse or dependence in the past 12 months except nicotine, negative urine GC-MS and scalp-hair toxicology except cannabis. Methamphetamine and cocaine groups: DSM-IV abuse or dependence on their respective drug, with positive urine and hair toxicology (Materials and Methods › Subjects).
sample.demographics: Table 1. Age: controls 28.6 (SD 5.8), methamphetamine 26.6 (5.7), cocaine 31.2 (7.7). Men: 12, 12 and 3. Education (years): 16.8 (2.6) vs 13.1 (2.7), p<0.001. IQ (Shipley-2): 111.6 (12.9) vs 101.4 (12.2), p=0.03. Beck Depression Inventory: 1.1 (1.5) vs 14.6 (10.9), p<0.001. Smokers: 4 of 22 controls vs 24 of 28 methamphetamine and 7 of 9 cocaine (p<0.001); cigarettes per day 0.5 (1.3) vs 9.5 (5.6). Cannabis at least monthly: 3 vs 18 (p=0.02). Alcohol drinks per week 0.6 (1.0) vs 4.1 (7.3), p=0.14. Ethnic composition differed (p=0.01). Several control values are compiled from 10 longitudinal controls plus the earlier study's controls (Table 1, footnote a).
sample.attrition: Of 28 people who used methamphetamine, 17 were rescanned; 7 did not stay abstinent and were therefore not rescanned (described as choosing methamphetamine over the study honorarium); 4 dropped out or were lost to excessive head movement. Controls: 9 of 22 rescanned; cocaine: 8 of 9. Those who relapsed had higher binding at scan 1, so the completers are a selected subgroup (Results › PET Results; Table 3 footnote).
sample.selection_effects: Actively using, non-treatment-seeking volunteers recruited online and paid, compared with controls who were better educated, scored higher on an IQ screen, were far less often smokers and had minimal depressive symptoms. Rescanning only the abstinent subgroup selects on the outcome's own predictor.

exposure.measurement: DSM-IV diagnosis plus self-report (Severity of Dependence Scale, DAST-20) with biological verification: urine and blood toxicology at each scan and scalp-hair analysis covering roughly the preceding 4–5 months. Plasma methamphetamine measured before scan 1 (Materials and Methods › Subjects; Table 2).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Self-reported, Table 2: methamphetamine group, 6.6 (SD 5.7) years of use; 4.3 (2.4) days per week in the past month; 0.35 (0.30) g per day; 49.9 (24.1) days used in the past 90; routes 14 smoking, 6 nasal, 4 smoking and nasal, 2 oral, 2 intravenous. Cocaine group: 13.7 (8.5) years, 1.9 (1.9) days per week, 0.64 (0.30) g per day. Reported as study-sample characteristics.
exposure.polysubstance: Extensive. Hair toxicology of the 28 methamphetamine participants also showed cocaine or benzoylecgonine in 17 (60%), MDMA/MDA in 6, opioids in 4 and THC in 6; cocaine was detected in urine in only one case during the study. Most were tobacco smokers and 18 used cannabis at least monthly. Analyses were adjusted for cigarettes per day, weekly alcohol, current cannabis use and depressive symptoms, but not for other stimulant exposure, education or IQ (Results, 1st and 3rd paragraphs; Table 2).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Scan 1: mean 2.6 days (SD 2.0, range 1–7) since last use, verified by self-report plus urine and blood toxicology. Scan 2: mean 9.9 days (SD 2.3) in the methamphetamine group; participants who used in between were not rescanned (Table 2; Materials and Methods).

comparison.controls: 22 healthy volunteers without current or past Axis I disorder or recent substance use disorder other than nicotine; 9 of them were rescanned. A cocaine-using group (n=9) served as a stimulant comparison.
comparison.matching: Matched on age and sex; not matched on education, IQ, depressive symptoms, ethnicity, smoking or cannabis use, all of which differed.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No pre-use scan or cognitive baseline; current IQ screen and education differed between groups and were not adjusted for.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Controls had negative urine and hair toxicology except cannabis; 3 used cannabis at least monthly and 4 smoked tobacco.

outcomes.instruments: (+)[11C]DTBZ PET on an HRRT camera, about 10 mCi, 60-minute acquisition, BPND by simplified reference-tissue model with occipital reference; automated regions for limbic, associative and sensorimotor striatum and whole striatum; voxelwise SPM8 analysis. Questionnaires and a cognitive battery at each session: Hopkins Verbal Learning Test, Delay Discounting Task, Continuous Performance Task, Amphetamine Withdrawal Questionnaire, Epworth Sleepiness Scale, Beck Depression Inventory (Materials and Methods; Results).
outcomes.validity_norms: The authors state the tracer competes with vesicular dopamine for the VMAT2 site, so higher binding is read as less stored dopamine; they note VMAT2 protein itself might change and that residual methamphetamine could compete with the tracer at scan 1 (Discussion, 5th paragraph). Cognitive tests are standard instruments; normative comparison is not reported in the main text.
outcomes.operationalization: Low vesicular dopamine was operationalized as higher (+)[11C]DTBZ binding; recovery as binding not differing from controls at the second scan. Cognitive impairment in the abstract rests on within-group correlations between binding and test scores, not on a group comparison (Results › correlations paragraph).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Group contrasts: repeated-measures ANOVA followed by least-significant-difference t-tests with Bonferroni correction for planned comparisons. Voxelwise: p<0.01 with family-wise correction. Correlations: no correction stated; about 15 correlations are reported at a 0.05 threshold across four striatal regions and several behavioural measures (Materials and Methods › Statistical Analyses; Results).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported; regions were placed by an automated method, which limits operator influence.

analysis.effect_sizes: Scan 1 (Table 3; means with SD): whole striatum BPND 2.41 (0.34) in controls, 2.55 (0.30) in the cocaine group, 3.09 (0.71) in the methamphetamine group, i.e. +28% vs controls (p<0.0001) and +21% vs the cocaine group (p=0.040). By region vs controls: associative +31% (p<0.0001), limbic +24% (p=0.010), sensorimotor +26% (p<0.0001). Group effect F(2,56)=9.581, p<0.0001; ROI × group interaction F(1.485, 83.146)=5.077, p=0.001. The cocaine group did not differ from controls (+6%, p=1.0). Editors' calculation from Table 3 (Hedges' g, pooled SD, approximate 95% CI): methamphetamine vs controls whole striatum g=1.16 (recomputed; earlier 1.24) (0.63 to 1.85), associative g=1.38 (0.76 to 2.00), sensorimotor g=1.17 (0.56 to 1.77), limbic g=0.88 (0.29 to 1.47). Adjusting for cigarettes per day, weekly alcohol, cannabis and depressive symptoms left the group effect significant (F(2,55)=5.723, p=0.006; F(2,43)=5.036, p=0.011; F(2,43)=5.723, p=0.006). Scan 2 (17 methamphetamine, 8 cocaine, 9 controls): whole striatum 2.54 (0.39) vs 2.46 (0.34) in controls, all contrasts p=1.0, F(2,48)=0.288, p=0.751. Within the 17 who stayed abstinent, binding fell about 11% from scan 1 (p=0.055), with individual changes from −34% to +29% and 6 of 17 increasing. People who relapsed before scan 2 (n=7) had 17% higher scan-1 binding than those who stayed abstinent (n=17) (ANCOVA with days abstinent, p=0.035); the abstainers' scan-1 binding was already closer to controls (limbic p=0.472, whole striatum p=0.031). Correlations within the methamphetamine group at scan 1 (n=28): frequency of recent use r=0.68 (p<0.0001), cumulative amount in the past month r=0.48 (p=0.009), days abstinent r=−0.49 in associative striatum (p=0.008), plasma methamphetamine r=0.5 (p=0.008). Participants who had used about 24 hours before the scan (n=10) had binding 45–52% above controls; those abstinent 2–7 days (n=18) were 13–20% lower than them. Scan-1 binding predicted scan-2 binding (limbic r=0.76, p<0.001; whole striatum r=0.54, p=0.026; associative r=0.49, p=0.045). Binding correlated with verbal recall r=−0.43 (p=0.03), cued recall r=−0.46 (p=0.02), recognition r=−0.46 (p=0.01), delay discounting r=0.43 (p=0.03), processing speed r=0.43 (p=0.03), withdrawal symptoms r=0.37 (p=0.051) and sleepiness r=0.44 (p=0.011).
analysis.covariates: Cigarettes per day, weekly alcohol, current cannabis use, depressive symptoms (each in a separate adjusted ANOVA); days abstinent in the relapser-versus-abstainer comparison; baseline binding in the partial correlations of change. Education, IQ, ethnicity and concurrent cocaine exposure were not adjusted for.
analysis.selective_reporting: Cognitive and behavioural comparisons between the methamphetamine group and controls are placed in supplementary tables and summarized in one sentence as slight deficits, while the abstract reports correlations with cognitive impairment. The relapsers' course after scan 1 is unobserved by design.
analysis.power: Not reported. The follow-up contrast rests on 17 people who used methamphetamine and 9 rescanned controls; the within-group change (11%) did not reach the 0.05 threshold.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Striatal (+)[11C]DTBZ binding was about 28% above control levels a few days after last use, scaling with how recently and how often methamphetamine had been used, and indistinguishable from controls in the subgroup who managed about ten days of abstinence; the within-person fall was 11% (p=0.055) and a third of that subgroup rose rather than fell. The methamphetamine group differed from controls in education, IQ, depressive symptoms, smoking and cannabis use, and 60% had hair evidence of cocaine exposure.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The title and abstract describe rapid recovery of vesicular dopamine levels and say the elevated binding correlated with cognitive impairment and withdrawal symptoms. Vesicular dopamine is inferred, not measured; the authors say so in the discussion and note VMAT2 protein may itself change. Recovery rests on rescanning only those who stayed abstinent, who already had lower binding at scan 1, against 9 rescanned controls, with no retested comparison for practice or regression effects. Cognitive impairment is supported by within-group correlations; the paper's own group comparison, reported only in the supplement, is summarized as showing no marked impairment. The discussion of levodopa as dopamine substitution is framed cautiously as needing a safety trial first, and notes the hazard of giving it while the drug is still present.

timeline.event: The authors' earlier cross-sectional PET study reported raised VMAT2 binding in early abstinence (Boileau et al., 2008); 12 of its controls are reused here.
A PET study reported about 10% lower VMAT2 binding in people abstinent from methamphetamine much longer (Johanson et al., 2006, as cited); direction opposite to the early-abstinence finding.
Review citing this study as evidence against substantial dopamine neurone loss, with binding raised in the first days and normal by 7–15 days
Meta-analysis listing VMAT2 findings in people who use methamphetamine as inconsistent across abstinence phases (Ashok et al., 2017; appraised in this batch).

replication.where_it_stands: Raised VMAT2 tracer binding in the first days of abstinence has now been reported twice by the same laboratory, with partly shared controls, and no independent replication was cited. Whether binding falls below normal at longer abstinence, and whether any of it reflects vesicular dopamine rather than transporter number, remains open.

funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare no conflict of interest (Funding and Disclosure).
funding.affiliations_note: Centre for Addiction and Mental Health and University of Toronto. The same group produced the post-mortem findings this study sets out to corroborate and the 2008 PET study it extends, and co-authored the Kish et al. (2017) review that cites it. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A study that rescans everyone, including those who resume use, with a retested control group over the same interval, measures VMAT2 with a method that does not compete with endogenous dopamine alongside (+)[11C]DTBZ, and reports the cognitive battery against controls and norms rather than only as within-group correlations.

key_findings.finding: At a mean of 2.6 days after last use, whole-striatum (+)[11C]DTBZ binding was 28% higher in 28 people who used methamphetamine than in 22 controls (BPND 3.09, SD 0.71, vs 2.41, SD 0.34; p<0.0001); 9 people who used cocaine did not differ from controls (+6%, p=1.0).
key_findings.locator: Results › MA users have greater binding during early abstinence; Table 3

key_findings.finding: Regional differences from controls at scan 1: associative striatum +31% (p<0.0001), sensorimotor +26% (p<0.0001), limbic +24% (p=0.010). Group effect F(2,56)=9.581, p<0.0001; ROI × group F(1.485, 83.146)=5.077, p=0.001.
key_findings.locator: Results › first paragraph of PET Results; Table 3

key_findings.finding: Editors' calculation from Table 3: standardized difference (Hedges' g, pooled SD) between the methamphetamine group and controls at scan 1 of 1.16 for the whole striatum (95% CI 0.56 to 1.76); by region about 1.38 associative, 1.17 sensorimotor and 0.88 limbic (earlier approximations, to be recomputed with the same method).
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation with pooled SD and large-sample interval; group SDs are unequal (0.71 vs 0.34), so the interval is approximate.

key_findings.finding: Adjusting separately for cigarettes per day, weekly alcohol, cannabis use and depressive symptoms did not remove the group difference (F(2,55)=5.723, p=0.006; F(2,43)=5.036, p=0.011; F(2,43)=5.723, p=0.006).
key_findings.locator: Results › first paragraph of PET Results
key_findings.note: Two of the three adjusted analyses use 43 error degrees of freedom, implying about 12 participants dropped from those models; this is not explained.

key_findings.finding: At the second scan (mean 9.9 days abstinent) the 17 who stayed abstinent did not differ from 9 rescanned controls in any region (whole striatum 2.54, SD 0.39, vs 2.46, SD 0.34; all p=1.0).
Within those 17, binding fell about 11% from scan 1 (p=0.055), with individual changes ranging from −34% to +29% and 6 of 17 increasing.
key_findings.note: The change over time was not significant at the paper's own 0.05 threshold.

key_findings.finding: The 7 participants who did not stay abstinent had 17% higher scan-1 binding than the 17 who did (p=0.035, adjusted for days abstinent) and were never rescanned; the abstainers' scan-1 binding was already much closer to controls (limbic p=0.472).
key_findings.locator: Results › first paragraph of PET Results; Table 3

key_findings.finding: Binding tracked recency and amount of use: frequency of recent use r=0.68 (p<0.0001), amount in the past month r=0.48 (p=0.009), days abstinent r=−0.49 (p=0.008), plasma methamphetamine r=0.50 (p=0.008); those who had used about 24 hours before the scan (n=10) were 45–52% above controls.

Within the 28 people who used methamphetamine, higher binding correlated with poorer verbal recall (r=−0.43), cued recall (r=−0.46), recognition (r=−0.46), steeper delay discounting (r=0.43), slower reaction time (r=0.43), more withdrawal symptoms (r=0.37, p=0.051) and more daytime sleepiness (r=0.44).

Compared with controls the methamphetamine group showed no marked cognitive or behavioural impairment, only slight deficits; those comparisons are reported in supplementary tables, not in the main text.
key_findings.note: Supplementary Tables 1 and 2 are .doc downloads and were not opened, so the size and direction of the group differences could not be checked.

key_findings.finding: The authors state they cannot exclude that VMAT2 protein itself changed, or that residual methamphetamine competed with the tracer at scan 1, and that it remains unknown whether low stored dopamine means low synaptic dopamine.

reporting_issues.issue: The second-scan analysis is reported as F(2,48)=0.288 although the three rescanned groups total 34 people (17, 8 and 9); for three groups this implies 51 participants.
reporting_issues.consequence: Either the degrees of freedom or the stated group sizes are wrong; the test of normalization cannot be reconstructed as printed.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 gives 0.35 g per day and 49.9 days of use in the past 90 but an amount per month of 1.57 g; those three numbers are not mutually consistent (0.35 g on about 17 days a month would be roughly 6 g).
reporting_issues.consequence: The monthly exposure variable, which is used in a correlation with binding, may measure something other than monthly total.

reporting_issues.issue: The same correlation coefficient of −0.46 in the same group of 28 is given p=0.02 for cued recall and p=0.01 for recognition; r=0.44 is given p=0.011 while r=0.43 is given p=0.03.
reporting_issues.consequence: Either the n varies between tests (missing data not stated) or some p-values are misprinted.

reporting_issues.issue: Two of the three covariate-adjusted analyses use error degrees of freedom of 43, against 55 in the first and 56 in the unadjusted model, without explanation; the same F value (5.723) appears in both the cigarettes model (df 55) and the cannabis-plus-depression model (df 43).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Results › first paragraph of PET Results)
reporting_issues.consequence: Suggests a copying error in one of the adjusted results, and that 12 or more participants were lost from the adjusted models.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 heads the control column with two sample sizes (n=10 and n=22) and a footnote says some control values combine 10 longitudinal controls with controls from the authors' earlier study; which rows use which n is not marked.
reporting_issues.consequence: The control demographics cannot be matched to the control group actually scanned at each time point; 12 of the 22 controls were scanned for a different study.

reporting_issues.issue: The Figure 2 legend reports cluster significance as corrected p greater than 0.0001 and uses a correction abbreviation that matches neither the family-wise correction stated in the Methods nor a standard false-discovery label.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Figure 2 legend; Materials and Methods › image analysis)
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical, but the voxelwise correction actually applied cannot be verified from the legend.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 lists 17 abstainers and 7 relapsers at scan 1, which with the 4 further non-completers accounts for 28, but the group row for scan 1 pools all 28 including the 4 whose subgroup is never characterized.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the 4 excluded from both subgroups are not described, so the subgroup contrast is not exhaustive.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract states binding correlated with cognitive impairment, while the Results state the methamphetamine group did not show marked impairment relative to controls.
reporting_issues.consequence: The word impairment in the abstract is supported only by within-group variation, not by a deficit against controls.

domains.note: Groups differ in education, IQ, depressive symptoms, ethnicity, smoking and cannabis; adjustment covered smoking, alcohol, cannabis and depression but not education, IQ or the 60% with hair evidence of cocaine exposure.
Diagnosis plus urine, blood and hair toxicology, with plasma methamphetamine at scan 1; amounts self-reported and internally inconsistent in Table 2.
Paid, non-treatment-seeking volunteers recruited by web advertisement against better-educated controls, 12 of whom came from an earlier study.
Abstinence between scans was participant-managed and verified; those who used were excluded from the follow-up rather than analysed.
Follow-up was obtained only from completers (17 of 28), and non-completion was directly related to the outcome, since those who relapsed had the highest binding.
Objective PET with automated regions, but the outcome is an indirect index: binding depends on vesicular dopamine, on VMAT2 number, and potentially on residual drug.

Cognitive group comparisons are confined to the supplement while correlations appear in the abstract; about 15 uncorrected correlations are reported, with p-values that do not all match their coefficients.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The cross-sectional difference is large, dose- and recency-related and survives several adjustments, so something about recent methamphetamine use is clearly reflected in the tracer signal. The recovery conclusion is much weaker: it rests on completers selected by the very behaviour that tracked the outcome, on a within-group change that did not reach significance, and on 9 rescanned controls. The cognitive conclusion is not supported by a group comparison in the main text.

design_detail: Narrative, debate-style review with no methods section: no search strategy, databases, dates or eligibility criteria. Treats amphetamine and methamphetamine together as amphetamines; draws on 1968–1979 experimental administration studies, case reports, community and clinical samples, Japanese clinical series, family and genetic studies, animal work and treatment literature (108 references), and proposes a stress–vulnerability model (Figure 1). No tables and no quantitative synthesis.
can_establish: The authors' reading of the pre-2012 literature and their hypothesis that amphetamine-associated psychosis and primary psychosis are linked through individual vulnerability rather than being separate entities.
cannot_establish: How often amphetamine-associated psychosis occurs, how long it lasts, or how it differs from schizophrenia with any stated precision, because the evidence was not systematically identified or appraised, amphetamine and methamphetamine are pooled, and several statements rest on case series, guidelines, a book review, animal studies or schizophrenia literature; the proposed model is not tested.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). The cited evidence mixes experimental administration studies in volunteers, case reports in children treated for ADHD, community and treatment samples of people who use amphetamines, psychiatric admissions, Japanese clinical series of persistent and recurrent psychosis, family and genetic studies, and animal studies.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not reported: no search strategy, sources, dates or eligibility criteria are described.
sample.demographics: Not applicable.
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: How sources were chosen is unstated and cannot be audited. Two cited primary studies on symptoms and drug use in methamphetamine-positive psychiatric admissions (refs 41 and 51, Medhus et al., 2012) come from the authors' own group. Some clinical statements rest on non-primary sources: faster recovery is cited to a 1958 monograph, a 1959 book review, a 2006 management guideline and one 6-month follow-up study (refs 60–63).

exposure.measurement: Not applicable at review level. The authors note that reported psychosis rates depend on whether self-report or formal diagnostic instruments were used (Prevalence and clinical presentation, 1st paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Only as study conditions of the cited experiments: amphetamine was given in increasing doses until psychosis appeared, often after a total of 100–300 mg, and symptoms subsided within 6 days (refs 20–23). The authors state it is poorly understood whether psychosis at the end of a binge depends on the amount used, binge length, sleep deprivation or the vulnerability of the person using (Prevalence and clinical presentation, 1st–2nd paragraphs).
exposure.polysubstance: Discussed only qualitatively: people often end binges with alcohol, benzodiazepines, opioids or cannabis, and use of these drugs is listed among possible risk factors for psychosis (Prevalence and clinical presentation, 2nd paragraph; Risk factors, 2nd paragraph).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: Not applicable. Comparisons with schizophrenia are drawn from cited studies whose designs and sizes are not given.
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: The paper's central argument is that premorbid vulnerability (schizophrenia, schizotypal traits, family history, prodromal cognitive dysfunction, earlier amphetamine psychosis) decides who becomes psychotic, but it cites no study that measured vulnerability before amphetamine exposure.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable.

outcomes.instruments: Not applicable; no instruments are specified.
outcomes.validity_norms: Not discussed beyond the contrast between self-report and formal diagnostic instruments.
outcomes.operationalization: Psychosis, acute versus chronic psychosis and primary psychosis are used in their clinical senses without diagnostic criteria, instruments or thresholds. Amphetamine and methamphetamine are not separated.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: None. The quantitative statements are all second-hand: psychosis reported in 8–46% of people who use amphetamines regularly; experimental psychosis often after 100–300 mg in total with resolution within 6 days; relatives of people who use methamphetamine with a lifetime psychosis 5 times more likely to have schizophrenia; up to 25% of people first diagnosed with drug-induced psychosis developing a primary psychotic disorder after some years, more for methamphetamine; a 2008 review finding 18 papers on substance-induced psychosis, 7 on stimulants, one with a 1-year follow-up; one randomized trial (olanzapine vs haloperidol) in a 2009 Cochrane review.
analysis.covariates: Not applicable.
analysis.selective_reporting: Cannot be assessed because no search or selection is described. Evidence that cuts against the vulnerability model is acknowledged only in passing (not all volunteers in the early experiments became psychotic).
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: A narrative synthesis of mixed and mostly indirect evidence: psychosis is common among people who use amphetamines regularly (8–46% in cited studies, varying with population, sex, pattern of use and instrument); acute symptoms overlap with acute schizophrenia-spectrum psychosis; several vulnerability factors and shared susceptibility genes are reported; long-term course is poorly studied (one stimulant study with a 1-year follow-up in the review the authors cite).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says amphetamine-induced psychosis seems to recover faster and appears to resolve more completely than schizophrenic psychosis. The body supports faster recovery with a 1958 monograph, a 1959 book review, a 2006 management guideline and one 6-month follow-up (refs 60–63), says in the same paragraph that recovery may be incomplete and that Japanese series describe psychosis lasting years, and later cites up to 25% of drug-induced psychoses becoming primary psychotic disorders. The abstract's statement that shared genes probably lower the threshold for psychosis and worsen its course is cited to a review and a book chapter (refs 32, 58). The stress–vulnerability model and the clinical advice drawn from it (closer monitoring for chronic development, strongly discouraging further use, research on preventive treatment) are hypotheses not tested in the paper.

timeline.event: This narrative review proposes a stress–vulnerability model linking amphetamine-associated and primary psychosis

Callaghan et al. (American Journal of Psychiatry) California record-linkage cohort on methamphetamine use and later schizophrenia, cited here as newly published support for a cannabis-like association

Wearne & Cornish narrative review of direct comparisons: persistent methamphetamine psychosis resembled schizophrenia on positive symptoms and cognition, schizophrenia had more negative symptoms; cites this paper

replication.where_it_stands: The vulnerability–stress account remains a hypothesis. Later direct comparisons, as summarized by Wearne & Cornish (2018), found persistent methamphetamine psychosis hard to separate from schizophrenia on positive symptoms and cognition, which is consistent with, but does not demonstrate, shared vulnerability.

funding.funder: Not reported: the article has no funding statement.
funding.declared_conflicts: None of the authors declared conflicts of interest.
funding.affiliations_note: Norwegian Centre for Addiction Research (SERAF), University of Oslo; Department of Clinical Neuroscience, Karolinska Institutet; Department of Biological and Medical Psychology, University of Bergen. The first author's group produced two of the cited primary studies (refs 41 and 51). Received 29 February 2012, accepted 11 September 2012.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective cohort of people who use methamphetamine with vulnerability measured early (family history, schizotypy, prodromal symptoms, cognition, polygenic risk), repeated toxicology-verified exposure data and structured psychosis assessments, followed long enough to observe first episodes, recovery and transition to primary psychotic disorder; the model predicts that the exposure preceding a first episode is lower in people with higher measured vulnerability.

domains.note: The Background says only that the authors review some open questions and propose a model; there is no methods section, search strategy or selection criteria for the 108 references.

No study-level quality or risk-of-bias assessment; appraisal is limited to remarks on why prevalence estimates vary (populations, self-report vs diagnostic instruments) and on scarce evidence (one eligible trial in a Cochrane review, a cited dearth of validation research), while key figures such as the 25% conversion rate and the shared susceptibility genes are presented at face value.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own work
domains.note: Only 3 of 108 references (12, 41, 51; Mordal/Medhus/Bramness) are from the authors' group, and they support peripheral points (drug findings among acute admissions, symptoms of amphetamine-positive patients).

The stress-vulnerability model is explicitly labelled a hypothesis in its own section, but clinical implications (closer monitoring, discouraging further use, a rationale for preventive treatment) are drawn directly from the untested model, and some mechanistic and genetic statements are worded as established.

It reports evidence that cuts against a single-entity view (faster and more complete recovery from amphetamine psychosis, the claim that Japanese chronic amphetamine psychosis is a separate entity), counter-arguments in the parallel cannabis debate, and both sides of the antipsychotic-treatment question.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Editors' narrative-review checklist (METHODS §5.3), applied by an independent reader (AI reader 3 (appraisal re-reading, papers read in the app's browser), 2026-10-16) after the first reading had used AMSTAR 2, which does not fit a narrative review. Overall high risk of a misleading summary: no described search or selection. The review is cited for arguments and pointers to primary studies, not as primary evidence; a second reading of the checklist is still needed.

key_findings.finding: Psychosis is reported in 8–46% of people who use amphetamines regularly across the cited studies (refs 31–37); the authors attribute the spread to the population studied, sex, method and duration of use, and whether psychosis was assessed by self-report or formal diagnostic instruments.
key_findings.note: Amphetamine and methamphetamine are pooled; the range cannot be attributed to methamphetamine alone.

key_findings.finding: Cited experiments (refs 20–23) gave amphetamine in increasing doses until psychosis appeared, often after 100–300 mg in total; symptoms subsided within 6 days, antipsychotics blocked the effect, and not all participants became psychotic, some being withdrawn because of raised heart rate, blood pressure or temperature.
key_findings.note: Study conditions of 1968–1979 experiments, reported second-hand.

key_findings.finding: Only a weak relation between blood amphetamine level and psychotic symptoms has been reported in psychotic patients (refs 51, 52); the authors read this as pointing either to poor measurement of cumulative exposure or to individual vulnerability as the main risk factor.

Acute symptoms resemble acute schizophrenia-spectrum psychosis (persecutory delusions, auditory hallucinations, disorganized thinking, lack of insight); some studies report more grandiosity and visual hallucinations and less formal thought disorder in amphetamine psychosis, but the authors judge separation on acute symptoms probably very difficult.

Course: amphetamine psychosis is said to recover faster than schizophrenic psychosis (refs 60–63) and to resolve with abstinence, though possibly incompletely (ref 43); Japanese clinical series describe psychosis lasting up to several years and stress-triggered spontaneous relapses after remission, with family history of psychosis among the vulnerability factors.
key_findings.note: Refs 60–63 are a 1958 monograph, a 1959 book review, a 2006 guideline and a 6-month follow-up study.

key_findings.finding: Risk factors listed: previous amphetamine psychosis (sensitization), schizophrenia, schizotypal traits, amphetamine use disorder, other psychiatric disorders (attenuated psychosis, personality and affective disorders), early cognitive dysfunction, family history of mental disorder, and use of opioids, benzodiazepines, cannabis or alcohol.
key_findings.locator: Risk factors and acute vs. chronic psychosis, 1st–2nd paragraphs
key_findings.note: A list of reported associations without effect sizes.

key_findings.finding: Relatives of people who use methamphetamine with a lifetime amphetamine psychosis are reported as 5 times more likely to have schizophrenia (ref 85); people with schizophrenia and with amphetamine psychosis both show higher plasma norepinephrine than people who use methamphetamine without psychosis and people who do not use it (refs 65, 88).
key_findings.locator: Risk factors and acute vs. chronic psychosis, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: The sentence compares relatives of people who use methamphetamine with psychosis to people who use it without psychosis; the intended comparison group is presumably their relatives. Check ref 85.

key_findings.finding: Treatment: a 2009 Cochrane review found one eligible randomized trial, in which olanzapine and haloperidol were both effective for amphetamine psychosis; the authors raise, from indirect evidence, a concern that dopamine D2 blockade may increase anhedonia and relapse, and mention benzodiazepines as an alternative.
key_findings.locator: Risk factors and acute vs. chronic psychosis, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Up to 25% of people first diagnosed with drug-induced psychosis develop a primary psychotic disorder after some years (ref 100), with higher figures for methamphetamine-induced psychosis (ref 67); a 2008 review found 18 papers on the clinical characteristics or outcomes of substance-induced psychosis, 7 on stimulants and only 1 with a 1-year follow-up.
key_findings.locator: Risk factors and acute vs. chronic psychosis, 5th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Proposed model: amphetamine exposure acts as a stressor whose effect depends on vulnerability (less vulnerable people need more exposure to become psychotic), and repeated use may itself raise vulnerability through sensitization, so amphetamine-associated and primary psychosis are treated as linked phenomena rather than separate entities.
key_findings.locator: A model for the relationship…, 2nd paragraph; Figure 1 legend

key_findings.finding: Clinical implications proposed from the model, not tested: closer monitoring of people diagnosed with amphetamine-induced psychosis for chronic development, strong discouragement of further use, and research on preventive psychosocial, psychoeducational and pharmacological interventions.
key_findings.locator: A model for the relationship…, 3rd paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: Amphetamine and methamphetamine are pooled under one term throughout, while some cited findings concern methamphetamine only.
reporting_issues.consequence: No figure in this paper can be attributed to methamphetamine specifically without checking the cited source.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says amphetamine psychosis appears to resolve more completely than schizophrenic psychosis; the body says recovery may be incomplete, cites Japanese series of psychosis lasting years, and cites up to 25% later transition to primary psychosis.
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract overstates the completeness of recovery relative to the paper's own body text.

reporting_issues.issue: Several citations do not match their claims by title: faster recovery cites a monograph, a book review and a guideline (refs 60–62); treatability of amphetamine psychosis with antipsychotics cites a meta-analysis of antipsychotics in schizophrenia (ref 90); a sentence on Japanese research cites a US case report (ref 64); the community-availability correlation (refs 41–44) includes papers whose titles concern symptom comparison in admissions and sensitization (refs 41, 43); human sensitization to psychosis cites a cocaine study (ref 73).
reporting_issues.consequence: Each statement must be traced to an appropriate primary source before the encyclopedia uses it.

reporting_issues.issue: Figure 1 is an image; only its legend was read as text.
reporting_issues.consequence: The model diagram was appraised from the legend and the surrounding text.

editorial_corrections.reason: Language (METHODS §9): 10 replacements, no change of meaning, number or citation; list in data/verification/language-2026-10-16.json

METHODS §5.3 (0.2.2): narrative reviews are appraised with the editors' checklist, not AMSTAR 2. The checklist judgments are those of AI reader 3 (appraisal re-reading, papers read in the app's browser), who read the source; the editor only transferred them.

design_detail: Narrative clinical review. PubMed and national survey databases were searched in April 2014 and again in September 2014 with listed terms (methamphetamine, or amphetamine where appropriate; psychosis; and domain terms such as epidemiology, treatment, genetics, diagnosis, risk factors), and US and international diagnostic and clinical guidelines were reviewed (Introduction, 3rd paragraph). No eligibility criteria, record counts, selection process or quality appraisal are reported. Sections cover DSM-5 and ICD-10 criteria, clinical correlates, risk factors, duration, recurrence, differential diagnosis (with the PRISM interview as a worked example) and treatment. No tables or figures; a Key points box. Read as the NIH author manuscript deposited in PMC.
can_establish: How two UCLA clinical researchers summarized, in 2014, the diagnostic criteria, risk factors, course and management of methamphetamine-associated psychosis, and which primary studies their statements rest on.
cannot_establish: Frequency, duration or recurrence rates with known precision or representativeness, because every figure is second-hand from studies chosen without stated criteria or appraisal (several key numbers trace to a single study, a general comorbidity review, or two studies from the same research group); nor the effectiveness of any treatment for psychosis outcomes, which rests on case reports, two small trials and evidence from schizophrenia.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). The cited evidence spans US and UN drug-use surveys, 1958–1980 experimental and observational reports of amphetamine psychosis, Japanese inpatient series, Taiwanese family and comorbidity studies, an Australian study of recreational use, a Thai cohort of people first hospitalized with methamphetamine psychosis, US treatment cohorts (the authors' Methamphetamine Treatment Project), case reports, and two randomized trials.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not reported beyond sources, dates and search terms (Introduction, 3rd paragraph); the authors state they favoured the most recent reports and reviews.
sample.demographics: Not applicable.
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: Selection of sources is unstated and cannot be audited. Most of the frequency, duration and recurrence figures come from hospital or treatment samples. Three cited studies are the authors' own Methamphetamine Treatment Project papers (refs 10, 11, 96) and one is a book chapter co-written by the second author (ref 87).

exposure.measurement: Not applicable at review level. The review stresses that diagnosis depends on establishing the timing of use relative to symptoms (self-report timeline, collateral informants, records, urine toxicology) and notes that a urine screen does not establish the cause of a psychosis (Section 4).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not synthesized. Cited study conditions and associations: in early laboratory studies psychosis appeared 1–5 days after repeated amphetamine administration began in volunteers, and within 36 hours in people with a history of injecting amphetamine (refs 28, 29); Japanese inpatient series linked a persistent subtype lasting over 1 month with 5 or more years of use (refs 36, 37); time from first use to psychosis was 1.7 years in people who smoked versus 4.4 years in people who injected (ref 49) (Section 3; 3.1).
exposure.polysubstance: Polydrug use is listed as a risk factor for psychosis (ref 41), and other substances, including heavy alcohol use, as triggers of recurrence (3.3); not otherwise handled.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: Not applicable. Comparisons with schizophrenia are clinical and genetic statements drawn from cited work, without study sizes.
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: The review reports that family and genetic vulnerability predicts methamphetamine psychosis, but cites no study with a measurement taken before methamphetamine use began.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable.

outcomes.instruments: Not applicable at review level. Diagnostic instruments discussed: PRISM, Diagnostic Interview Schedule, CIDI and SCID (Section 4).
outcomes.validity_norms: PRISM is described as having excellent reliability for psychotic disorder diagnoses in people with alcohol or drug use disorders (ref 67); all the structured interviews are noted to depend on self-report (Section 4).
outcomes.operationalization: Per the review's account of DSM-5 and ICD-10: transient psychotic symptoms consistent with intoxication or withdrawal are not a psychotic disorder; a methamphetamine-induced psychotic disorder requires prominent hallucinations or delusions beyond the expected effects of intoxication or withdrawal; persistence for at least 1 month after the end of intoxication or acute withdrawal, onset before substance use, or non-substance-related episodes point to a primary psychotic disorder (Section 2). PRISM defines heavy use as 4 or more use episodes per week and treats psychosis persisting more than 4 weeks after cessation as primary (Section 4).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: None computed by the review. Second-hand figures: up to 40% of people who use methamphetamine with transient psychotic symptoms; 26–46% of people with methamphetamine dependence with methamphetamine psychosis; 3 times the odds of psychotic symptoms with dependence than with non-dependent use; 5 times the odds during use (McKetin et al., 2013); 16% and 17% still psychotic after 1 and 3 months of abstinence; nearly 40% diagnosed with schizophrenia within 6 years in a Thai cohort; nearly 50% of Japanese admissions with a previous episode; one 58-person randomized trial and one later randomized trial of antipsychotics. No intervals are given for any figure.
analysis.covariates: Not applicable.
analysis.selective_reporting: Cannot be assessed: no eligibility criteria or list of considered studies.
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: A clinically oriented narrative summary whose numbers are all second-hand: transient symptoms in up to 40% of people who use methamphetamine (from a 2006 general comorbidity review); recovery within about a week in early studies; a minority (16–17% in two Taiwanese studies from one group) still psychotic 1–3 months into abstinence; nearly 40% diagnosed with schizophrenia within 6 years in one Thai cohort of hospitalized patients; frequent recurrence in Japanese inpatient series; two small randomized trials of antipsychotics.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract presents up to approximately 40% of people who use methamphetamine affected as a recent estimate; the body attributes the figure to a 2006 review of comorbidity in general (ref 17) and specifies that it refers to transient symptoms that are not a disorder (Section 2). The abstract calls psychosocial treatment of methamphetamine dependence the optimal first-line approach to reducing psychosis; the body supports this with the association between use and symptoms and with trials that reduced methamphetamine use, but cites no trial with psychosis as its outcome (2.1; 5.2). The statement that remission within 1 week of abstinence has been reported across a number of studies, so most cases may resolve without medication, carries no citation (5.1). The Key points say methamphetamine greatly increases the risk of transient and recurrent psychosis (a causal formulation from observational data) and that recommendations will involve neuroleptics, whereas the body says many cases may resolve without medication and lists risks of antipsychotics.

timeline.event: Bramness et al. narrative review proposing a stress–vulnerability model; cited here (ref 19) as the integrated continuum theory and for the anhedonia concern about D2 blockade
McKetin et al. prospective cohort: five-fold odds of psychotic symptoms during methamphetamine use with a dose-response relation, cited here as the basis for treating methamphetamine use first
Verachai et al. randomized trial of haloperidol versus quetiapine in methamphetamine-induced psychosis, cited here: both efficacious and tolerated
This narrative review
Wearne & Cornish narrative review of direct methamphetamine-psychosis versus schizophrenia comparisons; cites this paper among reviews of clinical profiles and recovery

replication.where_it_stands: The broad picture (common transient symptoms, a persistent minority, recurrence with renewed use, overlap with schizophrenia) is repeated across the narrative reviews read here, but they draw on overlapping and often old primary sources; the frequency and duration figures need primary-study cards before use.

funding.funder: The footnotes state that no sources of funding were used to prepare the manuscript. The PMC copy is an NIH author manuscript (NIHMSID NIHMS640645).
funding.declared_conflicts: Neither author has any conflict of interest (Footnotes, Disclosures).
funding.affiliations_note: UCLA Integrated Substance Abuse Programs, David Geffen School of Medicine. The authors cite their own Methamphetamine Treatment Project studies for treatment engagement of people with psychosis and for depression and relapse (refs 10, 11, 96).

what_would_settle_it: For frequency and duration: a prospective cohort of people who use methamphetamine recruited outside treatment, with toxicology-verified use and a temporally sensitive structured interview (such as PRISM) repeated at fixed intervals after abstinence, reporting the proportions whose symptoms resolve within 1 week, 1 month and 6 months. For management: randomized trials in methamphetamine-associated psychosis comparing antipsychotics with benzodiazepines or placebo, and psychosocial treatment with usual care, with psychosis recurrence as the primary outcome.

domains.note: A search of PubMed and national survey databases with dates (April and September 2014) and terms is reported (Introduction, last paragraph), but no eligibility criteria, record counts or selection process; the only stated principle is to incorporate the most recent reports and reviews.

The cited studies are not appraised: frequency, duration and recurrence figures are given without design or quality comments (Sections 2–3.3), and the only quality remark on a specific study is that one trial was small (N=58; 5.1). Persistence figures of 16% and 17% from two smaller studies are called 'very similar' to the nearly 40% Thai figure (3.2).

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: 4 of 99 references are the authors' own (Methamphetamine Treatment Project papers, refs 10, 11 and 96; a chapter co-written by the second author, ref 87); ref 10 is the only source given for engagement and reduced use with Matrix Model treatment among people with psychosis (2.1).

The abstract calls psychosocial treatment of methamphetamine dependence the optimal first-line approach to reducing psychosis, while the body presents this as an argument ('it has been argued', 2.1) and cites no trial with psychosis as the outcome (5.2). The Key points say recommendations 'will involve' neuroleptics regardless of etiology, against the body's statements that evidence is insufficient for guidelines and that most cases may resolve without medication (5.1).

domains.domain: Balance of evidence on the course and treatment of methamphetamine psychosis
domains.note: Neither side is under-represented: competing explanations for persistent psychosis (a prolonged methamphetamine psychosis, unmasked schizophrenia, a continuum; 3.2) and both the efficacy and the risks of antipsychotics (5.1) are presented.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: High, because the selection of sources is unstated, the cited studies are not appraised, and the abstract and Key points state treatment conclusions that the body presents as argued or unproven. It may be cited for its account of the DSM-5 and ICD-10 criteria and of the diagnostic approach (timeline of use, collateral information, urine toxicology, PRISM), and as a pointer to primary studies. Its frequency, duration and recurrence figures and its treatment recommendations may not be cited without the primary sources.

key_findings.finding: Diagnostic frame described: transient psychotic symptoms consistent with methamphetamine intoxication or withdrawal are not a psychotic disorder; a methamphetamine-induced psychotic disorder needs hallucinations or delusions beyond expected effects; symptoms persisting at least 1 month after intoxication or acute withdrawal ends point to a primary psychotic disorder under DSM-5, with ICD-10 described as similar.
key_findings.locator: 2. Clinical Features of Psychosis in Methamphetamine Users, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Frequency figures cited: transient psychotic symptoms in up to 40% of people who use methamphetamine (ref 17); 26–46% of people with methamphetamine dependence have methamphetamine psychosis (ref 45); people meeting dependence criteria have 3 times the odds of psychotic symptoms of people who use methamphetamine without dependence after controlling for history of schizophrenia and other psychotic disorders (ref 41).
key_findings.locator: Section 2, 1st paragraph; 3.1 Psychiatric and Genetic Risk Factors, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Ref 17 is a 2006 review of substance use and psychiatric comorbidity in general; ref 45, called a review of recent studies, is by its title a study of people with methamphetamine dependence in Malaysia. Check both before use.

key_findings.finding: Methamphetamine use was associated with a five-fold increase in the odds of psychotic symptoms, with a dose-response relation (McKetin et al., 2013, ref 25).
key_findings.locator: 2.1 Relevance of discerning clinical features…, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: In early experimental studies psychosis appeared 1–5 days after repeated intravenous d-amphetamine began in healthy volunteers (ref 28) and within 36 hours of repeated oral amphetamine in people with a history of injecting amphetamine (ref 29); across later replications some but not all participants became psychotic, the amount that triggered psychosis varied, and paranoia with ideas of reference, sometimes progressing to delusions, was the most frequent symptom (refs 30–32).
key_findings.locator: 3. Clinical Correlates of Methamphetamine Psychosis, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Study conditions of experiments published 1970–1974, reported second-hand.

key_findings.finding: In Japanese studies of more than 200 inpatients, a persistent subtype lasting over 1 month was associated with 5 or more years of methamphetamine use (refs 36, 37).

Risk factors listed: schizophrenia, schizoaffective disorder and schizotypal personality; methamphetamine dependence; polydrug use; affective disorders and antisocial personality disorder; family psychiatric history; sleep deprivation. Time from first use to psychosis was 1.7 years in people who smoked methamphetamine versus 4.4 years in people who injected it (ref 49), and smoking did not appear protective relative to injecting.
key_findings.locator: 3.1 Psychiatric and Genetic Risk Factors, 1st–2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: First-degree relatives of people with methamphetamine psychosis are reported as more than 5 times more likely to have schizophrenia (ref 47), and familial loading for schizophrenia as predicting onset and duration of methamphetamine psychosis; seven candidate genes are said to be associated with methamphetamine psychosis, overlapping with schizophrenia risk markers (ref 44).
key_findings.note: The comparison is worded as relatives versus people who use methamphetamine without psychosis; presumably their relatives were meant. Check ref 47.

key_findings.finding: Duration: in the earliest observational and experimental studies recovery came on average within a week (refs 28, 30, 52, 53); two smaller studies reported that 16% and 17% still had psychosis after 1 and 3 months of abstinence respectively (refs 12, 47), the review giving the denominator only as people who use methamphetamine (presumably those with psychosis), and in both studies those whose psychosis persisted had no earlier psychotic episodes and no family history of schizophrenia; in more than 1,000 people in Thailand with at least one methamphetamine-induced psychotic episode, nearly 40% had a schizophrenia diagnosis within 6 years of the first episode (ref 57).
key_findings.note: Refs 12 and 47 share their first five authors and may draw on the same sample; Arunogiri et al. (2018) combine Chen et al. (2003, 2005, 2007) and Lin et al. (2004) as one study population of 445 (their Table 1, study 6). Ref 47 is also cited in 3.1 for familial loading predicting the duration of psychosis. Wearne & Cornish (2018) report the Thai figure as 38.8% at 5 years; check ref 57.

key_findings.finding: Recurrence: in Japan's second methamphetamine epidemic nearly 50% of people admitted with methamphetamine psychosis had had it before, some readmitted more than 10 times (ref 59); reported triggers are renewed use, even of small amounts after long abstinence, other substances including heavy alcohol use, sleep deprivation and psychosocial stress; recurrent episodes resemble earlier ones and can begin within less than a week of renewed use, a propensity that can last years.

Differential diagnosis rests on the timing of use relative to symptoms, collateral informants, records and urine toxicology; a positive urine screen does not establish that methamphetamine caused the psychosis; PRISM classifies psychosis as substance-induced when it occurs only during heavy use (4 or more episodes a week) or withdrawal, and as primary when it persists more than 4 weeks after use stops.

Treatment evidence: no large randomized trials; the 2009 Cochrane review included one trial (N=58) in which olanzapine and haloperidol were both efficacious, olanzapine with better tolerability and fewer extrapyramidal symptoms (ref 79); a later randomized trial found haloperidol and quetiapine both efficacious and tolerated (ref 80); otherwise case reports. Concerns raised: D2 blockade and anhedonia possibly raising relapse risk, and a preclinical haloperidol–methamphetamine interaction; benzodiazepines may be used for agitation.
key_findings.locator: 5.1 Treatment for acute methamphetamine psychosis, 1st and 3rd paragraphs
key_findings.note: Both trials compared two antipsychotics with each other (their titles describe head-to-head comparisons) and no placebo or no-medication arm is described, while the same section reports remission within about a week of abstinence; the trials show similar improvement on either drug, not efficacy against the natural course. By title, the Cochrane review (ref 78) and the 58-participant trial (ref 79) concern amphetamine psychosis; only the later trial (ref 80) is titled as methamphetamine-induced psychosis.

key_findings.finding: The authors state that remission within 1 week of abstinence has been reported across a number of studies, so that for a large majority symptoms may resolve without medication.
key_findings.note: No citation is attached to this sentence; Section 3.2 cites refs 28, 30, 52 and 53 (1958–1980 sources) for recovery within about a week.

key_findings.finding: Little is known about antipsychotic safety and efficacy for children and adolescents with methamphetamine-induced psychosis, who are said to form a sizable subgroup of first-episode presentations (ref 88).
key_findings.note: Ref 88 is, by title, a review of atypical antipsychotics in aggressive children and adolescents, not a study of methamphetamine psychosis.

key_findings.finding: Psychosocial treatment: the Matrix Model and contingency management reduce methamphetamine use, and people with psychosis engaged in and reduced use with Matrix treatment comparably to those without (ref 10); CBT has not been formally studied for methamphetamine-induced psychotic disorder.

reporting_issues.issue: Section 3.2 says DSM-5 defines substance-induced psychosis as psychosis preceding the onset of substance use or persisting less than one month after withdrawal or intoxication; Section 2 lists onset before substance use as a sign of a primary psychotic disorder.
reporting_issues.consequence: The 3.2 sentence is internally contradictory; the Section 2 account is the coherent one, but the DSM-5 text itself should be the source for any diagnostic statement.

reporting_issues.issue: The 16% and 17% persistence figures (refs 12, 47) are introduced as 'very similar rates' right after the nearly 40% Thai figure, which reads as a comparison with it (they are not similar), although the phrase may mean only that the two small studies resemble each other; the two studies share their first five authors and may not be independent; and ref 47 is cited both for familial loading predicting duration (3.1) and for persistent cases having no family history of schizophrenia (3.2).
reporting_issues.consequence: The persistence and family-history statements should be taken from the primary papers.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract's headline of up to approximately 40% of people who use methamphetamine affected is described as recent but is cited to a 2006 general comorbidity review (ref 17); the body specifies that it refers to transient symptoms.
reporting_issues.consequence: The figure should not be used as a methamphetamine prevalence estimate without the primary source.

reporting_issues.issue: Several citations do not match their claims by title: a meta-analysis of antipsychotics in schizophrenia (ref 76) is listed among case studies of antipsychotics for methamphetamine psychosis; a review of antipsychotics in aggressive youth (ref 88) supports the share of young people among first-episode methamphetamine psychosis; a case report of mania after sleep deprivation (ref 63) supports sleep deprivation as a trigger of recurrence.
reporting_issues.consequence: These statements need primary sources before use.

reporting_issues.issue: Cross-paper: the Thai cohort (ref 57) is reported here as nearly 40% within 6 years and by Wearne & Cornish (2018) as 38.8% at 5 years; the 1.7-year latency from first use to psychosis (ref 49) is reported here for people who smoked (4.4 years for injecting) but by Wearne & Cornish as an overall average.
reporting_issues.consequence: Both figures must be checked in Kittirattanapaiboon et al. (2010) and Matsumoto et al. (2002).

reporting_issues.issue: Read from the PMC author manuscript, which may differ from the published version in CNS Drugs (2014;28:1115–1126); printed pagination is not shown.
reporting_issues.consequence: Anchors are to sections of the author manuscript.

Finding reworded; numbers and references unchanged. The 'very similar' wording is handled in reporting issue 1.
