design_detail: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover human laboratory study in an outpatient research unit (New York State Psychiatric Institute). Thirteen men who used methamphetamine recreationally completed five 2-day blocks (10 sessions). Day 1 of each block was a sample session: one intranasal amphetamine condition (placebo, or methamphetamine or d-amphetamine at 12 or 50 mg/70 kg, as study conditions) plus a monetary reinforcer (US$5 for 7 participants, US$20 for 6). Day 2 was a choice session in which participants worked on a progressive response schedule for portions of the sampled drug or the sampled money. Plasma amphetamine levels, cardiovascular measures, visual-analogue mood ratings, a drug-effect questionnaire and two psychomotor tasks were measured before and repeatedly after dosing, and again 24 h later as residual effects.
can_establish: Within these 13 experienced men, whether the two amphetamines, at the two tested dose levels and by the intranasal route, differed in how often each was chosen over money and in acute mood, cardiovascular and psychomotor measures; and how an alternative monetary reinforcer of $5 versus $20 changed drug choice.
cannot_establish: Whether methamphetamine and d-amphetamine differ in abuse potential outside this setting (choice was between a drug portion and money during a 4-hour working day, in people with methamphetamine but not necessarily d-amphetamine experience); whether the drugs differ at other dose levels, by other routes, in women, or in people without amphetamine experience; or whether any observed drug difference reflects pharmacology rather than familiarity with methamphetamine's effects. The $5-versus-$20 contrast is between participants (7 vs 6), not within.

sample.recruitment: Advertisement and word of mouth: word-of-mouth referral and newspaper and online advertisements in New York City; outpatient; paid $60 per day and debriefed about conditions at discharge (Methods › Participants).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Men who currently used methamphetamine; passed medical examination and psychiatric interview; within normal weight range by the 1983 Metropolitan Life tables; not seeking treatment; no other Axis I disorder. Three met criteria for current methamphetamine dependence; the diagnostic system is not named in the text. No women were enrolled and no reason is given. Other exclusion criteria are not listed.
sample.demographics: 13 men (1 Asian, 6 Black, 2 Hispanic, 4 White); mean age 37.4 years (SD 7.3); education 14.8 years (SD 2.0); BMI 24.9 (SD 2.7) (Methods › Participants).
sample.attrition: Not reported: the paper describes 13 completers and says nothing about enrolment, withdrawal or missing sessions.
sample.selection_effects: Advertisement-recruited, medically and psychiatrically screened men who used methamphetamine about 9 days a month, mostly without dependence (3 of 13), not seeking treatment, and already familiar with methamphetamine's effects but with no reported d-amphetamine experience. This asymmetry of experience sits directly on the study's comparison. Men only, so no data on women. Outpatient design means behaviour outside sessions was not controlled.

exposure.measurement: Experimental administration of methamphetamine HCl (supplied by NIDA) or d-amphetamine sulfate (Cambrex), prepared by the institute pharmacy with lactose as placebo and filler, double-blind; plasma amphetamine levels measured from an intravenous line at baseline and 15, 60, 90, 120, 180 and 240 min. Participants' own use was self-reported. Before each session participants passed a field sobriety test and gave a urine sample required to be negative for several drug metabolites, with amphetamines and THC excluded from that requirement (Methods › Procedure).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions: single intranasal doses of 0, 12 or 50 mg/70 kg of methamphetamine or of d-amphetamine on day 1 of each block, with blocks at least 48 h apart and condition order counterbalanced across participants; on day 2 participants could earn up to the same total amount in ten 10% portions. Participants' own reported use: methamphetamine on 9.4 (SD 4.7) days per month. Comparison with real-world patterns: the authors note that choice in this study occurred in the morning before a 4-hour period of computerized tasks, unlike recreational use, and that use outside the laboratory may occur in the evening in social settings (Discussion, 2nd paragraph).
exposure.polysubstance: Current use reported by participants: alcohol 7 of 13 (4 to 10 drinks a week), cocaine 7 of 13 (1 to 8 days a month), cannabis 3 of 13 (4 to 12 days a month), tobacco 4 of 13 (3 to 20 cigarettes a day). Handled only by pre-session sobriety testing and urine screens that did not include amphetamines or THC; this was an outpatient study, and the authors name undetected outside drug use as a limitation for the 24-hour residual findings (Discussion, 4th paragraph).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Same-day abstinence only, checked by field sobriety test and a urine screen that excluded amphetamines and THC from the negativity requirement. No washout beyond the 48 h between blocks; the 24-hour measures are explicitly residual-effect measures taken the morning after dosing.

comparison.controls: Two within-participant comparators: placebo, and the other amphetamine at the matched dose level. Each participant experienced all five conditions.
comparison.matching: Within-participant for drug and dose; condition order counterbalanced (sequences not reported). The monetary reinforcer magnitude ($5 vs $20) was a between-participant factor with 7 and 6 participants, not matched or randomized by any reported procedure, and the two groups are compared only on drug choice (the paper states they did not differ on physiological, subjective or performance measures, without giving those tests).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to within-person contrasts. The relevant unmeasured variables are prior d-amphetamine experience (not reported for any participant), expectancy (all had received the 50 mg/70 kg methamphetamine condition openly before the study), and tolerance to methamphetamine but not to d-amphetamine.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Same participants across conditions; see polysubstance.

outcomes.instruments: Self-administration: computerized 50-min choice task with 10 trials, response requirements rising from 50 to 2800 finger presses per trial (11,550 responses to obtain the full reinforcer); outcome is the number of drug options chosen out of 10. Plasma amphetamine. Heart rate, systolic and diastolic pressure at baseline and 5, 15, 30, 60, 90, 120, 180, 240 min. Computerized 100-mm visual-analogue mood scales at the same times, summed across the session (maximum 700). Drug-effect questionnaire at 45 min (good effects, bad effects, strength, desire to take the drug again on 0 to 4; liking on -4 to +4). Psychomotor battery: digit-symbol substitution task and divided attention task. Residual measures: the same subjective, cardiovascular and performance measures at baseline on the choice day, about 24 h after dosing (Methods › Procedure; Subjective-Effects and Psychomotor Battery).
outcomes.validity_norms: Standard human-laboratory abuse-liability measures; within-person contrasts, so norms are not required. Participants were trained on the tasks in two 3 to 4 h sessions before the study.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Abuse potential' was operationalized as the number of drug options chosen over money on the progressive-response choice task, plus positive subjective ratings. 'Equivalence' of the two drugs was inferred from non-significant between-drug comparisons, not from an equivalence test or a prespecified margin.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None: all tests at p<0.05 with Huynh-Feldt correction for sphericity where appropriate. The count is a lower bound: the VAS item list is given by example only, Table 2 shows 13 items, and the drug-effect questionnaire, cardiovascular, plasma, choice and two performance tasks add further measures, each tested acutely and again at 24 h.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Double-blind administration; blinding integrity not assessed, and participants were experienced with methamphetamine only. Outcomes are self-rated, automated or computerized.

analysis.effect_sizes: The paper reports p values, summed-rating means with SEM (Table 2) and figures; no F statistics for most analyses, no effect sizes and no confidence intervals. Choice data analysed by single-factor repeated-measures ANOVA separately in the $5 (n=7) and $20 (n=6) groups; sample-session cardiovascular, plasma and performance data by two-factor (condition x time) ANOVA; subjective ratings summed across the session and analysed by single-factor ANOVA; residual measures by single-factor ANOVA. Editors' calculation from Table 2 (SD = SEM x square root of 13, difference divided by the average of the two SDs, ignoring the within-person correlation, so approximate): summed 'high' and 'good drug effect' are not in Table 2; for drug-effect-questionnaire 'good drug effect' (0 to 4), 50 mg/70 kg methamphetamine vs placebo d about 2.3 and vs the matched d-amphetamine condition about 0.6; for summed 'stimulated', methamphetamine vs placebo about 1.1 and vs matched d-amphetamine about 0.5. These are indicative only. Key quantitative statements the paper does give: overall drug choice 41% under $5 versus 17% under $20; roughly 47 to 50% drug choice for either amphetamine at the larger dose under $5; 24-hour heart rate 76.8 (SEM 2.3) bpm after placebo versus 86.1 (1.9) after 12 mg/70 kg methamphetamine, 87.8 (2.3) after 50 mg/70 kg methamphetamine and 90.5 (3.4) after 50 mg/70 kg d-amphetamine.
analysis.covariates: None. No adjustment for period or for the between-group difference in monetary reinforcer in the pooled analyses.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or protocol is mentioned. The paper states two directional hypotheses in the Introduction (equal self-administration under $5, attenuation under $20; dose-dependent increases in positive ratings, cardiovascular values and performance).
analysis.selective_reporting: Table 2 lists only items with statistically significant effects, so the full VAS item set and its null results are unavailable; 'bad effects' from the drug-effect questionnaire is described in Methods but not reported anywhere. Figures 1 to 4 carry the plasma, cardiovascular, choice and performance values, which cannot be read as numbers. The statement that the $5 and $20 groups did not differ on any physiological, subjective or performance measure is given without the tests. Subjective ratings were analysed as session sums, which is not the same analysis used in the companion single-drug study.
analysis.power: Not reported. n=13 overall and 7 and 6 for the two choice analyses. The central claim (no difference between the drugs in self-administration) rests on non-significant tests in groups of 7 and 6, which cannot exclude a substantial difference; no equivalence margin was set.

interpretation_gap.results_show: With $5 as the alternative, both amphetamines at 50 mg/70 kg were chosen more often than placebo (n=7); with $20 as the alternative, money was chosen almost always and no dose effect appeared (n=6); overall 41% of choices were for drug under $5 versus 17% under $20. No significant difference between methamphetamine and d-amphetamine in number of drug choices. Both drugs raised plasma levels dose-dependently (peak 3 to 4 h) and raised heart rate and blood pressure at 50 mg/70 kg (peak within 15 min), with heart rate higher under methamphetamine. Summed ratings of alert, energetic, friendly, social, stimulated, talkative and nose burning rose and sleepy and tired fell at the larger doses of both drugs; at the matched larger dose, methamphetamine exceeded d-amphetamine on 'high', 'stimulated', heart pounding, drug-effect-questionnaire good drug effect and drug strength. At 24 h, heart rate remained above placebo after both 50 mg/70 kg conditions and after 12 mg/70 kg methamphetamine, diastolic pressure after 50 mg/70 kg methamphetamine, and ratings of 'content' were lower after 50 mg/70 kg methamphetamine than after every other condition. Both drugs raised maximum tracking speed on the divided attention task; only the smaller doses shortened hit latency; no digit-symbol effects.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that the drugs were self-administered equally, "indicating their equivalence for abuse potential", and the discussion states the data do not support the view that methamphetamine is a more potent reinforcer in humans. Gaps: (1) equivalence is inferred from non-significant tests in 7 and 6 participants with no equivalence margin, which is absence of evidence rather than evidence of equivalence; (2) participants were experienced with methamphetamine and no d-amphetamine experience is reported, an asymmetry the authors themselves raise for the subjective findings but not for the choice findings; (3) the abstract reports no significant differences on most measures while the same results show methamphetamine higher on several mood items, heart rate, drug strength and 24-hour 'content'; (4) the conclusion that methamphetamine use is likely influenced by non-pharmacological factors is an inference about population patterns from a 13-man laboratory choice task; (5) the 41% versus 17% contrast is between two small non-randomized groups.

timeline.event: Martin et al.: oral methamphetamine and d-amphetamine produced overlapping physiological and subjective effects (cited in this paper's Introduction).
Lamb and Henningfield: humans trained to discriminate d-amphetamine generalized to methamphetamine (cited in Introduction).
Sevak et al.: methamphetamine, d-amphetamine and methylphenidate produced similar discriminative-stimulus and subject-rated effects in people trained on methamphetamine (cited in Introduction).
This study: first direct comparison of the two amphetamines by a route associated with non-medical use, and the first with a self-administration endpoint.

replication.where_it_stands: The only direct human self-administration comparison of the two amphetamines found in this reading, with 13 men and 6 to 7 per choice group. Its finding of no difference in choice agrees in direction with animal self-administration work cited by the authors (Balster and Schuster 1973; Yokel and Pickens 1973) and with oral human comparisons, but the sample cannot exclude a moderate difference, and the single-drug intranasal dose-response data come from the same laboratory (Hart et al., 2008).

funding.funder: National Institute on Drug Abuse grant DA-19559 to Dr Hart (Acknowledgements). Study methamphetamine supplied by NIDA; d-amphetamine supplied by Cambrex (Methods › Drug).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare that apart from income from their primary employer they received no financial support or compensation from any individual or corporate entity in the past 3 years for research or professional service, hold no personal financial holdings that could be perceived as a conflict, and had no constraints on publishing the data (Declaration of interest).
funding.affiliations_note: Authors at Columbia University and the New York State Psychiatric Institute (Division on Substance Abuse), with one author at Wayne State University. Cambrex supplied d-amphetamine as a material donation only. Recorded as context, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A larger crossover self-administration study with a within-participant manipulation of the alternative reinforcer, a prespecified equivalence margin, participants with comparable prior experience of both amphetamines (or a sample with experience of neither), both sexes, and a choice context closer to real-world settings, would show whether the two amphetamines are genuinely equal in reinforcing efficacy rather than only not distinguishable in a small sample.

domains.note: Described as randomized and counterbalanced, but the sequence-generation and concealment methods are not described, and the $5 versus $20 assignment (7 vs 6 participants) is not stated to be randomized.

Blocks were separated by at least 48 h, yet the paper itself shows effects persisting at 24 h (heart rate, diastolic pressure, 'content'), so carryover into the next block cannot be excluded; period was not modelled; the example design in Table 1 shows both methamphetamine conditions in week 1 and both d-amphetamine conditions in week 2, with placebo last.

Double-blind in form, but all participants had received the 50 mg/70 kg methamphetamine condition openly before the study, all were experienced with methamphetamine and none is reported to have used d-amphetamine; blinding integrity was not assessed. Outpatient setting with no control of behaviour between sessions.
Only 13 completers are described; enrolment, withdrawals and missing sessions are not reported.

Choice and performance are computerized and cardiovascular measures automated (low concern), but the main subjective outcomes are self-ratings by participants who may have recognized their familiar drug.

No protocol or registration; only significant VAS items tabulated; 'bad effects' collected but never reported; between-group equivalence of the $5 and $20 groups asserted without tests; subjective data analysed as session sums without a stated plan.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The within-person dose-response findings (both drugs raised plasma levels, cardiovascular measures and positive ratings) are robust to these concerns. The headline comparative conclusion is not: it rests on non-significant differences in 6 to 7 participants per choice group, in people experienced with one of the two drugs but not reported as experienced with the other, without an equivalence margin, with possible carryover given the documented 24-hour residual effects, and with selective tabulation of outcomes.

key_findings.finding: Participants: 13 men, mean age 37.4 (SD 7.3), education 14.8 years (SD 2.0), using methamphetamine 9.4 (SD 4.7) days a month; 3 met criteria for current methamphetamine dependence; none sought treatment; no other Axis I disorder. No women enrolled; no prior d-amphetamine use is reported.

Design: 5 two-day blocks at least 48 h apart; day 1 sample session with one of 5 conditions (placebo; methamphetamine or d-amphetamine at 12 or 50 mg/70 kg as study conditions) plus $5 (7 participants) or $20 (6 participants); day 2 choice session with 10 trials for 10% portions of drug or money, response requirement rising from 50 to 2800 presses (11,550 for the full reinforcer).
key_findings.locator: Methods and Materials › Design; Procedure › Choice (self-administration) sessions; Table 1

key_findings.finding: Before the study each participant received the 50 mg/70 kg methamphetamine condition openly in a familiarization session; no untoward effects were noted.

Self-administration with $5 as the alternative (n=7): both drugs at 50 mg/70 kg were chosen more often than placebo (p<0.05), with no significant difference between methamphetamine and d-amphetamine; the discussion gives roughly 47 to 50% drug choice for either drug at that dose level. With $20 as the alternative (n=6), money was chosen almost always and no dose effect was significant. Overall drug choices: 41% under $5 versus 17% under $20.
key_findings.locator: Results › Methamphetamine and d-Amphetamine Choice; Figure 2; Abstract › Findings; Discussion, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: The 41% vs 17% comparison is between two small non-randomized groups and no test is reported for it. Choice counts appear only in Figure 2 (image).

key_findings.finding: Plasma concentrations of both drugs rose dose-dependently, with peaks 3 to 4 h after dosing; every active condition exceeded placebo and each 50 mg/70 kg condition exceeded the matched 12 mg/70 kg condition (p<0.0001). Values appear only in Figure 1.
key_findings.locator: Results › Plasma Methamphetamine and d-Amphetamine Levels; Figure 1

key_findings.finding: Both 50 mg/70 kg conditions raised heart rate and systolic and diastolic pressure above placebo and above the 12 mg/70 kg conditions (p<0.01), with peaks within 15 min; methamphetamine raised heart rate more than d-amphetamine (p<0.05). Magnitudes appear only in Figure 1.
key_findings.locator: Results › Cardiovascular Effects › Acute Effects; Figure 1

key_findings.finding: Residual cardiovascular effects at about 24 h: heart rate (mean, SEM) 76.8 (2.3) bpm after placebo versus 86.1 (1.9) after 12 mg/70 kg methamphetamine, 87.8 (2.3) after 50 mg/70 kg methamphetamine and 90.5 (3.4) after 50 mg/70 kg d-amphetamine (p<0.01); diastolic pressure 74.4 (2.2) versus 78.4 (2.4) mmHg after 50 mg/70 kg methamphetamine (p<0.05).
key_findings.note: Outpatient design: the authors note undetected drug use between sessions could contribute. The 12 mg/70 kg d-amphetamine condition is absent from the list of significant comparisons.

key_findings.finding: Summed visual-analogue ratings (maximum 700), placebo / 12 mg AMPH / 12 mg MA / 50 mg AMPH / 50 mg MA: energetic 271 / 319 / 361 / 414 / 468; stimulated 111 / 160 / 172 / 226 / 320; social 314 / 346 / 367 / 448 / 454; nose burning 37 / 48 / 41 / 102 / 107; heart pounding 26 / 24 / 19 / 29 / 66; sleepy 205 / 163 / 88 / 67 / 47; tired 224 / 176 / 127 / 68 / 56. Methamphetamine at 50 mg/70 kg exceeded the matched d-amphetamine condition on stimulated and heart pounding.

Drug-effect questionnaire (0 to 4 scale; liking -4 to +4), placebo / 12 mg AMPH / 12 mg MA / 50 mg AMPH / 50 mg MA: good drug effect 0.7 / 0.8 / 1.6 / 2.3 / 3.1; like drug -0.1 / 0.7 / 1.1 / 2.1 / 2.8; drug strength 1.1 / 1.0 / 1.7 / 2.5 / 3.1. Methamphetamine at 50 mg/70 kg exceeded the matched d-amphetamine condition on good drug effect and drug strength; both drugs at the larger dose exceeded placebo and their own smaller dose.

Ratings of 'high' and 'good drug effect' (VAS) and desire to take the drug again rose at both larger doses above placebo and above the smaller doses (p<0.05); methamphetamine at 50 mg/70 kg produced higher 'high' ratings than the matched d-amphetamine condition (p<0.05). Values appear only in Figure 3.
key_findings.locator: Results › Subjective Effects › Acute Effects; Figure 3

key_findings.finding: Residual subjective effect at 24 h: ratings of 'content' were lower after 50 mg/70 kg methamphetamine (40.7, SEM 10.0) than after placebo (54.6, 8.6) and than after every other active condition (p<0.05); no other residual subjective effect was significant.

Psychomotor performance: on the divided attention task all active conditions raised maximum tracking speed and the two 12 mg/70 kg conditions shortened mean hit latency (p<0.05); no other performance effects were significant, including on the digit-symbol task, and no residual performance effects at 24 h. Values appear only in Figure 4.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract states that both amphetamines dose-dependently increased self-administration under the $5 condition, but the results report only that the 50 mg/70 kg conditions exceeded placebo, with no significant step from the 12 to the 50 mg/70 kg condition described in the text.
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract claims a dose-response relation that the reported results support only as a two-point difference from placebo; Figure 2 carries the symbols but is an image.

reporting_issues.issue: Figure 2's legend defines a symbol for a difference from the 50 mg d-amphetamine condition, implying a drug difference in choice, while the text states there was no significant difference between the drugs.
reporting_issues.consequence: Whether any choice comparison differed between the two amphetamines cannot be resolved from the text; the figure is an image and its symbols cannot be read.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and discussion say the two drugs did not differ on most measures, while the same results list several measures on which 50 mg/70 kg methamphetamine exceeded the matched d-amphetamine condition (heart rate, 'high', stimulated, heart pounding, drug-effect-questionnaire good drug effect and drug strength), and the 12 mg/70 kg methamphetamine condition raised several ratings that the matched d-amphetamine condition did not.
reporting_issues.consequence: The summary of equivalence is based on counting non-significant tests; the significant differences all point the same way (methamphetamine larger), which an equivalence claim should address.

reporting_issues.issue: Subjective ratings were analysed as sums across the session by single-factor ANOVA, cardiovascular and performance data by condition x time ANOVA, with no F statistics or degrees of freedom printed for any analysis.
reporting_issues.consequence: Degrees of freedom cannot be checked against the sample size, and the error-term inflation visible in the companion study (Hart et al., 2008) cannot be ruled in or out here.

reporting_issues.issue: The drug-effect questionnaire is described as including 'bad effects', which is never reported; Table 2 presents only items with significant effects.
reporting_issues.consequence: Adverse subjective effects of either drug cannot be compared from this paper.

reporting_issues.issue: Pre-session urine screens were required to be negative for several drug metabolites but explicitly excluded amphetamines and THC, and no results are reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: Participants may have used amphetamines or cannabis between sessions; this bears directly on the 24-hour residual findings, as the authors acknowledge.

reporting_issues.issue: The claim that the $5 and $20 groups did not differ on any physiological, subjective or performance measure, which justifies pooling them (n=13), is made without reporting any test.
reporting_issues.consequence: The pooling cannot be verified; with 7 and 6 participants such tests would have little power to detect a difference.

reporting_issues.issue: Three participants are said to meet criteria for current methamphetamine dependence, but the diagnostic system (DSM-IV) is not named in the text.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the construct behind the dependence count is implicit.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC3475187 (author manuscript; all sections, Tables 1 and 2 rendered as text, acknowledgements and declaration of interest read; Figures 1 to 4 are images and their values were not extracted; no supplementary files)

editorial_corrections.reason: RoB 2 vocabulary: 'unclear' belongs to another tool; the judgment itself is unchanged (METHODS §5.3).

design_detail: Cross-sectional PET study of the dopamine transporter (DAT) ligand [11C]WIN-35,428 in 6 abstinent people who had used methamphetamine, 4 abstinent people who had used methcathinone, 10 non-using controls and 3 untreated early Parkinson's disease patients. One scan per person; outcome is the binding potential k3/k4 from a three-compartment model with arterial input, in caudate and putamen. No cognitive or psychiatric testing; the neurological examination is reported only in one summary sentence.
can_establish: That this very small group of people who formerly used methamphetamine (and a group who formerly used methcathinone) had lower mean striatal [11C]WIN-35,428 binding potential than this control group at a single time point.
cannot_establish: Whether methamphetamine caused the lower binding (no pre-use scan, three different recruitment sources, other drug use and smoking not measured), whether it reflects loss of terminals rather than transporter down-regulation or a change in affinity (the authors accept a neuroadaptive process is possible), whether it persists or recovers (one scan per person), or whether it raises the risk of parkinsonism (no follow-up).

sample.recruitment: The methamphetamine group from drug rehabilitation treatment groups; the methcathinone group identified through the US Drug Enforcement Administration while incarcerated on drug-related charges (the Discussion describes them as members of methcathinone distribution rings); controls from a university normal-volunteer office; newly diagnosed, untreated Parkinson's disease patients (Hoehn and Yahr stage II) from an outpatient neurology clinic (Materials and Methods › Subjects; Discussion, 5th paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Participants in the drug groups had to name methamphetamine or methcathinone as their drug of choice and greatest use. All participants were in good general health by history, physical examination, ECG, blood and urine chemistries, blood count, liver and thyroid tests, hepatitis and HIV screens; none took neuroleptics, methylphenidate or other therapeutic drugs at scanning; all agreed to avoid illicit drugs for at least 2 weeks and had blood and urine drug screens before PET. No minimum amount, frequency or duration of use is stated, and no psychiatric or head-injury exclusion is described (Materials and Methods › Subjects).
sample.demographics: Controls: mean age 30.5 (SD 10.0, range 18–48), 4 men and 6 women. Methamphetamine: 37.5 (SD 8.1, range 26–45), 3 and 3. Methcathinone: 31.2 (SD 5.6, range 26–39), 2 and 2. Parkinson's disease: 53.3 (SD 10.4, range 45–65), 2 and 1. Only the Parkinson's group differed significantly in age, F(3,19)=5.3, p=0.008 (Table 1; Results › Demographics). Education, IQ, ethnicity, smoking and psychiatric history are not reported.
sample.attrition: Not applicable (single scan). The number screened or excluded is not reported.
sample.selection_effects: Each group came from a different source: treatment groups (methamphetamine), prison through law enforcement (methcathinone), a university volunteer office (controls). The drug groups are tiny (6 and 4). All their members used several drugs, whereas controls had no history of drug abuse or dependence. The people who used methcathinone were drug manufacturers or distributors identified by law enforcement, an unusual group whose findings may not generalize.

exposure.measurement: Retrospective self-report from a telephone interview, a study questionnaire (number of uses, typical dose, frequency, last use, highest dose) and the drug-history section of the Addiction Severity Index; recent use excluded by enzyme immunoassay of blood and urine before PET (Materials and Methods › Drug use history; Drug screens). The authors concede drug histories and purity cannot be verified, but assert methcathinone purity was certain because the participants who used it made it (Discussion, 5th paragraph); this is an assertion, not a measurement.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Self-reported, per person (Table 2). Methamphetamine (n=6): usual amount ¼ g/day (3 people), ¼–½ g/day (2) or 3½ g/day (1); largest single-day amount from ½ g to 8 g; duration of use 3, 3, 10, 12, 20 and 18–20 years; all six snorted, three also smoked and two also injected. Methcathinone (n=4): usual amount 1 to 3½ g/day; duration 2–3 years; oral and/or snorted. Frequency of use and lifetime amount are not tabulated.
exposure.polysubstance: All participants in the drug groups had also used cannabis, LSD, benzodiazepines, cocaine and alcohol; amounts and frequency of these drugs were not reported or analysed (Materials and Methods › Subjects). Tobacco is not mentioned for any group. The authors argue that none of these drugs is known to cause lasting DAT changes (Discussion, 5th paragraph), although the same Discussion cites reports of cocaine-related DAT changes (Discussion, 2nd paragraph).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Negative blood and urine screens before PET (these detect only recent use); agreement to abstain for at least 2 weeks. From the last-use and scan dates in Table 2 (editors' calculation, month precision), the methamphetamine group had last used about 4, 5, 40, 42, 45 and 65 months before PET (mean about 34 months), and the methcathinone group 27–41 months before (mean about 35 months). The methcathinone group had been identified while incarcerated.

comparison.controls: 10 volunteers from a university normal-volunteer office with no history of drug abuse or dependence; 3 untreated early Parkinson's disease patients served as a disease reference group (Materials and Methods › Subjects; Results › Drug use).
comparison.matching: Not individually matched. Sex ratios similar; the methamphetamine group was on average 7 years older than controls (not significant). Age was handled by ANCOVA and, separately, by a fixed correction of 0.8% DAT decline per year taken from a published SPECT study (Table 3 legend). Education, IQ, socioeconomic status and smoking were not reported.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No pre-use DAT measure; no estimate of premorbid ability; psychiatric history not described; family history of parkinsonism not reported.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: History of drug abuse or dependence excluded; controls' alcohol, tobacco and occasional drug use not reported.

outcomes.instruments: PET (GE 4096Plus) after about 20 mCi intravenous [11C]WIN-35,428; 50 frames over 90 minutes; metabolite-corrected arterial input; caudate, putamen and cerebellum regions drawn on MRI-coregistered images; three-compartment model with K1/k2 constrained to the cerebellum value; outcome k3/k4, called binding potential (BP) (Materials and Methods › PET scans). Neurological examination by a neurologist experienced with movement disorders (Materials and Methods › Subjects).
outcomes.validity_norms: BP reflects both the number of transporters (Bmax) and their affinity (Kd); the authors argue from Parkinson's and animal data that Kd is unchanged but did not measure it (Discussion, 5th paragraph). The neurological examination is reported without a rating scale or scores.
outcomes.operationalization: Reduced DAT density was defined as a lower group-mean k3/k4 than controls. Absence of parkinsonism rests on the neurologist's examination, with no data shown. No cognitive or psychiatric outcome was measured, although the summary paragraph says the decreases were not associated with overt neurological or psychiatric illness.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Two regions, each analysed two ways (ANCOVA with age as covariate; ANOVA on age-corrected values), with Duncan's multiple range test for post hoc group contrasts. Duncan's test is a liberal procedure; there is no correction across regions or analysis strategies (Materials and Methods › Data analysis).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Regions of interest were outlined by an investigator unaware of participants' histories (Materials and Methods › PET scans). Blinding of the neurological examiner is not reported.

analysis.effect_sizes: BP (k3/k4), mean (SD), Table 3. Caudate: controls 7.5 (1.7), methamphetamine 5.8 (1.0), methcathinone 5.7 (0.9), Parkinson's 4.0 (0.9). Putamen: 7.3 (1.4), 5.5 (0.9), 6.1 (0.4), 2.3 (0.4). Printed percent differences from controls: methamphetamine −23% caudate and −25% putamen; methcathinone −24% and −16%; Parkinson's −47% and −68% (Abstract). Age-corrected values: caudate 8.7 (1.6) in controls vs 7.0 (1.2) methamphetamine and 6.7 (1.3) methcathinone; putamen 8.3 (1.4) vs 6.7 (0.9) and 7.1 (0.6), the methcathinone putamen difference no longer significant. ANCOVA: caudate F(3,18)=4.97, printed p=0.039; putamen F(3,18)=5.53, p=0.007 (Results › Caudate nucleus; Putamen). Editors' calculation (Hedges' g from the Table 3 means and SDs with pooled SD; approximate 95% CI from the large-sample standard error): methamphetamine vs controls, caudate g=1.08 (0.00 to 2.16), putamen g=1.37 (0.25 to 2.48); methcathinone vs controls, caudate g=1.09 (−0.13 to 2.32), putamen g=0.91 (−0.29 to 2.12). Simple two-group pooled-variance t-tests from the same table (editors' calculation, not age-adjusted) give p≈0.044 and p≈0.014 for the methamphetamine comparisons and p≈0.072 and p≈0.125 for the methcathinone comparisons, so significance of the methcathinone contrasts depends on the four-group error term and Duncan's test. Individual values are not shown; assuming normality, about 16% (caudate) and 10% (putamen) of controls would be expected to fall below the methamphetamine group mean (editors' calculation), so the distributions probably overlap.
analysis.covariates: Age only (ANCOVA covariate, or a fixed 0.8%/year correction that the authors say may be somewhat high). No adjustment for sex, smoking, other drug use or education.
analysis.selective_reporting: Individual BP values are not shown (Figure 1 shows one image per group), so the overlap between groups cannot be inspected. The neurological examination is summarized without data. No relation of BP to amount, duration or time since last use is reported, although per-person data exist in Table 2.
analysis.power: Not reported. With 6 people who used methamphetamine and 10 controls the 95% interval for the standardized difference runs from about 0 to above 2 (editors' calculation), so the size of the difference is very uncertain.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 6 people who formerly used methamphetamine and 4 who formerly used methcathinone, mean striatal binding potential for a DAT ligand was 16–25% lower than in 10 controls, with a very imprecise effect size, no individual data, a single scan per person and unmeasured confounders (other drugs, tobacco, education). Three older Parkinson's patients had larger reductions, especially in the putamen.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The title and abstract describe reduced DAT density and persistent reductions, and the abstract raises the possibility of increased risk of parkinsonism as people who use these drugs age (Abstract). Persistence is inferred from one scan after self-reported abstinence, and two of the six people who used methamphetamine had stopped only 4–5 months before scanning (Table 2). The Discussion weighs neuroadaptation against neurotoxicity and states the authors "tend to favor the view that DA neurotoxicity may be involved", on the strength of animal studies and the resemblance to Parkinson's disease, while conceding a neuroadaptive process is conceivable (Discussion, 2nd paragraph and summary). The Parkinson's comparison uses 3 patients about 20 years older. The summary says the decreases were not associated with overt psychiatric illness, but no psychiatric assessment is described in the Methods.

timeline.event: Post-mortem striatum of people who used methamphetamine chronically (Wilson et al., 1996, as described in this paper's Discussion): DAT and other dopamine markers reduced but dopa decarboxylase and the vesicular monoamine transporter normal, read by those authors as no terminal loss; McCann et al. answer that these markers may miss milder injury.
Baboon study from the same group (Villemagne et al., 1998) used by the authors to support a neurotoxic reading of lower [11C]WIN-35,428 binding.

VMAT2 PET in early abstinence: tracer binding raised in the first days and normal by 7–15 days, read as low vesicular dopamine rather than terminal loss (Boileau et al., 2016; appraised in this batch)

Critical assessment: striatal dopamine and DAT are low in people who use methamphetamine while metabolites, synthetic enzymes and VMAT2 are normal, unlike Parkinson's disease; whether methamphetamine damages dopamine neurones is called premature to decide

Meta-analysis of 9 DAT studies in people who use amphetamine-type stimulants (108 such participants, 126 controls): Hedges' g −1.47 (95% CI −1.83 to −1.10) (Ashok et al., 2017; appraised in this batch)

replication.where_it_stands: Lower striatal DAT binding in people who use methamphetamine is the most consistent finding in this literature: pooled across 9 amphetamine-type studies the standardized difference is about −1.5 (Ashok et al., 2017), and Kish et al. (2017) call it the most replicated dopamine-marker observation. What it means is unsettled. Markers that would also fall if terminals were lost (dopamine metabolites, synthetic enzymes, VMAT2) are normal in post-mortem striatum, VMAT2 tracer binding is raised rather than lowered in early abstinence, and PET has shown DAT rising with protracted abstinence, all of which favour regulation or dopamine depletion over terminal loss; no quantitative nigral cell counts exist in people who used methamphetamine. This paper's suggestion of later parkinsonism is addressed, without resolution, by two registry cohorts (Callaghan et al., 2012; Curtin et al., 2015), both limited by coded exposures and outcomes.

funding.funder: US Public Health Service grants DA05707, DA06275 (G.A.R.) and DA09482 (D.F.W.); National Institute of Mental Health Intramural Research Program (U.D.M.) (Footnotes).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from the NIMH Intramural Research Program and Johns Hopkins (Nuclear Medicine; Neurology). The baboon neurotoxicity study on which the Discussion relies (Villemagne et al., 1998) lists McCann, Wong, Dannals and Ricaurte among its authors (reference list). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: Prospective PET with both DAT and a terminal marker less subject to regulation (VMAT2) in people before and after starting regular methamphetamine use and after sustained abstinence, with matched controls rescanned at the same intervals, measured tobacco and other drug use, and individual values reported; post-mortem confirmation of terminal integrity in comparable people who used methamphetamine.

domains.note: Adjusted for age only. Other drug use (including cocaine) and tobacco not measured; education, IQ and psychiatric history not reported; no pre-use DAT.
Retrospective self-report of amounts and dates; one participant aged 29 in the methamphetamine group reports 18–20 years of use (Table 2).
Treatment groups, incarcerated drug distributors and university volunteers; very small groups.

Time since last use ranged from about 4 months to over 5 years; people who used methcathinone were identified in prison; if binding changes with abstinence, the group mean depends on when people were scanned.
No missing outcome data apparent; screening numbers not reported.
Arterial-input kinetic modelling with blinded region drawing. That BP mixes transporter number and affinity is an interpretation issue, not a measurement bias.
Two analysis strategies with a liberal post hoc test; the caudate p-value does not match its F statistic; no individual data; neurological findings not shown.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The PET measurement is careful and blinded, but a methamphetamine group of six from a treatment programme compared with university volunteers, with only age adjusted and other drug use and tobacco unmeasured, cannot attribute the lower binding to methamphetamine; the effect size is very imprecise and the significance of some contrasts depends on the post hoc procedure.

key_findings.finding: The methamphetamine group (n=6) had lower mean [11C]WIN-35,428 binding potential than controls (n=10): caudate 5.8 (SD 1.0) vs 7.5 (SD 1.7), 23% lower; putamen 5.5 (SD 0.9) vs 7.3 (SD 1.4), 25% lower; both significant by ANCOVA with age as covariate and Duncan's post hoc test.
key_findings.locator: Table 3; Results › Caudate nucleus and Putamen; Abstract

key_findings.finding: Methcathinone group (n=4): caudate 5.7 (SD 0.9), 24% lower; putamen 6.1 (SD 0.4), 16% lower; after age correction the putamen difference was no longer significant.

Untreated early Parkinson's patients (n=3, mean age 53): caudate 4.0 (SD 0.9), 47% lower; putamen 2.3 (SD 0.4), 68% lower. Putamen binding in Parkinson's was significantly lower than in both drug groups; caudate binding did not differ significantly between Parkinson's patients and the drug groups.
Four-group ANCOVA (age covariate): caudate F(3,18)=4.97, printed p=0.039; putamen F(3,18)=5.53, p=0.007.
key_findings.note: For F(3,18)=4.97 the p-value is about 0.011 (editors' calculation), not 0.039; see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: With a fixed age correction (0.8% per year), the methamphetamine group remained lower: caudate 7.0 (SD 1.2) vs 8.7 (SD 1.6); putamen 6.7 (SD 0.9) vs 8.3 (SD 1.4), about 19–20% lower.

Editors' calculation from Table 3: standardized differences (Hedges' g) for methamphetamine vs controls of 1.08 (95% CI 0.00 to 2.16) in caudate and 1.37 (0.25 to 2.48) in putamen; for methcathinone 1.09 (−0.13 to 2.32) and 0.91 (−0.29 to 2.12).
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation with pooled SD; values printed to one decimal, so approximate.

key_findings.finding: Time since last use, from the dates in Table 2: methamphetamine group about 4, 5, 40, 42, 45 and 65 months (mean about 34); methcathinone group 27–41 months (mean about 35). Two of the six in the methamphetamine group had stopped only 4–5 months before PET.
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation from month/year dates.

key_findings.finding: Self-reported use (Table 2): four of six in the methamphetamine group reported usual amounts of ¼ to ½ g/day and one reported 3½ g/day; durations ranged from 3 to about 20 years; all snorted, some also smoked or injected. All participants in the drug groups had also used cannabis, LSD, benzodiazepines, cocaine and alcohol, not quantified.
Neither drug group showed clinical signs of parkinsonism on a neurologist's examination; no rating scale or scores are reported.
The authors state that the lower binding could reflect a neuroadaptive process rather than neurotoxicity, while favouring neurotoxicity on the basis of animal data and the Parkinson's comparison.

reporting_issues.issue: Caudate ANCOVA reported as F(3,18)=4.97 with p=0.039; with 3 and 18 degrees of freedom, F=4.97 corresponds to p≈0.011 (editors' calculation). The putamen F(3,18)=5.53, p=0.007 is consistent.
reporting_issues.consequence: Either the F or the p is misprinted. The conclusion at p<0.05 is unchanged, but the exact strength of evidence is uncertain.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results say everyone in the drug groups reported about 3 years of abstinence, but Table 2 dates show two in the methamphetamine group (subjects 1 and 6) last used about 4 and 5 months before PET. The abstract's average of about 3 years matches the mean (editors' calculation about 34 months).
reporting_issues.consequence: The words persistent and lasting rest partly on people abstinent only a few months.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract lists the methcathinone putamen decrease (−16%) as significant without noting that the age-corrected comparison was not significant (Table 3); a simple two-group t-test from the table gives p≈0.13 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: The methcathinone putamen finding is fragile and depends on the analysis chosen.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion gives 30 and 37 as the mean ages of methamphetamine and control subjects respectively, the reverse of Table 1 (37.5 and 30.5). It also says age-related DAT decline does not occur between 30 and 37, while the paper's own correction assumes 0.8% per year from age 10 (about 5–6% over 7 years).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Discussion, 3rd paragraph; Table 1; Table 3 legend)
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the age argument is less secure than the text suggests, though the age-corrected values still show lower binding.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 lists a 29-year-old in the methamphetamine group with 18–20 years of use, which implies use from about age 9–11; not commented on.
reporting_issues.consequence: Either a data error or an atypical history; illustrates the unverified self-report.

reporting_issues.issue: Title and abstract call the outcome transporter density, but the measure is k3/k4 (binding potential), which depends on both Bmax and Kd; Kd was not measured.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Title; Materials and Methods › PET scans; Discussion, 5th paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: Lower BP is compatible with fewer transporters, lower affinity, or competition from endogenous dopamine.

reporting_issues.issue: The summary says the decreases were not associated with overt neurological or psychiatric illness, but no psychiatric assessment is described in the Methods and the neurological examination is reported without data.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Discussion, summary paragraph; Materials and Methods › Subjects)
reporting_issues.consequence: The absence of clinical consequences is asserted rather than shown.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC6792853 (all sections, Tables 1–3 as text, Figure 1 legend; Figure 1 is an image of one scan per group; no supplementary material exists)

editorial_corrections.reason: Language (METHODS §9): 43 replacements, no change of meaning, number or citation; list in data/verification/language-2026-10-16.json

design_detail: Cross-sectional comparison in early abstinence followed by a one-month retest with a retested control group. 27 non-treatment-seeking adults with current DSM-IV methamphetamine dependence lived on a UCLA research ward with urine-verified abstinence and were tested after 4–9 days (mean 6.19); 28 healthy comparison participants recruited the same way were tested as outpatients. 18 in the methamphetamine group (after a mean 25.44 days) and 21 controls (after a mean 43.50 days) were retested. Battery of 18 test scores in five domains, analysed by domain MANOVA, a composite standardized to the controls, and change scores.
can_establish: How this screened, advertisement-recruited group in its first week of verified abstinence compared with controls on a mostly verbal battery, and whether their test scores changed over the next three to four weeks more than controls' scores changed on retest.
cannot_establish: Whether the baseline differences were caused by methamphetamine (no pre-use data; groups differed in education and smoking), whether cognition changes after longer abstinence, or that no meaningful change occurs in the first month (the change estimate is too imprecise to exclude a moderate or large one).

sample.recruitment: Newspaper and Internet advertisements for both groups; people in the methamphetamine group were not seeking treatment and resided at the UCLA General Clinical Research Center for the study (Method › Participants, 1st paragraph; Procedure). Payment: $30 per assessment, $50 for completing both, and $60 per week of residence for the methamphetamine group.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Methamphetamine group: current DSM-IV methamphetamine dependence (SCID) and a positive urine test for methamphetamine at enrolment. Excluded for everyone: neurological disease (including head trauma with loss of consciousness over 5 minutes), systemic, cardiovascular or pulmonary disease, symptomatic hepatitis or cirrhosis, HIV infection, prescription psychotropic medication, and frank structural abnormality on MRI. People in the methamphetamine group excluded if they currently met abuse or dependence criteria for any drug other than methamphetamine except cannabis abuse, or had a current mood or psychotic disorder unrelated to methamphetamine. Controls: no methamphetamine use, no substance abuse or dependence, no illicit drug other than cannabis used more than twice (Method › Participants, paragraphs 1 and 4).
sample.demographics: Methamphetamine group vs controls at time 1 (Table 1): age 33.9 (7.5) vs 33.3 (7.9); men 17/27 vs 14/28; education 12.7 (1.9) vs 15.1 (2.5) years (p<0.01); mother's education 13.3 (2.6) vs 14.2 (2.2); Shipley-Hartford vocabulary 28.1 (4.6) vs 29.4 (4.3); Wender Utah Rating Scale 24.7 (17.2) vs 17.3 (18.2); cigarette smokers 21 vs 13 (p<0.01); White 17 vs 19. Hepatitis B positive 4 vs 2. Two in the methamphetamine group had substance-induced mood disorder, one substance-induced psychotic disorder, one social phobia; one control had a specific phobia (Method › Participants, 3rd and 4th paragraphs).
sample.attrition: 9 of 27 in the methamphetamine group (33%) chose not to stay 30 days and 7 of 28 controls (25%) did not return (Method › Participants, 5th paragraph). Those in the methamphetamine group who left did not differ from completers on demographics, smoking, education, Wender Utah score, use history, vocabulary, or time-1 domain and composite scores (all p>0.05, statistics not shown). Control completers were older (35.19 vs 27.57 years, p<0.05), had marginally higher vocabulary (30.25 vs 26.20, p=0.06) and differed on the attention/processing-speed domain at time 1 (Results › Change between first and second assessments, 1st paragraph).
sample.selection_effects: Advertisement-recruited, non-treatment-seeking participants who used methamphetamine and agreed to live on a research ward, screened free of HIV, other substance dependence, psychiatric and medical comorbidity; the authors note this limits generalization to the wider population of people with methamphetamine dependence (Discussion, last paragraph). Retest data come only from those in the methamphetamine group willing to stay a month. Control completers differed from control dropouts in age and vocabulary.

exposure.measurement: SCID DSM-IV diagnosis of current methamphetamine dependence; urine positive for methamphetamine at enrolment; frequency, quantity, duration and route by self-report (Method › Participants, 2nd paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Self-reported: use on 4.15 (2.24) days per week; 5.87 (3.46) times per day on use days; about 4.66 (5.76) g per week; regular use for 7.63 (6.89) years. Usual route: smoking 68%, snorting 12%, injection 16%, oral 4% (Method › Participants, 2nd paragraph; Table 1).
exposure.polysubstance: Dependence on other drugs excluded; 3 in the methamphetamine group met cannabis abuse criteria; both those with and without that diagnosis averaged fewer than 2 days of cannabis use in the past 30 days. Six controls reported infrequent past cannabis use. Cigarette smoking 21/27 in the methamphetamine group vs 13/28 controls; nicotine dependence not assessed; participants could take smoking breaks during testing (Method › Participants, 3rd and 4th paragraphs; Discussion, last paragraph). Alcohol use is not described for either group.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Methamphetamine group: on the research ward, urine drug screens every other day; first battery after at least 4 days of abstinence (mean 6.19, SD 1.47, range 4–9 days); retest after a mean 25.44 days (SD 3.20), i.e. about 31 days of verified abstinence. Controls: urine drug screen before each assessment (Procedure).

comparison.controls: 28 healthy volunteers recruited by advertisement, naive to methamphetamine, without substance abuse or dependence; tested as outpatients and retested after a mean 43.50 days (SD 15.81), longer than the methamphetamine group because of scheduling delays (Method › Participants, 4th paragraph; Results › Change, 2nd paragraph).
comparison.matching: Not individually matched. No significant difference in age, sex, ethnicity, hepatitis B, Wender Utah score, mother's education or vocabulary; the methamphetamine group had fewer years of education and more smokers (Results › First assessment, 1st paragraph). Education was used as a covariate in secondary analyses.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No pre-use testing. Premorbid ability estimated by Shipley-Hartford vocabulary (n.s., editors' d≈0.29 favouring controls) and mother's education (n.s., d≈0.37); own education differed by about 1.1 SD (editors' calculation from Table 1). Childhood ADHD symptoms by retrospective Wender Utah scale only (n.s., d≈0.42 toward more symptoms in the methamphetamine group). The authors note that education may be either a premorbid marker or a consequence of use (Discussion, 5th paragraph).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: No substance abuse or dependence; no illicit drug other than cannabis used more than twice; 6 with infrequent past cannabis use; 13/28 smoked cigarettes; alcohol not described.

outcomes.instruments: Attention/processing speed: Trail Making A, Stroop words and colours. Working memory: backward digit span, Sentence Span, Missing Digit Span. Learning/memory: Selective Reminding Test (12 trials; total and intrusions), Repeated Memory Test (word and picture recall and recognition). Timed executive: Trail Making B, Stroop colour-word, letter fluency (FAS). Untimed executive: computerized Wisconsin Card Sorting (perseverative errors), Discrimination Learning, Logical Problems. Premorbid estimate: Shipley-Hartford vocabulary (Measures). Several tests are the group's own adaptations without published norms.
outcomes.validity_norms: Normative data were available only for Trail Making, Stroop, FAS, Selective Reminding and WCST; on these the methamphetamine group's time-1 means fell between the 16th and 55th percentiles (Discussion, 7th paragraph); which test sat at the 16th percentile, and the controls' percentiles, are not reported. Alternate forms were used at retest for all tests except Trail Making, Stroop and backward digit span (Measures, last paragraph).
outcomes.operationalization: No individual impairment classification. Group differences by domain MANOVA, then t-tests only within domains with a significant omnibus test; a composite equal to the mean of test scores standardized to the controls' mean and SD; change = time 2 minus time 1 per test, analysed by domain MANOVA and as a composite change score standardized to the controls (Statistical methods). The authors define the impaired range as the 2nd percentile or below (Discussion, 7th paragraph).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Domain-wise MANOVA gatekeeping before individual t-tests (Statistical methods). Correlations of change with test interval and with use variables, and the paired practice-effect tests, were uncorrected (Results › Change, 2nd and 4th paragraphs; Discussion, 2nd paragraph).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported; testers could not have been blind to inpatient status.

analysis.effect_sizes: Time 1: composite −0.31 (0.45) in the methamphetamine group vs 0.01 (0.60) in controls, t(53)=2.21, p<0.05 (Table 2; Results › First assessment, 3rd paragraph). The −0.31 is in units of the controls' test-level SDs; on the composite's own scale the standardized difference is about 0.60 (95% CI 0.06 to 1.14; editors' calculation from Table 2). Stroop colours 68.8 (10.5) vs 75.6 (11.7), t(53)=2.26 (editors' d≈0.61). Both became non-significant with education as a covariate (no adjusted estimates given). Learning/memory MANOVA p=0.09 and timed executive p=0.09, so individual tests were not tested; editors' approximate d from Table 2 (assuming about 26 per group): Selective Reminding total 0.67, Repeated Memory word recall 0.61, picture recall 0.90, word recognition 0.56, Stroop colour-word 0.65; near zero for Trail Making A and B, Stroop words, Sentence Span, Missing Digit Span and FAS. Change: no domain MANOVA significant (p>0.10); composite change 0.14 in the methamphetamine group vs 0.00 in controls (standardized to controls' change), t(37)=−1.01, p=0.33; editors' d≈0.32 (95% CI −0.31 to 0.96). Time 2 (completers, Table 3; not tested by the authors): the methamphetamine group remained below controls on Repeated Memory word recall (2.11 vs 4.14), picture recall (5.17 vs 7.29), word recognition (10.72 vs 14.67) and picture recognition (17.61 vs 20.24); editors' d≈0.73–0.82.
analysis.covariates: Education (time-1 Stroop colours and composite; change MANOVAs); test interval and vocabulary (change MANOVAs). Smoking, sex and Wender Utah scores not adjusted.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration mentioned. The time-1 hypotheses (deficits in verbal memory, executive functioning and attention/processing speed) were stated in advance in the Introduction; the authors state they had no specific hypotheses about change (Introduction, last paragraph).
analysis.selective_reporting: Time-2 between-group comparisons are not reported although Table 3 shows sizeable differences on memory tests. MANOVA gatekeeping meant that medium-to-large memory differences at time 1 were not tested individually. Adjusted estimates after the education covariate are not given. Statistics for dropout comparisons and use-variable correlations are reported only as p>0.05.
analysis.power: Not reported; the authors attribute their null results partly to limited power (Discussion, 6th paragraph). Editors' approximation: about 44% power for a standardized difference of 0.5 at time 1 (27 vs 28) and about 33% for a change difference of 0.5 (18 vs 21), two-sided α=0.05.

interpretation_gap.results_show: After about 6 days of verified abstinence, the methamphetamine group scored below controls on the composite (editors' d≈0.6, wide interval) and significantly on one processing-speed test; the differences were no longer significant when years of education was a covariate. Memory tests showed medium-to-large differences that were not tested because their domain MANOVA was p=0.09. Over about 25 days, the methamphetamine group's change did not differ significantly from controls' change (editors' d≈0.32, 95% CI −0.31 to 0.96), and the group still scored below controls on memory tests at retest (untested). On the five normed tests, the methamphetamine group's means were between the 16th and 55th percentiles.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that people with methamphetamine dependence "do not show considerable cognitive gains in the first month of abstinence" and that a longer abstinence may be needed (Abstract, Conclusions). This is a no-change inference from a test with about one-third power whose interval includes a large differential improvement; the Discussion itself calls the indications of improvement equivocal (Discussion, 2nd paragraph). The abstract reports the 0.31-SD composite difference as significant but does not say it became non-significant after adjusting for education, a point the Discussion treats at length, raising the possibility that premorbid differences account for most of the variance (Discussion, 5th paragraph). The abstract's 0.31 SD is in test-level units and understates the standardized composite difference (about 0.6).

timeline.event: Longitudinal studies reporting improvement with abstinence (Chou et al., 2007; Jaffe et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2004) did not retest a control group, so practice effects cannot be separated (as summarized by Simon et al., Introduction, 5th paragraph).
Chang et al. (2005): people abstinent from methamphetamine for about a week did not differ from matched controls on a broad battery (as summarized by Simon et al., Introduction, 2nd paragraph).

Meta-analysis cited by Simon et al. for the largest methamphetamine–control differences in learning (d=−0.66), executive functions (−0.63), memory (−0.59) and processing speed (−0.52) (Introduction, 1st paragraph; values as reported by Simon et al.).

Iudicello et al. (2010): over about 13 months, self-reported abstainers' global change was close to that of retested controls; larger gains confined to 6 abstainers impaired at baseline (appraised in sc_iudicello_2010 from this reading batch).

replication.where_it_stands: Both controlled retest studies in this batch find the methamphetamine groups' overall change close to that of retested controls, one over the first month with verified abstinence (this study) and one over about a year with self-reported abstinence (Iudicello et al., 2010); neither is precise enough to exclude moderate recovery, and both show that practice effects in controls are of the same order as the methamphetamine groups' gains.

funding.funder: National Institutes of Health grants DA 022539, DA 020726 and DA 15179 and contract DA 50038, all awarded to Edythe D. London (title footnote).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement on the PMC page.
funding.affiliations_note: UCLA Department of Psychiatry and Biobehavioral Sciences and Semel Institute; two authors at the University of Southern California Department of Psychology. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A larger study (several dozen per group) of people with methamphetamine use disorder with biologically verified abstinence, retested at fixed intervals from the first week to a year alongside controls retested at identical intervals with alternate forms, with between-group comparisons reported at every time point, premorbid ability measured independently of education (for example school records), and pre-registered analyses.

domains.note: Groups differed by about 1.1 SD in education and in smoking (78% vs 46%); smoking and sex not adjusted; adjusting for education removed the time-1 differences, but education may partly be a consequence of use.
Current dependence by SCID, urine-positive at enrolment, abstinence verified every other day; use amounts self-reported.
An advertisement-recruited, non-treatment-seeking, heavily screened methamphetamine group willing to live on a ward; control retest completers older and with higher vocabulary than control dropouts.
People in the methamphetamine group were inpatients without treatment, controls outpatients; retest interval 25 vs 44 days.

33% of the methamphetamine group and 25% of controls not retested (dropouts compared, statistics not shown); WCST data for only 13 controls and 18 in the methamphetamine group; FAS not analysable at retest.
Alternate forms for most tests, but several in-house tests without norms; no assessor blinding possible for inpatient status.
Pre-specified MANOVA gatekeeping, but time-2 group comparisons and education-adjusted estimates not reported.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Abstinence is well verified and the retested control group is a real strength, but the time-1 methamphetamine–control difference is confounded by education and smoking, and the change comparison is small, uses different settings and intervals for the two groups, and cannot separate a null from a moderate effect.

key_findings.finding: After a mean 6.19 days (range 4–9) of urine-verified abstinence, 27 people who used methamphetamine scored below 28 controls on the battery composite: −0.31 (0.45) vs 0.01 (0.60), t(53)=2.21, p<0.05.
key_findings.note: The 0.31 is in test-level SD units; the standardized difference on the composite is about 0.60, 95% CI 0.06 to 1.14 (editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: Only the attention/processing-speed MANOVA was significant at time 1; within it, the methamphetamine group was slower on Stroop colours (68.8 vs 75.6, t(53)=2.26, p<0.05). Learning/memory and timed executive MANOVAs were p=0.09.
key_findings.note: The paper prints the MANOVA statistic as Wilks' lambda = 2.97, which is impossible for a lambda (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: The Stroop colours difference and the composite difference both became non-significant when years of education was entered as a covariate (no adjusted estimates given).

Memory tests not followed up because of the MANOVA gate showed medium-to-large differences at time 1: Selective Reminding total 110.3 vs 120.3; Repeated Memory picture recall 5.89 vs 8.11, word recall 2.56 vs 4.18, word recognition 11.30 vs 14.00 (editors' d≈0.56–0.90).
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation assuming about 26 per group; exact per-test n is given only as 24–28 controls and 25–27 in the methamphetamine group.

key_findings.finding: The methamphetamine group's time-1 means on the normed tests (Trail Making, FAS, Selective Reminding, Stroop, WCST) fell between the 16th and 55th percentiles, which the authors describe as low-average to average and not in the impaired range (2nd percentile or below).
Neither days of abstinence before testing (4–9) nor years of use or grams per week were related to time-1 scores (all p>0.05, statistics not shown).

18 in the methamphetamine group (retested after 25.44 days, SD 3.20) and 21 controls (after 43.50 days, SD 15.81, p<0.01 for the difference) completed both assessments; 9 in the methamphetamine group and 7 controls were lost.
key_findings.locator: Method › Participants, 5th paragraph; Results › Change between first and second assessments, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: No domain MANOVA on change scores differed between groups (p>0.10), with or without education, interval or vocabulary as covariates. Composite change was 0.14 in the methamphetamine group vs 0.00 in controls, t(37)=−1.01, p=0.33.
key_findings.note: Editors' d≈0.32, 95% CI −0.31 to 0.96: compatible with no differential change and with a large one.

key_findings.finding: Across all participants, 7 tests improved significantly on retest (Trail Making A, Stroop colours, words and colour-word, Logical Problems, Discrimination Learning, Sentence Span; uncorrected paired t-tests), including tests given in alternate forms.

At retest, the methamphetamine group still scored below controls on Repeated Memory word recall (2.11 vs 4.14), picture recall (5.17 vs 7.29), word recognition (10.72 vs 14.67) and picture recognition (17.61 vs 20.24); on the Selective Reminding total the gap narrowed (time 1, same subsample, 108.2 vs 120.9; time 2, 113.1 vs 117.1; editors' d about 1.0 and 0.2). The paper reports no between-group test at time 2.
key_findings.note: Editors' d≈0.73–0.82 (approximate p 0.01–0.03), computed from Table 3 with 21 vs 18.

key_findings.finding: Within the methamphetamine group only, a longer retest interval went with more improvement on Repeated Memory picture recognition and Logical Problems and less on backward digit span (uncorrected p<0.05); interval was unrelated to change in controls and across all participants.
key_findings.note: The methamphetamine group's interval varied little (SD 3.2 days).

reporting_issues.issue: MANOVA results are printed as Wilks' lambda = 2.97 (time 1) and 'all Wilks' lambdas < 1.36' (change); Wilks' lambda lies between 0 and 1, so these are presumably F statistics, printed without degrees of freedom.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › First assessment, 2nd paragraph; Results › Change, 3rd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The omnibus tests cannot be checked; the bound of 1.36 is uninformative as printed.

reporting_issues.issue: The chi-square for sex is printed as 0.34 and for smoking as 6.82; from the Table 1 counts (17/10 vs 14/14; 21/27 vs 13/28 smokers) the uncorrected values are 0.94 and 5.72 (editors' calculation), whereas the printed ethnicity (0.15) and hepatitis B (0.83) values reproduce exactly.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › First assessment, 1st paragraph; Table 1
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; conclusions unchanged (smoking p≈0.017).

reporting_issues.issue: The route percentages (smoking 68%, snorting 12%, injection 16%, oral 4%) are exact for 25 participants (17, 3, 4, 1) and cannot be obtained from 27.
reporting_issues.consequence: Route missing for 2 participants, not disclosed.

reporting_issues.issue: Retest intervals are 43.50 days (controls) and 25.44 days (methamphetamine group) in the Results and Procedure but 45 and 29 days in the Discussion.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Change, 2nd paragraph; Discussion, 3rd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the Results values are the reliable ones.

reporting_issues.issue: The note to Table 3 says data came from 19–17 people in the methamphetamine group, but only 18 completed both assessments.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor typographical error in the per-test n.

reporting_issues.issue: The vocabulary comparison is reported as t(50), implying 52 participants with vocabulary scores, and WCST data exist for only 13 controls and 18 in the methamphetamine group; Table 1 does not show these missing values.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › First assessment, 1st paragraph; Table 2 note
reporting_issues.consequence: Premorbid estimate and the untimed executive domain rest on incomplete data.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract reports the composite difference as significant without saying it was non-significant after adjusting for education, and expresses it as 0.31 SD in test-level units.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract; Results › First assessment, 3rd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Readers of the abstract cannot tell that the difference depends on whether education is adjusted, or that it is about 0.6 SD on the composite's own scale.
