disagreements.first_pass: At retest, the methamphetamine group still scored below controls on Repeated Memory word recall (2.11 vs 4.14), picture recall (5.17 vs 7.29), word recognition (10.72 vs 14.67) and picture recognition (17.61 vs 20.24); the paper reports no between-group test at time 2.
disagreements.reviewer: review round 2 (group M)
disagreements.resolution: Applied by the editor after adjudication against the source: Review round 2 (group M, finding 8): Table 3 shows the Selective Reminding total gap shrinking from about 1.0 to 0.2 SD (editors' pooled-SD calculation with 21 vs 18, recomputed) while the Repeated Memory gaps stayed or widened; the key finding should carry both directions, as the claim now does.

design_detail: Narrative review with a reported literature search: PubMed, PsycINFO and ScienceDirect with printed search terms, plus reference lists and Google Scholar. Inclusion criteria, stated to have been formulated before the literature search: participants aged 16 or older; methamphetamine specifically (not amphetamine or other stimulants); studies of methamphetamine psychosis that directly compared it with schizophrenia or a primary psychotic disorder; methamphetamine use preceding the psychosis; original research only; no case studies. Search dates, numbers of records screened and excluded, language limits, duplicate screening and any risk-of-bias tool are not reported, and one author conducted the review (Author contributions). Twelve direct-comparison studies published 1990–2017 are tabulated in Table 1; Table 2 appraises thirteen informally (it adds Hajebi et al., 2018). No meta-analysis: narrative synthesis organized by positive, negative and cognitive symptoms and by acute versus chronic (persistent) methamphetamine psychosis.
can_establish: What the small set of direct comparisons published up to 2018 reported about positive, negative and cognitive symptoms in methamphetamine psychosis versus schizophrenia, and which methodological weaknesses those studies share.
cannot_establish: That the eligible literature was found completely (undated search, no record flow, single reviewer); the size or consistency of any group difference (no effect sizes, no pooling); or that any symptom reliably separates methamphetamine psychosis from schizophrenia, because several headline differences rest on indirect comparisons or single small studies. The prevalence, duration and transition figures in its introduction are second-hand citations outside the review's own method.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (review). The included studies recruited mostly from psychiatric hospitals, emergency wards, in- and outpatient clinics and detention centres in Taiwan, Iran, Japan, Norway, South Africa, Thailand and the USA, plus two Australian samples of people who use methamphetamine (needle and syringe programmes, Hides et al., 2015; a treatment cohort, McKetin et al., 2017) (Table 1). Per-study sizes as printed in Table 1 range from 22 to 285.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Human participants aged 16 or older; methamphetamine only; studies of methamphetamine psychosis directly compared with schizophrenia or primary psychotic disorder; methamphetamine use had to precede the psychosis; original research only (reviews excluded); case studies excluded (Overview of review › Inclusion criteria). The criteria list numbers two items as (3).
sample.demographics: Not summarized at review level. Table 1 gives sex and age for a few studies only: 61% men, mean age 31.65 (Hides et al., 2015); 71% men, mean age 31.6 (McKetin et al., 2017); 52% men, mean age about 38–39 (Medhus et al., 2013).
sample.attrition: Not applicable. The review does not report how many records were retrieved, screened or excluded.
sample.selection_effects: Review level: an undated search with no flow diagram and no list of excluded studies, run by one author, leaves completeness unverifiable. Study level: most psychosis samples were hospitalized, which the authors note selects more severe cases (Methodological limitations, 3rd paragraph); in two studies the primary-psychosis comparison group were themselves people who use methamphetamine (Hides et al., 2015; McKetin et al., 2017); in one, the schizophrenia group was chosen because it responded poorly to medication (Srisurapanont et al., 2011) (Table 2).

exposure.measurement: Not measured by the review. In the included studies methamphetamine-associated psychosis was established by structured interview (DIGS-C, SCID-I, CIDI, MINI-Plus), hospital files or chart review, and in one study by urine or blood toxicology (Medhus et al., 2013) (Tables 1–2).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Barely reported: one psychosis group had used methamphetamine for a mean of 3.8 (SD 5.4) years (Srisurapanont et al., 2011); one recruited people who had injected moderate or high doses over an extended period (Tomiyama, 1990) (Table 1). No amounts, frequencies or routes are synthesized.
exposure.polysubstance: Not handled at review level. Table 2 records substantial other-drug use in psychosis groups: 66% with a history of other drug use (Ezzatpanah et al., 2014), 64% with other drug dependence (Tomiyama, 1990), 87% with at least one other psychoactive substance in blood or urine (Medhus et al., 2013). Shelly et al. (2016) excluded dependence on other drugs; most studies did not address it. The authors list uncontrolled polydrug use as a limitation (Methodological limitations, 3rd paragraph).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Mostly not reported. The authors classified every study that did not report abstinence as an acute-psychosis study (Methodological limitations, 1st paragraph). Where reported: no more than 4 weeks (Shelly et al., 2016); methamphetamine use in the past week (Srisurapanont et al., 2011); more than 1 month (Wang et al., 2016); the acute group of Chen et al. (2015) was assessed about 9 weeks after its episode (Table 2).

comparison.controls: A schizophrenia or primary-psychosis group in every included study; healthy controls in only three (Chen et al., 2015; Ezzatpanah et al., 2014; Okada et al., 2016) (Table 2). The comparison group of Hajebi et al. (2018) mixed schizophrenia (46), schizoaffective disorder (1) and brief psychotic disorder (3), and 9 of its members had used methamphetamine (Table 2).
comparison.matching: Varies by study: age and sex matched in Ezzatpanah et al. (also education), Okada et al. and Tomiyama; groups differed in age, ethnicity and place of birth in Jacobs et al. (2008); age not matched in Srisurapanont et al. (2011) (Table 2).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No included study had a pre-psychosis baseline. Premorbid ability was estimated only in some (Japanese Adult Reading Test in Okada and Yamamuro; WRAT reading in Jacobs). Family history and premorbid psychiatric risk are not compared between groups anywhere in the review.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Schizophrenia groups excluded substance use disorders in some studies (Chen 2015; Wang 2016; Shelly 2016), used methamphetamine in others (Hides 2015; McKetin 2017), and had unknown drug use in Srisurapanont 2011 (Table 2).

outcomes.instruments: Across the included studies: BPRS, PANSS (including a five-factor model), SANS, Manchester Scale, SCID-I first-rank symptom items, CIDI lifetime symptom items; cognition with BACS, WCST, Stroop, Visual Search and Attention Test (VSAT), Wechsler Memory Scale, RBANS, WASI, D-KEFS colour-word interference, a continuous performance test, Trail Making and Grooved Pegboard; prefrontal activation with near-infrared spectroscopy (Table 1).
outcomes.validity_norms: Instrument validity in methamphetamine samples is not discussed, except the authors' argument that total-score scales such as PANSS and BPRS cannot capture qualitative differences in hallucinations and delusions (Methodological limitations, 3rd paragraph). Cognitive findings are group comparisons; none is related to norms.
outcomes.operationalization: Acute versus persistent methamphetamine psychosis is defined by whether psychosis continued for more than 1 month after stopping use, following Chen et al. (2015) (Methodological limitations, 1st paragraph); studies with unknown abstinence were counted as acute. Differences are reported only as significant or not.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not addressed by the review. Several included studies compared many single symptoms or tests (first-rank symptom items, lifetime symptom items, item-level differential item functioning) with no correction mentioned.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported for any included study.

analysis.effect_sizes: None reported by the review, which gives directions and significance only. Editors' calculation for Shelly et al. (2016), from the review's percentages and the Table 1 group sizes (methamphetamine psychosis n=33, schizophrenia n=69; counts reconstructed by rounding): voices conversing 16/33 vs 14/69, odds ratio about 3.7 (95% CI 1.5 to 9.1), risk difference 28 percentage points (9 to 48); thought broadcasting 29/69 in schizophrenia vs 8/33, odds ratio about 2.3 (0.9 to 5.7), an unadjusted interval that includes no difference, consistent with the review's statement that this difference was significant only after controlling for age. Woolf intervals for odds ratios, Wald intervals for risk differences; approximate.
analysis.covariates: Not applicable at review level; adjustment in the included studies is listed per study in Table 2 and is mostly limited to matching.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: The text summarizes some studies differently from Table 1 (see reporting issues): the visual and tactile hallucination result of McKetin et al. (2017) appears in opposite directions in Table 1 and in the text, and Hajebi et al. (2018) is used in the text but missing from Table 1. Whether relevant studies were left out cannot be checked because excluded records are not listed.
analysis.power: Not assessed. The authors note that small samples may make the two disorders look more alike than they are (Methodological limitations, 3rd paragraph). Four of the twelve Table 1 studies had 15 or fewer people in at least one psychosis group: Medhus et al. (9 methamphetamine-positive), Okada et al. (14 schizophrenia), Tomiyama (11 and 11), Yamamuro et al. (15).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In the direct comparisons, positive-symptom severity was mostly similar in methamphetamine psychosis and schizophrenia; schizophrenia groups had more negative symptoms in every study that examined them in detail (Tomiyama, 1990; Wang et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2015; Hajebi et al., 2018); in the one study that separated acute from persistent cases, the persistent group performed like the schizophrenia group on cognitive tests and the acute group like people who used methamphetamine without psychosis and controls (Chen et al., 2015). Acute-sample studies found no methamphetamine–schizophrenia cognitive difference except on one attention test (VSAT) in one study of 30 vs 30. More visual and tactile hallucinations than in schizophrenia were shown directly only in a persistent-psychosis sample (Wang et al., 2016).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says visual and tactile hallucinations appear more prevalent in acute methamphetamine psychosis and that acute methamphetamine psychosis "could be clinically distinguished from a primary psychotic disorder" on behavioural and cognitive features. In the body, the authors themselves say the hallucination-modality differences for acute psychosis come from indirect, not direct, comparisons (Positive symptoms › Acute, 4th paragraph), call the thought-disorder evidence indirect and inconclusive (3rd paragraph), and conclude there is insufficient evidence on whether chronic methamphetamine psychosis is distinct (Summary and conclusions, 2nd paragraph). The parietal-cortex attribution rests on one VSAT difference with no imaging of parietal cortex. Figure 1 orders visual and tactile hallucinations acute > chronic > schizophrenia, which the review's own Table 1 summary of McKetin et al. (2017) contradicts. The management paragraph states as fact that acute symptoms resolve with abstinence, citing a StatPearls chapter rather than the reviewed studies (Summary and conclusions, 3rd paragraph), and the introduction infers methamphetamine-induced persistent changes independent of genetic predisposition from a case report with literature review (Grelotti et al., 2010) (Chronic methamphetamine psychosis paragraph).

timeline.event: McKetin et al. prospective cohort, cited by this review for psychotic symptoms about 5 times more likely during periods of methamphetamine use than during abstinence, with a dose-response relation (Acute methamphetamine psychosis, 3rd paragraph)

Chen et al. (Taiwan): the only included study separating acute (under 1 month) from persistent methamphetamine psychosis with healthy controls and controls who used methamphetamine without psychosis; persistent group resembled schizophrenia on BPRS positive scores and BACS cognition

McKetin et al. (Australia, 284 people with methamphetamine dependence): no significant difference in lifetime positive symptoms between persistent methamphetamine psychosis and primary psychosis, whose members also used methamphetamine
This narrative review

replication.where_it_stands: At the time of this review the direct-comparison literature was 12–13 mostly small, cross-sectional, hospital-based studies with inconsistent definitions of acute and persistent psychosis, little control of polydrug use or medication, and no pooled estimates.

funding.funder: No research funding statement. Acknowledgments: the first author held an Australian Postgraduate Award and acknowledges a Macquarie University Psychology Department Higher Degree Research Grant.
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare no commercial or financial relationships that could be construed as a potential conflict of interest. The handling editor (Julia M. Lappin, University of New South Wales) declared a shared affiliation, without other collaboration, with the first author.
funding.affiliations_note: Department of Psychology, Macquarie University, and School of Psychology, University of New South Wales, Sydney, Australia. Article received 28 June 2018, accepted 19 September 2018.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective study enrolling people at a first methamphetamine-associated psychotic episode with toxicology-confirmed use, assessed with the same structured, item-level instruments at fixed intervals after verified abstinence, against first-episode schizophrenia patients matched on age, sex, other drug use and antipsychotic exposure, with assessors blind to group; and, for the existing studies, a registered systematic review that pools item-level differences with confidence intervals.

domains.note: Three databases (PubMed, PsycINFO, ScienceDirect), reference lists and Google Scholar were searched with printed terms against inclusion criteria set before the search (Overview of review › Inclusion criteria; Search approach). There are no search dates, record counts or excluded-study list, one author conducted the review (Author contributions), and Hajebi et al. (2018), used in the text and Table 2, is missing from Table 1.

Table 2 records for each of 13 studies the comparison groups, acute/chronic distinction, abstinence and factors controlled, and the text names study limitations, but there is no validated tool. Okada, Yamamuro and Srisurapanont are assigned to acute or chronic psychosis differently across Table 1, Table 2 and the text, and the review's main contrasts depend on that assignment.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: Neither author appears in any of the 140 references, including the 13 compared studies (References; Tables 1–2).

The abstract concludes that acute methamphetamine psychosis could be clinically distinguished from schizophrenia by thought disorder, hallucination type and parietal-mediated attention, while the body calls the thought-disorder evidence 'indirect and inconclusive' and the hallucination comparisons not 'reliable' (Positive symptoms › Acute, 3rd–4th paragraphs) and the parietal link rests on one attention test without imaging (Cognitive symptoms › Acute, 2nd paragraph). The management paragraph states that acute symptoms will resolve with abstinence, citing a StatPearls chapter (Summary and conclusions, 3rd paragraph).

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for similarity and difference between methamphetamine psychosis and schizophrenia
domains.note: Neither side is under-represented: similar and divergent findings are reported study by study, and the introduction sets out competing explanations (shared vulnerability, methamphetamine-caused schizophrenia, a distinct disorder). The limitations section's arguments on power and total-score scales run only toward differences being missed (Methodological limitations, 3rd paragraph).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: High, because the abstract's central conclusion, that acute methamphetamine psychosis can be told apart from schizophrenia, rests on evidence the body itself calls indirect or inconclusive; the search and the appraisal of studies are reported but incomplete. It may be cited as a map of the 12–13 direct-comparison studies and their shared limitations (small, mostly hospital samples; unreported abstinence; uncontrolled polydrug use and medication) and for the point that few studies separate acute from persistent psychosis. It may not be cited for any symptom that distinguishes the two conditions, nor for its introductory prevalence and duration figures.

key_findings.finding: The review identified twelve studies directly comparing methamphetamine psychosis with schizophrenia or primary psychosis, published 1990–2017, with per-study sizes of 22 to 285 as printed; a thirteenth, a 12-month prospective study (Hajebi et al., 2018), is appraised in Table 2 and used in the text but absent from Table 1.
key_findings.locator: Overview of review › Inclusion criteria and Search approach; Table 1; Table 2

key_findings.finding: Positive-symptom severity did not differ between methamphetamine psychosis and schizophrenia in most acute-sample comparisons: PANSS in Medhus et al. (2013; 9 vs 33) and Okada et al. (2016; 21 vs 14), BPRS in Hides et al. (2015; substance-induced vs primary psychotic disorder among 198 people who use methamphetamine), and PANSS at admission, discharge, 6 and 12 months in Hajebi et al. (2018).
key_findings.locator: Positive symptoms › Acute meth psychosis vs. schizophrenia, 2nd paragraph; Table 1 rows 107, 110, 111
key_findings.note: The text attributes a BPRS result to Okada et al. (ref 111), but Table 1 lists PANSS for that study; see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Shelly et al. (2016; methamphetamine psychosis within 4 weeks of use n=33, schizophrenia n=69, SCID-I): voices conversing 48.5% vs 20.3%; thought broadcasting 42% in schizophrenia vs 24%, significant only after controlling for age; no difference in other first-rank symptoms.
key_findings.locator: Positive symptoms › Acute meth psychosis vs. schizophrenia, 4th paragraph; Table 1 row 112; Table 2 row 112
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: voices conversing OR about 3.7 (95% CI 1.5–9.1); thought broadcasting OR about 2.3 (0.9–5.7) unadjusted.

key_findings.finding: Srisurapanont et al. (2011; 168 methamphetamine psychosis vs 169 schizophrenia, recent use within the past week, Manchester Scale): Table 1 reports higher methamphetamine-group scores for delusions, hallucinations and incoherent speech, with incoherent speech the only item that differentiated the groups on differential item functioning analysis; negative-symptom severity did not differ.
key_findings.locator: Table 1 row 113; Positive symptoms › Acute, 3rd paragraph; Negative symptoms › Acute, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Table 1 prints n=61 for this study against groups of 168 and 169. The text uses this study as evidence that thought disorder marks schizophrenia without giving the direction of the incoherent-speech difference, while Table 1 places the higher score in the methamphetamine group; the direction must be checked in the primary paper.

key_findings.finding: Chen et al. (2015; healthy controls 67, methamphetamine use without psychosis 25, acute psychosis 50, persistent psychosis beyond 1 month of abstinence 56, schizophrenia 54): persistent psychosis equalled schizophrenia on BPRS total and positive scores, both above acute psychosis; negative symptoms schizophrenia > persistent > acute; on BACS, persistent psychosis equalled schizophrenia and both were below acute psychosis and methamphetamine use without psychosis, which did not differ from controls.
key_findings.locator: Table 1 row 105; Positive symptoms › Chronic, 2nd paragraph; Negative symptoms › Chronic; Cognitive symptoms › Chronic, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: The acute group was assessed about 9 weeks after its episode (Table 2), so its lower symptom scores may reflect resolution. Table 1 also says 160 people who used methamphetamine, but the three methamphetamine groups sum to 131.

key_findings.finding: Wang et al. (2016; persistent methamphetamine psychosis beyond 1 month of abstinence vs schizophrenia, 53 vs 53 in Table 1): similar delusion patterns and auditory hallucinations; visual and tactile hallucinations more frequent in methamphetamine psychosis; schizophrenia had more negative symptoms overall, with more blunted affect, emotional withdrawal and motor retardation.
key_findings.locator: Table 1 row 115; Positive symptoms › Chronic, 1st paragraph; Negative symptoms › Chronic
key_findings.note: The text gives 52 methamphetamine-psychosis participants and names conceptual disorganization as greater in schizophrenia; Table 1 gives 53 and names unusual thought content.

key_findings.finding: McKetin et al. (2017; 284 people with methamphetamine dependence: 110 without psychosis, 85 transient, 37 persistent beyond 1 month of abstinence, 52 primary psychosis; CIDI lifetime symptoms): no significant difference between persistent methamphetamine psychosis and primary psychosis on any positive symptom; the primary-psychosis group also used methamphetamine.
key_findings.locator: Table 1 row 109; Positive symptoms › Chronic, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: Table 1 says the persistent group exceeded the transient group on lifetime visual, olfactory and tactile hallucinations; the text says the persistent and primary groups reported fewer visual and tactile hallucinations than the transient group. The two cannot both be right.

key_findings.finding: Negative symptoms were milder in methamphetamine psychosis than in schizophrenia in the detailed comparisons: Tomiyama (1990; 11 vs 11, SANS) found less affective flattening and alogia but similar avolition–apathy, anhedonia–asociality and attention; Hajebi et al. (2018) found more severe negative symptoms in non-affective psychosis at admission and discharge.
key_findings.locator: Negative symptoms › Acute, 2nd paragraph; Negative symptoms › Chronic; Table 1 row 114

key_findings.finding: Cognition: Jacobs et al. (2008; 19 methamphetamine psychosis vs 20 paranoid schizophrenia) found no difference in any domain; Ezzatpanah et al. (2014; 30 vs 30 vs 30 healthy controls) found both psychosis groups below controls on WCST, Stroop, VSAT and Wechsler Memory Scale, with schizophrenia worse than methamphetamine psychosis only on VSAT; Yamamuro et al. (2015; 15 vs 19) found no BACS differences.
key_findings.locator: Cognitive symptoms › Acute, 1st–2nd paragraphs; Cognitive symptoms › Chronic, 1st paragraph; Table 1 rows 106, 108, 116

key_findings.finding: Prevalence figures cited in the introduction (second-hand, not appraised by the review): 7% to 76% across studies; a 2018 meta-analysis (Lecomte et al.) gave 36.5% for methamphetamine-induced psychotic disorder, 42.7% lifetime and 43.3% among people with methamphetamine use disorder; in an Australian non-treatment sample 13% screened positive for psychosis at assessment and 23% reported clinically significant symptoms in the past year; 60% of a US sample with methamphetamine dependence reported at least one psychotic symptom; risk 2–3 times the general population for recreational use and 11 times for regular use; mean 1.7 years from first use to onset.
key_findings.note: Secondary citations; each must be checked in its primary source before use. The 11-fold figure is cited to a paper whose title concerns crystalline methamphetamine and dependence (ref 41).

key_findings.finding: Duration figures cited (second-hand): most symptoms resolve within 1 month; up to 30% persist up to 6 months after abstinence; 15–28% of admitted patients needed more than 2–3 months in hospital; 10–28% remained psychotic beyond 6 months; 28% had schizophrenia-like symptoms 8–12 years after abstinence (a 1967 Japanese study); a 7% risk of psychotic symptoms during abstinent periods (McKetin et al., 2013); 5% of abstinent people with methamphetamine dependence met criteria for a psychotic disorder at 3-year follow-up.
key_findings.note: Secondary citations from heterogeneous, mostly hospital samples; not appraised by the review.

key_findings.finding: Diagnostic transitions cited (second-hand): 38.8% of Thai patients first hospitalized with methamphetamine psychosis had a schizophrenia diagnosis at 5 years; 5.0% of Chinese patients had their diagnosis changed to schizophrenia; 19.1% to 30% of people admitted with amphetamine-induced psychosis later received a schizophrenia diagnosis in register studies.
key_findings.locator: The relationship between METH-induced psychosis and schizophrenia, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Risk factors cited (second-hand): younger age at first use and larger amounts used, family history of schizophrenia, crystalline methamphetamine, and current use (about 5 times higher odds of psychotic symptoms during periods of use, with a dose-response relation).
key_findings.locator: Acute methamphetamine psychosis, 2nd–3rd paragraphs; The relationship between METH-induced psychosis and schizophrenia, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Indirect comparisons only (different samples, not head-to-head): negative symptoms in 25% and 21.4% of hospitalized methamphetamine-psychosis samples versus 58% (and 50–90% at first episode) in schizophrenia; visual hallucinations in 46.5% and tactile in 21.3% of one methamphetamine-psychosis sample and visual in 68.8% of another, versus 16–27% in schizophrenia. The authors state these hallucination comparisons are not based on direct comparisons.
key_findings.locator: Negative symptoms › Acute, 2nd paragraph; Positive symptoms › Acute, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Studies that did not report abstinence were classed by the authors as acute methamphetamine psychosis; the authors identify mixing of acute and persistent cases, small samples, uncontrolled polydrug use and medication, hospital samples and total-score scales as the main limitations of the literature.
key_findings.locator: Methodological limitations and considerations, 1st and 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Management remarks are explicitly labelled by the authors as not clinical recommendations: second-generation antipsychotics suggested as possibly appropriate for persistent methamphetamine psychosis, with caution about extrapyramidal effects of first-generation drugs; the authors call for randomized trials.

In its summary, the review cites ref. 140 (Farnia et al., 2014; by its title a randomized trial of aripiprazole versus risperidone for amphetamine-induced psychosis), with ref. 56, for the statement that first-generation antipsychotics such as haloperidol carry an elevated risk of extrapyramidal symptoms in methamphetamine-induced psychosis and should be used carefully; no results of that trial are reported, and the authors label their management remarks as not clinical recommendations.
key_findings.note: Added by the editor during review round 1 so that card and claim agree; the finding was first located by AI reader 2 and has not yet been re-found by a reader who had not seen it.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 summarizes McKetin et al. (2017) as persistent methamphetamine psychosis exceeding transient psychosis on lifetime visual, olfactory and tactile hallucinations; the text says persistent psychosis and primary psychosis reported fewer visual and tactile hallucinations than transient psychosis; Figure 1 orders visual and tactile hallucinations acute > chronic > schizophrenia.
reporting_issues.consequence: The review's headline that visual and tactile hallucinations mark acute methamphetamine psychosis depends on which version is right; the primary paper must be read before any claim about hallucination modality by phase.

reporting_issues.issue: The DSM-5 rule is stated two ways: a psychosis persisting longer than 6 months warrants a primary diagnosis (Relationship section, 1st and 3rd paragraphs), but the limitations section says patients psychotic more than 1 month after stopping should, under the DSM, receive a primary diagnosis (Methodological limitations, 2nd paragraph).
reporting_issues.consequence: The diagnostic threshold that separates substance-induced from primary psychosis must be taken from DSM-5 itself, not from this review.

reporting_issues.issue: Group sizes in Table 1 do not add up: Chen et al. (row 105) lists 160 people who used methamphetamine but its methamphetamine groups sum to 131 (25+50+56; 252 total with 67 controls and 54 schizophrenia); Medhus et al. (row 110) prints n=285 against groups of 33 and 9, while Table 2 says 35 of 38 tested positive for methamphetamine and that 13% had taken it recently; Srisurapanont et al. (row 113) prints n=61 against groups of 168 and 169.
reporting_issues.consequence: Sample sizes for these studies must be taken from the primary papers.

reporting_issues.issue: The same study is described with different instruments: Chen et al. (105) is said to use the PANSS for positive symptoms (Positive symptoms › Chronic, 2nd paragraph) but the BPRS in Table 1 and in the negative-symptom section; Okada et al. (111) is cited for a BPRS result (Positive symptoms › Acute, 2nd paragraph) but listed with the PANSS in Table 1 and in the negative-symptom section.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor for conclusions; instruments must be checked at source.

reporting_issues.issue: Acute versus chronic classification is inconsistent: Okada et al. (111) is classed as acute in Table 1 although Table 2 says 15 of its 21 methamphetamine participants had residual and late-onset psychosis; Yamamuro et al. (116) is classed chronic in Table 1, assumed acute in Table 2, and described as acute in the chronic positive-symptom paragraph; Srisurapanont et al. (113) is classed acute in Table 1 while Table 2 says it could include both.
reporting_issues.consequence: The review's acute-versus-chronic contrasts, which carry its main conclusions, rest on partly arbitrary assignments.

reporting_issues.issue: Wang et al. (115): 52 methamphetamine-psychosis participants in the text versus 53 in Table 1; conceptual disorganization (text) versus unusual thought content (Table 1) as the item greater in schizophrenia.
reporting_issues.consequence: The thought-disorder conclusion partly rests on this study, so the item matters; check at source.

reporting_issues.issue: The Ezzatpanah et al. VSAT result is called sustained visual attention in the cognitive section and selective visual attention in the abstract and summary.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the parietal-cortex inference in the abstract relies on the selective-attention reading.

reporting_issues.issue: Two secondary citations do not obviously match their claims by title: the 11-fold psychosis risk for regular use cites a paper on crystalline methamphetamine and dependence (ref 41), and the 58% prevalence of negative symptoms in schizophrenia cites a paper on cardiovascular risk and smoking in a schizophrenia cohort (ref 135).
reporting_issues.consequence: Neither figure should be reused without checking the cited source.

reporting_issues.issue: Figure 1 is an image (Venn diagram); only its legend could be read as text.
reporting_issues.consequence: The figure's content was appraised from the legend only.

design_detail: Systematic review without meta-analysis (PRISMA; PROSPERO 42016052223) of observational studies comparing adults who use illicit methamphetamine or amphetamine with and without psychotic symptoms or disorder (MAP vs MNP) on sociodemographic, drug-use, psychiatric, family-history and trauma factors. 20 papers from 13 study populations (5476 participants as reported); 11 cross-sectional and 2 cohort designs. Quality rated with a modified Newcastle–Ottawa Scale built for the review; evidence for each factor graded with reference to GRADE; synthesis by narrative and counting of studies with and without a significant association.
can_establish: Which factors have been reported, and how often, as correlates of psychotic symptoms among people who use methamphetamine, and how weak the underlying study designs are.
cannot_establish: That any factor, including frequency of use, causes psychosis, or how large any association is across studies: there is no pooled estimate, most included studies are cross-sectional with lifetime outcomes, and the comparison is between people who use methamphetamine with and without psychosis, not between people who use it and people who do not.

sample.recruitment: Included populations came from community and dance-venue samples, needle-syringe programmes, outpatient and residential treatment, psychiatric inpatient units, detention centres and prison (Table 1): 4 in Asia (China, Taiwan, Thailand, Malaysia), 5 in Australia, 3 in the USA and 1 in Sweden (Results › Study characteristics, 2nd paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Adults (>17 years) with illicit methamphetamine or amphetamine use in the past 12 months; those with current or lifetime psychotic symptoms compared with those without, psychosis measured by a validated instrument or structured interview; people with methamphetamine as primary drug analysed separately. Case reports, reviews and animal studies excluded (Method, 2nd paragraph; Study design and data extraction, 1st paragraph).
sample.demographics: Not summarized across studies; Table 1 gives setting, injecting proportion and exclusion of prior psychotic disorder per study.
sample.attrition: Not applicable. Screening: 402 records, 45 duplicates removed, 320 excluded on title or abstract, 17 full texts excluded, 20 included (Abstract; Figure 1, an image, not read).
sample.selection_effects: Most populations come from treatment, needle-syringe, custodial or psychiatric settings with heavy use; the authors note these may not represent adults who use methamphetamine generally (Implications for future research, 3rd paragraph). By Table 1, seven populations did not exclude people with primary psychotic disorders (studies 1, 2, 5, 7, 9, 11, 12) and one did not screen systematically (study 10); the Discussion lists only five of these populations (Strengths and limitations, 3rd paragraph).

exposure.measurement: In the primary studies: self-reported frequency, amount, duration, age at onset and route of methamphetamine use; dependence by DSM-IV symptom counts or the Severity of Dependence Scale. No biological verification described. In 8 of 13 populations, current use was related to a lifetime psychosis outcome, so use and psychosis may refer to different times (Strengths and limitations, 2nd paragraph).
exposure.polysubstance: Only six included papers (from five populations) adjusted for other drug use (Strengths and limitations, 4th paragraph). Alcohol dependence was associated with psychosis in 3 populations and frequent cannabis use in 1 (Table 2), so other drugs are both a confounder and a correlate.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Varied; not summarized. One included population required at least 3 weeks' abstinence (study 13, Table 1).

comparison.controls: People who use methamphetamine without psychotic symptoms or disorder (MNP), within the same populations. No comparison with people who do not use methamphetamine.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Whether psychosis or its risk factors preceded methamphetamine use is generally unknown in the cross-sectional studies; the authors state that the literature is insufficient to support a causal association (Strengths and limitations, 3rd paragraph).

outcomes.instruments: Psychosis measures in the primary studies: BPRS (current, past month), a 7-item psychosis screen (past year), PRISM-IV, MINI, MINI-plus and DIGS-C (current or lifetime psychotic disorder), hospitalisation coded as substance-induced psychosis (registry), the Methamphetamine Experience Questionnaire (lifetime paranoia) and CIDI-based questions (Table 1 and notes).
outcomes.validity_norms: Study quality by a modified Newcastle–Ottawa Scale developed for this review (representativeness 3, risk-factor assessment 3, psychosis absent at start 2, comparability and confounding 2, outcome assessment 3; total 13), which the authors acknowledge is not validated (Quality assessment; Strengths and limitations, 1st paragraph). Per-study scores are in Table 3, an online appendix not read.
outcomes.operationalization: A factor counts as associated when a primary study reports a significant association; Table 2 sorts studies into 'association' and 'no association' rows (vote counting). Outcome-level certainty judged with reference to GRADE by two authors.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable at review level; not addressed. 22 factors were synthesized from primary studies that each tested many correlates.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: No meta-analysis: it was planned for factors reported in three or more studies with acceptable heterogeneity, but inconsistent reporting prevented it (Study synthesis). No pooled estimates, I², τ², prediction intervals or publication-bias tests. Estimates quoted from single studies: frequency of use, 3 to 11 times higher odds of psychosis across four studies (intervals not given except one); within-person, 16 or more days of use per month vs fewer, OR 11.2 (95% CI 5.9–21.1) (McKetin et al., 2013); dependence vs none, 2 to 3 times higher odds (Ding et al., 2014; Kalayasiri et al., 2009, 2014); family history of schizophrenia, OR 5.4 (95% CI 2.0–14.7) (Chen et al., 2003); three or more adverse childhood experiences, OR 4.5 (95% CI 1.6–12.6) (Ding et al., 2014); hospitalisation for substance-induced psychosis, education OR 0.8 (95% CI 0.7–1.0) and past-month homelessness OR 2.5 (95% CI 1.1–5.3) (Rognli et al., 2014) (Results, factor sections).
analysis.covariates: Not applicable at review level. Moderators were discussed only qualitatively and at study level (current vs lifetime outcome, setting, East Asian populations for duration of use); no formal moderator analysis.
analysis.preregistration_detail: PROSPERO 42016052223, registered before data extraction (whether before searching and screening is not stated). The protocol was updated to add a Google Scholar forward-citation search after reference-list screening found five further citations (Method, 1st and 4th paragraphs).
analysis.selective_reporting: Search: MEDLINE (Ovid), PsycINFO and Embase from inception to 8 December 2016, no language restriction, plus reference lists of earlier reviews and a forward-citation search; the main search required a 'risk factor' concept, and the supplementary searches found five further citations (Method, 3rd and 4th paragraphs). No grey literature or registries. Overlap: earlier narrative reviews (Bramness et al., 2012; Glasner-Edwards and Mooney, 2014; Rognli and Bramness, 2015; Bramness and Rognli, 2016) and a 2004 systematic review of stimulant psychosis (Curran et al.) cited in the Introduction. The synthesis omits two findings that Table 1 reports for study 4 (transient symptoms associated with male sex and earlier onset of use) from the gender and age-at-onset rows of Table 2.
analysis.power: Not applicable. Vote counting treats non-significant results in small samples as evidence of no association.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Frequency of use was associated with psychotic symptoms in four populations and not in four others; dependence was associated in four by the review's count, but Table 1 records one of those four (Ding et al., 2014) as finding no association with dependence. The review dismisses the null frequency studies as lifetime-outcome, recall-biased and lower quality, yet Table 1 shows two of the four (McKetin et al., 2010; Hides et al., 2015) related current psychosis to current use, and their quality ratings overlap those of the positive studies. The strongest evidence is one within-person cohort (McKetin et al., 2013; OR 11.2). Certainty was judged moderate for frequency and low to very low for every other factor, and the authors state the evidence is insufficient to support causation.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says frequency of use and severity of dependence were "consistently found to be associated with psychosis" (Abstract, Results), and the conclusion calls them the most consistent predictors (Conclusion). The Discussion reads the pattern as adding to the concept that greater use results in a greater likelihood of psychosis (Discussion, 1st paragraph) while the limitations section says causation is not supported (Strengths and limitations, 3rd paragraph). 'Consistently' does not describe a four-to-four split for frequency, the dependence count includes a study the review's own table lists as null, and the moderate certainty for frequency rests on upgrading for effect size and a dose–response gradient from a single study without downgrading for that inconsistency.

timeline.event: Narrative review of amphetamine-induced psychosis, cited here as one of three earlier reviews without systematic methods.

Prospective within-person cohort of people with methamphetamine dependence: odds of psychotic symptoms during months of 16 or more days of use OR 11.2 (95% CI 5.9–21.1) as quoted in this review; the basis of its moderate certainty for frequency.
Narrative review of methamphetamine psychosis, cited here as an earlier non-systematic review (and, apparently in error, in place of an included primary study; see reporting issues).
Later systematic review and meta-analysis of mental-health outcomes of amphetamine use, including psychosis; appraised in its own card.

replication.where_it_stands: The within-person, dose-related association between days of methamphetamine use and psychotic symptoms rests mainly on one prospective cohort; the cross-sectional literature is split and mostly measures lifetime outcomes. This review adds a structured inventory and a quality rating, not a pooled estimate.

funding.funder: Australian National Health and Medical Research Council postgraduate scholarship (Grant 1093778), a stipend to the first author during PhD candidature (Funding).
funding.declared_conflicts: Dan Lubman has provided consultancy advice to Lundbeck and Indivior and received travel support and speaker honoraria from AstraZeneca, Bristol Myers Squibb, Janssen, Lundbeck and Servier. No other conflicts declared (Declaration of Conflicting Interests).
funding.affiliations_note: Turning Point, Eastern Health and Monash University (Arunogiri, Lubman); University of Otago (Foulds); National Drug Research Institute, Curtin University (McKetin). By the first three author names shown in the reference list, review authors co-authored at least included studies 1, 3, 4 and 5 (McKetin) and 1 and 4 (Lubman), including the cohort that carries the moderate rating; screening, extraction and quality rating were done by the two authors who were not on those studies (Arunogiri and Foulds). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: An individual-participant-data analysis, or new prospective cohorts, of people who use methamphetamine without prior psychotic disorder, with contemporaneous timeline follow-back of methamphetamine and other drug use (with biological checks), repeated structured psychosis assessments, within-person analysis adjusted for cannabis and alcohol, and pre-registered definitions of each risk factor.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Items 11, 12 and 15 do not apply because no meta-analysis was performed. One critical flaw (no list of excluded full texts) with several non-critical weaknesses gives low confidence under AMSTAR 2. Confidence in the headline conclusions is further reduced by internal inconsistencies in how studies were counted for frequency and dependence (see reporting issues), which AMSTAR 2 does not score directly.

key_findings.finding: Search of MEDLINE (Ovid), PsycINFO and Embase from inception to 8 December 2016 without language restriction, plus reference lists and a forward-citation search; 402 records screened, 20 papers from 13 populations included, 5476 participants as reported.
key_findings.locator: Abstract; Method, 3rd and 4th paragraphs; Results › Study characteristics, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Sample sizes in Table 1 sum to 5472; see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Eleven of 13 populations were studied cross-sectionally; five measured current psychosis (studies 1–5) and eight lifetime disorder or symptoms (studies 6–13).

Quality scores on the modified Newcastle–Ottawa Scale ranged from 5 to 12 of 13 (mean 7.85, SD 2.08); the commonest weaknesses were failure to exclude pre-existing psychotic disorder and insufficient control for other drug use. Only one population (McKetin et al., 2013) was rated in the top band.
key_findings.locator: Risk of bias within studies; Table 1

key_findings.finding: No meta-analysis was possible; synthesis was narrative, by counting studies with and without a significant association.

Frequency of use: associated with psychosis in four populations (McKetin et al., 2006, 2013; Ding et al., 2014; Kalayasiri et al., 2009), with odds 3 to 11 times higher in people who used more frequently; not associated in four (Glasner-Edwards et al., 2008; Hides et al., 2015; McKetin et al., 2010; Rognli et al., 2014). Rated the only factor with moderate certainty.
key_findings.locator: Results › Dose-amount and frequency of MA use; Table 2; Risk of bias across studies

key_findings.finding: In the one prospective within-person cohort (McKetin et al., 2013), which controlled for other drug use among other confounders, use on 16 or more days a month carried an odds ratio of 11.2 (95% CI 5.9–21.1) for psychotic symptoms, which the review describes as a comparison with use on fewer than 16 days.
key_findings.locator: Results › Dose-amount and frequency of MA use
key_findings.note: In the primary study as read for the encyclopedia (sc_mcketin_2013, Table), 11.2 compares months with 16–28 days of use with months of no use, and 1–15 days against no use gives 4.0; the review's comparator appears to be a misdescription (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Severity of dependence: associated in four populations by the review's count (dependent vs non-dependent odds 2 to 3 times higher), not associated in one (Hides et al., 2015).
key_findings.locator: Results › Severity of MA dependence; Table 2
key_findings.note: Table 1 lists Ding et al. (2014), one of the four, as not associated with dependence.

key_findings.finding: Amount of use was associated in three of four populations, all with lifetime outcomes; route of use (injecting) was not associated in any of four; age at onset and years of use gave inconsistent results.
key_findings.locator: Table 2; Results › Duration; Route of MA use

key_findings.finding: Sociodemographic factors (age, sex, employment, income, education) were generally not associated; one registry cohort found fewer years of schooling (OR 0.8, 95% CI 0.7–1.0) and recent homelessness (OR 2.5, 95% CI 1.1–5.3) associated with hospitalisation for substance-induced psychosis.
key_findings.note: Table 1 reports that in study 4 transient symptoms were associated with male sex, which the gender row of Table 2 omits.

key_findings.finding: Alcohol dependence was associated with psychosis in three populations and frequent cannabis use in one; antisocial personality or conduct disorder in four; current major depression in three; family history of schizophrenia in one (OR 5.4, 95% CI 2.0–14.7); three or more adverse childhood experiences in one (OR 4.5, 95% CI 1.6–12.6).
key_findings.locator: Table 2; Results › Other drug use, Personality factors, Family history, Trauma

key_findings.finding: Certainty was low to very low for all factors except frequency of use; the authors state the literature is insufficient to support a causal association.
key_findings.locator: Risk of bias across studies; Strengths and limitations, 3rd paragraph; Table 2 footnote b

key_findings.finding: Only six included papers adjusted for other drug use.

The Introduction cites a prevalence of psychotic symptoms of 15–23% among people using methamphetamine in community settings and up to 60% among people dependent on it in treatment; the Discussion cites up to 30% transition to persistent psychotic illness in longitudinal studies.
key_findings.locator: Introduction, 2nd paragraph; Strengths and limitations, 5th paragraph
key_findings.note: Background figures from cited studies, not results of this review.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 lists Ding et al. (2014) as not associated with methamphetamine dependence, but Table 2 counts it among the four studies in which dependence was associated with psychosis, and the text uses it for the 2-to-3-fold odds.
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Table 1 (study 9); Table 2 (Dependence); Results › Severity of MA dependence
reporting_issues.consequence: The 'consistent' dependence association may rest on three populations, all rated in the lowest quality band (studies 2, 11 and 12).

reporting_issues.issue: The null frequency studies are described as having measured lifetime psychosis (Table 2 comment) and three of them as reporting lifetime substance-induced psychotic disorder (text), but Table 1 shows McKetin et al. (2010) used a current (past-year) screen and Hides et al. (2015) related current psychotic disorder to current use; Rognli et al. (2014) used hospitalisation during follow-up.
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Table 2 (Frequency); Results › Dose-amount and frequency of MA use; Table 1
reporting_issues.consequence: The reason given for discounting the null studies, and hence for the moderate certainty rating, is not supported by the review's own table.

reporting_issues.issue: The statement that studies finding a frequency association were of higher quality is followed by a citation list that includes Chen et al. and Sulaiman et al., which are not among the four frequency-positive studies; by the Table 1 bands, positive studies (+, ++, ++, +++) and null studies (+, ++, ++, +) differ only by the single top-band study.
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Results › Dose-amount and frequency of MA use; Table 1
reporting_issues.consequence: The quality argument rests on one study.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 totals do not match Table 1 sample sizes: study 3 behaves as N=79 in every total (Table 1 prints 75; overall 5476 vs a Table 1 sum of 5472); the gender row says 6 studies but cites 7; the polydrug 'association' row cites studies 8 and 12 but its N (268) equals studies 3 and 9, which Table 1 lists with polydrug or other drug use as correlates (study 8 also appears in the 'no association' row); totals for frequency 'no association' (2503 vs 2508–2512), dependence 'association' (1577 vs 1450) and family history 'association' (912 vs 723) cannot be reproduced from the cited studies (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Participant counts per factor are unreliable; cite the primary studies for numbers.

reporting_issues.issue: Among studies finding no association with use variables, the text cites Glasner-Edwards and Mooney (2014), a narrative review, instead of the included study (Glasner-Edwards et al., 2008).
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Results › Patterns of MA use, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Citation error.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion lists seven papers (five populations) as not excluding primary psychotic disorders, but Table 1 records three further populations that did not exclude them (studies 1, 5 and 7), including one of the frequency-positive studies (McKetin et al., 2006, in which 10% had a previous psychotic disorder).
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Strengths and limitations, 3rd paragraph; Table 1
reporting_issues.consequence: Contamination by primary psychosis is understated, including in evidence for the frequency association.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 reports that in study 4 transient symptoms were associated with male sex and earlier onset of use, yet the text states that sex was not associated in any study and Table 2 omits study 4 from the gender and age-at-onset rows.
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Table 1 (study 4); Results › Sociodemographic factors; Table 2
reporting_issues.consequence: Findings from the highest-quality study are left out of the synthesis for two factors.

reporting_issues.issue: Quality bands overlap: '+' is defined as a total of 0–6 and '++' as 6–10.
reporting_issues.consequence: A score of 6 cannot be placed; minor.

reporting_issues.issue: The review describes the odds ratio of 11.2 (5.9–21.1) from McKetin et al. (2013) as 16 or more days of use a month compared with fewer than 16 days; in the primary study as read for the encyclopedia (sc_mcketin_2013), 11.2 compares months of 16–28 days of use with months of no use, and 1–15 days against no use gives 4.0.
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Results › Dose-amount and frequency of MA use
reporting_issues.consequence: Quoted from this review, 11.2 overstates the contrast between heavier and lighter use; cite the primary study with its reference category.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 lists Sulaiman et al. (2014; study 8) as finding no association with money spent on methamphetamine and names no amount variable among its correlates, yet Table 2 and the text count it among the three studies in which greater amounts of use went with psychosis.
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Table 1 (study 8); Table 2 (Amount of use); Results › Dose-amount and frequency of MA use
reporting_issues.consequence: The amount-of-use association may rest on two of four studies rather than three, the same pattern as the dependence count in reporting issue 0.

editorial_corrections.reason: Language (METHODS §9): 8 replacements, no change of meaning, number or citation; list in data/verification/language-2026-10-16b.json

design_detail: Short narrative review in CMAJ (4 pages, 38 references, single author) on the pharmacology of smoked methamphetamine hydrochloride: pharmacokinetics compared with therapeutic amphetamines, mechanism of monoamine release, the role of dopamine in liking and craving, whether methamphetamine damages the brain, and medication development. No methods section; peer reviewed according to the footnote.
can_establish: How a neurochemist who studies post-mortem brain in people who used methamphetamine summarized the drug's mechanism and the state of the brain-damage question in 2008, and which primary sources support each statement.
cannot_establish: Whether methamphetamine causes loss of dopamine terminals, cognitive impairment or any other harm in humans: the article reviews no cognitive data, gives no systematic account of the evidence, and its human neurochemical statements rest mainly on one post-mortem study from the author's laboratory.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable: narrative review; no search or selection method reported.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not reported.
sample.demographics: Not applicable.
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: Sources chosen by the author. Human evidence on dopamine and the dopamine transporter is cited only to the author's own post-mortem study (reference 20, Moszczynska et al., 2004); none of the in vivo PET studies of the dopamine transporter in people who use methamphetamine is cited. One source is a non-peer-reviewed drug-information website (reference 9) and one is a personal communication from Health Canada.

exposure.measurement: Not applicable (review).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Reported only as pharmacokinetic comparisons from cited studies: peak plasma d-amphetamine of about 10–110 ng/mL with long-term therapeutic extended-release mixed amphetamine salts; peak plasma methamphetamine of about 50 ng/mL after a single 30 mg smoked dose in a laboratory study; blood concentrations of 15–1600 ng/mL (median 190 ng/mL) in people using methamphetamine recreationally, sampled in a police investigation; elimination half-life about 11 hours for smoked, intranasal and intravenous routes (Introduction, 1st paragraph; Therapeutic uses, 3rd paragraph).
exposure.polysubstance: Not discussed.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: Not applicable (review).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not discussed. The article does not raise pre-existing differences or confounding as explanations for any human finding.

outcomes.instruments: Not applicable. Topics covered: monoamine release, cardiovascular activation, striatal dopamine and dopamine transporter, brain structure by imaging, relapse treatment.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Brain damage' is discussed as loss of striatal dopamine nerve terminals (animal data) versus lower dopamine and dopamine-transporter levels (human post-mortem data); cognitive impairment is mentioned but not defined or measured.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: None reported for any brain or cognitive outcome; human findings are described qualitatively (low striatal dopamine in post-mortem brain; modestly decreased striatal dopamine transporter in some people who use methamphetamine). Quantitative statements are pharmacokinetic only (see exposure).
analysis.covariates: Not applicable.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Not applicable to a narrative review; no protocol.
analysis.selective_reporting: The human neurochemical evidence is limited to the author's own post-mortem study; in vivo imaging of the dopamine transporter, including longitudinal evidence of change with abstinence, is not cited. No cognitive studies are cited although cognitive impairment is mentioned twice.
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: The article reports that high-dose regimens damage striatal dopamine terminals in animals; that in humans post-mortem striatal dopamine is low in people who used methamphetamine and the dopamine transporter is modestly lower in some; that whether this reflects terminal loss or has clinical consequences is debated; that there is no evidence of dopamine-terminal damage at therapeutic amphetamine doses; and that imaging data are too preliminary to define a characteristic pattern of brain abnormality.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract keeps to that uncertainty (whether low dopamine represents neuronal loss is uncertain). The body goes further in two places: it calls it reasonable to expect from animal findings that terminal damage would also occur in people exposed to some dose (Does methamphetamine cause brain damage?, 2nd paragraph), and it suggests that low dopamine could explain aspects of cognitive impairment, a link for which no human data are cited (Is there a role for dopamine, 1st paragraph). The statement that the crystalline form can cause more overall harm than other forms rests on pharmacokinetic reasoning and two epidemiological sources, not on comparative harm data.

timeline.event: PET follow-up of 5 people who used methamphetamine: dopamine transporter rose with protracted abstinence, which bears on the terminal-loss question this article leaves open; not cited here.

The author's post-mortem series (Moszczynska et al., 2004), the source of this article's human dopamine and transporter statements; its numbers are summarized in the encyclopedia's card for Kish et al. (2017).
A reply titled 'Limiting production of crystal meth' (CMAJ volume 179, page 558) is linked from the PMC page; not read.

London et al. (2015), narrative review reporting conflicting VMAT2 findings in people who use methamphetamine (higher in early abstinence, lower after more than 3 months, unchanged post-mortem); appraised in sc_london_2015 from this reading batch.

Critical review by the same author concluding that it is premature to say whether recreational methamphetamine does or does not damage dopamine neurones in humans (per the encyclopedia's first-pass card).

replication.where_it_stands: The author's own later review keeps the position taken here: lower striatal dopamine and transporter levels in people who used methamphetamine are established, while whether they reflect loss of dopamine terminals, and what they mean for cognition, remain unresolved. This article adds pharmacokinetic context, not evidence on either question.

funding.funder: The author's methamphetamine studies are supported by the US National Institutes of Health, National Institute on Drug Abuse (07186) (Acknowledgments).
funding.declared_conflicts: Competing interests: none declared.
funding.affiliations_note: Human Neurochemical Pathology Laboratory, Centre for Addiction and Mental Health, Toronto. The human evidence cited comes mainly from this laboratory. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: Post-mortem studies that measure several independent dopamine-terminal markers, terminal structure and nigral cell counts in the same brains of people with documented methamphetamine exposure and of matched controls, together with in vivo imaging and cognitive testing against controls and norms followed over abstinence.

domains.note: A short CMAJ 'Mechanisms and innovations' review with no methods section and no statement of how its 38 references were found or chosen; sources include Erowid, product monographs and a personal communication.

No formal quality or risk-of-bias assessment; evidence is graded only informally (labelled preliminary, very preliminary or needing confirmation), and some statements carry no citation (for example that dopamine-receptor blockers do not block methamphetamine liking).

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own work
domains.note: Only 1 of 38 references is from the author's group (ref 20, Moszczynska et al. 2004, introduced as the author's own finding), but it is cited three times and is the sole human source for striatal dopamine depletion and the modest transporter decrease, with no imaging studies cited for that point.

Hypotheses are consistently flagged with hedges (mechanism not completely understood, probably, could involve, still debated), and treatment ideas such as deep brain stimulation or cognitive enhancers are presented as strategies that might be considered.

It reports findings against simple readings: no evidence of dopamine-terminal damage at therapeutic doses, uncertainty whether the transporter decrease reflects terminal loss, receptor blockers not blocking liking, and a negative sertraline trial.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Editors' narrative-review checklist (METHODS §5.3), applied by an independent reader (AI reader 3 (appraisal re-reading, papers read in the app's browser), 2026-10-16) after the first reading had used AMSTAR 2, which does not fit a narrative review. Overall high risk of a misleading summary: no described search or selection. The review is cited for arguments and pointers to primary studies, not as primary evidence; a second reading of the checklist is still needed.

key_findings.finding: Methamphetamine raises extracellular dopamine, serotonin and norepinephrine by promoting release from nerve endings, apparently by moving transmitter from vesicles into the cytoplasm (via VMAT2) and reversing transport through the plasma-membrane transporter; the author states the mechanism is not completely understood.
key_findings.locator: Pharmacologic actions of methamphetamine, 2nd paragraph; Figure 2 legend

key_findings.finding: Cardiovascular activation is attributed largely to norepinephrine release from sympathetic nerve endings; the alerting action and efficacy in ADHD are said to involve, at least partly, brain norepinephrine.

Methamphetamine and amphetamine share the same mechanism of action, and a direct human comparison found similar behavioural effects and potencies (Martin et al., 1971), though some differences cannot be excluded.
key_findings.locator: Therapeutic uses of methamphetamine and amphetamine, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Elimination half-life is about 11 hours for smoked, intranasal and intravenous methamphetamine.

Blood concentrations in people using methamphetamine recreationally (police investigation) ranged from 15 to 1600 ng/mL (median 190), against about 50 ng/mL peak after a single 30 mg smoked laboratory dose and about 10–110 ng/mL peak d-amphetamine with long-term therapeutic extended-release mixed amphetamine salts.
key_findings.locator: Therapeutic uses of methamphetamine and amphetamine, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: Study conditions and forensic measurements, reported for comparison of exposure levels only.

key_findings.finding: High-dose methamphetamine damages striatal dopamine nerve terminals in animals; there is no evidence of dopamine-terminal damage in humans taking therapeutic amphetamine doses; some people who use methamphetamine recreationally show modestly lower striatal dopamine transporter, and whether this means loss of terminals or has clinical consequences is debated.
key_findings.locator: Does methamphetamine cause brain damage?, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: The author's post-mortem study found low striatal dopamine in people who used methamphetamine, taken to mean that recreational doses can deplete dopamine; low dopamine is proposed as a possible partial explanation for withdrawal dysphoria and aspects of cognitive impairment.
key_findings.locator: Is there a role for dopamine in methamphetamine-craving?, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: The cognitive link is a hypothesis; no cognitive data are cited.

key_findings.finding: Imaging studies have found various structural changes in some people who use methamphetamine, but the author judges the data too preliminary to say whether any specific pattern is characteristic of chronic exposure.
key_findings.locator: Does methamphetamine cause brain damage?, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: The brain regions and neurochemicals responsible for methamphetamine liking and the transition to craving in humans are stated to be unknown; dopamine-receptor blockers are said not to block liking, and opioid antagonists partly blocked liking, arousal and craving with amphetamine in amphetamine-dependent people in preliminary data.
key_findings.locator: Is there a role for dopamine in methamphetamine-craving?, paragraphs 1–3

key_findings.finding: No medication was approved in Canada for methamphetamine relapse prevention; bupropion and naltrexone had very preliminary support, a sertraline trial suggested no benefit and possibly lower abstinence, and substitution with oral amphetamine had only pilot data.

reporting_issues.issue: The statement that dopamine-receptor blockers do not block methamphetamine liking is attributed to clinical findings without a citation.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Is there a role for dopamine in methamphetamine-craving?, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Unverifiable from the article; needs a primary source before use.

reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Is there a role for dopamine in methamphetamine-craving?, 1st paragraph; References
reporting_issues.consequence: The imaging claim has no traceable primary source in this article.

reporting_issues.issue: The suggestion from rehabilitation centres that cognitive impairment reduces programme retention is cited to reference 20, a post-mortem neurochemistry study by its title.

reporting_issues.consequence: Apparent citation mismatch; the clinical claim is unsupported here.
