verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC2413312 (all sections, Figure 1–2 legends (images), acknowledgments, competing-interests footnote and reference list; no tables; supplementary file is a French-language abstract, not read)

editorial_corrections.reason: Language (METHODS §9): 5 replacements, no change of meaning, number or citation; list in data/verification/language-2026-10-16.json

METHODS §5.3 (0.2.2): narrative reviews are appraised with the editors' checklist, not AMSTAR 2. The checklist judgments are those of AI reader 3 (appraisal re-reading, papers read in the app's browser), who read the source; the editor only transferred them.

design_detail: Systematic review and meta-analysis, an update of McKetin et al. (2019) under that review's PROSPERO protocol (CRD42017081893), following PRISMA. Medline (PubMed in the abstract), EMBASE and PsycINFO searched May 2017 and updated July 2021; English-language, peer-reviewed human studies since 1950. Included: quantitative studies of methamphetamine or amphetamine use with depression or depressive symptoms measured by a validated scale or diagnostic tool, comparing levels of use and levels of depression (the last criterion added after the protocol). 14 studies: 11 cross-sectional and 3 longitudinal; 12 on any use and 2 on use disorder. Odds ratios pooled separately for unadjusted and adjusted estimates, by design and exposure level, with fixed or random effects chosen by the significance of Cochran's Q (MetaXL). Unmeasured confounding assessed with E-values and a five-item key-covariate checklist; no risk-of-bias tool.
can_establish: That, in the 14 eligible English-language studies to 2021, methamphetamine or amphetamine use was on average associated with modestly higher odds of depressive symptoms, more consistently in the three prospective cohorts than in the cross-sectional studies.
cannot_establish: That methamphetamine causes depression or how large any effect is: the prospective evidence is three subpopulation cohorts with one or two adjusted estimates pooled, the use-disorder estimate is one cross-sectional twin study, confounding and reverse causation are not resolved by the E-value method as applied, and there are no dose–response or longitudinal use-disorder data.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable at review level; participant numbers of the included studies are not reported in the main text. Included samples (Table 1): US national household survey (middle-aged and older community adults, by its title), US 8th- and 11th-grade students, Canadian secondary-school students followed from grade 10 to 11, South African high-school students, young people aged 14–29 in rural Thailand, community sentinel samples of people who use drugs (rural US people who use stimulants; Canadian LGBT people), HIV cohorts (Canadian gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men living with HIV; US HIV-positive and HIV-negative men who have sex with men), Cambodian transgender women, Nigerian commercial motorcyclists, US mothers recruited after birth in areas with high methamphetamine use, a US sample with methamphetamine use disorder, and male monozygotic twin pairs from the US military (Vietnam era). Most studies are North American.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Peer-reviewed quantitative studies; exposure methamphetamine or amphetamine use; outcome depression or depressive symptoms on a validated or diagnostic scale; usable data (e.g. odds ratio); cross-sectional, case-control, cohort or pre-trial RCT data. Added after the protocol: comparison groups had to differ in level of methamphetamine/amphetamine exposure (studies comparing methamphetamine with other drug use excluded) and in level of depression (studies comparing depression with another disorder excluded) (2.2).
sample.demographics: Not summarized; Table 1 gives setting and data years but no sample sizes, ages or sex distributions.
sample.attrition: Review level: 6606 records, 5821 unique screened, 5255 excluded, 566 full texts assessed, 14 included (3.1; Figure 1). Attrition within the three cohort studies is not reported.
sample.selection_effects: English-only, peer-reviewed-only search with no reference-list, registry or grey-literature search; title and abstract screening by a single reviewer. Several samples are high-risk subpopulations (HIV cohorts, transgender women, LGBT people who use drugs, mothers who used methamphetamine in pregnancy), which the authors say may not generalize. No included study sampled people in treatment for methamphetamine use disorder over time, so the authors state the findings may not apply to treatment populations (Discussion, 6th paragraph; 6.1).

exposure.measurement: Self-report in all included studies as tabulated; use-disorder diagnosis by DSM-IV (past 18 months, Casaletto et al., 2015) or DSM-III (lifetime, Lin et al., 1996) (Table 1).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Any use over varying windows: past 30 days, past 3 or 6 months, past year, lifetime, or daily/weekly use during pregnancy (Table 1). The authors state they had no data to analyse amount or frequency of use (Discussion, 6th paragraph; 6.1).
exposure.polysubstance: Handled only through each study's own adjustment: other substance use is one of five key covariates (age, gender, employment, other substance use, pre-morbidity/comorbidity), and adjustment sets vary widely, from none to cannabis use alone to extensive lists (Table 3). The exposure includes amphetamine: one longitudinal study measured meth/amphetamine (speed) use (Briere et al., 2012, by its title).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable; exposure and outcome were measured concurrently in the 11 cross-sectional studies.

comparison.controls: Within each study, people reporting no use (or less use) of methamphetamine/amphetamine, or without use disorder (Table 1).
comparison.matching: None at review level; the twin study compares co-twins within monozygotic pairs (Section 5.2).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: The authors note limited data on premorbid functioning, and that genetics, family history and life stressors were rarely measured (Discussion, 6th paragraph; 6.1). Only two longitudinal estimates adjusted for earlier depressive symptoms (Briere et al., 2012; Javanbakht et al., 2020) (Table 3).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Comparison groups in sentinel drug-using samples used other drugs; in general-population and school samples other drug use varied and was adjusted for in some studies only (Table 3).

outcomes.instruments: Depressive symptom scales with varying thresholds: CES-D (continuous, ≥16, ≥22, ≥23), PHQ-9 (continuous, ≥5), HADS, BDI, BDI-II; diagnoses of major depressive disorder by DSM-IV criteria in a national survey, by SCID (Casaletto et al., 2015) and by the Diagnostic Interview Schedule for DSM-III (Lin et al., 1996) (Table 1).
outcomes.validity_norms: All instruments are validated; thresholds differ (a PHQ-9 cut-off of 5 marks mild symptoms), so depression ranges from mild screening-positive symptoms to diagnosed major depression across studies. The authors could not analyse severity or major depressive disorder separately (6.1, 3rd paragraph).
outcomes.operationalization: Depression as a binary outcome (depressed vs not, or higher vs lower level), effect measure odds ratio; unadjusted odds ratios were calculated by the reviewers from descriptive data where studies did not report them (2.4).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; six pooled estimates (Table 2) plus one sensitivity analysis, without correction.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable at review level; not reported for included studies.

analysis.effect_sizes: Pooled odds ratios (Table 2). Any use, cross-sectional: unadjusted 1.40 (95% CI 1.08–1.80), 10 estimates, random effects, Q 39.92, I² 77%; adjusted 1.66 (1.34–2.05), 4 estimates, fixed effect because Q 7.35 was not significant (editors' calculation: p≈0.06 on 3 df), I² 59%. Any use, longitudinal: unadjusted 2.05 (1.53–2.75), 2 estimates, I² 0%; adjusted 1.18 (1.08–1.28), 2 estimates, Q 1.76, I² 43% (the Results text gives 1.24, 1.14–1.34). Use disorder, cross-sectional: unadjusted 3.46 (2.04–5.89), 2 estimates, I² 0%; adjusted 2.80 (1.40–5.90), a single study. Sensitivity without the major-depression study: 1.37 (1.06–1.76). τ² and prediction intervals not reported. Editors' reproductions (inverse-variance on log odds ratios from printed intervals): the adjusted cross-sectional result is matched by DiMiceli recent use 2.60, Embry 1.33 (the value in the text, not in Table 3), Marshall 1.67 and Pluddemann 2.65 under fixed effect (1.66, 1.34–2.04; Q 7.40; I² 59%); a DerSimonian–Laird random-effects model on the same four gives 1.85 (1.28–2.69). The two adjusted longitudinal estimates printed in Table 3 (Briere 1.60, 1.10–2.30; Javanbakht 1.50, 1.10–2.30) pool to 1.55 (1.19–2.01) with Q 0.06, so neither published longitudinal value can be reproduced from the paper's own study-level table.
analysis.covariates: Review-level adjustment not possible; included estimates adjusted for different covariate sets, from none to more than ten variables (Table 3). Five key covariates were used to grade confounding risk: age, gender, employment, other substance use, pre-morbidity/comorbidity (2.6).
analysis.preregistration_detail: PROSPERO CRD42017081893, registered for the earlier, broader review that this paper updates (2.1). Deviation reported and explained: an inclusion criterion on exposure and outcome comparison groups was added beyond the protocol (2.2). Planned funnel plots, meta-regression and analyses by frequency of use and sample type were not done for lack of data (2.5; 6.1). Whether the E-value analysis was pre-specified is not stated.
analysis.selective_reporting: Study-level estimates in Table 3 do not always match those used or quoted elsewhere (see reporting issues). Forest plots are only in the supplementary file, which was not read.
analysis.power: Not assessed; most pooled estimates rest on 1–4 studies. Publication bias not assessed because there were too few estimates (2.5).

interpretation_gap.results_show: A modest positive association between any methamphetamine/amphetamine use and depressive symptoms (adjusted cross-sectional OR 1.66 from four estimates; adjusted longitudinal OR 1.18 from two cohorts, a value that does not match the paper's own study-level table), with individual cross-sectional studies split four positive and five null; a larger association for use disorder rests on two cross-sectional studies, one adjusted. No dose–response, severity or longitudinal use-disorder data.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Discussion says people who use methamphetamine have higher risks of depression and that methamphetamine use, particularly use disorder, is a potential risk factor for depression, using risk language for odds ratios. It says the E-value analysis suggests very low to low risk of the associations being explained away by unmeasured confounding in most studies, but the E-values treat odds ratios as risk ratios although screening-positive depressive symptoms are common outcomes, and are computed for point estimates only: an unadjusted, non-significant estimate (Blazer and Wu, 3.42, 0.75–15.65) is classed as low risk. The twin study is said to provide strong evidence for causal inference and to show the association cannot be explained by genetics alone; its within-pair estimate is 7.0 (1.6–30.8) from one 1992 cohort, and the drug class of its use-disorder measure must be checked (its title concerns substance abuse/dependence generally). The Discussion also states that Colyer et al. reported significantly higher risk after adjusting for polydrug use, while the review itself extracted a null unadjusted estimate for that study. The abstract does hedge ("Based on limited data") and calls for causal-framework longitudinal studies.

timeline.event: Lin et al. Vietnam-era monozygotic twin study (included): use disorder associated with major depression within twin pairs, OR 7.0 (1.6–30.8)
McKetin et al. systematic review and meta-analysis of mental-health outcomes of amphetamine use; this paper reports its pooled adjusted odds ratio for depression as 1.3 (1.2–1.4)
This update: 14 studies; adjusted ORs 1.66 cross-sectional and 1.18 longitudinal; E-value analysis added

replication.where_it_stands: Two overlapping syntheses by largely the same authors agree on a modest positive association (pooled adjusted odds ratios between about 1.2 and 1.7). Prospective evidence is three subpopulation cohorts; temporal order, dose–response and confounding by shared risk factors remain unresolved, and the authors call for causal-framework longitudinal studies.

Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: Prospective cohorts that measure methamphetamine use (frequency and amount, toxicology-verified where possible) and depression by diagnostic interview repeatedly from before or near first use, including people with use disorder in treatment and community settings, analysed with methods that address reverse causation and time-varying confounding (within-person models or target-trial emulation); and a dose–response synthesis using consistent depression definitions.

domains.domain: Item 1: research question and inclusion criteria include population, exposure, comparator and outcome
Item 2 (critical): protocol established before the review
domains.note: PROSPERO protocol registered for the earlier review; the added comparison-group criterion is reported and justified; the E-value method is not stated as pre-specified.

domains.domain: Item 3: choice of study designs explained
domains.note: Observational designs included and cohort evidence explicitly prioritized (Introduction; 2.2).
Three databases with full strings (Table S3), language restriction justified, search within 24 months of publication; no reference-list, registry, expert or grey-literature search.
Title and abstract screening by one reviewer; full texts by two independent reviewers with a third for disagreements.
Four authors extracted; independent duplicate extraction is not stated.

domains.domain: Item 7 (critical): list of excluded studies with reasons
domains.note: 552 full texts excluded; no list in the main text, and none is mentioned among the supplementary items.

domains.domain: Item 8: included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Setting, data years, exposure and outcome definitions given; no sample sizes or demographics.

domains.domain: Item 9 (critical): satisfactory technique for assessing risk of bias in individual studies
domains.note: No risk-of-bias tool; only a covariate checklist and E-values for unmeasured confounding; selection bias and exposure and outcome measurement not assessed.

domains.domain: Item 10: funding sources of included studies reported
Item 11 (critical): appropriate methods for statistical combination
domains.note: Model chosen by significance of Q, giving a fixed-effect headline estimate despite I² 59% (random effects would give about 1.85, 1.28–2.69); the longitudinal pooled estimate cannot be reproduced from the study-level table; adjusted estimates with very different covariate sets pooled together.

domains.domain: Item 12: impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: Adjusted and unadjusted estimates are separated, but no analysis by study quality.

domains.domain: Item 13 (critical): risk of bias accounted for when interpreting results
domains.note: Confounding, reverse causation, subpopulation samples and the limits of regression adjustment are discussed; the E-value interpretation overstates robustness.
Analyses stratified by design, exposure level and adjustment; mixed cross-sectional findings discussed.

domains.domain: Item 15 (critical): publication bias investigated and discussed
domains.note: Not assessed because of too few estimates; likely impact not discussed.

domains.domain: Item 16: conflicts of interest and funding of the review reported

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Four critical items fail: no list of excluded studies, no risk-of-bias assessment of the included studies, problematic meta-analytic methods (model selection by Q test with a fixed-effect headline estimate, and a longitudinal pooled estimate inconsistent with the study-level table), and no assessment of publication bias. Under AMSTAR 2 rules more than one critical flaw gives critically low confidence. The registered protocol, multi-database search and E-value analysis are real strengths, and the direction of association is consistent with the earlier review by the same group; the pooled magnitudes, especially the longitudinal 1.18, should not be cited without checking against the primary studies.

key_findings.finding: Search and selection: 6606 records, 5821 unique titles and abstracts screened, 566 full texts assessed, 14 studies included: 11 cross-sectional and 3 longitudinal; 12 on any use and 2 on use disorder.
key_findings.locator: 3.1 Study selection; 3.2 Study characteristics; Figure 1 (PRISMA flowchart, image)

key_findings.finding: Of the nine cross-sectional studies of any use, four reported a positive association (DiMiceli, Mburu, Pluddemann, Marshall) and five no association (Blazer and Wu, Colyer, Daniulaityte, Embry, Obadeji).
Any use, cross-sectional: unadjusted pooled OR 1.40 (95% CI 1.08–1.80; 10 estimates; random effects; Q 39.92; I² 77%); adjusted pooled OR 1.66 (1.34–2.05; 4 estimates; fixed effect; Q 7.35; I² 59%).
key_findings.note: Editors' reproduction: fixed effect on DiMiceli 2.60, Embry 1.33, Marshall 1.67 and Pluddemann 2.65 gives 1.66 (1.34–2.04), Q 7.40, I² 59%; DerSimonian–Laird random effects on the same estimates gives 1.85 (1.28–2.69).

key_findings.finding: Any use, longitudinal: unadjusted pooled OR 2.05 (1.53–2.75; 2 estimates; I² 0%); adjusted pooled OR 1.18 (1.08–1.28; 2 estimates; Q 1.76; I² 43%) in Table 2, the abstract and the Discussion.
key_findings.note: The Results text gives 1.24 (1.14–1.34) (3.4). The adjusted longitudinal estimates in Table 3 (Briere 1.60, 1.10–2.30; Javanbakht 1.50, 1.10–2.30) pool to about 1.55 (1.19–2.01) with Q 0.06 (editors' calculation), so the published value cannot be reproduced; check the forest plot in the supplement or the primary papers.

key_findings.finding: The three longitudinal studies: Canadian secondary-school students followed from grade 10 to 11, adjusted for earlier depressive symptoms and other substance use, OR 1.60 (1.10–2.30); US cohort of HIV-positive and HIV-negative men who have sex with men followed 3.7 years, adjusted for unemployment, antidepressant use, earlier depressive symptoms and HIV status, OR 1.50 (1.10–2.30); mothers with prenatal methamphetamine use followed 36 months, unadjusted, OR 1.90 (1.00–3.70).

Use disorder, cross-sectional: unadjusted pooled OR 3.46 (2.04–5.89; 2 studies; I² 0%); the only adjusted estimate is a single study, OR 2.80 (1.40–5.90) (Lin et al., 1996); no longitudinal study of use disorder met the criteria.
key_findings.note: The abstract reports 2.80 alongside pooled estimates without saying it comes from one study.

key_findings.finding: Twin study (Lin et al., 1996; male monozygotic pairs): index-twin OR 3.50 (1.79–6.80), adjusted for household income, education and combat experience 2.80 (1.40–5.90); within monozygotic pairs OR 7.0 (1.6–30.8), adjusted 5.8 (1.3–27.11).
Sensitivity analysis: removing the one study with a major-depressive-disorder outcome changed the unadjusted cross-sectional estimate from 1.40 (1.08–1.80) to 1.37 (1.06–1.76).

E-values (point estimates): 1.28 to 6.30 for cross-sectional estimates and 2.37 to 3.21 for longitudinal ones; classified with cut-offs of 1.68, 3.47 and 6.71 adjusted for whether a study controlled for at least half of five key covariates (age, gender, employment, other substance use, pre-morbidity/comorbidity). Table 3 grades 11 of 18 estimates as low or very low risk of unmeasured confounding.
key_findings.note: All printed E-values match the rare-outcome formula with odds ratios used as risk ratios (Obadeji excepted: 2.26 from its OR vs 2.56 printed). With the square-root conversion advised for common outcomes they would be smaller (e.g. Briere 1.84, Javanbakht 1.75, Lin 2.73, Pluddemann 2.64), and the E-value for the confidence limit is 1.00 for the nine estimates whose intervals include 1 (editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: Depression definitions ranged from mild screening thresholds (PHQ-9 ≥5) through CES-D cut-offs of 16, 22 and 23 to diagnosed major depressive disorder (DSM-IV, SCID, DIS/DSM-III); exposure windows ranged from past 30 days to lifetime and prenatal use.
No data allowed analysis by amount or frequency of use, by sample type, by age group, or by depression severity; planned funnel plots and meta-regression were not done.
The earlier review that this paper updates reported a pooled adjusted OR for depression of 1.3 (1.2–1.4).

reporting_issues.issue: The adjusted longitudinal pooled OR is 1.18 (1.08–1.28) in the abstract, Table 2 and Discussion but 1.24 (1.14–1.34) in Results 3.4, and neither matches the two adjusted longitudinal estimates in Table 3 (1.60 and 1.50, which pool to about 1.55 with Q near 0, editors' calculation; the paper prints Q 1.76, I² 43%).
reporting_issues.consequence: The paper's headline prospective estimate is unverifiable from its own tables; the encyclopedia should cite the individual cohort estimates instead until resolved.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says heterogeneity was significant for the adjusted cross-sectional estimates (3.3), but Table 2 marks Q 7.35 as non-significant (p≈0.06 on 3 df, editors' calculation), so under the authors' rule a fixed-effect model was used despite I² 59%.
reporting_issues.consequence: A random-effects model would give a larger estimate with a wider interval (about 1.85, 1.28–2.69); the headline 1.66 understates uncertainty.

reporting_issues.issue: Study-level values differ between places: Embry et al. appears as 1.33 (1.01–1.76) in 5.1.1 and in the pooled analysis but as grade-specific 1.28 (0.80–2.06) and 1.36 (0.96–1.93) in Table 3; Pluddemann et al. is 2.60 (1.60–4.20) in 5.1.1 and 2.65 (1.64–4.28) in Table 3.
reporting_issues.consequence: Values must be taken from the primary papers.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion (7th paragraph) says Colyer et al. reported significantly higher depression risk after adjusting for polydrug use, but the review lists that study among those with no association (3.3) and extracted an unadjusted OR of 1.05 (0.92–1.19) (Table 3); the Discussion (4th paragraph) also cites Embry et al. among studies showing two-fold or higher odds, against its 1.28–1.36.
reporting_issues.consequence: The Discussion overstates the consistency of the subpopulation and low-confounding-risk evidence.

reporting_issues.issue: E-value risk categories do not follow the stated cut-offs: DiMiceli lifetime (2.60) and recent use (4.64) are both graded low, which no single rule yields; Mburu at CES-D ≥23 (3.64, no covariates) is graded moderate where the stated rule gives low; Pluddemann (age and cannabis only) and Lin (income, education, combat, other substances) are graded very low, which requires adjustment for at least half of the five key covariates. The ≥50% cut-off list also leaves a gap between 1.6 and 1.69.
reporting_issues.consequence: The detailed rules are in Table S4, which was not read; as printed, the confounding-risk grades cannot be relied on.

reporting_issues.issue: E-values are computed for point estimates only, with odds ratios treated as risk ratios; non-significant estimates (e.g. Blazer and Wu 3.42, 0.75–15.65, unadjusted) are graded low risk of unmeasured confounding.
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract's and Discussion's reassurance about unmeasured confounding is weaker than stated.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 gives 10 cross-sectional unadjusted estimates under a column defined as number of studies, while nine cross-sectional any-use studies are listed; the abstract names PubMed but Methods name Medline; Table 1 calls a national household survey, a school survey and a study of people with use disorder general population-based cohorts.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor, but study counts and sample types should be checked at source.

reporting_issues.issue: The use-disorder exposure in Lin et al. (1996) is labelled methamphetamine use disorder, while that paper's title concerns substance abuse/dependence in general; the review's eligibility accepted methamphetamine or amphetamine, and one cohort measured meth/amphetamine (speed) use.
reporting_issues.consequence: The pooled estimates concern amphetamine-type stimulants broadly; the specific drug class in Lin et al. must be checked before the twin result is attributed to methamphetamine.

reporting_issues.issue: Sample sizes of the included studies are not reported in the main text, and the supplementary file (forest plots, eligibility, search strings, E-value rules) is a .docx download that was not opened.
reporting_issues.consequence: Weights, participant totals and the forest plots could not be checked.

verification.source_read: Publisher full text (HTML), https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/dar.13670 (all sections, Tables 1–3 as text, Figure 1 caption only, author contributions, acknowledgements, conflict statement, reference list; supplementary .docx not read)

editorial_corrections.reason: Language (METHODS §9): 2 replacements, no change of meaning, number or citation; list in data/verification/language-2026-10-16.json

design_detail: Narrative review of structural MRI, diffusion tensor imaging, PET and SPECT (dopamine and serotonin transporters, VMAT2, D2/D3 receptors, translocator protein, glucose metabolism, blood flow), MR spectroscopy, task fMRI and resting-state fMRI studies in people who use methamphetamine, with sections linking the findings to executive function and to treatment. No methods section: no search strategy, inclusion criteria, appraisal of cited studies or quantitative synthesis. Four figures, three of them from studies first-authored by co-authors of the review (Morales et al., 2012; Kohno et al., 2014) and one from a monkey study (Groman et al., 2013).
can_establish: Which neuroimaging findings the authors considered central in 2014 and which primary studies a reader should check for each marker.
cannot_establish: That the imaging differences it describes are caused by methamphetamine, how large or consistent they are across studies, or whether they and the associated cognitive differences recover with abstinence, because it has no systematic search, no appraisal of the cited studies and no synthesis, and most of the studies it cites are small and cross-sectional.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable: narrative review of published studies chosen by the authors; no search, sources or dates reported.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not reported. The abstract defines the scope as structural, molecular and functional neuroimaging studies, with a focus on cortical and striatal abnormalities.
sample.demographics: Not applicable. Sample sizes and abstinence durations are given for only a few cited studies (for example 5 people in each of two DAT recovery studies; 13 vs 27 people in a blood-flow study).
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: Selection of studies is by the authors, with no stated criteria. Three of four figures come from studies first-authored by co-authors (Morales et al., 2012; Kohno et al., 2014), and two cited sources are unpublished conference presentations (Ballard et al., 2014; Robertson et al., 2013). The reference list does not include Hart et al. (2012), the critical review of whether cognition is impaired in people who use methamphetamine, while it does include Dean et al. (listed as 2012).

exposure.measurement: Not applicable (review). Exposure measurement in the cited studies is not described.
exposure.polysubstance: Discussed for cigarette smoking only: smoking is reported in 87–92% of people who use methamphetamine against 22% of the general population, and a cited study found smaller orbitofrontal and caudate grey matter in smokers with and without methamphetamine use (Structural Brain Imaging, 4th paragraph). Polydrug use is noted as a limitation of one D3 receptor study (Boileau et al., 2012). Alcohol, cannabis and other drug use in the cited studies are not discussed.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Reported study by study where relevant; ranges cited run from 4–10 days to 25 years of abstinence.

comparison.controls: Not applicable (review). Cited studies compare people who use methamphetamine with people who do not; matching is described only as 'matched' for the DAT studies.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: The review raises premorbid and familial explanations itself: brain structure and addiction are both heritable, and in a sibling study (Ersche et al., 2012) stimulant-dependent people and their siblings without drug use shared some differences from controls (larger putamen, amygdala and hippocampus; lower fractional anisotropy) (Structural Brain Imaging, 7th paragraph). It does not apply this reasoning to the molecular or functional findings.

outcomes.instruments: Grey-matter volume and density (MRI), fractional anisotropy (DTI), DAT ([11C]WIN-35,428, [11C]d-threo-methylphenidate, [99mTc]TRODAT), SERT ([11C](+)McN-5652), VMAT2 ([11C]dihydrotetrabenazine), D2/D3 receptors ([11C]raclopride, [18F]fallypride, [11C]-(+)-PHNO), translocator protein ([11C]PK11195), NAA, choline, creatine, myo-inositol and glutamate (MRS), glucose metabolism ([18F]FDG), blood flow ([99mTc]HMPAO), task and resting-state fMRI.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Deficit' and 'dysfunction' denote a group difference from people who do not use methamphetamine in an imaging marker, or a correlation of a marker with a task score; no study's effect size or normative comparison is given for cognition.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable to the review. Of its own figures, Figure 1 is shown at p<0.005 uncorrected with a 200-voxel cluster extent; Figures 2–4 are reported as corrected.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: No pooled estimates and no effect sizes for cognitive outcomes. Numbers cited: striatal DAT 11–28% lower in people abstinent from methamphetamine than in matched people who do not use it, across six PET studies; DAT increases of up to 38% in the first two weeks of abstinence in 5 people (Chou et al., 2007) and of 19% (caudate) and 16% (putamen) between early (<6 months) and later (12–17 months) abstinence in 5 people (Volkow et al., 2001b); striatal VMAT2 22%, 12% and 11% higher in early abstinence (Boileau et al., 2008) but 10% lower after more than 3 months (Johanson et al., 2006); striatal D2-type receptor availability 16% (caudate), 13% (putamen) and 8% (nucleus accumbens) lower in people abstinent 2 weeks to 35 months (Monoamine systems, 2nd–4th paragraphs).
analysis.covariates: Not applicable. The figures from the authors' own fMRI work are reported as controlled for age, sex, smoking and cannabis use (Figures 3–4 legends).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration; no methods section.
analysis.selective_reporting: Evidence is selected without stated criteria. The review cites Chou et al. (2007) as preliminary evidence that executive function recovers with DAT recovery, without the caveat raised in Simon et al. (2010), which shares its senior author, that Chou et al. had no control group for WCST practice effects. Simon et al. (2010) is cited only as support for common executive deficits, not for its null result on cognitive change over the first month. Hart et al. (2012) is not cited.
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: The body describes group differences from people who do not use methamphetamine in many imaging markers, mostly from small cross-sectional studies; concedes that human studies generally cannot attribute structural abnormalities to methamphetamine (Structural Brain Imaging, 6th paragraph); offers smoking and familial vulnerability as explanations for some structural findings (paragraphs 4 and 7); and supports recovery with abstinence by within-person changes in samples of about 5 or by a one-month grey-matter change shown at an uncorrected threshold.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The title and abstract present corticostriatal deficits of chronic use and state that people with a history of chronic methamphetamine use "often display several signs of corticostriatal dysfunction" linked to addiction-related phenotypes (Abstract), without mentioning confounding by smoking, premorbid or familial differences, or polydrug use. The white-matter findings are called consistent with drug-induced damage (Structural Brain Imaging, 5th paragraph). The Introduction cites Simon et al. (2010) for common executive-function deficits, although that study found no significant executive difference and placed the methamphetamine group's mean scores in the low-average to average range (see sc_simon_2010). A paragraph heading claim that cortical grey-matter deficits reverse with protracted abstinence rests on one month of abstinence (Figure 1, uncorrected) and a cross-sectional comparison (Structural Brain Imaging, 3rd paragraph). The treatment suggestions (anti-inflammatory drugs, exercise, D3 targets, cognitive remediation) are presented as possibilities and rest on animal or preliminary data.

timeline.event: DAT follow-up in 5 people (19% and 16% increases), cited by this review as Volkow et al., 2001b.
Thalamic metabolic recovery at 12–17 months in 5 people, cited by this review as associated with motor and verbal memory improvement.

Simon et al. (2010): no significant executive-function difference after about 6 days of abstinence and no significant differential cognitive change over a month against retested controls; cited by this review only for cognitive deficits.
Sibling study of stimulant dependence, cited for structural differences shared with unaffected siblings.
Critical review of whether cognition is impaired in people who use methamphetamine; not cited by this review.
Evaluation of the evidence that methamphetamine causes cognitive decline; cited by this review as Dean et al., 2012.

replication.where_it_stands: Useful as a map of imaging markers and their primary sources, each of which needs its own card. On the encyclopedia's questions it adds no independent evidence: causation is conceded to be unresolved for structural findings, magnitudes are given only as percentage differences in transporter and receptor binding, and the recovery evidence it cites consists of very small within-person studies.

funding.funder: Endowment from the Thomas P and Katherine K Pike Chair in Addiction Studies and a gift from the Marjorie M Greene Trust (EDL); T32 DA 024635 (MEB), F31 DA0331-17 (AMM), F31 DA033120-02 (MK) (Acknowledgements).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the PMC author manuscript.
funding.affiliations_note: All authors at UCLA (Department of Psychiatry and Biobehavioral Sciences; also Molecular and Medical Pharmacology and the Brain Research Institute for the first author). The review relies in part on the authors' own studies. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: For the review's own question, a registered systematic review that pools methamphetamine–control differences marker by marker, codes smoking, polydrug use and abstinence for every study, and keeps within-person longitudinal evidence separate from cross-sectional comparisons; for causation, imaging cohorts that begin before regular use, or methamphetamine-specific discordant-sibling designs, with controls scanned at the same intervals.

domains.note: There is no methods section: no databases, dates or selection criteria are reported, and only the scope (structural, molecular and functional imaging, focused on cortical and striatal abnormalities) is stated (Abstract).

There is no appraisal of the cited studies as such; limitations are named for some findings (smoking and familial explanations for structural data, polydrug use in Boileau et al., 2012, conflicting VMAT2 results; Structural Brain Imaging, 4th–7th paragraphs; Monoamine systems, 3rd and 5th paragraphs). The recovery evidence (two DAT studies of 5 people each; Figure 1 at p<0.005 uncorrected) is presented without comment on size or threshold (Structural Brain Imaging, 3rd paragraph; Monoamine systems, 2nd paragraph).

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: Six of the 142 bibliography entries name a review author (Ballard 2014, a poster; Kohno 2013, 2014; London 2004; Morales 2012; Payer 2011), and at least six 'et al.' entries are from the senior author's group by the author lists printed in Hart et al. (2012) and Dean et al. (2013) (e.g., Lee 2009, Monterosso 2005, Simon 2010). These supply 3 of the 4 figures, the grey-matter recovery claim, the risky decision-making and resting-state findings, and 3 of the 4 citations for common executive deficits (Introduction, 2nd paragraph).

The abstract presents group differences as corticostriatal 'dysfunction' without the body's caveats that human studies cannot assign structural differences to methamphetamine and that smoking or familial factors may explain some (Structural Brain Imaging, 4th–7th paragraphs). The claim that grey-matter deficits reverse with protracted abstinence rests on one month of abstinence shown at an uncorrected threshold (3rd paragraph; Figure 1), and lower fractional anisotropy is read as drug-induced damage in the 5th paragraph and as familial predisposition in the 7th.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for and against methamphetamine-caused brain and cognitive deficits
domains.note: Under-represented: evidence that the functional and cognitive differences are small, absent or not caused by methamphetamine; counter-evidence is given for structural findings (Structural Brain Imaging, 4th–7th paragraphs) and a few molecular ones (Monoamine systems, 2nd, 3rd and 5th paragraphs) but not for these. Hart et al. (2012) is not in the bibliography, and Simon et al. (2010), listed with no significant differences in Dean et al. (2013, Table 1), is cited only for common executive deficits (Introduction, 2nd paragraph).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: High, because there is no search or selection method, the abstract and section-level claims go beyond the evidence and caveats the body itself gives, and a notable share of the evidence comes from the authors' group. It may be cited as a pointer to primary imaging studies marker by marker, and for its own statement that human studies cannot attribute structural differences to methamphetamine. It may not be cited as evidence of methamphetamine-caused deficits, of recovery with abstinence, or of common executive-function deficits.

key_findings.finding: The review has no methods section: no search, inclusion criteria, appraisal or synthesis is reported.
The authors state that human studies generally do not allow structural abnormalities to be assigned to methamphetamine use itself and turn to animal studies for that question.
key_findings.locator: Structural Brain Imaging of Methamphetamine Users, 6th paragraph

key_findings.finding: In vervet monkeys given an escalating methamphetamine regimen, putamen grey matter increased (p<0.05 corrected), together with lower D2-type receptor and DAT availability and poorer cognitive flexibility (Groman et al., 2013, as summarized).
key_findings.locator: Structural Brain Imaging, 6th paragraph; Figure 2 legend
key_findings.note: The review describes the regimen as resembling a common pattern of human use ('escalating' comes from the Figure 2 title) and presents the D2-type receptor and DAT reductions as associated with the grey-matter increase; it gives no magnitudes and no data on persistence. Elsewhere it cites recovery of D2-type receptor availability with protracted abstinence in monkeys (Groman et al., 2012; Molecular Imaging › Monoamine systems, 4th paragraph).

key_findings.finding: Cigarette smoking is reported in 87–92% of people who use methamphetamine against 22% of the general population; in a cited study, smokers with and without methamphetamine use had smaller orbitofrontal and caudate grey matter than people who neither smoked nor used methamphetamine, so those deficits may partly reflect smoking or premorbid conditions.

In a sibling study of 50 cocaine- or amphetamine-dependent people, dependent people and their siblings without a history of chronic drug use both had larger putamen, amygdala and hippocampus and lower fractional anisotropy than controls; only the dependent people had smaller orbitofrontal and anterior insular volumes. The review concludes some but not all structural differences may predate drug use.
key_findings.note: The review gives no effect sizes, no breakdown of the 50 dependent participants by drug, and no sibling-versus-control comparison of inhibitory control; the next section reports only that fractional anisotropy near the right inferior frontal gyrus went with stop-signal performance across all three groups (Deficits in Brain Structure and Impaired Executive Functions, 1st paragraph).

key_findings.finding: Grey matter increased in several cortical regions between the first and fourth week of abstinence in the methamphetamine group, with no change in controls scanned a month apart; the figure is thresholded at p<0.005 uncorrected with a 200-voxel cluster extent.
key_findings.locator: Structural Brain Imaging, 3rd paragraph; Figure 1 legend

key_findings.finding: Striatal DAT was 11–28% lower in people abstinent from methamphetamine than in matched people who do not use it, across six PET studies; DAT rose by up to 38% in the first two weeks in 5 people (SPECT) and by 19% (caudate) and 16% (putamen) between early and later abstinence in 5 people (PET).
DAT availability correlated with cognitive or psychomotor performance in some studies (McCann et al., 2008; Volkow et al., 2001d) but not in another (Johanson et al., 2006).

Striatal VMAT2 was higher than controls in early abstinence (+22% caudate, +12% putamen, +11% ventral striatum) in one study and 10% lower after more than 3 months in another; a post-mortem study found no difference.

Striatal D2-type receptor availability was 16% (caudate), 13% (putamen) and 8% (nucleus accumbens) lower in people abstinent 2 weeks to 35 months; the authors state that no human study has followed D2-type receptors over abstinence.
key_findings.note: Cited to Volkow et al., 2001b, which in the review's own reference list is the DAT recovery paper (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: MRS markers of neuronal integrity (NAA/creatine in anterior cingulate) are lower in people who use methamphetamine and are described as recovering slowly with extended abstinence; one PET study found more translocator-protein binding in the methamphetamine group, lower with longer abstinence.

Lower right anterior cingulate blood flow was found in 13 people abstinent a mean 3 months (SD 2) than in 27 abstinent a mean 36 months (SD 40), taken as a sign of recovery (cross-sectional comparison).
The review cites Simon et al. (2010), among others, for the statement that cognitive deficits, particularly in executive functions, are common in people with a history of methamphetamine use.
key_findings.note: Simon et al. (2010) found no significant executive-function difference (sc_simon_2010).

key_findings.finding: Dopamine agonists (modafinil, methylphenidate, d-amphetamine) are described as not consistently efficacious; anti-inflammatory drugs, exercise, D3-receptor targets and cognitive remediation are proposed as possibilities on animal or preliminary evidence.

The review states that people who use methamphetamine generally have smaller cortical but larger striatal grey-matter volumes than people who do not. After under 3 weeks of abstinence, anterior cingulate, dorsolateral prefrontal, orbitofrontal, superior temporal and hippocampal volumes were smaller than in people who never used it (Nakama et al., 2011; Thompson et al., 2004), with an insular density deficit at up to 6 months of abstinence (Schwartz et al., 2010); people abstinent a mean 3–4 months had larger parietal, caudate, lenticular and accumbens volumes (Jernigan et al., 2005) and larger putamen and globus pallidus (Chang et al., 2005), and putamen volume was also larger in people still using (Jan et al., 2012b).
key_findings.locator: Structural Brain Imaging of Methamphetamine Users, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: Second-hand summaries of cross-sectional studies; the primary papers have not been read.

key_findings.finding: In places the authors lean toward neurotoxicity: they open the neuronal-integrity section by citing mounting evidence (reviews, largely of animal work) that repeated exposure can be neurotoxic, and suggest that dopamine agonists may have failed partly because of methamphetamine-induced neurotoxicity to dopamine nerve terminals, while their own summary reports partial DAT recovery with abstinence, inconsistent VMAT2 findings and no human longitudinal data on D2-type receptors.
key_findings.locator: Molecular Imaging › Neuronal integrity and neuroinflammation, 1st paragraph; Implications for Therapy, 2nd paragraph; Molecular Imaging › Monoamine systems, 2nd–4th paragraphs
key_findings.note: An interpretation, hedged by the authors (agonist failure 'may in part' reflect neurotoxicity); no human study of terminal counts is cited.

reporting_issues.issue: The D2 receptor findings (raclopride binding 16%, 13% and 8% lower; correlation with orbitofrontal metabolism) are cited to Volkow et al., 2001b, but the reference list assigns 2001b to the Journal of Neuroscience DAT recovery paper; the D2/orbitofrontal paper is listed as 2001a.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Molecular Imaging › Monoamine systems, 4th paragraph; Bibliography
reporting_issues.consequence: Anyone tracing these numbers must use the American Journal of Psychiatry 2001;158:2015–21 paper, not the DAT recovery paper.

reporting_issues.issue: The only Kim et al. (2006) entry in the reference list is titled as a study of prefrontal grey-matter changes, yet Kim et al. (2006) is cited for grey-matter density, WCST errors, a correlation of executive deficits with fractional anisotropy in the corpus callosum, and lower white-matter glucose metabolism in people abstinent 19 months (SD 27).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Deficits in Brain Structure, 2nd paragraph; Regional Brain Function, 4th paragraph; Bibliography
reporting_issues.consequence: The diffusion and metabolism attributions cannot be matched to the listed source; check the primary paper before any claim relies on them. Hart et al. (2012, Table 2, p. 594) list the white-matter glucose finding in men abstinent 19 (SD 27) months under Kim et al. (2005), so that part is probably a miscitation of the 2005 study.

reporting_issues.issue: People who use methamphetamine are said to have lower fractional anisotropy in the genu of the corpus callosum, but Stroop and WCST deficits are said to correlate with increased fractional anisotropy in the genu.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Structural Brain Imaging, 5th paragraph; Deficits in Brain Structure, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The direction of the structure–cognition relation is stated inconsistently; the primary studies (Salo et al., 2009a) must be checked.

reporting_issues.issue: A paragraph that opens by saying glucose metabolism remains abnormal throughout protracted abstinence cites mixed evidence: a prefrontal white-matter deficit at a mean 19 months of abstinence (attributed to Kim et al., 2006) and the absence of a striatal increase at 12–17 months fit the opening, while a thalamic increase at 12–17 months that went with better motor and verbal-memory performance (Wang et al., 2004) and higher anterior cingulate blood flow with longer abstinence (Hwang et al., 2006) point to partial recovery.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Regional Brain Function, 4th paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The opening sentence overstates persistence: the paragraph's own evidence shows persisting differences in some measures and partial recovery in others.

reporting_issues.issue: The Introduction cites Simon et al. (2010) as support for common executive-function deficits; that study found a significant difference on one processing-speed test only, none in executive domains, and none after adjusting for education.
reporting_issues.consequence: A citation overstates its source; claims should cite primary data, not this sentence.

reporting_issues.issue: One of the listed training grants is printed as F31 DA0331-17, which appears truncated.
reporting_issues.consequence: Trivial.

reporting_issues.issue: London et al. (2004) is cited for poorer sustained attention among people recently abstinent from methamphetamine that correlated negatively with metabolism in the anterior and middle cingulate and the insula (Regional Brain Function, 2nd paragraph). Hart et al. (2012) report that the groups in London et al. (2004) did not differ on task performance (p. 597) and place the attention deficit and these correlations in London et al. (2005; Table 2, p. 595), which is not in this review's bibliography.
reporting_issues.consequence: The attention finding belongs to London et al. (2005) and should be checked there; the 2004 study found no performance difference.

reporting_issues.issue: Salo et al. (2009a) is cited for lower fractional anisotropy in the genu of the corpus callosum in people who use methamphetamine (Structural Brain Imaging, 5th paragraph). Hart et al. (2012) report that in that study the groups did not differ on any DTI measure and that slower Stroop responses went with lower genu fractional anisotropy regardless of group (p. 601).
reporting_issues.consequence: The genu difference attributed to Salo et al. (2009a) is not supported by Hart's account, and the correlation runs with lower, not higher, fractional anisotropy (compare the issue on the direction of the genu correlation); check the primary paper before citing either.

reporting_issues.issue: Figure 1 (grey-matter increase over the first month of abstinence) is displayed at an uncorrected threshold (p < 0.005, clusters over 200 voxels), without comment in the text.
reporting_issues.consequence: The figure illustrates, but does not by itself establish, the increases described. The primary study (Morales et al., 2012) also reports these increases without correction for multiple comparisons, at a different threshold (voxel p < 0.001, clusters of 100 voxels or more; Table 3, as recorded on its study card).
