design_detail: Two linked analyses at 1.5 T with voxel-based morphometry (VBM8/SPM8, DARTEL, modulated gray-matter maps, 8 mm smoothing). (1) Cross-sectional comparison of three groups: 18 control non-smokers, 25 control smokers and 39 people with methamphetamine dependence who smoked cigarettes, scanned after 4–7 days of abstinence. (2) Longitudinal re-scan of 12 methamphetamine-dependent and 12 control participants over the first month of abstinence, testing group-by-time interactions. The design's point is to separate tobacco smoking from methamphetamine as an explanation for gray-matter differences.
can_establish: That some gray-matter differences previously attributed to methamphetamine (right orbitofrontal cortex, caudate) are also present in control smokers who do not use illicit drugs, and that other regional differences (superior temporal, parietal, precentral) distinguish the methamphetamine group from smoking controls; and, tentatively, that gray matter changed over the first month of supervised abstinence in the methamphetamine group but not in controls.
cannot_establish: Whether the remaining differences are caused by methamphetamine or precede use (no pre-use scan; no group of people using methamphetamine who do not smoke); what the gray-matter increase during abstinence means at tissue level (it could be inflammation or glial change rather than recovery); and whether any difference has a functional consequence (no cognitive or clinical outcome was measured).

sample.recruitment: Online and print advertisements at UCLA. Methamphetamine-dependent participants stayed as residents at the General Clinical Research Center with daily urine toxicology; control participants were outpatients tested at intake and each visit. About 60% of each longitudinal group had taken part in an earlier study from the same laboratory (Methods §2.2).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Ages 18–55. Excluded: central nervous system, cardiovascular, pulmonary or systemic disease, psychotropic medication, head trauma, HIV seropositivity, pregnancy, and any current Axis I diagnosis other than methamphetamine or nicotine abuse or dependence (SCID for DSM-IV). Smokers in either group had smoked on at least 25 of the previous 30 days; control non-smokers had smoked fewer than 5 cigarettes in their lifetime. People who had ever smoked more than 5 cigarettes, and methamphetamine-dependent people who did not smoke, could join the longitudinal but not the cross-sectional study, because only two methamphetamine-dependent participants were non-smokers (Methods §2.2).
sample.demographics: Table 1 (means with SEM). Cross-sectional: age 30.1 (2.2), 35.4 (1.8), 34.8 (1.5), F(2,79)=2.10, p=0.13; men 8 of 18, 13 of 25, 20 of 39 (chi-square 0.87); education 14.6 (0.4), 14.1 (0.3), 12.8 (0.3), F(2,79)=8.52, p<0.001, with the methamphetamine group lower than both control groups; mother's education 13.2, 13.6, 12.3, not significant (F(2,75)=1.74, p=0.18); alcohol days in the last 30: 2.4, 5.3, 5.4, not significant; cannabis days in the last 30: 0.1, 0.2, 1.1, p=0.01. Smoking did not differ between the two smoking groups (days used, cigarettes per day about 14 vs 13, pack-years about 11.5 vs 13.2, Fagerström about 3.8 vs 3.6, age of first cigarette; all p>0.2). Longitudinal: control 37.5 (2.3) and methamphetamine 33.8 (2.4) years old; 8 of 12 and 10 of 12 currently smoked; education 14.8 vs 12.7, p<0.005.
sample.attrition: Not stated for the cross-sectional study. For the longitudinal study only completers are described (12 per group); how many began and did not return, and how the 24 relate to the 82, is not reported.
sample.selection_effects: Advertisement-recruited volunteers; the methamphetamine group was studied as residents under supervised abstinence while controls were outpatients, so setting as well as drug status differs. People using methamphetamine who do not smoke are rare and were not recruited, so methamphetamine and tobacco cannot be fully crossed. Education was about 1.5 years lower in the methamphetamine group; the authors argue education is itself affected by use and point to similar maternal education.

exposure.measurement: DSM-IV dependence by SCID; Addiction Severity Index and a study drug-use survey; urine toxicology daily during residence for the methamphetamine group and at intake and each visit for controls (Methods §2.2).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Self-reported, Table 1: methamphetamine group used on 22.4 (SEM 1.3) of the previous 30 days, about 2.6 (0.4) g per week, 8.4 (1.3) years of heavy use (n=38) and 11.5 (1.5) years of use (n=33), first use at 21.7 (1.2) years. Longitudinal methamphetamine group: 21.1 days, 1.9 g per week, 6.8 years of heavy use, first use at 21.6 years. Route is not reported. Reported as study-sample characteristics.
exposure.polysubstance: Tobacco is the study's exposure of interest and was matched between the two smoking groups. Cannabis use was higher in the methamphetamine group (about 1.1 vs 0.1–0.2 days in 30) and was entered as a covariate; alcohol days did not differ; cannabis or alcohol abuse or dependence were exclusions. Other drug use is not described.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: First scan at 4–7 days of abstinence, verified by daily urine toxicology during residential admission. Second scan a mean of 23.5 days (SD 1.6) later in the methamphetamine group and 31.6 days (SD 13.1) later in controls (Methods §2.1).

comparison.controls: Two comparison groups: 18 lifetime non-smokers and 25 cigarette smokers, neither using illicit drugs beyond light alcohol or cannabis. The longitudinal control group was described as matched for smoking (8 of 12 current smokers against 10 of 12).
comparison.matching: Groups were similar in age, sex and alcohol use and, among smokers, in smoking history. Analyses covaried age, sex and cannabis frequency. Education was not a covariate in the main models; the authors report that adding it left results supported only at a more liberal uncorrected threshold of p<0.005.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No pre-use scan; maternal education is the only premorbid proxy. The authors state explicitly that group differences may reflect premorbid risk factors.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Light alcohol or cannabis permitted; no illicit drug use; verified by urine testing.

outcomes.instruments: 1.5 T Siemens Sonata, T1 MPRAGE, 1 mm slices; VBM8 for SPM8 with DARTEL normalization, modulation without linear head-size scaling, 8 mm smoothing; gray-matter mask. A supplementary semi-automatic delineation of the caudate (FSL FIRST) was run for comparison with earlier volumetric studies.
outcomes.validity_norms: Modulated VBM intensity is a relative gray-matter volume index, not cortical thickness. No cognitive, behavioural or clinical outcome was measured in this paper.
outcomes.operationalization: Deficit was defined as a significantly smaller voxel-wise gray-matter value than a comparison group; change with abstinence as a significant group-by-time interaction with a within-group time effect.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Cross-sectional: voxel height p<0.001 with cluster-extent family-wise error correction at p<0.05, in a gray-matter mask. Longitudinal: voxel height p<0.001 uncorrected with a 100-voxel cluster extent and no family-wise correction (Table 3 footnote states uncorrected voxel-level p). So the recovery analysis is held to a weaker standard than the group comparison.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable for automated VBM; blinding is not reported for the supplementary caudate delineation.

analysis.effect_sizes: Reported only as cluster-level corrected p-values with cluster extents, peak F/T and Z values and MNI coordinates (Tables 2 and 3); no group means, SDs or percentage differences are printed, so standardized differences and overlap cannot be computed from the paper. Editors' calculation from peak T values (which are selected maxima and therefore upward-biased): control non-smokers versus the methamphetamine group, peak T 6.35 corresponds to about d=1.8; control non-smokers versus control smokers, T 5.59, about d=1.7; control smokers versus the methamphetamine group, T 5.10, about d=1.3. Cross-sectional findings: the three groups differed in bilateral orbitofrontal and precentral gyri, right frontal pole, left superior temporal and left superior frontal gyri. Control non-smokers had more gray matter than control smokers in one cluster only, the right orbitofrontal cortex (1043 voxels, p<0.001 corrected). Control non-smokers exceeded the methamphetamine group in ten clusters (right frontal pole/orbitofrontal, left orbitofrontal, left superior frontal, left insula, bilateral precentral, right middle temporal, right precuneus, left caudate, right cingulate). Control smokers exceeded the methamphetamine group in four clusters (left superior temporal, right inferior temporal, right supramarginal, left precentral); no region was larger in the methamphetamine group. The supplementary caudate delineation found smaller bilateral and left caudate in both smoking groups than in control non-smokers, with no difference between control smokers and the methamphetamine group. Measures of smoking and of methamphetamine use were not related to gray-matter values (no dose-response). Longitudinal: group-by-time interactions in bilateral superior temporal gyrus, right angular gyrus, right insula, left precuneus, left inferior frontal gyrus, left occipital pole and left cerebellum; within the methamphetamine group gray matter increased in those cortical regions between weeks 1 and 4 and decreased in the cerebellum, while no region changed in controls at the stated threshold.
analysis.covariates: Age, sex and frequency of cannabis use in all cross-sectional models. Not education (addressed only in a sensitivity analysis at an uncorrected threshold), not alcohol, not depressive symptoms (not measured here).
analysis.preregistration_detail: Directional hypotheses are stated in the Introduction (smaller prefrontal, cingulate and insular gray matter in both smoking groups; striatal and pallidal differences specific to methamphetamine), but there is no registration. The striatal hypothesis was not borne out in the predicted direction: the methamphetamine group's caudate was smaller, not larger, and did not differ from control smokers.
analysis.selective_reporting: The caudate result in the abstract combines a voxel-wise finding (methamphetamine versus control non-smokers) with a supplementary region-of-interest finding (control smokers versus control non-smokers); the supplement is a separate download. The longitudinal analysis is reported at an uncorrected threshold while the cross-sectional analysis is corrected.
analysis.power: Not formally reported. The authors name modest sample size as a limitation and note that the longitudinal sample is comparable to or larger than earlier within-subject imaging studies in this field.

interpretation_gap.results_show: After 4–7 days of abstinence, people with methamphetamine dependence who smoked had less gray matter than non-smoking controls in a wide set of regions, but compared with smoking controls the difference was confined to four clusters; the right orbitofrontal and caudate differences were as large in control smokers as in the methamphetamine group. Over the first month of supervised abstinence, gray matter rose in several cortical regions in the methamphetamine group and not in controls, on an uncorrected threshold, with the two groups rescanned after different intervals (about 24 versus 32 days).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that orbitofrontal and caudate deficits may be partly attributable to cigarette smoking or premorbid conditions, which the data support, and that the gray-matter increase with abstinence suggests some deficits are partly attributable to methamphetamine use, which is a weaker inference: it rests on an uncorrected longitudinal analysis in 12 per group with unequal scan intervals, and on regions that mostly did not differ from control smokers at baseline. The discussion is careful, naming premorbid risk, the absence of dose-response, and the possibility that an increase in gray matter reflects inflammation or reactive gliosis rather than repair. The claim to be first to show smaller parietal and caudate volume, and the inference that early deficits precede the expansion seen in long-abstinent samples, mixes cross-sectional comparisons across different studies.

timeline.event: Cingulate and hippocampal gray-matter deficits reported in people who used methamphetamine, with a largely smoking versus non-smoking group contrast (Thompson et al., 2004; appraised in this batch). This study did not reproduce the hippocampal finding, which the authors attribute to different methods.
Larger striatal volumes reported in long-abstinent samples (Chang et al., 2005; Jernigan et al., 2005, as cited), the opposite direction to the caudate finding here in early abstinence.
This study separates smoking from methamphetamine and finds the orbitofrontal and caudate differences also in control smokers.

replication.where_it_stands: Gray-matter differences in people who use methamphetamine are partly shared with tobacco smoking; the direction of striatal findings varies with abstinence duration across studies; longitudinal change during abstinence has been shown only once, at an uncorrected threshold, in 12 people.

funding.funder: US NIH grants P20 DA022539, R01 DA015179 and R01 DA020726 (E.D.L.); training grants T90 DA022768 and T32 DA024635; M01 RR00865 (UCLA General Clinical Research Center); a Eugene V. Cota-Robles Fellowship; endowments from the Thomas P. and Katherine K. Pike Chair in Addiction Studies and the Marjorie M. Greene Trust. The sponsors had no role in design, data, writing or submission (Acknowledgments; Role of Funding Source).
funding.declared_conflicts: The senior author declares research support for projects other than this one under a UCLA contract (number 20063287) with Philip Morris USA (Conflict of Interest).
funding.affiliations_note: The declared tobacco-industry contract is recorded because this paper's conclusion assigns part of the gray-matter difference in people who use methamphetamine to cigarette smoking; the authors state the support was for other projects and the funders had no role. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, never a reason to discount the results. The senior author also authored the earlier Thompson et al. (2004) study whose hippocampal finding is not reproduced here.

what_would_settle_it: A four-group design with people who use methamphetamine and do not smoke (hard to recruit but decisive), or a prospective study scanning people before and after the onset of use, both with longer follow-up, corrected longitudinal statistics, equal rescan intervals and cognitive outcomes measured alongside the imaging.

key_findings.finding: Control non-smokers had more gray matter than control smokers in exactly one cluster, the right orbitofrontal cortex (1043 voxels, cluster-level p<0.001, family-wise corrected), and no other region differed between the two control groups.
key_findings.locator: Results §3.2; Table 2, Control Nonsmoker > Control Tobacco Smoker

key_findings.finding: Compared with control non-smokers, the methamphetamine group had less gray matter in ten clusters: right frontal pole/orbitofrontal (7314 voxels), left orbitofrontal, left superior frontal, left insula, bilateral precentral, right middle temporal, right precuneus, left caudate and right cingulate (all cluster-level p<0.05 corrected).

Compared with control smokers, the methamphetamine group had less gray matter in only four clusters (left superior temporal, right inferior temporal, right supramarginal, left precentral); no region was larger in the methamphetamine group.
key_findings.locator: Results §3.2; Table 2, Control Tobacco Smoker > Methamphetamine-Dependent Tobacco Smoker

key_findings.finding: A supplementary anatomical delineation of the caudate found smaller bilateral and left caudate volumes in both control smokers and the methamphetamine group than in control non-smokers (p<0.05), with no significant difference between the two smoking groups.
key_findings.locator: Results §3.2, final paragraph (Supplemental Results, Supplemental Table 1)
key_findings.note: The supplement is a .docx download and was not opened; the numbers behind this statement were not checked.

key_findings.finding: Neither smoking measures nor methamphetamine-use measures correlated with gray-matter values: no dose-response was detected.

Over the first month of abstinence, group-by-time interactions appeared in bilateral superior temporal gyrus, right angular gyrus, right insula, left precuneus, left inferior frontal gyrus, left occipital pole and left cerebellum; gray matter rose in those cortical regions in the methamphetamine group and fell in the cerebellum, while no region changed in controls.
key_findings.note: Table 3 is explicitly labelled uncorrected voxel-level p, with a 100-voxel extent; unlike the cross-sectional analysis, these results are not corrected for multiple comparisons.

key_findings.finding: The two longitudinal groups were rescanned after different intervals: a mean of 23.5 days (SD 1.6) in the methamphetamine group and 31.6 days (SD 13.1) in controls.
key_findings.note: Relevant to the group-by-time interaction, since the control group had the longer interval and still showed no change.

key_findings.finding: Groups did not differ in age, sex or alcohol use; the methamphetamine group had about 1.5 fewer years of education (F(2,79)=8.52, p<0.001) but maternal education did not differ (F(2,75)=1.74, p=0.18). The two smoking groups were comparable on cigarettes per day, pack-years and Fagerström score.
The authors did not reproduce the smaller hippocampal volumes reported by their own laboratory in 2004, attributing the difference to method.

Editors' calculation from the peak T values in Table 2 (upward-biased because peaks are selected maxima): about d=1.8 for control non-smokers versus the methamphetamine group, d=1.7 for control non-smokers versus control smokers, and d=1.3 for control smokers versus the methamphetamine group.
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation d = T × sqrt(1/n1 + 1/n2) at the peak voxel; the paper gives no means, SDs or percentage differences.

reporting_issues.issue: The cannabis ANOVA is given as F(2,79)=4.55, p=0.01 in the Results but as F=6.210, p=0.003 in the Table 1 footnote; the table marks the cannabis row with three asterisks while the footnotes define only one and two.
reporting_issues.consequence: The covariate's group difference cannot be verified as printed; p=0.0135 and p=0.0031 are the values implied by the two F statistics (editors' calculation).

reporting_issues.issue: Two rows of Table 2 print identical T and Z values (right supramarginal gyrus 4.43/4.43; left precentral gyrus 4.24/4.24), whereas Z is below T in every other row.
reporting_issues.consequence: Transcription error in two of the four clusters that distinguish the methamphetamine group from control smokers, the comparison that carries the paper's main inference.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 3 the left precuneus appears with coordinates −3, −60, 34 in the interaction list and −3, 60, 34 in the within-group list, and a cluster at x=−46 is labelled right frontal operculum.
reporting_issues.consequence: Coordinate or label errors; the anatomical attribution of two longitudinal clusters is unreliable.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says that control smokers and the methamphetamine group both had smaller orbitofrontal and caudate gray matter than control non-smokers, but the caudate part of that statement comes from the supplementary region-of-interest analysis, not from the voxel-wise results where only the methamphetamine group differed in caudate.
reporting_issues.consequence: A reader of the abstract would attribute to the main analysis a result that rests on a supplementary method.

reporting_issues.issue: The longitudinal analysis uses an uncorrected threshold with a 100-voxel extent, while the cross-sectional analysis uses family-wise cluster correction; the difference in standard is not discussed.
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstinence findings, which carry the recovery claim, are substantially less protected against false positives than the group differences.

reporting_issues.issue: How the 24 longitudinal participants relate to the 82 cross-sectional participants is not stated, and the longitudinal inclusion rules differed (non-smoking methamphetamine participants and ex-smokers were allowed).
reporting_issues.consequence: The degree of sample overlap, and whether the longitudinal methamphetamine group is representative of the cross-sectional one, cannot be judged.

reporting_issues.issue: Education was excluded from the main models; the sensitivity analysis including it is reported only as supporting the results at a more liberal uncorrected threshold of p<0.005, without a table.
reporting_issues.consequence: Whether the methamphetamine-versus-smoker differences survive adjustment for education at the paper's own corrected threshold is not shown.

reporting_issues.issue: Years of use (11.5) is reported for 33 of 39 participants and years of heavy use (8.4) for 38, without explanation of the missing data.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Table 1 and footnotes b and c)
reporting_issues.consequence: Exposure duration rests on partial data.

domains.note: The study's design directly addresses the main confounder (tobacco) and covaries age, sex and cannabis; education still differs and is handled only in a sensitivity analysis, and premorbid differences cannot be excluded.
DSM-IV diagnosis with daily urine toxicology during residence; self-reported amounts incomplete for some participants.
Advertisement-recruited volunteers; residential versus outpatient participation differs with group; non-smoking methamphetamine participants could not be recruited.

The methamphetamine group lived in a research unit under supervised abstinence between scans, so the longitudinal change includes the effects of that environment; scan intervals differed between groups.
Attrition into the longitudinal sample is not described; several exposure variables have smaller n.
Automated VBM with a standard pipeline, identical for all groups.
Corrected statistics cross-sectionally but uncorrected longitudinally; the abstract merges a supplementary analysis into the main caudate claim.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: This is the methodologically strongest of the structural studies read in this batch: it adds the comparison group the earlier literature lacked, verifies abstinence, and reports that the orbitofrontal and caudate differences are shared with tobacco smoking. Its weaknesses are the absence of non-smoking participants who use methamphetamine, residual confounding by education, and a longitudinal analysis that is small, unequal in interval and uncorrected.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC3427723 (accepted author manuscript; all sections, Tables 1–3 as text, both figure legends, acknowledgments, contributor and conflict statements; Figures 1–2 are statistical maps as images; the supplementary .docx with the caudate delineation methods and results was not opened because it is a download)

editorial_corrections.reason: ROBINS-E vocabulary: 'moderate' belongs to another tool; the judgment itself is unchanged (METHODS §5.3).
ROBINS-E vocabulary: 'moderate' belongs to another tool; the judgment itself is unchanged (METHODS §5.3).

design_detail: Cross-sectional structural MRI study at 3 T in 22 people with a history of methamphetamine dependence and 21 people without a substance-use history. Cortical pattern matching produced maps of gray-matter density (proportion of gray matter within a 15 mm sphere at each cortical point); hippocampi were traced and modelled for volume and radial size; lobar gray and white matter and ventricles were measured. A four-item memory test was given and correlated with hippocampal measures within the sample.
can_establish: That in this sample, gray-matter density around the right cingulate and limbic cortex was lower, hippocampal volumes smaller and white-matter volume larger than in these controls, and that hippocampal size covaried with word recall.
cannot_establish: That methamphetamine caused any of these differences (no pre-use scan; groups differ in education, smoking and depressive symptoms), that the differences are progressive or reversible (one scan), or that the participants' memory was impaired relative to controls or norms (no group comparison of the memory scores is reported).

sample.recruitment: Not stated in this paper; selection criteria are referred to the companion PET paper (London et al., 2004). Participants screened at UCLA; a partially overlapping subsample (17 people who used methamphetamine, 18 controls) had PET in that study (Materials and Methods › Participants; Figure 1 legend).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Both groups healthy on examination, history and laboratory tests. Excluded: psychoactive medication; cardiovascular, pulmonary or systemic disease; HIV seropositivity. By SCID-I, any current Axis I diagnosis other than methamphetamine or nicotine dependence excluded people in the methamphetamine group; controls could have no lifetime substance-use diagnosis and no current Axis I disorder. Axis II disorders were not exclusionary (Materials and Methods › Participants).
sample.demographics: Table 1 (means with SEM): age 31.9 (1.47) in controls vs 35.3 (1.66) in the methamphetamine group; 10 of 21 controls and 15 of 22 in the methamphetamine group were men; education 15.2 (0.50) vs 12.8 (0.42) years, p<0.001; mother's education 14.2 (0.48, n=20) vs 13.0 (0.68); race and handedness similar. Table 3: Beck Depression Inventory 1.25 (1.25, n=20) vs 9.77 (1.89), p<0.0005; Spielberger state anxiety 31.4 (3.77) vs 38.67 (2.64) in 15 per group, reported as not significant (p=0.0506); trait anxiety 31.9 (2.41) vs 38.7 (2.63), reported p<0.001.
sample.attrition: Not applicable (single session), but Table 2 shows incomplete drug-use data (duration n=21, weekly amount n=19, age of first use n=12 of 22) and Table 3 incomplete questionnaire data (anxiety in 15 per group).
sample.selection_effects: A dependent, mostly tobacco-smoking group with markedly more depressive symptoms and about 2.4 fewer years of education (editors' calculation from the printed SEMs: standardized difference about 1.1 for education and about 1.1 for depression scores) compared with screened healthy volunteers. Recruitment source is not reported in this paper, so the selection route cannot be judged.

exposure.measurement: Self-report only: an intake questionnaire, a drug-use survey and the Addiction Severity Index; DSM-IV dependence by SCID-I. No toxicological verification is described in this paper (Materials and Methods › Drug use).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Self-reported, Table 2: 10.5 years of use (SEM 1.09, n=21), about 3.44 g per week (SEM 0.79, n=19), used on 18.9 of the previous 30 days (SEM 1.75, n=21), first use at 26.1 years (SEM 1.77, n=12); route primarily smoking (stated in the text, not tabulated). Reported as study-sample characteristics.
exposure.polysubstance: Tobacco: 15 of 22 in the methamphetamine group vs 2 of 21 controls smoked more than 5 cigarettes a day (p<0.001 by the editors' Fisher test). Cannabis: 2.38 vs 0.14 days in the previous 30 (p<0.05). Alcohol days similar (3.24 vs 2.38). Six people in the methamphetamine group with heavy cannabis use or cannabis dependence were removed in sensitivity analyses, which did not change significance. Smoking was acknowledged as a limitation but not adjusted for (Materials and Methods › Drug use; Discussion, limitations paragraph).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Mean 6.64 days (SD 5.2), printed only in the mood table; how abstinence was established or verified is not described in this paper (Table 3).

comparison.controls: 21 screened volunteers with no history of substance abuse (Materials and Methods › Participants).
comparison.matching: Described as age-matched; not matched on sex (10 of 21 vs 15 of 22 men), education, smoking or mood. Hippocampal analyses adjusted for age and sex and, separately, for brain size; the cortical maps are described as a regression on group membership, with no covariates stated.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No pre-use imaging or cognitive baseline; current education and mother's education are the only proxies for premorbid circumstances, and education differed.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: No lifetime substance-use diagnosis; 2 smoked tobacco and cannabis use was minimal.

outcomes.instruments: 3 T GE scanner, 3D T1-weighted SPGR (1.22 mm slices); automated tissue segmentation; cortical surface extraction and cortical pattern matching using 30 sulci per hemisphere traced by an analyst blind to diagnosis, sex and age; gray-matter density as the proportion of gray matter within a 15 mm sphere; hippocampal surface models with radial distance from a central axis; lobar gray and white matter and ventricular volumes. Memory: a repeated memory test with 25 words and 25 line drawings, tested after a 10-minute distraction, giving word recall, picture recall, word recognition and picture recognition. Mood: Beck Depression Inventory and State-Trait Anxiety Inventory (Materials and Methods).
outcomes.validity_norms: Gray-matter density is a local proportion measure, not cortical thickness or volume, although the text also calls the same 11.3% figure a difference in gray-matter volume. Memory scores are raw counts correct; no norms are applied and no group comparison of memory is reported.
outcomes.operationalization: Deficit was defined as a lower group mean in a structural measure; impaired memory performance in the abstract rests on a within-sample correlation between hippocampal measures and word recall.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Cortical and hippocampal maps: permutation testing with 1,000,000 permutations giving one corrected p per map; lateral-surface maps were not significant after correction. Volumetric tests (hippocampus total and by side, with and without brain-size adjustment; ventricles; total and hemispheric white matter; four lobar white-matter regions; total gray matter) are reported uncorrected. The four memory correlations were Bonferroni-corrected for the left-hippocampus radial analysis (p=0.01 uncorrected, p<0.05 corrected).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: The analyst who traced sulci was blind to group, sex and age; blinding for hippocampal tracing is referred to earlier methods and not restated.

analysis.effect_sizes: Reported as percentage differences with p-values; no means, SDs or standardized effect sizes are printed for the brain measures (volumes appear only in Figure 3, an image), so standardized differences cannot be computed by the editors. Cortical gray matter: cingulate, subgenual and paralimbic region 11.3% below controls (p<0.05 in the Results; the Figure 1 and Figure 3 legends give p<0.034, corrected); adjacent medial frontal cortex 3.6% lower (p<0.1); left cingulate 0.7% lower (p=0.4 in the Results, p>0.1 in the Lateralization section); lateral surfaces not significant after correction. Hippocampus: 7.8% smaller overall (p<0.01), left 8.2% (p=0.01), right 7.5% (p<0.05), adjusted for age and sex, and still significant after adjustment for brain size and after excluding the 6 people who used cannabis heavily. White matter: 7.0% larger overall (p<0.01), left 6.6% (p=0.01), right 7.5% (p<0.01 in the Results, p<0.001 in the Discussion), with temporal (left p<0.005, right p<0.05) and occipital (left p<0.05, right p<0.01) excess; mean net white-matter gain 24.3 cc against a mean gray-matter reduction of 6.3 cc. Right frontal horn of the lateral ventricle 25.2% larger (p<0.05). No group difference in total cerebral volume or total gray matter (p>0.1). Memory: total and right hippocampal volume correlated positively with word recall (both p<0.05; coefficients not printed); left hippocampal radial atrophy related to group (p<0.05) and to word recall (p=0.01, p<0.05 corrected); picture recall and both recognition measures were not related to hippocampal measures.
analysis.covariates: Age and sex in the hippocampal volume regressions; brain size in a secondary analysis; cannabis handled by exclusion in a sensitivity analysis. No adjustment for education, tobacco smoking or depressive symptoms, all of which differed between groups; covariates for the cortical maps are not stated.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Two regions were predicted in advance from the companion PET study (cingulate) and from the memory literature (hippocampus), but no registration exists.
analysis.selective_reporting: Memory scores are used only in correlations; the groups' memory performance is never compared. Correlation coefficients are not given for the hippocampal-volume analyses. Percentages are reported without SDs or confidence intervals.
analysis.power: Not reported. With 22 and 21 participants, only differences of roughly one standard deviation or more are reliably detectable; the authors note that correlations with other cognitive measures might appear in a larger cohort.

interpretation_gap.results_show: A cross-sectional pattern of lower right cingulate and limbic gray-matter density, smaller hippocampi, larger white-matter volume and a larger right frontal horn in 22 people who had used methamphetamine than in 21 controls who were better educated, mostly non-smoking and much less depressed, with hippocampal size correlating with word recall within the sample.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract states that the maps suggest chronic methamphetamine abuse causes a selective pattern of cerebral deterioration that contributes to impaired memory performance, and that methamphetamine may selectively damage the medial temporal lobe and cingulate-limbic cortex; it also offers therapeutic targets for drug-induced brain injury. The title is descriptive, but the discussion compares the changes with early dementia and schizophrenia in effect size, calls the hippocampi severely atrophied, and describes neurodegeneration. None of this follows from one cross-sectional scan: there is no baseline, no adjustment for education, smoking or depression, and no demonstration that these participants' memory was worse than controls'. The discussion acknowledges that it is unknown whether the deficits are progressive or reversible, and that the smoking imbalance is a limitation, but argues from one published smoking study that the pattern differs.

timeline.event: Companion PET study in a partially overlapping sample reported cingulate and limbic metabolic differences correlated with self-reported mood (London et al., 2004, as cited here).
An independent sample recruited within an HIV study was reported in abstract form to show enlarged lobar volumes (Jernigan et al., 2003, as cited here).
Gray-matter volume compared in people using methamphetamine with and without cigarette smoking, and with abstinence (Morales et al., 2012; appraised in this batch).

replication.where_it_stands: Smaller limbic and hippocampal gray matter in people who use methamphetamine has been reported repeatedly, but the smoking confound was not separated here; the white-matter excess has had little replication, and whether the differences precede use or change with abstinence is unresolved.

funding.funder: US National Institute on Drug Abuse contract Y01 DA50038 (E.D.L., W.L.) and grant R01 DA15179 (E.D.L.); National Center for Research Resources M01 RR00865; algorithm development by NIBIB and NCRR grants R21 EB01651 and R21 RR019771 (P.M.T.); a Human Brain Project grant to the International Consortium for Brain Mapping funded by NIMH and NIDA (P20 MH/DA52176, P41 RR13642) (Footnotes).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: UCLA Laboratory of Neuroimaging and departments of psychiatry and pharmacology. The imaging method (cortical pattern matching) is the senior imaging authors' own; the comparison PET map in Figure 1 comes from the same group's companion study. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: Longitudinal MRI in people before and after the onset of regular methamphetamine use, with a non-using comparison group scanned at the same intervals, tobacco-smoking and education matched or adjusted, and the memory battery administered to both groups against norms; or at minimum a cross-sectional study with a smoking control group, as later attempted by Morales et al. (2012).

domains.note: Education (about 2.4 years), tobacco smoking (15 of 22 vs 2 of 21) and depressive symptoms all differ and none is adjusted for; cortical map covariates are not stated; no pre-use measurement.
Self-report only, with no toxicology described in this paper; key exposure variables are missing for some participants (weekly amount n=19, age of first use n=12 of 22).
Recruitment source is not reported here; people dependent on methamphetamine against screened healthy volunteers; sample partly overlaps the group's earlier PET study.
Abstinence averaged 6.64 days with a wide spread (SD 5.2) and no stated verification; any acute withdrawal effect on tissue water or volume is not addressed.
Mood and drug-use data are incomplete for several participants; anxiety measures from only 15 per group.
Blinded sulcal tracing and automated segmentation, but gray-matter density is a derived proportional measure reported interchangeably with volume.

Memory scores reported only as correlations with brain measures, never as a group comparison; correlation coefficients omitted; volumetric tests reported uncorrected while the maps are corrected; figure legends and text give different p-values for the same results.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The imaging methods are careful and the maps are permutation-corrected, but the design cannot separate drug effects from education, tobacco smoking and depression, and the central clinical claim (impaired memory) rests on a within-group correlation with no group comparison of the memory test.

key_findings.finding: Gray-matter density in a cingulate, subgenual and paralimbic region was 11.3% lower in 22 people who had used methamphetamine than in 21 controls, with the effect on the right medial surface; the overall cortical map was significant after permutation correction.
key_findings.locator: Results › Mapping cortical gray-matter deficits; Figures 1 and 3e
key_findings.note: Results text gives p<0.05; the Figure 1 and Figure 3 legends give p<0.034 corrected.

key_findings.finding: Left cingulate gray-matter density was 0.7% lower (not significant), and adjacent medial frontal cortex 3.6% lower (p<0.1); lateral-surface differences did not survive correction.
key_findings.locator: Results › Mapping cortical gray-matter deficits; Lateralization section; Figure 2

key_findings.finding: Hippocampal volume was 7.8% smaller overall (p<0.01), 8.2% on the left (p=0.01) and 7.5% on the right (p<0.05), adjusted for age and sex; the difference persisted after adjusting for brain size and after excluding 6 participants with heavy cannabis use.

Total white-matter volume was 7.0% larger in the methamphetamine group (p<0.01; left 6.6%, right 7.5%), with temporal and occipital excess; mean net white-matter gain 24.3 cc against a mean gray-matter reduction of 6.3 cc.
key_findings.locator: Results › Whole-brain gray- and white-matter measures; Discussion, white-matter paragraph

key_findings.finding: The right frontal horn of the lateral ventricle was 25.2% larger (p<0.05); total cerebral volume and total gray matter did not differ (p>0.1).
key_findings.locator: Results › Whole-brain gray- and white-matter measures

key_findings.finding: Hippocampal volume (total and right) correlated with word recall (both p<0.05), and left hippocampal radial atrophy correlated with word recall (p=0.01, p<0.05 after Bonferroni correction for four memory tests); picture recall and word and picture recognition showed no relation.
key_findings.note: Correlation coefficients are not printed; only p-values.

key_findings.finding: The memory test scores were never compared between the groups; the paper reports no test of whether the methamphetamine group recalled fewer words than controls.
key_findings.locator: Materials and Methods › Neuropsychological testing; Results › Hippocampal deficits

key_findings.finding: Group characteristics: the methamphetamine group had 12.8 vs 15.2 years of education (p<0.001), 15 of 22 vs 2 of 21 smoked more than 5 cigarettes a day, Beck Depression Inventory 9.77 vs 1.25 (p<0.0005), and had been abstinent a mean of 6.64 days (SD 5.2) by self-report.

Self-reported use: about 10.5 years, about 3.44 g per week, on 18.9 of the previous 30 days, primarily by smoking; exposure data were missing for some participants (weekly amount reported for 19 of 22, age of first use for 12 of 22).
key_findings.locator: Table 2; Materials and Methods › Drug use

key_findings.finding: Editors' calculation from the printed means and SEMs: standardized group differences of about 1.1 for education and about 1.1 for depression scores, and about 0.5 for age (not significant), indicating that the groups differ on these variables about as strongly as the brain measures differ.
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: SEM converted to SD, Hedges' g with pooled SD.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results refer to Figure 2b, 2c and 2d for ventricular, gray-matter and white-matter volumes, but those panels are in Figure 3; Figure 2 shows lateral-surface maps.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Results › Whole-brain gray- and white-matter measures)
reporting_issues.consequence: Readers checking the volumetric data are sent to the wrong figure.

reporting_issues.issue: The right-hemisphere white-matter excess is given as 7.5% with p<0.01 in the Results and p<0.001 in the Discussion.
reporting_issues.consequence: One of the two p-values is wrong; the finding's strength is uncertain.

reporting_issues.issue: The cingulate deficit is reported as p<0.05 in the Results but p<0.034 corrected in the Figure 1 and Figure 3 legends; the left cingulate is p=0.4 in the Results and p>0.1 in the Lateralization section.
reporting_issues.consequence: Inconsistent reporting of the same tests.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 1 the significance marker also appears on the mother's education row, implying p<0.001; from the printed means and SEMs (14.2 vs 13.0) the difference is about t=1.4, p≈0.16 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: The asterisk appears to be misplaced; readers could conclude the groups differed strongly in parental education.

reporting_issues.issue: Trait anxiety is marked p<0.001 (31.9 vs 38.7, SEM 2.41 and 2.63, 15 per group); from those figures the editors calculate t≈1.9, p≈0.07. State anxiety is given as p=0.0506 where the same calculation gives p≈0.13.
reporting_issues.consequence: Either the printed statistics or the sample sizes are wrong; the mood differences between groups cannot be verified as printed.

reporting_issues.issue: The same 11.3% figure is described as gray-matter density in the Methods and Lateralization section and as gray-matter volume in the abstract and Results.
reporting_issues.consequence: Density here is a proportion within a 15 mm sphere; calling it volume overstates what was measured.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 reports drug-use variables for different subsets (duration n=21, weekly amount n=19, age of first use n=12) without explaining the missing data; Table 3 reports anxiety for 15 of each group.
reporting_issues.consequence: Exposure characterization rests on partial data, and the mood comparison on two-thirds of the sample.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract describes the groups as age-matched, but the sex ratio differs (15 of 22 men vs 10 of 21) and age differs by 3.4 years in the same direction as the structural findings.
reporting_issues.consequence: Sex and age are adjusted in the hippocampal analyses but their handling in the cortical maps is not stated.

reporting_issues.issue: No toxicological verification of abstinence or of control status is described in this paper; abstinence appears only as a row in the mood table.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Materials and Methods › Drug use; Table 3)
reporting_issues.consequence: Recent use at the time of scanning cannot be excluded from the information given here.

editorial_corrections.reason: ROBINS-E vocabulary: 'serious' belongs to another tool; the judgment itself is unchanged (METHODS §5.3).
ROBINS-E vocabulary: 'serious' belongs to another tool; the judgment itself is unchanged (METHODS §5.3).
Language (METHODS §9): 9 replacements, no change of meaning, number or citation; list in data/verification/language-2026-10-16.json

design_detail: Prospective observational study of symptom course during monitored inpatient abstinence. 56 adults with methamphetamine dependence, not seeking treatment, were admitted to a research ward (UCLA General Clinical Research Center) for neuroimaging studies lasting 2 or 5 weeks and rated daily on a 30-item rater-scored Methamphetamine Withdrawal Questionnaire (MAWQ) and weekly on the Beck Depression Inventory (BDI), Brief Symptom Inventory (BSI) and a visual analogue scale (VAS) for craving; 89 healthy outpatient controls completed the BDI and BSI weekly. Analyses used subsets of 25–32 participants with methamphetamine dependence; linear mixed-effects models for time, ANCOVA with Bonferroni correction for group comparisons, Pearson correlations for craving and depression.
can_establish: How self-reported depressive and general psychiatric symptoms and craving changed over 2–5 weeks of monitored inpatient abstinence in 25–32 non-treatment-seeking people with methamphetamine dependence and no other current psychiatric diagnosis, relative to healthy outpatients.
cannot_establish: The course of withdrawal in people who seek treatment, have psychiatric comorbidity or stay in their usual surroundings; whether the changes reflect abstinence rather than hospitalization, decline from a peak at admission, or repeated testing (no inpatient comparison group); how often psychosis occurs in withdrawal (only symptom-distress subscales and three questionnaire items were used); or when relapse risk is highest (relapse was not measured).

sample.recruitment: Advertisement (print, radio, internet) for paid research participation; participants with methamphetamine dependence were not seeking treatment and were studied as inpatients in a series of neuroimaging studies; controls were studied as outpatients (Methods › Participants; In-patient milieu).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Methamphetamine group: DSM-IV methamphetamine dependence, active use with a positive urine screen at entry, self-reported use within 7 days before admission, no dependence on other substances except nicotine. Controls: no history of substance use disorder except nicotine dependence, negative urine tests throughout. Both: no major medical illness including HIV seropositivity, no other current Axis I diagnosis on the SCID-IV, no recent psychotropic medication; light alcohol use (described as equivalent to 7.5 drinks a week) allowed. Participants whose self-reported last use disagreed with urine toxicology were excluded from analysis (number not given) (Methods › Participants; MAWQ section).
sample.demographics: Controls vs methamphetamine group: age 31.7 (SD 8.3) vs 33.8 (8.2); men 50.6% vs 62.5%; years of education 14.8 (2.1) vs 12.6 (1.3); maternal education 14.4 (2.7) vs 12.7 (2.7); married 20.2% vs 5.4%; unemployed 25.8% vs 80.3%; on parole or probation 0% vs 21.4%; cigarette smokers 44.9% vs 91.1%; white 66.3% vs 53.6%, Hispanic 5.6% vs 26.8%, Black 12.4% vs 1.8%, Asian 10.1% vs 3.6% (Table 1).
sample.attrition: Of 56 enrolled, the analyses include 32 (MAWQ, days 1–14), 28 (BDI), 26 (craving VAS and craving–BDI correlations) and 25 (BSI); BSI controls n=85 of 89. Studies lasted 2 or 5 weeks, so weeks 3–5 come from a further unreported subset; the number assessed at each week is not given. The authors state the analysed subsets did not differ demographically from the whole group (data not shown) (Results › Demographics; Table 2; figure legends).
sample.selection_effects: Non-treatment-seeking, paid volunteers for imaging research, with other current psychiatric disorders excluded: people most likely to have persisting depression or psychosis were screened out, which biases towards fast resolution; the authors note treatment-seeking people may have more severe or longer symptoms (Limitations). Analysed subsets (25–32 of 56) were not shown to be comparable with the full sample. Inpatients were compared with outpatient controls.

exposure.measurement: SCID-IV diagnosis of methamphetamine dependence; recent use confirmed by positive urine screen at entry; abstinence on the ward confirmed by daily urine and breath-alcohol tests; days since last use from self-report corroborated by entry toxicology (urine kit detection window typically 48–72 hours, per the manufacturer) (Methods).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Mean 11.1 (SD 7.2) years of methamphetamine use and 20.4 (SD 8.6) days of use in the past 30 days (Table 1); most named smoking as their main route (In-patient milieu). Amounts not reported.
exposure.polysubstance: Dependence on other substances except nicotine excluded; light alcohol use allowed; 91.1% smoked tobacco and smoking was allowed freely on the ward to avoid nicotine withdrawal. Craving for alcohol, opioids and cocaine was measured by VAS but not reported.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Study entry is defined as days 0–1 of abstinence in the Figure 3 legend, although participants could have last used up to 7 days before admission; weekly assessments are described both as weeks of abstinence and as weeks of hospitalization. Abstinence was verified daily on the ward.

comparison.controls: 89 healthy outpatients without substance use disorder (other than nicotine dependence), recruited by the same advertisements, assessed weekly with BDI and BSI only.
comparison.matching: Described as matched; groups did not differ in age or sex but differed in education, maternal education, ethnicity, marital status, employment, parole or probation and smoking (Table 1). BSI comparisons adjusted for ethnicity, education, maternal education and smoking; BDI comparisons for demographic and behavioural variables that differed (Methods › Data analysis; Results).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No measurement before methamphetamine use; premorbid depression, childhood adversity and family history not reported. Unemployment and parole or probation status, which differed sharply, were not among the listed covariates.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: No substance use disorder other than nicotine; negative urine tests throughout; 44.9% smoked tobacco.

outcomes.instruments: MAWQ: 30 items plus vital signs, rater-scored on a four-point scale, adapted from the Amphetamine Withdrawal Questionnaire by one of the authors and expanded with symptoms seen anecdotally in clinical practice (joint pain, red or itchy eyes, headache, anger), given daily at about 9 a.m.; BDI and BSI (11 subscales) weekly in both groups; VAS craving weekly in the methamphetamine group (Methods).
outcomes.validity_norms: No validation data are reported for the adapted MAWQ, and the authors found it gave lower symptom intensities than the self-report scales (Limitations). BDI entry scores are interpreted against treatment-seeking psychiatric outpatients and BSI entry scores against general adult psychiatric outpatients. The BSI psychoticism and paranoid-ideation subscales are self-report distress scales, not diagnostic measures of psychosis.
outcomes.operationalization: Withdrawal was operationalized as MAWQ item endorsement and change over days 1–14; depression as BDI score; psychopathology including psychotic symptoms as BSI subscale scores; craving as VAS score. No severity thresholds or definitions of resolution are given; resolved is used to mean a decline to stable low levels or to the control level.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Partial: group comparisons used Bonferroni-corrected post hoc tests; the 33 MAWQ rows (30 items, 3 vital signs) were each tested at P<0.05 without correction (about 1.7 false positives expected; a Bonferroni threshold would be about 0.0015); the five craving–BDI correlations were uncorrected.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable for self-report scales; MAWQ raters knew participants' group and day of abstinence.

analysis.effect_sizes: None reported: P values only, and BDI, BSI and craving values are shown only in figures (images, not extracted). Editors' calculations: entry prevalence on the MAWQ (n=32, Wilson 95% CI): thinking often about methamphetamine 72% (55–84), craving 69% (51–82), increased appetite 63% (45–77), tiredness or low energy 56% (39–72), depressed 25% (13–42), sleep difficulties 22% (11–39), feeling watched or talked about 9% (3–24), suicidal thoughts 6% (2–20), hearing voices 3% (0.6–16), feeling touched 3% (0.6–16). Education difference between groups from Table 1 means and SDs: standardized difference about 1.2 (t about 7.0), not the printed F 4.4, P 0.04.
analysis.covariates: Group comparisons adjusted for ethnicity, education, maternal education and cigarette smoking (BSI), and for demographic and behavioural variables that differed (BDI); within-group time effects unadjusted.
analysis.selective_reporting: Craving for alcohol, opioids and cocaine was measured but not reported; control-group BDI time course and analysed-subset demographics are described as not shown; n at each weekly time point not reported; correlation coefficients appear only in Figure 3.
analysis.power: Not reported. With 25–32 participants per analysis, and fewer after week 2, a non-significant difference from controls at week 4 (P=0.07) cannot be read as equivalence.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among 28 participants, BDI scores averaging about 12 at entry fell over the first 2 weeks to stable low levels but stayed above controls' scores for the first 3 weeks and only approached them at week 4 (P=0.07). BSI subscale scores, including psychoticism and paranoid ideation, were raised at entry and fell to a low baseline by the end of week 2 (n=25). VAS craving stayed high through week 1, fell after 2 weeks and persisted at a lower level to week 5 (n=26). On the rater-scored MAWQ, craving and depressed mood items did not change significantly over 14 days; 3 of 32 endorsed feeling watched or talked about and 1 of 32 hearing voices at entry.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes: "Depressive and psychotic symptoms accompany acute withdrawal from methamphetamine but resolve within 1 week." The Results show depressive symptoms above controls for 3 weeks, and the Discussion itself speaks of a reduction within 2 weeks and of withdrawal symptoms resolving within 14 days. The abstract calls psychotic symptoms prevalent, but no prevalence of psychotic symptoms is reported beyond 1–3 of 32 item endorsements and raised BSI subscale means. The Discussion says the correlation data, with the literature, give strong evidence that days 7–14 are the most vulnerable time for relapse, although relapse could not occur or be measured on a locked research ward, the correlation rests on 26 people at two uncorrected time points, and symptoms at entry may partly reflect the end of a period of use and sleep loss rather than withdrawal. Withdrawal is described as mild and well tolerated with reference to Table 2, which reports only how many endorsed each item, not severity.

timeline.event: Newton et al.: 19 non-treatment-seeking people with methamphetamine dependence; generally mild depressive symptoms that varied widely and resolved within 2 weeks of abstinence (as described in this paper's Introduction)

McGregor et al.: 21 treatment-seeking people followed 3 weeks; acute phase of 7–10 days peaking about 24 hours after last use, then a milder subacute phase for about 2 more weeks (as described in this paper's Introduction)
Simon et al.: neuropsychological change during early abstinence, one of the same UCLA inpatient research programme's reports that this paper lists as based on its participants (refs 22–29)
This study: depressive and psychiatric symptoms fall over 1–2 weeks of inpatient abstinence; craving persists at a lower level to 5 weeks

replication.where_it_stands: Three small studies (19, 21 and 25–32 analysed participants) agree that depressive symptoms are highest at the start of abstinence and fall over the first 1–3 weeks, and that craving outlasts them; none followed treatment-seeking people with psychiatric comorbidity in their usual environment, and none measured relapse.

funding.funder: NIH grants P20 DA022539, R01 DA020726, R01 DA15179 (Edythe D. London) and M01 RR 00865 (UCLA General Clinical Research Center) (Acknowledgments).
funding.declared_conflicts: None (Declarations of interest).
funding.affiliations_note: Department of Psychiatry and Biobehavioral Sciences, Brain Research Institute, and Department of Molecular and Medical Pharmacology, University of California at Los Angeles. The MAWQ was adapted by one of the authors (Richard Rawson). Read as the PMC author manuscript of Addiction 2010;105:1809–1818.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective study of treatment-seeking and community samples, including people with psychiatric comorbidity, with toxicology-verified time since last use, a validated withdrawal scale and structured interviews for depression and psychosis assessed daily in the first week and weekly to 3 months, a design that separates abstinence from hospitalization and repeated-testing effects (an inpatient comparison group or outpatient follow-up), and relapse recorded after discharge.

domains.note: For the comparison with controls: large differences in education (standardized difference about 1.2), employment, parole or probation and smoking, only partly adjusted; inpatient versus outpatient setting. For the time course: no comparison group for hospitalization, regression from a peak at admission or repeated testing.

Dependence by SCID and abstinence verified daily, but time since last use at entry is self-reported and the entry time point is defined inconsistently (days 0–1 of abstinence versus last use up to 7 days earlier).
Paid non-treatment-seeking imaging volunteers with other current psychiatric disorders excluded; analyses on unexplained subsets of 25–32 of 56.
Cue-free, monitored ward with individual housing and medication for physical complaints only; neuroimaging procedures. Symptom and craving trajectories may differ outside such a setting.
Up to 31 of 56 participants missing from each analysis; numbers at weeks 3–5 unreported; exclusions for discrepant self-report not counted.

Validated self-report scales, but unblinded repeated administration; the adapted MAWQ has no reported validation and disagreed with self-report; psychosis measured only by symptom-distress subscales and single items.
Many outcomes (46 measures) with figures only; craving for other drugs and control-group BDI course not reported; abstract emphasizes resolution within 1 week.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The direction of the within-group change (symptoms highest at admission and falling over 1–2 weeks) is plausible and agrees with two earlier small studies, but its timing and size cannot be separated from hospitalization, regression from an admission peak and repeated testing, the sample was selected to exclude psychiatric comorbidity, and about half the participants are missing from each analysis. Comparisons with controls are confounded by setting and sociodemographic differences.

key_findings.finding: Sample: 56 people with methamphetamine dependence (mean 11.1 years of use, 20.4 days of use in the past 30; 91.1% tobacco smokers; 80.3% unemployed) and 89 healthy controls; groups similar in age (33.8 vs 31.7) and sex (62.5% vs 50.6% men) but different in education (12.6 vs 14.8 years), ethnicity, employment, parole or probation and smoking.

At entry (n=32) the most frequent MAWQ symptoms were thinking often about methamphetamine (23, 72%), craving (22, 68%), increased appetite (20, 63%), tiredness or low energy (18, 56%), restlessness (13, 40%), lack of motivation (12, 38%) and anxiety (11, 34%); depressed mood 8 (25%); suicidal thoughts 2 (6%).

Over days 1–14 of abstinence, MAWQ items with a significant time effect were red or itchy eyes (F 4.33, P<0.001), tiredness or low energy (F 5.36, P<0.001), increased appetite (F 3.23, P<0.001), sleep difficulties (F 3.16, P<0.001), lack of motivation (F 2.8, P=0.001), reduced sexual pleasure (F 2.22, P=0.008), feeling watched or talked about (F 2.19, P=0.009) and thinking often about methamphetamine (F 2.04, P=0.02); the craving item (P=0.79) and depressed item (P=0.26) did not change significantly. Vital signs did not change.
key_findings.note: 33 rows tested at P<0.05 without correction; degrees of freedom not given. The authors say substantial changes occurred only within the first 14 days.

key_findings.finding: Psychotic-type items at entry on the rater-scored MAWQ: feeling watched or talked about 3 of 32 (9%), feeling touched when no one is there 1 of 32 (3%), hearing voices 1 of 32 (3%).

BDI (n=28 vs 89 controls): mean about 12 at entry (mild–moderate range), decreasing over the first 2 weeks to stable low levels (time effect P<0.001); still significantly higher than controls during the first 3 weeks after adjustment (P<0.05); approaching control levels only at the end of week 4 (P=0.07).
key_findings.note: Weekly means appear only in Figure 1 (image, not extracted).

key_findings.finding: BSI (n=25 vs 85 controls): most subscales except phobia were raised at entry, fell significantly during week 1 and reached a low baseline by the end of week 2 (P<0.004); time effects included psychoticism P=0.003 and paranoid ideation P=0.003; by week 2 all subscales except additional symptoms were at the control level, although the same paragraph says the methamphetamine group scored higher than controls at most time points.
key_findings.locator: Results › Psychiatric symptoms; Figure 4 legend (panels A–K)

key_findings.finding: Craving VAS (n=26): high at entry and through week 1, significantly lower after more than 2 weeks of abstinence (P<0.01 vs entry), and still present at a reduced level through week 5.
key_findings.locator: Results › Craving for MA; Figure 2 legend
key_findings.note: The number of participants assessed in weeks 3–5 (5-week studies only) is not reported.

key_findings.finding: Craving and BDI were not correlated at entry (P=0.29) but were at the end of week 1 (P=0.004) and week 2 (P=0.03), and not at weeks 3 (P=0.8) or 4 (P=0.09); n=26.
key_findings.locator: Results › Craving for MA and depressive symptoms; Figure 3 legend
key_findings.note: Correlation coefficients are printed only inside Figure 3 (image, not extracted); five uncorrected tests.

key_findings.finding: Ward conditions: individual housing, cues and media restricted, daily urine and breath tests, questionnaires daily at about 9 a.m., medication only for physical symptoms (none for insomnia, anxiety or fatigue), free tobacco smoking, concurrent MRI and PET studies.

The authors list as limitations the small, non-treatment-seeking sample, inpatient cases versus outpatient controls, follow-up of no more than 5 weeks, and lower symptom ratings on the rater-scored MAWQ than on self-report.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 prints education as 14.8 (SD 2.1) vs 12.6 (SD 1.3) years with F 4.4, P 0.04; those means and SDs give t about 7.0 (F about 49, P below 0.0001; standardized difference about 1.2) with the full groups, so the printed test understates the difference by far (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Education differed much more than the paper suggests; it was a covariate, but residual confounding in comparisons with controls is more likely.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 smoking: 44.9% (40/89) vs 91.1% (51/56) gives a chi-square of about 31 (29 with continuity correction), not the printed 13.2 (editors' calculation); the F tests have error df of 111, 107 and 105, implying about 113, 109 and 107 participants rather than 145, with the missing demographic data not reported; age F 2.4 on 1 and 111 df gives P≈0.12, not 0.15.
reporting_issues.consequence: Conclusions about group differences unchanged, but the table's statistics cannot be reproduced and demographic data were incomplete.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says depressive and psychotic symptoms resolve within 1 week; the Results report BDI scores above controls for 3 weeks and approaching controls only at week 4, and the Discussion describes resolution within 2 weeks (BDI) and 14 days (withdrawal symptoms).
reporting_issues.consequence: The encyclopedia should not cite this paper for one-week resolution of depressive symptoms.

reporting_issues.issue: In the BSI paragraph, all subscales are said to reach the control level by the end of week 2 (except additional symptoms), but the same paragraph says the methamphetamine group scored higher than controls at most time points.
reporting_issues.consequence: Which BSI comparisons remained significant after week 2 cannot be determined from the text; the figure (image) was not extracted.

reporting_issues.issue: Study entry is defined as days 0–1 of abstinence (Figure 3 legend), yet participants could have used up to 7 days before admission, time since last use was used to align participants, and BSI time points are described as weeks of hospitalization (Figure 4 legend).
reporting_issues.consequence: The time axis (days since last use or days since admission) is ambiguous, which matters for any statement about how many days after stopping symptoms resolve.

reporting_issues.issue: Analyses use 25–32 of the 56 participants, and the number assessed at weeks 3–5 is never given; the abstract reports the full 56 without saying this.
reporting_issues.consequence: Late time points, including craving at week 5, rest on an unknown and probably small number of people.

reporting_issues.issue: Figure 1 gives the BDI range as 0–69 without naming the BDI version; the cited reference compares BDI-IA and BDI-II, which (editors' note) have 21 items scored 0–3, a maximum of 63.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the version used should be confirmed before comparing scores with norms.

reporting_issues.issue: Figures 1–4 are images; the weekly means, standard deviations and correlation coefficients were not extracted (the images could not be rendered without bringing the browser tab to the front).
reporting_issues.consequence: Magnitudes of change and of the craving–depression correlations are not on this card.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC3071736 (NIH author manuscript; all sections, Tables 1–2 as text, Figures 1–4 legends only, acknowledgments, declarations, references; no supplementary material)

design_detail: Qualitative interview study (Harm Reduct J 2022;19:4; open access, CC BY), the qualitative component of a larger sequential mixed-methods study of methamphetamine use in Nevada and New Mexico. 21 loosely structured interviews, December 2019 to February 2020, with people aged 18 or over who reported using methamphetamine in the previous 3 months, recruited by street and agency outreach and chain referral. Four questions concerned negative experiences and overdose: drawbacks and negative experiences; whether the respondent or anyone they knew had experienced what they believed to be a methamphetamine overdose and what it looked or felt like; experiences of seeking medical care; and strategies used to reduce harms. Interviews were recorded, transcribed verbatim and analysed inductively (thematic analysis) by a single analyst, with team discussion of memos and codes and a second researcher joining for the final organization of themes. No tables or figures; findings are presented as themes with quoted extracts labelled by respondent number, ethnicity, race, sex, age band, state and drugs used.
can_establish: How these 21 people described, in their own terms, what happens when too much methamphetamine is taken ('overamping'), how they distinguished it from opioid overdose, what they did about it, and what help they found when they sought care.
cannot_establish: How common any of these experiences is, whether methamphetamine rather than sleep deprivation or other drugs caused them, whether route of administration changes the risk (the authors say explicitly that their data cannot be used for this), or how often fatal methamphetamine overdose occurs; a purposive sample of 21 people in two states supports none of these.

sample.recruitment: Street and agency-based outreach in both states (flyers and one-to-one outreach at encampments of people experiencing homelessness, syringe service programmes and bars) plus chain referral through existing participants. Community partners (public health authorities, treatment providers, harm reduction agencies) took part in design and gave access to their premises. Interviews took place in private or semi-private settings, including partner offices, encampments and participants' dwellings. Participants were paid 40 US dollars immediately after consent, and reminded they could stop at any time, to limit any sense of coercion.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: age 18 or over and self-reported methamphetamine use in the past 3 months. All interviews were conducted in English, although Spanish was offered. No exclusion criteria are reported.
sample.demographics: 48% female and 52% male; 2 participants Black, 10 White, 3 multiracial, 6 Latinx; median age 35 years (IQR 30 to 43); 48% homeless; 81% had completed 12 or more years of education; 38% employed full or part time.
sample.attrition: Not applicable (single interview). The number approached or declining is not reported, and no saturation criterion is given for stopping at 21 interviews.
sample.selection_effects: Named by the authors: a convenience sample recruited where many people experiencing homelessness are found, from two western states with high rates of methamphetamine and opioid deaths, so findings may not transfer to people with more stable housing or to other regions. In addition, 17 of 21 also used opioids, so the sample is not of people who use methamphetamine alone; people who had died of an overdose are by definition absent, which bears directly on the central finding that fatal overdose was said to be rare.

exposure.measurement: Self-report in interview; no toxicology, no quantification of amount or frequency, and no instrument. Eligibility was self-reported use within 3 months.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not measured. 'Overconsumption' is the respondents' own notion, not a quantity. Respondents repeatedly tied symptoms to runs of two to three days without sleep rather than to an amount. Route was not asked about systematically; the paper reports that nearly half the sample named injecting as making delusions and hallucinations more likely, and gives accounts of people changing route afterwards.
exposure.polysubstance: Central and not controllable: 17 of 21 used opioids (heroin, methadone or prescription opioids) as well as methamphetamine, and all but two quoted extracts are labelled 'MA+heroin' or 'MA+methadone'. Alcohol was not asked about systematically; of the four respondents who described memory lapses, two said they drank and one had cut down. The authors state that symptoms could be due to sleep deprivation or other substances rather than methamphetamine itself.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable; no requirement of abstinence and no account of intoxication at interview.

comparison.controls: None (qualitative design). Comparison is internal and conceptual: respondents contrasted methamphetamine 'overamping' with opioid overdose, and one contrasted methamphetamine paranoia (after days awake) with cocaine paranoia (immediate).
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No information on psychiatric history, prior psychosis, sleep disorders or medical comorbidity, any of which bears on the symptoms described.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable.

outcomes.instruments: A loosely structured interview guide with four overdose-related questions (reproduced in the Methods) plus a short demographic questionnaire. Analysis was inductive thematic coding with a hierarchical code scheme; no software, coding frame, saturation assessment, member checking or reporting checklist (such as COREQ) is named.
outcomes.validity_norms: Not applicable. Credibility rests on team discussion of memos and codes, involvement of researchers and service providers including people with lived and living experience of substance use, and illustrative quotation.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Overdose' was left to the respondents to define, which is the point of the study; the authors group what respondents described into psychological and physical symptoms and appraise each for desirability, discomfort, concern about health or safety, and perceived need for emergency care.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (no hypothesis testing).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable; a single analyst coded all transcripts, with the research team discussing and refining codes.

analysis.effect_sizes: None, and none would be appropriate: this is a thematic analysis without quantitative comparison. The only counts reported are descriptive: 2 of 21 interviews containing an account of an apparently fatal methamphetamine overdose (both second-hand and apparently the same event), 17 of 21 using opioids as well, 4 of 21 describing memory lapses, and 'nearly half' naming injecting as raising the chance of hallucinations.
analysis.covariates: Not applicable.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol registration or published analysis plan is mentioned; approval was by the University of Nevada, Reno institutional review board, with the University of New Mexico deferring under a single-IRB agreement.
analysis.selective_reporting: Quotations are attributed to respondent identifiers, so the reader can see that several themes rest on the same few people (for example R8, R10 and R14 each appear three times); the number of respondents endorsing each theme is usually not given. Full transcripts are not available because of the sensitivity of the content; redacted excerpts can be requested through the university's research integrity office.
analysis.power: Not applicable. No sampling target or saturation criterion is stated for the 21 interviews.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In this group, acute fatal methamphetamine overdose was described as rare or, by some, impossible; what respondents described instead was 'overamping', a continuum of psychological symptoms (memory lapses, anxiety, paranoia, delusions, hallucinations, some experienced as spiritual and some as terrifying) and physical symptoms (an overwhelming urge to sleep, pounding heart, uncontrollable 'flailing'), usually attributed by respondents to several days awake without food or water rather than to the drug itself; medical care was rarely sought and, when sought, was experienced as having little to offer.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and conclusions stay close to this, which is the strength of the paper: the authors say explicitly that their respondents claimed fatal overdose is rare or impossible, that symptoms may be due to sleep deprivation or polysubstance use rather than methamphetamine, and that their findings should not be used to draw conclusions about routes of administration or combinations. Two small stretches: the Results report that nearly half the sample identified injecting as increasing the chance of delusions and hallucinations, a quantified statement derived from a question that was not systematically asked (the limitations acknowledge this); and the limitations state that respondents were asked specifically about witnessing fatal methamphetamine overdoses, whereas the question printed in the Methods asks whether they or anyone they knew had experienced what they believed to be an overdose. The Discussion's policy proposals (overdose prevention sites, drug checking, safer supply) go beyond what 21 interviews can support, and are offered as directions rather than findings.

timeline.event: Darke, Kaye & Duflou: 7-year Australian national study of methamphetamine-related deaths, cited here as background (toxicology detected other substances in 83% of cases and methamphetamine toxicity alone was the cause in 6.1%; 1649 deaths)
This study (interviews December 2019 to February 2020)

Wagner, Chase, Anderson, Reyes, Harding, Fiuty & Page: survey of 420 people who use drugs in the same two states, from the same programme of work, comparing self-reported symptoms of acute methamphetamine toxicity with opioid and mixed overdose (Acad Emerg Med 33(1):e70217; not read for this card)

replication.where_it_stands: The standard qualitative reference for how people who use methamphetamine describe 'overamping', widely cited for the claim that methamphetamine overdose does not fit the opioid overdose template. It should be cited for the description and the vocabulary, never for frequency. The same group's 2026 survey of 420 people is the quantitative successor and is the place to look for symptom proportions; the two are not independent, sharing authors, sites and programme.

funding.funder: Clinical Translational Research Infrastructure Network, grant 5U54GM104944-07 (a US National Institute of General Medical Sciences award).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors and research staff declare no competing interests.
funding.affiliations_note: School of Public Health, University of Nevada, Reno; University of New Mexico Health Sciences Center; and The Mountain Center Harm Reduction Center, Santa Fe (one author is a harm reduction service provider). The research team is described as including people with lived and living experience of substance use, which is a strength for interpretation and is declared.

what_would_settle_it: For frequency and clinical meaning: a prospective study in which people who use methamphetamine record symptom episodes as they happen, with contemporaneous measurement of sleep, other substances taken and, where possible, physiological measures, so that the contributions of methamphetamine, sleep deprivation and polysubstance use can be separated; linked to emergency-department and toxicology data so that the described continuum can be mapped onto clinically recognizable events.

domains.domain: Research design appropriate to the question (qualitative appraisal, CASP-style)
domains.note: The question is how people define and experience methamphetamine overdose; interviews are the right method and the four questions are printed in full.

Convenience and chain-referral sampling in outreach settings; no account of how many were approached or declined, no sampling frame and no saturation criterion for stopping at 21. People who died are necessarily absent from a sample used to characterize fatal overdose as rare.
