The issue is kept and its consequence now separates the article side, which both readers confirmed, from the registry side, which stays single-reader. The same applies to the protocol details in analysis.preregistration_detail and to the PROSPERO funding sentence in funding.funder. This is the item that keeps the card at first-pass.

disagreements.first_pass: not recorded
disagreements.reviewer: missed: the review states the 1999 withdrawal in Discussion 4.1 citing two reports that predate it, so the date is unreferenced in the review; the claim's 1999 date should be anchored to a primary regulatory source or worded as 'according to the review'
disagreements.resolution: Added as a reporting issue. Checked in the source: Discussion 4.1 gives the year and the two reasons with references 64 and 65, and the reference list dates those two reports to 1996 and 1998. I also checked the cross-reference in siefried_2020, which I read for this round: its amineptine paragraph gives no year and no reference, so it does not corroborate the date. Key finding 11 already attributes the statement to the review; the issue records why that attribution matters.

disagreements.first_pass: not recorded
disagreements.reviewer: missed: Results 3.9 classifies 8 of 9 trials while Discussion 4.2 says four gave nothing and another four gave prose-only descriptions; minor, and it does not affect the statement that only one trial reported adverse events by arm
disagreements.resolution: Added as a reporting issue after counting both passages: Results 3.9 names one trial with events by arm, three with prose descriptions and four with nothing, which accounts for eight of nine and leaves out the 1997 amineptine trial, while Discussion 4.2 gives four and four.

disagreements.first_pass: first-pass
disagreements.reviewer: kept first-pass; key findings flagged: 1; reporting issues flagged: 1; risk of bias: agree
disagreements.resolution: Kept at first-pass after adjudication. Key finding 12 is corrected and both missed items are added, but reporting issue 10 rests on the PROSPERO record, which neither the second reader nor this adjudication could open, so the registry half of that item, and with it the protocol details in analysis.preregistration_detail, have had only one reader; the card therefore does not meet the standard for ai-checked. It needs a targeted registry check by a reader with web access. The risk-of-bias appraisal (AMSTAR 2, critically low confidence, items 11 and 15 critical and answered no) is agreed; item 2 is partial yes on the article alone, and the reader notes that the detailed PROSPERO-based note under item 2 shares the same limitation.

design_detail: Completed systematic review with random-effects meta-analysis (not a protocol) of placebo-controlled parallel-group randomized trials of 'psychostimulants' (classical stimulants dexamphetamine and methylphenidate, plus bupropion and modafinil) for amphetamine or methamphetamine use disorder in people aged 14 or older. Searched MEDLINE, EMBASE, PsycINFO, Cochrane CENTRAL and CINAHL to August 2016 without language limits. 17 trials (1387 participants) included; end-of-treatment abstinence pooled from 5 trials and retention from 14 (odds ratios, RevMan 5.3); Cochrane risk-of-bias tool in duplicate; GRADE. Methods set in an unpublished a priori protocol; PROSPERO registration was submitted but not accepted.
can_establish: That, in trials published to August 2016, bupropion and modafinil (the only drugs in the abstinence analysis) did not increase urine-verified abstinence in the final 2 weeks of treatment, and that the four drugs together did not detectably improve retention to the end of trials; with very low certainty for both.
cannot_establish: Whether the classical stimulant agonists (dexamphetamine, methylphenidate) affect abstinence, because none of their trials entered the abstinence meta-analysis; whether any drug is harmful or safe (adverse events were not analysed quantitatively and denominators are not given); or whether longer treatment improves retention (a subgroup of two trials, one in incarcerated men).

sample.recruitment: Not applicable at review level. Trials from the USA (10), Sweden (2), Australia (2), Iran (1), Finland (1) and Finland with New Zealand (1), per Table 1 (editors' count); populations included adults with any frequency of use, people using less than daily, one adolescent trial, men who have sex with men, people with ADHD (one trial in incarcerated men) and people who inject.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: randomized controlled trials comparing any psychostimulant with an inactive control (placebo) in people aged 14 or older with a DSM diagnosis of amphetamine or methamphetamine use disorder (abuse or dependence), or DSM-5 stimulant use disorder with amphetamine or methamphetamine data extractable. Excluded: non-randomized or quasi-randomized designs, cocaine-only trials, trials managing withdrawal rather than dependence, and laboratory administration studies with non-substance outcomes. Psychostimulants identified from the ATC and AHFS classifications following earlier Cochrane reviews, including bupropion and modafinil (Methods › Inclusion and exclusion criteria).
sample.demographics: Table 1 gives per-trial n, percentage men (47.4% to 100%) and mean ages (17.5 to 42 years). Two trials enrolled only men (one of men who have sex with men, one of incarcerated men with ADHD); one trial was in adolescents; three trials restricted entry to non-daily or low-frequency use.
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level. The review reports that most trials lost more than half of participants before completion; in the retention meta-analysis 332 of 626 (53.0%) on psychostimulants and 268 of 558 (48.0%) on placebo completed (Table 2).
sample.selection_effects: Trials are small (47% had 30 or fewer participants per arm) and many excluded people with other substance use disorders. The five trials in the abstinence analysis were all of methamphetamine dependence and tested only bupropion (3) or modafinil (2).

exposure.measurement: The exposure is the assigned medication, as study conditions (Table 1): modafinil 200 or 400 mg daily (3 trials); bupropion 150 mg twice daily or 300 mg daily (6 trials); methylphenidate up to 54, 72 or 180 mg daily (6 trials); dexamphetamine 60 mg daily or titrated to a maximum of 110 mg daily (2 trials). Treatment periods 8 to 24 weeks.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only, as above. A planned dose subgroup analysis was not possible because doses were similar within each drug.
exposure.polysubstance: Many trials excluded comorbid substance use disorders (references 13, 24 to 26, 28 to 30, 33, 35), which the review treats as indirectness.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: Inactive placebo in all 17 trials; the placebo substance was reported in three (lactose in two, gelatin in one).
comparison.matching: Not applicable (randomized trials). Random sequence generation was adequately reported in fewer than half of trials and allocation concealment was not adequately reported in over 75% (80% in the GRADE footnote).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Same populations as the active arms.

outcomes.instruments: Primary: (1) abstinence, as the proportion of participants with methamphetamine-free urine tests over the longest substance-free period assessed across trials, which in the five pooled trials was the final 2 weeks of treatment ('terminal abstinence'); (2) retention, as the proportion remaining in treatment at the end of the trial. Secondary: serious adverse events, defined as any event causing hospitalization or dropout.
outcomes.validity_norms: Urinalysis is objective; retention is a process measure whose meaning depends on trial context (one trial enrolled incarcerated men, in whom the authors note expectations about parole may have affected retention).
outcomes.operationalization: Benefit is a higher odds of terminal urine-verified abstinence or of trial completion with medication than with placebo. Harm was to be the incidence of serious adverse events, but these were only described qualitatively.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. 8 counts the two primary pooled estimates and the six tests for subgroup differences (abstinence by drug and by use frequency; retention by diagnosis, drug, use frequency and treatment duration), which together produced 14 subgroup estimates. The only significant result (retention with treatment longer than 12 weeks; subgroup difference p = 0.05) emerged from this set.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable at review level. Screening, full-text review (kappa 0.84), extraction and risk-of-bias assessment (kappa 0.83) were done independently by two reviewers.

analysis.effect_sizes: Random-effects, inverse-variance odds ratios. Abstinence (5 trials, 642 participants: 70 of 353 on medication, 19.8%, versus 62 of 289 on placebo, 21.5%): OR 0.97 (95% CI 0.65 to 1.45), p = 0.87, I2 2%; GRADE very low; absolute effect 5 fewer per 1000 (64 fewer to 69 more). Editors' calculation from the pooled counts (crude, not stratified by trial): risk difference -1.6 percentage points (95% CI -7.9 to 4.7). Subgroups: modafinil OR 0.86 (0.46 to 1.61), I2 0%; bupropion OR 1.12 (0.54 to 2.33), I2 47%; difference p = 0.59; non-daily use OR 1.24 (0.34 to 4.48), I2 74%; unspecified frequency OR 0.92 (0.54 to 1.54); difference p = 0.67. Retention (14 trials, 1184 participants: 332 of 626, 53.0%, versus 268 of 558, 48.0%): OR 1.20 (0.91 to 1.58), I2 15%; GRADE very low; 46 more per 1000 (23 fewer to 113 more). Editors' calculation: crude risk difference 5.0 percentage points (-0.7 to 10.7). Retention subgroups: amphetamine use disorder OR 1.54 (0.48 to 4.99), I2 57%; methamphetamine use disorder OR 1.11 (0.86 to 1.44), I2 0%; dexamphetamine OR 2.50 (0.80 to 7.87), p = 0.12; treatment longer than 12 weeks (2 trials) OR 2.45 (1.14 to 5.25), p = 0.02, subgroup difference chi-square 3.93, df 1, p = 0.05.
analysis.covariates: None (trial-level aggregate data).
analysis.preregistration_detail: The paper states the methods were set a priori in an unpublished protocol available on request, and that PROSPERO registration was submitted but did not meet eligibility at the time. The protocol was not seen, so adherence to it cannot be checked; one planned subgroup analysis (dose) was abandoned and three (age, diagnosis, duration) could not be run for abstinence.
analysis.selective_reporting: Sensitivity analyses (removing special populations and removing trials at high risk for selective reporting or incomplete outcome data) are reported only as not changing the results, without numbers. Serious adverse events are reported as counts of dropouts without denominators. The review used published data only and did not seek unpublished outcome data.
analysis.power: Not addressed formally. The abstinence analysis has 642 participants and about 132 events; its interval (OR 0.65 to 1.45; roughly 6 percentage points either way) does not exclude a modest benefit or harm.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Across five trials of bupropion or modafinil, about one in five participants on either medication or placebo had urine-verified abstinence in the last 2 weeks of treatment, with no difference (OR 0.97). Across 14 trials of four drugs, about half completed, with a non-significant 5-point difference favouring medication (OR 1.20). Certainty was very low for both. Of the five planned retention subgroup contrasts, only treatment duration was borderline (p = 0.05), with OR 2.45 in two trials longer than 12 weeks. Several individual methylphenidate trials reported fewer positive urines (Table 1), but none contributed to the pooled abstinence estimate.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and conclusions state that psychostimulants had no effect on sustained abstinence or retention. For abstinence this generalizes from bupropion and modafinil to the whole class: no dexamphetamine or methylphenidate trial was in that analysis, which the abstract does not say. The conclusions also state that longer treatment may favour retention, which rests on two trials, a borderline subgroup difference among several subgroup tests, and a trial-classification problem (see reporting issues); the Discussion itself calls the finding non-generalizable. The abstract's statement that serious adverse events did not differ between groups rests on qualitative reports and dropout counts without denominators. The overall conclusion of very low certainty and the call for standardized outcomes are well supported.

timeline.event: Pérez-Mañá et al., Cochrane review and meta-analysis of psychostimulants for amphetamine abuse or dependence, which found no effect (cited as reference 7; this review updates it).
This review: 17 trials to August 2016; no pooled effect on terminal abstinence (5 trials) or retention (14 trials).

Siefried et al., narrative systematic review of all medications to June 2019 (43 trials); includes 14 of this review's 17 trials but not Das 2010 or the two Konstenius methylphenidate trials, and describes the Ling 2014 methylphenidate trial and the Elkashef 2008 bupropion trial differently (no urine difference; 156 rather than 151 participants).

replication.where_it_stands: The abstinence result is a statement about bupropion and modafinil, consistent with the null primary results of those trials as summarized by Siefried et al. (2020). Whether classical stimulant agonists improve abstinence was not answered by this review and remained open in the later reviews read for the encyclopedia. The overlap with Pérez-Mañá et al. (2013) and Siefried et al. (2020) means these reviews are not independent replications.

funding.funder: Population Genomics Program and the Peter Boris Centre for Addictions Research (McMaster University and St Joseph's Healthcare Hamilton); the senior author is supported by a Hamilton Academic Health Sciences Organization Innovation Grant. The funders are stated to have had no role in design, review, analysis, interpretation or reporting.
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare no competing interests.
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from McMaster University (Clinical Epidemiology and Biostatistics, Neuroscience, Medicine, Health Sciences Library), St Joseph's Healthcare Hamilton, Hamilton Health Sciences and St George's University of London. None of the authors appears among the authors of the included trials listed in the references.

what_would_settle_it: Adequately powered placebo-controlled trials of classical stimulant agonists (dexamphetamine or lisdexamfetamine, methylphenidate) in people with moderate to severe methamphetamine use disorder, using a common responder outcome (urine-verified abstinence or a prespecified reduction over the last weeks of treatment) and treatment of more than 12 weeks, with systematic adverse-event reporting; or an individual-participant-data meta-analysis of the existing trials using one outcome definition.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population, interventions, placebo comparator and outcomes specified.
An a priori protocol is stated to exist (unpublished, available on request); PROSPERO registration was submitted but not accepted; deviations (abandoned dose subgroup) are explained.
Restriction to randomized trials is stated without rationale.

Five databases from inception to August 2016 with a strategy developed with a health-sciences librarian (in an additional file), no language or date limits, reference lists of past reviews and included trials hand-searched, ClinicalTrials.gov searched for unpublished and ongoing trials; no other grey literature and no expert contact, and published data only. The search ended in August 2016 and the article was published on 14 November 2016; the saved full text has no submission date, so the interval to submission cannot be stated.
Two reviewers independently; kappa 0.84 at full text.
Two authors with a pilot-tested form.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: No list of excluded full texts in the article or among the three additional files described (PRISMA checklist, search strategy, extraction form).

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 1 gives diagnosis and population, length, drug and dose, n, sex, age and each trial's substance-use result.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: Cochrane risk-of-bias tool, in duplicate (kappa 0.83); per-trial judgments in Figures 2 and 3 (images).

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Only a general statement that most trials were not industry funded.

AMSTAR 2 item 11 is yes or no for randomized trials. Judged yes: the review gives a rationale for pooling psychostimulants as a class (agents sharing a dopaminergic mechanism with the drugs used, Background; a published classification approach, Inclusion criteria), pools with random-effects inverse-variance weighting, reports I2 with a stated threshold, and investigates heterogeneity through a priori subgroup analyses. Two caveats that do not make the methods inappropriate: the class pooling puts four pharmacologically different drugs in one estimate, which the review itself carries as GRADE indirectness; and the exclusion of the 151-participant bupropion trial (Elkashef 2008) from the retention analysis follows a prespecified rule (of trials with overlapping participants, keep the larger, Methods › Data synthesis; Anderson 2015 had 204), but the overlap itself is asserted and never explained (reporting issue 1).

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: AMSTAR 2 item 12 is yes, no or no meta-analysis. Judged yes: sensitivity analyses were run removing trials at high risk of bias for selective outcome reporting and for incomplete outcome data, one at a time, for both pooled outcomes (Results › Sensitivity analyses). Only the conclusion is given (estimates did not change appreciably) and no numbers are reported, which limits what a reader can check but does not mean the impact was not assessed.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: GRADE very low for both outcomes, with risk of bias, indirectness and imprecision discussed.
Prespecified subgroup analyses and discussion; but see the reporting issue on overlapping intervals.
Funnel plots for both outcomes, visually symmetrical and discussed; with five trials for abstinence the plot cannot detect asymmetry, which the review does not acknowledge.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding and absence of competing interests declared.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: AMSTAR 2 critical items here are 2, 4, 7, 9, 11, 13 and 15. After the second reading, one critical item is answered no (item 7, no list of excluded full texts) and two critical items are partly met (item 2, an unpublished protocol with a PROSPERO submission that was not accepted; item 4, a search without grey literature or expert contact), with non-critical weaknesses at items 3 and 10. Under AMSTAR 2 one critical flaw, with or without non-critical weaknesses, gives low confidence, so the overall rating stays low confidence after items 11 and 12 were changed from an unavailable response to yes. The review is otherwise well conducted (duplicate screening, extraction and risk-of-bias rating with kappas reported, the Cochrane risk-of-bias tool, GRADE with absolute effects, funnel plots for both outcomes), and its null pooled estimates are credible for the drugs that entered them. The main limitation for the encyclopedia is scope, not bias: the abstinence estimate covers bupropion and modafinil only, and the one significant subgroup estimate rests on two trials.

key_findings.finding: 17 placebo-controlled parallel-group trials (1387 participants) were included: bupropion 6, methylphenidate 6, modafinil 3, dexamphetamine 2; after screening 1251 unique citations.

End-of-treatment abstinence (urine-verified, final 2 weeks), 5 trials of bupropion or modafinil in methamphetamine dependence: 70 of 353 (19.8%) on medication versus 62 of 289 (21.5%) on placebo; OR 0.97 (95% CI 0.65 to 1.45), p = 0.87, I2 2%; 5 fewer per 1000 (64 fewer to 69 more); GRADE very low.
key_findings.locator: Results › Meta-analyses: abstinence; Figure 4a; Table 2; Table 3
key_findings.note: Editors' crude risk difference from the pooled counts: -1.6 percentage points (95% CI -7.9 to 4.7). No dexamphetamine or methylphenidate trial contributed.

key_findings.finding: Abstinence subgroups: modafinil OR 0.86 (0.46 to 1.61), bupropion OR 1.12 (0.54 to 2.33), subgroup difference p = 0.59; non-daily use OR 1.24 (0.34 to 4.48, I2 74%), unspecified frequency OR 0.92 (0.54 to 1.54), difference p = 0.67.
Retention to end of trial, 14 trials: 332 of 626 (53.0%) on medication versus 268 of 558 (48.0%) on placebo; OR 1.20 (0.91 to 1.58), I2 15%; 46 more per 1000 (23 fewer to 113 more); GRADE very low.
key_findings.locator: Results › Meta-analyses: retention; Figure 5a; Tables 2 and 3
key_findings.note: Editors' crude risk difference: 5.0 percentage points (-0.7 to 10.7).

key_findings.finding: Retention subgroups: amphetamine use disorder OR 1.54 (0.48 to 4.99), methamphetamine use disorder OR 1.11 (0.86 to 1.44); no drug subgroup significant (dexamphetamine, 2 trials, OR 2.50, 0.80 to 7.87); treatment longer than 12 weeks, 2 trials, OR 2.45 (1.14 to 5.25), p = 0.02, subgroup difference p = 0.05.
key_findings.locator: Results › Subgroup analyses (retention); Figure 5b to 5e; Discussion, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Individual trial results as tabulated: methylphenidate trials reporting fewer positive urines than placebo (Tiihonen 2007 OR 0.42, 0.24 to 0.72; Ling 2014 OR 0.18 at week 14, p = 0.025; Rezaei 2015 at week 10, p = 0.03; Konstenius 2014, 23% versus 16% negative urines, p = 0.047) did not enter the abstinence meta-analysis; the adolescent bupropion trial favoured placebo (5.0 versus 8.9 negative screens, p = 0.043).

Risk of bias (Cochrane tool): random sequence generation adequately reported in fewer than half of trials; allocation concealment inadequately reported in over 75%; 16 of 17 blinded participants and personnel; all unclear or high risk for blinding of outcome assessment; high risk for incomplete outcome data in half of trials; 47% of trials had 30 or fewer participants per arm.
key_findings.locator: Results › Risk of bias assessment; Discussion, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Safety: only 3 of 17 trials used a standardized adverse-event instrument; dropouts attributed to serious adverse events were 8 (modafinil), 11 (bupropion) and 7 (methylphenidate) against 11 on placebo, without denominators; no trial attributed serious events to study medication.

Sensitivity analyses removing trials in specific populations (men who have sex with men; ADHD; incarcerated men with ADHD) or trials at high risk for selective reporting or incomplete outcome data did not change either primary result (numbers not shown); funnel plots showed no visible asymmetry.
key_findings.locator: Results › Sensitivity analyses; Publication bias; Figure 6

reporting_issues.issue: The 'longer than 12 weeks' retention subgroup contains two trials (references 26 and 28), but Table 1 gives study lengths over 12 weeks for ten trials (for example Shearer 2009, 22 weeks; Anderson 2012, 16 weeks), and the Description of studies names references 25, 28 and 32 as the trials with 20 to 24 weeks of treatment, while Table 1 gives reference 25 a length of 13 weeks and reference 26 a length of 24 weeks.
reporting_issues.consequence: The classification behind the only significant subgroup result (OR 2.45) cannot be reproduced from the paper; the duration finding should not be cited without the primary trials' treatment periods.

reporting_issues.issue: The bupropion trial by Elkashef et al. (2008; 151 participants, 18 weeks) is excluded from the retention meta-analysis for an 'overlapping sample' with Anderson et al. (2015; 204 people using less than daily, 12 weeks), with no explanation; the two trials differ in size, duration and eligibility in Table 1, and Siefried et al. (2020) list them as separate trials.
reporting_issues.consequence: A sizeable bupropion trial may have been omitted from the retention estimate without justification; its direction of effect is unknown here.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion states that individual trial odds ratios showed little to no overlap of confidence intervals, and GRADE downgrades both outcomes for inconsistency, while the pooled analyses report I2 of 2% (abstinence) and 15% (retention).
reporting_issues.consequence: The inconsistency downgrade and the description of non-overlapping intervals are not supported by the reported heterogeneity statistics; the very low rating is driven mainly by risk of bias, indirectness and imprecision.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract states that the incidence of serious adverse events did not differ between groups, but no incidence was calculated: the review reports only counts of dropouts attributed to serious events (26 across medication arms, 11 on placebo) without denominators.
reporting_issues.consequence: The review provides no quantitative evidence on safety; a claim of no difference in serious adverse events cannot rest on it.

reporting_issues.issue: The publication-bias section introduces both funnel plots as being for treatment retention, then describes Figure 6a as built from the five abstinence trials; and it argues the abstinence plot would stay symmetrical if other trials were added.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor drafting error; a funnel plot of five trials cannot assess publication bias, so this domain is effectively unassessed for abstinence.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says drug subgroups in the retention analysis contained two to six trials, but after the stated exclusions (references 22, 32 and 33) the largest drug subgroup (methylphenidate) can contain at most five of the 14 trials (editors' count from Table 1).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; suggests the subgroup composition was not reported exactly.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC5109734 (all sections, Tables 1 to 3 rendered as text, funding, contributions, competing interests and reference list read; Figures 1 to 6 (PRISMA flow, risk-of-bias graphs, forest plots, funnel plots) are images and their values were not extracted beyond what the text states; Additional files 1 to 3 not read).

disagreements.first_pass: partial-yes
disagreements.reviewer: 'partial yes' is not an AMSTAR 2 response for item 11; on the instrument's criteria the item would be 'yes', or 'no' if the editors treat the unexplained exclusion of Elkashef 2008 as an inappropriate method
disagreements.resolution: Changed to yes. AMSTAR 2 offers partial yes only for items 2, 4, 7, 8 and 9 (METHODS §5.3), so the first-pass response was not available for this item. Decided from the source: item 11 asks for a justification for combining, an appropriate weighted technique and investigation of heterogeneity, and the review does all three (Background and Inclusion criteria for the class rationale; random-effects inverse variance with I2; prespecified subgroup analyses explicitly run to explore heterogeneity). The Elkashef 2008 exclusion follows the prespecified larger-sample rule in Methods › Data synthesis rather than an ad hoc choice, so it is a reporting gap (already reporting issue 1), not an inappropriate method. Item 11 is critical, so this changes the count of critical flaws.

disagreements.first_pass: partial-yes
disagreements.reviewer: 'partial yes' is not an AMSTAR 2 response for item 12; the item would be 'yes', since sensitivity analyses removing high-risk trials were run, though reported without numbers
disagreements.resolution: Changed to yes. Checked at Results › Sensitivity analyses: trials at high risk for selective outcome reporting and for incomplete outcome data were removed one at a time for both primary outcomes and the pooled estimates are reported as unchanged. The missing numbers are a reporting weakness, kept in the note; item 12 is not a critical item, so the overall rating is unaffected.

disagreements.first_pass: …search within 3 months of submission…
disagreements.reviewer: the claim that the search ended within 3 months of submission could not be checked: the article-notes panel with the submission date is not in the saved text
disagreements.resolution: Reworded to what the source shows: search to August 2016, publication 14 November 2016 (the journal line in the saved page). The judgment 'partial yes' is unchanged, since it rests on the absence of grey literature and expert contact, not on the date.

disagreements.first_pass: low-confidence (from one critical no and three partly met items)
disagreements.reviewer: agrees with low confidence; notes that treating item 11 as a critical no would give critically low
disagreements.resolution: Overall recomputed under the AMSTAR 2 critical-item rule after items 11 and 12 were decided from the source: critical items 2 and 4 partly met, 7 no, 9, 11, 13 and 15 yes. One critical flaw with non-critical weaknesses gives low confidence, so low-confidence stands; the reasoning now states the count.

disagreements.first_pass: …which together produced 16 subgroup estimates…
disagreements.reviewer: recounted from the Results as 14 (abstinence by drug 2 and by frequency 2; retention by diagnosis 2, by drug 4, by frequency 2, by duration 2)
disagreements.resolution: Corrected to 14. Recounted independently from the Results: abstinence by medication 2 (modafinil, bupropion) and by use frequency 2; retention by diagnosis 2, by medication 4 (the subgroup-difference test has 3 degrees of freedom), by use frequency 2 and by treatment duration 2. The six subgroup-difference tests and the statement that only the longer-than-12-weeks retention estimate reached significance are both right.

verification.checked_by: AI reader 2 (blind reading and adjudication, round 2)

design_detail: Natural-history follow-up of a stratified random sample (by gender, ethnicity and treatment modality) of admissions, mostly from 1996, to publicly funded Los Angeles County substance-use treatment for methamphetamine use. Monthly methamphetamine-use timelines were reconstructed retrospectively from the Natural History Interview at about 3 years after the index treatment episode (n=350) and at a second interview 2 to 4 years later (n=277). Outcome: months of continuous methamphetamine abstinence from discharge until the first month with any use. Kaplan–Meier-type survival description and a Cox proportional-hazards model with data-driven predictor selection.
can_establish: How often, and how soon, people discharged from usual-care treatment for methamphetamine use in one US county in the mid-1990s reported resuming any use, how often they later regained abstinence, and which self-reported characteristics were associated with time to first use in this sample.
cannot_establish: That any predictor causes earlier or later relapse (observational, self-selected exposures, data-driven model); in particular, the strong association with post-discharge self-help or further treatment is built into the way that variable was coded (participation before relapse, treated as a baseline characteristic), so it cannot show that continuing care prevents relapse. Nor can it show what current treatment achieves (index treatment 1996, data collected 1999 to 2003) or the effect of treatment against no treatment (no untreated comparison).

sample.recruitment: Treatment registry: admission records sampled from the California Alcohol and Drug Data System for the publicly funded Los Angeles County treatment system, mostly 1996 admissions; 62% residential and 38% outpatient index episodes (Methods › 2.1; Table 1).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Admissions of clients using methamphetamine to the county system; no further eligibility criteria are given in this paper (sampling details are in earlier reports from the project, which were not read).
sample.demographics: 56.3% men; 16.6% African-American, 29.7% Hispanic, 47.1% non-Hispanic White, 6.6% other or mixed; mean age at admission 29.4 (SD 6.9); 32.0% with less than high-school education; employed in 29.9% of the months in the 2 years before admission; 51.4% admitted under legal pressure; 19.1% self-reported an ever-diagnosed major mental illness; 33.1% reported sexual abuse before age 15; 56.0% reported parental alcohol or drug problems (Table 1).
sample.attrition: 75% of sampled admissions were located and 76% of those located were interviewed, so roughly 57% of the sampled records are in the analysis (editors' calculation; deaths and incomplete data are among the losses). 277 of 350 (79%) had the second interview. Those without a second interview contributed shorter histories (mean 39 versus 66 months) and were right-censored. Two missing predictor values were filled by multiple imputation (Methods › 2.1, 2.4).
sample.selection_effects: Only people who survived, could be found and agreed to be interviewed about 3 years after treatment are analysed; the authors report no differences between analysed and non-analysed admissions on the admission-record variables (education, age at first use, age at admission, prior treatment, employment, homelessness, pregnancy, legal supervision), but people who died or were not located may differ in exactly the outcome studied. The strata were sampled within gender, ethnicity and modality, and no sampling weights are mentioned, so the descriptive percentages describe the sample rather than necessarily the 1996 admission population.

exposure.measurement: Not a drug-exposure study: the 'exposures' are 17 candidate predictors, all self-reported at the Natural History Interview about 3 years after the index treatment (post-discharge self-help or further treatment from both interviews). Several are lifetime ('ever') measures recorded after the outcome period had begun: ever sold methamphetamine, ever injected, ever diagnosed with major mental illness, having experienced paranoia, hallucinations and violent behaviour attributed to methamphetamine.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Pre-treatment use: methamphetamine on a mean of 15.7 (SD 10.3) days per month in the 2 years before admission; 30.0% first used before age 16; 46.6% had ever injected drugs (Table 1). Index treatment lasted a mean of 3.7 months (SD 3.2; range 1 to 18).
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed; only methamphetamine use is analysed. The predictor set includes lifetime injection of any drug; other substance use after treatment is not reported.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable; abstinence is the outcome. Relapse is defined as any methamphetamine use in a month, so a single use counts; 36% are counted as relapsing in the first month, including people who were still using when they left treatment.

comparison.controls: No untreated or alternative-treatment comparison group; comparisons are between subgroups of the treated sample defined by the predictors.
comparison.matching: None. The reduced Cox model adjusts each of its five predictors for the other four only.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Motivation, self-efficacy, social networks, quality of life and clinically assessed psychiatric diagnoses were not measured, as the authors acknowledge (Discussion › 4.1); these plausibly drive both self-help participation and abstinence.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable.

outcomes.instruments: Natural History Interview: a face-to-face life-history interview with memory aids and corroborative information, from which a monthly methamphetamine-use timeline was built from reported use frequency and changes in frequency. Outcome: months of continuous abstinence after discharge until the first month with any use; also abstinence status in months 12, 24, 36, 48 and 60 (Methods › 2.2, 2.3).
outcomes.validity_norms: Reliability checks reported in this study: 88% agreement between self-reported current or recent use and urinalysis at the first interview; differences under 0.08 in measures of association with the predictors between proximal and distal recall of the same year. There is no biological verification of the month-by-month history itself.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Relapse' is the first calendar month with any methamphetamine use after discharge; 'continuing abstinence' is its complement. No distinction is made between a single lapse and a return to regular use.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. 17 candidate predictors were screened (4 dropped at p > 0.65 in univariate models, 13 entered a full model whose results are not presented, 5 retained at p < 0.20); the authors acknowledge that the several analyses raise the risk of type I error (Discussion › 4.1).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable: predictors and outcome were collected in the same interviews.

analysis.effect_sizes: Descriptive (n=350 unless stated): relapse within 12 months of discharge 61% (editors' 95% CI about 56 to 66%), comprising 36% with no abstinent month, 14% in months 2 to 6 and 11% in months 7 to 12; relapse in year 2 7%, years 3 and 4 3% each, year 5 2%, years 6 to 7 1%; 23% abstinent throughout their observed follow-up. Continuing abstinence for at least 2, 3, 4 and 5 years: 32%, 26%, 21% and 13% of the whole sample; 32%, 32%, 26% and 23% of those followed at least that long (n=350, 325, 277, 206). At least 5 years of continuous abstinence: 47 of 350 (13%; editors' 95% CI 10 to 17%) and 47 of 206 with 5 years of follow-up (23%; 18 to 29%). Abstinent in month 12: 66%; month 24: 75%; months 36, 48, 60: 77%, 80%, 79% of those observable. Among the 206 followed 60 months: mean 44 abstinent months out of 60; the 159 who relapsed did so after a mean of 7 months, 94% of them later had at least 6 months of abstinence, and they averaged 39 abstinent months. Reduced Cox model (n=350; likelihood-ratio chi-square 106.46, df 5): parental alcohol or drug problems HR 1.35 (95% CI 1.05 to 1.73), p = 0.020; ever sold methamphetamine HR 1.48 (1.15 to 1.90), p = 0.002; all three methamphetamine-related problems (paranoia, hallucinations, violence) HR 0.75 (0.58 to 0.97), p = 0.027; each additional month in the index treatment HR 0.93 (0.89 to 0.97), p = 0.001; post-discharge self-help or other treatment before relapse HR 0.29 (0.22 to 0.39), p < 0.001. HR above 1 means earlier relapse.
analysis.covariates: The five predictors are mutually adjusted in the reduced model; demographics, education, employment, age at first use, injection, use frequency, legal pressure, age at admission and modality were screened out by p-value. No adjustment for treatment programme clustering (intraclass correlation under 0.001).
analysis.preregistration_detail: None reported; the authors state they used a model-building approach because there were no prespecified hypotheses (Methods › 2.4).
analysis.selective_reporting: The full 13-predictor model is not presented, so the reader sees only the predictors that survived p-value selection. Sensitivity analyses are described only as showing 'substantial robustness' and are in an unread supplement. Use of other substances after treatment is not reported.
analysis.power: Not reported. With 350 participants and about 270 relapse events (77%), the model has ample events for five predictors; the issue is selection and coding bias rather than precision.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In this 1996 county treatment sample, 61% reported using methamphetamine again within a year of discharge (36% within the first month), and relapse then slowed: 7% in year 2 and 2 to 3% a year afterwards. Most people who relapsed also regained abstinence: point abstinence was 66% in month 12 and about 77 to 80% in months 36 to 60, and those followed 5 years averaged 44 abstinent months out of 60. In the Cox model, post-discharge self-help or further treatment before relapse had the largest association (HR 0.29), with smaller associations for parental substance problems, selling methamphetamine, more months in treatment and self-reported methamphetamine-related psychiatric problems.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract states that 61% relapsed within a year and 25% during years 2 to 5, and names the predictors as protective and risk factors; the conclusion says the results support early and long-term continuing care. Gaps: (1) the Results' own year-by-year figures give 15% relapsing in years 2 to 5 (editors' calculation: 7 + 3 + 3 + 2); the abstract's 25% matches the fall in unconditional continuing abstinence from 39% to 13%, which counts people whose follow-up ended before 5 years as no longer abstinent. (2) The 'protective' self-help variable was coded as participation after discharge and before relapse but entered as a fixed baseline characteristic, so people who relapsed early had almost no time to be classified as participants; this immortal-time construction biases the hazard ratio towards protection and is not discussed. Several other predictors ('ever' sold, 'ever' diagnosed) were recorded after the outcome period began, so their timing relative to relapse is unknown. (3) The abstract omits the point-abstinence and re-abstinence results, which give a much more favourable picture of long-term course than the relapse figures alone. (4) The continuing-care recommendation is reasonable as a hypothesis but rests on these associations, not on any comparison of care.

timeline.event: Brecht, von Mayrhauser and Anglin: preliminary analysis of the first 98 interviewees from this cohort, with 57% one-year continuous abstinence and age at first use predicting relapse; neither finding held in the complete sample (Discussion, 2nd and 9th paragraphs).
Rawson et al.: status of people who used methamphetamine, 2 to 5 years after outpatient treatment (cited as an earlier long-term follow-up).
Mooney et al.: 22% three-year continuous abstinence in the Methamphetamine Treatment Project, close to this study's 26% (cited in the Discussion).
McKetin et al. (MATES, Australia): 31% one-year continuous abstinence after residential treatment, against 39% here (cited in the Discussion).
This study: the longest follow-up of continuous post-treatment methamphetamine abstinence identified by its authors (mean 60.5 months).

replication.where_it_stands: The pattern of frequent early relapse followed by repeated periods of abstinence is consistent with the shorter follow-ups the authors cite, from different countries and treatment settings. The predictor findings have not been replicated and one of them (self-help) is structurally biased; another earlier predictor from the same cohort (age at first use) did not survive in the complete sample. Data reflect 1996 usual care in one US county.

funding.funder: National Institute on Drug Abuse grants R01DA11020, R01DA025113 and P30 DA016383-06 (first author); R01DA025113 (second author).
funding.declared_conflicts: Neither author declares a conflict of interest.
funding.affiliations_note: Both authors at UCLA Integrated Substance Abuse Programs (Department of Biobehavioral Sciences, David Geffen School of Medicine). The first author designed the study and did the analysis; the cohort is the authors' own long-running natural-history project.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective cohort of people leaving current methamphetamine treatment, with frequent biologically verified use measurement and continuing-care participation recorded as a time-varying exposure from discharge (or, for continuing care itself, a randomized trial of continuing care against usual discharge), reporting both time to first use and point and sustained abstinence over 5 years, with deaths and incarceration tracked as competing events.

domains.note: Associations adjusted only for the other selected predictors; motivation, social support, psychiatric diagnoses and post-discharge circumstances were not measured and plausibly drive both self-help participation and abstinence.

The self-help or further-treatment variable is defined by participation before relapse but entered as a fixed covariate from discharge (immortal-time bias favouring protection). 'Ever' predictors were recorded about 3 years after discharge and may post-date relapse. All predictors are self-reported.
About 57% of sampled admissions were interviewed; no differences on admission-record variables, but people who died or were not located are missing, and stratified sampling is not weighted.
Subsequent treatment episodes, incarceration and other events that constrain use during follow-up are not modelled, apart from their partial inclusion in the self-help or further-treatment variable.
73 participants without a second interview were censored at a mean of 39 months; censoring may be informative. Only two predictor values were imputed.

Month-by-month use reconstructed by retrospective self-report over several years; reliability checks (88% agreement with urinalysis for current use; similar associations under proximal and distal recall) support but do not verify the timeline.
Predictors chosen by univariate screening (p > 0.65 dropped) and then by p < 0.20 from a full model that is not reported; sensitivity analyses are only in a supplement.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: For the predictor associations, and above all the headline association with post-discharge self-help or further treatment (HR 0.29), the coding of that variable builds in a survival advantage, and selection of predictors by p-value without the full model shown makes the remaining hazard ratios optimistic. The descriptive relapse and abstinence figures are at lower risk: they depend mainly on retrospective self-report and on who could be found and interviewed, and are best read as describing survivors of a 1996 county treatment cohort.

key_findings.finding: Sample: 350 people from a stratified random sample of (mostly 1996) admissions to publicly funded Los Angeles County treatment for methamphetamine use, interviewed about 3 years after the index episode; 277 (79%) re-interviewed 2 to 4 years later. Mean post-discharge follow-up 60.5 months (SD 14.8); 93% followed at least 36 months, 80% at least 48, 59% at least 60.
61% resumed methamphetamine use within 12 months of discharge: 36% had no abstinent month after discharge, 14% relapsed in months 2 to 6 and 11% in months 7 to 12.
key_findings.note: Editors' 95% CI for 61% of 350: about 56 to 66% (Wilson). Relapse means any use in a month.

key_findings.finding: After the first year relapse slowed: 7% of the sample relapsed in year 2 (3% in months 13 to 18, 4% in months 19 to 24), 3% in each of years 3 and 4, 2% in year 5 and 1% in years 6 to 7; 77% relapsed within their observed follow-up and 23% stayed abstinent throughout (abstinence durations 22 to 90 months).

At least 5 years of continuous abstinence: 47 people, 13% of the full sample (editors' 95% CI 10 to 17%) and 23% of the 206 with at least 5 years of follow-up (18 to 29%). Continuing abstinence for at least 2, 3, 4 and 5 years was 32%, 26%, 21% and 13% of the full sample.
key_findings.note: The full-sample figures fall partly because of censoring (41% were followed less than 5 years), so they are lower bounds; the conditional figures are closer to survival estimates.

key_findings.finding: Point abstinence (no use in that month) was 66% in month 12 and 75% in month 24; among those observable, 77% in month 36, 80% in month 48 and 79% in month 60.

Among the 206 followed for 60 months, participants averaged 44 abstinent months out of 60; the 159 who relapsed did so after a mean of 7 months, 94% of them later had at least 6 months of abstinence within the 60 months, and they averaged 39 abstinent months.

Reduced Cox model (n=350): post-discharge self-help or other treatment before relapse HR 0.29 (95% CI 0.22 to 0.39), p < 0.001; each additional month in the index treatment HR 0.93 (0.89 to 0.97), p = 0.001; all three methamphetamine-related problems (paranoia, hallucinations, violent behaviour) HR 0.75 (0.58 to 0.97), p = 0.027; parental alcohol or drug problems HR 1.35 (1.05 to 1.73), p = 0.020; ever sold methamphetamine HR 1.48 (1.15 to 1.90), p = 0.002. Model chi-square 106.46 (df 5) against 110.71 (df 13) for the unreported full model.
key_findings.note: Editors' check: each hazard ratio and interval is reproduced from its printed coefficient and standard error. The self-help variable is coded as participation before relapse but treated as a baseline covariate, which biases its hazard ratio towards protection (immortal time).

key_findings.finding: 38.3% reported self-help and/or further treatment after discharge and before relapse (21% self-help only, 6% other treatment only, 11% both).

Race/ethnicity, sexual abuse before 15, self-reported major mental illness and treatment modality (residential versus outpatient) showed little univariate relation to time to relapse (p > 0.65) and were dropped; age at first use, which predicted relapse in an earlier analysis of the first 98 participants, was not retained in the complete sample.
Agreement between self-reported current or recent methamphetamine use and urinalysis at the first interview was 88%.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract states that 25% relapsed during years 2 to 5, whereas the Results give year-by-year relapse of 7%, 3%, 3% and 2% of the sample for years 2 to 5, which sums to 15% (editors' calculation). The 25% appears to correspond to the fall in unconditional continuing abstinence from 39% at 1 year to 13% at 5 years, which treats participants censored before 5 years as if they had relapsed.
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract overstates later relapse by about 10 percentage points; claims about relapse after the first year should use the Results' year-by-year figures.

reporting_issues.issue: The conditional 3-year continuing-abstinence figure (32% of the 325 followed at least 3 years) is inconsistent with the unconditional figure for the same duration (26% of 350, about 91 people, which is 28% of 325; editors' calculation) and with the reported 3% relapse during year 3, since it equals the 2-year figure.
reporting_issues.consequence: One of the 3-year figures is wrong; the Discussion's comparison with Mooney et al. uses the 26% figure. Claims should not cite the 32% conditional 3-year value.

reporting_issues.issue: The second interview is described as 2 to 3 years after the first in the abstract and as 2 to 4 years later in the Methods.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; follow-up duration is given precisely elsewhere (mean 60.5 months).

reporting_issues.issue: Several predictors are lifetime measures recorded at an interview about 3 years after discharge ('ever sold methamphetamine', 'ever diagnosed with major mental illness', methamphetamine-related paranoia, hallucinations and violence), and the post-discharge self-help variable is defined as participation before relapse but analysed as a fixed covariate.
reporting_issues.consequence: Temporal order between predictors and relapse is not established, and the strongest 'protective' association is inflated by design; none of this is discussed in the paper.

reporting_issues.issue: The full 13-predictor model is described but its results are not presented, and the sensitivity analyses are only summarized as robust, with details in a supplement.
reporting_issues.consequence: Readers cannot see the adjusted associations of the predictors that were dropped, so null findings for demographics, injection, use frequency, legal pressure and modality cannot be quantified.

reporting_issues.issue: The sample was drawn within gender, ethnicity and modality strata, but the paper does not say whether sampling was proportional or whether weights were applied.
reporting_issues.consequence: The descriptive relapse percentages may not represent the 1996 admission population of the county system.

design_detail: Single-site, double-blind, placebo-controlled, two-arm randomized trial (1:1) in an outpatient research clinic of the San Francisco Department of Public Health, August 2013 to September/October 2017; a larger and longer replication of Colfax et al. (2011) by an overlapping team. 120 cisgender men (115) and transgender women (5) who have sex with men, with SCID-diagnosed methamphetamine dependence and a methamphetamine-positive urine, received mirtazapine (15 mg for 1 week, then 30 mg daily) or matched placebo for 24 weeks, then 12 weeks of follow-up off medication, with weekly 30-minute counselling (CBT and motivational interviewing) and weekly urine tests. Primary analysis: GEE log-link model of piecewise linear trends in weekly urine positivity (week 1 omitted), with treatment effects at 12, 24 and 36 weeks. ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01888835.
can_establish: Whether, in this population receiving weekly counselling, mirtazapine reduced the modelled rate of methamphetamine-positive weekly urines over 12 and 24 weeks of treatment and 12 weeks after stopping, and how often mirtazapine produced short-term abstinence compared with placebo.
cannot_establish: That mirtazapine produces abstinence (abstinence outcomes were not significantly different and most participants never achieved sustained abstinence); whether the effect holds outside cisgender men and transgender women who have sex with men, in people with depression or psychotic disorders, or with better adherence; or that the self-reported sexual-behaviour changes reduce HIV transmission (not measured). Nor can it serve as independent replication of the 2011 trial, which came from the same team, site, design and analysis model.

sample.recruitment: Community recruitment through clinics, community-based organizations, nightlife venues and websites; telephone pre-screen, two screening visits and two run-in visits (with urine collection) to test retention before enrolment. Participants could receive up to 595 dollars for study visits (Methods › Recruitment; Procedures).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included (per the paper): age 18 to 65; SCID-diagnosed DSM-IV-TR methamphetamine dependence; interest in reducing or stopping use; assigned male at birth (any gender identity) or assigned female at birth and identifying as male; anal sex with men while using methamphetamine within the prior 6 months; methamphetamine-positive urine; for people with HIV, CD4 above 200 or 100 to 199 with viral load below 200 copies/mL. Excluded: prior mirtazapine trial; mirtazapine, MAO inhibitors or antidepressants in the past 30 days except five named SSRIs; current major depression or any psychiatric condition precluding safe participation; liver tests above 5 times the upper limit; eGFR below 40; pending legal proceedings with high risk of incarceration; other research participation.
sample.demographics: Mean age 43.3 (SD 9.8); 50.8% White, 25.8% African American, 12.5% Latinx; 115 cisgender men and 5 transgender women (1 mirtazapine, 4 placebo); 51.7% HIV-positive; 68.3% not employed; 56.7% with income below 20,000 dollars. Methamphetamine use 5 to 7 days a week in 51.7%, 2 to 4 days in 30.8%, at most 1 day in 17.5% (23.3% placebo vs 11.7% mirtazapine); routes: smoked 84.2%, snorted 38.3%, injected 40.8%, rectal 27.5%, oral 16.7%. Mean CES-D 20.2 (Table 1).
sample.attrition: Dropout 20 of 60 (33%) on mirtazapine and 13 of 60 (22%) on placebo (P = .21); final (week 36) visit completed by 38 and 42. Mean weekly visit completion 66% (69% vs 63%). Urine samples were missing for 34%, 41% and 36% of participants at weeks 12, 24 and 36, against 10%, 15% and 20% assumed in the power calculation (Results › Retention and adherence; Methamphetamine use).
sample.selection_effects: Of 241 assessed, 120 were enrolled; the commonest exclusions were psychotic disorder (40), absence of methamphetamine dependence (18), no positive urine (10), inability to adhere to procedures (8) and excluded antidepressants (5). Run-in visits selected people able to attend. The population is restricted to people who have sex with men, without major depression or psychotic disorders, and paid for attendance.

exposure.measurement: Assigned study medication: mirtazapine or identical over-encapsulated placebo prepared off site; 15 mg (or placebo) in week 1, then 30 mg daily to week 24; dispensed at baseline, weekly for 2 weeks, then every 4 weeks in WisePill electronic dispensers. Adherence by WisePill events and by self-report.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions as above (oral, daily, 24 weeks, then 12 weeks without medication). WisePill adherence: weeks 2 to 12, 38.5% (SD 27.0) mirtazapine vs 39.5% (26.2) placebo; weeks 13 to 24, 28.1% (23.4) vs 38.5% (27.0) as printed; at least 50% adherence in 37% vs 35% (week 12) and 22% vs 20% (week 24).
exposure.polysubstance: Other substance use was assessed weekly by audio computer-assisted self-interview but is not reported; one participant on mirtazapine died of an unintentional opioid overdose. Four participants (3%) were taking SSRIs, with no association with urine results.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable: participants were actively using (80% urine-positive at baseline: 85% mirtazapine, 75% placebo) and the outcome is urine positivity during and after treatment.

comparison.controls: Matched placebo on the same schedule, with the same weekly counselling, HIV risk-reduction counselling and visit payments.
comparison.matching: 1:1 sequence generated by the study biostatistician; allocation known only to the off-site biostatistician and pharmacist; block size not stated. Baseline differences: methamphetamine-positive urine 85% vs 75% (P = .16); craving 5.8 vs 4.7 (P = .08); use on at most 1 day a week 11.7% vs 23.3%; high school or less 30.0% vs 45.0%; full-time employment 18.3% vs 8.3%.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to a randomized comparison.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Same population; not reported for either arm.

outcomes.instruments: Primary: weekly methamphetamine-metabolite urine test (MedTox EZ-Screen, qualitative), analysed as a repeated binary indicator over weeks 2 to 12, 13 to 24 and 25 to 36. Secondary: six self-reported sexual-risk measures by audio computer-assisted self-interview (past 4 weeks). Also craving, Severity of Dependence Scale, Athens Insomnia Scale, sleep hours, CES-D, adherence, adverse events, end-of-study abstinence (no methamphetamine in the last 2 weeks of each evaluation period) and 'beyond-threshold weeks of success'.
outcomes.validity_norms: Urine testing is objective but qualitative and covers only recent use; abstinence measures are urine-defined. Sexual-risk outcomes are self-reported counts.
outcomes.operationalization: Benefit is a greater decline in the modelled probability of a positive weekly urine on mirtazapine than on placebo, after accounting for the fitted baseline difference, expressed as relative risks at 12 weeks and as 'net' relative risks at 24 and 36 weeks.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; the authors acknowledge a large number of secondary outcomes at multiple time points without adjustment. 33 counts 3 primary time points, 18 sexual-behaviour estimates (6 measures at 3 time points), 6 sleep and depression estimates, 3 end-of-study abstinence comparisons and 3 beyond-threshold comparisons; adherence, craving, dependence-severity and as-treated comparisons come on top.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Double-blind (registry: participant, investigator and outcomes assessor masked). At week 24, 46% on mirtazapine and 49% on placebo guessed their assignment correctly (P = .83), although fatigue or drowsiness was reported by 30% on mirtazapine and 10% on placebo.

analysis.effect_sizes: Primary (intention-to-treat GEE, robust SEs): RR for a positive urine 0.67 (95% CI 0.51 to 0.87), P = .003, at 12 weeks; 'net' RR 0.75 (0.56 to 1.00), P = .05, at 24 weeks; 'net' RR 0.73 (0.57 to 0.96), P = .02, at 36 weeks (12 weeks after stopping). Raw positivity among samples provided: week 12, 25 of 38 (66%) vs 32 of 41 (78%); week 24, 20 of 32 (63%) vs 29 of 39 (74%); week 36, 25 of 35 (71%) vs 37 of 42 (88%). Editors' calculation from these counts (cross-sectional, ignoring the baseline difference and missing samples): risk differences -12.3 (95% CI -32.0 to 7.4), -11.9 (-33.5 to 9.8) and -16.7 (-34.6 to 1.2) percentage points. End-of-study abstinence (last 2 weeks): 11 (18%) vs 5 (8%) at weeks 12 and 24 (OR 2.50, 0.80 to 7.61; P = .11), 7 (12%) vs 3 (5%) at week 36 (OR 2.50, 0.62 to 10.20; P = .19); reported numbers needed to treat 10, 10 and 15; editors' risk difference at week 12, 10.0 points (-2.0 to 22.0). Beyond-threshold weeks of success: median 0 (IQR 0 to 0) in both arms at all time points. As-treated (upper half of adherence): cumulative adherence RR 0.70 (0.38 to 1.28) at 12 weeks and 0.69 (0.50 to 0.95) at 24 weeks; past-week adherence 0.64 (0.36 to 1.13) and 0.73 (0.50 to 1.08). Sexual risk at 24 weeks: male partners RR 0.52 (0.27 to 0.97); condomless anal sex with serodiscordant partners 0.47 (0.23 to 0.97); condomless receptive anal sex with serodiscordant partners 0.37 (0.14 to 0.93); all P = .04; three other measures not significant; no differences at 12 or 36 weeks. CES-D net -6.18 (-11.07 to -1.30) at 24 weeks only; Athens Insomnia Scale -1.40 (-2.74 to -0.07) at 24 weeks only.
analysis.covariates: None in the primary model beyond the fitted baseline difference; a sensitivity model adjusted for imbalanced baseline characteristics and baseline correlates of missing or positive urines.
analysis.preregistration_detail: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01888835, first submitted 25 June 2013 and posted 28 June 2013, before the August 2013 start. The registered primary outcome (number of methamphetamine-positive urine tests, efficacy at 12 and 24 weeks of treatment and whether sustained to week 36) and secondary outcome (sexual risk: male partners, partners with whom methamphetamine was used, unprotected anal sex with serodiscordant partners) are unchanged since registration and match the paper; adherence and adverse events are registered as other outcomes. Depression, insomnia and abstinence-based outcomes are not registered. Registry eligibility differs from the paper's (age 18 to 69 vs 18 to 65; anal sex within 3 vs 6 months; all antidepressants excluded vs five SSRIs allowed; bipolar or psychotic disorder excluded). No results are posted on the registry. The protocol is in a supplement that was not read.
analysis.selective_reporting: Sensitivity-analysis estimates (week 1 included, missing imputed positive, adjusted, out-of-window visits, stratified by use intensity) are given only qualitatively in the text, with numbers in an unread supplementary table; stratification by baseline use intensity showed no significant effect. Other substance use and self-reported methamphetamine use are not reported.
analysis.power: 80% power for RRs of 0.81 (weeks 2 to 12), 0.86 (13 to 24) and 0.85 (25 to 36), assuming 90%, 85% and 80% retention and within-person correlation of 0.45. Observed missing urine rates (34% to 41%) were well above the assumed 10% to 20%; the authors state minimum detectable effects were nonetheless similar.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Modelled urine positivity fell more on mirtazapine (RR 0.67 at 12 weeks; 0.75 at 24 weeks, upper limit 1.00; 0.73 at 36 weeks). In absolute terms most samples stayed positive in both arms (63% to 71% on mirtazapine, 74% to 88% on placebo at weeks 12 to 36), the mirtazapine arm started with more positive urines (85% vs 75%), a third or more of samples were missing at each assessment, and abstinence did not differ significantly (18% vs 8% end-of-study abstinence; median 0 weeks of sustained success in both arms). Adherence was below 40% in both arms. Sexual-risk differences appeared only at 24 weeks, for 3 of 6 measures at P = .04, without multiplicity correction.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Key Points state that mirtazapine is the first medication to show efficacy for methamphetamine use disorder in 2 independent randomized trials and that the sexual-risk findings were consistent with the earlier study; the abstract concludes that mirtazapine reduced methamphetamine use and some HIV risk behaviours with benefits lasting after treatment. The two trials share investigators, site, population and analysis model, so 'independent' is overstated; the earlier trial found sexual-risk reductions at 12 weeks, this one found none at 12 weeks. The Discussion is more measured, calling the reduction modest overall and non-significant on abstinence-based analyses, and the Limitations note the unadjusted multiple secondary comparisons.

timeline.event: Colfax et al.: 12-week trial in 60 MSM at the same health department (RR 0.57 for a positive urine at 12 weeks); this trial is its planned expansion.
This trial: 120 participants, 24 weeks of treatment plus 12 weeks of follow-up; direction of the urine effect reproduced (RR 0.67 at 12 weeks).
Siefried et al. systematic review (search to June 2019) describes this trial in its Discussion as a replication but does not include it among its 43 trials.

replication.where_it_stands: Two trials from one team, one site and one population show the same direction of effect on urine positivity with the same analysis model; the effect on abstinence is not significant in either. Replication by an independent group, in other populations and with abstinence or use-days outcomes, had not been identified in this reading.

funding.funder: National Institutes of Health grant R01DA034527 and National Institute on Drug Abuse grant R01DA031678; the funders had no role in design, conduct, analysis, interpretation, writing or the decision to submit.
funding.declared_conflicts: The first author has led NIH-funded studies receiving donated ledipasvir-sofosbuvir from Gilead Sciences (2016 to 2017), outside this work, and has received grant or contract support from NIH, CDC, SAMHSA, AHRQ and UCSF; the other authors report grant or contract support from public and foundation funders (NIH, CDC, HIV Prevention Trials Network, MPact Global Action, DARPA, PCORI, Alzheimer's Foundation, American Cancer Society, Buffett Foundation, Department of Defense, Department of Veterans Affairs); one reports NIDA grants during the conduct of the study.
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from the San Francisco Department of Public Health and the University of California San Francisco. Five authors (G-M Santos, Vittinghoff, Matheson, D Santos, Colfax) were authors of the 2011 trial this study replicates; the co-first authors had full access to the data. No industry funding of this trial is reported. Second reading: the funding and conflict-of-interest details on this card could not be re-checked, because the saved page used for the second reading has no Article Information block; treat the funder, the disclosures and the role-of-funder statement as single-reader.

what_would_settle_it: An independent multi-site placebo-controlled trial of mirtazapine in a broader population of people with methamphetamine use disorder (including women, heterosexual men and people with depression), with a registered primary outcome on urine-verified use days or abstinence, strategies that keep missing urine data low, verified adherence, follow-up of at least 6 months after stopping, and HIV or STI incidence if the prevention claim is to be tested.

domains.note: Statistician-generated sequence with allocation held off site by the biostatistician and pharmacist and identical over-encapsulation; baseline differences (85% vs 75% positive urine; craving; frequency of use) are compatible with chance, though the primary-outcome imbalance matters for a model that estimates divergence from baseline.
Double-blind with an intention-to-treat analysis; similar (low) adherence in both arms; week-24 guesses no better than chance despite more drowsiness on mirtazapine.

34% to 41% of urine results missing at weeks 12, 24 and 36, more dropout on mirtazapine (33% vs 22%); the primary analysis assumes missingness completely at random given time and arm. Imputing missing samples as positive reportedly preserved significance, but the estimate is only in an unread supplement.
Objective urine testing applied identically in both arms.

Primary and secondary outcomes registered before enrolment and unchanged, matching the paper; the analysis model is described as prespecified, with the protocol supplied as a supplement. Exploratory outcomes (depression, insomnia, abstinence) are reported alongside without adjustment.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A prospectively registered, well-concealed double-blind trial with an objective primary outcome whose analysis follows its registration. The concern is missing data: more than a third of urine results are missing at each assessment, dropout is higher on mirtazapine, and the primary analysis relies on missing-completely-at-random assumptions, with the conservative imputation result not shown in the article. The relative risks are also model-based divergences that are larger than the raw cross-sectional contrasts, partly because the mirtazapine arm started with more positive urines.

key_findings.finding: 120 participants randomized 60:60 (115 cisgender men, 5 transgender women who have sex with men) from 241 assessed; mean age 43.3; 51.7% HIV-positive; 80% urine-positive at baseline (85% mirtazapine, 75% placebo).
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Results; Results › Participants; Table 1; Results › Methamphetamine use, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Primary outcome (intention to treat): RR of a methamphetamine-positive urine 0.67 (95% CI 0.51 to 0.87), P = .003, at 12 weeks; net RR 0.75 (0.56 to 1.00), P = .05, at 24 weeks; net RR 0.73 (0.57 to 0.96), P = .02, at 36 weeks (12 weeks after medication stopped).
key_findings.locator: Table 2, Primary outcomes; Results › Methamphetamine use
key_findings.note: Model-based divergence of piecewise linear trends after accounting for the fitted baseline difference; the meaning of the 'net' 24- and 36-week estimates is defined only in footnotes (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Raw urine positivity among samples provided: week 12, 25 of 38 (66%) mirtazapine vs 32 of 41 (78%) placebo; week 24, 20 of 32 (63%) vs 29 of 39 (74%); week 36, 25 of 35 (71%) vs 37 of 42 (88%). Editors' calculation: risk differences -12.3 (95% CI -32.0 to 7.4), -11.9 (-33.5 to 9.8) and -16.7 (-34.6 to 1.2) percentage points; ratios of 0.84, 0.84 and 0.81.

Abstinence: end-of-study abstinence (no positive urine in the last 2 weeks) in 11 (18%) vs 5 (8%) at weeks 12 and 24 (OR 2.50, 0.80 to 7.61; P = .11) and 7 (12%) vs 3 (5%) at week 36 (OR 2.50, 0.62 to 10.20; P = .19); median beyond-threshold weeks of success 0 (IQR 0 to 0) in both arms at all points.
key_findings.locator: Table 2; Results › Number of beyond-threshold weeks of success

key_findings.finding: Missing urine results: 41 of 120 (34%) at week 12, 49 (41%) at week 24 and 43 (36%) at week 36, against 10%, 15% and 20% assumed; dropout 20 (33%) on mirtazapine vs 13 (22%) on placebo (P = .21).
key_findings.locator: Results › Methamphetamine use, 2nd paragraph; Retention and adherence

key_findings.finding: Adherence by WisePill dispenser was low and similar by arm: 38.5% vs 39.5% over weeks 2 to 12 (P = .77); over weeks 13 to 24 printed as 28.1% vs 38.5% (P = .59); self-reported 44.3% vs 46.1% and 38.8% vs 37.5%.
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Results; Table 2; Results › Medication adherence
key_findings.note: The week-24 placebo values repeat the week-12 mirtazapine values exactly and are hard to reconcile with P = .59 (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Sexual risk (self-report): no differences at 12 weeks; at 24 weeks fewer male partners (RR 0.52, 0.27 to 0.97), fewer condomless anal sex episodes with serodiscordant partners (0.47, 0.23 to 0.97) and fewer condomless receptive episodes with serodiscordant partners (0.37, 0.14 to 0.93), all P = .04; partners with whom methamphetamine was used 0.54 (0.26 to 1.14) and anal sex with serodiscordant partners 0.53 (0.28 to 1.01) not significant; no differences at 36 weeks.

Depression and sleep: CES-D net 6.18 points lower on mirtazapine at 24 weeks (1.30 to 11.07; P = .01), not at 12 or 36 weeks; Athens Insomnia Scale 1.40 points lower at 24 weeks (0.07 to 2.74; P = .04); no differences in craving or dependence severity.
key_findings.locator: Table 2; Results › Craving, severity of dependence, depressive symptoms, and sleep

key_findings.finding: Safety: serious adverse events reported as nine, none judged drug-related; listed on mirtazapine: a death from unintentional opioid overdose and hospitalizations for deep venous thrombosis, congestive heart failure and soft-tissue infection; on placebo: shoulder injury, COPD, assault and lower respiratory infection. Fatigue or drowsiness 18 (30%) vs 6 (10%); weight gain 4 (7%) vs 1 (2%); hyperglycaemia 14 (23%) vs 11 (18%).
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: drowsiness risk difference 20 percentage points (6.1 to 33.9), Fisher's exact p = 0.011. Only eight serious events are itemized.

key_findings.finding: Registration NCT01888835, first submitted 25 June 2013 (before the August 2013 start); registered primary outcome (methamphetamine-positive urine tests at 12 and 24 weeks and sustained to 36 weeks) and secondary sexual-risk outcomes unchanged since registration; no results posted on the registry.
key_findings.page: ClinicalTrials.gov record NCT01888835 (current version and history)
key_findings.locator: Outcome Measures; Study Record History; Eligibility
key_findings.note: Read from the registry, not from the article, and not re-checked: neither reading of this card had access to ClinicalTrials.gov, so the registration date, the outcome history and the absence of posted results remain single-reader. The article prints only the registration number (Abstract, Trial Registration) and states that the analysis model was prespecified in the protocol, which is in a supplement that was not read. A reader with web access should confirm this finding at the registry.

reporting_issues.issue: Trial completion is given as 38 participants (48%) on mirtazapine and 42 (53%) on placebo, but 38 of 60 is 63% and 42 of 60 is 70% (the same counts are given correctly as 63% and 70% for week-36 visits).
reporting_issues.consequence: The completion percentages are wrong; retention to the final visit was 63% and 70%.

reporting_issues.issue: Week-24 visit completion is 43 of 60 (72%) in both arms but is reported with P = .28; identical proportions cannot give that P value.
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical error, probably a P value copied from another comparison.

reporting_issues.issue: WisePill adherence over weeks 13 to 24 is printed as 28.1% (SD 23.4) on mirtazapine versus 38.5% (SD 27.0) on placebo with P = .59; the placebo figures duplicate the mirtazapine figures for weeks 2 to 12, and a 10-point difference with these SDs would give P of roughly .03 to .06 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: One of the adherence values is likely a copying error; the claim that adherence was similar by arm in the second period cannot be checked, and secondary sources quoting '28.1 to 39.5%' inherit the error.

reporting_issues.issue: The 24- and 36-week estimates are labelled 'net treatment effects' that account for differences from the beginning of each period, and the 36-week footnote describes weeks 25 to 36 as 'receiving treatment', although medication stopped at week 24.
reporting_issues.consequence: It is unclear whether the 24- and 36-week RRs are cumulative divergences from baseline or period-specific increments; editors' check: the raw positivity ratios at weeks 24 and 36 divided by the baseline ratio are about 0.74 and 0.72, close to the reported 0.75 and 0.73, which fits the cumulative reading. Claims about effects after stopping should state this uncertainty.

reporting_issues.issue: The text gives the 12-week Athens Insomnia Scale difference as 1.2 points lower with a 95% CI of 0.02 to 2.3 and P = .06, whereas Table 2 gives -1.15 (-2.33 to 0.02), an interval that includes zero.
reporting_issues.consequence: Sign error in the text's interval; the 12-week sleep effect is not significant.

reporting_issues.issue: Nine serious adverse events are reported but eight are itemized (four per arm).
reporting_issues.consequence: One serious event is unaccounted for in the article.

reporting_issues.issue: Eligibility in the paper differs from the registry: age 18 to 65 (registry 18 to 69), anal sex while using within 6 months (registry 3 months), five SSRIs permitted (registry excludes all antidepressants in the past 30 days).
reporting_issues.consequence: The registry was not updated to the criteria applied, or the paper describes them differently; four participants (3%) were taking SSRIs. Status of this item: the article side is confirmed by both readers (ages 18 to 65, anal sex with men while using methamphetamine within the prior 6 months, five named SSRIs permitted, at Methods › Recruitment, and the four participants in the sensitivity analyses). The registry side is single-reader: ClinicalTrials.gov was not accessible in the second reading, so the 18-to-69 age range, the 3-month window and the antidepressant exclusion have not been re-checked.

reporting_issues.issue: The Key Points describe this trial and Colfax et al. (2011) as two independent randomized trials, although five authors, the site, the population, the counselling and the analysis model are shared.
reporting_issues.consequence: The two trials are a replication by the same team, not independent confirmation; claims should not count them as independent.

reporting_issues.issue: The wording of the 24-week result overstates its own interval. Results › Methamphetamine Use, 1st paragraph, puts weeks 12, 24 and 36 under one verb, saying the rate of methamphetamine-positive urine samples significantly declined by week 12 (RR 0.67, 0.51-0.87), week 24 (RR 0.75, 0.56-1.00) and week 36 (RR 0.73, 0.57-0.96); the abstract says mirtazapine resulted in reductions at 24 weeks. The 24-week interval reaches 1.00, and Table 2 gives P = .05 for it.
reporting_issues.consequence: Any claim that mirtazapine lowered use at 24 weeks should print the interval, which is what makes the borderline result visible. The word significant cannot be carried over from this sentence for the 24-week estimate.

reporting_issues.issue: Visit completion is reported as a mean of 66% with an SD of 47%, while the arm figures are 69% (SD 32%) and 63% (SD 31%) (Results › Retention and Adherence, and the abstract). An SD of 47% is what a yes-or-no visit indicator with a mean of 0.66 gives, so the overall figure is computed over visits while the arm figures are computed over participants.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor, but the overall SD is not comparable with the arm SDs and should not be quoted as participant-level variability in visit completion.

Registration, outcome and eligibility history additionally read from ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01888835.

The interval and the P value are as the card already records them.
