design_detail: Narrative clinical review with two illustrative case vignettes, by four stroke clinicians at Harborview Medical Center, University of Washington (Front Neurol 2024;15:1397677; received 8 March, accepted 8 April 2024). Sections: US and global epidemiology of methamphetamine use; haemorrhagic stroke (vignette of a 47-year-old man with a basal-ganglia haemorrhage; epidemiology; pathophysiology; treatment and outcomes); ischaemic stroke (vignette of a 33-year-old man with a middle cerebral artery occlusion and vasospasm; epidemiology; pathophysiology; acute treatment); diagnosis, cessation and withdrawal. No methods section: no search strategy, eligibility criteria or appraisal. 106 references. Five figures (CT and angiography images of the two vignettes; two mechanism schematics). Read as the published version deposited in PMC.
can_establish: How stroke clinicians in a western US centre summarized, in 2024, the observational and case literature on methamphetamine and haemorrhagic and ischaemic stroke, which primary studies carry each statement, and where they judged the evidence weak (vasculitis, ischaemic stroke, acute treatment).
cannot_establish: The size of any stroke risk attributable to methamphetamine, because sources were not systematically identified or appraised, the two risk estimates cited are given without intervals or covariates, and the two vignettes are single cases in which other causes (untreated hypertension; an unmonitored cardiac source) were not excluded.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). Cited stroke evidence: two hospital-database studies of stroke risk (Westover et al. 2007; Huang et al. 2016), single-centre cohorts comparing methamphetamine-positive and negative patients with intracerebral haemorrhage (Swor et al. 2019, n=41; Zhu et al. 2020, n=61) or ischaemic stroke (Zhu et al. 2023), aneurysm series (Beadell et al. 2012; Moon et al. 2015; Noblett et al. 2021; Caton et al. 2022), autopsy series (Citron et al. 1970; Karch et al. 1999; Darke et al. 2018), case reports, the Lappin et al. 2017 review, and rodent and monkey experiments. Two patients from the authors' centre are described as vignettes.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: None reported.
sample.demographics: Vignettes: a 47-year-old man with untreated hypertension and a urine screen positive for methamphetamine; a 33-year-old man with a urine screen positive for methamphetamine and no further use history. Young is used for patients under 50 in the abstract.
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: Selection of sources is unstated. The review leans on hospital series from the western United States, where the authors note methamphetamine use has historically been highest. The vignettes were chosen to illustrate, not sampled.

exposure.measurement: Not described at review level. The review notes that urine toxicology detects methamphetamine for up to about 4 days, that amphetamine immunoassays have many false positives (some antihistamines, decongestants, bupropion, trazodone, chlorpromazine, promethazine, a labetalol metabolite), that confirmation by LC–MS separates true from false positives, and that history is unreliable: in Zhu et al. (2020), 29 of 379 (7.7%) people with haemorrhagic stroke who denied methamphetamine use screened positive (Diagnostic challenges and management, 1st–2nd paragraphs).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not synthesized. The authors state that route of administration is rarely reported and that its effect on risk is unclear; dose and duration are not reported by the aneurysmal haemorrhage outcome studies. In the vignettes, use history was unclear or not documented.
exposure.polysubstance: Discussed as a limitation: the aneurysmal haemorrhage outcome studies are said to be hampered by high rates of polysubstance use; reversible cerebral vasoconstriction and PRES cases attributed to methamphetamine occurred with other substances; people who use methamphetamine are more likely to use nicotine, cannabis, cocaine, opioids and other drugs (Introduction › Epidemiology, 4th paragraph). Not otherwise handled.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: Not applicable at review level. Cited comparisons: methamphetamine-negative patients with intracerebral haemorrhage (Swor; Zhu 2020), age-matched controls with aneurysmal haemorrhage (Beadell), people without methamphetamine use with aneurysmal haemorrhage (Moon; Caton), propensity-matched ischaemic stroke controls (Zhu 2023), hospitalized controls in Westover and Huang.
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: The review notes that methamphetamine-associated haemorrhage occurs in younger people with fewer comorbidities but higher smoking rates; pre-existing aneurysms, untreated hypertension and smoking are discussed as contributors but no cited study is said to have measured them before use began.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not reported.

outcomes.instruments: Not applicable at review level. Outcomes discussed: incidence of intracerebral and subarachnoid haemorrhage and ischaemic stroke; haemorrhage location; aneurysm size and morphology; NIHSS, GCS, ICH score, modified Rankin Scale, Glasgow Outcome Scale; ischaemic stroke subtype; white-matter hyperintensities; cardiomyopathy, ventricular thrombus, QTc, atrial fibrillation, endocarditis side.
outcomes.validity_norms: Not discussed.
outcomes.operationalization: Methamphetamine-related stroke is not defined; in the vignettes it means a stroke with a positive urine screen for methamphetamine.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: None computed. Second-hand figures: methamphetamine raises the likelihood of intracerebral haemorrhage by as much as 2–5 times (refs 11, 37: Huang et al.; Westover et al.; no intervals); among people who used methamphetamine in Huang et al., incidence of subarachnoid haemorrhage 6.2 and of intracerebral haemorrhage 20.8 per 100,000 person-years (no comparison-group rates given); aneurysmal haemorrhage outcomes worse with methamphetamine: median Glasgow Outcome Score 3 versus 5 at discharge (p<0.001; Beadell), OR 5 (95% CI 1.03 to 24) at 1 year and OR 7.2 (1.2 to 30) at 3 years (Moon); ischaemic stroke subtypes in people with versus without methamphetamine use 31% vs 28% small-vessel, 25% vs 24% large-vessel, 34% vs 46% cardioembolic (not significant; Zhu 2023); ventricular thrombus in 10 of 30 people with methamphetamine cardiomyopathy (Schürer); QTc prolongation in 27% of 158 people who used methamphetamine (Haning & Goebert); 86% higher risk of a diagnosis of atrial fibrillation in a 2022 California database analysis; relapse in 61% of 350 people within a year of treatment (Brecht & Herbeck).
analysis.covariates: Not reported for any second-hand estimate except that the white-matter association is described as independent of other cardiovascular risk factors and the Moon association as independent.
analysis.selective_reporting: Cannot be assessed (no eligibility criteria). The review does report null and conflicting findings: no association with ischaemic stroke in the two population studies, no outcome difference in the larger intracerebral haemorrhage cohort, no change in mean arterial pressure with chronic methamphetamine in small animals, no necrotizing angiitis in two autopsy series.
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Haemorrhagic stroke is the best-documented association: two hospital-database studies (one of amphetamine-use codes) with estimates of about 2 to 5, case series in which over 80% of reported methamphetamine-associated strokes were haemorrhagic, and single-centre cohorts showing that methamphetamine-associated intracerebral haemorrhage occurs in younger patients, mostly in deep (hypertensive-pattern) locations. The evidence for vasculitis is weak (one 1970 polysubstance series; two autopsy series without necrotizing angiitis), the population studies found no association with ischaemic stroke, outcome comparisons conflict, and acute-treatment evidence consists of case reports.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The conclusion states that methamphetamine "poses a clear risk of hemorrhagic stroke", a causal formulation resting on two observational database studies without intervals in the review. The abstract says methamphetamine may partly explain rising stroke rates in the young and calls it an increasingly prevalent cause of strokes in young patients, while the Introduction concedes that the cited trends in substance use among young people with stroke (4.4% to 28.9% in one registry) were not specific to methamphetamine and no methamphetamine-specific trend is presented. The conclusion says patients with methamphetamine-related stroke have a greater increase in disability; the cited cohort found no difference in discharge function or mortality, only a larger change from pre-stroke mRS, which follows from better pre-stroke function. The abstract describes the literature as case studies and series, while the body also relies on cohort and database studies. The haemorrhagic vignette is attributed to methamphetamine in a 47-year-old with untreated hypertension in whom MRI was not done because the cause was not felt to be in question; the ischaemic vignette is attributed to methamphetamine-induced vasospasm, though the spasm was seen during catheter instrumentation and long-term cardiac monitoring was not performed. Against this, the review is careful on vasculitis (to be invoked rarely and with skepticism), on ischaemic stroke and on treatment; the gap lies in the abstract and conclusion, two of whose statements (disability, rising contribution to stroke in the young) are not supported by the evidence the body cites.

timeline.event: Citron et al. necrotizing angiitis series: 14 people who injected several drugs, 12 reporting methamphetamine, 1 exclusively; the basis of the vasculitis hypothesis, judged weak by this review
Karch, Stephens & Ho: over 400 San Francisco deaths with methamphetamine detected, no necrotizing angiitis at autopsy (as reported here)
Westover et al. population-based hospital study, ages 18–44: amphetamine use and haemorrhagic stroke; no association with ischaemic stroke

Huang et al. 10-year Taiwanese cohort of people who used methamphetamine: haemorrhagic stroke increased; incidence 20.8 (intracerebral) and 6.2 (subarachnoid) per 100,000 person-years; no association with ischaemic stroke
Lappin, Darke & Farrell review of 98 published cases: over 80% haemorrhagic (cited here as ref 13)
Darke, Lappin, Kaye & Duflou national study of 38 fatal methamphetamine-related strokes in Australia: no necrotizing angiitis (as reported here)
Zhu et al. single-centre cohort of 61 methamphetamine-associated intracerebral haemorrhages: younger, deep locations, no difference in discharge outcome or mortality
This narrative review

replication.where_it_stands: Consistent with Lappin et al. (2017) on the predominance of haemorrhagic stroke, and more sceptical than that review about vasculitis as a mechanism. The risk estimates it cites (Westover 2007; Huang 2016) and the outcome cohorts (Swor 2019; Zhu 2020; Beadell 2012; Moon 2015) need their own cards before any claim of magnitude; Lappin 2017 and this review cite overlapping sources and are not independent support.

funding.funder: No financial support received for the research, authorship or publication (Funding Statement).
funding.declared_conflicts: None: the authors declare no commercial or financial relationships that could be construed as a potential conflict of interest.
funding.affiliations_note: All four authors at Harborview Medical Center, University of Washington, Seattle (stroke neurology). Two first authors contributed equally. Peer reviewers and editor are named on the article.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective cohort of young adults that verifies methamphetamine exposure by confirmed toxicology and history, with a comparison group matched on smoking, hypertension and other drug use, reporting incidence of intracerebral haemorrhage, aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage and ischaemic stroke as absolute rates with intervals; for treatment, a registry of thrombolysis and thrombectomy outcomes in patients with confirmed methamphetamine exposure.

domains.note: No methods section of any kind: no search, dates, databases or inclusion criteria, and no statement of how the 106 references were chosen.

Several cited bodies of work are appraised in the text: the 1970 necrotizing-angiitis series is called a limited basis for extrapolation, the aneurysmal-haemorrhage outcome studies are said to be hampered by small samples, selection bias, polysubstance use and missing dose and duration, and the studies suggesting ethnic differences are called small and selected. But the headline epidemiological figures are passed on without design, interval or adjustment (2 to 5 times for intracerebral haemorrhage; up to 6.5 times for stroke in people who use drugs; 86% higher odds of atrial fibrillation, taken from a two-page editorial; over 80% of published cases haemorrhagic).

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: Only the two case vignettes come from the authors' own centre. No reference in the list is authored by any of the four authors.

The body marks speculation as such (aneurysm growth after a single case, the plausibility of chronic hypertension, stroke risk after cessation "not clearly documented"). The abstract and Conclusion do not: methamphetamine "poses a clear risk of hemorrhagic stroke", haemorrhagic stroke is "the more common type" of complication, and greater disability is stated as fact and attributed to the younger age of the population, where the body reports no difference in discharge function or mortality and only a greater change in modified Rankin Scale score.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for and against a methamphetamine-stroke link
domains.note: The body is even-handed: it reports the null and conflicting results (no difference in blood pressure, ICU stay or discharge outcome in the larger intracerebral-haemorrhage cohort; no necrotizing angiitis in over 400 autopsies or in 38 fatal methamphetamine-related strokes; no consensus on vasospasm or Hunt and Hess grades; a paucity of epidemiological evidence for ischaemic stroke). The under-represented side is in the abstract and Conclusion, which carry the adverse readings only.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS §5.3), so the editors' narrative-review checklist is used. The review makes no claim to be systematic and has no methods, which fixes the first domain at high and therefore the overall judgment at high, since the overall can be no milder than the worst domain. Within that limit the review is a careful one: it appraises the weakest literature it cites, draws on no work of its own, and hedges its mechanisms, but its abstract and conclusion state more than its body supports. It may be cited for the map of stroke-specific cohorts published since Lappin et al. (2017), for its scepticism about vasculitis and for the clinical points on toxicology and withdrawal; every number in it must be taken from the primary source, and it is not evidence for the relative frequency of haemorrhagic and ischaemic stroke.

key_findings.finding: Methamphetamine is said to raise the likelihood of intracerebral haemorrhage by as much as 2–5 times (refs 11, 37: Huang et al. 2016; Westover et al. 2007). In Huang et al.'s 10-year cohort, incidence among people who used methamphetamine was 6.2 per 100,000 person-years for subarachnoid haemorrhage and 20.8 for intracerebral haemorrhage. Over 80% of methamphetamine-related strokes in published case reports and series were haemorrhagic (Lappin et al. 2017).
key_findings.locator: Methamphetamine-related hemorrhagic stroke › Epidemiology & characteristics, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: No intervals or comparison-group rates are given. As reported in Lappin et al. (2017, Table 3), Westover's estimate (OR 4.95) concerns amphetamine use and haemorrhagic stroke, and Huang's (HR 2.09) haemorrhagic stroke.

key_findings.finding: Methamphetamine-related haemorrhagic stroke is described as affecting younger people with better pre-stroke function and fewer comorbidities (cited to Lappin et al. 2017, Swor et al. 2019 and Zhu et al. 2020) and more often men (Lappin 2017 and Zhu 2020); lower rates of hypertension and antithrombotic use and higher rates of smoking come from Zhu et al. (2020) alone, and of these only the smoking difference is described as significant. Haemorrhages are mostly deep (basal ganglia, thalamus, pons), with significantly less lobar involvement than non-methamphetamine haemorrhage in the largest single-centre cohort.
key_findings.locator: Methamphetamine-related hemorrhagic stroke › Epidemiology & characteristics, 2nd–3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Subarachnoid haemorrhage with methamphetamine use is usually aneurysmal and occurs at younger ages; in 23 patients with methamphetamine-associated aneurysmal haemorrhage, aneurysm type and location did not differ from patients without methamphetamine exposure, but aspect ratio was larger (Caton et al. 2022). Whether vasospasm or Hunt–Hess grade differ is unsettled.
key_findings.locator: Epidemiology & characteristics, 4th paragraph; Pathophysiology of hemorrhagic stroke, last paragraph

key_findings.finding: Vasculitis: the hypothesis rests on Citron et al. (1970), 14 people who injected several drugs, 12 reporting methamphetamine and only 1 exclusively; 4 fatal cases described in detail (2 with confirmed and 1 with possible methamphetamine use), diagnosed mostly from other organs. Rhesus monkeys given methamphetamine showed calibre changes, perivascular infiltration and microaneurysms but no clear necrotizing arteritis. Over 400 San Francisco autopsies with methamphetamine detected and an Australian study of 38 fatal methamphetamine-related strokes found no necrotizing angiitis. The authors conclude vasculitis should be invoked rarely and with skepticism.
key_findings.locator: Pathophysiology of methamphetamine-related hemorrhagic stroke, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Chronic hypertension as a pathway is poorly documented: chronic methamphetamine did not change mean arterial pressure in small-animal studies; methamphetamine use was associated with more white-matter hyperintensities independent of other cardiovascular risk factors (Zhu et al. 2023).
key_findings.locator: Pathophysiology of methamphetamine-related hemorrhagic stroke, 5th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Aneurysm size: in 62 people with intracranial aneurysms and methamphetamine use, ruptured aneurysms had a median diameter of 5.5 mm (mean 6.3 mm) (Noblett et al. 2021); the authors set this against a meta-analytic mean of 6.1 mm for ruptured aneurysms in general, so size alone does not show higher rupture risk with methamphetamine.
key_findings.locator: Pathophysiology of methamphetamine-related hemorrhagic stroke, last paragraph

key_findings.finding: Outcomes after intracerebral haemorrhage conflict: methamphetamine-positive patients (n = 41) had higher mean arterial and diastolic pressure, more days of intravenous antihypertensives and longer ICU and hospital stays (Swor et al. 2019); in a slightly larger cohort (n = 61) there was no difference in blood pressure, ICU or hospital stay, NIHSS, GCS, ICH score, discharge function or mortality, though more participants underwent surgery (Zhu et al. 2020). The review states, citing both studies, that the change in modified Rankin Scale score from pre-stroke to discharge was greater in the methamphetamine group, that is, a larger worsening of disability, since the scale rises with disability.
key_findings.locator: Therapeutic considerations & outcomes in meth-related hemorrhagic stroke, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage with methamphetamine use: median Glasgow Outcome Score at discharge 3 versus 5 in age-matched controls (p<0.001; Beadell et al. 2012); worse outcome at 1 year, OR 5 (95% CI 1.03 to 24), and at 3 years, OR 7.2 (95% CI 1.2 to 30) (Moon et al. 2015). The authors note small samples, selection bias, polysubstance use and no dose or duration data.
key_findings.locator: Therapeutic considerations & outcomes in meth-related hemorrhagic stroke, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: The 3-year interval is not symmetric around 7.2 on the log scale (geometric midpoint about 6.0, editors' calculation); this may reflect an exact interval or rounding; check in Moon et al.

key_findings.finding: Ischaemic stroke: incidence with methamphetamine use is unknown; the two population-based studies (Westover; Huang) found no statistical association, and both identified cohorts by ICD codes among hospitalized patients. In a California single-centre comparison of ischaemic stroke admissions, subtypes did not differ (small-vessel 31% vs 28%, large-vessel 25% vs 24%, cardioembolic 34% vs 46%), but microvascular ischaemic disease on MRI was greater than in propensity-matched controls (Zhu et al. 2023).

Cardioembolic pathways cited: ventricular thrombi in 10 of 30 (33%) people with methamphetamine cardiomyopathy and reduced ejection fraction (Schürer et al. 2017); QTc prolongation as the commonest ECG abnormality, 27% of 158 people who used methamphetamine (Haning & Goebert 2007); 86% higher risk of atrial fibrillation diagnosis in a 2022 California database analysis; among people injecting stimulants (75% methamphetamine), endocarditis was evenly left- and right-sided, versus 66% right-sided among people injecting opioids (Johnstone et al. 2022).
key_findings.locator: Pathophysiology of methamphetamine-related ischemic stroke, 2nd–3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Acute ischaemic stroke treatment evidence in people who use methamphetamine consists of one case report of intravenous thrombolysis (a woman with carotid dissection, NIHSS 21, alteplase within 80 minutes, with improvement), a 29-patient cocaine-positive series without thrombolysis complications, and isolated thrombectomy and angioplasty case reports; the authors recommend standard therapies for eligible patients and warn against bias related to substance use.
key_findings.locator: Therapeutic considerations in methamphetamine ischemic stroke, 1st–3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Among patients with haemorrhagic stroke who denied methamphetamine use, 29 of 379 (7.7%) screened positive for amphetamines after exclusion of recent false-positive medications (Zhu et al. 2020); urine screens detect methamphetamine for up to about 4 days.

Stopping methamphetamine is associated with reversal of cardiac dysfunction (moderate-strength evidence, Manja et al. 2023 systematic review); reduced stroke risk after stopping is described as reasonable but not documented. In 350 people treated in Los Angeles, 61% relapsed within the first year (Brecht & Herbeck 2014).

Vignettes: a 47-year-old man with untreated hypertension, systolic pressure over 250 mm Hg and a 7.4 × 4.5 × 5.1 cm left basal-ganglia haemorrhage, urine screen positive for methamphetamine, use history unclear, discharged with mRS 4; a 33-year-old man with a right middle cerebral artery occlusion (NIHSS 15), urine screen positive, treated with thrombolysis and thrombectomy, with vasospasm during catheter access and in MCA branches that improved after intra-arterial milrinone, otherwise unremarkable work-up (2 days of telemetry; no long-term cardiac monitoring), attributed to methamphetamine-induced vasospasm.
key_findings.locator: Methamphetamine-related hemorrhagic stroke › Case vignette; Methamphetamine-related ischemic stroke › Case vignette; Figures 1, 3, 4 (images)

key_findings.finding: Withdrawal time course as the review gives it: an early crash of 12 to 24 hours with exhaustion and fatigue, a withdrawal phase of 2 to 4 weeks with depressive symptoms, increased sleeping and eating, and an extinction phase of up to 6 to 12 months with continuing cognitive and mood changes. The review notes that this period can overlap stroke recovery, making the cause of new mood or mental-status changes hard to tell apart.
key_findings.note: Second-hand: cited to references 105 and 106, Acheson et al. (2023) and the 2009 Cochrane review of treatment for amphetamine withdrawal. The same phases appear in acheson_2023 (Introduction), itself citing earlier sources, so the figures should be traced to the primary studies before use.

reporting_issues.issue: The regional shares of US methamphetamine drug submissions in 2022 are given as 39% West, 33% South, 29% Midwest and 8% Northeast, which sum to 109%, and 39% is called the majority.
reporting_issues.consequence: At least one figure is wrong; the NFLIS 2022 report should be used directly for any regional claim.

reporting_issues.issue: The review states that people who used methamphetamine in the US in 2015–2019 were 50.9% women (citing Han et al. 2021); this encyclopedia's card for Han et al. (first-pass) records 50.9% women as the weighted composition of the whole survey sample of 195,711 adults, not of people who used methamphetamine.
reporting_issues.consequence: Probably a misattribution; the sex distribution of people who use methamphetamine must be taken from Han et al. directly.

reporting_issues.issue: Stroke risk among people using drugs is said to be as high as 6.5 times that of people who do not use drugs, cited to Kaku and Lowenstein (1990) (Introduction › Epidemiology ¶5). The first reader recorded that Lappin et al. (2017, Table 3) give the same study's relative risks as 6.5 for ischaemic and 11.7 for haemorrhagic stroke at ages 35 and below; that comparison is outside this source and has not been re-checked by the second reader.
reporting_issues.consequence: Kaku and Lowenstein must be read before either figure is used, and the 6.5 should not be carried as a methamphetamine-specific or stroke-type-specific estimate. The Lappin figures remain single-reader.

reporting_issues.issue: The 86% higher risk of atrial fibrillation is attributed to a 2022 California database analysis but cited to ref 85, which by title and length (3 pages) is an editorial comment, not the database study.
reporting_issues.consequence: The primary analysis is not cited; the figure cannot be checked from this review.

reporting_issues.issue: The statement that cardiotoxicity occurs with acute, chronic and binge use and that severity of use independently predicts outcomes (Pathophysiology of methamphetamine-related ischemic stroke ¶2, last sentence) is cited to references 12 and 86-88: a case report of myocardial infarction with normal coronary arteries, an echocardiographic comparison of young people with cardiomyopathy, and a study of binge administration whose title names no species. None of the three concerns severity of use as a predictor of outcomes. The first reader also recorded that the corresponding sentence in Kevil et al. (2019), reference 12, carries no citation of its own; that is outside this source and has not been re-checked.
reporting_issues.consequence: The claim that severity of use predicts outcomes has no traceable support in the references given here, and should not be carried into a monograph without a primary source.

reporting_issues.issue: Two case reports described as involving methamphetamine (refs 92 and 94) are titled as amphetamine-induced cardiomyopathy and amphetamine-induced arterial occlusion.
reporting_issues.consequence: The substance in these cases should be checked before they are counted as methamphetamine cases.

reporting_issues.issue: The 2-to-5-fold figure is worded as methamphetamine increasing the likelihood of intracerebral haemorrhage (Epidemiology & characteristics ¶1), with no interval, no adjustment and no design given, and one of its two citations (reference 37) is titled for amphetamines or cocaine rather than methamphetamine. The first reader additionally recorded, from Lappin et al. (2017), that the underlying estimates are for haemorrhagic stroke generally rather than intracerebral haemorrhage; that lies outside this source and has not been re-checked.
reporting_issues.consequence: Not citable as a causal or intracerebral-haemorrhage-specific estimate; the primary studies (references 11 and 37) are needed, and the stroke-type question stays open until Lappin et al. is read.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract's statement that haemorrhagic rather than ischaemic stroke is the more common neurovascular complication of methamphetamine use rests on the share of published case reports and series (over 80% haemorrhagic, cited to Lappin et al. 2017, at Epidemiology & characteristics ¶1). The population studies the review cites give relative risks against people who do not use methamphetamine, not the ratio of haemorrhagic to ischaemic stroke among people who do, and the review itself notes a paucity of epidemiological evidence for ischaemic stroke.
reporting_issues.consequence: The share of published cases reflects what gets written up, not relative incidence. No monograph should state that haemorrhagic stroke is the more common type on this basis; the same inference appears in sc_paulus_2020 and both cards now carry the caveat.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC11076881 (published version; all sections including both case vignettes, figure legends, author contributions, funding and conflict-of-interest statements, article notes and the full reference list; Figures 1–5 are images and were not extracted; no tables; no supplementary material)

disagreements.first_pass: Methamphetamine-associated intracerebral haemorrhage affects younger patients with better pre-stroke function and fewer comorbidities, more often men, with lower rates of hypertension and antithrombotic use and higher rates of smoking (Zhu et al. 2020); haemorrhages are mostly deep (basal ganglia, thalamus, pons), with less lobar involvement than in non-methamphetamine haemorrhage in the largest single-centre cohort.
disagreements.reviewer: attribution is narrower than the source: refs 13, 38 and 39 for younger age, better pre-stroke function and fewer comorbidities, refs 13 and 39 for male predominance, ref 39 alone for hypertension, antithrombotics and smoking, of which only smoking is significant
disagreements.resolution: Rewritten. Checked at Epidemiology & characteristics ¶2: the first clause carries three citations (13, 38, 39), male predominance two (13, 39), and only the hypertension, antithrombotic and smoking comparison is attributed to reference 39 (Zhu et al. 2020), with "significantly higher" used of smoking alone. The card had given the whole sentence to Zhu et al. (2020). Locator (¶2-3) is right and unchanged.

disagreements.first_pass: Pathophysiology of methamphetamine-related hemorrhagic stroke, 5th paragraph
disagreements.reviewer: the content is exact but sits in Pathophysiology of methamphetamine-related hemorrhagic stroke ¶4; the card counts the Figure 2 legend as a paragraph
disagreements.resolution: Corrected to the 4th paragraph. Counting only running text, the section runs: hypertensive surge (¶1), vasospasm and reversible cerebral vasoconstriction (¶2), blood-brain-barrier breakdown (¶3), vasculitis (¶4), chronic hypertension and white-matter hyperintensities (¶5), aneurysms (¶6). The Figure 2 legend between ¶1 and ¶2 is a caption, not a paragraph (locator convention, docs/VERIFICATION-BRIEF.md).

disagreements.first_pass: Pathophysiology of methamphetamine-related hemorrhagic stroke, 6th paragraph
disagreements.reviewer: content confirmed; the location is ¶5 by text paragraphs, the card having counted the Figure 2 legend
disagreements.resolution: Corrected to the 5th paragraph, by the same recount. Content re-checked there: no change in mean arterial pressure with chronic methamphetamine in small-animal work (reference 65, a rat study of cardiovascular and respiratory function), and more white-matter hyperintensities independent of other cardiovascular risk factors (reference 66, Zhu et al.).

disagreements.first_pass: Outcomes after intracerebral haemorrhage conflict: methamphetamine-positive patients (n=41) had higher mean arterial and diastolic pressure, more days of intravenous antihypertensives and longer ICU and hospital stays (Swor et al. 2019); in a larger cohort (n=61), there was no difference in blood pressure, ICU or hospital stay, NIHSS, GCS, ICH score, discharge function or mortality, but more surgery and a larger fall from pre-stroke mRS (Zhu et al. 2020).
disagreements.reviewer: two fixes: 'a larger fall from pre-stroke mRS' should be a larger worsening (increase), and the mRS point is cited to refs 38 and 39 together, not to Zhu 2020 alone
disagreements.resolution: Both accepted and rewritten. Checked at Therapeutic considerations & outcomes ¶2: the sentence on the change from pre-morbid to discharge modified Rankin Scale score carries references 38 and 39 together, and the modified Rankin Scale rises with disability, so a word meaning a decrease reversed the meaning of the result. The n = 41 and n = 61 figures are confirmed, as is the review's misprint of IV hypertensive agents for antihypertensives.

disagreements.first_pass: Pathophysiology of methamphetamine-related ischemic stroke, 3rd–4th paragraphs
disagreements.reviewer: content confirmed; the location is ¶2-3 by text paragraphs, the card having counted the Figure 5 legend
disagreements.resolution: Corrected to the 2nd and 3rd paragraphs. (2017, Table 3) report the same study's relative risks as 6.5 for ischaemic and 11.7 for haemorrhagic stroke at ages 35 and below.

Confirmed in this source: the 6.5-fold figure is in Introduction › Epidemiology ¶5 with reference 9, and the reference list gives reference 9 as Kaku and Lowenstein (1990). The Lappin Table 3 comparison is in another paper, which this reading did not cover and which no reader has re-checked, so the issue now says so and the card no longer asserts it as verified.

(2019), where the corresponding sentence carries no citation, and to a case report, an echocardiographic comparison and a rat binge-dosing study (refs 86–88), none of which by title concerns severity of use as a predictor.

Confirmed from the source and its reference list: reference 86 is a case report of methamphetamine-associated myocardial infarction with normal coronary arteries, 87 an echocardiographic comparison in young adults with cardiomyopathy, 88 a study of binge administration whose title names no species (so the card no longer calls it a rat study), and none addresses severity of use as a predictor. The claim about Kevil et al. (2019) is now marked as not re-checked.

The stroke-type point is marked as single-reader and unchecked.

disagreements.first_pass: AMSTAR 2 (13 items recorded, overall critically-low confidence)
disagreements.reviewer: wrong instrument for the design: a narrative review uses the editors' narrative-review checklist (instrument none-applicable), which scripts/rob_vocab.py flags; proposed judgments high / some-concerns / low / some-concerns / some-concerns, overall high
disagreements.resolution: Re-appraised with the editors' narrative-review checklist (METHODS §5.3, modelled on sc_kish_2017). AMSTAR 2 is for systematic reviews and meta-analyses, and scoring a narrative review against it only restates that it is not systematic. My own five judgments, made from the text, agree with the second reader's: no methods or search (high); real but uneven appraisal of the cited studies, with the headline risk figures passed on unappraised (some concerns); nothing of the authors' own cited (low); speculation marked in the body but not in the abstract or conclusion (some concerns); the balance of adverse against null findings even in the body but not in the abstract or conclusion (some concerns). Overall high, the worst domain. The substance of the earlier reasoning, that every number must be taken from the primary source, is kept.

design_detail: Narrative review by nine vascular-biology and clinical authors at LSU Health Sciences Center, Shreveport, in Arteriosclerosis, Thrombosis, and Vascular Biology (2019;39(9):1739–1746). Sections: pharmacology and binding sites; vasoconstriction and pulmonary hypertension; atherosclerotic disease; arrhythmias; cardiomyopathy; summary and future directions; highlights. There is no methods section: no search strategy, eligibility criteria or appraisal of the cited studies. 64 references. Most mechanistic statements rest on rodent, ex vivo and cell-culture work; only five passages give numbers from human studies. Two schematic figures and a graphical abstract (images; legends read). Read as the NIH author manuscript deposited in PMC.
can_establish: Which mechanisms and which human, animal and cell studies these authors considered relevant to methamphetamine and cardiovascular disease in 2019, and where they themselves judged the evidence to be thin.
cannot_establish: How common any cardiovascular outcome is in people who use methamphetamine, or by how much methamphetamine raises its risk, because no search, selection criteria or appraisal is reported, the few human figures are second-hand, unadjusted and without intervals, and much of the causal account comes from rodent and cell experiments.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). Cited human evidence: autopsy and coronial series from the USA and Australia (refs 14, 40, 41, 50), a US National Inpatient Sample analysis published as a meeting abstract (ref 49), a 20-versus-21 comparison of vasodilator function (ref 31), a human laboratory study of cardiovascular response (ref 24), a single ECG study (ref 52), case reports and clinical series of cardiomyopathy and pulmonary hypertension (refs 32, 33, 51, 54, 55, 59–61). Animal evidence: mouse, rat and one other animal model (refs 25–27, 42, 43, 53, 56, 62). Cell and tissue evidence: endothelial cells, macrophages, T lymphocytes, cardiomyocytes, rat aorta (refs 29, 30, 34, 36, 39, 45, 46, 48, 57, 58, 63, 64).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: None reported.
sample.demographics: Not applicable.
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: Selection of sources is unstated and cannot be audited. All the human figures come from people who died or reached hospital (autopsy, coronial and inpatient records, case series), so they describe severe end-points in selected groups, not risk in people who use methamphetamine. Several statements carry no citation at all (see reporting issues).

exposure.measurement: Not applicable at review level. The review does not say how methamphetamine use was established in any cited human study (self-report, toxicology or records).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not synthesized. The review cites plasma concentrations averaging 2–3 μM in people who use methamphetamine, up to 17 μM in people arrested for erratic behaviour and 87 μM in post-mortem samples from deaths not due to overdose (refs 21–23), and compares them with binding values at the dopamine transporter (Ki 0.46 μM), noradrenaline transporter (Ki 0.11 μM), TAAR1 (EC50 about 1–3 μM), sigma-1 receptor (Ki about 2 μM) and alpha-2 adrenergic receptors (Ki about 1 μM) (refs 15–19). Doses and schedules of the animal and cell studies are not given. Intravenous methamphetamine is said to accumulate mainly in the lung (refs 34, 35).
exposure.polysubstance: Not discussed. The review does not mention tobacco, alcohol, cocaine or other drug use as a possible confounder of any cited human association.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: Not applicable at review level. Of the cited human figures, only the 1999 autopsy comparison (19% versus 0.5% in sex- and age-matched controls, ref 40) and the 20-versus-21 vasodilation study (ref 31) are described with a comparison group; the Australian autopsy figures are said not to have been seen in control cohorts without saying who those were.
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not discussed. Pre-existing cardiovascular risk (family history, hypertension, smoking, lipids) is not addressed for any cited human study; the review only remarks, without a citation, that methamphetamine use lowers serum cholesterol and obesity.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not reported for any cited study.

outcomes.instruments: Not applicable at review level. Outcomes discussed: heart rate and blood pressure, arterial constriction and vasodilator response, pulmonary hypertension, coronary atherosclerosis at autopsy, sudden cardiac death in records, QT interval on 12-lead ECG, ventricular fibrosis on endomyocardial biopsy and cardiac MRI, dilated cardiomyopathy and its recovery after stopping use.
outcomes.validity_norms: Not discussed.
outcomes.operationalization: Not defined. The review does not give the cited studies' definitions of sudden cardiac death, of 'minimal to severe' or 'extremely severe' coronary disease, or of methamphetamine-associated cardiomyopathy or pulmonary hypertension.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: None computed by the review. Second-hand figures, all without intervals: coronary atherosclerosis in 19% of methamphetamine-related deaths versus 0.5% of sex- and age-matched controls (ref 40); coronary artery disease in 54% and extremely severe coronary disease in up to 10% in two Australian autopsy series (refs 14, 41; which figure comes from which is not stated); a 27% increased risk of sudden cardiac death in a US National Inpatient Sample analysis of more than 35 million patients including over 180,000 who used methamphetamine (ref 49); 6.5% of non-accidental deaths in people who used methamphetamine attributed to sudden cardiac death in Australian coronial data (ref 50); reduced nitroglycerin-mediated vasodilation in 20 people who used methamphetamine versus 21 age-matched controls (ref 31, magnitude not given). The 27% figure has no stated comparator, adjustment, interval or absolute risk.
analysis.covariates: Not applicable.
analysis.selective_reporting: Cannot be assessed (no eligibility criteria or list of considered studies). No cited human study is reported with a null result; absence of evidence is acknowledged for chronic systemic hypertension and for prospective arrhythmia incidence. The meeting abstract cited as ref 49 is titled as reporting stroke as well as sudden cardiac death; the review reports only the sudden-death result.
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: The human evidence actually cited is autopsy and coronial series, one inpatient-database meeting abstract, case reports and clinical series, one 20-versus-21 vasodilation study and one ECG study; the mechanistic account rests mainly on rodent, rat-aorta and cell-culture experiments. In the body, the authors say the mechanisms remain largely unknown, that most sudden-death figures are biased by retrospective adjudication from records, that no prospective study of arrhythmia incidence exists, and (in the closing paragraph) that the prevalence of methamphetamine-associated cardiovascular pathology still needs systematic study.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract ranks cardiovascular disease as the leading cause of death in people who use methamphetamine after overdose and accidents and attributes it to methamphetamine's effects on vasoconstriction, pulmonary hypertension, plaque formation, arrhythmias and cardiomyopathy, without figures. The atherosclerosis section opens by saying methamphetamine use "clearly increases the rate of coronary artery disease", on the basis of unadjusted autopsy comparisons, and calls the apolipoprotein-E-knockout mouse experiments direct evidence linking methamphetamine use to plaque formation. The summary says methamphetamine use clearly induces cardiovascular dysfunction, that its acute effects often result in myocardial infarction (no citation or frequency) and that it significantly enhances susceptibility to pulmonary hypertension (no statistic; one cited genetic study whose sample size is not given). The highlights state mechanisms (vasospasm plus plaque in myocardial infarction; remodelling leading to dilated cardiomyopathy) as established. The causal and frequency language of the abstract, summary and highlights is stronger than the observational, selected, unadjusted or non-human evidence in the body, and stronger than the authors' own caveats.

timeline.event: Karch, Stephens & Ho: autopsy series of methamphetamine-related deaths (San Francisco, by title); cited here (ref 40) for coronary atherosclerosis in 19% versus 0.5% of controls

Kaye, Darke, Duflou & McKetin: Australian methamphetamine-related fatalities with major organ pathology; cited here (ref 41) with ref 14 for coronary disease in 54% and extremely severe disease in up to 10%

Darke, Duflou & Kaye national study of cardiovascular disease in methamphetamine-related death (ref 14), and Darke, Kaye & Duflou 7-year national coronial study (ref 50: 6.5% of non-accidental deaths attributed to sudden cardiac death)

Schürer et al.: clinical and histopathological series of methamphetamine-associated cardiomyopathy; cited here (ref 55) for fibrosis related to duration of use and predicting recovery after stopping, and for no improvement in anyone who continued use
Parekh et al. meeting abstract (JACC Cardiovascular Interventions supplement) on the US National Inpatient Sample: 27% increased risk of sudden cardiac death; cited here as ref 49
This narrative review

Hemphill et al. stroke review cites this review (its ref 12) for vasoconstriction, TAAR1 and cardiotoxicity after acute, chronic and binge use; the last statement is uncited here, so the chain of citation ends without a primary source

replication.where_it_stands: A mechanistic overview written by vascular biologists. For any claim about how often cardiovascular disease occurs in people who use methamphetamine, or how much methamphetamine raises the risk, the primary studies (the autopsy and coronial series of Karch 1999, Kaye 2008 and Darke 2017; Schürer 2017; the inpatient-sample analysis, which exists here only as a meeting abstract) need their own cards. The authors' closing statement that prevalence and mechanisms remain to be established should govern how this review is cited.

funding.funder: NIH National Institute of General Medical Sciences Institutional Development Award (IDeA) P20GM121307 to C.G.K.; NIH R01 HL098435, HL133497 and HL141155 to A.W.O.; HL131844 to M.D.W.; HL122354 and HL145753 to M.S.B. (Acknowledgments › Sources of Funding).
funding.declared_conflicts: Disclosures: none (Footnotes).
funding.affiliations_note: All nine authors are at LSU Health Sciences Center, Shreveport (pathology and translational pathobiology, physiology, cell biology and anatomy, pharmacology and toxicology, microbiology and immunology, medicine). Ref 44, cited for the general description of atherosclerosis, is from two of the authors' own group (Orr, Woolard). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective cohort of people who use methamphetamine and a comparison group matched on age, sex, smoking and other stimulant use, with toxicology-verified exposure and repeated echocardiography, ECG and coronary imaging, reporting incident cardiomyopathy, pulmonary hypertension, arrhythmia and coronary events as absolute rates; and, for the causal pathway, within-person follow-up of cardiac structure and function after people stop using.

domains.note: The Abstract says only that the authors examine the current literature; there is no methods section, search strategy or selection criteria for the 64 references.

Studies are taken at face value: autopsy series are summarised as showing that methamphetamine clearly increases coronary artery disease, and apolipoprotein E knockout mouse studies are called direct evidence, with no discussion of confounding (tobacco, cocaine or other drug use are not mentioned); the only appraisal remark is that sudden-death studies suffer from retrospective adjudication bias.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own work
domains.note: Only 1 of 64 references (ref 44, Vozenilek et al.) includes an author of the review, and it supports a general point on atherosclerosis biology rather than a key finding.

Mechanistic proposals in the body are usually hedged (may, could, would be predicted to, mechanisms remain unknown), but the Summary restates associations and animal findings as established human effects (methamphetamine clearly induces cardiovascular dysfunction; induces mitochondrial dysfunction and myocyte death driving cardiomyopathy).

Little that cuts against the thesis is presented: the review notes minimal data for persistent hypertension and lower cholesterol and obesity in users, but cites no null or conflicting studies and does not consider alternative explanations for the associations.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Editors' narrative-review checklist (METHODS §5.3), applied by an independent reader (AI reader 3 (appraisal re-reading, papers read in the app's browser), 2026-10-16) after the first reading had used AMSTAR 2, which does not fit a narrative review. Overall high risk of a misleading summary: no described search or selection, and the cited studies are taken at face value. The review is cited for arguments and pointers to primary studies, not as primary evidence; a second reading of the checklist is still needed.

key_findings.finding: Cardiovascular disease is described as the second leading cause of death in people who use methamphetamine, after accidental overdose (ref 14, Darke, Duflou & Kaye 2017); no proportion of deaths is given.
key_findings.note: The abstract ranks it after overdose and accidents; the introduction after accidental overdose only. See reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Binding values cited: dopamine transporter Ki 0.46 μM, noradrenaline transporter Ki 0.11 μM (ref 15); TAAR1 EC50 about 1–3 μM, sigma-1 receptor Ki about 2 μM, alpha-2 adrenergic receptor Ki about 1 μM (refs 16–19). Blood concentrations cited: average 2–3 μM in people who use methamphetamine, up to 17 μM in people arrested for erratic behaviour, 87 μM in post-mortem samples from deaths not due to overdose (refs 21–23). The authors conclude that human plasma levels are sufficient to engage all these sites.
key_findings.note: Which concentration comes from which of refs 21–23 is not stated, and the review does not discuss whether post-mortem values are comparable with plasma values in living people. Ref 19 (1977) is by title a characterization of alpha-noradrenergic receptor binding that does not name methamphetamine.

key_findings.finding: Methamphetamine given to people acutely raises heart rate and blood pressure (ref 24). In mice, acute exposure constricted pial and intracerebral arteries (refs 25, 26) and chronic exposure produced vasoconstriction with persistent cerebral hypoperfusion (ref 27). Proposed mechanisms: endothelial endothelin-1 release (ref 25) or arterial TAAR1 signalling (ref 29), with neuronal catecholamine and adrenergic receptor signalling apparently not involved (ref 30).
key_findings.locator: Methamphetamine-mediated vasoconstriction and pulmonary hypertension, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Refs 29 and 30 are, by title, rat-aorta studies of trace amines (beta-phenylethylamine) and amphetamines.

key_findings.finding: In 20 people who used methamphetamine and 21 age-matched controls, nitroglycerin-mediated vasodilation was reduced in the methamphetamine group (ref 31, Nabaei et al. 2016); the authors infer smooth-muscle dysfunction and reduced nitric-oxide sensitivity. No magnitude, test statistic or adjustment is reported.
key_findings.locator: Methamphetamine-mediated vasoconstriction and pulmonary hypertension, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: A cross-sectional comparison; the inference that methamphetamine caused the dysfunction is the review's.

key_findings.finding: Evidence for chronic systemic hypertension is described as minimal; pulmonary hypertension is linked to prolonged use (refs 32, 33: a three-page 1993 report and a 2006 study asking whether methamphetamine use is associated with idiopathic pulmonary arterial hypertension). Nearly all patients with methamphetamine-associated pulmonary hypertension examined in one study carried one copy of a carboxylesterase 1 variant predicted to lower its activity (ref 34); the number examined is not given.
key_findings.locator: Methamphetamine-mediated vasoconstriction and pulmonary hypertension, 2nd paragraph (after Figure 2)
key_findings.note: The summary turns this into methamphetamine use significantly enhancing susceptibility to pulmonary hypertension, with no statistic.

key_findings.finding: Autopsy evidence: a 1999 study reported minimal-to-severe coronary atherosclerosis in 19% of decedents who had used methamphetamine versus 0.5% of sex- and age-matched controls (ref 40); two Australian autopsy studies reported coronary artery disease in 54% and extremely severe disease in up to 10%, said not to occur in control cohorts (refs 14, 41). Chronic methamphetamine increased atherosclerosis in apolipoprotein-E-knockout mice (refs 42, 43).
key_findings.locator: Methamphetamine in atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Unadjusted autopsy proportions; the review does not give denominators, ages, smoking or other drug use. The text places the 1999 decedents in southern California; ref 40's title names San Francisco.

key_findings.finding: Proposed atherogenic mechanisms come from mice and cells: endothelial permeability and pro-inflammatory gene expression (refs 45, 46), raised ICAM-1, VCAM-1 and MCP-1 mRNA in treated mice (refs 42, 43), macrophage ROS, IL-6 and IL-1β (ref 47), mitochondrial ROS (ref 48), and plaque features (more smooth muscle, raised interferon-gamma, lower TGF-beta) read as a vulnerable-plaque phenotype. The authors state little is known about methamphetamine's effect on vascular smooth-muscle phenotype.
key_findings.locator: Methamphetamine in atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: Ref 47 is by title a 2002 general review of immunity in atherosclerosis, not a methamphetamine study.

key_findings.finding: Sudden cardiac death: a US National Inpatient Sample analysis of more than 35 million patients, including over 180,000 who used methamphetamine, reported a 27% increased risk (ref 49); Australian coronial data attributed 6.5% of non-accidental deaths in people who used methamphetamine to sudden cardiac death (ref 50). The authors caution that most such studies are biased by retrospective adjudication from records.
key_findings.note: Ref 49 is a meeting abstract (journal supplement page S29, no DOI listed). No interval, comparator definition, adjustment or absolute risk is given for the 27%.

key_findings.finding: No prospective observational study of arrhythmia incidence in people who use methamphetamine exists, according to the authors; evidence consists of isolated case reports of monomorphic ventricular tachycardia (ref 51), QT prolongation on 12-lead ECG (ref 52, one study, described as growing evidence), and one animal study in which atrial and ventricular ectopic beats and sinus tachycardia occurred in the 30 minutes after methamphetamine, without sustained ventricular arrhythmias (ref 53).
key_findings.note: Ref 53 is by title a study of electronic control device exposure in a methamphetamine-intoxicated animal model, not a study designed around cardiac rhythm alone.

key_findings.finding: Structural and electrical remodelling: biopsies in methamphetamine-associated cardiomyopathy showed inflammation and fibrosis (sentence uncited); ventricular fibrosis was corroborated by cardiac MRI (ref 54); the extent of fibrosis correlated with duration of use and predicted recovery after stopping (ref 55). In animals, potassium and L-type calcium channel expression fell and largely recovered by week 8 of withdrawal (ref 56); in isolated rat myocytes, methamphetamine inhibited potassium and L-type calcium currents dose-dependently (ref 57), while another study found increased beating rate and calcium sparks (ref 58).
key_findings.note: No numbers are given for the correlation between fibrosis and duration of use.

key_findings.finding: Cardiomyopathy: methamphetamine-associated cardiomyopathy is described as severe systolic dysfunction with left-ventricular dilation (refs 55, 59), most commonly dilated (ref 61); clinical and autopsy reports describe necrosis, fibrosis, hypertrophy and cardiac enlargement (ref 60); in one series the degree of fibrosis predicted recovery after stopping use, and cardiac function did not improve in any patient who continued use (ref 55). Rat studies show myocyte disarray, oedema, abnormal mitochondria and myofilament loss (ref 62).
key_findings.note: No numbers of patients, recovery proportions or follow-up times are given.

key_findings.finding: The authors state that proposed mechanisms of methamphetamine cardiomyopathy (catecholamine excess, ROS, mitochondrial dysfunction, vasospasm, ischaemia) are "primarily based on cursory observations" and that the molecular targets remain unknown; isolated-cardiomyocyte studies are taken as support for direct, catecholamine-independent toxicity (refs 57, 63, 64).
The authors conclude that methamphetamine-associated cardiovascular complications need systematic study to establish the prevalence of pathology and the mechanisms of disease progression.

reporting_issues.issue: The 1999 autopsy study is described as a study of decedents from southern California, but the cited paper (ref 40, Karch, Stephens & Ho 1999) is titled as a study of methamphetamine-related deaths in San Francisco.
reporting_issues.consequence: Either the location or the citation is wrong; the 19% versus 0.5% figures must be checked in the primary paper before use.

reporting_issues.issue: Several statements carry no citation: a case report of vasospasm-related myocardial infarction unresponsive to vasodilators; methamphetamine use lowering serum cholesterol and obesity; increased T cells and macrophages in plaques of treated mice (only Figure 2B is referenced); biopsy findings of inflammation and fibrosis in methamphetamine cardiomyopathy; cardiotoxicity after acute, chronic and binge administration; and, in the summary, acute effects often resulting in myocardial infarction.
reporting_issues.consequence: None of these statements can be traced to a source from this review; they cannot support claims.

reporting_issues.issue: Citations that do not match their claims by title: the figure of up to 51 million people worldwide using amphetamine-type stimulants is cited to two psychosis papers (refs 8, 9: McKetin et al. 2013; Wearne & Cornish 2018) rather than an epidemiological source; macrophage production of ROS, IL-6 and IL-1β after methamphetamine is cited to a 2002 general review of immunity in atherosclerosis (ref 47); an alpha-2 adrenergic Ki for methamphetamine is cited to a 1977 receptor-binding characterization (ref 19); the TAAR1 vasoconstriction mechanism is cited to a beta-phenylethylamine rat-aorta study (ref 29); the only animal study of the acute effect on cardiac rhythm is a study of electronic control device exposure (ref 53).
reporting_issues.consequence: These statements need their primary sources; the global prevalence figure should come from UNODC or equivalent, not from this review.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract places cardiovascular disease after overdose and accidents as a cause of death; the introduction calls it second only to accidental overdose. Neither gives a proportion.
reporting_issues.consequence: The ranking cannot be cited from this review; the coronial data (Darke et al. 2017) should be used directly.

reporting_issues.issue: The 27% increased risk of sudden cardiac death is reported as demonstrated by a database analysis of more than 35 million patients; the source (ref 49) is a meeting abstract in a journal supplement, and the review gives no comparator, adjustment, interval or definition of sudden cardiac death in an inpatient database.
reporting_issues.consequence: Not citable as a risk estimate without the full analysis; a relative figure without a base rate cannot be turned into absolute risk.

reporting_issues.issue: Read from the PMC author manuscript, which may differ from the published version (Arterioscler Thromb Vasc Biol 2019;39(9):1739–1746); printed pagination is not shown.
reporting_issues.consequence: Anchors are to sections and paragraphs of the author manuscript.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC6709697 (NIH author manuscript; all sections, highlights, both figure legends, sources of funding, disclosures, author affiliations and the full reference list; Figures 1–2 and the graphical abstract are images and were not extracted; no supplementary material)

editorial_corrections.reason: METHODS §5.3 (0.2.2): narrative reviews are appraised with the editors' checklist, not AMSTAR 2. The checklist judgments are those of AI reader 3 (appraisal re-reading, papers read in the app's browser), who read the source; the editor only transferred them.

design_detail: Literature review with a systematic search and descriptive synthesis, no meta-analysis (J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2017;88(12):1079–1091; review article, free). EMBASE, MEDLINE and PsycINFO searched to 10 February 2017, plus reference lists; English or a detailed English abstract; no year limit. 370 records screened, 77 papers included: 3 post-mortem series (Table 2), 11 case-control, cohort and case-series studies (Table 3) and 63 case reports and series describing 98 strokes in people aged 44 or younger (Table 1: 81 haemorrhagic, 17 ischaemic). Cases were pooled by counting; no protocol, risk-of-bias assessment or causality assessment of the case attributions. Methamphetamine and other amphetamines were both eligible (non-medical use only).
can_establish: What kinds of stroke have been reported in young people after non-medical methamphetamine or amphetamine use, with what imaging findings and reported outcomes, and which epidemiological studies had examined the association by early 2017.
cannot_establish: How often stroke occurs in people who use methamphetamine, the relative share of haemorrhagic and ischaemic stroke, or case fatality, because 63 of the 77 sources are case reports selected by publication, about half the cases involved amphetamine rather than methamphetamine, deaths ascertained at autopsy are pooled with clinical cases, and the epidemiological estimates are reported without intervals or adjustment details.

sample.recruitment: Bibliographic search (EMBASE, MEDLINE, PsycINFO) to 10 February 2017 with hand-searching of reference lists (Methods). Cases in Table 1 date from 1945 to 2016 and come from clinical reports, coroner and forensic reports and three autopsy series. Table 3 studies come from US, Australian and Taiwanese hospital series, a US population-based database of hospitalized stroke (Westover et al. 2007), a case-control study of women (Petitti et al. 1998) and a Taiwanese cohort of 1315 people who used methamphetamine (Huang et al. 2016).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: peer-reviewed publications (or ones referenced in a relevant journal article) on methamphetamine use and incident stroke, reporting cases aged 44 or younger; ischaemic and haemorrhagic stroke; non-medical use only, excluding prescribed amphetamines (dextroamphetamine only when used non-medically). Polydrug use was recorded where reported (Methods › Inclusion criteria).
sample.demographics: Case reports (Table 1): ages 16 to 44. Haemorrhagic: 51 men and 30 women by the editors' count (text: 2:1); ischaemic: 12 men and 5 women. Editors' count from Table 1: 46 of the 98 cases list amphetamine, dextroamphetamine or amphetamine with ecstasy and do not name methamphetamine (43 of 81 haemorrhagic, 3 of 17 ischaemic).
sample.attrition: Not applicable. Figure 1 (flow diagram) is an image and was not extracted; the abstract gives 370 screened and 77 included.
sample.selection_effects: Case reports are published when they are striking, severe or unusual; the authors acknowledge that this may explain the 80% haemorrhagic share and the poor outcomes. Ten of the 81 haemorrhagic cases come from autopsy series (Table 1 footnote †) and other deaths from coroner and forensic reports, so case fatality is inflated by design. English-language restriction. Attribution of each stroke to the drug rests on the original case authors; several cases had other causes or risk factors (syphilis, carotid dissection, bacterial embolus, arteriovenous malformation, aneurysm, hypertension, pregnancy-induced hypertension, smoking, oral contraceptive use) or long intervals since last use (2 weeks, 4 days, 3 months).

exposure.measurement: Not described at review level: the review does not say whether use in each case was established by toxicology, self-report or records. The drug column of Table 1 records what the case report named.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not synthesized for dose. Route is reported only as ratios: haemorrhagic oral:injection:inhalation 3:3:1; ischaemic 1:1:4 (Results). Table 1 has no route column and the number of cases with a known route is not stated. Time from use to symptoms ranged from minutes to weeks; in Table 1 one ischaemic stroke occurred 3 months after reported last use.
exposure.polysubstance: Recorded but not analysed. Editors' count from Table 1: 17 of 98 cases list another drug (heroin, cocaine, ecstasy or MDMA, cannabis, methylphenidate or caffeine): 15 haemorrhagic, 2 ischaemic. The Westover estimate is compared with cocaine and tobacco in the source study, but the review does not say what it was adjusted for.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: None for the case reports. Table 2: one post-mortem series compared 413 methamphetamine-positive deaths with 114 drug-free trauma deaths (Karch et al. 1999). Table 3: Petitti et al. (1021 controls), Westover et al. (hospitalized stroke patients by drug-use coding), Huang et al. (a control group, not described), Beadell et al. (age-matched controls).
comparison.matching: Not applicable at review level.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: For the case reports, pre-existing vascular malformations, aneurysms and hypertension could be identified only where investigated; the authors note that many reports did not record other risk factors and that unreported risk factors cannot be excluded (Discussion › Individual and use-related characteristics).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not reported.

outcomes.instruments: Stroke type, site, angiographic or autopsy findings and clinical outcome as recorded in each case report (Table 1); proportions, odds ratios, hazard ratios and Glasgow Outcome Scale results as reported by the primary studies (Tables 2 and 3).
outcomes.validity_norms: Not discussed.
outcomes.operationalization: Stroke in a person aged 44 or younger in whom the case authors linked the event to non-medical amphetamine-type stimulant use. Outcomes were classified by the reviewers as death, complete recovery or residual deficit from the case descriptions; criteria for complete recovery are not stated.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (descriptive).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: No pooled estimates; counts and proportions only. Second-hand estimates, all without confidence intervals: Westover et al. (ages 18–44, 937 haemorrhagic and 998 ischaemic hospitalized strokes) OR 4.95 for haemorrhagic and 1.04 for ischaemic stroke with amphetamine use; Petitti et al. (women aged 15–44) 3.8 times the risk of stroke with amphetamine use; Kaku & Lowenstein (ages 15–44) relative risk of stroke with any illicit drug use 6.5 (ischaemic) and 11.7 (haemorrhagic) at age 35 or below; Huang et al. (1315 people who used methamphetamine, all ages, 54 stroke events) HR 2.09 (p=0.001) for haemorrhagic stroke, no significant difference for ischaemic stroke or subarachnoid haemorrhage. Amphetamines were implicated in 6–13% of haemorrhagic and 2–6% of ischaemic strokes in hospital series, and intracranial haemorrhage caused 1.4–5% of methamphetamine-related deaths in post-mortem series. Editors' calculation from Table 2: Karch et al.'s 10 of 413 (2.4%) versus 0 of 114 trauma controls gives a two-sided Fisher exact p of about 0.13, so these counts alone do not show the strong association attributed to that study.
analysis.covariates: Not reported for any second-hand estimate.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration mentioned. The search strategy is in online supplementary figure s1 (PDF, not read).
analysis.selective_reporting: Cannot be fully assessed. The excluded-studies list and search strategy are in supplements (not read). Outcome proportions in the abstract are given only for the case reports, not for the epidemiological studies.
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: 98 published cases of stroke in people aged 16–44 after non-medical use of methamphetamine or amphetamine (about half amphetamine), 83% haemorrhagic, with a third of haemorrhagic cases fatal in a pool that includes 10 autopsy-series deaths; three post-mortem series attributing 1.4–5% of methamphetamine-related deaths to intracranial haemorrhage; and a small epidemiological literature in which amphetamine use was associated with haemorrhagic stroke (Westover OR 4.95; Huang HR 2.09) but not with ischaemic stroke (Westover OR 1.04; Huang not significant).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and conclusions speak of methamphetamine throughout, while about half of the pooled cases involved amphetamine without methamphetamine. The conclusion that there is a preponderance of haemorrhagic stroke rests on case reports that the Discussion itself says may reflect reporting bias; the epidemiological support (two studies) is real but uses amphetamine-use codes in one and is given without intervals. The abstract states that the incidence of methamphetamine-related stroke "will increase" as a certainty, which is a projection, not a finding. The Discussion infers that, because many reports did not mention other risk factors, haemorrhagic strokes were related primarily to methamphetamine use, which treats unreported as absent (the authors add that unreported risk factors cannot be excluded). The outcome figures in the abstract do not say that deaths identified at autopsy were included. The Discussion calls methamphetamine likely to be making a disproportionate contribution to rising stroke incidence in young people, citing no study that measured this.

timeline.event: Kaku & Lowenstein case-control study of stroke in people aged 15–44: illicit drug use relative risk 6.5 (ischaemic) and 11.7 (haemorrhagic) at age 35 or below; 12 strokes attributed to amphetamine (Table 3)
Petitti et al. case-control study of women aged 15–44: amphetamine use associated with 3.8 times the risk of stroke (Table 3)
Westover, McBride & Haley population-based study of hospitalized stroke at ages 18–44 (Texas): OR 4.95 for haemorrhagic and 1.04 for ischaemic stroke with amphetamine use (Table 3)
Ho et al. series of 30 methamphetamine-associated strokes (20 haemorrhagic, 10 ischaemic, all ages); one autopsy showed accelerated atherosclerosis without vasculitis
Huang et al. 10-year follow-up of 1315 people who used methamphetamine: HR 2.09 for haemorrhagic stroke, no difference for ischaemic stroke (Table 3)
This review
Darke, Lappin, Kaye & Duflou national study of 38 fatal methamphetamine-related strokes in Australia; reported by Hemphill et al. (2024) as finding no necrotizing angiitis

Hemphill et al. narrative review of methamphetamine and stroke in the young: cites this review for the over-80% haemorrhagic share and the inhalation-predominant route in ischaemic cases, describes Beadell et al. as an aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage cohort, and judges vasculitis a rare mechanism to be invoked with skepticism

replication.where_it_stands: The most-cited review of methamphetamine and stroke in young adults, but its headline proportions (80% haemorrhagic; a third fatal) are properties of the published case literature, not of people who use methamphetamine. The association with haemorrhagic stroke rests on two epidemiological studies (Westover 2007; Huang 2016) that need their own cards; the absence of an association with ischaemic stroke in both deserves equal weight.

funding.funder: Not reported (no funding statement in the published article).
funding.declared_conflicts: Competing interests: none declared (Footnotes). Provenance: not commissioned; externally peer reviewed.
funding.affiliations_note: All three authors at the National Drug and Alcohol Research Centre, UNSW Sydney (first author also School of Psychiatry, UNSW). Shane Darke is a co-author of one of the three included post-mortem series (Kaye et al. 2008, Table 2) and of several background references. The contributors statement says the first author ran the searches and analyses; no second screener or extractor is named (an acknowledged colleague assisted with the literature review).

what_would_settle_it: A population-based cohort or a large case-control study of young adults with stroke that verifies methamphetamine exposure by toxicology, separates methamphetamine from other amphetamines, adjusts for smoking, hypertension, other stimulants and vascular malformations, and reports incidence of haemorrhagic and ischaemic stroke as absolute rates with confidence intervals; for prognosis, a registry comparing outcomes of drug-associated and other strokes at the same ages, excluding cases ascertained at autopsy.

domains.domain: Item 1: research question and inclusion criteria include population, exposure, comparator and outcome
domains.note: Population (aged 44 or younger), exposure (non-medical methamphetamine or amphetamine use) and outcome (stroke) are stated; no comparator.

domains.domain: Item 2 (critical): protocol established before the review
Item 3: choice of study designs explained
domains.note: Case reports, autopsy series and epidemiological studies were all included without justification or separate weighting.
Three databases, listed terms, full strategy in a supplement, reference-list searching; English-language restriction not justified, no grey literature or expert contact.
Not described; the first author performed the searches.
Not described.

domains.domain: Item 7 (critical): list of excluded studies with reasons
domains.note: Only a flow diagram (image); no list in the article.

domains.domain: Item 8: included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Tables 1–3 give each case or study; route of administration and how drug use was established are not shown per case.

domains.domain: Item 9 (critical): satisfactory technique for assessing risk of bias in individual studies
domains.note: No appraisal of the epidemiological studies and no causality assessment of the case attributions.

domains.domain: Item 10: funding sources of included studies reported
Item 13 (critical): risk of bias accounted for when interpreting results
domains.note: Reporting bias and severity bias of the case literature are acknowledged, but confounding in the epidemiological studies is not discussed and the conclusions are not tempered.
Differences in drug-implicated proportions across hospital series are attributed to local use rates and time trends; no formal exploration.

domains.domain: Item 16: conflicts of interest and funding of the review reported
domains.note: Competing interests declared (none); no funding statement.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Four of the applicable critical items are not met (no protocol, no list of excluded studies, no risk-of-bias or causality assessment, risk of bias not accounted for in interpretation); items 11, 12 and 15 do not apply because there is no meta-analysis. The search is reasonable and the case table is unusually complete, which makes the review a good catalogue of published cases; but the headline proportions describe what gets published, not what happens to people who use methamphetamine.

key_findings.finding: Search of EMBASE, MEDLINE and PsycINFO to 10 February 2017 plus reference lists; 370 records screened and 77 papers included: 3 post-mortem series, 11 case-control and epidemiological studies, 63 case reports and series.
key_findings.locator: Abstract; Methods, 1st paragraph; Results, 1st paragraph; Figure 1 (image, not extracted)

key_findings.finding: Post-mortem series: intracranial haemorrhage caused 2 of 146 (1.4%; berry aneurysm with subarachnoid haemorrhage), 10 of 413 (2.4%) and 17 of 371 (5%) all-age methamphetamine-related deaths (Logan et al. 1998; Karch et al. 1999; Kaye et al. 2008). Karch et al. found no such cases in 114 drug-free trauma deaths; Kaye et al. found cerebrovascular complications significantly more common in women.
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: 10/413 versus 0/114 gives a two-sided Fisher exact p of about 0.13; the strong association attributed to Karch et al. is not shown by these counts alone.

key_findings.finding: Hospital series implicated amphetamines in 6–13% of haemorrhagic strokes and 2–6% of ischaemic strokes; in an Adelaide series of ischaemic stroke at ages 15–50, 19 of 326 (6%) involved amphetamines, predominantly injected, compared with 1 of 51 (2%) in a US series a decade earlier.
key_findings.note: The 6% from Kaku & Lowenstein is 12 of 214 strokes of both types, not a share of haemorrhagic strokes.

key_findings.finding: Westover et al. (population-based, hospitalized stroke at ages 18–44; 937 haemorrhagic, 998 ischaemic): amphetamine use associated with haemorrhagic stroke, OR 4.95, and not with ischaemic stroke, OR 1.04; the haemorrhagic association was more than double that for cocaine or tobacco, and amphetamine use was associated with higher mortality after haemorrhagic stroke.
key_findings.note: No confidence intervals or covariates are given in the review; the text calls the odds ratio a 4.95 increased risk. Exposure is described as amphetamine use.

key_findings.finding: Huang et al. (1315 people who used methamphetamine, all ages, 54 stroke events, 10-year follow-up): HR 2.09 (p=0.001) for haemorrhagic stroke versus a control group; no significant difference for ischaemic stroke or subarachnoid haemorrhage. Petitti et al. (women aged 15–44; 1021 controls): amphetamine use associated with 3.8 times the risk of stroke, with no separate estimate by stroke type.

Case reports: 98 strokes at ages 16–44, of which 81 haemorrhagic (83%) and 17 ischaemic. Haemorrhagic: men to women 2:1 (editors' count 51:30); route oral:injection:inhalation 3:3:1; 60 intracerebral and 32 subarachnoid haemorrhages (13 both); intraventricular haemorrhage in 5 (1 without intracerebral haemorrhage); aneurysm 17%, arteriovenous malformation 8%, other vascular abnormalities (beading, arteritis, small-artery occlusion) in a third, no vascular abnormality in 47%.
key_findings.note: Denominators for 17%, 8% and 47% are not stated. Editors' count from Table 1: 11 definite and 1 possible aneurysm (6 of them from autopsy series) and 5 arteriovenous malformations among 81 cases. Route cannot be checked: Table 1 has no route column.
