key_findings.finding: Haemorrhagic stroke outcomes: death in a third, complete recovery in a quarter, residual deficits in about 40%. Editors' count from Table 1: 26 of 81 died (32%) and 19–21 recovered fully (23–26%, depending on whether 'fair' and 'almost asymptomatic' recovery are counted); excluding the 10 autopsy-series cases, 16 of 71 died (23%).
key_findings.locator: Results › Haemorrhagic stroke, 2nd paragraph; Table 1 (footnote † marks autopsy series)

key_findings.finding: Ischaemic stroke (17 cases): men to women 12:5; route oral:injection:inhalation 1:1:4; mostly anterior-circulation territory; where angiography was done, beading in 3, intimal thickening in 1, normal in 4; other causes in 3 (bacterial embolus 1, carotid dissection 2). Death about 20%, complete recovery about 20%, residual deficits about 60%.
key_findings.note: Editors' count from Table 1: 3 of 17 died, 3 of 17 recovered fully; 7 of 17 are recorded as smokers.

key_findings.finding: The authors state that the 80% haemorrhagic share is far above the 40–55% expected in stroke at ages under 45 and may partly reflect reporting bias, and that the reported outcomes may reflect the severe end of the spectrum because minor events would not be reported.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 1st paragraph; Discussion › Prognosis and outcomes

key_findings.finding: Proposed mechanisms are hypertension and tachycardia, vasculitis (necrotizing angiitis, beading on angiography, in some cases resolving on repeat angiography after stopping use or after corticosteroids), direct vascular toxicity, vasospasm and accelerated atherosclerosis; supporting evidence is case reports, a 2009 series of 30 cases that found no vasculitis in ischaemic stroke, and a 1971 study in rhesus monkeys given intravenous methamphetamine over 2 weeks.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Pathogenesis of haemorrhagic stroke; Pathogenesis of ischaemic stroke

key_findings.finding: Methamphetamine-associated aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage had worse outcomes than age-matched controls at discharge (Beadell et al., 28 of 374 with methamphetamine) and methamphetamine use independently predicted poorer Glasgow Outcome Scale scores at 1 and 3 years (Moon et al., 31 of 398).

reporting_issues.issue: The inclusion criteria restrict cases to people aged 44 or younger, but Table 2 (three post-mortem series) and most of Table 3 (Ho, Beadell, Moon, Nakagawa, Huang; Phillips at 15–50) are all-age or older-age studies.
reporting_issues.consequence: The post-mortem and epidemiological findings do not describe young adults specifically; any claim about young people should rest on Westover et al. (18–44), Petitti et al. and Kaku & Lowenstein (15–44), or the case reports.

reporting_issues.issue: Title, abstract and conclusions refer to methamphetamine, but by the editors' count 46 of the 98 cases in Table 1 (43 of 81 haemorrhagic) involved amphetamine, dextroamphetamine or amphetamine with ecstasy without methamphetamine being named; the Westover estimate concerns amphetamine use.
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims should say methamphetamine or amphetamine; the proportions are not specific to methamphetamine.

reporting_issues.issue: Ischaemic case fatality is given as one-fifth in the abstract and about 20% in the Results, but as one quarter in the Discussion (Prognosis and outcomes); Table 1 shows 3 of 17 (18%).
reporting_issues.consequence: Use one-fifth (3 of 17) if cited at all.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says haemorrhagic stroke was associated with vascular abnormalities in a third of cases; the Results give aneurysm 17%, arteriovenous malformation 8%, other abnormalities a third and no abnormality 47%, implying abnormalities in about half.
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract understates pre-existing or coexisting vascular lesions, which bear on whether the drug was the cause.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results say intracerebral haemorrhages were predominantly temporal, parietal and occipital; in Table 1 the editors count frontal involvement in 13 cases, parietal in 15, temporal in 5 and occipital in 2 (mixed sites counted under each lobe).
reporting_issues.consequence: The anatomical distribution in the text does not match the case table; do not cite it.

reporting_issues.issue: The text cites three studies of haemorrhagic stroke (refs 32–34) as reporting methamphetamine use in 7–13% of cases; refs 33 and 34 are single case reports (one of them an ischaemic infarction), and Table 3 assigns the 7% and 8% figures to refs 30 and 31.
reporting_issues.consequence: Citation numbering error; the figures belong to Beadell et al., Moon et al. and Nakagawa et al.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 describes Beadell et al. (ref 30) as an all-age spontaneous intracerebral haemorrhage cohort; the reference title and the Discussion describe aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage.
reporting_issues.consequence: The stroke type of that cohort must be checked in the primary paper before its 7% figure is used; Hemphill et al. (2024) also describe it as an aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage study.

reporting_issues.issue: Background figures for the haemorrhagic share of stroke in young people differ: 33.5% at ages 20–44 in the Introduction (ref 13) versus 40–55% under 45 in the Discussion (ref 12). The outcome comparator in the Discussion (ref 67) is described as all-cause stroke at ages 16–45, but by title it is a study of ischaemic stroke in young adults.
reporting_issues.consequence: The contrast between methamphetamine-related cases and young stroke in general is drawn against inconsistent or mismatched baselines.

reporting_issues.issue: The haemorrhagic death rate pools 10 autopsy-series cases (Table 1 footnote †) with clinical cases, and one counted death (Ago et al. 2006) is attributed in Table 1 to methamphetamine poisoning with renal failure from rhabdomyolysis rather than to the stroke.
reporting_issues.consequence: Case fatality is overstated by design; excluding autopsy-series cases it falls from 32% to 23% (editors' calculation).

reporting_issues.issue: No confidence intervals are given for any odds ratio, relative risk or hazard ratio, and covariates are not reported; odds ratios are described as increased risk.
reporting_issues.consequence: Each estimate must be taken from its primary paper with its interval and adjustment set.

reporting_issues.issue: The article carries no funding statement; supplementary files (search strategy, full references for Table 1) are PDFs and were not read.
reporting_issues.consequence: Funding is recorded as not reported; individual case citations not given in the reference list could not be checked.

verification.source_read: Publisher full text (HTML), https://doi.org/10.1136/jnnp-2017-316071 (jnnp.bmj.com; all sections, Tables 1–3 read in full from the publisher's table view with footnotes, contributors, competing interests, provenance, affiliations and reference list; Figure 1 flow diagram is an image and was not extracted; supplementary files s1 and s2 are PDFs and were not opened; no rapid responses had been posted)

design_detail: Narrative pharmacology review of methamphetamine-induced hyperthermia (Pharmacol Ther 2014;144(1):28–40), by seven authors at West Virginia University, the University of Chicago, Vanderbilt and the CDC's National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health. Sections: normal thermoregulation (anatomy, neurochemistry, body-mass scaling); methamphetamine and temperature regulation, with environmental and disease modulators; clinical considerations, including emergency presentation, diagnosis and symptomatic management; preclinical pharmacological and molecular studies by target system (noradrenaline, dopamine, serotonin, reactive species, immune, miscellaneous) including manipulations that failed; conclusions. No methods section: no search strategy, eligibility criteria or appraisal. 153 references. Two tables: Table 1 contrasts physiological responses to environmental heat with those to high-dose methamphetamine; Table 2 lists compounds tested against hyperthermia in preclinical models with their molecular targets (structures are images). One schematic figure (image). Read as the NIH author manuscript in PMC; the manuscript carries a publisher's disclaimer that it is an unedited accepted version.
can_establish: What was known in 2014 about the mechanisms proposed for methamphetamine-induced hyperthermia, almost entirely from rodent experiments, and which manipulations raised, lowered or did not change body temperature in those models.
cannot_establish: Anything quantitative about hyperthermia in people: no human incidence, no temperature distributions, no case-fatality, no dose–temperature relation and no treatment effect, because the review cites no human series with numbers other than an annual emergency-department count and a clinical threshold, and because the authors themselves state that rodent thermoregulation does not scale to humans.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). The evidence base is overwhelmingly preclinical: rats, mice (including C57BL/6J, ICR and several knockout lines), rhesus macaques, isolated rat hepatocytes and synaptosomes. Human sources cited are a 1970 series of acute high-dose toxic reactions in Haight-Ashbury, a 2002 report of acute liver failure, clinical toxicology and emergency-medicine reviews, a 1978 study of induced hyperthermia in sedated people, and US agency statistics.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: None reported.
sample.demographics: Not applicable.
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: Selection of sources is unstated and cannot be audited. The review is weighted towards the authors' own programme: several cited studies of sigma-receptor compounds against methamphetamine hyperthermia are by the corresponding author's group (AC927, AZ66, CM156, SN79), and two authors (Miller, O'Callaghan) wrote several of the cited temperature-and-neurotoxicity studies in mice.

exposure.measurement: Not applicable at review level; the cited animal studies administered known amounts under controlled conditions, which the review does not tabulate.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Reported only as study conditions and rarely: the review states that lower, stimulant amounts do not have significant effects on body temperature while high amounts can produce lethal hyperthermia, and gives exactly one animal dose (a bolus of 30 mg/kg in ICR mice in a study where two dopamine antagonists failed to block the temperature rise). Doses, schedules and ambient temperatures of the other cited experiments are not given, although ambient temperature is repeatedly named as decisive (protective effects of several drugs disappeared at 28.5, 29 or 33 degrees C; one inhibitor worked only at 20 degrees C).
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed as a confounder. Co-exposure is discussed only mechanistically (the comparison with MDMA, and amphetamine formed as a metabolite being itself capable of raising temperature).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: Not applicable at review level. The cited experiments compare treated with untreated animals, knockout with wild-type mice, or drug-pretreated with vehicle-pretreated animals.
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable (experimental literature). For the human statements, no comparison group is described anywhere.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable.

outcomes.instruments: Not specified at review level: core or brain temperature in animals, measured by means the review does not describe; in the clinical sections, core body temperature and the laboratory and histological markers of liver injury (AST, ALT, histopathology).
outcomes.validity_norms: The review notes a clinical threshold: hyperthermia is diagnosed when core temperature exceeds 40 degrees C, at which point thermoregulation is said to fail.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Hyperthermia' is used for any drug-induced elevation of body or brain temperature in animals and for the clinical syndrome in people, without a stated quantitative criterion for the animal studies. The review explicitly distinguishes hyperthermia from fever and notes that anti-inflammatory drugs do not affect it.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: None computed, and almost none reported: no temperature changes in degrees, no sample sizes, no intervals and no test statistics are given for any cited experiment, with one exception (tryptophan hydroxylase 2 knockout mice lacking brain serotonin showed a hyperthermic response about 1 degree C greater than controls). Effects are described only as attenuation, prevention, no significant effect or enhancement. Two human figures: an estimated 94,000 US emergency-department admissions a year attributed to methamphetamine (a 2011 agency source) and 65% of heat-related deaths resulting from exposure to excessive heat (a 2006 CDC report, which is a statement about heat deaths generally, not about methamphetamine).
analysis.covariates: Not applicable.
analysis.selective_reporting: Cannot be assessed for source selection, but the review is unusually explicit about negative results: a whole section lists manipulations that did not change methamphetamine-induced hyperthermia (non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, an interleukin-1 receptor antagonist, several neuroprotective agents, interleukin-6 knockout), and divergent findings are reported (dopamine antagonists failing in one mouse study; a serotonin-enhancing drug lowering rather than raising temperature; a radical scavenger that blocks peroxynitrite but not hyperthermia).
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: A mechanistic literature in rodents in which many unrelated interventions lower methamphetamine-induced hyperthermia and several expected ones do not; no single mechanism is identified; ambient temperature, group housing, stress and exercise modulate the effect; and the relationship between temperature, neurotoxicity and death is correlational in animals. The human content is a clinical description of presentation and symptomatic cooling, with no numbers beyond an annual admission count and the 40 degrees C threshold.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract states that reports of methamphetamine-related emergency room visits suggest elevated body temperature is a universal presenting symptom, and the introduction repeats 'universal'. No study, proportion or temperature distribution supports this in the text; the citation given for the admission count is an agency fact sheet on drug-related emergency visits. The abstract also says lethal overdoses are generally associated with extreme hyperthermia, again without a source reporting temperatures at death. By contrast, the body is careful: it says the mechanisms are largely unknown and relatively unexplored, that the mechanistic relationship between methamphetamine, hyperthermia, neurotoxicity and mortality has not been established, that rodent-to-human extrapolation is limited by body-mass scaling, and that it is unknown whether cooling improves outcomes in methamphetamine overdose because no prospective studies exist. The gap is therefore confined to the two universality claims in the abstract, which are the sentences most likely to be quoted.

timeline.event: Greenblatt & Osterberg: lethality of stimulants greater in grouped than isolated mice ('aggregate toxicity'), cited here as the origin of the social-housing effect
Smith & Fischer: 310 cases of acute high-dose methamphetamine toxicity in Haight-Ashbury, cited here for hepatitis as the second commonest presenting complaint

Bowyer et al. and Miller & O'Callaghan: lowering ambient temperature prevents methamphetamine hyperthermia and attenuates dopaminergic neurotoxicity in rodents, the finding on which the temperature-neurotoxicity link rests
Albers & Sonsalla: pharmacological profile of agents protective and non-protective against methamphetamine hyperthermia in mice, the single most-cited source in this review's drug sections
Numachi et al.: dopamine transporter knockout mice show only a modest, non-significant reduction in hyperthermia but a higher lethal dose; serotonin transporter knockout mice show no change
Ito et al.: dopamine D1 and D2 knockout mice show reduced hyperthermia and reduced lethality; surviving animals had lower temperatures than those that died
Thomas et al.: reducing brain serotonin pharmacologically attenuates hyperthermia, while mice genetically lacking brain serotonin show hyperthermia about 1 degree C greater
This review

replication.where_it_stands: Still the standard mechanistic reference on methamphetamine hyperthermia, and useful chiefly for its negative results and its explicit statement that no mechanism, and no specific treatment, has been established. It supports no numerical claim about people; the clinical toxicology reviews it cites (Albertson 1999; Schep 2010) and primary emergency-department series would be needed for that.

funding.funder: National Institutes of Health grants DA013978 and GM081741 supported some of the described studies and the authors (Acknowledgments).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors state they have no conflicts of interest to disclose (Footnotes, Declaration of interest).
funding.affiliations_note: West Virginia University School of Pharmacy and Center for Neuroscience, Department of Neurosurgery; University of Chicago; Vanderbilt University; and the CDC's National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health. The sigma-receptor compounds presented in Table 2 as potential therapeutic options come from the corresponding author's own research programme, funded by the NIH grants acknowledged here; recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: For the human question: a prospective emergency-department cohort of people presenting after methamphetamine use that records core temperature on arrival for every patient, with outcomes, so that the frequency and distribution of hyperthermia and its relation to death can be estimated rather than asserted. For the mechanism: experiments that separate temperature from neurotoxicity, in species whose thermoregulation resembles human thermoregulation, using local rather than systemic manipulation to locate the peripheral and central sites involved, with ambient temperature reported as a controlled variable.

domains.note: No methods section, search, dates or criteria; the paper moves straight from the introduction to thermoregulatory physiology, and how its references were chosen is never stated.

No methodological appraisal of any cited study: sample sizes, randomization, blinding, doses and effect magnitudes are almost never reported, so the animal literature that carries the review is never weighed the way SYRCLE would weigh it. Against that, the review is explicit about the limits of the evidence as a body: a whole subsection on body-mass scaling and why rodent thermoregulation does not extrapolate to humans, repeated notes that effects differ between rats and mice and with ambient temperature, the statement that no manipulation has produced a clear picture of how monoamines are involved, and the observation that the plasma-serotonin and body-temperature association was never examined.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: Much of the evidence is other groups' work, but the reference list carries repeated citations of the authors' own studies (the corresponding author and two co-authors appear many times), two co-authors are the source of several of the temperature-and-neurotoxicity results relied on, and the four sigma-receptor compounds that Table 2 offers among potential pharmacotherapy options come from the corresponding author's own programme.

The body is careful, marking what is unknown or unexplored and labelling proposed mechanisms as proposed. The abstract is not: it states that elevated body temperature is a universal presenting symptom in methamphetamine-related emergency visits and that lethal overdoses are generally associated with extreme hyperthermia, neither of which the body supports with a human series, and the statement about emergency presentations rests on an in-text citation that has no entry in the reference list. Section 3.2 also extends the argument to children and adults treated for amphetamine salts for ADHD and to sport in hot weather, with no evidence offered.

domains.domain: Balance of positive against null and contradictory mechanistic findings
domains.note: Negative and contradictory results are given their own space: a dedicated subsection on manipulations that do not affect methamphetamine hyperthermia (non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, an interleukin-1 receptor antagonist, several neuroprotective agents), species reversals reported wherever they occur, and the unexplained protective effect of fenfluramine left unexplained.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS §5.3), so the editors' narrative-review checklist is used. The absence of any search or selection method fixes that domain at high and therefore the overall judgment at high, since the overall can be no milder than the worst domain. Within that limit this is a careful mechanistic survey: it is balanced about null findings, open about species differences and body-mass scaling, and sceptical about its own evidence base. Its weaknesses for this encyclopedia are that it reports almost no magnitudes, so nothing in it can anchor a quantitative claim; that its two human generalizations sit in the abstract unsupported by the body; and that some of its own citations do not support the statements they are attached to. Cite it for the map of mechanisms tested and for its negative findings, and take every number from the primary study.

key_findings.finding: The review states that methamphetamine at lower, stimulant amounts does not have significant effects on body temperature, while high amounts can produce lethal hyperthermia; the mechanisms combine increased heat production (central and skeletal-muscle activation) with impaired heat loss (vasoconstriction).
key_findings.locator: 3. METH and temperature regulation, 1st paragraph; 3.1 Body temperature dysregulation by METH; Figure 1 legend; Table 1

key_findings.finding: Table 1 contrasts the response to environmental heat (hypothalamic heat-sensitive neuron activation; reduced metabolic and muscle activity; increased skin blood flow and sweating) with the response to high-dose methamphetamine (raised brain temperature, heat-shock protein expression, vasoconstriction and piloerection, with saliva spreading as the only heat-loss mechanism listed in animals).
key_findings.note: The table is a conceptual summary without data, and the animal items (piloerection, saliva spreading) do not transfer to people.

key_findings.finding: Rodent-to-human extrapolation is limited: small animals have a large surface-area-to-volume ratio and regulate surface temperature by passive heat dissipation and metabolic change, whereas humans depend on sweating and peripheral vasomotor mechanisms, making rodents more vulnerable to ambient temperature than humans.

Modulators of the temperature response in animals: raising ambient temperature enhances and cold prevents methamphetamine hyperthermia and attenuates oxidation products and neurotoxicity; group housing increases toxicity and lethality ('aggregate toxicity'), with brain temperature rising before and above body temperature; unpredictable stress enhances hyperthermia in rats (preventable by a 5-HT2 antagonist) while restraint stress in mice lowers body temperature and confers resistance to dopaminergic neurotoxicity.
key_findings.locator: 3.2 Modulators of thermoregulation and METH hyperthermia

key_findings.finding: Clinical description: the commonest presenting feature in emergency departments after a methamphetamine overdose is said to be extreme hyperthermia, which can be lethal untreated; other features listed are hypertension, tachycardia, breathlessness, chest pain, agitation, altered mental status, pupil dilation, shivering and possible seizures. Hyperthermia is diagnosed clinically above a core temperature of 40 degrees C.
key_findings.note: No proportions, temperature distributions or case numbers are given; the symptom list is cited to a 1999 clinical review.

key_findings.finding: No approved pharmacotherapy exists for methamphetamine hyperthermia; management is symptomatic cooling, and the authors state it is unknown whether cooling improves outcomes in methamphetamine overdose because no prospective studies have been done.
key_findings.locator: 4.2 Treatment of METH hyperthermia, 2nd paragraph; 6. Summary and conclusions, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Liver: hepatitis was the second commonest presenting complaint in a 1970 series of acute toxic reactions; acute liver damage has been reported without viral hepatitis; in a rat binge model, aminotransferases rose with histopathological changes; raising temperature exogenously worsened methamphetamine hepatotoxicity in vitro, and hyperthermia contributed to liver damage and raised peripheral ammonia in vivo.
key_findings.locator: 4.3 Clinical consequences of METH hyperthermia, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: No numbers from the human reports are given; the mechanistic evidence is from rats and isolated hepatocytes.

key_findings.finding: Damage to dopaminergic nerve terminals in rats and mice tracks core temperature: raising ambient temperature worsens it, lowering core temperature by pharmacological, genetic or physiological means reduces it, and raising brain methamphetamine levels has no neurotoxic effect if body temperature is kept low. The authors state that elevated temperature appears to be an obligatory component of neurotoxicity in these models but that the controlling mechanism is unknown and the relationship between methamphetamine, hyperthermia, neurotoxicity and mortality has not been established.
key_findings.locator: 4.3 Clinical consequences of METH hyperthermia, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Catecholamines: peripheral chemical sympathectomy with 6-hydroxydopamine blocked methamphetamine hyperthermia, and blocking catecholamine synthesis with alpha-methyl-p-tyrosine attenuated it in rats but not mice, and in rats only at room temperature, not at a raised ambient temperature of 28.5 degrees C. Within the noradrenaline section the species differ: the beta-adrenoceptor antagonist propranolol prevented methamphetamine hyperthermia in mice, whereas the series supporting noradrenaline-driven thermogenesis in skeletal muscle under glucocorticoid permission is in rats, where sympathectomy or adrenalectomy prevented hyperthermia, dexamethasone restored it in adrenalectomized animals, and the muscle calcium-release inhibitor dantrolene prevented it. The receptor subtypes responsible are unidentified.
key_findings.locator: 5.1 Monoaminergic systems, 2nd–3rd paragraphs; 5.1.1 Norepinephrine systems, 2nd paragraph (propranolol, mice) and 3rd paragraph (sympathectomy, adrenalectomy, glucocorticoid and dantrolene series, rats)

key_findings.finding: Dopamine: methamphetamine failed to produce hyperthermia in dopamine D2 knockout mice; D2 and D1 antagonists attenuated it, but the protection was lost at higher ambient temperatures (29 and 33 degrees C), and in one study in ICR mice a D1 and a D2 antagonist did not attenuate the temperature rise after a 30 mg/kg bolus. In D1 and D2 knockout mice both hyperthermia and lethality were reduced, and in both knockout and wild-type groups animals that survived had lower temperatures than those that died. Dopamine transporter knockout mice showed only a modest, non-significant reduction in hyperthermia but a higher lethal dose.
key_findings.note: This is the review's only direct temperature-mortality observation, and it is in mice.

key_findings.finding: Serotonin: depleting brain serotonin pharmacologically attenuated hyperthermia in mice, yet mice genetically lacking brain serotonin showed a hyperthermic response about 1 degree C greater, which the authors read as compensation by other systems; serotonin transporter knockout mice showed unchanged hyperthermia. A 5-HT1A antagonist blocked the temperature rise while a 5-HT1A agonist did not attenuate it, and a serotonin-releasing drug paradoxically reduced hyperthermia. The authors conclude serotonin modulates but is not required.

Reactive species: an antioxidant, melatonin and an iron chelator each attenuated hyperthermia in rodents, and mice lacking neuronal nitric oxide synthase resisted it, but nitric oxide synthase inhibitors worked only at 20 degrees C and not at normal or raised ambient temperature, and one radical scavenger blocked peroxynitrite without affecting temperature. Older rats were more sensitive than young rats to peroxynitrite formation and to the hyperthermic and lethal effects.

Other targets: a protein kinase C delta inhibitor reduced hyperthermia and knockout mice resisted it; sigma-receptor antagonists (AC927, AZ66, CM156, SN79) attenuated hyperthermia in mice; an anticonvulsant attenuated it without changing temperature alone; a GABA transaminase inhibitor, an NMDA antagonist and ibogaine reduced it but caused hypothermia alone; systemic but not intracerebroventricular interferon-gamma reduced it, as did an immunosuppressive antibiotic that inhibits a transcription-factor family.
key_findings.note: Table 2 lists these compounds with their molecular targets; chemical structures are images and were not extracted.

key_findings.finding: Manipulations without effect on methamphetamine hyperthermia: ibuprofen and aspirin in mice; an interleukin-1 receptor antagonist (which nevertheless reduced deaths); and a list of neuroprotective agents and genetic modifications including edaravone, carnosine, minocycline, memantine, an alpha-7 nicotinic antagonist, calcitriol, ketamine and interleukin-6 knockout. Hypothalamic interleukin-1 beta expression did not correlate with body temperature.
key_findings.locator: 5.5 Mechanisms that do not affect METH hyperthermia
key_findings.note: These negative results separate hyperthermia from fever and separate neuroprotection from temperature control.

key_findings.finding: Conclusion as drawn by the authors: no single mechanism underlies methamphetamine hyperthermia, no pharmacological profile predicts protection, broad classes of drugs with no clear thermoregulatory action can act as countermeasures in animals, and most studies used systemic administration or whole-body knockouts so central and peripheral sites cannot be separated; peripheral mechanisms and muscle heat generation appear important.

The review states that it is unclear whether the maximum methamphetamine-induced rise in body temperature is related specifically to peak plasma concentration or rather to cumulative exposure, so no dose-temperature relation is established. It also notes that metabolites may contribute to a sustained hyperthermic effect, amphetamine having been reported to raise body temperature on its own.
key_findings.locator: 4.1 Pharmacokinetic parameters of METH, 1st paragraph (last sentence) and 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: Recorded as the authors' own acknowledgement that no dose-temperature relation exists in this literature; it supports the card's cannot_establish. Route and bioavailability figures from the same paragraph are deliberately not extracted, as no claim needs them.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract's statement that elevated body temperature is a universal presenting symptom of methamphetamine-related emergency room visits has no supporting data anywhere in the text; the only citation near the equivalent sentence in the introduction is an agency fact sheet on drug-related emergency visits used for the figure of about 94,000 admissions a year.
reporting_issues.consequence: Not citable. Any claim about how often people presenting after methamphetamine use are hyperthermic needs an emergency-department series that measured temperature in all patients.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract's statement that lethal overdoses are generally associated with extreme hyperthermia is likewise unsupported in the text; the only temperature-mortality data given are from mice (survivors had lower temperatures than animals that died).
reporting_issues.consequence: The human generalization rests on animal data; claims must say so.

reporting_issues.issue: In section 3.2, 1st paragraph, the statement that 65% of heat-related deaths result from exposure to excessive heat is cited to a CDC report on heat-related deaths in general and concerns neither methamphetamine nor drug-related deaths; the review then infers, by analogy with MDMA, that the clinical condition would be expected to be greatly exaggerated with methamphetamine co-exposure.
reporting_issues.consequence: An expectation by analogy, not a finding; the figure does not belong in any methamphetamine claim.

reporting_issues.issue: Two in-text citations have no matching entry in the reference list: 'Bowyer et al., 1984' and 'Bowyer et al., 1995' (the list contains Bowyer et al. 1992, 1994 and 2013 and Bowyer & Holson 1995). The 1984 citation supports the statement that hyperthermia is the major presenting symptom in emergency rooms, and the 1995 citation supports several statements about the temperature dependence of neurotoxicity.
reporting_issues.consequence: The emergency-room statement cannot be traced to a source at all; the neurotoxicity statements probably intend Bowyer & Holson (1995), a book chapter.

reporting_issues.issue: Effect magnitudes are absent throughout: no cited experiment is reported with a sample size, a temperature change in degrees, an interval or a test statistic, except one roughly 1 degree C enhancement in serotonin-deficient mice. Animal doses and ambient temperatures are given only sporadically, while the review itself shows that ambient temperature determines whether a drug protects.
reporting_issues.consequence: Nothing in this review can anchor a quantitative claim; each primary study must be read for its conditions and magnitudes.

reporting_issues.issue: Statements about serotonin manipulation are internally confusing: pharmacological inhibition of tryptophan hydroxylase is said to attenuate hyperthermia, while 'treatment of mice with tryptophan hydroxylase' (apparently a word missing, probably an inhibitor of a specific isoform) is said not to alter it, in the same sentence as the knockout result.
reporting_issues.consequence: The serotonin section cannot be paraphrased precisely from this text; the primary study must be read.

reporting_issues.issue: Two antipsychotic drug names are given in non-standard spellings in the text and in Table 2 ('risperidol'; 'p-cholorphenyl-alanine' in Table 2 versus 'p-chlorophenylalanine' in the text), and one author's surname is spelled two ways in the reference list and text.
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical only, but the compound identities should be confirmed from the primary studies before any claim names a drug.

reporting_issues.issue: Read from the NIH author manuscript, which carries a publisher's disclaimer that it is an unedited accepted version; printed pagination is not shown in the HTML. The PMC line gives the final edited form as Pharmacol Ther 2014 May 14;144(1):28-40, so the only date visible in this save is 14 May 2014; the first reader also recorded an October 2014 print issue, which this reading could not check.
reporting_issues.consequence: Anchors are to sections of the author manuscript rather than printed pages; the citation year is 2014 on either date.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 files vasoconstriction and piloerection in animals under activation of heat production mechanisms in the methamphetamine column, while section 2 lists vasoconstriction and insulation (including piloerection in furred animals) among heat retention strategies, and section 3.1 describes methamphetamine-induced vasoconstriction as contributing to hyperthermia by preventing heat dissipation. Table 1 also files saliva spreading in animals under activation of heat loss mechanisms for methamphetamine, which matches the text.
reporting_issues.consequence: The table contradicts the paper's own physiology: vasoconstriction retains heat and blocks dissipation rather than producing it. Table 1 is the part of this review most likely to be reused, so its headings should not be carried over as the paper's classification of mechanisms.

reporting_issues.issue: Several citations in section 3.1 do not support the statements they are attached to. The sentence that methamphetamine causes vasoconstriction carries four references: a study of the autonomic thermoregulatory response of the rat to MDMA, an emergency-department study of the frequency of acute coronary syndrome in people presenting with chest pain after methamphetamine use, a case report of methamphetamine-induced myocardial infarction with raised troponin, and a study of electrocardiographic abnormalities. None measured vasoconstriction, and the first concerns a different drug. The statement about drooling and saliva spreading in methamphetamine-treated animals cites a general review of central thermoregulatory pathways.
reporting_issues.consequence: Vasoconstriction is central to the review's account of how methamphetamine raises body temperature, and the citations given do not evidence it. Any claim about methamphetamine-induced vasoconstriction needs a study that measured it; this belongs with the citation problems already recorded for this source.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 gives the molecular target of fenfluramine as a serotonin-transporter inhibitor, while the text (5.1.3, 7th paragraph) describes it as enhancing serotonin function through several mechanisms, calls it a serotonin indirect agonist, and notes that it also enhances noradrenaline release, which the authors suggest may explain its protective effect against methamphetamine hyperthermia.
reporting_issues.consequence: A text-table inconsistency of the same kind as the other table problems on this card. The pharmacology in Table 2 should not be quoted without reading the matching passage, and fenfluramine's mechanism in this context is explicitly unresolved in the text.

reporting_issues.issue: Section 3.2, 3rd paragraph, extends the heat argument from methamphetamine to children and adults treated with a mixture of amphetamine salts for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, who are said to be prone to more difficulty in extreme temperature situations such as playing sport in hot summer months. No evidence is cited for that sentence, and no study of people taking prescribed stimulants is reported anywhere in the review.
reporting_issues.consequence: An unevidenced clinical extrapolation to a different substance and a different population, including children. It should not be carried into any monograph from this review.

design_detail: Narrative clinical review in JAMA Psychiatry (published title 'Neurobiology, Clinical Presentation, and Treatment of Methamphetamine Use Disorder: A Review'; the PMC author manuscript read here is titled 'Methamphetamine Use Disorder: The Next Addiction Crisis'). No methods section, search strategy or eligibility criteria for the narrative parts. Three themes: molecular and neural mechanisms beyond monoamine release (oxidative stress, excito- and neurotoxicity, neuroinflammation), clinical presentation with emphasis on cardiovascular and cerebrovascular disease, and treatment. The one quasi-systematic element is a count of ClinicalTrials.gov intervention studies containing the term 'methamphetamine' (Table 1, with an unread supplementary table). Two authors from one research institute; 94 references.
can_establish: The authors' synthesis and research agenda: which mechanisms and clinical problems they consider important, a rough audit of how many registered methamphetamine trials reported results and publications, and pointers to primary sources for prevalence, course, comorbidity, cardiovascular harm and treatment.
cannot_establish: Any of the figures it quotes (all are second-hand and must be taken from the primary sources), that methamphetamine causes the cognitive, 'degenerative' or metabolic brain states it describes (the mechanistic evidence cited is largely preclinical or in vitro, and the authors themselves say the human neurobiology is almost entirely cross-sectional), or that no medication has shown any benefit (the mirtazapine trials are not discussed).

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). Cited sources range from US surveillance (NSDUH, CDC mortality reports, ARCOS), cell and animal studies of mechanism, cross-sectional imaging and neuropsychology, single-country clinical samples (China, Taiwan, South Africa, Australia, Thailand), systematic reviews of pharmacotherapy and psychosocial treatment, and the authors' own imaging studies.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: None stated for the narrative sections. For the ClinicalTrials.gov count: all registered intervention studies containing the term 'methamphetamine', with no search date, no definition of 'intervention trial' and no rule for classifying publications as showing 'no effect', 'some effect' or 'unclear' given in the text (details are in an unread supplementary table).
sample.demographics: Not applicable.
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: Selection is the authors'. Eight of the cited imaging and relapse-prediction studies are from the authors' group (references 29 to 31 and 33 to 37). The treatment section does not cite either randomized trial of mirtazapine (Colfax et al., 2011; Coffin et al., published online December 2019), which bear directly on its statement that there are no pharmacological treatments.

exposure.measurement: Not applicable at review level.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not synthesized. Forms are mentioned (ice, powder, pills) without route-specific evidence; one cited study reports a progression from first use to craving, regular use and compulsive use within about 50, 60 and 85 days in a single Chinese sample (reference 48).
exposure.polysubstance: Discussed only as co-use with opioids (methamphetamine as an opioid substitute or adjunct; presence of methamphetamine in opioid deaths).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: Not applicable.
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: The review itself notes that the scarcity of longitudinal studies makes it hard to tell whether cognitive dysfunction pre-dates use, results from it, or reflects behaviours common to substance use disorders (Biological pathways, 3rd paragraph), and that childhood adversity and pre-existing psychiatric risk are common in people with methamphetamine use disorder.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable.

outcomes.instruments: Not applicable at review level.
outcomes.operationalization: Not defined. 'Cognitive impairment', 'degenerative' and 'disease-modifying' are used without operational definitions.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (no statistical synthesis).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: None computed. Figures quoted second-hand: past-year methamphetamine use in people aged 12 or older up 195% from its 2010 low to 2018, 1.86 million people in the US using it in 2018 (NSDUH); age-adjusted overdose death rate involving methamphetamine more than tripled 2011 to 2016; deaths involving cocaine, amphetamines or both up 42.4%, from 12,122 (2015) to 17,258 (2016); methamphetamine present in 63% of opioid deaths; psychotic symptoms reported by 36.5% (42.7% lifetime); mood disorders 16.0%, psychotic disorders 13.0%, anxiety disorders 7.0% in one sample; moderate to severe childhood abuse or neglect 44% in one sample; more than two-thirds with cognitive impairment in one study; 5-year remission up to 30% without treatment; after treatment 61% relapse within 12 months and another 14% in years 2 to 5; 51% dropout within 2 weeks of a large programme. ClinicalTrials.gov audit (Table 1): 159 studies, 65 randomized (40.9%), 25 with results (38.5% of randomized), 14 with publications; of these 8 no effect, 3 some effect, 3 unclear; of the 11 with results but no publication, 5 no effect, 0 some effect, 6 unclear.
analysis.covariates: Not applicable.
analysis.selective_reporting: Evidence selection cannot be audited. The pharmacotherapy summary relies on earlier reviews (Lee et al., 2018; Chan et al., 2019; Morley et al., 2017; German guidelines) and omits the two mirtazapine trials; the course-of-illness summary quotes relapse rates from Brecht and Herbeck (2014) but not that study's findings of frequent later abstinence.
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: A clinically oriented synthesis: a list of mechanisms documented mainly in cell and animal studies; cross-sectional imaging and neuropsychological differences; second-hand epidemiological, psychiatric and cardiovascular figures from heterogeneous single samples; a registry audit in which 3 of 14 published randomized trials reported some effect; and summaries of earlier reviews showing no medication with sufficient evidence and modest evidence for contingency management and CBT.
interpretation_gap.claimed: Gaps between the review's statements and its own content: (1) the abstract says prevalence and mortality 'doubled' over 10 years, while the text gives a 195% increase in prevalence (nearly a tripling) and a more than threefold increase in methamphetamine-involved overdose death rates over 5 years; (2) a fourfold increase in methamphetamine 'consumption' is attributed to ARCOS data in a study whose cited title concerns prescription stimulants, not illicit use; (3) the conclusion states that the disorder results in significant long-term cognitive and neurological deficits and describes it as possibly degenerative, while the body calls the cognitive literature debated, notes the lack of longitudinal studies and states that the neurobiology is almost entirely cross-sectional; (4) the claim that methamphetamine puts the brain into a Warburg-type metabolic state rests on a cancer-biology reference and preclinical work; (5) exercise is said to help maintain abstinence, but the cited exercise studies measured craving, inhibitory control, depression and anxiety; (6) the statement that there are no pharmacological treatments is reasonable as regards approval, but the review does not discuss the randomized mirtazapine evidence.

timeline.event: Hart et al. critical review questioning cognitive impairment in people who use methamphetamine (cited as reference 38 for the debate)

Brecht and Herbeck: long-term relapse after treatment; this review quotes its 61% first-year relapse and 'another 14%' in years 2 to 5 (that paper's abstract says 25% and its year-by-year results sum to 15%).
Chan et al. systematic review and meta-analysis of pharmacotherapy for methamphetamine/amphetamine use disorder (cited as reference 78).
This review; Siefried et al. (2020) reach the same conclusion on pharmacotherapy from a systematic search.
McKetin et al. argue similarly that pharmacotherapy should target the wider neurobiological changes of methamphetamine use.

replication.where_it_stands: An influential agenda-setting review rather than an evidence synthesis. Its pharmacotherapy conclusion agrees with the systematic reviews read for the encyclopedia; its neurobiological framing (oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, degeneration) is a hypothesis built mostly on preclinical data, and its epidemiological figures need to be taken from primary sources.

funding.funder: The William K. Warren Foundation; National Institute on Drug Abuse (U01 DA041089); National Institute of General Medical Sciences Center Grant (1P20GM121312).
funding.declared_conflicts: The first author is an advisor to Spring Care, Inc. (a behavioural health start-up) and has received royalties for an UpToDate article about methamphetamine; no disclosures are listed for the second author.
funding.affiliations_note: Both authors at the Laureate Institute for Brain Research and the Department of Community Medicine, University of Tulsa. Several cited imaging and relapse-prediction studies are the authors' own. The text read is the NIH author manuscript, whose title differs from the published title; copyedits in the published version were not checked.

what_would_settle_it: For the central neurobiological thesis: prospective human cohorts with repeated measures of neuroinflammation and oxidative-stress markers (for example TSPO PET, peripheral cytokines) and cognition across periods of use and abstinence, compared with matched people who do not use methamphetamine, and randomized trials of agents targeting these pathways with clinical outcomes (use, retention, cognition).

domains.note: No search, dates or criteria for the narrative sections; the ClinicalTrials.gov audit has a single search term, no date and no classification rules in the text.
No appraisal of the quality of cited studies; figures from single samples (China, Taiwan, South Africa) and from studies of other constructs are presented as general findings.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: Eight cited imaging and relapse-prediction studies are from the authors' group; they are used for the argument about neural markers, which the review itself says are not yet clinically useful.
Preclinical mechanisms and a cancer-metabolism concept are presented as characterizing the human disorder; 'degenerative' and 'results in' are used without longitudinal human evidence.
The cognition debate is acknowledged, but positive pharmacotherapy trials (mirtazapine) and the favourable long-term course data in a cited cohort are not mentioned.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No standard risk-of-bias instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS §5.3); if AMSTAR 2 were applied it would fail every applicable critical item (no protocol, no described search, no list of exclusions, no appraisal of included studies) and be rated critically low. The review is useful for its research agenda, for pointers to primary sources on cardiovascular harm and for the registry audit; none of its quoted figures should be cited from it, and its mechanistic statements should be cited as hypotheses.

key_findings.finding: Past-year methamphetamine use among people aged 12 or older increased by 195% from its 2010 low to 2018, with an estimated 1.86 million people in the US using methamphetamine in 2018 (NSDUH, as cited); the age-adjusted rate of overdose deaths involving methamphetamine more than tripled from 2011 to 2016; overdose deaths involving cocaine, amphetamines or both rose 42.4%, from 12,122 in 2015 to 17,258 in 2016.
key_findings.note: The abstract summarizes these trends as a doubling of prevalence and mortality. Figures are second-hand (references 4 and 5 and NSDUH); cite the primary sources.

key_findings.finding: The review attributes a fourfold increase in methamphetamine 'consumption' between 2015 and 2016 to ARCOS data, citing a study titled as concerning prescription stimulants (reference 3).
key_findings.note: This figure does not describe illicit methamphetamine use and should not be cited as such.

key_findings.finding: Course after treatment, as quoted from Brecht and Herbeck (2014): 61% relapse within the first 12 months and another 14% during years 2 to 5; without treatment, 5-year remission up to 30% (Lanyon et al., 2019).
key_findings.note: The source paper's abstract gives 25% for years 2 to 5 and its results sum to 15%; the review omits that source's findings of later abstinence in most people who relapsed.

key_findings.finding: Psychiatric figures as quoted: psychotic symptoms in 36.5% of people using methamphetamine (42.7% lifetime; reference 50, a meta-analysis titled as concerning substance-induced psychotic disorder); co-occurring mood 16.0%, psychotic 13.0% and anxiety 7.0% disorders in one sample (reference 55); moderate to severe childhood abuse or neglect 44% in one sample (reference 53).

Cognition: the review states that the effect of methamphetamine on cognition is debated and that the lack of longitudinal studies prevents separating pre-existing from drug-related dysfunction, then concludes that methamphetamine is associated with moderate dysfunction in several cognitive processes; more than two-thirds of people with methamphetamine use disorder are said to show cognitive impairment on the basis of one study (reference 43).
key_findings.locator: Biological Pathways, Neural Basis and Cognition, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Methamphetamine is said to be present in 63% of opioid deaths, citing a CDC report on 25 states, July 2017 to June 2018 (reference 73).
key_findings.note: Not verified against the source; take the figure and its denominator from the MMWR report.

key_findings.finding: ClinicalTrials.gov audit (term 'methamphetamine'): 159 registered studies; 65 randomized (40.9%); 25 of those with results (38.5%); 14 with identifiable publications, of which 8 reported no effect, 3 some effect and 3 effects not bearing on efficacy; of the 11 with results but no publication, 5 no effect, none some effect, 6 unclear.
key_findings.note: No search date or classification rules in the text; the trial list is in an unread supplementary table.

key_findings.finding: Pharmacotherapy, second-hand: a systematic review of 49 studies of 20 medications found limited evidence of benefit for methylphenidate, bupropion, modafinil and naltrexone but none sufficient for routine use (reference 75); anticonvulsants, antipsychotics, opioid antagonists, varenicline and atomoxetine showed low-strength or insufficient evidence on abstinence of 3 or more weeks (reference 78). The review concludes there is not sufficient evidence that medications by themselves are useful.

Psychosocial treatment, second-hand: in a network meta-analysis of cocaine and amphetamine addiction, only contingency management plus community reinforcement increased end-of-treatment abstinence over treatment as usual (reference 81); brief CBT reduced use frequency and severity in one trial in methadone patients; behavioural activation was beneficial in 7 of 8 studies across several substances; exercise studies reported reduced craving and improved inhibitory control, depression and anxiety. 51% dropped out within 2 weeks in one large pooled dataset of pharmacotherapy trials (reference 89).

Mechanistic thesis: beyond monoamine release, methamphetamine engages oxidative stress, neuro- and excitotoxicity and neuroinflammation (including TLR4 binding and inflammasome activation in microglia), which the authors argue amount to an altered brain state resembling degenerative CNS disease and a Warburg-type metabolic shift.
key_findings.locator: Biological Pathways, Neural Basis and Cognition, 1st paragraph; Figure 2
key_findings.note: Supported in the text mainly by cell, animal and cancer-biology references (references 10 to 22); presented by the editors as the authors' hypothesis.

key_findings.finding: The authors state that the neurobiology of the disorder is almost entirely derived from cross-sectional studies, and that imaging markers used to predict relapse have not yet proved clinically useful.
key_findings.locator: Conclusion and Relevance, last part; Biological Pathways, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Cardiovascular and cerebrovascular disease is presented as the most severe medical problem and the leading cause of death in methamphetamine use disorder (reference 66). Methamphetamine-related strokes are said to be rising, to occur most often in young men and to be primarily haemorrhagic (67); methamphetamine is associated with vasoconstriction, pulmonary hypertension, atherosclerotic plaque formation, cardiac arrhythmias and cardiomyopathy (68); the associated cardiomyopathy is described as left ventricular dilatation with impaired ejection fraction and raised tissue markers of inflammation and fibrosis (69, 70), and the electrocardiogram as frequently showing tachyarrhythmias, right axis deviation, left ventricular hypertrophy, P pulmonale, inferior Q waves, lateral T wave inversion and a longer QTc interval (71); symptoms preceding death attributed solely to methamphetamine toxicity are given as collapse, breathing difficulty and hyperthermia (72).
key_findings.note: All of it is second-hand, and two of the inferences do not follow from the sources cited. The leading-cause-of-death statement rests on a 10-year follow-up study of cardiovascular and stroke risk, which estimates risk and does not establish what people who use methamphetamine most often die of. The statement that strokes are primarily haemorrhagic rests on a review of published cases, which reflects what gets reported rather than relative incidence; the same inference is recorded on sc_hemphill_2024. Every figure and description here must be taken from the primary source.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says prevalence and mortality doubled over the past 10 years; the text gives a 195% increase in past-year use from 2010 to 2018 and a more than threefold rise in the methamphetamine overdose death rate from 2011 to 2016.
reporting_issues.consequence: The headline trend is stated inconsistently; claims about trends must come from NSDUH and CDC sources directly, with years and measures.

reporting_issues.issue: The 'fourfold increase in methamphetamine consumption' is cited to ARCOS via a study of prescription stimulant trends.
reporting_issues.consequence: A prescription-distribution figure is presented in the context of an illicit-drug crisis; it should not be cited for illicit use.

reporting_issues.issue: The relapse figure for years 2 to 5 after treatment (14%) attributed to Brecht and Herbeck (2014) matches neither that paper's abstract (25%) nor its year-by-year results (15%).
reporting_issues.consequence: Secondary quotation drift; the primary paper's results section is the source to cite.

reporting_issues.issue: Several cited sources concern different constructs from the statements they support: a meta-analysis of substance-induced psychotic disorder for 'psychotic symptoms'; a network meta-analysis of cocaine and amphetamine addiction for 'MUD patients'; a pooled analysis of pharmacotherapy trials for dropout from 'intervention programs'; a review of 49 studies called a meta-analysis; and the 42.4% rise in overdose deaths from 12,122 in 2015 to 17,258 in 2016 is cited to a report titled for drug overdose deaths involving cocaine and psychostimulants with abuse potential, 2003 to 2017, while the sentence reads cocaine, amphetamines, or both substances combined.
reporting_issues.consequence: Each figure must be re-anchored in its primary source before use.

reporting_issues.issue: The Interventions section gives the registry address as 'clinicialtrials.gov' and contains a garbled sentence on the number of Phase II studies in the cited review ('35 studies related to 33 Phase II quality').
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical; the counts from the cited review cannot be relied on as quoted.

reporting_issues.issue: The PMC text is the accepted author manuscript, whose title (Methamphetamine Use Disorder: The Next Addiction Crisis) differs from the published title recorded by the first reader from PubMed (Neurobiology, Clinical Presentation, and Treatment of Methamphetamine Use Disorder: A Review). The author-manuscript title is confirmed from the saved page; the published title could not be re-checked in this reading, which had no access to PubMed or the publisher, so that half of the issue remains single-reader.
reporting_issues.consequence: Anchors refer to the author manuscript; wording may differ slightly in the published version, so the reference record should use the Crossref title.

reporting_issues.issue: Two causal-sounding generalizations rest on single studies. Clinical Presentation ¶1 reports that the transition from casual to compulsive use takes on average about 50 days to first craving, 60 days to regular use and 85 days to compulsive use, from one sample (reference 48). Clinical Presentation ¶2 reports that rising adolescent cannabis use may increase the probability of initiating other illicit drugs including methamphetamine through biological and social processes, from one longitudinal study (61), offered as evidence for the gateway hypothesis (62).
reporting_issues.consequence: Neither can be cited from this review as a general pattern. The day counts need their primary sample, population and measurement before use, and the gateway sentence is a single longitudinal association presented as a mechanism.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC8098650 (NIH author manuscript; all sections, Table 1 rendered as text, acknowledgements with funding, financial disclosures and the full reference list read; Figure 1 (trends) and Figure 2 (pathways) are images and their values were not extracted; the supplementary eTable was not read). Published title and abstract checked on PubMed (PMID 32267484).

disagreements.reviewer: content confirmed exactly, but it is in Clinical Presentation ¶2, not ¶3; the section has only three paragraphs, and the 5-year remission figure of up to 30% without treatment is in the same paragraph
disagreements.resolution: Corrected to the 2nd paragraph. Recounted in the source: Clinical Presentation has three paragraphs of running text (acute and psychiatric presentation; trajectories and course; cardiovascular and cerebrovascular disease), and the relapse and remission figures are all in the second, with the remission figure cited to a five-year community cohort.

disagreements.first_pass: Clinical Presentation, 4th paragraph
disagreements.reviewer: content confirmed; the location is Clinical Presentation ¶3, not ¶4, there being no ¶4
disagreements.resolution: Corrected to the 3rd paragraph, the last of the section. The sentence states that methamphetamine is also present in 63% of opioid deaths, citing the CDC report, and the existing note to take the figure and its denominator from that report is kept.

disagreements.first_pass: The PMC text is the accepted author manuscript, whose title ('Methamphetamine Use Disorder: The Next Addiction Crisis') differs from the published title ('Neurobiology, Clinical Presentation, and Treatment of Methamphetamine Use Disorder: A Review', confirmed on PubMed).
disagreements.reviewer: partly-confirmed: the author-manuscript title is confirmed from the saved text; the published title could not be checked, as this session had no browser and the save contains no PubMed or publisher page
disagreements.resolution: Reworded so that the card distinguishes what this reading confirmed (the author-manuscript title, from the saved page) from what rests on the first reader's PubMed check (the published title). disagreements.first_pass: not recorded beyond the 63% opioid-death figure
disagreements.reviewer: missed: the cardiovascular and cerebrovascular paragraph has no key finding except the 63% figure, although these are the statements most likely to be cited from this review; and two of its inferences (leading cause of death from a risk cohort; primarily haemorrhagic strokes from a case-report review) do not follow from the sources
disagreements.resolution: Added as one key finding covering the paragraph with its reference numbers, and the two inference problems recorded in its note after checking both references in the reference list: reference 66 is a 10-year follow-up study of cardiovascular and stroke risk, and reference 67 is the 2017 review of stroke and methamphetamine use in young adults. Whether the interpretation_gap text should also carry these two points is a matter of judgment and is listed for the senior author.

disagreements.first_pass: the day counts are held in the exposure field; neither item is flagged
disagreements.reviewer: missed: the gateway statement and the 50, 60 and 85-day trajectory claim are causal-sounding generalizations from single studies, and neither is flagged
