design_detail: Inpatient pharmacokinetic study in 8 men, balanced crossover of two conditions about a week apart (intranasal methamphetamine 50 mg; smoked methamphetamine, 40 mg placed in the device). In each session a 10 mg dose of deuterium-labelled methamphetamine was infused intravenously over 15 minutes at the same time as the unlabelled dose, so that absolute bioavailability of the unlabelled route could be computed from the labelled intravenous clearance. Plasma was sampled to 72 hours and urine collected to 72 hours; concentrations of methamphetamine and amphetamine, labelled and unlabelled, were measured by gas chromatography–mass spectrometry and analysed by non-compartmental methods. No placebo condition.
can_establish: Absolute bioavailability, peak concentration, time to peak, terminal half-life, clearance, volume of distribution and renal handling of methamphetamine and its metabolite amphetamine after intranasal and smoked dosing in 8 men, each serving as his own intravenous reference within the same session.
cannot_establish: The subjective or cardiovascular profile of either route on its own (every session also contained an intravenous dose, and the delivered doses differed between routes, as the authors state); anything about repeated dosing, women, or people who use methamphetamine more heavily; and any clinical outcome, since none was measured.

sample.recruitment: Newspaper advertisement or referral from previous participants, at a university general clinical research centre in San Francisco (pp. 476–477).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Men and women aged 21 to 45 within 30% of ideal body weight, not dependent on methamphetamine by DSM-IV criteria, with methamphetamine experience at least once in the previous 6 months and experience of the intranasal, smoked or intravenous route; nobody used methamphetamine only by mouth. Medical history, examination, blood count, chemistry, hepatitis C serology and electrocardiogram excluded significant physical and psychiatric illness (pp. 476–477).
sample.demographics: 8 men completed; mean age 40 years (range 31–45). Self-reported ethnicity: 1 Black, 1 Hispanic, 4 non-Hispanic white, 2 mixed. Reported methamphetamine use ranged from 3 times a week to 3 times a year; 7 of the 8 had used all three routes and one had no intravenous experience. All smoked tobacco and used caffeine, and other illicit drug use was infrequent (pp. 477, 478–479).
sample.attrition: Eight completed; no dropouts are reported. The authors note that women were eligible but few enquired and none entered (p. 476).
sample.selection_effects: Men only, recruited by advertisement, not dependent and using relatively infrequently: a healthier and lighter-using sample than people who seek treatment, which matters for clearance, tolerance and the subjective ratings. The mean age of 40 is high for a methamphetamine laboratory sample.

exposure.measurement: Drug administered and measured in the laboratory: plasma and urine methamphetamine and amphetamine, deuterated and non-deuterated, by gas chromatography–mass spectrometry, with documented within-day and between-day precision and accuracy in plasma (down to 1 ng/mL for methamphetamine and 0.5 ng/mL for amphetamine) and in urine; the stated limits of quantification of 10 ng/mL (methamphetamine) and 1 ng/mL (amphetamine) are urine limits, and no plasma limit is stated (pp. 477–478). Participants' own use was self-reported. Urine toxicology and a report of recent use were taken on admission (p. 476).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: intranasal dextromethamphetamine 50 mg (base equivalent) as a solution of the hydrochloride salt; smoked dextromethamphetamine 40 mg (base equivalent) placed in the device, of which a mean of 22.2 mg (SD 8.4, range 11.3–36.4) was estimated to have left it; and, in both sessions, 10 mg of deuterium-labelled methamphetamine infused intravenously over 15 minutes. Participants abstained from drugs and alcohol other than nicotine and caffeine for 48 hours before admission and were inpatients for 48 hours after dosing (pp. 476–477, 479).
exposure.polysubstance: All participants smoked tobacco and used caffeine, both continued; other illicit drug use was described as infrequent and was not quantified; an admission urine screen and a report of recent use were required before dosing (pp. 476, 477).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: 48 hours' abstinence from drugs and alcohol (except nicotine and caffeine) before admission, with an admission urine screen; sessions about a week apart, which the authors judged sufficient because more than 90% of the drug is eliminated within 48 hours (pp. 476, 477).

comparison.controls: Each participant's own simultaneous intravenous deuterated dose is the reference for bioavailability, and the two routes are compared within person. There is no placebo condition and no non-using comparison group.
comparison.matching: Within-person design; the order of the two route conditions was balanced across participants (p. 476).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to the pharmacokinetic questions. For the physiological and subjective measures there is no drug-free session, so pre-dose values within the session are the only baseline.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable (no separate control group); tobacco and caffeine use continued in all participants.

outcomes.instruments: Non-compartmental pharmacokinetics (WinNonlin 3.0): Cmax, tmax, AUC to the last measurable concentration and to infinity, terminal rate constant and half-life, clearance, terminal and steady-state volume of distribution, mean residence time, renal clearance from 0–24-hour urine, and absolute bioavailability computed as intravenous clearance × extravascular AUC / extravascular dose. Cardiovascular monitor for heart rate and blood pressure, rate-pressure product, respiratory rate by counting; verbal 0–100 ratings of intoxication and craving and 100-mm visual analogue scales for good drug effect, bad drug effect, desire for methamphetamine and drug quality (pp. 477–478).
outcomes.validity_norms: The assay is validated in-house with stated precision and accuracy; the subjective scales are standard laboratory visual analogue scales with no norms.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Bioavailability' is the fraction of the administered (or, for the smoked condition, the estimated delivered) dose reaching plasma, computed against the simultaneous intravenous dose. Nothing is operationalized as harm or impairment.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Three pharmacokinetic comparisons are tested (bioavailability between routes on the nominal doses and on the estimated delivered doses; tmax between routes, after excluding one outlier) and about fourteen physiological and subjective measures were analysed by repeated-measures ANOVA with Huynh-Feldt correction for sphericity only; significance was set at P = .05 (p. 478).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: None: the study was open, participants and staff knew which route was being given, and the subjective ratings are self-reports in that open condition.

analysis.effect_sizes: Means (SD) are reported without confidence intervals. Absolute bioavailability: intranasal 79.4% (SD 13.1); smoked 37.4% (SD 14.2) of the 40 mg placed in the device, and about 67% of the estimated delivered dose (p. 481; p. 479). Peak plasma methamphetamine: intranasal 113 ng/mL (SD 23.1) at 2.66 h (SD 1.16); smoked 50.9 (SD 24.7) at 2.47 h (SD 3.91); AUC to infinity 2000 (SD 599) and 801 (SD 526) ng·h/mL (Table II, p. 480). Terminal half-life: intranasal 10.7 h (SD 2.39), smoked 10.7 h (SD 2.11), intravenous 11.8 h (SD 3.59) in the intranasal session and 11.0 h (SD 2.68) in the smoked session (Tables I–II, p. 481). Intravenous clearance 272 (SD 73.3) and 271 (SD 70.8) mL·h⁻¹·kg⁻¹; steady-state volume of distribution 4.30 (SD 0.930) and 4.02 (SD 0.607) L/kg; mean residence time 16.6 (SD 4.34) and 15.5 (SD 3.55) h (Table I, p. 481). Amphetamine half-life 15.2–16.9 h; amphetamine AUC 15.5–19.3% of methamphetamine AUC (Tables III–IV, p. 481). Only two P values are printed for the pharmacokinetic comparisons (P<.02 and P<.1 for bioavailability on the two dose definitions; P<.03 for tmax with one outlier excluded) (pp. 479–480).
analysis.covariates: None; within-person comparisons of means. Urine pH, which the authors note strongly affects renal clearance, was not controlled and was measured only infrequently (pp. 483–485).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol, registration or pre-specified primary outcome is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: The physiological and subjective data are reported mainly as a null comparison between routes, with figures rather than tables for the time courses; individual bioavailability values are not shown, only the range of the amount recovered from the device. The 67% figure (smoked bioavailability on the delivered dose) appears in the text and abstract but in no table.
analysis.power: Not reported; no sample-size calculation. With 8 participants the standard deviations are large relative to the means for the smoked condition (for example AUC 801 ± 526 ng·h/mL), so the route comparison is imprecise.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Methamphetamine is well absorbed by both non-injection routes studied: about four-fifths of an intranasal dose and between a third (of the amount placed in the device) and two-thirds (of the amount estimated to have left it) of a smoked dose reached the circulation; peak plasma concentrations came at about 2.5–2.7 hours by both routes, and the terminal half-life was about 11 hours by all three routes, with amphetamine appearing later and with a longer half-life.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and discussion conclude that exposure after intranasal or smoked use, and the possibility of drug-related complications, remain substantial, and that the findings may help risk assessment and treatment planning. This is supported for systemic exposure but not for complications, which were not measured. The abstract also reports single values (intravenous half-life 11.4 hours, clearance 272 mL·h⁻¹·kg⁻¹, volume of distribution 4.2 L/kg, mean residence time 16 hours, amphetamine half-life 16.2 hours) that are averages or one of the two tabulated condition values, so a reader cannot match them to the tables. The time-to-peak values in the abstract (2.7 and 2.5 hours) conceal a standard deviation of 3.91 hours in the smoked condition and the exclusion of one outlier from the only test of that difference. The authors are explicit that the physiological and subjective comparisons between routes are confounded by the simultaneous intravenous dose and by unequal delivered doses, and say the intravenous tracer dose should have been smaller (pp. 480, 482, 485).

timeline.event: Smoked and intravenous pharmacokinetics in 6 men: bioavailability 90.3% of the amount that left the device, geometric mean half-life 11.1 h (smoked) and 12.2 h (intravenous)
Oral sustained-release dosing in 8 volunteers: plasma half-life 9.3–11.1 h, time to peak 5.4–7.5 h, amphetamine AUC about 21% of methamphetamine

Intravenous enantiomer study in 12 men from the same San Francisco laboratory: d-methamphetamine half-life 10.2–10.7 h, l-methamphetamine 13.3–15.0 h (shared investigators, not an independent replication)
Intranasal laboratory study with plasma sampling (Hart et al., 2008): plasma concentrations still rising at the 4-hour sample, consistent with the late peak found here

replication.where_it_stands: This is the first report of intranasal bioavailability and remains the main source for it. The half-life of about 10–12 hours is consistent across this study, Cook et al. (1993) and the oral study of Schepers et al. (2003). Smoked bioavailability differs between this study (37% of the amount placed in the device, 67% of the amount estimated delivered) and Cook et al. (90% of the amount that left the device), a difference the authors attribute to device temperature and technique; the two figures are not measuring the same denominator.

funding.funder: US Public Health Service grants DA12393 and DA00053 and contract N01DA-4-8306 from the National Institute on Drug Abuse, National Institutes of Health; carried out in part in the General Clinical Research Center at the University of California, San Francisco, with support from NIH grant 5 M01 RR-00079 (p. 475).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors state that they have no financial or personal relationships that could be perceived as influencing the research (p. 485).
funding.affiliations_note: University laboratory (Drug Dependence Research Center, Langley Porter Psychiatric Institute, UCSF); no industry sponsor.

what_would_settle_it: A randomized, placebo-controlled crossover with each route given alone (no concurrent intravenous tracer), equal delivered doses verified by recovery, both sexes, dense early sampling to capture the rise, and urine pH measured throughout; and, for the smoked route, a standardized delivery device so that bioavailability is reported against a defined delivered dose.

domains.domain: Randomization process (order of the two route conditions)
domains.note: The order is described only as a balanced crossover; no randomization method, sequence generation or allocation concealment is described, and no period effect is modelled.

Open administration with no placebo; each session also contained an intravenous dose that made up roughly a fifth to two-fifths of the total, and the delivered doses differed between routes, so the two conditions are not comparable for any pharmacodynamic outcome. The authors state this (pp. 480, 485).

All 8 completed both sessions, but plasma values below the limit of quantification were treated as missing and dropped from the analysis, and one participant's tmax was excluded as an outlier from the only test of the route difference.
Assays and cardiovascular monitoring are objective and validated (low on their own); the self-rated subjective measures were collected in an unblinded, placebo-free design (some concerns).

No protocol or pre-specified outcome; the headline smoked bioavailability of 67% rests on an estimated delivered dose that varied between 11.3 and 36.4 mg across participants and appears in no table; summary values in the abstract do not match either tabulated condition.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: For the pharmacokinetic parameters the design is strong: each participant is his own intravenous reference within the same session, which removes day-to-day variability, and the assay is validated. The overall judgment is set by the unblinded, placebo-free administration with a concurrent intravenous dose, which the authors themselves identify as making the between-route comparison of physiological and subjective effects uninterpretable. The source can be cited for bioavailability, half-life, clearance, volume of distribution, time to peak and the amphetamine-to-methamphetamine ratio by route in 8 men who used methamphetamine infrequently; it cannot be cited for the relative subjective or cardiovascular effects of the two routes, nor for any statement about complications.

key_findings.finding: Absolute bioavailability of intranasal methamphetamine (50 mg condition) was 79.4% (SD 13.1), computed against each participant's simultaneous intravenous dose.
key_findings.locator: Table II, continuation columns (F), row 'Intranasal 50 mg'

key_findings.finding: Absolute bioavailability of the smoked condition was 37.4% (SD 14.2) of the 40 mg placed in the device, and about 67% of the mean 22.2 mg (SD 8.4) estimated to have left it; the route difference was significant on the nominal doses (P<.02) but not on the estimated delivered doses (P<.1).
key_findings.locator: Results › Pharmacokinetic measures, 2nd paragraph (p. 479); Table II, continuation columns (F) (p. 481)
key_findings.note: The amount estimated to have left the device ranged from 11.3 to 36.4 mg (28%–91%) across the 8 participants, so the 67% figure rests on a mean that is itself highly variable.

key_findings.finding: Terminal half-life was essentially the same by all three routes: 10.7 h (SD 2.39) intranasal, 10.7 h (SD 2.11) smoked, and 11.8 h (SD 3.59) and 11.0 h (SD 2.68) for the two intravenous reference doses.
key_findings.locator: Tables I and II, continuation columns (t1/2)

key_findings.finding: Peak plasma methamphetamine was 113 ng/mL (SD 23.1) at 2.66 h (SD 1.16) after the intranasal condition and 50.9 ng/mL (SD 24.7) at 2.47 h (SD 3.91) after the smoked condition; AUC to infinity was 2000 (SD 599) and 801 (SD 526) ng·h/mL.

From the intravenous reference doses, clearance was 272 (SD 73.3) and 271 (SD 70.8) mL·h⁻¹·kg⁻¹, steady-state volume of distribution 4.30 (SD 0.930) and 4.02 (SD 0.607) L/kg, and mean residence time 16.6 (SD 4.34) and 15.5 (SD 3.55) h.
key_findings.locator: Table I, continuation columns (CL, Vss, MRT)

key_findings.finding: Amphetamine appeared late and persisted longer than the parent drug: peak 9.12 ng/mL (SD 2.39) at 17.3 h (SD 5.95) after the intranasal condition and 3.71 (SD 2.88) at 15.3 h (SD 5.12) after the smoked condition, with a half-life of 15.2–16.9 h and an AUC 15.5–19.3% of that of methamphetamine.
key_findings.locator: Tables III and IV, main and continuation columns

key_findings.finding: Renal clearance of methamphetamine (94.4–102 mL·h⁻¹·kg⁻¹) was about a tenth of that of amphetamine (957–1270), with a ratio of about 10 to 13; 34–39% of the dose appeared in urine as unchanged drug over 24 hours, and the Results note that the fraction excreted varied from about 10% to 90% between people.
key_findings.locator: Results › Pharmacokinetic measures, 1st paragraph (p. 479); Tables V and VI (p. 482)
key_findings.note: Urine pH was not controlled and was measured only infrequently, and the authors attribute much of this variability to it (pp. 483–485).

key_findings.finding: Under stated assumptions (complete hepatic metabolism, hepatic blood flow 25 mL·min⁻¹·kg⁻¹, linear kinetics), the hepatic extraction ratio was estimated at about 19%, consistent with a low-extraction drug.

In the intranasal condition, systolic pressure rose from 121 (SD 10) to a peak of 141 (SD 13) mm Hg, diastolic from 76 (SD 7) to 86 (SD 7) mm Hg and heart rate from 73 (SD 9) to 94 (SD 13) beats/min; in the smoked condition, systolic from 121 (SD 10) to 137 (SD 11), diastolic from 73 (SD 10) to 83 (SD 8) and heart rate from 76 (SD 10) to 106 (SD 19).
key_findings.locator: Results › Pharmacodynamic measures, last paragraph (p. 480) continuing on p. 481
key_findings.note: Both conditions also contained the 10 mg intravenous dose, so these changes cannot be attributed to the named route alone.

key_findings.finding: No significant differences in physiological or subjective effects were found between the two conditions; the authors attribute this to the shared intravenous dose and the unequal delivered doses, estimating the absorbed intranasal dose at about 40 mg and the absorbed smoked dose at about 15 mg.

In a preliminary comparison in 4 men (mean age 34, SD 9), who were given one 15-minute intravenous infusion of 10 mg of a 50/50 mixture of deuterium-labelled and unlabelled methamphetamine (5 mg of each), plasma concentrations over time did not differ significantly between the two forms; the bioavailability calculation rests on this assumption.
key_findings.locator: Results › Comparison of deuterated versus nondeuterated methamphetamine plasma levels (p. 478); Figure 1 (p. 479)

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract gives a single intravenous elimination half-life of 11.4 hours, which appears nowhere in the tables; Table I gives 11.8 (SD 3.59) and 11.0 (SD 2.68) hours for the two intravenous reference doses, whose average is 11.4.
reporting_issues.consequence: A reader quoting the abstract cites a number with no printed variability and no corresponding row; the same applies to the abstract's clearance (272, the intranasal-session value), steady-state volume of distribution (4.2 L/kg, the average of 4.30 and 4.02) and mean residence time (16 hours).

reporting_issues.issue: Table I reports a time to peak of 3.55 h (SD 8.27) for a 15-minute intravenous infusion in the intranasal session, against 1.00 h (SD 0.641) for the same infusion in the smoked session. A standard deviation more than twice the mean, for a route whose peak must occur at the end of the infusion, indicates one or more aberrant values.
reporting_issues.consequence: Intravenous tmax as printed cannot be used; it also casts doubt on the tmax comparison between the extravascular routes, which is reported as significant only after one outlier was excluded (P<.03).

reporting_issues.issue: All tables give the terminal rate constant λz in units of L/h; a first-order rate constant has units of h⁻¹ (the printed values, about 0.06, are consistent with h⁻¹).
reporting_issues.consequence: A units error in the table headers only; the values themselves are internally consistent with the printed half-lives (0.693/0.0672 = 10.3 h, editors' calculation).

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract gives a single amphetamine half-life of 16.2 hours for all routes, while Tables III and IV give 16.2, 16.9, 15.2 and 16.3 hours for the four conditions; and the abstract's renal clearances of 'about 100 and 1100 mL·h⁻¹·kg⁻¹' are rounded from 94.4–102 and 957–1270.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor, but the abstract's single values should not be quoted as measured parameters.

reporting_issues.issue: Table I prints the steady-state volume of distribution for the first row as '4.30 ± 0.930)', with an unmatched closing parenthesis.
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical only.

reporting_issues.issue: Smoked bioavailability is reported against two different denominators (the 40 mg placed in the device, giving 37.4%, and the mean 22.2 mg estimated to have left it, giving about 67%), and the comparison with the 90% reported by Cook et al. (1993) is made against the second denominator.
reporting_issues.consequence: Quoting a single 'smoked bioavailability' for methamphetamine without the denominator is meaningless; the encyclopedia must carry the denominator with the number.

reporting_issues.issue: Table VI (p. 482) prints the intravenous clearance for the intranasal session as 284 (SD 59.0) mL·h⁻¹·kg⁻¹, whereas Table I (p. 481) gives 272 (SD 73.3) for the same 10 mg infusion; the value for the smoked session (271, SD 70.8) is the same in both tables.
reporting_issues.consequence: Table VI applies the intravenous clearance to its nasal and smoked rows (asterisked), so the percent-of-dose-excreted value for the nasal route depends on which of the two clearances is correct; the discrepancy is not explained.

verification.source_read: PDF pp. 475–486 (PDFs/Methamphetamine/Harris_2003_BioavailabilityIntranasalSmoked..pdf)
verification.checked_by: AI readers 10 and 11 (card check against the PDF) and the AI adjudicator

disagreements.first_pass: with limits of quantification of 10 ng/mL (methamphetamine) and 1 ng/mL (amphetamine) in plasma and documented within-day and between-day precision
disagreements.reviewer: Reader 11 (missed): the card places the limits of quantification (10 ng/mL methamphetamine, 1 ng/mL amphetamine) in plasma, but both sentences stand at the end of the urine assay paragraph (p. 478), and the plasma precision data run down to 1 ng/mL for methamphetamine, so a plasma limit of 10 ng/mL is not established by the paper.
disagreements.resolution: Confirmed on pp. 477-478: the plasma precision and accuracy data (methamphetamine from 1 ng/mL, amphetamine from 0.5 ng/mL) come first, and the limit-of-quantitation sentences (10 and 1 ng/mL) close the urine paragraph. Card text corrected to say so.

disagreements.first_pass: (not on the first-pass card)
disagreements.reviewer: Reader 11 (missed): Table VI (p. 482) prints the intravenous clearance for the intranasal session as 284 (SD 59.0) mL/h/kg, while Table I (p. 481) gives 272 (SD 73.3) for the same 10 mg infusion; the asterisked rows of Table VI apply that intravenous clearance to the nasal and smoked rows.
disagreements.resolution: Confirmed on the rendered tables (Table I, p. 481: 272 and 271; Table VI, p. 482: 284 and 271, with the intravenous-CL footnote). Added as a reporting issue; key finding 4 quotes Table I and is unchanged.

disagreements.first_pass: In a preliminary comparison in 4 men (mean age 34, SD 9), plasma curves after 5 mg of deuterium-labelled and 5 mg of unlabelled methamphetamine given intravenously did not differ, which is the assumption the bioavailability calculation rests on.
disagreements.reviewer: Reader 11 (note on a confirmed finding): accurate as the paper words it (Fig 1 caption and Introduction), but the 4 men in fact received one 15-minute infusion of 10 mg of a 50/50 labelled-unlabelled mixture, that is 5 mg of each, not two separate doses.
disagreements.resolution: Confirmed on p. 478 (Results, Comparison of deuterated versus nondeuterated methamphetamine plasma levels: 10 mg of a 50/50 mixture given intravenously for 15 minutes by infusion pump; no significant difference over time, Figure 1 on p. 479). The finding now says it was one infusion of a mixture and uses the paper's no significant difference instead of did not differ; the numbers are unchanged.

design_detail: Twenty-day residential laboratory study of oral methamphetamine self-administration in 8 volunteers, double-blind. On days 1, 5, 9, 13 and 17 participants received a sample capsule (0, 5 or 10 mg methamphetamine) and a sampled alternative of a $1 voucher; at the remaining dosing times that day and on the next two days they chose, on each of eight occasions, between the sampled capsule and the voucher. Active methamphetamine was available on days 5–7 and 13–15 and placebo on all other dosing days, with the order of the 5 mg and 10 mg conditions counterbalanced; days 1–3 were an acclimation period excluded from analysis. Outcomes were the number of drug choices, visual-analogue subjective ratings after the sample dose, psychomotor performance and continuously monitored food intake.
can_establish: That, under these conditions, adults with stimulant experience chose an oral methamphetamine capsule more often than placebo when a $1 voucher was the alternative, and that the sampled 10 mg dose produced larger positive subjective ratings than placebo while both active doses reduced measured daily food intake.
cannot_establish: A dose–response relation for self-administration (the two active doses did not differ); the role of the alternative's value (only $1 was used); the relation between subjective effects and drug taking in any quantitative way, because ratings were analysed only after the sample dose while choices were counted over three days; and anything about smoked, intranasal or injected use, about dependence, or about use outside a residential laboratory.

sample.recruitment: Word-of-mouth referral and newspaper advertisement in New York City; participants lived in a residential laboratory at the New York State Psychiatric Institute in groups of two or three (p. 76).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Healthy volunteers who passed medical and psychological evaluations and were within normal weight ranges; all reported previous stimulant use. The woman volunteer had a serum pregnancy test at screening and random urine pregnancy tests during the study (p. 76). No diagnostic criteria for stimulant use disorder are reported as inclusion criteria, and dependence status is not stated.
sample.demographics: 8 completers: 1 woman (Hispanic-American) and 7 men (3 Black-American, 3 White-American, 1 Hispanic-American), aged 23–42 years (mean 31.1), mean weight 71.5 kg (SD 13) (p. 76).
sample.attrition: Three other men began and did not complete: two for personal reasons unrelated to the protocol and one because he reported difficulty sleeping during the 10 mg phase (p. 76). The abstract and conclusions describe only the 8 completers.
sample.selection_effects: Volunteers recruited by advertisement and word of mouth who were willing to live in a laboratory for 20 days, mostly with cocaine rather than methamphetamine experience: only 3 of the 8 reported ever using methamphetamine before the study, and all received a 10 mg dose during pre-study training. Losing one participant because of a drug-related effect at the higher dose removes a person whose choices might have differed.

exposure.measurement: Drug administered in the laboratory: repackaged 5 mg methamphetamine hydrochloride tablets (a commercial product) in opaque capsules with lactose filler, or lactose alone for placebo, under double-blind conditions with capsule colour changing between conditions. Participants' own drug use was self-reported at screening; food intake was reported by bar-code scanner, acknowledged by staff, recorded by hand and validated against the daily trash (pp. 77).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: oral capsules containing 0, 5 or 10 mg of methamphetamine hydrochloride, available at 1000, 1400 and 1800 hours on three consecutive days per condition, with a maximum of eight choice occasions per condition; a 10 mg dose was also given once before the study for familiarization. The authors state the doses were chosen because they had produced dose-dependent subjective effects in an earlier study from the same laboratory (p. 77).
exposure.polysubstance: Self-reported at screening: 7 of 8 had used cocaine at least once and 3 had used methamphetamine at least once; 1 reported current cocaine use 4 times a week, 1 current cannabis use 4 times a week, 7 current alcohol use (1–15 drinks a week), 5 current tobacco use (7–20 cigarettes a day) and all 8 current caffeine use (2–30 cups a week). During the study tobacco was available under supervision except overnight; alcohol and other drugs were excluded by residence (p. 76).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Residential throughout the 20 days, so abstinence from non-study drugs other than tobacco and caffeine follows from the setting; no urine screening is reported. Each 3-day dose condition was separated by a day without any dose (p. 77).

comparison.controls: Placebo capsules in the same participants, in the 3-day condition that followed each active condition; the monetary alternative ($1 voucher) is the comparator within each choice.
comparison.matching: Within-person. The order of the two active doses was counterbalanced, but placebo conditions always occupied the same positions relative to the active ones (days 9–11 and 17–19), so the placebo comparison is not order-balanced.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable: each participant serves as his or her own control.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable (no separate control group).

outcomes.instruments: Number of capsule choices over the eight choice occasions per condition; a 50-item visual analogue scale (0–100 mm) of mood and drug-effect items; a visual-analogue sleep questionnaire; a drug-effect questionnaire rating good effects, bad effects, drug strength and desire to take the drug again on 5-point scales and liking on a 9-point scale; a psychomotor battery (digit-symbol substitution, repeated acquisition, divided attention, rapid information processing, immediate and delayed digit recall); and continuous food-intake recording with calculation of total calories, macronutrient grams, number of eating occasions and intake per occasion (pp. 76–77).
outcomes.validity_norms: Standard laboratory instruments with no external norms; food intake is measured rather than self-estimated, which is a strength.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Reinforcing effect' is operationalized as choosing the capsule over a $1 voucher more often than in the matched placebo condition; nothing is operationalized as harm.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Four planned pairwise comparisons were made for each outcome family, but the subjective battery alone has 50 items, of which 23 are tabulated for the 10 mg condition and 4 for the 5 mg condition, plus food-intake measures and six psychomotor tasks. The significance threshold was set at P<0.03 without justification (p. 77).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Double-blind administration; the outcomes are participant-generated (choices, ratings, food reports) and machine-recorded, so assessor blinding is less relevant, but blinding integrity was not tested.

analysis.effect_sizes: No effect sizes or confidence intervals are reported; F values appear in Tables 1 and 2 without degrees of freedom, and other results are given as means with P values. Mean number of drug choices out of eight: 4.3 (5 mg) against 1.4 in its placebo condition (P<0.02) and 4.4 (10 mg) against 1.3 (P<0.01), with no difference between the two active conditions or between the two placebo conditions. Peak subjective ratings after the 10 mg sample against its placebo (mean, SEM): good drug effect 36.42 (4.43) against 13.46 (0.96); high 26.30 (4.00) against 10.38 (1.34); stimulated 28.50 (6.38) against 4.38 (1.45); alert 59.50 (6.47) against 30.20 (5.52); hungry 11.46 (3.94) against 26.50 (7.18); sedated 3.54 (1.74) against 17.54 (2.24). After the 5 mg sample only four items differed: alert 59.40 (4.08) against 44.17 (2.58), energetic 34.25 (1.40) against 21.46 (3.03), talkative 46.46 (1.67) against 37.46 (2.99) and headache 5.13 (2.19) against 0.67 (0.15). Food intake fell by about 43% (5 mg) and about 37% (10 mg) relative to the matched placebo conditions (P<0.01), which the discussion converts to about 1415 kcal on average (Tables 1–2 and text, pp. 78–80).
analysis.covariates: None; repeated-measures ANOVA with planned comparisons, on data from the sample day for subjective and food-intake outcomes and across three days for choices.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: Tables 1 and 2 list only the subjective items that reached significance, so the remaining items of the 50-item scale (including bad drug effect, anxious, irritable and paranoid-type items) cannot be evaluated; psychomotor results are dismissed in one sentence as showing no consistent effects and are not tabulated; food-intake values appear only in a figure.
analysis.power: Not reported; no sample-size calculation. With 8 participants and no confidence intervals, the absence of a dose difference in choice cannot be read as evidence of equivalence; the authors themselves offer two post-hoc explanations for it.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 8 residential volunteers, an oral methamphetamine capsule was chosen about 4.3–4.4 times out of 8 when active drug was available against 1.3–1.4 times in the matched placebo conditions; the 10 mg sample raised a range of positive subjective ratings and lowered hunger and sedation ratings, while the 5 mg sample moved only four items; both active doses cut measured daily food intake by roughly 37–43%; and self-administration did not increase from 5 mg to 10 mg.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that oral methamphetamine is a positive reinforcer in humans, and the discussion that the data are the first to show this under controlled conditions. In this sample and against a $1 alternative that is supported. Three qualifications the abstract does not carry: only 3 of the 8 participants reported ever having used methamphetamine before the study, so the sample is best described as stimulant-experienced rather than methamphetamine-experienced; the alternative reinforcer was a single $1 voucher per choice, and the authors' own argument that it was competitive rests on vouchers being chosen about 80% of the time under placebo; and the dissociation claimed between subjective and reinforcing effects compares ratings taken after one sample dose with choices counted over three days, which the authors acknowledge makes the relationship impossible to quantify.

timeline.event: Repeated oral methamphetamine administration in the same laboratory (Comer et al., 2001), the source of the dose selection and of comparable food-intake reductions of about 1150 and 1450 kcal; shares investigators and setting
Intranasal methamphetamine in the same research group: dose-related increases in positive subjective ratings and reduced hunger ratings, without a self-administration procedure

Intranasal self-administration against monetary alternatives of $5 and $20 in 13 men from the same group: drug chosen on 41% of occasions against $5 and 17% against $20, showing that the alternative's value matters

replication.where_it_stands: That methamphetamine functions as a reinforcer in human laboratory choice procedures is now supported by this study and by later work from the same laboratory using a different route and larger monetary alternatives; because the studies share investigators and setting they are not independent replications. The absence of a dose difference between 5 and 10 mg has not been resolved: the later intranasal work found drug choice to depend more on the size of the alternative than on the dose.

funding.funder: Grant DA-03746, printed without the agency name (p. 80); the National Institute on Drug Abuse is the editors' inference from the DA- grant prefix.
funding.declared_conflicts: Not reported: the article carries no conflict-of-interest statement.
funding.affiliations_note: Academic laboratory (New York State Psychiatric Institute and Columbia University). The study medication was a commercial methamphetamine product, repackaged by the institute pharmacy; no industry sponsorship is declared.

what_would_settle_it: A choice procedure with several monetary alternatives crossed with a wider dose range in the same participants, with subjective ratings taken at every choice rather than only after the sample dose, enough participants to estimate dose effects with intervals, and recruitment of people who actually use methamphetamine rather than stimulant-experienced volunteers in general.

domains.note: The order of the 5 mg and 10 mg conditions was counterbalanced across participants rather than randomized, and the placebo conditions always followed their matched active condition, so placebo is confounded with position in the study.

A drug-free day separated the 3-day conditions and days 1–3 were discarded as acclimation, but residual effects were found the morning after the 10 mg sample (more trouble sleeping and jitteriness), and the first three days of each condition contribute choices that may carry over.
Double-blind with matched capsules, but every participant had taken a 10 mg dose openly before the study and capsule colour changed with each condition; blinding integrity was not assessed.
Three of eleven who began did not complete, one of them because of difficulty sleeping during the 10 mg phase, which is a drug-related reason; only completers are analysed.
Choices and food intake are behavioural and machine-recorded, with the food records validated against the trash; subjective ratings are self-reports but that is the measure of interest.

Only the significant items of a 50-item scale are tabulated; psychomotor results are reported in one sentence without data; food-intake values appear only in a figure; F values are printed without degrees of freedom; the significance threshold is an unexplained P<0.03 and no protocol exists.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The core comparison (capsule chosen more often when it contained methamphetamine than when it did not) is behavioural, within person and double-blind, and is unlikely to be explained by these concerns. The overall rating is set by the reporting: a 50-item battery tabulated only where significant, undocumented degrees of freedom, a non-standard significance threshold and no protocol. The source can be cited for the demonstration that an oral methamphetamine capsule functions as a reinforcer against a $1 alternative in stimulant-experienced volunteers, for the subjective-effect profile of the sampled 10 mg dose against its placebo, and for the measured reduction in daily food intake; it cannot be cited for a dose–response relation, for the magnitude of reinforcement at other alternative values, or for a quantitative link between subjective effects and drug taking.

key_findings.finding: Capsule choice rose when the capsule contained methamphetamine: a mean of 4.3 of 8 choices in the 5 mg condition against 1.4 in its placebo condition (P<0.02) and 4.4 against 1.3 in the 10 mg condition (P<0.01), with no difference between the two active conditions or between the two placebo conditions.
key_findings.locator: Results › Reinforcing effects (p. 77, right column, continuing on p. 78); Figure 1 (p. 78)

key_findings.finding: Individual choices varied widely: in the 5 mg condition five participants chose the drug at least four times (range 4–8) and three chose it 0–2 times; in the 10 mg condition three chose it seven or eight times, three chose it four times and two chose it never.

The sampled 10 mg dose raised ratings of good drug effect (36.42, SEM 4.43, against 13.46, SEM 0.96), high (26.30 against 10.38), stimulated (28.50 against 4.38), alert (59.50 against 30.20), self-confident, social and talkative, and lowered ratings of hungry (11.46 against 26.50), sedated (3.54 against 17.54), sleepy, tired and depressed, all at P<0.03.

The sampled 5 mg dose changed only four of the fifty rated items against its placebo: alert (59.40 against 44.17), energetic (34.25 against 21.46), talkative (46.46 against 37.46) and headache (5.13 against 0.67).
No significant effects were found on the drug-effect questionnaire, including the items for drug strength and desire to take the drug again, in any condition.
key_findings.locator: Results › Subjective effects, last sentence of the 1st paragraph (the paragraph runs from p. 78 to p. 79); Discussion, on the desire-to-take-again and drug-strength items (p. 80)

key_findings.finding: The morning after the 10 mg sample day, participants reported more trouble sleeping and more jitteriness than after the matched placebo and after the 5 mg sample day (P<0.01); no other next-day differences were found.

Both active doses reduced measured total daily caloric intake relative to their placebo conditions, by about 43% (5 mg) and about 37% (10 mg) (P<0.01), with no significant difference between the two doses; intake of fat, carbohydrate and protein fell in parallel, so no macronutrient was selectively affected.
key_findings.note: The absolute intakes appear only in Figure 4; the Discussion states an average reduction of about 1415 kcal (p. 80).

key_findings.finding: The two doses reduced intake by different routes: at 5 mg through fewer eating occasions and longer intervals between them (both P<0.01), at 10 mg through a smaller mean intake per eating occasion (P<0.01).
key_findings.locator: Results › Food intake, last sentences (data reported as not shown)

key_findings.finding: Methamphetamine produced no consistent effects on the psychomotor battery, and those data are not reported.
key_findings.locator: Materials and methods › Data analysis (p. 77); Discussion, paragraph beginning 'Finally, methamphetamine produced little effect' (p. 80)

key_findings.finding: Vouchers were chosen on about half of the occasions when active methamphetamine was available and on about 80% of occasions under placebo, which the authors offer as evidence that the $1 alternative was a working reinforcer.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, paragraph beginning 'There are at least two possible explanations'

key_findings.finding: Only 3 of the 8 participants reported ever having used methamphetamine before the study, while 7 reported having used cocaine at least once; all received a single 10 mg methamphetamine dose during pre-study training.
key_findings.locator: Materials and methods › Participants (p. 76); Materials and methods › Procedure, 1st paragraph (p. 77)

reporting_issues.issue: The F values in Tables 1 and 2 are printed without degrees of freedom, and no degrees of freedom appear anywhere for the repeated-measures analyses; with 8 participants a planned pairwise within-person comparison would have 1 and 7 degrees of freedom.
reporting_issues.consequence: No test statistic in the paper can be checked against its sample size, and the P values cannot be recomputed.

reporting_issues.issue: The two active doses reduced caloric intake by about 43% (5 mg) and about 37% (10 mg), that is, the lower dose produced the larger reduction, while the Discussion gives a single average reduction of about 1415 kcal; the absolute intakes are only in Figure 4.
reporting_issues.consequence: The percentages and the kcal figure cannot be reconciled from the printed text, and the ordering of the two doses runs against the dose-ordering of the subjective effects; the figure would have to be digitized to check either.

reporting_issues.issue: The significance threshold is set at P<0.03 with no justification, and individual results are reported at P<0.01, P<0.02 and P<0.03.
reporting_issues.consequence: A non-standard, unexplained threshold applied across a 50-item rating battery and several behavioural outcomes, with no correction for multiplicity.

reporting_issues.issue: Three of the eleven people who began did not complete, one of them because of difficulty sleeping during the 10 mg phase, but the abstract and conclusions describe only the eight completers.
reporting_issues.consequence: A drug-related dropout is omitted from the paper's summary; the tolerability of the higher dose is better than it looks from the abstract.

reporting_issues.issue: Some standard errors in Table 1 are implausibly small for an 8-person sample on a 0–100 visual analogue scale, for example 'content' 30.80 with a standard error of 0.07 and 'withdrawn' 11.04 with 0.33 under placebo.
reporting_issues.consequence: Either those placebo values were almost identical across all participants or the dispersion is mistyped; the corresponding F values (16.24 for 'content') cannot be checked without degrees of freedom.

reporting_issues.issue: Tables 1 and 2 list only the subjective items that reached significance, out of a 50-item scale that included bad drug effect, anxious, irritable and similar items.
reporting_issues.consequence: The absence of adverse subjective effects cannot be inferred from the tables, because unaffected and unreported items are indistinguishable.

reporting_issues.issue: The Data analysis section says that choice was also analysed by time of capsule administration (afternoon versus evening), with morning choices left out because the morning dose on the first day of each condition was a sample dose, but no result of this analysis is reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: Whether time of day affected choice cannot be known; an analysis that was run and not reported adds to the selective-reporting concern, alongside the psychomotor data (key finding 8).

design_detail: Six-session, double-blind, placebo-controlled, Latin-square balanced crossover in 12 men who used methamphetamine intravenously and were not dependent. Each received, about a week apart, single intravenous doses of d-methamphetamine 0.25 and 0.5 mg/kg, l-methamphetamine 0.25 and 0.5 mg/kg, racemic methamphetamine 0.5 mg/kg (0.25 mg/kg of each enantiomer) and saline placebo, each over 1 minute. Plasma was sampled to 48 hours and analysed with an enantioselective gas chromatography–mass spectrometry assay; cardiovascular, respiratory, temperature, subjective (verbal and visual analogue), mood-questionnaire and monetary-value measures were taken repeatedly over 48 hours.
can_establish: How the two methamphetamine enantiomers, given separately and as a 1:1 mixture, differ in plasma pharmacokinetics (AUC, peak, clearance, half-life, metabolite formation) and in acute cardiovascular and subjective effects, within the same people under double-blind, placebo-controlled conditions with a balanced order.
cannot_establish: What happens after repeated or sustained dosing, which is where the authors expect the enantiomers to differ most; effects by any other route (only intravenous was studied); effects in women (none were recruited) or in people who are dependent; and the health consequences of either isomer, since no outcome beyond acute physiology and ratings was measured.

sample.recruitment: Not described beyond the setting: a university drug-dependence research laboratory in San Francisco, with inpatient stays at a general clinical research centre (pp. 406–407).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Men aged 21–45 in good physical health by examination, laboratory tests and electrocardiogram, within 15% of ideal body weight, reporting intravenous methamphetamine use between once weekly and once or twice every 6 weeks, not dependent on methamphetamine, alcohol or other drugs by DSM-IV criteria and not seeking treatment. Excluded: significant medical or psychiatric illness, substance-use treatment in the last 12 months, current dependence on any drug except caffeine or nicotine, medications affecting the study or drug kinetics, and sensitivity to the study drugs. Hepatitis C and HIV status were not assessed (p. 406).
sample.demographics: 12 men; mean age 32.3 years (SD 7.4, range 23–43); mean weight 73.5 kg (SD 7.0, range 68.2–90.9); mean height 177.6 cm (SD 6.1, range 165–185); 9 white and 3 Black by self-report (p. 408). The paper states that although women were not excluded, none was recruited (p. 406).
sample.attrition: All 12 completed all six sessions; missing data accounted for less than 1% of values and were replaced by the group mean at that time point (pp. 407–408).
sample.selection_effects: Men only, not dependent, using intravenously as rarely as once every six weeks, healthy enough to pass a medical screen: a sample with some tolerance but far from the heaviest use, and the subjective ratings and monetary valuations come from people already experienced with this route.

exposure.measurement: Drug administered in the laboratory under double-blind conditions and measured directly: an enantioselective assay (chiral capillary column, trifluoroacetyl derivatives, deuterated internal standards) quantified d- and l-methamphetamine and d- and l-amphetamine in plasma, linear from 0.5 to 500 ng/mL with a limit of quantification of 1 ng/mL (pp. 406–407).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only, each given once intravenously over 1 minute: d-methamphetamine 0.25 and 0.5 mg/kg; l-methamphetamine 0.25 and 0.5 mg/kg; racemic methamphetamine 0.5 mg/kg; placebo (saline). Doses were prepared by the investigational pharmacist from stock solutions of material obtained commercially and recrystallized in the authors' laboratory, with purity, identity and sterility established under an investigational new drug application; each aliquot was diluted to the same volume to preserve the blind (pp. 406–407).
exposure.polysubstance: Current dependence on any drug other than caffeine or nicotine was an exclusion; participants were asked to abstain from drugs and alcohol except caffeine and nicotine for 48 hours before admission, and urine toxicology at admission delayed a session if recent use was evident (pp. 406–407). Tobacco and caffeine use are not quantified.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: 48 hours' self-reported abstinence before each admission, checked by urine toxicology; sessions about one week apart, with 48 hours of inpatient observation after each dose (pp. 406–407).

comparison.controls: Saline placebo in the same participants, one of the six sessions; the enantiomers are also compared with each other and with the racemate within person.
comparison.matching: Within-person crossover with a Latin-square balanced order across the six conditions.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable: every comparison is within person against the same participant's placebo session.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable (no separate control group).

outcomes.instruments: Non-compartmental pharmacokinetics (WinNonlin): AUC to the last measurable concentration and to infinity, peak concentration, terminal rate constant, half-life, systemic clearance and volume of distribution in the elimination phase; relative exposure as the ratio of d- to l-enantiomer AUC with 90% confidence intervals, judged against the 80–125% bioequivalence range. Pharmacodynamics: automated blood pressure and heart rate, rate-pressure product, manual respiratory rate, skin and tympanic temperature by thermocouple; verbal 0–100 intoxication rating; 0–100 visual analogue scales for any drug effect, good drug effect, drug liking, bad drug effect, intoxication and high; Profile of Mood States; Beck Depression Inventory; State-Trait Anxiety Inventory; Buss Aggression Scale; and a monetary value from $0 to $20 for the dose received (pp. 407–408).
outcomes.validity_norms: Standard laboratory scales and validated questionnaires; the monetary-value measure is a laboratory analogue of drug valuation with no external norms.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Abuse liability' is inferred from positive subjective ratings and the monetary value participants assigned to the dose; no self-administration or choice procedure was used.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None at the family level: significance was set at P ≤ .05, with post-hoc Fisher least-significant-difference or Scheffé tests after a significant F. Table I reports ten pharmacokinetic parameters for each of six dosing conditions and Table II eighteen peak measures for each of six conditions, with pairwise comparisons against placebo and against three other conditions (pp. 407–408, 414).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Double-blind administration with identical injection volumes; blinding integrity was not tested, and participants experienced with intravenous methamphetamine may well have distinguished the active conditions from placebo.

analysis.effect_sizes: Table I gives means (SD) with 95% confidence intervals for every pharmacokinetic parameter. Half-life: d-methamphetamine 10.2 (SD 2.3), 10.3 (SD 2.6) and 10.7 (SD 2.6) h at 0.25 mg/kg, 0.5 mg/kg and in the racemate; l-methamphetamine 13.6 (SD 3.8), 13.3 (SD 3.5) and 15.0 (SD 4.6) h (overall P<.0001; at 0.5 mg/kg P = .0049). Clearance 0.257–0.266 L·h⁻¹·kg⁻¹ for the d-isomer and 0.188–0.221 for the l-isomer; volume of distribution 3.73–4.17 L/kg with no significant difference between isomers (P = .2206). Peak concentration 76.7 (SD 25.3) and 131.9 (SD 24.4) ng/mL for d-methamphetamine at the two doses, 65.4 (SD 18.1) and 125.9 (SD 30.7) for l-methamphetamine. Relative exposure (d/l AUC ratio): 0.910 (90% CI 0.837–0.983) at 0.25 mg/kg and 0.894 (0.821–0.967) at 0.5 mg/kg, against 0.679 (0.622–0.736) after the racemate, which falls outside the 80–125% range. Amphetamine formation differs sharply by isomer: amphetamine-to-methamphetamine AUC ratio 0.162–0.173 for the d-isomer and 0.029–0.038 for the l-isomer. Pharmacodynamics (Table II, mean peak change with SD): systolic pressure +34.5 (18.9) mm Hg after 0.5 mg/kg d-methamphetamine and +33.4 (17.8) after the racemate, against +19.5 (11.3) after 0.5 mg/kg l-methamphetamine and +4.3 (9.9) after placebo; heart rate +13.5 (18.5), +18.7 (23.4), +10.7 (10.2) and +3.7 (9.8) beats/min; visual-analogue intoxication 46.0 (35.3), 24.7 (27.4), 30.3 (24.9) and 1.7 (4.7); drug liking 47.7 (35.1), 33.3 (28.7), 28.6 (24.8) and 2.1 (3.9); monetary value $14.60 (9.6), $10.70 (9.2), $11.30 (8.8) and $1.10 (2.4). No standardized effect sizes are given; the standard deviations are large relative to the means for most subjective measures.
analysis.covariates: None; repeated-measures ANOVA on change scores from pre-dose values, with dosing condition and time as within-subject factors.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration is mentioned; the study was conducted under investigational new drug application 58,189 with institutional review board approval (pp. 406–407).
analysis.selective_reporting: Time courses appear in figures without printed values; the Profile of Mood States, Beck Depression Inventory, State-Trait Anxiety Inventory and Buss Aggression Scale results are reported mainly as null findings; urinary excretion and p-hydroxylation, named in the limitations as important, were not examined.
analysis.power: Not reported; no sample-size calculation. With 12 participants the pharmacokinetic contrasts are reasonably precise (the confidence intervals are printed), while the subjective contrasts have standard deviations close to or above their means and are much less precise.

interpretation_gap.results_show: The two enantiomers have similar volumes of distribution and broadly similar exposure when given separately, but l-methamphetamine is eliminated more slowly (half-life about 13–15 hours against 10–11 hours) and is converted to amphetamine about four to seven times less. After the racemate, exposure to the l-isomer exceeded exposure to the d-isomer. Acutely, doses containing d-methamphetamine raised blood pressure, heart rate and positive subjective ratings more and for longer (up to about 6 hours) than l-methamphetamine, whose effects returned to baseline by about 2–4 hours; the racemate behaved much like d-methamphetamine on most measures, and l-methamphetamine at 0.5 mg/kg was not inert.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract states that 0.5 mg/kg l-methamphetamine produced peak intoxication and drug-liking ratings "similar to" the same dose of d-methamphetamine, and prints the pairs (46.0 ± 35.3 versus 30.3 ± 24.9; 47.7 ± 35.1 versus 28.6 ± 24.8) in an order that reads as if the higher value were the l-isomer's. In Table II the higher value in each pair is the d-isomer's, and the Results state that 0.5 mg/kg l-methamphetamine produced significantly smaller effects than 0.5 mg/kg d-methamphetamine on intoxication, any drug effect and drug liking (P<.0001) and than the racemate (P<.05). The conclusion that racemic methamphetamine would have an abuse liability comparable to d-methamphetamine is supported by these acute data in this sample, but it is a prediction about products and markets drawn from single intravenous doses in 12 non-dependent men, and the authors' own limitations section lists the single route, the narrow dose range, the single dose and the absence of repeated dosing (p. 418).

timeline.event: Smoked and intravenous pharmacokinetics of S-(+)-methamphetamine in 6 men: half-life 11.1–12.2 h, consistent with the d-isomer values here
Intranasal and smoked bioavailability study from the same San Francisco laboratory, sharing two authors: half-life about 10.7 h
Oral sustained-release dosing: half-life 9.3–11.1 h for the d-isomer, the form given in all these studies

replication.where_it_stands: This remains the only controlled human comparison of the methamphetamine enantiomers with a stereoselective assay; no independent replication was found in the sources read for this card. The d-isomer half-life agrees with three other laboratories, which supports the assay and the design; the l-isomer values and the racemate exposure finding rest on this study alone and should be labelled single-study.

funding.funder: Grants DA12521, DA18179 and DA12393 from the National Institute on Drug Abuse, National Institutes of Health; carried out in part at the General Clinical Research Center, University of California, San Francisco, with NIH support (grant RR-00079). One author was supported in part by a Merck, Sharp & Dohme International Fellowship in Clinical Pharmacology, with two of the authors as US sponsors (p. 403).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors report no conflict of interest (p. 419).
funding.affiliations_note: Author affiliations include a pharmaceutical company (ALZA, Palo Alto) alongside the university laboratories, and the fellowship above is industry-funded. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results. The paper's framing question is the likely consequence of precursor regulation, a policy question, which is relevant to how its conclusions are worded (pp. 403–405, 417).

what_would_settle_it: A repeated-dosing crossover with the racemate and each enantiomer, with stereoselective plasma sampling long enough to measure accumulation of the l-isomer, including women, and with a self-administration or choice procedure rather than ratings alone, so that the prediction about the relative abuse liability of racemic and d-methamphetamine is tested on behaviour.

domains.domain: Randomization process (Latin-square allocation of the six conditions)
domains.note: A Latin-square balanced crossover is described, but the sequence generation and allocation concealment are not, and no period effect is reported.
Sessions about a week apart, which is more than ten half-lives for the d-isomer and about eight for the l-isomer; no methamphetamine was detectable before dosing (p. 408).

Double-blind with matched injection volumes, but blinding integrity was not assessed and the placebo and l-methamphetamine 0.25 mg/kg conditions were plainly less intoxicating, so participants experienced with the drug could probably tell the conditions apart.
All 12 completed all six sessions; under 1% of values were missing and were replaced by the group mean at that time point.
Stereoselective assay and automated cardiovascular measurement are objective (low); the subjective ratings and monetary valuations are self-reports whose blinding cannot be assumed (some concerns).

No protocol or pre-specified primary outcome; about forty outcomes with uncorrected pairwise tests; time courses only in figures; the abstract's description of the subjective comparison does not match Table II.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The design is the strongest among the pharmacokinetic studies read here: placebo-controlled, double-blind, balanced crossover, with an enantioselective assay and every participant receiving all six conditions, so the pharmacokinetic contrasts between isomers are internally valid. The concerns are the untested blind, the uncorrected multiplicity across many outcomes, and an abstract that describes the subjective comparison in a way its own table does not support. The source can be cited for the enantiomer differences in half-life, clearance, amphetamine formation and relative exposure after the racemate, and for the acute cardiovascular and subjective profile of single intravenous doses; it cannot be cited for repeated dosing, other routes, women, or for a market-level prediction about abuse liability.

key_findings.finding: The elimination half-life was shorter for d-methamphetamine than for l-methamphetamine in every condition: 10.2 h (SD 2.3), 10.3 (SD 2.6) and 10.7 (SD 2.6) against 13.6 (SD 3.8), 13.3 (SD 3.5) and 15.0 (SD 4.6) at 0.25 mg/kg, 0.5 mg/kg and within the racemate (P<.0001 overall; P = .0049 at 0.5 mg/kg).
key_findings.locator: Results › Pharmacokinetic results, penultimate paragraph of the section, the one beginning with the volume of distribution (p. 408, right column); Table I, t½ row (pp. 410–411)

key_findings.finding: Systemic clearance was higher for the d-isomer (0.257–0.266 L·h⁻¹·kg⁻¹) than for the l-isomer (0.188–0.221), while the volume of distribution was 3.73–4.17 L/kg and did not differ between isomers (P = .2206).
key_findings.locator: Results › Pharmacokinetic results, 1st–2nd paragraphs (p. 408, right column); Table I, CL and Vd rows (pp. 410–411)

key_findings.finding: Given separately, the two isomers produced nearly equal exposure: d/l AUC ratio 0.910 (90% CI 0.837–0.983) at 0.25 mg/kg and 0.894 (0.821–0.967) at 0.5 mg/kg. After the racemate the ratio fell to 0.679 (90% CI 0.622–0.736), outside the 80–125% range, that is, exposure to the l-isomer exceeded exposure to the d-isomer within the same injection.
key_findings.note: The Results describe this as the l-isomer AUC being '30% greater' than the d-isomer's; from the printed ratio the correct statement is that the d-isomer's AUC was about 32% smaller, or the l-isomer's about 47% greater (editors' calculation, 1/0.679 = 1.47).

key_findings.finding: Both AUC and peak concentration roughly doubled from 0.25 to 0.5 mg/kg for each isomer, consistent with linear kinetics over this range; peak concentrations were 76.7 (SD 25.3) and 131.9 (SD 24.4) ng/mL for d-methamphetamine and 65.4 (SD 18.1) and 125.9 (SD 30.7) for l-methamphetamine.
key_findings.locator: Results › Pharmacokinetic results, 3rd paragraph (left column, p. 408); Table I, AUC and Cmax rows (pp. 410–411)

key_findings.finding: Conversion to amphetamine is strongly stereoselective: the amphetamine-to-methamphetamine AUC ratio was 0.162–0.173 for the d-isomer and 0.029–0.038 for the l-isomer, a four- to sevenfold difference, and amphetamine peaked 12–18 h after dosing with a half-life of 32.5–64.6 h.
key_findings.locator: Results › Pharmacokinetic results, last paragraph (p. 408, right column); Table I, amphetamine rows (pp. 410–411)

key_findings.finding: Peak increases in systolic blood pressure were 34.5 mm Hg (SD 18.9) after 0.5 mg/kg d-methamphetamine and 33.4 (SD 17.8) after the racemate, against 19.5 (SD 11.3) after 0.5 mg/kg l-methamphetamine and 4.3 (SD 9.9) after placebo; peak heart-rate increases were 13.5 (SD 18.5), 18.7 (SD 23.4), 10.7 (SD 10.2) and 3.7 (SD 9.8) beats/min.
key_findings.note: Heart-rate changes were not ordered by dose: the 0.25 mg/kg d-methamphetamine condition gave the second-largest mean (18.0, SD 11.7), larger than the 0.5 mg/kg condition.

key_findings.finding: Cardiovascular effects peaked about 5–15 minutes after the 1-minute infusion in every condition; after l-methamphetamine they returned to baseline within 2–4 hours, while after conditions containing d-methamphetamine they persisted for up to 6 hours.
key_findings.locator: Results › Pharmacodynamic measures › Physiologic measures, paragraph beginning 'phetamine produced greater and longer-lasting cardiovascular effects'; Figure 4 (p. 413)

key_findings.finding: Peak visual-analogue intoxication was 46.0 (SD 35.3) after 0.5 mg/kg d-methamphetamine, 36.7 (SD 25.6) after 0.25 mg/kg d-methamphetamine, 30.3 (SD 24.9) after 0.5 mg/kg l-methamphetamine, 24.7 (SD 27.4) after the racemate, 14.6 (SD 20.3) after 0.25 mg/kg l-methamphetamine and 1.7 (SD 4.7) after placebo; peak drug liking for the same conditions was 47.7, 38.9, 28.6, 33.3, 14.9 and 2.1, so the order differs from intoxication: the racemate was rated above 0.5 mg/kg l-methamphetamine.
key_findings.locator: Table II, visual analog scales block

key_findings.finding: At 0.5 mg/kg, l-methamphetamine produced significantly smaller effects than the same dose of d-methamphetamine on intoxication, any drug effect and drug liking (P<.0001) and smaller than the racemate (P<.05); its subjective effects approached baseline at about 3 hours, while conditions containing d-methamphetamine remained intoxicating for up to 6 hours. The 0.25 mg/kg l-methamphetamine condition did not differ from placebo on any subjective measure.
key_findings.locator: Results › Pharmacodynamic measures › Subjective measures, 1st–2nd paragraphs (p. 410); Figure 5 (p. 415)

key_findings.finding: Participants valued all doses containing d-methamphetamine and the higher l-methamphetamine dose at a mean of $10.70 to $14.60 per dose, against $1.10 for placebo and $4.60 for 0.25 mg/kg l-methamphetamine; monetary value was the one subjective measure on which 0.5 mg/kg l-methamphetamine matched the d-methamphetamine conditions.
key_findings.locator: Results › Pharmacodynamic measures › Subjective measures, 2nd–3rd paragraphs (p. 410); Table II, Monetary value row (p. 414); Figure 6 (p. 416)

key_findings.finding: All doses were tolerated: no serious adverse events occurred and no clinically significant changes in electrocardiography, examination, vital signs or laboratory tests were observed. The authors state that the responses obtained were 25–50% of the maximum they considered safe.
key_findings.locator: Results › Tolerability of methamphetamine (p. 408); Discussion › Study limitations (p. 418)

key_findings.finding: The authors list their own limitations: only the intravenous route, only two doses over a narrow range, only single doses with no repeated-dosing arm, and no examination of p-hydroxylation or urinary excretion.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract reports the systolic blood-pressure changes (33.4 ± 17.8 and 34.5 ± 18.9 against 19.5 ± 11.3) in units of beats per minute; Table II and the Results give them in mm Hg.
reporting_issues.consequence: A reader quoting the abstract would attribute a blood-pressure change to heart rate; the mm Hg values in Table II are the correct ones.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract describes 0.5 mg/kg l-methamphetamine as producing peak intoxication and drug-liking ratings similar to the same dose of d-methamphetamine, listing the pairs 46.0 ± 35.3 versus 30.3 ± 24.9 and 47.7 ± 35.1 versus 28.6 ± 24.8 in an order that attributes the larger value to l-methamphetamine. Table II shows the larger value in each pair belongs to d-methamphetamine, although without a significant difference between the two 0.5 mg/kg conditions in peak intoxication or drug liking, and the Results report the l-isomer's effects as significantly smaller (P<.0001) in the analysis across time.
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract's pairs are in reversed order; its description of the peak ratings as similar is consistent with Table II (no significant peak difference), but the across-time comparison favours d-methamphetamine and the l-isomer's effects are shorter-lived, so the Results and Table II should be used instead.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results state that after the racemate the AUC for l-methamphetamine was 30% greater than that for d-methamphetamine, while the printed mean ratio of 0.679 corresponds to the d-isomer being about 32% smaller, or the l-isomer about 47% greater (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Two incompatible percentages for the same comparison circulate within the paper (the abstract's 'd 30% smaller' is the one consistent with the ratio); the ratio with its confidence interval should be cited rather than either percentage.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table I, the peak amphetamine concentration after the racemate (d-enantiomer) is printed as 4.9 ± 1.8 with a 95% confidence interval of 4.9–7.6; a mean cannot coincide with the lower bound of its own symmetric interval, and the interval's midpoint is about 6.3.
reporting_issues.consequence: Either the mean or the interval is mistyped; the amphetamine peak for that condition cannot be read from the table with confidence.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results give the amphetamine half-life range as 33.0 to 65.0 hours, while Table I lists 32.5, 64.6, 33.5, 43.6 and 40.6 hours for the five conditions in which it could be estimated.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor rounding mismatch between text and table.

reporting_issues.issue: The legends of Figures 4, 5 and 6 state that mean data are shown for N = 12 except for the 0.5 mg/kg d- and l-methamphetamine conditions, for which means with standard deviations are given.
reporting_issues.consequence: Dispersion is displayed for two of the six conditions only, so the figures cannot be used to compare variability across conditions.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table I, the amphetamine AUC0–t after 0.25 mg/kg l-methamphetamine is printed as 32.1 ± 21.6 with a 95% confidence interval of 13.4–45.8; the interval's midpoint is 29.6, not the mean, and its half-width (16.2) is wider than the 13.7 implied by the SD with 12 participants (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Either the mean or the interval is mistyped, as for the amphetamine peak after the racemate; the cell cannot be read from the table with confidence.
