design_detail: Controlled oral administration study on a closed research ward. Eight volunteers received four daily 10-mg doses of S-(+)-methamphetamine hydrochloride as a sustained-release tablet formulation within 7 days; three weeks later five of them received four daily 20-mg doses. Doses were given under subject-blind conditions with placebo capsules at other times, in a fixed order (low regimen first). Plasma was sampled to 24 h and oral fluid to 72 h in the first session of each regimen, with 200 plasma and 590 oral fluid specimens analysed by gas chromatography–mass spectrometry; three oral-fluid collection methods were compared, and heart rate, blood pressure, respiration, oxygen saturation, temperatures and pupil diameter were recorded in the first session of each regimen and in a placebo session.
can_establish: Plasma and oral-fluid concentration–time profiles, half-life, time to peak and detection windows for methamphetamine and its metabolite amphetamine after a sustained-release oral formulation, in 8 volunteers; how much oral-fluid concentrations depend on the collection method; and whether oral-fluid concentrations can predict plasma concentrations.
cannot_establish: The pharmacokinetics of methamphetamine as people usually take it (the formulation was a sustained-release pharmaceutical given by mouth, and time to peak is formulation-dependent); dose-proportionality beyond two dose levels given in a fixed order to partly different people; and the physiological effects of these doses with any precision, since those analyses rest on five participants.

sample.recruitment: Volunteers resident on the secure clinical ward of the National Institute on Drug Abuse Intramural Research Program, Baltimore; the recruitment route is not described (p. 122).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Medical, physical and psychological evaluation before admission, including a history of past and recent drug use; participants lived on the closed ward for two weeks before the first dose so that previously self-administered drugs would be eliminated (p. 122). No other eligibility criteria are given.
sample.demographics: Four men and four women; mean age 35.3 years (SD 4.2, range 26.3–39.8); mean height 171.5 cm (SD 9.8, range 149.9–177.8); mean weight 72.0 kg (SD 17.6, range 54.7–103.2) (p. 124). Their own pattern of methamphetamine use is not reported.
sample.attrition: Two participants were disqualified for medical reasons and a third chose to stop after the fourth dose, so only five of the eight received the 20-mg regimen; no plasma was obtained from one participant after the first 10-mg dose because of blood-collection difficulties, and no physiological data were collected for one participant (pp. 122–124).
sample.selection_effects: A small residential sample with no reported characterization of the participants' own drug use, studied under two weeks of supervised abstinence; whoever remained for the second regimen had tolerated the first, so the 20-mg results come from a selected five.

exposure.measurement: Drug administered on the ward and measured directly: methamphetamine and amphetamine in plasma and oral fluid by solid-phase extraction and gas chromatography–mass spectrometry, with limits of detection and quantification of 2.5 µg/L for both analytes and between-run imprecision of 1.4–12% across control concentrations (pp. 123–124).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: four daily oral doses of 10 mg, and in five participants four daily oral doses of 20 mg three weeks later, each as one or two 10-mg sustained-release tablets inside a gelatin capsule with lactose filler; placebo capsules contained lactose alone. The formulation releases 20–40% of the drug within 30 minutes, 35–55% within 1 hour and 60–80% within 4 hours. The authors state they chose a sustained-release oral formulation for participant safety, although methamphetamine is less commonly taken by mouth (p. 122).
exposure.polysubstance: Two weeks of residence on a closed ward before dosing is the control for other drug use; no urine screening results, tobacco use or caffeine use are reported (p. 122).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Two weeks on a closed ward before the first dose; three weeks between the two regimens (p. 122).

comparison.controls: Placebo sessions within the same participants provide the comparison for the physiological measures; there is no separate control group and no placebo comparison for the pharmacokinetics.
comparison.matching: Within-person, but the two dose levels were given in a fixed order (10 mg first, 20 mg three weeks later) and to partly different people, so dose is confounded with time and with who remained in the study.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to the pharmacokinetics. For the physiological comparisons, tolerance acquired during the first regimen cannot be separated from the dose difference, because the high dose always came second.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable (no separate control group).

outcomes.instruments: Non-compartmental pharmacokinetics (WinNonlin): lag time, time to peak, peak concentration, half-life by log-linear regression of the terminal phase, AUC from dosing to 24 h by the trapezoidal rule, volume of distribution and total body clearance; a one-compartment model with first-order input and output for the plasma profiles. Three oral-fluid collection methods (citric-acid candy-stimulated expectoration, citric-acid-treated cotton swab, neutral cotton swab) and pH indicator sticks with a resolution of 0.4 pH units. Physiological measures with a bedside monitor and pupillometry with an adapted camera (pp. 122–124).
outcomes.validity_norms: Assay validated in-house with stated imprecision; oral-fluid pH measured only to within 0.4 units, which the authors do not discuss as a limitation when interpreting the pH-dependence of concentrations.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Detection window' is the time over which concentrations stay at or above 2.5 µg/L, or above the cutoffs proposed in 2001 by the US Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (50 µg/L methamphetamine with amphetamine at or above the limit of quantification); 'detection rate' is the proportion of specimens positive in a time period.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None reported beyond post-hoc Scheffé and Bonferroni tests inside each ANOVA; the α level was 0.05 throughout (p. 124). Fourteen pharmacokinetic parameters are tabulated per dose level, and about six inferential analyses are reported (AUC by dose; oral-fluid AUC by dose, device and subject; pH by device and subject; the oral fluid–plasma regression; physiological AUCs by dose).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Administration was subject-blind only; no blinding of staff is described. Assays are objective and were run against calibrators and controls.

analysis.effect_sizes: Means (SD) with ranges; no confidence intervals except for the ratios between collection devices. Plasma after the first dose, 10 mg (n=7 with plasma) and 20 mg (n=5): lag time 1.5 (SD 0.8) and 1.1 (SD 0.5) h; time to peak 5.4 (SD 2.5) and 7.5 (SD 3.4) h; peak 20.2 (SD 6.4) and 32.4 (SD 7.7) µg/L; half-life 9.3 (SD 3.7) and 11.1 (SD 7.2) h; AUC to 24 h 269.1 (SD 94.3) and 468.1 (SD 151.8) h·µg/L; volume of distribution 5.8 (SD 2.6) and 5.3 (SD 2.1) L/kg; clearance 32.2 (SD 13.7) and 33.5 (SD 15.9) L/h. Oral fluid: time to peak 5.0 (SD 1.9) and 4.7 (SD 3.9) h; peak 106.1 (SD 100.8) and 192.2 (SD 120.8) µg/L; half-life 7.1 (SD 2.3) and 8.1 (SD 1.9) h (Table 1, p. 125). Plasma AUC was 2.1 (SD 0.7) times higher after the high dose (P = 0.009). Amphetamine AUC was 21% (SD 25%) of methamphetamine in plasma and 24.0% (SD 11.4%) in oral fluid on a molar basis. Oral-fluid AUCs were 3.8 (SD 2.3) times the plasma AUCs (P = 0.009); the oral fluid-to-plasma ratio had a median of 2.0 and ranged from 0.0 to 23.0 (n=67), and the regression of oral-fluid on plasma concentrations gave R² = 0.222 (P = 0.005) (pp. 125–127).
analysis.covariates: Mixed-effects models with subject as a random effect for the oral-fluid analyses; no adjustment for sex, weight or oral-fluid pH in the pharmacokinetic comparisons.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned; the study was approved by the institutional review board.
analysis.selective_reporting: Pharmacokinetic results for the other two oral-fluid collection methods are placed in an online data supplement that was not read for this card; urine results are cited to a separate publication by the same group.
analysis.power: Not reported; no sample-size calculation. Eight participants (five at the higher dose) with standard deviations approaching or exceeding the means for several oral-fluid parameters (peak 106.1 ± 100.8 µg/L; AUC 1118.0 ± 983.4 h·µg/L) make every oral-fluid estimate imprecise.

interpretation_gap.results_show: After a sustained-release oral formulation, plasma methamphetamine appeared within 0.25–2 h, peaked at about 5–8 h and had a half-life of about 9–11 hours; amphetamine reached about a fifth to a quarter of the parent drug's AUC and peaked later. Oral-fluid concentrations were on average about twice to four times plasma concentrations but varied so widely, and depended so much on the collection method and on oral-fluid pH, that they could not predict plasma concentrations (R² 0.222).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The conclusion that oral fluid is practical for detecting use but inferior to urine in concentration and detection window follows from the data. Two cautions for anyone citing the pharmacokinetics: the time to peak (5.4–7.5 h) belongs to this sustained-release formulation, as the authors show by comparing it with 2.9–3.6 h for other oral formulations, while the half-life is formulation-independent and agrees with other studies; and the cardiovascular findings rest on five participants and only two of eight physiological measures reached significance, so they bound the effects of these doses rather than establishing them. The paper repeatedly describes 13 person-sessions as '13 individuals' although only 8 people took part.

timeline.event: Oral methamphetamine pharmacokinetics with repeated daily dosing (Cook et al., 1992): half-life 9.1–11.2 h, time to peak 2.9–3.3 h with a capsule formulation
Smoked and intravenous pharmacokinetics in 6 men: half-life 11.1–12.2 h
Intranasal and smoked bioavailability and pharmacokinetics in 8 men: half-life about 10.7 h by both routes
Intravenous enantiomer study: d-methamphetamine half-life 10.2–10.7 h, l-methamphetamine 13.3–15.0 h, showing that the half-life quoted for 'methamphetamine' depends on which isomer was given

replication.where_it_stands: The half-life of about 10 hours is now consistent across oral, smoked, intranasal and intravenous studies from three laboratories. Time to peak is formulation- and route-dependent and should never be quoted without both. The oral fluid-to-plasma relationship remains too variable for oral fluid to stand in for plasma concentrations, which later oral-fluid work has not overturned.

funding.funder: Intramural Research Program of the National Institute on Drug Abuse, National Institutes of Health: the acknowledgements state that the research was sponsored by NIDA Intramural Research Program funds (p. 132); the authors' affiliations are on p. 121.
funding.declared_conflicts: Not reported: the article carries no conflict-of-interest statement.
funding.affiliations_note: One author is affiliated with Amgen Inc. (Clinical Affairs) and one with a private research company, ConeChem Research; the study drug was a commercial sustained-release product. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results (p. 121).

what_would_settle_it: A randomized crossover of an immediate-release and a sustained-release oral dose with the same participants, balanced in order, with plasma sampling beyond 24 hours so that the terminal phase is captured, oral-fluid pH measured with a meter rather than indicator sticks, and enough participants to estimate the oral fluid-to-plasma ratio with a usable interval.

domains.note: No randomization: every participant received the 10-mg regimen first and, if still in the study, the 20-mg regimen three weeks later, so dose is confounded with order, with time on the ward and with who remained. RoB 2 is used because the design enum has no category for a fixed-order controlled administration study; the editors note that no validated instrument fits this design.
Administration was subject-blind with placebo capsules, but staff blinding is not described and the dose sequence was known; dosing itself was supervised on a closed ward, so adherence is secure.

Three of eight did not complete the second regimen (two disqualified medically, one withdrew), one participant has no plasma data for the first dose and one no physiological data; the physiological analyses rest on five participants.
Validated gas chromatography–mass spectrometry with calibrators and duplicate controls in each batch; automated physiological monitoring.

No protocol; two of the three collection methods are reported only in an online supplement; the modelling parameters appear with different values and units in the Results and the Discussion (see reporting issues).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The assays and the controlled residential setting are strengths, and the concentration–time data are the most reliable part of the paper. The overall judgment is set by the fixed dose order with substantial attrition before the higher dose, which makes the dose comparison and the physiological results weak. The source can be cited for the plasma and oral-fluid pharmacokinetics of a sustained-release oral formulation (half-life, time to peak, peak concentration, amphetamine ratio), for the dependence of oral-fluid concentrations on the collection method and pH, and for detection windows; it cannot be cited for dose-proportionality, for time to peak after other oral preparations, or for precise cardiovascular effects.

key_findings.finding: After the first 10-mg sustained-release oral dose, plasma methamphetamine peaked at 20.2 µg/L (SD 6.4) at 5.4 h (SD 2.5), with a lag of 1.5 h (SD 0.8) and a half-life of 9.3 h (SD 3.7); after the first 20-mg dose, peak 32.4 µg/L (SD 7.7) at 7.5 h (SD 3.4) with a half-life of 11.1 h (SD 7.2).

The overall mean plasma half-life was 10.0 h (SD 5.2) and did not differ between doses; the authors place it alongside previously reported values of 9.1–13.1 h after oral, inhaled and intravenous dosing.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, paragraph beginning 'In our study, plasma METH half-lives were not dose dependent' (p. 128); Table 3 (p. 130)
key_findings.note: The comparison values in Table 3 are taken from other published studies, not measured here.

key_findings.finding: Time to peak with this sustained-release formulation (overall mean 6.3 h, SD 3.0) was longer than the 2.9–3.6 h reported for other oral formulations, including a study using the same product with more frequent sampling (3.0 h).
key_findings.locator: Discussion, paragraph beginning 'Mean plasma METH tmax values reported in our study' (p. 128)

key_findings.finding: Plasma AUC over 24 h was 2.1 times higher (SD 0.7, range 1.2–3.1) after the 20-mg than after the 10-mg dose (P = 0.009).
key_findings.locator: Results › METH and AMP pharmacokinetics in plasma and oral fluid, 1st paragraph after Table 1

key_findings.finding: Amphetamine, the active metabolite, peaked later than the parent drug (plasma time to peak 11.9 h, SD 6.9, after the low dose and 14.3 h, SD 5.5, after the high dose) and reached a 24-h AUC of 21% (SD 25%) of methamphetamine in plasma and 24.0% (SD 11.4%) in oral fluid, on a molar basis.
key_findings.locator: Results › METH and AMP pharmacokinetics in plasma and oral fluid, 2nd paragraph (p. 125) and the oral-fluid paragraphs (p. 125); Table 2 (p. 127)

key_findings.finding: Oral-fluid concentrations were higher than plasma concentrations (mean AUC ratio 3.8, SD 2.3, range 1.8–8.7; P = 0.009), but the oral fluid-to-plasma ratio was highly variable within and between people (median 2.0, range 0.0–23.0, n=67) and plasma concentrations could not be predicted from oral fluid (R² = 0.222, P = 0.005).
key_findings.locator: Results › METH and AMP pharmacokinetics in plasma and oral fluid, last three paragraphs (p. 125; the last continues at the top of p. 127); Figure 2 (p. 127)

key_findings.finding: The collection method changed the measured concentration: AUCs from neutral cotton swabs were on average 1.47 times those from citric-acid-treated swabs and 1.92 times (95% CI 1.06–3.51; P<0.05) those from citric-acid candy-stimulated expectoration, with significant effects of dose (P<0.001), device (P = 0.006) and subject (P = 0.003).
key_findings.locator: Results › Comparison of the different oral fluid collection methods, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Oral-fluid pH differed sharply by device: 2.8 (SD 0.3) with citric-acid-treated swabs, 4.3 (SD 0.8) with candy stimulation and 6.0 (SD 0.6) with neutral swabs (both device and subject P<0.001), which is the mechanism the authors propose for the concentration differences.

Detection at 24 hours after a single dose: plasma methamphetamine exceeded 2.5 µg/L in 5 of 7 participants after 10 mg (4.8–6.9 µg/L) and 4 of 5 after 20 mg (5.2–15.9 µg/L), while all candy-stimulated oral-fluid specimens at 24 h were positive (2.5–33.2 and 10.5–68.1 µg/L).
key_findings.locator: Results › Windows of detection, 1st paragraph (plasma) and 2nd paragraph (oral fluid)

key_findings.finding: After four doses, methamphetamine remained above 2.5 µg/L in candy-stimulated oral fluid for 36–72 h (mean 58.3 h, SD 14.5); 48 h after the last dose all specimens were below the cutoffs proposed by the US Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (50 µg/L methamphetamine with amphetamine at or above the limit of quantification).
key_findings.locator: Results › Pharmacologic effects, preceding paragraph on SAMHSA cutoffs (p. 128); Discussion, paragraph beginning 'After four 10- or 20-mg doses' (p. 131)
key_findings.note: The Results (p. 127) print the same window as 36–76 h; see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: With those proposed cutoffs applied to this study, only 1 of 13 person-sessions was positive 24 h after a single dose, and 23 of 130 specimens collected within 24 h of dosing met them (18%).
key_findings.locator: Results › SAMHSA cutoff paragraph (p. 128); Discussion, windows-of-detection paragraph (p. 131)

key_findings.finding: Physiological effects of these oral doses were modest: across 12-hour AUCs, only diastolic blood pressure (+10.1%, P = 0.003) and heart rate (+21.7%, P = 0.036) differed from placebo, and only at 20 mg; systolic blood pressure, skin and core temperature, oxygen saturation and pupil diameter did not differ. The analysis rests on five participants.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 1, the Range column of the 20-mg oral-fluid block is displaced by one row: the half-life row has no range, the AUC row carries '5.5–10.5' (which fits the half-life), the volume-of-distribution row carries '673.8–3891.0' (which fits the AUC), and the clearance row carries '4.5–24.7'.
reporting_issues.consequence: Three of the four printed ranges in that block belong to the row above; anyone reading ranges from this table for the 20-mg oral-fluid parameters will take the wrong values.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1's column heading says '10 mg (n = 8)' for both the plasma and the oral-fluid blocks, although footnote b states that no plasma samples were collected from one volunteer and the Results give n = 7 for the plasma peak.
reporting_issues.consequence: The plasma parameters at the low dose rest on 7 participants, not 8.

reporting_issues.issue: The one-compartment model parameters are given twice with different values and different units: the Results print K01 as 1.07 ± 0.60 h and K10 as 10.76 ± 4.20 h (n = 13), while the Discussion gives K01 = 0.93 ± 0.61 h⁻¹ and K10 = 0.085 ± 0.067 h⁻¹ for the same fits. Rate constants cannot have units of hours, and a K10 of 10.76 h⁻¹ would imply an elimination half-life of about 4 minutes, against the measured 9–11 hours.
reporting_issues.consequence: The Results values are unusable; the Discussion values are the internally consistent ones (0.693/0.085 = 8.2 h, editors' calculation) and are the ones that can be compared with the other studies cited there.

reporting_issues.issue: The model fits are reported for n = 13 although only 12 plasma profiles exist (7 at the low dose plus 5 at the high dose), as the paper itself implies when it reports initial plasma detection for n = 12.
reporting_issues.consequence: One profile in the modelling count is unaccounted for; the discrepancy is small but it is the same count (13) that is elsewhere described as '13 individuals'.

reporting_issues.issue: Person-sessions are repeatedly called individuals: '8 of 13 individuals', '1 of 13 individuals', '9 of 12 participants', although only 8 people took part, 5 of them twice.
reporting_issues.consequence: Detection rates read as if they came from 12 or 13 people; they come from 8, which makes them less independent and the proportions less precise than they appear.

reporting_issues.issue: In the discussion of oral-fluid detection, work by Suzuki et al. is cited as reference 17, which in this article's list is Cook et al. (1993) on smoked methamphetamine; Suzuki et al. is reference 22.
reporting_issues.consequence: A reader following the citation lands on the wrong paper; the 48-hour oral-fluid detection in two cases belongs to Suzuki et al.

reporting_issues.issue: The detection window after four doses is printed as 36–76 h in the Results (p. 127) but as 36–72 h (mean 58.3, SD 14.5) in the abstract (p. 121) and the Discussion (p. 131).
reporting_issues.consequence: The upper end of the window differs by 4 hours between sections and the paper does not say which is right; key finding 9 uses the Discussion's 36–72 h.

design_detail: Cross-sectional PET study with [11C]WIN-35,428 (2-β-carbomethoxy-3β-(4-[11C]fluorophenyl)tropane) in 11 men who had used only methamphetamine and 9 men who had not, at one Japanese centre. Dopamine transporter binding potential (k3/k4, three-compartment four-parameter model, arterial input function, cerebellar cortex as the reference for K1/k2) was measured in the caudate/putamen, nucleus accumbens and prefrontal cortex and correlated, within the methamphetamine group only, with duration of use, duration of abstinence, Brief Psychiatric Rating Scale (BPRS) scores and a craving score.
can_establish: That in this small sample, men abstinent from methamphetamine (7 days to 1.5 years) had lower dopamine transporter binding potential in all three regions than men who had not used it, and that within the methamphetamine group lower striatal and accumbens binding went with longer reported use and higher ratings of positive psychiatric symptoms.
cannot_establish: That methamphetamine caused the lower binding (no pre-use scan, no dose data, and the psychiatric symptoms that brought most participants into care could themselves mark a pre-existing difference; the authors concede this on p. 1213); that the lower binding means lost dopamine terminals rather than reduced transporter expression; that the reduction is lasting (the null correlation with abstinence rests on 11 people); or the direction of the symptom association in time.

sample.recruitment: The methamphetamine group was referred from three Japanese psychiatric services (Hamamatsu University Hospital, Seimei Hospital, Hattori Mental Hospital); how the comparison group was recruited is not stated (p. 1207).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: All participants men, with no parkinsonism or other neurological abnormality and no history of seizures, dyskinesia or coma. Nicotine, alcohol and other drug use screened with the SCID (non-patient version): no participant met nicotine or alcohol abuse criteria; the methamphetamine group had used no drug other than methamphetamine and the comparison group no drug at all. The comparison group had no psychiatric disorder, including substance use disorders, on the SCID (p. 1207).
sample.demographics: Methamphetamine group: 11 men, mean age 27.4 years (SD 5.6), education 11.5 years (SD 1.2). Comparison group: 9 men, mean age 26.9 (SD 4.5), education 11.8 (SD 0.7). Age and education did not differ significantly (pp. 1207–1208). Individual ages, durations of use (1 month to 15 years), abstinence (7 days to 1.5 years) and route (7 intravenous, 4 smoked) are in Table 1 (p. 1207).
sample.attrition: Not applicable; single scan, no follow-up.
sample.selection_effects: A clinically selected group: participants were referred from psychiatric services and 8 of 11 had previously experienced methamphetamine psychosis, so the sample is weighted towards people with psychiatric consequences of use, not towards people who use methamphetamine generally. The comparison group's source is not stated, and whether the two groups came from comparable populations cannot be checked. Only men were studied.

exposure.measurement: Self-report corroborated by interviews with family members and by medical records; recent use excluded by urine drug screening, including on the day of the scan (p. 1207; p. 1212).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Duration of use only, defined as the interval between first and last use with abstinence periods longer than 1 month subtracted: 1 month to 15 years (Table 1, p. 1207). Route as reported: intravenous in 7, smoked in 4 (Table 1 footnotes, p. 1207). No dose, frequency or cumulative amount was measured anywhere in the paper, although the discussion states that participants used methamphetamine recreationally and had no history of high-dose use (p. 1211).
exposure.polysubstance: By design, people who used any drug other than methamphetamine were excluded, and the comparison group had used no drug; both groups were described as occasional smokers and drinkers who met no nicotine or alcohol abuse criterion (p. 1207). This is the study's main strength over earlier PET work, in which other drug use was present or unknown (p. 1210).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: 7 days to 1.5 years (Table 1, p. 1207), verified by regular urine drug screens including one on the scan day (p. 1212). Four participants had received neuroleptics previously (last exposure 1 week to 1 year before); none was taking them at the scan (p. 1208).

comparison.controls: 9 men with no history of psychiatric disorder, substance use disorder or any illicit drug use (SCID), scanned with the same tracer and scanner (p. 1207).
comparison.matching: Selected to be similar in age and education; no formal matching procedure, covariate adjustment or sex comparison is described, and no comparison of smoking or drinking quantity is given beyond the statement of similar occasional habits (p. 1207).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No pre-use scan, no premorbid IQ or psychiatric baseline. The authors note that the methamphetamine group had no psychotic symptoms before use (from interview and records), but a pre-existing difference in transporter density cannot be excluded and they say so (p. 1213).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: None reported: the comparison group had no experience of any other drug and occasional alcohol and tobacco use only (p. 1207).

outcomes.instruments: PET (SHR2400 scanner) with [11C]WIN-35,428, 450 MBq bolus, 38 frames over 90 minutes, arterial sampling with metabolite correction; regions of interest drawn by hand on the PET display, with the corresponding 0.3 T MRI images referred to as anatomical landmarks (the paper does not describe co-registration); dopamine transporter binding potential expressed as k3/k4 (p. 1207). Symptoms: BPRS total and the positive- and negative-symptom subscales, rated by one trained psychiatrist blind to the PET data; craving on a 0–5 scale adapted from the Subjective Craving Scale for Alcohol Dependence (p. 1207).
outcomes.validity_norms: No normative data for binding potential; comparison is with the 9 scanned men. The craving scale was adapted from an alcohol instrument and no validation for methamphetamine is given.
outcomes.operationalization: Transporter 'reduction' is the group difference in mean binding potential; 'persistent psychiatric symptoms' are BPRS ratings on the scan day in people abstinent at least 7 days, with recent use excluded by urine screen (pp. 1207, 1212).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Statistical significance was set at p<0.05 for all tests (p. 1207): three group comparisons of binding potential, thirteen reported rank correlations and five prefrontal correlations reported only as absent ('data not shown', p. 1209); the Methods also describe group comparisons of K1, k2, k3, k4 and K1/k2 whose results are not reported.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Partial and stated in both directions: the closing sentence of the PET paragraph says the procedure (region drawing and binding-potential calculation, which share one paragraph) was done blind to the clinical data, and the BPRS was rated blind to the PET data by the first author (Y.S., p. 1207). Blinding to group membership is not stated, and who collected the use histories, and whether the BPRS rater knew them, is not stated.

analysis.effect_sizes: Binding potential (k3/k4), comparison group vs methamphetamine group: caudate/putamen 4.40 (SD 0.18) vs 3.51 (SD 0.45), 20.2% lower; nucleus accumbens 4.16 (SD 0.64) vs 2.93 (SD 0.77), 29.6% lower; prefrontal cortex 0.18 (SD 0.05) vs 0.12 (SD 0.03), 33.3% lower (pp. 1208–1209). Mann-Whitney U: caudate/putamen U=1.0, N=20, p<0.001; nucleus accumbens U=8.5, N=20, p<0.001; prefrontal cortex U=23.5, N=20, p<0.05 (p. 1209). No confidence intervals are given. Editors' calculation from the printed means and SDs (Hedges' g, pooled SD, approximate because the groups are small and the distributions are not described): caudate/putamen about 2.4, nucleus accumbens about 1.6, prefrontal cortex about 1.4; the intervals around these values are wide with 11 and 9 participants. Correlations are Kendall's tau within the methamphetamine group (n=11).
analysis.covariates: None. Unadjusted rank tests throughout; age, education, duration of use, route, prior neuroleptic exposure and abstinence were not entered into any model.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned (the study predates trial-registry practice for such work).
analysis.selective_reporting: Prefrontal correlations are reported only as 'data not shown' (p. 1209), and the group comparisons of the individual rate constants described in the Methods are not reported. The craving-scale correlations are given with statistics only where significant; the non-significant ones are described in words (p. 1209).
analysis.power: Not reported; no sample-size calculation. With 11 and 9 participants only large differences could be detected, and the rank correlations in 11 people have very wide intervals (a Kendall tau of −0.48 in n=11 is at the edge of significance).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 11 men abstinent from methamphetamine and 9 men who had not used it, dopamine transporter binding potential was lower in the caudate/putamen (20.2%), nucleus accumbens (29.6%) and prefrontal cortex (33.3%). Within the methamphetamine group, lower caudate/putamen and accumbens binding went with longer reported duration of use and with higher BPRS positive-symptom scores, and the duration of use itself correlated with positive symptoms; binding did not correlate with how long people had been abstinent, and craving correlated only with abstinence duration.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that "longer use of methamphetamine may cause more severe psychiatric symptoms" and greater transporter reduction, that the reduction "may be long-lasting" after use stops, and that persistent psychiatric symptoms may be attributable to it (p. 1206); the discussion states that longer use induces greater reduction, which in turn is associated with more residual symptoms (p. 1212). Three gaps: (1) causal and temporal language from one cross-sectional scan per person, in a sample selected through psychiatric services; (2) the persistence claim rests on a non-significant correlation with abstinence duration in 11 people, which is absence of evidence rather than evidence of persistence, and the authors' support for it is a previous study rather than their own data (p. 1212); (3) duration of use is treated as a proxy for cumulative dose (pp. 1211–1212) although no dose, frequency or amount was measured, and the statement that nobody had used high doses has no measurement behind it. The paper's own closing caveat, that pre-existing transporter reduction cannot be ruled out, is stated only on p. 1213 and does not reach the abstract.

timeline.event: PET with the same tracer in 6 people abstinent from methamphetamine or methcathinone: caudate and putamen binding 23–25% lower than in 10 controls, but all participants reported other illicit drug use
PET with [11C]d-threo-methylphenidate in 15 people with methamphetamine dependence: caudate 27.8% and putamen 21.1% lower than 18 controls, with other drug use not quantified

The same Hamamatsu group reported transporter reductions with longer-lasting psychiatric symptoms in a larger sample (Sekine et al., 2003), which shares investigators and site and is therefore not an independent replication
Critical review summarizing this study as about 20% lower striatal binding in people without other illicit drug use, while noting that the imaging difference has no established functional meaning
Critical assessment of whether lower transporter binding in people who use methamphetamine indicates damage to dopamine neurons

replication.where_it_stands: The direction (lower striatal transporter binding) is consistent across independent groups, tracers and post-mortem tissue. This study adds the strongest available control for polysubstance use, and extends the finding to the nucleus accumbens and prefrontal cortex, but with 11 and 9 men and no dose data. Whether the difference reflects lost terminals, transporter regulation or a pre-existing trait, and whether it recovers, remain open.

funding.funder: Scientific Research grant from the Ministry of Health and Welfare of Japan and a Target-Oriented Research and Development grant from the Ministry of Science and Technology of Japan (p. 1213).
funding.declared_conflicts: Not reported: the article carries no conflict-of-interest statement.
funding.affiliations_note: At least one author is from the Central Research Laboratory of Hamamatsu Photonics K.K., the company that made the PET scanner and is credited with it in the Methods; the affiliation note lists three institutions without saying which authors belong to which, so the number of authors from the company cannot be checked from the PDF (pp. 1207, 1213). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective study with transporter imaging before and after the onset of regular use (or a discordant-sibling or twin design) in people without other drug use, with a transporter-independent terminal marker such as VMAT2 measured in the same people, blinded symptom ratings at several time points, and measured dose rather than duration as the exposure.

domains.note: No adjustment of any kind. Groups are small and the methamphetamine group differs in psychiatric status by selection; prior neuroleptic exposure in 4 participants is dismissed by citation rather than modelled; no dose data; age and education similar but unadjusted.

Duration of use comes from self-report corroborated by family and records, which is better than self-report alone, but dose, frequency and purity are absent, so 'longer use' cannot be read as 'more drug'. Abstinence is urine-verified.

Referred from three psychiatric services, with 8 of 11 having had methamphetamine psychosis, against a comparison group of unstated origin; the symptom–transporter correlation is estimated inside this selected group.
Four participants had received neuroleptics (up to a year before the scan); abstinence ranged from 7 days to 1.5 years, so time since use varies by a factor of about 80 across the group.
All 20 participants contributed scans and all 11 in the methamphetamine group contributed clinical ratings.

Binding potential is quantified with arterial input and metabolite correction and computed blind to clinical data, and the BPRS was rated blind to the PET data; but regions were drawn by hand and the prefrontal binding potential (0.12–0.18) is close to the tracer's non-specific floor, as the authors themselves note in calling for a tracer with a higher specific-to-nonspecific ratio (p. 1211).
Twenty-one or more tests at p<0.05 with no correction; prefrontal correlations and the rate-constant comparisons are reported only as absent or not at all.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The group difference in transporter binding is large and measured with a quantitative method applied blind to clinical data, and the exclusion of other drug use removes a confounder that weakens most comparable studies. But the methamphetamine group was recruited through psychiatric services and most had had psychosis, there is no dose measurement, nothing is adjusted, and the symptom and duration correlations come from 11 people with no correction for multiplicity. The source can be cited for the direction and approximate size of the group difference in people without other illicit drug use, and for the existence of a within-group association between transporter binding and positive symptoms; it cannot be cited for causation, for persistence after abstinence, or for a dose–response relationship.

key_findings.finding: Dopamine transporter binding potential (k3/k4) in the caudate/putamen was 4.40 (SD 0.18) in the 9 men of the comparison group and 3.51 (SD 0.45) in the 11 men of the methamphetamine group, 20.2% lower.
key_findings.locator: Results, last paragraph of p. 1208 continuing on p. 1209 (right column of p. 1208); Figure 4 (p. 1210)

key_findings.finding: In the nucleus accumbens the binding potentials were 4.16 (SD 0.64) and 2.93 (SD 0.77), 29.6% lower; in the prefrontal cortex 0.18 (SD 0.05) and 0.12 (SD 0.03), 33.3% lower.
key_findings.note: The prefrontal values are an order of magnitude smaller than the striatal ones and, in the editors' reading, close to the tracer's non-specific binding (the paper does not say so); the authors call for a tracer with a higher specific-to-nonspecific ratio before prefrontal conclusions are drawn (p. 1211).

key_findings.finding: All three regional differences were significant on the Mann-Whitney U test: caudate/putamen U=1.0, N=20, p<0.001; nucleus accumbens U=8.5, N=20, p<0.001; prefrontal cortex U=23.5, N=20, p<0.05.
Within the methamphetamine group (n=11), binding potential fell as reported duration of use rose: caudate/putamen Kendall's tau −0.48 (p<0.05), nucleus accumbens tau −0.73 (p<0.01).
key_findings.note: Duration of use, not dose: no quantity of drug was measured anywhere in the study.

key_findings.finding: Binding potential did not correlate with duration of abstinence (7 days to 1.5 years) in either the caudate/putamen or the nucleus accumbens.
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph (left column, continuing right column); Figure 5 (p. 1211)
key_findings.note: A non-significant correlation in 11 people; the discussion nonetheless reads it as evidence that the reduction is long-lasting (p. 1212).

key_findings.finding: Caudate/putamen binding correlated negatively with the BPRS total score (tau −0.62, p<0.05); the nucleus accumbens did not. Both regions correlated negatively with the BPRS positive-symptom subscale (caudate/putamen tau −0.73, p<0.01; nucleus accumbens tau −0.50, p<0.05).

The BPRS positive-symptom score rose with duration of methamphetamine use (tau 0.64, p<0.01), and the craving score fell as abstinence lengthened (tau −0.50, p<0.05) but was unrelated to duration of use and to binding potential in either region.
No correlation was found between prefrontal cortex binding and any clinical measure; these analyses are reported only as 'data not shown'.

Eight of the 11 men in the methamphetamine group had previously experienced methamphetamine psychosis. In the 2 weeks before the scan, 3 had no psychiatric symptoms, 4 had persistent anxiety-like but not psychotic symptoms and 3 had persistent psychotic symptoms; a further man (participant 1), whose psychotic symptoms began during use, still had them on the scan day, so 4 of the 11 had psychotic symptoms at the scan. None had a history of psychotic symptoms before methamphetamine use, none showed negative symptoms at the examination, and none was taking neuroleptics, although 4 had received them earlier.

Participants used only methamphetamine: the SCID excluded any other illicit drug use in the methamphetamine group and any illicit drug use in the comparison group, and neither group met nicotine or alcohol abuse criteria.

The reduction here (about 20% in the caudate/putamen) is compared by the authors with about 80% striatal transporter loss measured with the same scanner and tracer in unmedicated Parkinson's disease; no participants with Parkinson's disease were studied here.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, paragraph beginning 'In a previous study using the same PET scanner'

key_findings.finding: Duration of use was defined as the interval between first and last use with abstinence periods longer than one month subtracted, and ranged from 1 month to 15 years; 7 participants had used methamphetamine intravenously and 4 by smoking.
key_findings.locator: Table 1 and its footnotes; Method › Subjects, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: No participant had a history of seizures, dyskinesia or coma, complications the authors link to intoxication with high-dose methamphetamine; all were men without signs of parkinsonism or other neurological abnormality. The paper does not say whether this was an exclusion rule or a description of the group.
key_findings.note: If it was an exclusion rule, the most severe cases are absent from the methamphetamine group (editors' reading), which bears on how far the 20–33% reductions generalize.

reporting_issues.issue: Every Kendall's tau is reported with 'df=10'. A rank correlation has no degrees of freedom, and for n=11 the conventional correlation degrees of freedom would be n−2=9; the printed df appears to be n−1.
reporting_issues.consequence: The p-values can be approximately reconstructed from tau and n = 11 (editors' calculation, normal approximation without tie correction: tau −0.48 gives p of about 0.04, −0.50 about 0.03, −0.62 about 0.008, 0.64 about 0.006 and −0.73 about 0.002), so the printed thresholds are consistent and only the df label is non-standard; a tau of −0.48 is still near the significance boundary, so the exact test would matter for the weaker correlations.

reporting_issues.issue: The mean age printed for the methamphetamine group (27.4 years, SD 5.6) does not match the ages listed for the same 11 participants in Table 1, which give a mean of 28.0 and an SD of 5.7 (editors' calculation from the eleven values).
reporting_issues.consequence: Small, but it shows that the demographic text and Table 1 were not reconciled; the age comparison between groups is unaffected in substance.

reporting_issues.issue: Duration of use is treated in the discussion as a proxy for cumulative dose ('the duration of methamphetamine use ... may represent this dose dependency'), and the claim that nobody had used high doses is made in the same paragraph, although no dose, frequency or amount was measured in the study.
reporting_issues.consequence: The dose–response reading of the duration correlation is unsupported by any measured exposure quantity; the correlation can only be read as with time since first use.

reporting_issues.issue: Twenty-one or more statistical tests are reported at an uncorrected p<0.05, and the prefrontal correlations are reported only as 'data not shown'.
reporting_issues.consequence: At least one of the weaker significant correlations (tau around −0.48 to −0.50) would be expected by chance; the absent prefrontal results cannot be checked.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract states that the transporter reduction was significantly associated with the duration of use and closely related to the severity of persistent psychiatric symptoms, without saying that both associations are rank correlations inside a group of 11 people drawn from psychiatric services.
reporting_issues.consequence: A reader who stops at the abstract will take a within-group correlation in 11 people for an established dose–symptom relationship.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion suggests that methamphetamine causes a reduction of transporter density in the human brain, qualified only by the small number of participants (p. 1210), and says that the small caudate/putamen reduction appears to have predictive value for psychiatric signs and that people who use methamphetamine may have a greater risk of Parkinson's disease as they age (p. 1212), although each person was scanned once, nobody was followed and nobody was assessed for Parkinson's disease beyond the exclusion of signs of parkinsonism.
reporting_issues.consequence: The causal, predictive and Parkinson's-disease-risk readings go beyond a cross-sectional comparison of 11 and 9 men, and the authors' own caveat that a pre-existing reduction cannot be ruled out (p. 1213) does not reach these sentences.

reporting_issues.issue: The BPRS was rated by a research psychiatrist identified only by initials (Y.S., the first author), stated to be blind to the PET data; who collected the use histories is not stated and blinding to them is not claimed.
reporting_issues.consequence: The correlation of positive-symptom scores with duration of use (tau 0.64) is not shown to have been rated blind to duration, and the rater is also an author.

design_detail: Systematic review with random-effects meta-analysis (Review Manager 5.4.1, inverse variance) of placebo-controlled randomized trials of bupropion, alone or combined with another medication or psychosocial treatment, for amphetamine-type stimulant use disorder diagnosed by DSM-IV or DSM-5; PROSPERO CRD42022362962; searched to 31 October 2022. Eight trials (nine reports, because the two stages of Trivedi et al., 2021, were entered separately); 1239 participants as counted by the review. Main outcome: the proportion of amphetamine-positive urine samples (or positive weeks), pooled as a risk ratio; secondary outcomes retention, adherence, craving, addiction severity, depressive symptoms, dropout after adverse events and serious adverse events.
can_establish: The direction and rough size of the difference between bupropion and placebo in the share of amphetamine-positive urine samples, and in retention, adherence, craving, depression and adverse events, across the trials published to October 2022, with the review's own GRADE ratings.
cannot_establish: A precise effect of bupropion on use (the urine outcome counts each of 15,664 samples as an independent observation, so its intervals are too narrow); any effect on abstinence or on how many people stop using (not analysed); the effect of bupropion alone apart from its combination with naltrexone (about half of the review's participants come from one combination trial); absolute effects (no event rates are given in the article); or effects beyond 12 weeks.

sample.recruitment: Database search of MEDLINE, CINAHL, PsycINFO, EBM Reviews, EMBASE, PubMed and Web of Science, six trial registries, Google Scholar and the FDA, Health Canada and EMA websites, plus reference lists, to 31 October 2022; strategies designed by a librarian and peer-reviewed with the PRESS checklist (2.2, p. 2). 2623 records, 2142 screened, 35 sought in full text, 34 assessed, 8 trials included (Figure 1, p. 4). Primary trials: seven in the USA and one in Iran, run between 2003 and 2019 (Table 1, p. 5).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: randomized placebo-controlled trials with a bupropion arm at any dose, with or without another medication (such as naltrexone) or psychosocial treatment, in people with amphetamine-type stimulant use disorder diagnosed by DSM-IV or DSM-5; reports in English, Spanish, Portuguese, German, Arabic, Persian or French. Excluded: open-label, human-laboratory and animal studies, and trials with fewer than five participants per arm (2.3, p. 2).
sample.demographics: Trials of 19 to 403 participants; mean or median ages 17.5 to 42 years (one adolescent pilot, Heinzerling et al., 2013); 42% to 100% men (two trials in men only, Das et al., 2010, and Ghoreishi et al., 2017). Study conditions: bupropion SR 300 mg daily for 8 or 12 weeks in seven trials; 450 mg daily with injectable naltrexone for two 6-week stages in Trivedi et al. (2021). Psychosocial co-interventions are listed for six trials and given as not available for Ghoreishi et al. (2017) and Trivedi et al. (2021) (Table 1, p. 5).
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level; retention was pooled as an outcome (seven reports, 786 participants).
sample.selection_effects: Two trials contributed no urine data because their results were unavailable after the authors were contacted: Anderson et al. (2015), with 204 participants the largest bupropion-alone trial, and Ghoreishi et al. (2017), with 50 (Table 2, p. 6). The urine outcome therefore rests on five bupropion-alone trials with 357 participants (editors' sum from Table 1) and on the two stages of the naltrexone-plus-bupropion trial (403 people, of whom the 225 placebo non-responders re-randomized in stage 2 are entered again). The authors note that trials excluded many people with physical and mental comorbidity and included few women.

exposure.measurement: Bupropion or placebo as assigned in the primary trials.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions in the primary trials: bupropion SR 300 mg daily by mouth for 8 to 12 weeks (seven trials); 450 mg daily by mouth with extended-release injectable naltrexone every 3 weeks for two 6-week stages (Trivedi et al., 2021) (Table 1 and its footnotes, p. 5).
exposure.polysubstance: Not analysed; the authors note that most trials did not report other substance use disorders such as opioid or alcohol use disorder, so the results may not apply to people who use several drugs (4.1, p. 10).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: Placebo in each primary trial, with the same co-interventions as the bupropion arm.
comparison.matching: Randomization within each trial; the review pools within-trial comparisons.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to randomized comparisons; whether participants used amphetamine or methamphetamine was not distinguished across trials (4.1, p. 10).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not reported.

outcomes.instruments: Urine tests for amphetamine or methamphetamine during the randomized phase (proportion of positive samples; positive weeks in Elkashef et al., 2008; derived from a treatment-effectiveness score, the mean number of negative urine samples, in the two Heinzerling trials); retention to the end of the randomized phase; adherence by pill counts or MEMS caps; craving by visual analogue scale or Brief Substance Craving Scale at week 4 and at end of treatment; Addiction Severity Index sub-scores; depressive symptoms (HAM-D, BDI, PHQ-9); dropout after adverse events; serious adverse events. Self-reported use, withdrawal, anxiety and cognition were planned but dropped for lack of data (2.4, p. 3; Table 2, p. 6).
outcomes.validity_norms: Urine testing is objective; the pooled proportion combines collection once, twice or three times a week, which the review treats as comparable (3.3, p. 4). Primary trials were appraised with RoB 2 (cited as Higgins et al., 2011) in duplicate, and each outcome was rated with GRADE in duplicate (2.6, p. 3).
outcomes.operationalization: Benefit on use is a lower proportion of amphetamine-positive urine samples (or positive weeks) on bupropion than on placebo, pooled across trials as a risk ratio in which each urine sample counts as one observation (2.4, p. 3; 3.4.1, p. 4; Table 3, p. 7).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; P of .05 or less was used for each of 15 pooled estimates (eight outcomes, with addiction severity split into seven sub-scores) and for four sets of subgroup analyses per outcome (2.7, p. 3; Tables 3 and 4).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Title and abstract screening, full-text selection, data extraction, risk-of-bias assessment and GRADE were each done independently by two reviewers with consensus (2.3, 2.5, 2.6, pp. 2–3).

analysis.effect_sizes: Urine outcome (7 reports, 15,664 samples): RR 0.90 (95% CI 0.84 to 0.96), P < .001, I² 89%, GRADE very low; excluding the trial at high risk of bias, 0.87 (0.83 to 0.92); excluding Elkashef et al. (positive weeks), 0.91 (0.85 to 0.97). By medication (Table 4): bupropion 300 mg without naltrexone, 5 trials, 0.90 (0.81 to 1.00); 450 mg with naltrexone, the 2 stages of Trivedi et al., 0.92 (0.89 to 0.94); difference between subgroups not significant. By duration: 12-week trials (4) 0.85 (0.78 to 0.93) vs shorter trials (Trivedi's two stages and Heinzerling et al., 2013) 0.98 (0.89 to 1.08), a significant subgroup difference. Less-than-daily use (2 trials) 1.09 (0.56 to 2.11). Retention (7 reports, 786 participants): RR 0.97 (0.89 to 1.05), I² 6%, GRADE high. Adherence (6 reports, 119,680 pills): RR 0.91 (0.84 to 0.99), favouring placebo, I² 99%, GRADE very low. Craving at week 4 (4 reports, 373): SMD 0.04 (−0.16 to 0.24), I² 0%, GRADE moderate; at end of treatment (6 reports, 939): SMD −0.38 (−0.63 to −0.13), I² 64%, all six at high risk of bias, GRADE very low. Depressive symptoms (5 reports, 874): SMD −0.06 (−0.26 to 0.14). Addiction Severity Index legal status (2 reports, 148): SMD −0.47 (−0.83 to −0.11); six other sub-scores not significant. Dropout after adverse events (4 reports, 391): RD 0.03 (−0.01 to 0.07). Serious adverse events (8 reports, 1189): RD −0.01 (−0.02 to 0.01), GRADE low. No tau², prediction intervals or event rates are given in the article.
analysis.covariates: Not applicable; subgroup analyses by co-medication with naltrexone and dose, baseline frequency of use, sex and treatment duration, all at study level (2.7.2, p. 3; Table 4, p. 9).
analysis.preregistration_detail: PROSPERO CRD42022362962, registered on 7 October 2022, after a limited scoping search and before the full search (to 31 October 2022); the protocol is Appendix 1 (not read) (2.1, p. 2). Declared deviation: four planned outcomes (self-reported use, withdrawal, anxiety and cognition) dropped for lack of poolable data (2.4, p. 3). Whether the subgroup and sensitivity analyses were planned is not stated in the article.
analysis.selective_reporting: Per-trial risk-of-bias judgments, forest plots, funnel plots, GRADE tables and the list of excluded studies are only in the appendices, which were not read. The largest bupropion-alone trial (Anderson et al., 2015) and Ghoreishi et al. (2017) are absent from the main outcome because their urine data were unavailable (Table 2, p. 6).
analysis.power: Not applicable; several pooled outcomes rest on two to four reports.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Across seven reports, the share of amphetamine-positive urine samples was about 10% lower in relative terms on bupropion (RR 0.90, 0.84 to 0.96), with very high heterogeneity (I² 89%) and very low certainty by the review's own GRADE. Each urine sample is treated as an independent observation, so all the urine intervals are too narrow. For bupropion alone (five trials, 357 participants) the estimate is 0.90 (0.81 to 1.00). About half of the review's participants come from one trial that combined bupropion with naltrexone, with 225 of its participants counted twice. Retention did not differ (0.97, 0.89 to 1.05), adherence was lower on bupropion, and no absolute rates are reported.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Abstract and Conclusion report a significant, modest reduction in use and craving rated as very low-quality evidence, larger in men (craving) and with longer treatment (use); the Conclusion adds that the clinical relevance of such a small effect should be verified, a fair caution, and the Discussion acknowledges that the combination trial may have pulled results towards benefit (pp. 1, 10). But the finding in men rests on one men-only trial at high risk of bias for craving (Ghoreishi et al., 2017) (Discussion, 9th paragraph, p. 10), and the duration finding compares 12-week bupropion-alone trials with the 6-week stages of the naltrexone combination plus one 19-person adolescent pilot, so duration is confounded with medication and population (Table 4, p. 9). The total of 1239 participants counts 225 people twice, and the unit-of-analysis problem behind the urine and adherence intervals is not mentioned.

timeline.event: Bhatt et al.: in a meta-analysis of psychostimulants, bupropion did not increase urine-verified abstinence at the end of treatment (bupropion subgroup OR 1.12, 0.54 to 2.33); this review notes that Bhatt et al. analysed abstinence, not the share of positive samples, and predates the 2021 combination trial.
Siefried et al.: systematic review described by this review as showing possible benefits of bupropion on use that were not statistically significant in the included trials.
Trivedi et al.: two-stage trial of injectable naltrexone plus bupropion, entered here as two reports.
Apuy et al.: meta-analysis of bupropion with cognitive behavioural therapy (five studies), described by this review as finding no overall reduction in recurrence of use (not read).
This review: RR 0.90 (0.84 to 0.96) for the share of positive urine samples across seven reports; 0.90 (0.81 to 1.00) for bupropion alone.

replication.where_it_stands: On the share of positive urine samples, the pooled estimate leans slightly towards bupropion, but the method overstates its precision and much of the estimate comes from the naltrexone combination trial; for bupropion alone the interval reaches no effect. No difference has been shown in end-of-treatment abstinence (Bhatt et al., 2016) or in retention (this review).

funding.funder: Canadian Institutes of Health Research (grant REN-181675), Université de Montréal and the Centre de recherche du Centre hospitalier de l'Université de Montréal (CRCHUM); the sponsor had no role in conceptualization, data acquisition and analysis, interpretation of results, or drafting and editing (Funding sources/sponsors, pp. 10–11). Individual authors' salary or career awards are listed in the Acknowledgements (p. 11).
funding.declared_conflicts: As printed (Declaration of Competing Interest, p. 11): PB is site principal investigator for an upcoming trial of psychostimulants for methamphetamine use disorder; CGS is a consultant at Clearmind Medicine; NE has NHMRC funding for a study of lisdexamfetamine for methamphetamine use disorder; KS has NCCRED funding for a pilot study of lisdexamfetamine for methamphetamine withdrawal; BLF reports funding, in-kind donations, study medication or consultancy from Pfizer, Indivior, Aurora Cannabis, Bioprojet Pharma, Brainsway, Canopy Growth, Alcohol Countermeasure Systems, Alkermes, Universal Ibogaine and Shionogi (printed 'Shinogi'); DJA receives study material from Cardiol Therapeutics and Exka for trials funded by the Quebec Ministry of Health and Social Services. All other authors declare no conflict of interest.
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from Montréal (CRCHUM, Université de Montréal), Toronto (CAMH and the University of Toronto), Vancouver (BC Centre on Substance Use, UBC) and Sydney (St Vincent's Hospital, NCCRED, NDARC). No review author appears among the authors of the included trials in the reference list; Steven Shoptaw is thanked for providing results from his trial; the reference list shows him as an author of five of the eight trials (Das et al., 2010; Heinzerling et al., 2013 and 2014; Shoptaw et al., 2008; Trivedi et al., 2021), so the trials are not fully independent of one another. Walter Ling is an author of Elkashef et al. (2008), Shoptaw et al. (2008) and Trivedi et al. (2021), and Elkashef et al. (2008) shares eight authors with Anderson et al. (2015) (Elkashef, Anderson, Li, Holmes, Chiang, Kahn, Campbell and Haning); only Ghoreishi et al. (2017), from Iran, shares no author with the others, and it gave no urine data. Every one of the seven urine reports therefore shares at least one author with another (reference list, pp. 11–12). Ezard and Siefried are authors of the 2020 systematic review that this review discusses.

what_would_settle_it: A participant-level meta-analysis of the bupropion-alone trials that analyses urine results within people (allowing for repeated samples) and reports abstinence and use days, or a large independent trial of bupropion alone with a urine-verified primary outcome and follow-up after treatment ends.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (DSM-IV or DSM-5 amphetamine-type stimulant use disorder), intervention (bupropion, alone or combined), comparator (placebo) and outcomes are specified (2.3, 2.4).

PROSPERO CRD42022362962, registered on 7 October 2022 before the full search, with the protocol in Appendix 1 (not read); the dropped outcomes are explained, but whether the subgroup and sensitivity analyses were planned is not stated.

The review states that it focuses on placebo-controlled randomized trials of efficacy and safety, and excludes open-label, laboratory and animal studies and trials with fewer than five per arm to limit small-sample bias; the explanation is brief.

Seven databases, six trial registries, grey literature, regulators' websites and reference lists, librarian-designed and peer-reviewed strategies, search about a year before online publication (31 October 2022; online 4 November 2023) and authors contacted for data; but reports were limited to seven languages without a stated reason (2.3, p. 2). AMSTAR 2 gives partial yes only when publication restrictions such as language are justified, so the item is not met.
Two reviewers screened titles and abstracts and assessed full texts independently, with consensus (2.3).
Two reviewers extracted independently, with consensus (2.5).

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: The article says the excluded full-text reports and the reasons are in Appendix 5, which was not read; Figure 1 gives the reasons with counts (17 duplicate study populations, 1 wrong population, 2 wrong comparator, 4 wrong design, 1 probable duplicate, 1 with fewer than five per group).

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 1 gives dates, country, size, age, sex, frequency of use, ADHD, medication and dose, duration and co-interventions; setting, recruitment source and whether participants used amphetamine or methamphetamine are not given.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: RoB 2 applied in duplicate, by outcome, which covers allocation concealment, blinding and selection of the reported result; per-trial judgments are only in Appendix 8 (not read), and the tool is cited with the 2011 paper describing the original Cochrane tool.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Not reported.

Random-effects inverse-variance pooling is appropriate in itself, but the main outcome pools per-arm counts of positive urine samples (15,664 samples) as if each sample were an independent observation, ignoring repeated measures within people, and adherence is pooled in the same way over 119,680 pills; the two stages of Trivedi et al. (2021) are entered as separate studies although the 225 stage-2 participants were already in stage 1. Both are unit-of-analysis errors that make intervals too narrow; heterogeneity of 89% to 99% is pooled without a prediction interval.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: Sensitivity analyses excluding trials at high risk of bias are reported for use (RR 0.87) and adherence (RR 0.89) (3.4.1, 3.4.3).

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: Risk of bias and the very low GRADE ratings are carried into the Abstract, Discussion and Conclusion, which call the evidence low quality and the effect small.
I² is reported for every outcome, subgroup analyses explore it and the Discussion says they explain only part of it (Discussion, 10th paragraph).

Funnel plots for outcomes with five or more reports, with asymmetry recorded for each outcome in Table 3 and carried into GRADE; with five to eight reports and visual inspection only, the investigation has little power, and its likely impact is discussed only for adherence and depression.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding, sponsor role and each author's competing interests are declared.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Provisional, because item 7 can only be judged from Appendix 5, which was not read; but no answer to item 7 could raise the rating. Two critical items are not met. The search (item 4) is wide but limits reports to seven languages without a stated reason, and AMSTAR 2 gives partial yes only when publication restrictions are justified. The statistical methods (item 11) fail because the main urine outcome and the adherence outcome treat repeated measurements within people (urine samples, pills) as independent observations, and the re-randomized stage of the combination trial is entered as a separate study, so the intervals and P values for use are too optimistic. Two critical flaws give critically low confidence. The other critical items are met or partly met: the review is registered, selected and extracted in duplicate, appraised trials with RoB 2 and graded every outcome. It can be cited for the direction of the pooled urine result, for no difference in retention, for lower adherence on bupropion and for the frequency of adverse events; it should not be cited for a precise or statistically secure effect of bupropion on use, for bupropion alone apart from the naltrexone combination, or for abstinence.

key_findings.finding: Eight placebo-controlled trials, counted by the review as 1239 participants: 611 in seven trials of bupropion alone (300 mg daily) and 628 in the two stages of Trivedi et al. (2021, bupropion 450 mg daily with naltrexone), entered as two reports; stage 2 consisted of stage-1 placebo non-responders who were re-randomized.
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Results (p. 1); 3.2 Characteristics of included studies, 1st paragraph (begins p. 3); Table 1 and footnotes d and e (p. 5)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: the 225 stage-2 participants were already among the 403 in stage 1, so the trials enrolled about 1014 distinct people (611 + 403), not 1239.

key_findings.finding: Main outcome, amphetamine-positive urine samples (7 reports, 15,664 samples or weeks): RR 0.90 (95% CI 0.84 to 0.96), P < .001, I² 89%; risk of bias low in 3, some concerns in 3, high in 1; minor funnel-plot asymmetry; GRADE very low. Excluding the trial at high risk of bias: 0.87 (0.83 to 0.92); excluding Elkashef et al. (2008), which reported positive weeks: 0.91 (0.85 to 0.97).
key_findings.locator: 3.4.1 Amphetamine-type stimulant use by UA, 1st paragraph (p. 4); Table 3, row ATS use by urinalysis (p. 7)
key_findings.note: The unit of analysis is the urine sample, not the person (see reporting issues), so the interval is too narrow.

key_findings.finding: Subgroups of the urine outcome: bupropion 300 mg without naltrexone (Das 2010, Elkashef 2008, Heinzerling 2013, Heinzerling 2014, Shoptaw 2008) RR 0.90 (0.81 to 1.00); 450 mg with naltrexone (the two stages of Trivedi 2021) 0.92 (0.89 to 0.94), difference not significant. Four 12-week trials 0.85 (0.78 to 0.93) vs shorter trials (Trivedi's two stages and Heinzerling 2013) 0.98 (0.89 to 1.08), a significant difference; two trials of less-than-daily use 1.09 (0.56 to 2.11); men-only (Das 2010) 0.80 (0.71 to 0.90).
key_findings.locator: 3.4.1, 2nd paragraph (p. 4); Table 4, column ATS use by UA, and its footnotes 1 to 10 (p. 9)
key_findings.note: Editors' sum from Table 1: the five bupropion-alone trials in the urine outcome enrolled 357 participants (73 + 151 + 30 + 19 + 84). Table 4 marks the bupropion-alone estimate, 0.90 (0.81 to 1.00), as individually significant (P < 0.05), so the review counts it as a reduction; at the printed precision its interval reaches 1, and with urine samples as the unit a person-level interval would be wider.

key_findings.finding: The urine outcome pools, for each arm, the overall proportion of positive urine samples (or positive weeks); samples were collected weekly in one trial, twice weekly in two and three times weekly in three. Urine results of Anderson et al. (2015; 204 participants) and Ghoreishi et al. (2017; 50) were unavailable after the authors were contacted.
key_findings.locator: 2.4 Outcome measures, 2nd paragraph (p. 3); 3.3 Selected outcomes, 1st paragraph (p. 4); Table 1 (p. 5); Table 2, column ATS use, cells for Anderson 2015 and Ghoreishi 2017 coloured as unavailable (p. 6)

key_findings.finding: Retention (7 reports, 786 participants): RR 0.97 (0.89 to 1.05), I² 6%, GRADE high. Adherence by pill count (6 reports, 119,680 pills): RR 0.91 (0.84 to 0.99), favouring placebo, I² 99%, major funnel-plot asymmetry, GRADE very low; 0.89 (0.81 to 0.98) without trials at high risk of bias.
key_findings.locator: 3.4.2 Retention in treatment (begins p. 4); 3.4.3 Treatment adherence (p. 6); Table 3 (p. 7)
key_findings.note: The retention pool has seven of the eight reports with retention data; stage 1 of Trivedi et al. (2021) appears to have been left out (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Craving: at week 4 (4 reports, 373 participants) SMD 0.04 (−0.16 to 0.24), I² 0%, GRADE moderate; at the end of treatment (6 reports, 939) SMD −0.38 (−0.63 to −0.13), I² 64%, all six at high risk of bias, GRADE very low; in the one men-only trial −1.26 (−1.87 to −0.65).
key_findings.note: For Trivedi et al. (2021) the end-of-treatment craving and depression scores were built by adding the reported change to the baseline score and using the baseline SD (3.3, p. 4; Table 2 footnote, p. 6).

key_findings.finding: Depressive symptoms (5 reports, 874): SMD −0.06 (−0.26 to 0.14), I² 44%. Addiction Severity Index (2 reports, 148): legal status SMD −0.47 (−0.83 to −0.11), six other sub-scores not significant. Dropout after adverse events (4 reports, 391): RD 0.03 (−0.01 to 0.07). Serious adverse events (8 reports, 1189): RD −0.01 (−0.02 to 0.01), GRADE low.

Methods: search to 31 October 2022 in seven databases, six trial registries and grey literature; PROSPERO registration on 7 October 2022; screening, extraction, RoB 2 and GRADE in duplicate; random-effects inverse-variance pooling in Review Manager 5.4.1; funnel plots for outcomes with five or more studies; reports limited to seven languages.

The authors contrast their result with Bhatt et al. (2016), who found no effect of bupropion on sustained abstinence, noting that Bhatt et al. analysed different outcomes and did not include Trivedi et al. (2021); they add that the large Trivedi trial may have pulled the results towards benefit, although its estimate did not differ significantly from the other trials in subgroup analyses.
key_findings.locator: 4. Discussion, 3rd paragraph (p. 8) and 10th paragraph (p. 10); 4.1 Strengths and limitations (p. 10)

key_findings.finding: Conclusion: bupropion may have modest benefits for amphetamine-type stimulant use disorder, the clinical relevance of such a small effect should be verified, and the overall quality of evidence is low.

reporting_issues.issue: The review's total of 1239 participants adds the 403 participants of stage 1 and the 225 of stage 2 of Trivedi et al. (2021), but the stage-2 participants were stage-1 placebo non-responders who were re-randomized (3.2; Table 1 footnote e), so 225 people are counted twice; editors' calculation: the trials enrolled about 1014 distinct people.
reporting_issues.consequence: The evidence base is overstated by about a fifth, and the two stages are not independent samples; entering both as separate studies is a unit-of-analysis error.

reporting_issues.issue: The main outcome is analysed with urine samples as the unit: per-arm counts of positive samples among 15,664 samples are pooled as risk ratios as if each sample were an independent event (2.4; 2.7.1; 3.4.1; Table 3). Repeated samples from the same person are correlated. Adherence is pooled the same way over 119,680 pills. The review does not state its unit of analysis, but Table 3 gives N as samples and pills, and Table 4 gives the 30-participant men-only trial (Das et al., 2010) a urine interval of 0.80 (0.71 to 0.90), narrower than a yes-or-no outcome in 30 people could produce (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: The confidence intervals and P values of every urine and adherence estimate (overall, sensitivity and subgroup) are too narrow; the statistical significance of RR 0.90 (0.84 to 0.96), and of 0.90 (0.81 to 1.00) for bupropion alone, cannot be taken at face value. The editors cannot recompute them without participant-level data.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 4 shows that adding Heinzerling et al. (2013), a 19-person adolescent pilot, moves two pooled estimates noticeably: the 12-week bupropion-alone trials give 0.85 (0.78 to 0.93) and all five bupropion-alone trials 0.90 (0.81 to 1.00); Trivedi's two stages give 0.92 (0.89 to 0.94) and the shorter-trials subgroup, which adds Heinzerling et al. (2013), 0.98 (0.89 to 1.08).
reporting_issues.consequence: A pilot this small can carry such weight only if its many urine samples are counted as independent observations under high heterogeneity; the subgroup estimates, including the duration finding in the Abstract, are fragile. The forest plots (Appendix 9) were not read.

reporting_issues.issue: RoB 2 is cited with Higgins et al. (2011), which describes the original Cochrane risk-of-bias tool; the judgments in Table 3 use RoB 2's words. Table 3 also rates the dropout outcome 'Medium', which is not a GRADE level, and the text cites the GRADE table once as Appendix 8 and elsewhere as Appendix 10.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor citation and labelling errors; the dropout rating is presumably moderate.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 marks retention as available for eight reports, including both stages of Trivedi et al. (2021), but the pooled retention analysis has seven reports and 786 participants (3.4.2, p. 4; Table 3, p. 7), and Table 4 lists one 450-mg report. The eight reports enrolled 1189 people by Table 1 (p. 5); 786 is that total less the 403 of stage 1 (editors' calculation), so stage 1 appears to have been left out without comment.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the retention estimate (0.97, 0.89 to 1.05) probably omits the larger stage of the combination trial, which avoids counting stage-2 participants twice in this outcome, but the choice is not explained.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says that Trivedi et al. combined 450 mg bupropion with naloxone (p. 10); the trial used extended-release injectable naltrexone (Table 1 footnote c, p. 5; Introduction, p. 2).
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical error with no consequence for the results.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 4 the urine subgroup with mixed use frequency is printed with N = 5, but its footnote 3 lists three trials (Das et al., 2010; Elkashef et al., 2008; Shoptaw et al., 2008); the other two reports are presumably the two stages of Trivedi et al. (2021), the only urine reports not in the less-than-daily subgroup (footnote 4).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor labelling omission; the subgroup composition can be inferred.
