design_detail: Population birth cohort (Christchurch Health and Development Study; 1265 children born in Christchurch, New Zealand, in 1977). Self-reported use of methamphetamine or other amphetamine-type stimulants for the period since the previous interview, and self-reported psychotic symptoms over the past month at ages 18, 21 and 25 and since the previous assessment at 30 and 35, both reported at the interviews at ages 18, 21, 25, 30 and 35 (use periods 16–18 to 30–35); population-averaged logistic and negative binomial generalized estimating equations, unadjusted and adjusted for fixed childhood, family and adolescent confounders and for time-varying covariates; dose-response by lifetime highest frequency of use; comparison of symptoms at 30–35 by past and current use. Read: all pages of the online-first PDF (pp. 1–8, pages numbered as printed on that version; print pages 987–994); Figure 1 is an image whose values were not extracted; Supplementary Tables S1 to S3 not read.
can_establish: Whether, in a general-population cohort, periods of methamphetamine use go with more self-reported psychotic symptoms at the same interview after adjustment for measured childhood, family, adolescent and time-varying factors, and whether that excess is concentrated in frequent use.
cannot_establish: Which came first (use and symptoms were reported at the same interviews, and at ages 18, 21 and 25 over different windows: use since the previous interview, symptoms over the past month); effects on clinical psychotic disorder (the outcome is self-reported symptom items with high base rates); effects of very frequent use (few participants used often); and whether the findings hold outside one city's 1977 birth cohort.

sample.recruitment: Birth cohort of 1265 children (635 male, 630 female) born in Christchurch, New Zealand, in 1977, studied at birth, at 4 months, yearly to age 16 and at 18, 21, 25, 30 and 35 (p. 2).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Cohort members with at least one completed wave of data at ages 18 to 35 (p. 3).
sample.demographics: 635 male and 630 female at birth; the analysed samples (79–82% of the surviving cohort at each age) under-represented people from socially disadvantaged backgrounds (low parental education, low socioeconomic status, single parenthood) (pp. 3–4).
sample.attrition: 18–21% of the surviving cohort missing at each wave; the GEE models used everyone with at least one wave, and weighting for the pattern of missing data gave essentially the same results (p. 4); the authors note that people with psychotic symptoms, particularly paranoid ideas, are less likely to be retained (p. 7).
sample.selection_effects: Little selection into the study (a birth cohort); selective loss of disadvantaged participants, and possibly of people with paranoid symptoms, could bias estimates toward the null if those groups also used methamphetamine more; frequent use is rare (51 people ever used at least weekly).

exposure.measurement: Self-report at each interview of any use of 'methamphetamine, speed, P, ice, etc' since the previous interview, and how often; amphetamine-type stimulants were not distinguished, but the authors state that methamphetamine was by far the most common in New Zealand over the period (p. 2). Use or no use in each period for the repeated-measures models; lifetime highest frequency (never, once or twice, up to about monthly, at least weekly) for the dose-response model.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Use in the period: 3.3% (ages 16–18), 5.5% (18–21), 22.4% (21–25), 14.4% (25–30), 7.8% (30–35); ever 28.8% (Table 1, p. 4). Highest frequency: once or twice 124 (11.9%), up to about monthly 117 (11.3%), at least weekly 51 (4.9%) (Table 3, p. 7). Amount and route not measured.
exposure.polysubstance: Frequency of cannabis use and alcohol use disorder were time-varying covariates in the fully adjusted model; other illicit drug use was not adjusted for, beyond adolescent affiliation with substance-using peers (pp. 2–3).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable; use and symptoms were reported at the same interviews (symptoms over the past month at ages 18, 21 and 25, and since the previous assessment at 30 and 35).

comparison.controls: Within the cohort: periods with and without reported use (population-averaged estimates), and people by lifetime highest frequency against those who never used.
comparison.matching: None; regression adjustment. Fixed confounders: family living standards; family instability; parental intimate-partner violence; parental alcohol problems, criminality and illicit drug use; parental bonding; childhood sexual abuse and physical punishment; sex; childhood conduct and attention problems; adolescent self-esteem, novelty seeking, conduct disorder, anxiety disorder and affiliation with delinquent or substance-using peers. Time-varying covariates: major depression, anxiety disorder, alcohol use disorder, frequency of cannabis use and life stress (pp. 2–3).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Family history of psychosis and earlier psychotic experiences are not among the listed covariates, and genetic liability is unmeasured; the E-value indicates that an unmeasured confounder associated with both exposure and outcome by an odds ratio of about 1.6 could explain the fully adjusted association (p. 4).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Periods without methamphetamine use include use of other drugs; cannabis and alcohol are adjusted for, other drugs are not.

outcomes.instruments: Psychotic symptom items from the Symptom Checklist 90 (ages 18, 21 and 25; past month) and from the Diagnostic Interview Schedule (ages 30 and 35; since the previous assessment), covering hallucinations, delusions, paranoid ideation and related symptoms; the items are in Supplementary Tables S1 and S2, not read (p. 2).
outcomes.validity_norms: Coefficient alpha 0.71 to 0.75; an earlier factor analysis found the SCL-90 items formed one scale (p. 2). The authors note that some SCL-90 items (for example feeling lonely with others) arguably do not capture genuine psychotic experiences; 35.2% to 41.8% reported at least one symptom in the periods to age 25 (Table 1; p. 7).
outcomes.operationalization: At least one symptom in the period (dichotomous) and number of symptoms (count); not a diagnosis of psychotic disorder (p. 2).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; two outcome measures at three levels of adjustment, plus a dose-response model, a comparison of past and current use and a sensitivity analysis.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable; exposure and outcome were both self-reported in the same interview.

analysis.effect_sizes: Any use vs none, at least one psychotic symptom: OR 1.88 (95% CI 1.55–2.30) unadjusted; 2.14 (1.70–2.71) adjusted for fixed confounders; 1.33 (1.03–1.72) adjusted also for time-varying covariates (p = 0.033). Number of symptoms: IRR 1.50 (1.26–1.78), 1.52 (1.26–1.85) and 1.24 (1.02–1.50) (p = 0.030) (Table 2, p. 6; p. 4). E-value 1.571 (confidence limit 1.11) (p. 4). Dose-response, adjusted for fixed confounders only: once or twice 1.37 (0.86–2.17), up to about monthly 1.32 (0.82–2.11), at least weekly 2.85 (1.21–6.69; p = 0.016) (Table 3, p. 7). Population attributable fraction 8.0% (2.2%–14.7%), assuming causality (p. 6). Symptoms at 30–35: 5.1% of those who never used (n = 672), 7.4% of those who used only before 30 (n = 215), 15.9% of those who used before 30 and at 30–35 (n = 69), p = 0.0009 (Table 4, p. 7).
analysis.covariates: Fixed confounders and time-varying covariates as listed under comparison. The dose-response model used only the fixed confounders that were significant predictors in Model 1: family socioeconomic status, sex, child IQ, adolescent anxiety disorder, childhood physical and sexual abuse, deviant peer affiliation and attention problems (p. 6).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or analysis plan is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: All three levels of adjustment are reported for both outcomes; the dose-response estimate that the abstract reports beside the fully adjusted one comes from a model with a smaller covariate set chosen by statistical significance and no time-varying covariates.
analysis.power: With an effective sample of 1056, at least 90% power to detect odds ratios of 1.2 (p. 3); sparse frequent use prevented repeated-measures dose-response models (p. 3).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Periods of any methamphetamine use went with modestly higher odds of self-reported psychotic symptoms at the same interview after full adjustment (OR 1.33, 1.03–1.72); the excess was concentrated in the 5% who had ever used at least weekly (OR 2.85, adjusted for fixed confounders only); people who had used only before age 30 reported symptoms at 30–35 about as often as those who never used (7.4% vs 5.1%).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The conclusion states that "methamphetamine use is an independent risk factor for psychosis in the general population" (p. 7). Gaps: (1) the outcome is self-reported psychotic-like symptoms with high base rates, not psychosis as a disorder; (2) use and symptoms were reported at the same interviews (at ages 18 to 25 over different windows, although the abstract says both covered the period since the previous interview), so the phrase risk factor implies an order the design cannot show; (3) the abstract places the at-least-weekly estimate (2.85) directly after the estimate adjusted for concurrent cannabis use, but the 2.85 is adjusted only for fixed childhood, family and adolescent factors; (4) the discussion's statement that no long-term persistence was found among people with frequent use rests on Table 4, which groups people by any use, not by frequency; (5) the abstract calls the comparison at 30–35 incidence, but Table 4 gives the share reporting symptoms in that period, including people with earlier symptoms. The authors acknowledge the measurement problem and the sparse frequent use (p. 7).

timeline.event: Prospective within-person cohort of people who use methamphetamine showing dose-related psychotic symptoms (McKetin et al., 2013), sharing an author with this study.
Systematic review of risk factors for methamphetamine-associated psychosis: frequency of use the factor with the strongest evidence (Arunogiri et al., 2018).
Meta-analysis of mental-health outcomes of amphetamine use, mostly from clinical and criminal-justice samples (McKetin et al., 2019); this cohort is not in it (search May 2017).
This study (online 2021, print 2023): the first longitudinal general-population estimate, by the authors' account (p. 6).
Ten-year retrospective cohort of incident psychosis in people with illicit amphetamine records (Huang et al., 2022); identified by the currency check of 2026-10-16, not yet read.

replication.where_it_stands: The only general-population longitudinal estimate read so far. It agrees in direction with the clinical literature and gives a smaller association after adjustment for concurrent cannabis use and other time-varying factors, concentrated in frequent use. It shares an author (McKetin) with the 2013 cohort and the 2019 meta-analysis but uses an independent sample.

funding.funder: The Christchurch Health and Development Study is funded by the Health Research Council of New Zealand (Programme Grant 16/600) (p. 8).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors report no conflicts of interest (p. 8).
funding.affiliations_note: University of Otago (Christchurch and Wellington) and the National Drug and Alcohol Research Centre, University of New South Wales; R. McKetin is also an author of the 2013 within-person cohort and of the 2019 meta-analysis that this paper compares itself with.

what_would_settle_it: A pooled analysis of several general-population cohorts with frequent assessments, clinically validated psychosis outcomes, measured family history of psychosis and other drug use, and enough frequent methamphetamine use to model within-person changes in frequency, so that the timing of use relative to symptom onset and recovery after stopping can be estimated.

domains.note: Rich prospective adjustment for childhood, family and adolescent factors and for concurrent cannabis use, alcohol use disorder, depression, anxiety and life stress; family history of psychosis and other drug use not adjusted. Adjusting for depression and anxiety, which may follow from use or accompany psychotic symptoms, could bias toward the null. The dose-response estimate (2.85) is adjusted for fixed confounders only and on its own would be at high risk in this domain.
Self-reported use over periods of up to five years, without biological verification; amphetamine-type stimulants not distinguished; coarse frequency categories.
Birth cohort followed from before exposure; losses at follow-up are judged under missing data.
No intervention relevant to the question.
18–21% of the surviving cohort missing at each wave, under-representing disadvantaged participants; weighting gave the same pattern; possible differential loss of people with paranoid symptoms.

Self-reported symptom items reported in the same interview as drug use, and at ages 18, 21 and 25 for the past month while use covered the years since the previous interview, so exposure and outcome windows differ in three of the five waves (the paper says the difference was corrected in the analyses without saying how, p. 2); the instrument changed between ages 25 and 30 (the scale-by-exposure interaction was not significant, p = 0.13); some items of doubtful validity, though removing two of them did not change the results.
No registered analysis plan; the dose-response model uses a covariate set chosen by statistical significance; otherwise every adjustment level and both outcomes are reported.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No domain is at high risk, but concerns in five domains bear on a modest estimate (OR 1.33, lower limit 1.03): unmeasured confounding of the size the E-value describes (about 1.6), same-interview self-report of exposure and outcome and differential attrition could each move it to the null or beyond, which substantially lowers confidence in it as an estimate of the effect of use (ROBINS-E: some concerns in several domains). A second reader may reasonably judge some concerns overall; the study remains the best general-population evidence read so far. It may be cited for the adjusted association with self-reported psychotic symptoms and for its concentration in frequent use, not for causation or for psychotic disorder.

key_findings.finding: Birth cohort of 1265 (635 male, 630 female) born in Christchurch in 1977; 1025, 1011, 1003, 987 and 962 analysed at ages 18, 21, 25, 30 and 35 (79–82% of the surviving cohort), under-representing socially disadvantaged backgrounds; weighting for missing data gave essentially the same results.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Participants (p. 2); Sample size and sample bias (pp. 3–4)

key_findings.finding: Use in the period: 3.3% (ages 16–18), 5.5% (18–21), 22.4% (21–25), 14.4% (25–30), 7.8% (30–35), ever 28.8%; at least one psychotic symptom: 35.2%, 41.8%, 36.4%, 9.9% and 6.4%, ever 66.3%; the drop after age 25 partly reflects the change of instrument.
key_findings.locator: Table 1; Results › Rates of methamphetamine use and psychotic symptoms over time

key_findings.finding: Any methamphetamine use in a period vs none, odds of reporting at least one psychotic symptom at the same interview: 1.88 (1.55–2.30) unadjusted; 2.14 (1.70–2.71) adjusted for fixed childhood, family and adolescent confounders; 1.33 (1.03–1.72) adjusted also for time-varying major depression, anxiety disorder, alcohol use disorder, frequency of cannabis use and life stress (p = 0.033). Number of symptoms: IRR 1.50 (1.26–1.78), 1.52 (1.26–1.85), 1.24 (1.02–1.50) (p = 0.030).
key_findings.locator: Methods › Time-dynamic covariate factors (p. 3); Results › Associations … before and after control for covariates, numbered points 1 and 2 (p. 4); Table 2 (p. 6)
key_findings.note: Table 2 calls the fully adjusted model Model 2; the results text calls it Model 3.

key_findings.finding: The E-value for unmeasured confounding was 1.571 (confidence limit 1.11); the scale-by-exposure interaction was not significant (p = 0.13).
key_findings.locator: Results › Associations … before and after control for covariates, numbered points 3 and 4

key_findings.finding: Lifetime highest frequency (adjusted for fixed confounders only): once or twice 1.37 (0.86–2.17), up to about monthly 1.32 (0.82–2.11), at least weekly 2.85 (1.21–6.69; p = 0.016), against never (747, 71.9%); 51 people (4.9%) had ever used at least weekly.
key_findings.note: The model's covariates are childhood family socioeconomic status, sex, child IQ, adolescent anxiety disorder, childhood physical and sexual abuse, deviant peer affiliation and attention problems; child IQ is not among the confounders listed in the methods. The categories are not monotonic (1.37 for once or twice, 1.32 for up to about monthly, 2.85 for at least weekly), so the pattern is a contrast between at least weekly use (51 people) and the rest rather than a gradient.

key_findings.finding: Removing two SCL-90 items of doubtful face validity gave equivalent results; the population attributable fraction was 8.0% (2.2%–14.7%), assuming causality.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Population attributable fraction (PAF) estimate (p. 3); Results › Sensitivity analyses; Estimate of the population attributable fraction (p. 6)

key_findings.finding: At ages 30–35, at least one psychotic symptom was reported by 5.1% of those who never used (n = 672), 7.4% of those who used only before age 30 (n = 215) and 15.9% of those who used before 30 and at 30–35 (n = 69; Mantel-Haenszel p = 0.0009); among those with a symptom before 30, 6.3% (415), 8.3% (156) and 21.6% (51) (p = 0.001).
key_findings.locator: Results › Proximal/distal use of methamphetamine (p. 6); Table 4 (p. 7)
key_findings.note: Grouped by any use, not by frequency; the text describes the third group as having used both before age 35 and at 30–35. The never against past-only comparison is not tested separately: counts reconstructed from the percentages (34 of 672 and 16 of 215) give a relative risk of about 1.47 (95% CI about 0.83 to 2.6; editors' calculation), so the data do not exclude a moderate lasting excess, and the abstract's finding of no evidence for a persistent vulnerability is an absence of evidence.

key_findings.finding: The authors name as limitations the change of psychosis measure during follow-up, SCL-90 items that may not capture genuine psychotic experiences, a sample born in one place and year, likely lower retention of people with paranoid ideas, and sparse use and symptoms in later periods.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 labels the fully adjusted model Model 2, while the results text calls it Model 3 (numbered point 2).
reporting_issues.consequence: Labelling only; the 1.33 and 1.24 estimates come from the model with both fixed and time-varying covariates.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract reports the at-least-weekly odds ratio (2.85) immediately after the estimates adjusted for time-varying factors including concurrent cannabis use, but Table 3 is adjusted for fixed confounders only.
reporting_issues.consequence: The frequency gradient has not been adjusted for concurrent cannabis or alcohol use and should not be cited as if it had.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract describes the comparison at ages 30–35 as incidence of psychotic symptoms, but Table 4 gives the share reporting symptoms in that period, including people with earlier symptoms; the text describes the third group as having used before age 35 rather than before 30.
reporting_issues.consequence: The persistence analysis is a period prevalence by any past use; it does not test persistence after frequent use.

reporting_issues.issue: The covariates of the dose-response model include child IQ, which is not among the confounding factors listed in the methods.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the dose-response covariate set is not fully described where the confounders are defined.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says that at each interview participants reported their use and their psychotic symptoms for the period since the previous interview, but the Methods give the past month for symptoms at ages 18, 21 and 25 (since the previous assessment only at 30 and 35), and say the difference in time frames was corrected in the analyses without saying how.
reporting_issues.consequence: Exposure and outcome windows differ in three of the five waves; a claim should say that use and symptoms were reported at the same interviews, not for the same periods.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 gives the window of the highest frequency of use and of the symptom outcome as ages 18–35, while the Methods (p. 3) and the dose–response paragraph (p. 6) call it lifetime, ages 16–35.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor labelling inconsistency; whether use at 16–18 counts in the dose–response categories is unclear.

design_detail: Systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis (PROSPERO CRD42021286619; PRISMA and MOOSE; R metafor) of observational studies comparing positive- and negative-symptom severity between people with methamphetamine-induced psychosis and people with schizophrenia or a related disorder intended to be free of drug use: 12 studies, 624 vs 527 people; standardized mean differences (Hedges' g) from baseline or single-time scores; quality rated with a modified Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. Read: all nine pages; Table 1 and Figures 1 to 3 checked on the rendered pages, with the study values of the two forest plots read from the images; supplementary tables S1 to S5 and figures S1 to S12 not read.
can_establish: The average reported difference in positive- and negative-symptom scores between treated clinical groups with methamphetamine psychosis and with schizophrenia, across small samples published to December 2022.
cannot_establish: Whether the two conditions differ at onset or without treatment (most participants were treated and described as stable); whether any difference holds separately for acute and persistent methamphetamine psychosis (mixed in the pools); whether any symptom tells an individual's diagnosis (no diagnostic-accuracy data); and why any difference exists (cross-sectional comparisons).

sample.recruitment: PubMed, Embase and PsycINFO to 16 December 2022 (English, human, ages 18 to 65), with snowball searching of reference lists; 2052 records (pp. 182–183). Included studies came from Japan (3), Taiwan (2), Australia (2), China, Iran, Canada and South Africa (1 each) and one multinational WHO study (Australia, Japan, the Philippines, Thailand); mostly outpatients, five studies with both in- and outpatients (3.2, p. 184).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: observational studies of adults aged 18 to 65 with schizophrenia, schizoaffective or a related disorder by DSM or ICD, and of people currently using methamphetamine or with persistent psychotic symptoms after recent cessation of intoxication or acute withdrawal (within one month), methamphetamine being the primary or only drug. Excluded: reports of current or recent (within two years) use of other substances except tobacco (the text does not say to which group this applies); first-episode psychosis and mood disorders; case reports and qualitative studies (2.4, p. 183). Two studies of acute exacerbation after methamphetamine intake were excluded (Medhus 2013; Tomiyama 1990) (3.1).
sample.demographics: Mean ages 31.35 years (methamphetamine psychosis) and 32.46 years (schizophrenia); men 67.98% and 63.3%, which are unweighted means of the study percentages in Table 1 (editors' check); one study (Zhang 2018) was much younger (means 21.0 and 23.8 years) (3.1; 3.2; Table 1).
sample.attrition: Not applicable: baseline or single-time scores; follow-up data from the cohort and prospective studies were not used.
sample.selection_effects: Treated clinical samples described as stable, with mean antipsychotic doses of about 440 to 1,360 mg/day chlorpromazine equivalents where reported (Table 1); only five studies specified a minimum period of clinical stability (3.2). The methamphetamine-psychosis groups mix persistent psychosis after abstinence, psychosis with current use and lifetime substance-induced psychosis, and comparison groups were not always free of drug use (Hides 2015; Hajebi 2018; see comparison).

exposure.measurement: Diagnosis of methamphetamine-induced or -associated psychosis by DSM-III, DSM-IV(-TR), DSM-5, ICD-10 or the MINI in each study; only one study specified that methamphetamine was the main drug, one reported the dose (Chen 2015), and five the age at first use (3.2, p. 184).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not synthesized; dose reported in one study, route and quality of the drug mostly unreported (4.6, p. 188).
exposure.polysubstance: Six studies reported concomitant use of alcohol, cannabis, cocaine, heroin, MDMA, ketamine, opioids or nicotine and five did not report it (3.2; 4.6); other drug use was not accounted for in the analysis.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Heterogeneous and often unreported (4.6; Supplementary Table S2, not read); some groups were people currently using methamphetamine.

comparison.controls: People with schizophrenia or a related psychotic disorder, intended to be people who did not use drugs. Departures visible in Table 1 and the references: in Hides 2015 the 20 people with a primary psychotic disorder were drawn from 198 people who had used methamphetamine in the previous month; Hajebi 2018 compared first-episode non-affective psychosis (title, p. 189) although first-episode psychosis was an exclusion criterion; Alexander 2019 recruited 39 people with schizophrenia and stimulant dependence besides the 18 without, and the interval widths in Figs. 1 and 2 correspond to about 39 people per group (editors' calculation). The most heavily weighted study (Srisurapanont 2011; 30.4% of the positive-symptom pool and 13.9% of the negative, Figs. 1 and 2) drew its two groups from two different studies, the WHO multi-site project on methamphetamine psychosis and a Thai trial of long-acting injectable risperidone in schizophrenia (Table 1, p. 186): a comparison between groups recruited for different purposes, not a direct comparison.
comparison.matching: None at review level; within studies, mostly unmatched clinical groups.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Premorbid functioning, family history, duration of illness and duration of antipsychotic treatment are not synthesized; antipsychotic dose is reported for six studies (Table 1) and not analysed, although antipsychotics can cause secondary negative symptoms.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Intended to be none; not met in at least one study (Hides 2015) and unreported in others.

outcomes.instruments: PANSS (6 studies), BPRS (5), Manchester scale (1); depressive symptoms by PANSS, BPRS, CDSS or HDRS items (6 studies) (3.2).
outcomes.operationalization: Positive- and negative-symptom severity as baseline or single-time scores, standardized as Hedges' g, methamphetamine psychosis minus schizophrenia (negative values mean fewer symptoms in methamphetamine psychosis) (2.2; 2.7).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Two primary outcomes (positive, negative), depressive symptoms and two negative-symptom dimensions (diminished expression, amotivation), plus sensitivity, leave-one-out and meta-regression analyses.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable at review level; not reported for the included studies.

analysis.effect_sizes: Negative symptoms: SMD -0.35 (95% CI -0.54 to -0.16), 12 studies, I2 54% (tau2 0.057 in Fig. 2); studies with Newcastle-Ottawa scores above 5: -0.44 (-0.82 to -0.07); leave-one-out as reported (the study left out is not named), -0.254 (-0.37 to -0.13), I2 58.0%. Positive symptoms: -0.01 (-0.13 to 0.11), I2 0%, heterogeneity p = 1.00 (Fig. 1). Depressive symptoms (6 studies): -0.01 (-0.41 to 0.39), I2 83%; without one outlier -0.16 (-0.36 to 0.04). Negative-symptom dimensions (3 studies): not significant. Editors' recalculation (Hedges' g, DerSimonian-Laird) from the Table 1 means and dispersions, reading those of Dawe 2011 and Hajebi 2018 as standard errors: positive symptoms -0.29 (-0.67 to 0.10), I2 89%; negative symptoms -0.44 (-0.72 to -0.16), I2 79%; from the Fig. 2 study values, -0.35 (-0.54 to -0.16), I2 54%, as reported, and without Mikami 2003 -0.28 (-0.44 to -0.12), I2 30% (common-effect model: -0.25, -0.38 to -0.13).
analysis.covariates: None; unadjusted group means. Meta-regression on publication year and mean age was not significant for either outcome (3.6).
analysis.preregistration_detail: PROSPERO CRD42021286619. The text dates the protocol to 14 July 2020, while the registration number carries the year 2021; the registry record was not read. Departures from the stated eligibility criteria (comparison groups using methamphetamine, a first-episode comparison group) are not acknowledged.
analysis.selective_reporting: All stated outcomes are reported; the Newcastle-Ottawa scores and the number of studies in the sensitivity analysis appear only in supplements.
analysis.power: Not addressed; 12 small studies with 14 to 169 people per group (Table 1).

interpretation_gap.results_show: A small-to-moderate average difference in negative-symptom scores (SMD -0.35) between treated, mostly stable groups with methamphetamine psychosis and with schizophrenia, with moderate heterogeneity and 5 of 12 studies individually significant; for positive symptoms a reported null with near-perfect agreement across studies, which the paper's own Table 1 does not reproduce (editors' recalculation -0.29, -0.67 to 0.10, I2 89%, reading two studies' printed dispersions as standard errors; -0.35, -0.90 to 0.20, I2 94%, taking them as printed).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The results conclude that "there are no differences regarding positive symptoms" (p. 184) and the conclusions speak of similar levels of positive symptoms (p. 189): a non-significant difference read as similarity, on a pooled result that cannot be reproduced from Table 1. The abstract's p values (p = 1, p = 0.01) are the heterogeneity tests of Figs. 1 and 2, not tests of the pooled differences; the abstract calls the samples stable outpatients, though five studies included inpatients and only five specified stability; and the discussion's neurobiological accounts (self-medication, sensitization, a continuum of vulnerability) go beyond cross-sectional symptom scores, although they are labelled as hypotheses.

timeline.event: Srisurapanont et al. (2011): 168 people with methamphetamine psychosis from the WHO multi-site project compared with 169 people with schizophrenia from a Thai trial of long-acting injectable risperidone (Table 1, p. 186); the largest included study and the one weighted most heavily in both pools (30.4% of the positive-symptom pool, 13.9% of the negative).
Chen et al. (2015) and Wang et al. (2016a), by the same seven Taiwanese authors, enter both pools with near-identical groups and values (reporting issue 5).
Narrative review of 12 direct comparisons (Wearne & Cornish, 2018), sharing at least three primary studies with this meta-analysis (Chen 2015, Srisurapanont 2011, Wang 2016).
Systematic review of the symptom profile, cited here for the rarity of negative symptoms (Voce et al., 2019).
This meta-analysis, the first systematic meta-analytic comparison of these symptoms by the authors' account (p. 189).
Meta-analysis of cognition in substance-induced psychotic disorders versus schizophrenia-spectrum disorders (Semancikova et al., 2026); identified by the currency check of 2026-10-16, not read.

replication.where_it_stands: The only meta-analysis of symptom severity in methamphetamine psychosis versus schizophrenia. The negative-symptom difference is reproducible from the review's own data (direction robust, size uncertain) and was measured in treated patients; the positive-symptom null is not reproducible as reported and should be cited as a non-significant, imprecise difference, not as similarity. Because it shares primary studies with the 2018 narrative review, the two are not independent support.

funding.funder: Internal funding only (p. 189).
funding.declared_conflicts: S. Kaiser has received royalties from Boehringer Ingelheim; all other authors declare no conflict of interest (p. 189).
funding.affiliations_note: Faculty of Medicine, University of Geneva, and Division of Adult Psychiatry, Geneva University Hospitals; none of the authors is an author of an included study (references, pp. 189–190).

what_would_settle_it: A prospective study enrolling people at first presentation with psychosis after recent methamphetamine use, with verified abstinence, blinded ratings of positive and negative symptoms at presentation and at 1, 6 and 12 months, and a first-episode schizophrenia comparison group without drug use matched for antipsychotic exposure, analysing resolving and persistent cases separately and testing how well symptom profiles predict the later diagnosis.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population, comparison group, outcomes and designs are specified (2.2, 2.4).

Registered in PROSPERO (2.1); the registry record was not read, the year implied by the number (2021) does not match the stated date (14 July 2020), and departures from the stated eligibility criteria are not acknowledged.
The restriction to observational designs is stated (2.4) but not explained; only observational designs can compare diagnostic groups, so this is a strict reading of a non-critical item.

Three databases to 16 December 2022 with search terms given and reference-list snowballing (2.3); but English-language, human and adult-age limits were applied without any justification, and AMSTAR 2 gives 'partial yes' only when such publication restrictions are justified, so the item is not met. No grey literature or registries were searched either.
Three authors independently inspected titles, abstracts and methods (2.3, 2.5).

The extraction description (2.5) lists study characteristics and says disagreements were resolved by consensus, but does not say who extracted the symptom scores or whether in duplicate; the mismatches between Table 1 and the forest plots (reporting issues 1 to 4) indicate the extracted values were not cross-checked.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Reasons for exclusion are given only in a supplementary flow chart (2.5; 3.1) and two excluded studies are named in the text; no list of excluded full texts with reasons is described.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 1 gives design, key inclusion criteria, diagnostic criteria, group sizes, sex, age, baseline scores and antipsychotic dose; drug use, abstinence and dependence are only in supplements (S2, S3) not read.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: Two authors independently applied a modified Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (2.6), which covers selection, comparability and ascertainment but not selection of the reported result; study scores are only in a supplement.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Not reported.

Random-effects pooling of Hedges' g is appropriate in principle, but unadjusted group means were pooled without justification across acute and persistent psychosis and across comparison groups that did not meet the review's own criteria; two included studies probably share participants; and the positive-symptom study estimates in Fig. 1 cannot be reproduced from the extracted means in Table 1, so the pooled positive-symptom result cannot be verified (reporting issue 1). Judged not met. The leave-one-out estimate also appears to come from a common-effect model although random effects are stated for every analysis (key finding 2). With items 4 and 7 also not met, the overall rating would stay critically low even if this item were met.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: Sensitivity analysis restricted to studies with Newcastle-Ottawa scores above 5 (3.5).

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The limitations name the heterogeneity of populations, polysubstance use, unreported abstinence and medication and the cross-sectional design (4.6), and the quality-restricted sensitivity analysis is reported.
I2 reported, leave-one-out and meta-regression on year and age performed, and sources of heterogeneity discussed (3.3.2, 3.6, 4.6).
Funnel plots for both outcomes and Egger's test for negative symptoms (t = -1.09, df = 10, p = 0.303) (3.3); with 12 studies the test has little power.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Internal funding and one author's royalties are declared (p. 189).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Three critical items are not met (4: English-language, human and age limits without justification; 7: no list of excluded studies; 11: pooled positive-symptom values that the review's own table does not reproduce, unadjusted means pooled across mixed and partly ineligible groups, and probable double counting of one sample), with items 2 and 9 only partly met: critically low confidence. Items 4 and 11 alone give this rating, so it does not depend on item 7, which was judged from the article's description of a supplementary flow chart that was not read. The negative-symptom estimate is reproducible from the review's data and may be cited as a small-to-moderate difference in treated patients, with these caveats; the positive-symptom result may be cited only as a non-significant and imprecise difference.

key_findings.finding: From 2052 records (PubMed, Embase, PsycINFO to 16 December 2022), 12 studies were included: 624 people with methamphetamine-induced psychosis and 527 with schizophrenia or a related disorder; designs given as 6 cross-sectional (two with a case-control design), 3 case-control, 2 cohort and 1 prospective study.
key_findings.locator: Abstract (p. 182); 2.3 (p. 183); 3.1 Literature search and 3.2, 1st paragraph (p. 184); Table 1 (pp. 185–186)
key_findings.note: The abstract gives 524 people with schizophrenia; the results text and Table 1 give 527.

key_findings.finding: Negative symptoms were less severe in methamphetamine psychosis: SMD -0.35 (95% CI -0.54 to -0.16), 12 studies, I2 54%. Five of the 12 study intervals exclude no difference (Mikami 2003 -1.05, Hajebi -0.68, Dawe -0.41, Chen -0.41, Wang -0.41); two point estimates are zero or above (Howells 0.00, Alexander 0.17).
key_findings.note: Study values read from Fig. 2, an image, which labels Hajebi as 2016 (2018 in Table 1 and the references).

key_findings.finding: Robustness of the negative-symptom result: restricted to studies with Newcastle-Ottawa scores above 5, SMD -0.44 (-0.82 to -0.07, p = 0.04), positive symptoms unchanged; a leave-one-out analysis for potential outliers (the funnel plot flagged Mikami 2003) gave -0.254 (-0.37 to -0.13) with I2 58.0%, without naming the study left out; Egger's test t = -1.09, df = 10, p = 0.303.
key_findings.note: The number of studies in the sensitivity analysis is not given in the text. Editors' recalculation from the Fig. 2 values, reproduced by the second reader: omitting Mikami 2003 gives -0.28 (-0.44 to -0.12), I2 30%, with random effects (DerSimonian-Laird) and -0.25 (-0.38 to -0.13) with a common-effect model, which matches the printed estimate; the printed I2 of 58.0% matches omitting one of several other single studies (for example Zhang 2018), not Mikami. The printed result therefore looks like a common-effect leave-one-out, although 2.7 states random effects for every analysis.

key_findings.finding: Positive symptoms did not differ significantly: SMD -0.01 (-0.13 to 0.11); Fig. 1 shows I2 0%, tau2 0 and a heterogeneity p of 1.00, with all 12 study values between -0.19 and 0.15.
key_findings.note: These study values cannot be reproduced from Table 1 (reporting issue 1).

key_findings.finding: Editors' recalculation from Table 1 (Hedges' g, DerSimonian-Laird random effects; the dispersions printed for Dawe 2011 and Hajebi 2018 treated as standard errors, as their negative-symptom values in Fig. 2 require): positive symptoms -0.29 (-0.67 to 0.10), I2 89%, with study values from -1.93 (Mikami 2003) and -1.11 (Alexander 2019) to 0.54 (Srisurapanont 2011); negative symptoms -0.44 (-0.72 to -0.16), I2 79%, with 11 of the 12 study values in Fig. 2 reproduced (Mikami 2003: about -2.1 from Table 1, -1.05 in Fig. 2).
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation, recomputed by the second reader (AI reader 15) and by the adjudicator, with the same results. Taking every Table 1 dispersion as an SD, as printed: positive symptoms -0.35 (-0.90 to 0.20), I2 94%, study values from -1.98 to 1.20; negative symptoms -0.99 (-1.66 to -0.33), I2 96%.

key_findings.finding: Depressive symptoms (6 studies) did not differ: SMD -0.01 (-0.41 to 0.39), I2 83%; without the outlying study (Srisurapanont 2011) -0.16 (-0.36 to 0.04, p = 0.08). Diminished expression and amotivation (3 studies) did not differ significantly.

Samples departed from the stated criteria: Hides 2015's primary psychotic disorder group (20) came from 198 people who had used methamphetamine in the previous month; Hajebi 2018's comparison group had first-episode non-affective psychosis although first-episode psychosis was an exclusion criterion; five studies included inpatients although the abstract describes stable outpatients; only five specified a period of clinical stability; only one specified that methamphetamine was the main drug; six reported other substance use.
key_findings.locator: Abstract (p. 182); 2.4 Eligibility criteria (p. 183); 3.2, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 184); Table 1, Hides and Hajebi rows (p. 185)
key_findings.note: Hajebi's comparison group is identified from the reference title (p. 189). Its baseline PANSS positive means (31.9 and 33.4; Table 1) are those of acutely ill people, consistent with a first-episode cohort assessed at admission rather than with stable outpatients (editors' inference).

key_findings.finding: Chen 2015 and Wang 2016a, by the same seven Taiwanese authors, report near-identical groups and values: 56 vs 54 and 53 vs 53 people; negative symptoms 9.0 vs 10.5 and 9.1 vs 10.6; positive symptoms 17.0 vs 18.2 and 16.8 vs 18.2; mean antipsychotic doses 1100 ± 600 vs 1200 ± 600 mg/day chlorpromazine equivalents in both; both enter every pool.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, rows Chen et al., 2015 and Wang et al., 2016a (pp. 185–186); references (pp. 189–190)
key_findings.note: Editors' inference: probably overlapping samples, so one sample may be counted twice; the review does not discuss it.

key_findings.finding: The authors state that the cross-sectional design of the included studies allows no causal interpretation, that participants with methamphetamine psychosis also used other substances, and that abstinence, methamphetamine dose, severity of dependence and current medication were heterogeneous or unreported.

reporting_issues.issue: The 12 study SMDs for positive symptoms in Fig. 1 (-0.19 to 0.15; I2 0%) cannot be reproduced from the means and dispersions in Table 1. Reading the dispersions printed for Dawe 2011 and Hajebi 2018 as standard errors (reporting issue 2), Table 1 implies study values from -1.93 to 0.54 and a pooled -0.29 (-0.67 to 0.10) with I2 89%; taking every dispersion as an SD, as printed, study values from -1.98 to 1.20 and a pooled -0.35 (-0.90 to 0.20) with I2 94% (editors' recalculations, reproduced by the second reader). Either way none of the Fig. 1 values is reproduced; for example Mikami 2003, 1.7 ± 2.1 vs 7.3 ± 3.8, appears in Fig. 1 as -0.04. The Fig. 1 values themselves pool to the reported -0.01 (-0.13 to 0.11), I2 0%, so the fault lies in the study-level inputs, not in the pooling.
reporting_issues.consequence: The headline positive-symptom result (-0.01, -0.13 to 0.11) cannot be verified; either Table 1 or the analysis input is wrong. It should not be cited as evidence that positive symptoms are similar.

reporting_issues.issue: Mikami 2003's negative-symptom values in Table 1 (1.4 ± 2.3 vs 7.5 ± 3.6) imply an SMD of about -2.1, while Fig. 2 shows -1.05.
reporting_issues.consequence: With the value in Table 1 the pooled negative-symptom estimate would be about -0.44 instead of -0.35 (editors' recalculation); the direction is unaffected.

reporting_issues.issue: The dispersions printed for Dawe 2011 (0.52 to 1.07) and Hajebi 2018 (0.7 to 0.9) in Table 1, headed mean ± SD, behave as standard errors: only as standard errors do they reproduce these studies' negative-symptom SMDs in Fig. 2 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Readers computing effects from Table 1 would get grossly inflated values for these two studies.

reporting_issues.issue: The interval widths in Figs. 1 and 2 match the group sizes in Table 1 for 9 studies but correspond to about 39 vs 39 people for Alexander 2019 (Table 1: 39 vs 18), 20 vs 20 for Hides 2015 (81 vs 20) and 28 vs 28 for Howells 2018 (24 vs 28) (editors' calculation from the printed intervals).
reporting_issues.consequence: The analysis appears to have used group sizes, and for Alexander 2019 possibly the comparison group with stimulant dependence, other than those in Table 1.

reporting_issues.issue: Chen 2015 and Wang 2016a share all seven authors and report near-identical group sizes, symptom scores and identical antipsychotic doses (Table 1).
reporting_issues.consequence: Probable double counting of one Taiwanese sample in every pool (editors' inference), which narrows the intervals and adds a duplicated weight to the negative-symptom difference.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract's p values for the pooled effects (p = 1 for positive, p = 0.01 for negative symptoms) are the heterogeneity-test p values printed in Figs. 1 and 2; from the printed intervals the pooled differences would have p of about 0.87 and 0.0003 (editors' arithmetic).
reporting_issues.consequence: Does not change direction; indicates that output was transcribed without checking.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract gives 524 people with schizophrenia (results and Table 1: 527), and its design counts (6 cross-sectional, 3 case-control, 2 cohort) sum to 11 of the 12 studies.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor.

reporting_issues.issue: The PROSPERO number CRD42021286619 carries the year 2021, while the text dates the protocol's publication to 14 July 2020.
reporting_issues.consequence: Whether registration preceded the work cannot be checked from the article; the registry record was not read.

reporting_issues.issue: Section 3.2 says six studies assessed depression and anxiety but cites eight, including Wang 2016b, the aripiprazole-risperidone trial, which is not an included study; Hajebi is dated 2016 in the forest plots and 2018 in Table 1 and the references; 67.0% men is not a possible proportion of 53 (Wang 2016a, schizophrenia group); Dawe 2011 is described in Table 1 as 98 outpatients while its title describes inpatients.
reporting_issues.consequence: Labelling errors that lower confidence in data handling without changing the estimates.

reporting_issues.issue: The score ranges given in 3.3.1 and 3.3.2 as PANSS ranges (positive 14.5-19.8 for methamphetamine psychosis and 14-19.8 for schizophrenia; negative 7-17 and 8.9-19.8) do not match Table 1: they include values from Dawe 2011, which used the BPRS (19.84, 7.12, 8.98), and leave out Hajebi 2018 (31.9 and 33.4) and Howells 2018 (8 and 12). Section 3.3.1 also says the positive-symptom data came from 12 studies using PANSS positive scores, while 3.2 says 6 used the PANSS, 5 the BPRS and 1 the Manchester scale.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor for the estimates; a further sign that values were transcribed without being checked.

design_detail: Prospective general-population birth cohort (Christchurch Health and Development Study; 1,265 children born in Christchurch, New Zealand, in 1977), with self-reported methamphetamine (or amphetamine) use and violence over four periods (ages 18–21, 21–25, 25–30, 30–35) reported at interviews at 21, 25, 30 and 35. Population-averaged logistic GEE models relate any use in a period to violence perpetration, violence victimisation and intimate-partner violence perpetration and victimisation in the same period, unadjusted, adjusted for childhood and adolescent confounders (Model 1) and additionally for time-varying covariates (Model 2). A separate logistic regression relates the heaviest frequency of use at ages 18–35 to violence at any time in those years (dose-response, adjusted for fixed confounders only). Ecstasy use is analysed the same way as a comparison, and population attributable fractions are estimated.
can_establish: Whether, in an unselected birth cohort, periods with self-reported methamphetamine use go with more self-reported violence perpetration and victimisation in the same period after adjustment for a wide set of prospectively measured childhood and adolescent factors and for concurrent mental-health, alcohol and cannabis disorders.
cannot_establish: That methamphetamine use preceded or caused the violence (use and violence are reported for the same three-to-five-year periods, as the authors state), that other illicit drug use or involvement in drug markets does not explain the association (not adjusted for), or anything about methamphetamine as distinct from amphetamine (both are in the exposure question).

sample.recruitment: Birth cohort: 1,265 children (635 male, 630 female) born in Christchurch in 1977, studied at birth, 4 months, yearly to 16 and at 18, 21, 25, 30 and 35 (p. 2).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: All cohort members interviewed at any of the last four waves; no exclusions are described.
sample.demographics: Born 1977; equal numbers of boys and girls at birth; ethnicity (Māori or Pacific against European or other) is a covariate, but its distribution is not given in the article (details in an online supplement, not read).
sample.attrition: Interviewed: 1,025 at 21, 1,003 at 25, 987 at 30 and 962 at 35, 76–81% of the original cohort (p. 2); 1,044 people contribute to the dose-response analysis (Table 3). How missing waves were handled, and whether people lost to follow-up differed in drug use or violence, is not reported.
sample.selection_effects: Unselected general-population cohort; losses of about a fifth by age 35 could be selective, because people who use drugs often and are involved in violence are often harder to retain.

exposure.measurement: At each interview, self-reported use of "methamphetamine, speed, P, ice, etc" since the last interview, coded as any or no use in each period; for the dose-response analysis, the highest frequency reported in any period (never; once or twice only; up to about monthly; at least weekly) (pp. 2–3). No biological verification.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Frequency categories only; any use in the periods was 5.5% (18–21), 22.4% (21–25), 14.4% (25–30) and 7.8% (30–35); over ages 18–35, 71.9% never used, 11.9% used once or twice only, 11.3% up to about monthly and 4.9% at least weekly in at least one period (p. 3). Amount and route not measured.
exposure.polysubstance: Model 2 adjusts for alcohol and cannabis use disorders in each period (Table 2 note); other illicit drug use (opioids, cocaine, ecstasy) is not adjusted for. Ecstasy, used by 38.5% of the cohort, is analysed separately and shows no statistically significant adjusted association with violence, which the authors describe as inconclusive evidence (p. 3; p. 5; results in a supplement, not read).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: Within the cohort: periods (or, for the dose-response analysis, people) without methamphetamine use.
comparison.matching: No matching. Model 1 adjusts for parental age, family socioeconomic status at birth, family living standards, family instability, parental intimate-partner violence, parental alcohol problems, criminality and illicit drug use, quality of parenting, childhood sexual and physical abuse, sex, ethnicity, child IQ, school performance, childhood conduct and attention problems, self-esteem, novelty seeking, adolescent conduct disorder, depression, anxiety, smoking and delinquent or substance-using peers; Model 2 adds depression, anxiety disorder, alcohol and cannabis use disorders, life stress, unemployment and psychotic symptoms in each period (Table 2 notes).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Childhood and adolescent factors were measured prospectively, an unusual strength; antisocial personality in adulthood, involvement in drug markets or sex work and concurrent use of other illicit drugs were not adjusted for.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: The comparison periods may include use of other drugs; only alcohol and cannabis use disorders are adjusted for.

outcomes.instruments: Violence perpetration outside intimate relationships: Self-Report Delinquency Inventory with custom items (attacking with a weapon, hitting, attacking with intent to hurt seriously or kill, armed robbery, brawls, sexual coercion, animal cruelty; carrying a hidden weapon as a proxy). Victimisation: two items on physical or sexual assault from a life-events measure derived from the Feeling Bad Scale. Intimate-partner violence: 22 items from the Revised Conflict Tactics Scale, perpetration and victimisation separately, for people in a relationship of at least a month (pp. 2–3).
outcomes.validity_norms: Established self-report instruments; no record or informant corroboration, as the authors note (p. 6).
outcomes.operationalization: At least one reported act in a period classified the person as a perpetrator or victim for that period (pp. 2–3).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None across four outcomes, three model sets, the dose-response analysis, the ecstasy comparison and the interaction terms.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable; exposure and outcomes were reported in the same interview.

analysis.effect_sizes: Population-averaged odds ratios for any use in a period against none (Tables 1–2, p. 4). Violence perpetration: unadjusted 2.51 (95% CI 1.75–3.59), Model 1 2.42 (1.56–3.76), Model 2 1.60 (1.01–2.54). Victimisation: 2.93 (2.08–4.10), 2.64 (1.74–4.01), 1.57 (1.00–2.47). Intimate-partner violence perpetration: 2.11 (1.50–2.98), 1.87 (1.27–2.74), 1.55 (1.04–2.30). Intimate-partner violence victimisation: 1.53 (1.15–2.04), 1.43 (1.06–1.93), 1.09 (0.80–1.49). Sex by use interaction for victimisation b = 0.62 (SE 0.13), stronger in women (p. 4). Dose-response, heaviest frequency against never, adjusted for fixed confounders only (Table 3, p. 5): perpetration once or twice 1.13 (0.64–2.02), up to monthly 1.40 (0.81–2.42), at least weekly 4.84 (2.48–9.46); victimisation 1.87 (1.13–3.11), 1.89 (1.15–3.11), 3.62 (1.88–6.96); intimate-partner perpetration 1.75 (1.05–2.90), 1.89 (1.15–3.11), 2.44 (1.26–4.71); intimate-partner victimisation 1.12 (0.72–1.74), 1.45 (0.95–2.22), 2.28 (1.24–4.19). Population attributable fractions: perpetration 14.5% (0.8–23.0), victimisation 13.5% (2.6–20.6), intimate-partner perpetration 12.9% (1.2–18.7), intimate-partner victimisation 2.8% (0–8.0) (p. 5).
analysis.covariates: See comparison; the dose-response models use a reduced set of fixed confounders (family socioeconomic status, sex, child IQ, adolescent anxiety disorder, childhood physical and sexual abuse, deviant peers, attention problems; p. 5).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or analysis plan is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: Full Model 2 results, the ecstasy models and the confounder details are only in an online supplement (not read). The pairwise tests between frequency categories that the methods describe (p. 3) are not reported.
analysis.power: Not addressed. Only 51 people used at least weekly, and data sparseness prevented repeated-measures dose-response models (p. 3).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Periods with any self-reported methamphetamine or amphetamine use went with about 1.6 times the odds of self-reported violence perpetration and victimisation and of intimate-partner violence perpetration in the same period after full adjustment, with lower limits of 1.00–1.04; the association with intimate-partner victimisation was not clear (1.09, 0.80–1.49). Adjustment for concurrent mental-health, alcohol and cannabis disorders and life circumstances roughly halved the excess odds. Higher odds were concentrated in the 51 people who used at least weekly, in an analysis adjusted for fixed childhood and adolescent factors only and not period-matched.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes: "Methamphetamine use is an independent risk factor for violence perpetration and victimisation" (p. 1). The discussion says methamphetamine plays a substantial role in violence where its use is common (p. 5), a reading that rests on attributable fractions, which assume a causal effect; and that the associations are not fully accounted for by antisocial personality and concurrent use of other substances (p. 5), although adult antisocial personality was not measured and only alcohol and cannabis use disorders were adjusted for. The abstract describes the dose-response as compared with people who used less often, but only comparisons with people who never used are reported (Table 3). Against this, the discussion states that the temporal order within periods was unknown, which limited causal inference, and that most people who used did not engage in or experience violence (p. 5).

timeline.event: Within-person analysis of an Australian treatment cohort (McKetin et al., 2014), described here as showing a strong dose-dependent association between days of use and high hostility (p. 1, p. 5); on the encyclopedia's reading list, not yet read
Meta-analysis (sharing authors with this paper): pooled adjusted odds ratio for violence with any amphetamine use 1.4 (0.8–2.4); this cohort was published later and is not in it
This study: first general-population longitudinal analysis, by the authors' account
Analysis of methamphetamine use and crime in Australian longitudinal data by an overlapping author group (McKetin, Boden, Foulds and others); not yet read

replication.where_it_stands: The adjusted associations are in the same direction as the within-person treatment-cohort finding and close to the meta-analysis's adjusted point estimate, but they come from one cohort, sit near no association after full adjustment, and share authors with both the meta-analysis and the later crime analysis, so agreement among these sources is partly agreement within one research group.

funding.funder: Health Research Council of New Zealand (Programme grant 16/600); the study was previously funded by the National Child Health Research Foundation, the Canterbury Medical Research Foundation and the New Zealand Lottery Grants Board (Acknowledgements, p. 6). The 'Role of funding source' statement reads 'None' (p. 6).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict declared (p. 6).
funding.affiliations_note: University of Otago (Christchurch and Wellington; Christchurch Health and Development Study) and Curtin University (p. 1). Two authors (Foulds, McKetin) are authors of the 2019 meta-analysis cited in the same claim. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: Repeated short-interval measurement (for example monthly or diary-based) of methamphetamine use, other drug use and violence within the same people in a general-population or high-risk cohort, with biological verification of use, records-based violence outcomes and adjustment for involvement in drug markets, so that use can be shown to precede violence within person; the authors themselves propose micro-longitudinal designs (p. 6).

domains.note: An unusually wide set of prospectively measured childhood and adolescent confounders, plus concurrent mental-health, alcohol and cannabis disorders. Not adjusted for: other illicit drug use, involvement in drug markets or sex work, adult antisocial traits. Use and violence are reported for the same three-to-five-year period, so violence or victimisation may precede use (reverse causation), as the authors acknowledge. Model 2 also adjusts for factors that may lie on the causal path (psychotic symptoms, depression), which would bias towards no association.

Self-report of use of 'methamphetamine, speed, P, ice, etc', without biological verification, so methamphetamine is not separated from amphetamine; coarse frequency categories reported retrospectively for periods of three to five years.
Unselected birth cohort; selection into the analysis through attrition is considered under missing data.
Treatment, arrest or imprisonment after use, which could change both use and opportunities for violence, are not considered; probably uncommon in this general-population sample.
19–24% of the cohort missing at each of the four waves; the handling of missing waves and any comparison of retained and lost participants are not reported.

Self-reported violence without corroboration, collected in the same interview as drug use; people more willing to disclose drug use may also disclose more violence, which would inflate the association. Repeated interviews with a long-trusted study team may reduce under-reporting, as the authors argue.
No pre-specified plan; several model sets with interaction terms, a dose-response analysis adjusted for a reduced covariate set, and key results (full Model 2, ecstasy models) only in a supplement.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No single domain is high, but concerns in six domains act in part in the same direction (reverse causation within periods, unadjusted other drug use, correlated self-report), and the fully adjusted estimates sit at the margin of no association (lower limits 1.00–1.04), so together they substantially lower confidence that the adjusted association is real. The study is stronger than the cross-sectional literature: an unselected cohort, prospective childhood confounders and repeated measures. It may be cited for an adjusted association in the same periods in a general-population cohort, and for higher odds with at least weekly use; not for a causal effect, not for methamphetamine as distinct from amphetamine, and not for the population attributable fractions as shares of violence caused by methamphetamine.

key_findings.finding: Birth cohort of 1,265 children (635 male, 630 female) born in Christchurch in 1977; interviewed at 21 (1,025), 25 (1,003), 30 (987) and 35 (962), 76–81% of the original cohort. Use of methamphetamine (asked as methamphetamine, speed, P or ice) since the last interview was coded as any or none in each of four periods.
key_findings.locator: Methods › 2.1. Participants, 1st paragraph; 2.2. Methamphetamine use, age 18–35, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Any use was reported by 5.5% at 18–21, 22.4% at 21–25, 14.4% at 25–30 and 7.8% at 30–35. Over ages 18–35, 751 (71.9%) never used, 124 (11.9%) used at most once or twice, 118 (11.3%) used more often but at most monthly, and 51 (4.9%) used at least weekly in at least one period.
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.1. Methamphetamine use age 18–35, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
key_findings.note: 293 of 1,044 people used at least once (28.1%, editors' calculation); the abstract gives 28% and the methods 28.2%.

key_findings.finding: Unadjusted population-averaged odds ratios for any use in a period against none: violence perpetration 2.51 (95% CI 1.75–3.59), victimisation 2.93 (2.08–4.10), intimate-partner violence perpetration 2.11 (1.50–2.98), intimate-partner violence victimisation 1.53 (1.15–2.04). Violence perpetration in the period with use: 19 of the people using at 18–21 (33.9%) against 67 not using (7.0%).

Adjusted for childhood and adolescent confounders (Model 1): perpetration 2.42 (1.56–3.76), victimisation 2.64 (1.74–4.01), intimate-partner perpetration 1.87 (1.27–2.74), intimate-partner victimisation 1.43 (1.06–1.93). Further adjusted for depression, anxiety, alcohol and cannabis use disorders, life stress, unemployment and psychotic symptoms in each period (Model 2): 1.60 (1.01–2.54), 1.57 (1.00–2.47), 1.55 (1.04–2.30) and 1.09 (0.80–1.49).
key_findings.locator: Table 2; Results › 3.3. Adjusted models…, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The association with victimisation was stronger in women than in men (sex by use interaction b = 0.62, SE 0.13); no other age or sex interaction was significant.

Dose-response (heaviest frequency at ages 18–35 against never; adjusted for fixed confounders only): violence perpetration 1.13 (0.64–2.02) for once or twice, 1.40 (0.81–2.42) for up to about monthly and 4.84 (2.48–9.46) for at least weekly use; victimisation 1.87 (1.13–3.11), 1.89 (1.15–3.11) and 3.62 (1.88–6.96); intimate-partner perpetration 1.75 (1.05–2.90), 1.89 (1.15–3.11) and 2.44 (1.26–4.71); intimate-partner victimisation 1.12 (0.72–1.74), 1.45 (0.95–2.22) and 2.28 (1.24–4.19).
key_findings.note: Not adjusted for the time-varying covariates of Model 2 (alcohol and cannabis use disorders, mental health); repeated-measures dose-response models were not possible because of sparse data (p. 3). The analysis relates the heaviest frequency reported in any period to violence at any time from 18 to 35 (Methods 2.7, 3rd paragraph, p. 3), so the heaviest use and the violence need not fall in the same period or in that order.

key_findings.finding: Ecstasy (MDMA) use, analysed the same way, showed no statistically significant association with any of the four outcomes after full adjustment (all p > 0.05; the authors call the evidence inconclusive); 38.5% of the cohort reported ecstasy use against 28.2% methamphetamine use.
key_findings.locator: Methods › 2.8, 1st paragraph (p. 3); Results › 3.5. Comparison with ecstasy exposure, 1st paragraph (p. 5)
key_findings.note: Estimates only in the online supplement (not read).

key_findings.finding: Population attributable fractions for any use, with the relative risk calculated from the Model 2 population-averaged odds ratio: perpetration 14.5% (0.8–23.0), victimisation 13.5% (2.6–20.6), intimate-partner perpetration 12.9% (1.2–18.7), intimate-partner victimisation 2.8% (0–8.0).

The authors state that they could not be sure of the order of use and violence within each interview period, which limited causal inference; that use and violence were self-reported and not corroborated; and that most people who used did not engage in or experience violence.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 gives identical results, OR 1.89 (1.15–3.11), for victimisation and for intimate-partner violence perpetration in the up-to-monthly category.
reporting_issues.consequence: Possibly a copying error in one of the two cells (each interval is symmetric on the log scale, so neither cell is impossible as printed); both values should be confirmed with the authors before citation.

reporting_issues.issue: The models behind Table 2 include age by use and sex by use interaction terms (Table 2 note e), but the paper does not say how age and sex were coded, so the printed odds ratios may describe the reference sex and period rather than everyone; for victimisation the sex interaction was significant (b = 0.62, SE 0.13).
reporting_issues.consequence: The single victimisation odds ratio may not describe both men and women; how to read the main-effect odds ratios is uncertain.

reporting_issues.issue: The row '% Pooled over ages 18–35' in Table 1 is not defined. For intimate-partner victimisation it matches the person-period percentage computed from the counts (11.2% and 18.2%, editors' calculation), but not for violence perpetration (4.5% and 11.3% against the printed 11.8% and 26.3%) or the other two outcomes.
reporting_issues.consequence: The row cannot be read as one consistent quantity and should not be cited.

reporting_issues.issue: The lowest frequency category is described as once or twice only in any age period (Methods 2.2, p. 2; Table 3, p. 5) but as never more than 1–2 times per year (Results 3.1, p. 3).
reporting_issues.consequence: The boundary between the two lowest categories is unclear.

reporting_issues.issue: The results text says Table 3 displays percentages of each outcome by frequency of use (p. 5), but Table 3 shows odds ratios only.
reporting_issues.consequence: The absolute frequency of violence by category of use is not reported.

reporting_issues.issue: The time-varying covariates are listed as cannabis use disorder in the methods and the Table 2 note but as cannabis dependence in the results text, and the results list omits psychotic symptoms, which the methods and the note include (pp. 3–4).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the adjustment set of Model 2 is reported inconsistently.

reporting_issues.issue: The 'Role of funding source' statement reads 'None' (p. 6), while the acknowledgements name a Health Research Council programme grant (p. 6).
reporting_issues.consequence: Probably means the funder had no role; the funding itself is as given in the acknowledgements.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 note a says the dose-response models are adjusted for fixed confounding factors (see Table 2 Model 1), while Methods 2.7 and Results 3.4 say that only the factors significant in Model 1 were used and list seven of them (p. 5).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the note can be read as the full Model 1 set. The reduced set given in the text, which analysis.covariates records, is the better-supported reading.
