design_detail: Secondary analysis of the 2007 Australian National Survey of Mental Health and Wellbeing (NSMHWB; 8,841 respondents aged 16–85; stratified multistage household probability sample; response 60%). For each of five substance classes (alcohol, cannabis, stimulants, sedatives, opioids), respondents who reported use and a valid age of first use form a subsample (stimulants: 579). Two quantities are reported: a descriptive conditional probability (the weighted share of the subsample with a lifetime DSM-IV use disorder, abuse or dependence, at interview) and a cumulative probability by years since first use from discrete-time survival analysis, in which people without a disorder are censored at their age at interview. Pre-existing mood, anxiety and substance use disorders enter the survival models as time-varying predictors.
can_establish: For Australians aged 16–85 in 2007 who reported having used stimulants (class not defined), the share who had ever met DSM-IV criteria for stimulant abuse or dependence, a projected cumulative probability of doing so by years since first use, and associations between earlier-onset disorders and the transition, all from one retrospective interview.
cannot_establish: A figure for methamphetamine (the paper names no drug in its stimulant class), a dependence-only figure comparable with older surveys, causal effects of pre-existing disorders on the transition (timing recalled at one interview), or differences between substances (the subsamples overlap and the authors state that direct comparison between substances was not possible).

sample.recruitment: Community household survey: stratified, multistage probability sample of households, one member aged 16–85 selected for the diagnostic interview; response rate 60% (p. 137).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Subsamples: respondents who reported using each substance and gave a valid age of first use. Excluded from the analysis: people who could not remember or refused an age of onset, or who dated disorder onset before first use (stimulants n = 6) (p. 137). Diagnostic criteria were asked only of people who had used a drug at least five times in their life (alcohol: frequency and quantity thresholds) (p. 137); the paper does not say whether people who used stimulants fewer than five times are in the subsample of 579.
sample.demographics: Stimulant subsample (weighted estimates): mean age 32.6 (95% CI 31.5–33.6); 65.0% men; 6.8% unemployed; 85.3% born in Australia; 77.4% completed year 12 or higher; family history of alcohol or drug problems 28.6%; lifetime anxiety disorder 47.4%, affective disorder 31.4%, any substance use disorder 77.7%, any mental disorder 86.6% (Table 1, p. 139).
sample.attrition: Not applicable (single interview); 40% of selected households did not respond (p. 137).
sample.selection_effects: Household frame (people in institutions or without a home are not sampled); a 60% response with no non-response analysis reported here; survivors only (people who died before 2007 cannot be interviewed); the substance subsamples overlap, because use of several substances was common (p. 138; Table 1 note).

exposure.measurement: Self-reported lifetime use and exact age of first use in a modified WMH-CIDI 3.0, with recall probes linking first use to developmental milestones (p. 137).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not measured beyond lifetime use; the diagnostic section required at least five occasions of drug use (p. 137). Frequency, route and duration are not analysed.
exposure.polysubstance: Common and not excluded (subsamples not mutually exclusive); earlier use of, and earlier disorders for, other substances enter the survival models as time-varying covariates (p. 138; Table 2).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: No separate comparison group: within each subsample, the survival models compare person-years of people who did and did not go on to develop the disorder.
comparison.matching: Not applicable. All models controlled for age, sex, education, age of first use, family history of alcohol or drug problems, number of comorbid mental disorders with earlier onset and number of other substance use disorders with earlier onset (p. 138; Table 2 note).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Socioeconomic status, area-level deprivation and externalizing spectrum disorders were not examined, as the authors note (p. 141); childhood adversity is not included.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Other substance use and disorders are covariates, not exclusions.

outcomes.instruments: Modified WMH-CIDI 3.0: lifetime DSM-IV abuse or dependence for each substance class, with age of onset taken as the earliest onset of either; DSM-IV mood and anxiety disorders without hierarchy rules; lifetime daily tobacco use (p. 137).
outcomes.validity_norms: The instrument is described as calibrated against the SCID-IV (p. 137). No biological or record verification; ages of first use and of onset are recalled retrospectively, in some cases over decades.
outcomes.operationalization: Use disorder = DSM-IV abuse or dependence (not dependence alone). Time at risk starts at first use for drugs and at the first year with more than 12 standard drinks for alcohol (p. 137).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate across covariates; bold type in Table 2 marks associations significant after correction (p. 138; Table 2 note).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable (structured interview).

analysis.effect_sizes: Descriptive conditional probability of a lifetime use disorder: stimulants 45.7% (95% CI 39.5–51.8), opioids 44.7% (35.2–54.2), sedatives 39.0% (27.5–50.4), alcohol 34.5% (32.9–36.2), cannabis 31.8% (28.5–35.2); median age of onset of stimulant use disorder 20 years (IQR 18–24) (p. 138). Survival analysis: probability of a stimulant use disorder within the first year after first use 12.2%; cumulative 50.4% by 14 years after first use (data right-censored at 14 years; no interval given); half of the stimulant cases had onset about 3 years (IQR 1–5) after first use (p. 138). Predictors of stimulant use disorder significant after false-discovery-rate correction: generalized anxiety disorder OR 3.89 (2.01–7.53), PTSD 2.51 (1.58–3.99), any anxiety disorder 2.13 (1.35–3.36), earlier cannabis use disorder 7.03 (4.02–12.29), any other earlier substance use disorder 5.09 (3.26–7.94); not significant after correction although the interval excludes 1: sedative use 1.91 (1.08–3.40), opioid use disorder 2.37 (1.04–5.46) (Table 2, p. 140).
analysis.covariates: Age, sex, education, age of first use, family history, number of earlier comorbid mental disorders and number of earlier other substance use disorders (p. 138).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: The year-by-year cumulative probabilities are only in a supplement, which was not read (p. 138). The abstract gives the survival figure (50.4%) but not the descriptive one (45.7%, with its interval).
analysis.power: The stimulant subsample (579) gives an interval of about ±6 points for the descriptive proportion; the authors note wide intervals for the sedative and opioid subsamples (p. 141).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Of 579 Australians who reported using stimulants, 45.7% (39.5–51.8) had ever met DSM-IV criteria for stimulant abuse or dependence by the interview; projecting over time since first use, the survival analysis estimated 50.4% by 14 years after first use, 12.2% within the first year, with half of the cases starting within about 3 years. The outcome includes abuse, the class is undefined, and all timing is recalled.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract states that 50.4% of people who used stimulants would develop a use disorder (p. 136), and the conclusion that one-third to one-half of people who use substances go on to develop one, with the highest rates for stimulants and opioids (p. 141). Gaps: (1) the substances are ranked although the limitations say direct comparison between substances was not possible (p. 141); (2) the figure called a lifetime cumulative probability is truncated at 14 years after first use (p. 138); (3) the discussion describes the transition as from regular use (p. 139) while the analysis starts at first use for drugs (pp. 137–138); (4) odds ratios from the survival models are described as risk ('more than trebled the risk', p. 140); (5) the call for early identification of mood and anxiety disorders to prevent secondary use disorders (p. 141) rests on associations from recalled timing. The authors do say that their estimates are substantially higher than in other surveys and that counting abuse as well as dependence raises them (p. 139).

timeline.event: US National Comorbidity Survey: 11.2% of people who had ever used psychostimulants other than cocaine extramedically had ever met DSM-III-R dependence criteria, a proportion at one interview among everyone who had ever used

Wittchen et al. (2008), as reported here: transitions from first use to abuse 9.6–38.6% and to dependence 4.6–17.9% across substances; abuse or dependence for other illicit drugs 23.2% in men and 16.1% in women (p. 140); not read
McBride et al. (2009), as reported here: conditional dependence higher in Australia than in the United States for all substances except alcohol (p. 139); not read
NESARC survival analysis of transition to dependence for nicotine, alcohol, cannabis and cocaine; no amphetamine or methamphetamine estimate

This survey analysis: stimulant use disorder (abuse or dependence) 45.7% at interview and 50.4% by 14 years after first use, which the authors describe as substantially higher than earlier estimates of about one in four (p. 139)

replication.where_it_stands: The only population estimate seen so far that reports a stimulant-specific cumulative probability by years since first use. Its figures are much higher than older dependence-only proportions, and the authors attribute part of the difference to counting abuse and to Australian conditions; no survey reports a methamphetamine-specific figure, and none reproduces this one with the same measure.

funding.funder: The 2007 NSMHWB was funded by the Australian Government and conducted by the Australian Bureau of Statistics; the NHMRC Centre of Research Excellence in Mental Health and Substance Use is funded by the National Health and Medical Research Council; the National Drug and Alcohol Research Centre is supported by the Australian Government under the Substance Misuse Prevention and Service Improvements Grants Fund; NHMRC Fellowships to M. Teesson and K. Mills and a Society for Mental Health Research Fellowship to C. Marel (p. 141).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict declared (p. 141).
funding.affiliations_note: All authors are at the National Drug and Alcohol Research Centre and the NHMRC Centre of Research Excellence in Mental Health and Substance Use, University of New South Wales (p. 136). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective cohort followed from first use, separating methamphetamine from other stimulants, assessing DSM-5 use disorder (and dependence-level, moderate to severe, disorder separately) at fixed intervals, and reporting both the cumulative incidence by years since first use with intervals and the proportion affected at fixed follow-up times, in more than one country.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: National household frame of Australians aged 16–85; people in institutions and people without a home, among whom stimulant use disorders may be more common, are not sampled.
Stratified multistage probability sample with sampling weights, replicate weights and jackknife standard errors (pp. 137–138).
579 people in the stimulant subsample give an interval of about ±6 points for the descriptive proportion; cells for individual predictors and later years since first use are small.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Table 1 describes each subsample, but the stimulant class is never defined and the 'weighted prevalence' row is not explained (see reporting issues).

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: Exclusions for invalid ages are small (stimulants 6), but whether people who had used fewer than five times, who were not asked the diagnostic questions, are in the denominator is not stated.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: WMH-CIDI 3.0 DSM-IV diagnoses by structured interview, but self-report only, with ages of first use and onset recalled retrospectively (a limitation the authors state, p. 141) and coded by inconsistent rules (p. 137).

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: The same instrument and algorithm for all respondents.

Discrete-time survival analysis with time-varying covariates, design-based standard errors and false-discovery-rate control is appropriate, but the cumulative probabilities have no intervals, the 'lifetime' figure is truncated at 14 years, and two different probabilities are given for the same transition without explaining how they differ.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low rate managed
domains.note: Response 60%, described as comparable with other national surveys; weights are applied, but no non-response analysis is reported.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A large national probability survey with a standard diagnostic interview and an appropriate survival framework. What limits its numbers for this encyclopedia is less bias than scope: the stimulant class is undefined, the outcome includes DSM-IV abuse, the time at risk and the onset are recalled at one interview, and the denominator may or may not include people who used only a few times. It may be cited for the share of Australians who had used stimulants who had ever had a stimulant use disorder (abuse or dependence) and for the projected cumulative probability by years since first use, each labelled as such; not for methamphetamine specifically, not as a dependence figure, and not to rank substances.

key_findings.finding: Data from the 2007 Australian NSMHWB: 8,841 respondents aged 16–85 from a stratified multistage household probability sample, response 60%. Subsamples with valid age of first use: alcohol 5,456, cannabis 1,629, stimulants 579, opioids 156, sedatives 137; the subsamples are not independent.

Diagnostic criteria were asked only of people who had used a drug at least five times in their life; lifetime DSM-IV abuse or dependence was assessed with a modified WMH-CIDI 3.0, and the age of onset of the disorder was the earliest age of onset of either abuse or dependence.
key_findings.locator: Methods › 2.1. Sample, 2nd paragraph; Methods › 2.2. Measures, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Conditional probability of a lifetime use disorder (descriptive): stimulants 45.7% (95% CI 39.5–51.8), opioids 44.7% (35.2–54.2), sedatives 39.0% (27.5–50.4), alcohol 34.5% (32.9–36.2), cannabis 31.8% (28.5–35.2); median age of onset of stimulant use disorder 20 years (IQR 18–24).
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.2.1. Discrete Time Survival Analysis, 3rd paragraph; Methods › 2.3. Statistical analysis, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: The Methods describe these as descriptive estimates for each subsample, although they are printed under the survival-analysis heading.

key_findings.finding: Survival analysis for stimulants: data right-censored at 14 years after first use; probability of a use disorder within the first year after first use 12.2%; cumulative probability 50.4% within an estimated 14 years after first use; half of the stimulant cases had onset about 3 years (IQR 1–5) after first use. No intervals are given for the cumulative probabilities, and the year-by-year values are in a supplement (not read).
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.2.1. Discrete Time Survival Analysis, 1st paragraph; Results › 3.3. Cumulative conditional probability and speed of transitioning, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Editors' reasoning: the cumulative probability by 14 years assumes that people who started using recently will pass to a disorder at the same yearly rates as those who started earlier (no change across birth cohorts or periods) and that censoring at the interview is uninformative; the later years after first use are informed only by people who started long ago, whose ages of first use and onset were recalled over longer spans. The paper does not discuss these assumptions. Allowing for people who started recently is part of why 50.4% exceeds the descriptive 45.7%.

key_findings.finding: Cumulative incidence curves from first use to disorder are shown for each class; values were not extracted beyond those given in the text.

Predictors of the transition from stimulant use to stimulant use disorder, significant after false-discovery-rate correction: generalized anxiety disorder OR 3.89 (2.01–7.53), PTSD 2.51 (1.58–3.99), any anxiety disorder 2.13 (1.35–3.36), earlier cannabis use disorder 7.03 (4.02–12.29), any other earlier substance use disorder 5.09 (3.26–7.94). Major depressive episode 1.25 (0.73–2.13) was not associated.
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.4.1. Psychiatric predictors, 2nd paragraph; Results › 3.4.2. Substance use predictors, 2nd paragraph (pp. 138–139); Table 2, stimulant use disorder column (p. 140)

key_findings.finding: The authors write that their estimates are substantially higher than in other surveys, where the highest cumulative probabilities had been around one in four for cocaine, opioids and alcohol; that most earlier studies counted dependence without abuse and so give lower estimates; and that earlier comparative work found higher conditional dependence in Australia than in the United States.

Limitations stated by the authors: retrospective recall of ages of first use and onset; small sedative and opioid subsamples; overlapping subsamples, so that direct comparison between substances was not possible; socioeconomic status, area-level deprivation and externalizing disorders not examined.

Stimulant subsample characteristics: weighted prevalence 3.3% (2.8–3.9); mean age 32.6; 65.0% men; lifetime any substance use disorder 77.7%; lifetime any mental disorder 86.6%; 12-month substance use disorder 28.8%.
The stimulant class is not defined anywhere in the paper; no drug (amphetamine, methamphetamine, cocaine, ecstasy) is named as belonging to it.
key_findings.locator: Whole text, including Methods › 2.2. Measures, 1st paragraph (p. 137)
key_findings.note: Editors' observation from reading the whole text.

reporting_issues.issue: Two different probabilities are given for the same transition: 45.7% (95% CI 39.5–51.8), described in the Methods as a descriptive estimate (p. 138), and 50.4% (no interval) from the survival analysis (p. 138); the abstract and the Discussion use only the second (pp. 136, 139), while the Conclusion's range of one-third to one-half (p. 141) names neither, and the paper never explains how the two differ.
reporting_issues.consequence: A reader can mistake one for the other; the descriptive share at interview and the projected cumulative probability by 14 years must be cited separately.

reporting_issues.issue: The figure called a lifetime cumulative probability is truncated at 14 years after first use, the point beyond which no stimulant onsets were observed (p. 138).
reporting_issues.consequence: It is a cumulative probability by 14 years after first use, not over a lifetime.

reporting_issues.issue: The denominator is ambiguous: diagnostic criteria were asked only of people who had used a drug at least five times (p. 137), but the paper does not say whether people with fewer uses are in the stimulant subsample of 579.
reporting_issues.consequence: If they are excluded, the probabilities are conditional on more than occasional use and cannot be compared with figures among everyone who ever used.

reporting_issues.issue: Age of first use is coded by different rules for exact ages and for answers to the recall probes: a reported first use before age 14 is bottom-coded at 13 (Methods 2.1), while people who could not recall an exact age and placed their first use before their teens are coded 12, before their twenties 19 and after their twenties 20 (Methods 2.2). The rules do not conflict, but comparable answers are coded differently (an exact age of 11 becomes 13, before the teens becomes 12).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the coding affects the time from first use to onset, not the shares with a disorder.

reporting_issues.issue: The first row of Table 1, 'Weighted prevalence (%)', is not defined. Read as the prevalence of use, it conflicts with the subsample sizes (stimulants 3.3% against 579 of 8,841 = 6.5% unweighted; alcohol 22.1% against 61.7%); divided by the conditional probabilities it gives 7.2% for stimulants, 64.1% for alcohol and 19.5% for cannabis, close to the unweighted shares, so it is probably the weighted prevalence of the use disorder (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: The row should not be cited as the prevalence of stimulant use in Australia.

reporting_issues.issue: The discussion says the study estimated the transition from regular use to use disorder (p. 139), while for drugs the time at risk starts at first use (pp. 137–138); section 3.4 is headed transition to dependence although the outcome is abuse or dependence (p. 138).
reporting_issues.consequence: Inconsistent labels for both the starting point and the outcome.

reporting_issues.issue: The discussion says only an earlier sedative use disorder significantly increased the transition to opioid use disorder (p. 141), but Table 2 also marks any other earlier substance use disorder (OR 5.57, 1.93–16.07) as significant for opioids (p. 140).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor and not about stimulants; text and table disagree.

reporting_issues.issue: Odds ratios from discrete-time survival models are described as multiples of risk ('more than trebled the risk', p. 140).
reporting_issues.consequence: The wording overstates what an odds ratio of the yearly transition shows.

disagreements.first_pass: The rules for coding age of first use conflict: first use before age 14 is bottom-coded at 13 in Methods 2.1, while first use before the teens is coded at 12, before the twenties at 19 and after the twenties at 20 in Methods 2.2.

design_detail: Phase 3, investigator-led, multisite, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group randomized trial (1:1, stratified by sex at birth and by a PHQ-9 depression score of 10 or more) at six government-run outpatient alcohol and other drug clinics in Australia (Wollongong, Geelong, Townsville, Perth, Brisbane, Adelaide), 16 November 2022 to 1 May 2025, sponsored and coordinated by the University of New South Wales. 344 adults with DSM-5 moderate or severe methamphetamine use disorder were randomized and the 339 who received trial medication were analysed. Study condition: mirtazapine 30 mg each evening for 12 weeks, or matching placebo, followed by a 28-day taper; no protocolised psychosocial treatment (participants were free to use other services). Primary end point: change from baseline to week 12 in self-reported days of methamphetamine use in the past 28 days (timeline follow-back), analysed with a negative binomial mixed model (condition by time). ANZCTR ACTRN12622000235707.
can_establish: Whether, in adults with moderate or severe methamphetamine use disorder treated at public outpatient clinics, 12 weeks of mirtazapine reduced self-reported days of methamphetamine use compared with placebo, and how often it caused adverse effects and stopping of the medication over those 12 weeks.
cannot_establish: Whether mirtazapine reduced use as measured by drug tests (the oral-fluid measure did not differ); whether any benefit lasts beyond the 12 weeks of treatment (no later follow-up is reported); whether it improves depression, sleep, HIV risk behaviour, quality of life or functioning (none differed); its effect in people taking antidepressants, pregnant people or people with a suicide attempt in the past year (all excluded); or rare and long-term harms (172 people treated for 12 weeks).

sample.recruitment: Mainly social media, flyers at health services and word of mouth; telephone screening, then a face-to-face eligibility assessment at the trial clinic, where participants were enrolled as patients; A$50 (US$35.59) per assessment. Of 1267 assessed, 923 were excluded (475 declined or could not be recontacted, 419 did not meet the inclusion criteria, 29 incomplete screening) (Methods › Procedures, pp. 582–583; Figure 1, p. 583).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: age 18 to 65; DSM-5 moderate or severe methamphetamine use disorder in the past year; methamphetamine use at least twice a week in the past 4 weeks; a positive drug screen for amphetamines. Excluded: prescribed antidepressant medication; suicide attempt in the past year; pregnancy or lactation; need for acute medical care; inpatient treatment; incarceration; contraindications to mirtazapine. Detailed criteria are only in the eMethods (Supplement 3, not read) (Methods › Participants, p. 582).
sample.demographics: Mean age 42.0 (SD 8.6); 126 women (37.2%); 16% born outside Australia; median 10 years of schooling; 179 (52.8%) unemployed; 136 (40%) with a prison history; mean duration of methamphetamine use 21 years; median 24 (IQR 17 to 28) of the past 28 days used at baseline; injecting methamphetamine 48.5% (placebo) vs 43.0% (mirtazapine); PHQ-9 of 10 or more at eligibility 82 (49.1%) vs 83 (48.3%) (Abstract › Results, p. 581; Table 1, p. 584; Results › Participants, pp. 584–585).
sample.attrition: Five people randomized to placebo never received medication (3 did not attend the baseline visit, 1 was incarcerated, 1 withdrew consent) and are excluded from every analysis. Medication was discontinued by 36 of 167 (22%) on placebo and 49 of 172 (28%) on mirtazapine (P = .14); week-12 outcome data were available for 293 of 339 (86%: 88% on mirtazapine, 85% on placebo). Reasons in Figure 1: chose to stop because they did not like the medication's effects or did not feel it was working, 19 (placebo) vs 29 (mirtazapine); adverse events or other health risks, 4 vs 10 (Figure 1, p. 583; Results › Participants, p. 584; Table 3, p. 586).
sample.selection_effects: Participants sought treatment enough to enrol at a clinic but were recruited mainly by advertisement and paid for assessments. Use was heavy and long-standing (median 24 of 28 days; mean 21 years). People taking prescribed antidepressants or with a suicide attempt in the past year were excluded, which removes part of the depressed population the authors aim to generalize to. About three in four people assessed were not enrolled. 'Routine clinical practice' here still includes research assessments, electronic pill bottles and payments.

exposure.measurement: Assigned trial medication: mirtazapine or matching placebo tablets (placebo supplied by Syntro Pty Ltd), taken by mouth each evening, dispensed in bottles of 35 tablets fitted with MEMS caps and replaced at weeks 4 and 8. Clinicians could offer a half-tablet rescue dose to people who stopped for tolerability reasons (8 participants: 6 on mirtazapine, 2 on placebo). Adherence: percentage of days in the 12 weeks on which the bottle was opened (Methods › Procedures and End Points, pp. 582–583; Results › Participants, p. 584).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions: 30 mg daily by mouth for 12 weeks, then a taper at 15 mg for 28 days from week 12. MEMS adherence: median 52% (IQR 26% to 78%) overall and 62% (40% to 81%) when periods after discontinuation are excluded; adherence by arm is not reported in the article (Results › Participants, p. 584).
exposure.polysubstance: Days of other substance use, summed over tobacco, alcohol, cannabis, cocaine, ecstasy, hallucinogens, inhalants and heroin, at baseline mean 35.8 (SD 20.5) on placebo vs 33.5 (19.2) on mirtazapine (Table 1, p. 584); the arms did not differ in days of other substance use during the trial (Results › Exploratory End Points, p. 586; estimates only in eTable 2, not read).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable: participants were using at entry, and the outcome is use during treatment.

comparison.controls: Matching placebo tablets on the same schedule, with the same referral information, harm-reduction brochure, assessments and payments; both arms were free to use other drug treatment and health services.
comparison.matching: Randomized 1:1, stratified by sex at birth and by PHQ-9 score of 10 or more. The article does not describe how the sequence was generated or how allocation was concealed (protocol in Supplement 1, not read). Baseline characteristics were similar (Table 1, p. 584): mean days of use in the past 28 days 22.0 (placebo) vs 23.1 (mirtazapine) (Results › Change in Methamphetamine Use, p. 585).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to a randomized comparison.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Same population; days of other substance use similar at baseline (Table 1, p. 584).

outcomes.instruments: Primary: self-reported days of methamphetamine use in the past 28 days by timeline follow-back at baseline and weeks 4, 8 and 12, with week 12 the primary end point. Secondary: PHQ-9 (depression), Athens Insomnia Scale 5-item version, HIV Risk-Taking Behavior Scale of the Opiate Treatment Index, EQ-5D-5L utility score, and methamphetamine-negative oral fluid (cut-off 25 ng/mL) at weeks 4, 8 and 12. Exploratory: suicide risk (C-SSRS screener score of 3 or more), days of other substance use, adherence. Safety: participant-reported adverse events coded by MedDRA system organ class (Methods › End Points, p. 583).
outcomes.validity_norms: The timeline follow-back is cited as 88% sensitive and 96% specific against urine tests in earlier work; in this trial, self-reported use over the past 3 days had 89% sensitivity and 83% specificity against methamphetamine-positive oral fluid (Methods › End Points, 1st paragraph, p. 583). The oral-fluid test is objective but detects only recent use.
outcomes.operationalization: Benefit is a larger fall in self-reported use days from baseline to week 12 on mirtazapine than on placebo (the condition-by-time interaction of a negative binomial mixed model with a random intercept and time as a factor), reported as a mean difference in days and as an incidence rate ratio; the average over weeks 4, 8 and 12 is a further estimand (Methods › Statistical Analysis, pp. 583–584).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; the authors state that the width of confidence intervals was not adjusted for multiple comparisons (Statistical Analysis, p. 583). The count of 8 covers the primary end point, five secondary end points and two exploratory end points named in the Methods; each was estimated at weeks 4, 8 and 12 or as an average, and subgroup interactions by sex and by depression come on top.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Double-blind: all clinicians, researchers and investigators were blinded to allocation (Methods › Trial Design, p. 582). The primary outcome is the participant's own report to a blinded researcher. No check of blinding is reported in the article, although drowsiness (47% vs 33%) and weight gain (10% vs 3%) were more common on mirtazapine and could have revealed allocation.

analysis.effect_sizes: Primary (339 analysed): change in days of use from baseline to week 12, −7.0 (95% CI −8.5 to −5.6) on mirtazapine vs −4.8 (−6.2 to −3.4) on placebo; treatment estimand −2.2 days of 28 (−4.2 to −0.2), P = .02; incidence rate ratio 0.89 (0.80 to 0.98). Week 4: −1.3 (−3.3 to 0.6), P = .20; week 8: −1.9 (−3.9 to 0.1), P = .06; average over the 12 weeks: −1.8 (−3.5 to −0.1), P = .03. Secondary: methamphetamine-negative oral fluid averaged over weeks 4, 8 and 12, 12.0% vs 13.2% (difference 1.3 percentage points, −4.7 to 7.2; P = .68); at week 12, PHQ-9 −0.2 (−1.3 to 1.0); AIS-5 −0.6 (−1.4 to 0.2); HIV risk −0.3 (−1.0 to 0.3); EQ-5D 0.9 (−3.1 to 4.9). Editors' calculation (baseline mean plus mean change; approximate, because the changes are model estimates): about 16.1 vs 17.2 days of use in the past 28 days at week 12. Editors' calculation from the counts in Table 3: drowsiness risk difference 13.6 percentage points (95% CI 3.3 to 23.9); weight gain 6.9 (1.7 to 12.0).
analysis.covariates: None in the primary model. A prespecified adjusted analysis (baseline days of use, injecting, PHQ-9 score, age and sex) and multiple imputation by chained equations are said to leave the primary estimate unchanged, with numbers only in Supplement 3 (eFigure 2, eTables 7 to 9, not read) (Results › Change in Methamphetamine Use, p. 585).
analysis.preregistration_detail: ANZCTR ACTRN12622000235707, described as prospectively registered; the protocol was published (Trials, 2024; reference 14) and is Supplement 1, and the statistical analysis plan is Supplement 2; the article states that all analyses were prespecified in that plan (Methods › Trial Design, p. 582; Statistical Analysis, p. 584). The registry record, protocol and analysis plan were not read, so registered and reported outcomes have not been compared.
analysis.selective_reporting: Supplements 1 to 4 were not read. Sensitivity, adjusted and subgroup estimates, model details, other substance use and the full adverse-event tables are only in Supplement 3. No outcome after the 12 weeks of treatment is reported. Adherence is not reported by arm.
analysis.power: 340 participants for 90% power to detect a rate ratio of 0.75 on the primary end point (two-sided α .05), assuming 75% follow-up at week 12, with the effect size taken from Coffin et al. (2020) (Statistical Analysis, pp. 583–584). The observed rate ratio (0.89) is smaller than the planned minimum; follow-up (86%) was better than assumed.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Self-reported use fell more on mirtazapine: from baseline to week 12 the fall was 2.2 days of 28 larger than on placebo (7.0 against 4.8 days; 95% CI for the difference 0.2 to 4.2; rate ratio 0.89), with smaller, non-significant differences at weeks 4 and 8. Because the mirtazapine arm started about 1 day higher, the arms differed by only about 1 day at week 12, both still using on about 16 to 17 of 28 days (editors' calculation). The one drug-test measure did not differ (12.0% vs 13.2% of oral-fluid samples negative), nor did depression, sleep, HIV risk behaviour or quality of life. Drowsiness (47% vs 33%) and weight gain (10% vs 3%) were more common on mirtazapine, and 23% vs 15% stopped the medication for reasons related to it. No follow-up after treatment is reported.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Key Points conclude "Mirtazapine is safe and effective when used in routine clinical practice" (p. 582), and the abstract's Conclusions say that mirtazapine reduced methamphetamine use (p. 581), causal wording for a self-reported outcome whose objective counterpart did not differ. The Discussion says the trial confirms the phase 2 benefits and generalizes them to routine practice and a broader population (pp. 586–587). The Discussion fairly calls the effect diluted compared with the phase 2 trials (p. 587), but it cites strong agreement between self-report and biological measures, including in this trial, without addressing the oral-fluid result that showed no difference between arms (Discussion › Strengths and Limitations, p. 587); the Results describe secondary end points as trending towards benefit although their intervals are centred near zero (p. 585); and the Discussion infers a direct effect on addictive processes from the absence of effects on depression and insomnia, without a mediation analysis (p. 587). 'Safe' rests on 172 people treated for 12 weeks.

timeline.event: Colfax et al.: 12-week placebo-controlled trial in 60 men who have sex with men in San Francisco; risk ratio 0.57 for a methamphetamine-positive urine at 12 weeks. Steven Shoptaw, second author of this trial, is one of its authors.

Coffin et al.: 120 cisgender men and transgender women who have sex with men in San Francisco, 24 weeks of treatment and 12 weeks of follow-up; risk ratio 0.67 at 12 weeks. No author in common with this trial.
Naji et al. meta-analysis of the two San Francisco trials, cited by this trial as showing a 14% difference in methamphetamine-positive urine tests (not read).

This trial: 339 adults at six Australian public clinics, including women (37%) and people with depressive symptoms (49%); a 2.2-day larger fall in self-reported use days of 28 (rate ratio 0.89), the oral-fluid measure not different.

replication.where_it_stands: Three placebo-controlled trials point the same way on their primary measures of use: two from one San Francisco team on urine positivity in sexual-minority men, and this larger trial from a different team (one investigator in common with the first trial) on self-reported use days in a broader population. The effect is smaller in this trial, its one drug-test measure did not differ, and only the second San Francisco trial reports outcomes after the medication stopped.

funding.funder: Australian Government Medical Research Future Fund (grant 2007155); the National Drug and Alcohol Research Centre is supported by the Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing; Drs Degenhardt and Berk were supported by NHMRC Leadership grants (2016825 and 2017131). The funders had no role in design, conduct, data handling, analysis, interpretation, writing or the decision to submit. Placebo tablets were supplied by Syntro Pty Ltd (Methods › Procedures, p. 582; Article Information › Funding/Support and Role of the Funder/Sponsor, p. 588).
funding.declared_conflicts: As printed (Article Information › Conflict of Interest Disclosures, p. 588): Drs McKetin, Turner, Degan and Christmass reported Medical Research Future Fund grants during the study; Dr Shoptaw reported medications for a different study provided by Alkermes, Gilead Sciences and Indivior during the study and personal fees from Clear Scientific outside the submitted work; Dr Clare reported personal consulting fees outside the work and support from a New South Wales Ministry of Health programme; Dr Dore reported grants from AbbVie and Gilead Sciences during the study; Dr Dean reported NHMRC grants during the study and owning shares in Medigrowth; Dr Arunogiri reported speaker honoraria and advisory board fees from Camurus and Indivior outside the work; Dr Degenhardt reported NHMRC grants; Dr Goodman-Meza reported grants from the National Institutes of Health, St Vincent's Hospital and UNSW outside the work; Dr Hayllar reported speaker fees from Camurus and Indivior, donated to a medical charity, outside the work; Dr Colledge-Frisby reported employment by the National Drug Research Institute, which has Australian Government core funds; Dr Berk reported an NHMRC grant during the study and many other research grants and honoraria (including from Janssen) outside the work, and two issued patents. No other disclosures were reported.
funding.affiliations_note: Led from the National Drug and Alcohol Research Centre, UNSW Sydney, with clinicians from the six public clinics among the authors. Dr Shoptaw (UCLA) is second author and an author of Colfax et al. (2011), the first San Francisco trial; he is listed for concept and design and critical review here. No other author appears in the author lists of the two San Francisco trials (Colfax et al., 2011; Coffin et al., 2020, from their reference records), so Coffin et al. (2020) shares no author with this trial. Outside the mirtazapine trials, Coffin (first author of the 2020 trial) and Shoptaw are both authors of a bupropion–naltrexone trial (Trivedi et al., 2021; reference list of Bakouni et al., 2023, and its reference record). Mirtazapine is a generic drug; no industry funding of the trial is reported.

what_would_settle_it: An independent multi-site placebo-controlled trial in a broad population of people with methamphetamine use disorder, with a drug-test-verified primary outcome (for example urine-confirmed use days or abstinence), a check of blinding, adherence support, and follow-up of at least 6 months after the medication stops, powered for an effect of the size seen here (about 2 days in 28).

domains.note: Randomized 1:1 with stratification by sex and depression, and matching placebo tablets with all clinicians, researchers and investigators blinded, but the article does not describe how the sequence was generated or how allocation was concealed (protocol not read). Baseline characteristics were well balanced (Table 1), so the concern is only the missing description.

Double-blind; estimands use all available data whether or not participants stopped the medication or took the rescue dose. Five people randomized to placebo who never received medication (1.5% of those randomized) are excluded, which is unlikely to matter. Other treatment was open to both arms.
Week-12 data for 86% (88% vs 85%); mixed models use all assessments, and multiple imputation is reported to leave the primary estimate unchanged (numbers only in the unread supplement).

The primary outcome is self-reported to blinded researchers. Participants could have guessed their allocation from drowsiness (47% vs 33%) or weight gain (10% vs 3%), no blinding check is reported, and the objective oral-fluid measure showed no difference between arms (12.0% vs 13.2% negative). Self-report agreed reasonably with oral fluid overall (sensitivity 89%, specificity 83%), but agreement by arm is not reported.

Prospectively registered, with a published protocol and a statistical analysis plan; the primary end point (week 12) and the analysis are reported as prespecified. The registry record and the plan were not read, so this judgment rests on the article's statements.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A well-conducted, adequately sized pragmatic trial with low attrition and a prespecified analysis. The concerns are that the article does not describe allocation concealment, and above all that the only significant result is on a self-reported outcome while the one objective measure did not differ and side effects may have revealed allocation; a modest expectancy effect on self-report could account for a difference of about 2 days in 28. The trial can be cited for a small reduction in self-reported use over 12 weeks and for the frequency of drowsiness, weight gain and stopping; it cannot be cited for reduced use on drug tests, for effects after treatment, or for long-term safety.

key_findings.finding: 1267 people assessed, 344 randomized (172 to each arm); 339 received trial medication (167 placebo, 172 mirtazapine) and all 339 were analysed; the 5 not treated were all in the placebo arm (3 did not attend baseline, 1 incarcerated, 1 withdrew consent).
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Results (p. 581); Figure 1 (p. 583); Results › Participants, 1st paragraph (p. 584)

key_findings.finding: Sample: mean age 42.0 (SD 8.6); 126 women (37.2%); a PHQ-9 score of 10 or more at eligibility in 82 (49.1%) on placebo and 83 (48.3%) on mirtazapine; injecting 48.5% (placebo) vs 43.0% (mirtazapine); median 10 years of schooling; 179 (52.8%) unemployed; 136 (40%) with a prison history; mean 21 years of methamphetamine use; median 24 (IQR 17 to 28) of the past 28 days used at baseline.
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Results (p. 581); Table 1 (p. 584); Results › Participants, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (pp. 584–585)

key_findings.finding: Primary end point: mean days of use in the past 28 days at baseline 22.0 (95% CI 20.3 to 23.8) on placebo and 23.1 (21.3 to 24.9) on mirtazapine; change to week 12, −4.8 (−6.2 to −3.4) vs −7.0 (−8.5 to −5.6); treatment estimand −2.2 days (−4.2 to −0.2), P = .02, which the authors express as an 8% reduction in the risk of use on a given day (8 fewer use days per 100 possible days); incidence rate ratio 0.89 (0.80 to 0.98).
key_findings.locator: Results › Change in Methamphetamine Use, 1st paragraph; Table 2, Primary end point
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation (baseline mean plus mean change; approximate because the changes are model estimates): about 17.2 days of use in the past 28 days on placebo and 16.1 on mirtazapine at week 12. The rate ratio equals the ratio of the two arms' week-12 to baseline ratios (16.1/23.1 divided by 17.2/22.0 = 0.89). The −2.2 days is a difference in the fall from baseline: because the mirtazapine arm began 1.1 days higher, the arms differ by only about 1.1 days at week 12. The model enters baseline as one of the time points rather than as a covariate (Statistical Analysis, pp. 583–584), so part of the larger fall on mirtazapine could be regression from its higher baseline; the prespecified adjusted analysis uses covariates from the eligibility assessment, with its estimates only in Supplement 3 (editors' reasoning).

key_findings.finding: Other time points: treatment estimand −1.3 days (95% CI −3.3 to 0.6), P = .20, at week 4 and −1.9 (−3.9 to 0.1), P = .06, at week 8; average over the 12 weeks −1.8 (−3.5 to −0.1), P = .03. The primary estimate is reported as robust to multiple imputation and to adjustment for baseline covariates, with the numbers only in Supplement 3.
key_findings.locator: Results › Change in Methamphetamine Use, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Secondary end points, none significant: methamphetamine-negative oral-fluid samples averaged over weeks 4, 8 and 12, 12.0% (placebo) vs 13.2% (mirtazapine), difference 1.3 percentage points (95% CI −4.7 to 7.2), P = .68; at week 12, PHQ-9 change −0.2 (−1.3 to 1.0), P = .77; AIS-5 −0.6 (−1.4 to 0.2), P = .13; HIV risk behaviour −0.3 (−1.0 to 0.3), P = .32; EQ-5D 0.9 (−3.1 to 4.9), P = .66.
key_findings.locator: Methods › End Points (p. 583) and Statistical Analysis (p. 584); Table 2, Secondary end points; Results › Secondary End Points (p. 585)
key_findings.note: By the editors' calculation 86.8% and 88.0% of oral-fluid samples were not methamphetamine-negative, consistent with continued use by most participants.

key_findings.finding: By depression at eligibility, use-days estimand −2.8 (95% CI −5.7 to 0.0) in people not depressed and −1.4 (−4.2 to 1.4) in people depressed; estimands described as similar by sex and by depression (interaction tests only in the supplement). Among people depressed at baseline, insomnia improved more on mirtazapine at week 12 (−1.2, −2.3 to 0.0; P = .04), and depression did not (−1.2, −2.8 to 0.5; P = .16).

Medication discontinued by 85 (25%): 36 (22%) on placebo vs 49 (28%) on mirtazapine (P = .14); for reasons related to the medication 25 (15%) vs 40 (23%). Eight took the half-tablet rescue dose (6 mirtazapine, 2 placebo). MEMS adherence median 52% (IQR 26% to 78%), 62% (40% to 81%) excluding periods after discontinuation. Week-12 data for 293 of 339 (86%).

Safety over 12 weeks (placebo vs mirtazapine): drowsiness 55 (33%) vs 80 (47%), P = .01; weight gain 5 (3%) vs 17 (10%), P = .01; nervous system disorders 78 (47%) vs 111 (65%), P = .001; investigations 8 (5%) vs 19 (11%), P = .03; any adverse event 145 (87%) vs 155 (90%); serious adverse events 11 (7%) vs 7 (4%), none judged related to the medication; suicide risk (C-SSRS screener 3 or more) 6 (4%) vs 5 (3%); suicidal ideation 11 (7%) vs 11 (6%).
key_findings.locator: Table 3; Results › Safety; Results › Exploratory End Points
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation from the counts: drowsiness risk difference 13.6 percentage points (95% CI 3.3 to 23.9); weight gain 6.9 (1.7 to 12.0).

key_findings.finding: In this trial, self-reported methamphetamine use over the past 3 days had 89% sensitivity and 83% specificity against methamphetamine-positive oral fluid.

Design: prospectively registered (ACTRN12622000235707), protocol and statistical analysis plan supplied; all analyses stated to be prespecified. Sample size of 340 for 90% power to detect a rate ratio of 0.75, assuming 75% follow-up; confidence intervals not adjusted for multiple comparisons.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Trial Design (p. 582); Methods › Statistical Analysis, 1st paragraph (p. 583) and last paragraph (p. 584)

key_findings.finding: The authors judge the effect diluted compared with the phase 2 trials: an 8% reduction in the risk of use on a given day against a 14% reduction in methamphetamine-positive urine tests in the earlier trials, attributing the difference to a heterogeneous population with entrenched use, poor adherence and frequent discontinuation.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 3rd paragraph; Discussion › Strengths and Limitations
key_findings.note: The 8% is an absolute difference (2.2 of 28 days); the relative reduction implied by the rate ratio is 11% (see reporting issues).

reporting_issues.issue: The Abstract prints the primary result as a mean difference of 2.2 days with a 95% CI of −4.2 to −0.2 days: the point estimate is positive and lies outside its own interval. Table 2 and the Results give −2.2 (−4.2 to −0.2).
reporting_issues.consequence: Sign slip in the Abstract; the result is a reduction of 2.2 days.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results and Discussion call the primary result an 8% reduction in the risk of methamphetamine use on a given day. The 8% is 2.2 of 28 days, an absolute difference of about 8 percentage points of days. The Discussion then compares the 8% with a 14% reduction in methamphetamine-positive urine tests in the phase 2 trials, a different outcome (the Introduction, 3rd paragraph, p. 582, calls it a 14% difference). Editors' calculation: the relative reduction implied by the incidence rate ratio of 0.89 is 11%.
reporting_issues.consequence: The comparison of 8% with 14% mixes outcomes and possibly scales; claims should give the days and the rate ratio rather than an 8% reduction in risk.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 gives medication discontinuation due to adverse reactions as 25 of 167 (15%) on placebo vs 40 of 172 (23%) on mirtazapine with P = .19. Editors' calculation from these counts: P = .053 (chi-square) or .055 (Fisher's exact test), while every other P value in the table matches its counts by an uncorrected chi-square test (for example all discontinuations, P = .14) except suicide risk (6 of 167 vs 5 of 172, printed .68; .72 by recalculation), a trivial difference.
reporting_issues.consequence: The printed P value is probably wrong; the excess of medication-related discontinuation on mirtazapine is borderline rather than clearly non-significant.

reporting_issues.issue: The Abstract says 40 (23%) discontinued mirtazapine due to adverse events vs 25 (15%) on placebo; the Results call these discontinuations for reasons related to the trial medication and Table 3 calls them due to adverse reactions. Figure 1 shows that most were people who chose to stop because they did not like the medication's effects or did not feel it was working (29 on mirtazapine, 19 on placebo), with adverse events or other health risks given for 10 and 4.
reporting_issues.consequence: Read the 23% vs 15% as stopping for reasons related to the medication, not as stopping for adverse events.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 gives baseline EQ-5D utility scores as median 0.92 (IQR 0.85 to 0.97), on a scale whose maximum is 1, but Table 2 reports mean changes of 1.3 (placebo) and 2.2 (mirtazapine) with an estimand of 0.9 (−3.1 to 4.9), which cannot be on the same scale; the unit of the change is not stated.
reporting_issues.consequence: The quality-of-life result cannot be interpreted as printed; it is null either way.

design_detail: Systematic review with random-effects meta-analysis (Comprehensive Meta-analysis version 2) of quantitative studies of people presenting to general emergency departments, psychiatric emergency services or trauma centres with methamphetamine (or related amphetamine) intoxication or dependence. 23 studies were included (17 from the USA, 7 of them from one centre). Clinical features were summarized narratively, study by study, because the studies measured them inconsistently; only three quantities were pooled: the share of attendees who were methamphetamine-positive (17 studies), sex (11 studies) and age (7 studies) of methamphetamine-positive versus methamphetamine-negative attendees. No protocol registration is reported. Pages are the online-first article pages 1–12 printed on this PDF (print issue pp. 567–578).
can_establish: Which clinical features individual emergency-department, psychiatric-emergency and trauma-centre studies (1988 to 2016 data, mostly US) reported in people presenting after methamphetamine use, with their study-level percentages, and, with strong caveats, how the share of methamphetamine-positive attendees and their sex and age differed between studies.
cannot_establish: Pooled frequencies of any clinical feature (none were computed), case fatality among presentations (no deaths are reported), whether the features are caused by methamphetamine rather than other drugs or the reason for presentation (no comparison group for most features; three included studies counted cocaine or other stimulants), or a meaningful average share of methamphetamine-positive attendees (the pool mixes all emergency visits, psychiatric visits, trauma admissions, patients with rhabdomyolysis or chest pain and street-involved youth, and counts one data set more than once).

sample.recruitment: Database search of PubMed, PsycINFO, CINAHL and Scopus covering 1990–2017, run in April 2017 and updated to December 2017, plus hand searching (one study added) (pp. 2–3). Included studies came from general emergency departments (11 in the prevalence pool), trauma centres (4) and psychiatric emergency services (2); 17 were from the USA (7 from the University of California, Davis, Sacramento; 3 from Hawaii), 4 from Australia, 1 from Taiwan and 1 from Canada (p. 4; p. 7).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: English-language quantitative studies conducted in an emergency department, psychiatric emergency department or trauma centre and focused on methamphetamine and related amphetamines. Excluded: qualitative research, samples under 10, opinion pieces, case series, reports, and studies in non-emergency psychiatric inpatient units (p. 2). Several included studies are nevertheless series in which every patient was methamphetamine-positive (Lan et al., 1998, 44 patients; Turnipseed et al., 2003; Hawley et al., 2013; Table 1, pp. 5–6).
sample.demographics: Pooled attendees in the prevalence studies: 56% male (p. 7). Mean ages of 28.4 years for methamphetamine-positive and 38.4 years for methamphetamine-negative attendees are given in the abstract and on p. 8 without a source, SD, number of studies or method of calculation (Figure 4 shows only odds ratios); study-level mean ages of methamphetamine-positive patients range from 21 (street-involved youth) to a median of 46 (chest-pain patients) (Table 1).
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level.
sample.selection_effects: English-only search ending in 2017 with no grey literature or registries; heavy weighting to one US centre (7 of 23 studies, with overlapping study periods); two sets of linked studies drawn from the same data (Fatovich et al., 2012, a subset of Gray et al., 2007; Cloutier et al., 2013, and Hendrickson et al., 2008 and 2010) (p. 4). Most source studies are chart reviews of selected presentations (trauma admissions, chest pain, rhabdomyolysis, psychiatric visits), so their percentages describe very different denominators.

exposure.measurement: Whatever each study used: urine toxicology screens (positive results likely include other amphetamine-like compounds, p. 4) or self-report and clinical attribution in records. Three included studies counted cocaine or other stimulant use (p. 10). The pooled share of methamphetamine-positive attendees was about four times higher with toxicology (22.8%) than with self-report (5.7%) (p. 8; ratio, editors' calculation).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not reported in the review; the authors note that the pattern and frequency of use, the time of last use and the type of methamphetamine were rarely recorded (p. 10).
exposure.polysubstance: Not handled: the authors state that poly-drug use was poorly recorded in chart reviews and that toxicology screens stay positive for about 72 hours, which makes it difficult to link use accurately to the acute presentation (p. 10).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable; time of last use was not accurately assessed, which the authors say prevents separating intoxication from withdrawal in psychotic presentations (p. 10).

comparison.controls: For sex and age only: methamphetamine-negative attendees in the same studies (Figures 3–4, pp. 8–9). For clinical features there is no comparison group, except within individual studies (for example Bunting et al., 2007, against other patients with toxicology-related problems; Pasic et al., 2007, a matched case-control study), whose comparative results the review does not pool.
comparison.matching: Not applicable at review level; Pasic et al. (2007) is described in Table 1 as a case-control study using matched samples, without the matching variables; its odds ratios for sex (3.523) and age (2.445; Figures 3–4) show that it was not matched on sex or age.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Psychiatric history, other drug use and reason for presentation are not used in any analysis.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not recorded; methamphetamine-negative attendees may have used other drugs.

outcomes.instruments: Study-level presenting problems as recorded in each source (Table 1 column 'Behaviour or presenting problem (%)'); share of methamphetamine-positive attendees; sex; age.
outcomes.validity_norms: Primary-study risk of bias assessed with a modified Hoy et al. (2012) prevalence tool of 10 items; all studies but one (Marshall et al., 2012) were rated low risk, with a kappa of 1.00 between two raters described as all authors (pp. 2–3). Per-study ratings are not shown.
outcomes.operationalization: Clinical features are whatever each study recorded; the percentages in Table 1 have no stated denominator and no common case definition (for example agitated delirium, agitation, aggression, violent behaviour).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Three pooled quantities (prevalence, sex, age) with subgroup analyses by measurement method and setting.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Screening by at least two raters independently (p. 2); data extraction not described as duplicate (all authors contributed, p. 11).

analysis.effect_sizes: Pooled share of methamphetamine-positive attendees 11.3% (95% CI 6.3–19.7%; 17 studies; 120,111 attendees); toxicology 22.8% (15.4–32.5%; 8 studies) against self-report 5.7% (2.8–11.2%; 9 studies), Q = 12.42, p < 0.001; by setting, emergency departments 9.3% (11 studies), psychiatric emergency 13.4% (2), trauma 17.9% (4), not significantly different (p. 8; Figure 2). Methamphetamine positivity, men versus women: OR 1.422 (1.236–1.636), 11 studies, I² 50.16, Q 20.66, df 10, p = 0.029; toxicology subgroup interval 1.25–1.83 without a point estimate; by setting, emergency 1.36 (5 studies), psychiatric 2.22 (2), trauma 1.35 (4) (p. 8; Figure 3). Age: methamphetamine-positive attendees younger, pooled OR 2.251 (1.421–3.567), 7 studies; emergency 3.108 (3), psychiatric 2.228 (2), trauma 1.286 (0.745–2.222) (p. 8; Figure 4). No heterogeneity statistic for the prevalence or age pools, no prediction interval, no publication-bias assessment.
analysis.covariates: None; all pooled estimates are unadjusted.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned; PRISMA and MOOSE are cited as reporting guides (p. 2).
analysis.selective_reporting: Sensitivity analyses restricted to low-risk studies are said to have been run for all meta-analyses (p. 4), but no results are reported. The age analysis is reported as an odds ratio converted from age data without describing the conversion.
analysis.power: Not addressed. Subgroups by setting rest on two to five studies.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Study by study, people presenting after methamphetamine use had tachycardia in 42% and 85% and hypertension in 6.4% and 69% (two studies), acute coronary syndrome in 9 of 36 methamphetamine-positive chest-pain patients, psychosis in 12% to 80%, agitation in 13% to 48%, aggression in 18% to 50% and suicidal thoughts or behaviour in 6% to 50%, in very different settings and without stated denominators. Nothing about these features was pooled, no comparison group was used for them, and no deaths are reported. The only pooled results are the share of methamphetamine-positive attendees (11.3%, much higher with toxicology than with self-report) and their sex and age.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says presentations were characterised by cardiac complications, psychiatric symptoms and aggression with safety risk to health personnel (p. 1), and the discussion calls methamphetamine intoxication or dependence "a catalyst for aggressive and agitated behaviour" (p. 10); both rest on study-level descriptions without comparison groups. The implications section says nearly half of patients were acutely psychotic and nearly one-quarter depressed (p. 10), figures that match no pooled estimate and, for depression, only one study's 12 of 60. The title promises risk factors, but the only correlates analysed are sex and age among attendees, which describe who tested positive, not who is at risk of presenting. The abstract reports a 'pooled variance' of 57.1% in men and 42.9% in women, a quantity that is not defined. The Discussion's statement that people presenting with methamphetamine use were on average 10 years younger, citing Figure 4 (p. 8), rests on these mean ages, whose source and method are not given; Figure 4 shows only odds ratios. Against this, the critical reflection (p. 10) states plainly that the clinical characteristics could not be pooled and lists the measurement problems.

timeline.event: Narrative review of methamphetamine clinical pharmacology giving second-hand frequencies for non-fatal presentations; among its four sources for them is Gray et al. (2007), also included here, so the two reviews are not independent
Scoping review of methamphetamine use and Australian emergency services (Ross, Adams & Beovich, 2017), cited here as consistent on sex and age; not read
Integrative review (Jones, Woods & Usher, 2018), cited here as finding that methamphetamine accounted for 2.3% or less of emergency presentations; not read
This review: by the authors' account the first meta-analysis characterising emergency presentations with methamphetamine intoxication or dependence

replication.where_it_stands: The only systematic synthesis of emergency presentations seen so far in this encyclopedia, but its clinical content is a study-by-study listing from 23 mostly single-centre US chart reviews up to 2016 data, with no pooled frequencies and no mortality. It can be cited as a pointer to the primary series and for the range of reported frequencies, not for how often any feature occurs in presentations generally.

funding.funder: Not reported (no funding statement in the article).
funding.declared_conflicts: No potential conflict of interest was reported by the authors (p. 11).
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from the University of Tasmania (School of Health Sciences) and the University of Sydney (Psychiatry; Addiction Medicine) (p. 1). Published in a mental-health nursing journal; the implications section argues for mental-health staff and beds in emergency departments (pp. 10–11). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective multicentre study of consecutive emergency presentations with toxicology-confirmed and quantified methamphetamine exposure (other drugs measured), recording vital signs, temperature, creatine kinase, ECG and troponin, psychiatric features and outcomes including death in a standard way, so that frequencies and case fatality can be given with denominators by setting, and fatal cases compared with non-fatal ones.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (people presenting to emergency settings), exposure (methamphetamine intoxication or dependence), comparison (methamphetamine-negative attendees, for demographics) and outcomes (clinical characteristics, prevalence, sex, age) are stated in the aims (p. 2), although the exposure admits 'related amphetamines' and the clinical outcomes are not defined.
No protocol or registration is mentioned.
Quantitative studies were included and case series excluded without explanation, and several included studies are series of methamphetamine-positive patients only.

Four databases with subject headings and keywords listed (p. 2), but the English-language restriction is not justified, which AMSTAR 2 requires even for partial yes; no grey literature or registries; the text says reference-list searching added nothing (p. 2) while the flow diagram adds one study from hand, reference-list and forward searches (p. 3).
Source material was reviewed independently by at least two raters (p. 2).
All authors contributed to extraction (p. 11); duplicate or checked extraction is not described.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Of the 100 full texts excluded for not meeting the criteria and the 11 excluded on critical appraisal (Figure 1, p. 3), only four are named with reasons (p. 2).

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 1 gives country, period, mode of arrival, exposure measure and setting, presenting problems, prevalence and age, but not the design of each study (only Pasic et al., 2007, is labelled as case-control), the comparators, the denominators of the percentages or the case definitions. AMSTAR 2 gives 'partial yes' only when populations, interventions, comparators, outcomes and research designs are all described, so the item is not met.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: A published prevalence tool (modified Hoy et al., 2012) covering selection and non-response was applied by two raters (pp. 2–3), but per-study ratings are not shown, and rating 22 of 23 mostly retrospective chart reviews as low risk, with perfect agreement, does not match the measurement problems the authors themselves list (p. 10).

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Not reported.

Random-effects pooling was used, but the prevalence pool combines non-comparable denominators (all emergency visits, psychiatric visits, trauma admissions, patients with rhabdomyolysis or chest pain, street-involved youth) and counts linked studies from one data set separately (Hendrickson et al., 2008 and 2010; Figure 2), with no heterogeneity statistic reported; the age analysis is expressed as an unexplained odds ratio.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: Sensitivity analyses restricted to low-risk studies are said to have been done (p. 4), but no results are given; with 22 of 23 studies rated low risk they could hardly differ.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The critical reflection lists measurement problems (p. 10), but the abstract and conclusions describe presentations as characterised by cardiac, psychiatric and aggressive features without taking them into account.

Variation in prevalence was explored by measurement method (toxicology against self-report, Q = 12.42) and setting, and the wide variation is acknowledged (p. 8); a close call, because no heterogeneity statistic is given for the main pool.
Not assessed.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: The authors report no potential conflict of interest (p. 11); no funding statement.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Critical items 2, 4, 7, 11, 13 and 15 are not met and item 9 is only partly met, so confidence in the review's pooled results is critically low. For this encyclopedia the decisive point is scope rather than the score: the review pooled no clinical feature and reports no deaths, so it cannot supply frequencies of toxicity features or case fatality. It may be cited for the study-level figures it lists, labelled as such and second-hand, and as a pointer to the primary series; not for the 11.3% pooled share of methamphetamine-positive attendees as a description of emergency departments generally, because that pool mixes incompatible denominators and counts one data set twice.

key_findings.finding: Searches of PubMed, PsycINFO, CINAHL and Scopus for 1990–2017, run in April 2017 and updated to December 2017; English-language quantitative studies from emergency departments, psychiatric emergency departments or trauma centres; case series, samples under 10, qualitative studies and opinion pieces excluded; selection by at least two raters independently.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Data sources and search strategy, 1st paragraph; Methods › Selection criteria, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Pages are the online-first article pages printed on this PDF (1–12); the print issue runs pp. 567–578.

key_findings.finding: 850 records, 706 after removal of duplicates, 573 excluded on title and abstract, 133 assessed for eligibility and 100 excluded, 1 added from hand, reference-list and forward searching, 34 assessed for quality, 11 excluded on critical appraisal, 23 included; only four excluded studies are named with reasons.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Search results and outcome, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 2); Figure 1 (p. 3)

key_findings.finding: Risk of bias was assessed with a modified Hoy et al. (2012) prevalence tool of 10 items; every study except Marshall et al. (2012) was rated low risk, with a kappa of 1.00 between raters; per-study ratings are not shown.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Risk of bias assessment, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Of the 23 studies, 17 are from the USA (7 from the University of California, Davis, Sacramento, and 3 from Hawaii), 4 from Australia, 1 from Taiwan and 1 from Canada. Two sets of linked studies use the same data (Fatovich et al., 2012, is a subset of Gray et al., 2007; Hendrickson et al., 2010, used the same data set as the linked Oregon studies), and one pair is a 20-year repeat at the same emergency department. Positive urine toxicology likely includes other amphetamine-like compounds.

Cardiac features, study by study: 9 (25%) of 36 methamphetamine-positive patients with chest pain had acute coronary syndrome, with mean heart rates of 114 against 98 beats per minute in those without it (Turnipseed et al., 2003); mean systolic pressure 148 mm Hg (95% CI 144–152), diastolic 86 (83–89) and heart rate 116 per minute (97.3–134.7), with 3 episodes of ventricular tachycardia and 15 of cardiac ischaemia and no denominator given (Hawley et al., 2013); tachycardia in 42% and hypertension in 6.4% (Fatovich et al., 2012) against 85% and 69% (Lan et al., 1998).
key_findings.locator: Results › Systematic review: Clinical characteristics associated with methamphetamine presentations › Cardiac complications, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
key_findings.note: Table 1 (p. 6) lists Turnipseed et al. (2003) with 171 subjects, all methamphetamine-positive, against 36 in the text.

key_findings.finding: Behavioural and psychiatric features: police attended 57% of presentations in Pasic et al. (2007) and 12% in Richards et al. (1999a); aggression towards others in 50% (Szuster, 1990); agitation and anxiety in 48% (Toles et al., 2006); of 60 methamphetamine-related presentations to a psychiatric emergency service, 48 (80%) were acutely psychotic and 12 depressed (Pasic et al., 2007); auditory hallucinations in 9 (64%), paranoid thoughts in 12 (86%), suicidal ideation in 4 (29%) and attempted suicide in 1 (7%) (Szuster, 1990).
key_findings.locator: Results › Systematic review › Behavioural and psychiatric problems, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
key_findings.note: 12 of 60 is printed as 23% (it is 20%); Szuster's percentages imply 14 people, while Table 1 lists 32 methamphetamine-positive presentations.

key_findings.finding: Presenting problems listed per study without stated denominators: bizarre behaviour 20%, aggression 18%, violence 3% (Bunting et al., 2007); suicidal 25%, psychotic 12%, anxiety 10%, depression 8% (Cloutier et al., 2013); agitated delirium 20%, psychosis 12%, assault 8%, suicidal thoughts 6% (Gray et al., 2007, amphetamine-related presentations, Perth); life-threatening complication 9%, ECG abnormalities 6%, chest pain 2% (Hawley et al., 2013); suicide attempts 50% among 44 patients admitted for methamphetamine intoxication (Lan et al., 1998); psychosis 80%, suicidal 40%, agitation 13%, hypertension or tachycardia 42% (Pasic et al., 2007); aggression 50%, paranoia 86%, suicidal 29% (Szuster, 1990); agitation 48%, suicidal 47%, homicidal 10% (Toles et al., 2006).

Trauma presentations: motor vehicle accidents were the most common trauma presentation in four studies; London et al. (2009) report motor vehicle accidents in 49%, assaults in 22% and gunshot wounds in 8.6% of presentations, and Tominaga et al. (2004) 36%, 17.9% and 3.6%.
key_findings.locator: Results › Systematic review › Trauma presentations, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
key_findings.note: Table 1 (p. 6) attributes motor vehicle accidents 36% to Schermer and Wisner (1999) and gives only intentional injury 37% for Tominaga et al. (2004), so the text and the table do not line up on the trauma figures.

key_findings.finding: Pooled share of methamphetamine-positive attendees across 17 studies (120,111 attendees): 11.3% (95% CI 6.3–19.7%); 22.8% (15.4–32.5%) in 8 studies using toxicology against 5.7% (2.8–11.2%) in 9 using self-report (Q = 12.42, p < 0.001); emergency departments 9.3% (11 studies), psychiatric emergency 13.4% (2), trauma 17.9% (4), not significantly different. Study denominators range from all emergency visits (461 of 32,617) to patients with rhabdomyolysis (166 of 387), patients with chest pain (318 of 875) and street-involved youth (30 of 133); both Hendrickson et al. (2008) and (2010) are pooled.
key_findings.locator: Results › Meta-analysis: Prevalence and demographics associated with methamphetamine presentations, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Figure 2 (p. 7)

key_findings.finding: Sex: methamphetamine positivity in men against women, OR 1.422 (95% CI 1.236–1.636), 11 studies with 23,434 men (as printed) and 21,365 women, I² 50.16, Q 20.66, df 10, p = 0.029; toxicology subgroup interval 1.25–1.83 (no point estimate printed); emergency 1.36 (5 studies), psychiatric 2.22 (2), trauma 1.35 (4).
key_findings.locator: Results › Meta-analysis: Prevalence and demographics…, 3rd paragraph; Figure 3

key_findings.finding: Age: 7 studies with 1,597 methamphetamine-positive and 40,545 methamphetamine-negative attendees; mean age 28.4 against 38.4 years (no source, SD, number of studies or method given; Figure 4 shows only odds ratios); pooled OR 2.251 (95% CI 1.421–3.567), higher values meaning younger methamphetamine-positive attendees; emergency 3.108 (3 studies), psychiatric 2.228 (2), trauma 1.286 (0.745–2.222; 2 studies, p = 0.367).
key_findings.locator: Results › Meta-analysis: Prevalence and demographics…, 4th paragraph (p. 8); Figure 4 (p. 9)

key_findings.finding: The authors state that the studies had no consistent measures of clinical characteristics, which limited the meta-analyses to sex, age and prevalence; that chart reviews identified use, its pattern, the type of methamphetamine and other drug use poorly; that three included studies counted cocaine or other stimulant use; that toxicology screens stay positive for 72 hours, which makes it difficult to link use accurately to the acute presentation; and that time of last use was not accurately assessed, which prevents separating intoxication from withdrawal in psychotic presentations.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Critical reflection of the literature, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: No study row and no part of the results reports deaths or case fatality among presentations; mortality appears only in the introduction, cited from other sources.
key_findings.locator: Introduction, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 1) and 4th paragraph (p. 2); Results; Table 1 (pp. 5–6)
key_findings.note: Editors' observation from reading the whole text.

reporting_issues.issue: Turnipseed et al. (2003) has 36 methamphetamine-positive patients in the text (p. 4) and 171 subjects, all methamphetamine-positive, in Table 1 (p. 6).
reporting_issues.consequence: The denominator of the 25% acute coronary syndrome figure is uncertain until the primary study is read.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says nine studies used urine or other toxicology (p. 7), while the subgroup analysis has 8 toxicology and 9 self-report studies (p. 8); Table 1 lists Lee et al. (2009) as using both, and Richards et al. (1999a) as using urine screens and emergency visits, entered in Figure 2 with the all-visits denominator.
