reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 prints Marshall et al. (2012) as 30/133 (45.3%) and London et al. (2009) as 557/6193 (9.3%); the fractions are 22.6% and 9.0% (editors' calculation), as Figure 2 shows (0.226 and 0.090).
reporting_issues.consequence: Table 1 percentages are not reliable without checking the fraction; Figure 2 appears to carry the values pooled.

reporting_issues.issue: The sex analysis is said to include 23,434 men; the men in Figure 3 sum to 28,434 (editors' calculation), while the women sum to the printed 21,365.
reporting_issues.consequence: Probably a typing error; it does not change the pooled odds ratio.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and results give a 'pooled variance' of methamphetamine-positive cases of 57.1% in men and 42.9% in women. In Figure 3, men are 2,052 of 2,852 methamphetamine-positive cases (72%, editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: The quantity is undefined and cannot be reproduced; it should not be cited as the sex distribution of methamphetamine-positive attendees.

reporting_issues.issue: For the sex analysis, I² 50.16 and p = 0.029 correspond to Q of about 20.06 with 10 degrees of freedom; the printed Q of 20.66 would give I² 51.6% and p 0.024 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; probably a typing error in Q.

reporting_issues.issue: Hendrickson et al. (2010), which the review says used the same data set as the linked Oregon studies (p. 4), is pooled beside Hendrickson et al. (2008) and Cloutier et al. (2013) as separate studies, and their attendees are added into the 120,111 total (Figure 2).
reporting_issues.consequence: Overlapping data are counted more than once, which overstates the precision of the pooled share and the number of attendees.

reporting_issues.issue: Pasic et al. (2007): 12 of 60 depressed is printed as 23% (it is 20%); the implications section's 'nearly one-quarter … depressed' appears to rest on this figure.
reporting_issues.consequence: The depression figure in the implications section is overstated and comes from one study.

reporting_issues.issue: Szuster (1990): the percentages for hallucinations (9, 64%), paranoid thoughts (12, 86%), suicidal ideation (4, 29%) and attempted suicide (1, 7%) imply a denominator of 14, while Table 1 lists 32 methamphetamine-positive presentations of 343.
reporting_issues.consequence: The figures may describe a subgroup; their denominator cannot be checked without the primary study.

reporting_issues.issue: The search section says no new studies were added after manually reviewing reference lists (p. 2), while the flow diagram and the results add one study from hand, reference-list and forward searches (pp. 2–3); the search section attributes the one added study to updating the search to December 2017 (p. 2).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the search process is not reported consistently.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says 17 studies could be used in the meta-analysis, but 18 distinct studies appear across the three forest plots: Pasic et al. (2007), a matched case-control study, enters the sex and age analyses but not the prevalence pool.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor: the abstract's count of 17 understates the studies pooled. Pasic's odds ratios for sex (3.523) and age (2.445; Figures 3–4) show that its groups were not matched on sex or age, and an odds ratio comparing methamphetamine-positive with methamphetamine-negative people by sex or age is not distorted by sampling on methamphetamine status; the matching variables of this one case-control study are not stated.

reporting_issues.issue: Sensitivity analyses restricted to low-risk studies are said to have been completed for all meta-analyses (p. 4), but no result is reported anywhere.
reporting_issues.consequence: Selective reporting cannot be excluded; with 22 of 23 studies rated low risk the analyses could hardly differ.

reporting_issues.issue: Horyniak et al. (2014), whose title (reference list) concerns ecstasy and related drug presentations, is pooled as amphetamine-related presentations (255 of 1,347; Table 1).
reporting_issues.consequence: The exposure, or the denominator (1,347 may be drug-related presentations rather than all attendees), of at least one pooled study is broader than methamphetamine presentations among all attendees; either way its 18.9% is not comparable with the other rows.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results say that 120,111 attendees of the 17 pooled studies were tested for methamphetamine (p. 7), but nine of the 17 used self-report, and Richards et al. (1999a) enters Figure 2 with all 32,617 emergency visits (461, 1.4%), although Table 1 gives 461 of 3,102 urine screens (14.9%) for the same year. The same all-visits figures enter the sex pool (295 of 17,016 men and 166 of 15,601 women; Figure 3) and the age pool (461 against 32,156 methamphetamine-negative; Figure 4), so unscreened attendees count as methamphetamine-negative.
reporting_issues.consequence: This lowers the pooled 11.3% and, if the study was counted as toxicology, the toxicology subgroup; it also biases the sex and age comparisons of the largest single study, in a direction the review does not allow one to tell.

design_detail: Systematic review with frequentist random-effects network meta-analysis (R netmeta; protocol on the Open Science Framework, osf.io/5pqxb; PRISMA extension for network meta-analysis) of short-term parallel randomized trials of approved antipsychotics in adults with methamphetamine psychosis. Six head-to-head trials (395 participants) comparing six drugs (aripiprazole, haloperidol, olanzapine, paliperidone extended-release, quetiapine, risperidone); no trial had a placebo arm. Outcomes: main psychotic symptoms (primary), positive and negative symptoms, dropout; certainty rated with the GRADE approach for network estimates. Read: all eight pages; Tables 1 to 3 as text; Figures 1 to 3 (PRISMA flow, network graphs, forest plots) checked on the rendered pages; supplementary appendices 1 to 7 (search strategy, trial-level risk of bias, funnel plots, league tables) not read.
can_establish: Which antipsychotics had been compared in randomized trials of methamphetamine psychosis up to June 2020, what each trial found, and, if the trials are similar enough to be chained, how the drugs might rank on short-term symptom scores and dropout.
cannot_establish: Whether any antipsychotic speeds recovery beyond abstinence and usual care (no trial had a placebo or no-medication arm); whether one drug is truly better than another (no direct comparison was significant, and every significant difference is an indirect estimate in a network without a closed loop); effects beyond six weeks, on relapse or on side effects (not synthesized); and effects outside the short inpatient trials of three countries.

sample.recruitment: Searches of ClinicalTrials, the Cochrane Library, PubMed, Scopus and Web of Science from inception to 15 June 2020, without language limits, plus the reference lists of two recent systematic reviews (Chiang et al., 2019; Fluyau et al., 2019) (2.2). The six trials were single-site, published 2005 to 2020, two each in Thailand, Iran and China; five recruited inpatients and one outpatients (Leelahanaj 2005) (Table 1, p. 4).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: parallel randomized trials in adults with methamphetamine psychosis diagnosed by any recognized definition, of an antipsychotic approved for clinical use, against placebo or another antipsychotic, reporting main psychotic symptoms or dropout (2.1). Four full texts excluded (3.1; Fig. 1): an 8-week placebo-controlled trial of aripiprazole in people who had recovered from psychotic symptoms (Sulaiman 2013; Fig. 1 gives a mean PANSS total of 51.6, below mild psychosis), a case report, a retrospective study, and a trial in mental disorders due to amphetamine-type stimulants with unclear diagnosis (Xue 2018), which, the discussion reports, also found no difference between olanzapine and haloperidol (p. 6).
sample.demographics: Arm mean ages 21.3 to 41.1 years in Table 1 (the text gives 25.2 to 38.8); 54.6% to 100% men per arm. Diagnosis by DSM-IV or DSM-IV-TR criteria, in three trials with a BPRS, PANSS or CGI-S threshold, and in one by clinical interview with a methamphetamine-positive urine test (Verachai 2014) (Table 1).
sample.attrition: Dropout was computed as randomized minus completers; one trial (Samiei 2016) did not report dropout and 0.5 was added to its cells; five trials did not compare dropout between arms statistically (2.4; 3.5; 3.6).
sample.selection_effects: Short (21 to 42 days), single-site, mostly inpatient trials in three countries; two trials (Leelahanaj 2005; Farnia 2014) describe amphetamine psychosis in their titles and the review treats all six as methamphetamine psychosis; only one trial required a positive urine test. People with milder or rapidly resolving psychosis who are never admitted are not represented.

exposure.measurement: The randomized antipsychotic, at each trial's fixed or flexible dose range for 21 to 42 days (Table 1; reported here only as study conditions). Co-interventions were extracted but are not described in the article.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: oral antipsychotics at the trials' dose ranges (maximum doses listed in 3.3), for 21 to 42 days. Methamphetamine use before admission (amount, route, duration) is not reported for any trial.
exposure.polysubstance: Not reported; whether trials excluded people using other substances is not stated in the review.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not reported; most participants were inpatients, so abstinence during treatment is likely but not documented.

comparison.controls: Another antipsychotic in every trial; no placebo or no-medication arm. Direct comparisons: aripiprazole vs risperidone (2 trials), olanzapine vs haloperidol, haloperidol vs quetiapine, haloperidol vs risperidone, paliperidone extended-release vs risperidone (1 each) (Table 1; Fig. 3A).
comparison.matching: Randomization within trials; across trials, populations, settings, scales and durations differ, and the authors downgrade every network estimate for intransitivity (3.9).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not an issue within randomized trials; across trials, illness severity, duration of methamphetamine use and earlier psychosis are not reported, which is what makes the chained comparisons doubtful.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not reported.

outcomes.instruments: Main symptoms: BPRS (1 trial), SAPS (2), PANSS (3); positive symptoms: SAPS or PANSS positive (4 trials); negative symptoms: SANS or PANSS negative (3 trials); dropout (6 trials) (Table 1).
outcomes.validity_norms: Standard psychosis rating scales developed for schizophrenia; no validation in methamphetamine psychosis is reported.
outcomes.operationalization: Efficacy as endpoint scores converted to standardized mean differences (Hedges' g) against risperidone, negative values favouring the drug compared; endpoint rather than change scores were used for all symptom analyses because change scores were rarely reported; missing SDs imputed, for Farnia 2014 by substituting baseline SDs. Dropout as odds ratios (2.4; 2.7; 3.6).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Four outcomes (main, positive and negative symptoms, dropout), negative symptoms reviewed only qualitatively; 15 pairwise network estimates for the main outcome (Table 3).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Varies by trial: two trials were open-label (Samiei 2016; Wang 2016); the trial-level risk-of-bias judgments are in Appendix 2, not read.

analysis.effect_sizes: Main symptoms, network estimates against risperidone (negative favours the drug named): olanzapine SMD -1.09 (95% CI -1.89 to -0.28) and quetiapine -0.86 (-1.61 to -0.11), both without a direct comparison; haloperidol -0.60 (-1.20 to 0.01) and paliperidone extended-release -0.33 (-0.69 to 0.03), one trial each; aripiprazole 0.27 (-0.13 to 0.68), two trials; global I2 0%. Aripiprazole against olanzapine 1.36 (0.46 to 2.26), quetiapine 1.13 (0.28 to 1.98), haloperidol 0.87 (0.14 to 1.60) and paliperidone extended-release 0.60 (0.06 to 1.14), all indirect. No direct (within-trial) comparison was significant (Table 3). Positive symptoms (4 trials): quetiapine against risperidone -0.84 (-1.59 to -0.09), others not significant. Dropout odds ratios against risperidone from 0.18 to 2.77, every interval including 1 (olanzapine 0.18, 0.00 to 50.14; Fig. 3C), I2 72.5%.
analysis.covariates: None; no meta-regression or sensitivity analysis (too few trials, 3.8).
analysis.preregistration_detail: Protocol registered on the Open Science Framework (osf.io/5pqxb), titled as a review of efficacy and acceptability (p. 7); its date, its content and any deviations are not reported in the article, and the protocol was not read. Negative symptoms could only be reviewed qualitatively because the network could not be connected.
analysis.selective_reporting: All outcomes named in the methods are reported; side effects (extrapyramidal and cardiovascular) discussed in the introduction were not synthesized.
analysis.power: Not addressed. Trials of 42 to 120 participants cannot show that two drugs work equally well, and the dropout network is uninformative (intervals as wide as 0.00 to 218.26) (editors' sums of trial sizes from Table 1).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Six small head-to-head trials, none finding a significant difference between its two drugs. Chained through a network without a closed loop, they give indirect differences in favour of olanzapine and quetiapine over risperidone and of four drugs over aripiprazole on short-term symptom scores, all rated low certainty by the authors. Dropout cannot be compared, and nothing can be said about benefit beyond abstinence (no placebo arm).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that "olanzapine or quetiapine may be a preferred antipsychotic for MAP" (p. 1; again p. 7), and the discussion describes the superiority as relatively large (p. 6). The abstract's results state that olanzapine and quetiapine were superior to risperidone without saying that these are indirect estimates only (p. 1), and the discussion's first paragraph calls both drugs probably superior to aripiprazole and risperidone (p. 6). Gaps: (1) the preference rests entirely on indirect estimates, while the trials that compared these drugs directly found no difference; (2) both advantages over risperidone pass through one open-label pilot trial of haloperidol against risperidone (44 participants) that the authors rate at high risk of bias; (3) without a closed loop, agreement between direct and indirect evidence cannot be checked, yet the authors judge transitivity doubtful for every outcome. The caveats (low quality, indirect comparisons, no placebo) are stated in the abstract and discussion, so the gap lies mainly in the word preferred and in calling indirect differences large.

timeline.event: Cochrane review of treatment for amphetamine psychosis (Shoptaw et al., 2009), cited in this review's discussion as concluding that olanzapine and haloperidol both reduced symptoms (p. 6).
Narrative review describing the Cochrane review's single trial and a later haloperidol-quetiapine trial (Glasner-Edwards & Mooney, 2014).
Narrative review citing the aripiprazole-risperidone trial by title only (Wearne & Cornish, 2018).
Systematic review of antipsychotics for amphetamine psychosis (Fluyau et al., 2019), one of the two reviews whose reference lists were searched here; not yet read for this encyclopedia.
This review: the first quantitative synthesis of antipsychotics for methamphetamine psychosis, by the authors' account (p. 6).
A meta-analysis of symptoms in methamphetamine psychosis versus schizophrenia cites this review's conclusion with its low-quality caveat (Cohen-Laroque et al., 2024, p. 188).
Systematic review of drug, dose and duration of antipsychotics after amphetamine- and cannabis-induced psychosis (Hall et al., 2026); identified by the currency check of 2026-10-16, not yet read.
24-month randomized trial of aripiprazole or paliperidone against treatment as usual in stimulant-induced psychosis (Chung et al., 2026); identified by the currency check, not yet read.

replication.where_it_stands: The only network meta-analysis identified, and the most complete trial inventory read so far: six head-to-head trials, no placebo arm, searches to June 2020. Its ranking of drugs rests on indirect chains through small, partly open-label trials and should not be read as established superiority. A 2026 systematic review and a 2026 trial against treatment as usual are on the reading list.

funding.funder: Partially supported by Chiang Mai University, Thailand; the funder had no role in design, data collection, analysis, interpretation, writing or the decision to submit (p. 7).
funding.declared_conflicts: M. Srisurapanont received honoraria from Lundbeck A/G, Sumitomo Dainippon Pharma and Janssen (Thailand); the other authors declare no conflict of interest (p. 7).
funding.affiliations_note: All seven authors are from the Department of Psychiatry, Chiang Mai University; none is listed as an author of the six included trials (reference list, pp. 7-8).

what_would_settle_it: A multi-site randomized trial in acute methamphetamine psychosis comparing an antipsychotic with placebo (with sedation available to both arms) under supervised abstinence, with blinded ratings over the first four weeks and follow-up of persistence and relapse; and head-to-head trials large enough to test equivalence of the drugs now favoured only by indirect comparison.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Adults with methamphetamine psychosis; approved antipsychotics; placebo or another antipsychotic; main symptoms and dropout (2.1, 2.4).
A protocol registered on the Open Science Framework is cited (pp. 2, 7), but its date, content and any deviations are not reported in the article, and it was not read.
The restriction to short-term parallel randomized trials is stated (2.1) but not explained; a conventional choice for a treatment comparison, judged strictly.

Five sources from inception to 15 June 2020 including a trial registry, no language limit, and the reference lists of two reviews; the full strategy is in a supplement not read. No grey literature or expert contact is reported and the included trials' reference lists were not searched, so 'yes' is not met.
Two reviewers independently selected records and examined the full texts (2.2).
Two reviewers independently extracted the data with a record form (2.3).

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: All four excluded full texts are named with reasons in the text (3.1) and the reasons are repeated in Fig. 1.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 1 gives each trial's country, setting, diagnostic method, arms with dose ranges, sample size, age, sex, duration and scales.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: Two reviewers independently applied the Cochrane Handbook risk-of-bias guidance (2.6), which covers sequence generation, concealment, blinding, incomplete data and selective reporting; trial-level results are in Appendix 2 (not read) and the text summarizes open-label status and concealment (3.4).

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Not reported.

Random-effects frequentist network meta-analysis is an appropriate technique, but the authors judge every comparison intransitive (participants and designs varied, 3.9) without explaining why the trials could nevertheless be chained; the network has no closed loop, so the local inconsistency approach named in 2.8 could not be applied and indirect estimates are sums of single-trial estimates; the heterogeneity of the dropout network (I2 72.5%) was not investigated. A reader weighing the technique alone could judge the item met, which would make the overall rating moderate confidence.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: No sensitivity analysis excluding the two open-label trials or otherwise testing the effect of risk of bias (3.8); risk of bias enters only the GRADE ratings.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: Risk of bias is carried into the GRADE ratings (3.9) and named in the abstract's conclusion and the discussion.

The moderate heterogeneity of the dropout network (I2 72.5%) and the intransitivity the authors identify are reported but neither investigated nor discussed for their effect on the results (3.7, 3.9).

Funnel plots inspected for each outcome and the dropout evidence downgraded for undetermined publication bias (3.8, 3.9); with six trials or fewer per plot no method can detect small-study effects, which the authors acknowledge by not applying statistical tests.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding and the first author's honoraria are declared (p. 7).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: One critical item is not met (11: trials the authors themselves judge intransitive are chained in a network without a closed loop, without justification), the other critical items are met (7, 9, 13, 15) or partly met (2, 4), and there are several non-critical weaknesses (3, 10, 12, 14): low confidence. The rating concerns the network estimates. The review's descriptive content, the inventory of six head-to-head trials and their individually non-significant results, can be cited as such; its ranking of drugs only as low-certainty indirect evidence, stating that both advantages over risperidone pass through one open-label pilot trial.

key_findings.finding: Searches of five sources to 15 June 2020, without language limits, found six randomized trials with 395 participants with methamphetamine psychosis. All six were head-to-head comparisons of two antipsychotics and none had a placebo arm: aripiprazole vs risperidone (2 trials), olanzapine vs haloperidol, haloperidol vs quetiapine, haloperidol vs risperidone, and paliperidone extended-release vs risperidone (1 each).
key_findings.locator: 2.2; 3.1 Study selection; 3.2 Network structure and geometry, 1st paragraph; Table 1
key_findings.note: The text of 3.2 names the last comparison as paliperidone extended-release vs aripiprazole; Table 1, Fig. 3A and the discussion (p. 6) give risperidone.

key_findings.finding: Arms: risperidone in 4 trials (129 participants), haloperidol 3 (93), aripiprazole 2 (48), paliperidone extended-release 1 (60), quetiapine 1 (36), olanzapine 1 (29). Trials lasted 21 to 42 days and were single-site, two each in Thailand, Iran and China; five recruited inpatients and one (Leelahanaj 2005, olanzapine 29 vs haloperidol 27) outpatients.
key_findings.note: The two Chinese trials (Wang 2016; Wang 2020) share three author names (G. Wang, W. Hao, M. C. Chawarski; reference list, p. 8), so they are not from independent teams.

key_findings.finding: Each of the six trials reported no significant difference between its two drugs on the main psychotic symptoms; four reported none on positive symptoms and three none on negative symptoms; five did not compare dropout statistically.

Network estimates against risperidone on main symptoms: olanzapine SMD -1.09 (95% CI -1.89 to -0.28) and quetiapine -0.86 (-1.61 to -0.11), neither with a direct comparison; haloperidol -0.60 (-1.20 to 0.01) and paliperidone extended-release -0.33 (-0.69 to 0.03), one direct trial each; aripiprazole 0.27 (-0.13 to 0.68), two trials. Global I2 0% for main symptoms.

key_findings.finding: Aripiprazole was inferior to olanzapine (SMD 1.36, 0.46 to 2.26), quetiapine (1.13, 0.28 to 1.98), haloperidol (0.87, 0.14 to 1.60) and paliperidone extended-release (0.60, 0.06 to 1.14); all four are indirect estimates rated low quality. Every direct (within-trial) estimate was rated very low and none was significant.
key_findings.locator: Table 2A and 3.9 Rating the quality of evidence, 2nd paragraph (p. 6); Table 3 (p. 7)

key_findings.finding: Positive symptoms (4 trials): only quetiapine differed from risperidone (SMD -0.84, -1.59 to -0.09); negative symptoms (3 trials) could not be joined in a network and were reviewed qualitatively.
key_findings.note: The legend of Fig. 3 gives 5 RCTs for positive symptoms; the text, the legend of Fig. 2 and the four comparisons in Fig. 3B give 4. In two of the four positive-symptom trials (Farnia 2014; Samiei 2016) the main-symptom scale is itself the SAPS (Table 1), and the haloperidol–risperidone estimate is identical in both networks (−0.60, −1.20 to 0.01; Table 2A and 2B; Fig. 3A and 3B), so the positive-symptom result is not independent confirmation of the main-symptom result.

key_findings.finding: Dropout (6 trials): odds ratios against risperidone, olanzapine 0.18 (0.00 to 50.14), quetiapine 0.85 (0.00 to 218.26), paliperidone extended-release 1.13 (0.07 to 18.19), haloperidol 1.00 (0.01 to 114.39), aripiprazole 2.77 (0.32 to 23.95); none significant; I2 72.5%. One trial did not report dropout and 0.5 was added to its cells.
key_findings.note: The odds ratios were read from Fig. 3C, an image; the text says only that no difference was significant.

key_findings.finding: Risk of bias: two open-label trials (Samiei 2016; Wang 2016) were at high risk in two domains, allocation concealment was not explicit in four, and two trials (Verachai 2014; Wang 2020) had no risk of bias identified. The authors' GRADE started high and downgraded every outcome one level for indirectness (intransitivity), comparisons using data from the open-label trials for risk of bias, and estimates whose interval included no difference for imprecision; all main-symptom estimates were low or very low.
key_findings.locator: 3.4 Risk of bias in individual trial (p. 5); 3.9, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 6); Table 3 (p. 7)

key_findings.finding: The only placebo-controlled trial found, an 8-week trial of aripiprazole in people who had recovered from psychotic symptoms (Sulaiman 2013; mean PANSS total 51.6, less than mildly psychotic, in Fig. 1), was excluded; the discussion lists the absence of any placebo control among the limitations.
key_findings.locator: 3.1, 1st paragraph and Fig. 1 (p. 3); 4. Discussion, 3rd paragraph (p. 6); reference list, Sulaiman et al. (2013) (p. 8)

key_findings.finding: The authors argue that methamphetamine psychosis, as a self-limited disorder under DSM-5, should not last beyond four weeks after stopping, so antipsychotics should be tapered once symptoms resolve and psychosis lasting longer calls for reconsidering the diagnosis. This is the authors' clinical reasoning, not a result of the trials.

reporting_issues.issue: Section 3.6 prints the quetiapine estimate as SMD 0.86 with a 95% CI of -1.61 to -0.11, a point estimate outside its own interval; the abstract, Fig. 3A and Table 3 give -0.86.
reporting_issues.consequence: Sign error in the text; -0.86 is correct.

reporting_issues.issue: Section 3.2 says one trial compared paliperidone extended-release with aripiprazole; Table 1, the network graph in Fig. 2A (p. 4), Fig. 3A (one direct comparison with risperidone) and the discussion show that Wang 2020 compared paliperidone extended-release with risperidone.
reporting_issues.consequence: A network rebuilt from the text would have the wrong geometry; Table 1 is right.

reporting_issues.issue: The legend of Fig. 3 gives 5 RCTs for the positive-symptom network; the text, the legend of Fig. 2 and Fig. 3B (four comparisons) give 4.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; four trials is correct.

reporting_issues.issue: The text of 3.1 reports 775 records retrieved and 641 screened, while Fig. 1 shows 1,120 database records plus 7 from other sources, 841 screened after de-duplication, 830 excluded and 10 full texts (841 minus 830 is 11).
reporting_issues.consequence: The search yield cannot be reconstructed; the ten full texts and six included trials agree in text and figure.

reporting_issues.issue: Section 3.3 gives mean ages of 25.2 to 38.8 years, while Table 1 lists arm means from 21.3 (Leelahanaj, haloperidol) to 41.1 years (Farnia, aripiprazole); in the same Leelahanaj row, 96.6% men is not a possible proportion of 27 participants (26 of 27 is 96.3%; 96.6% fits 28 of 29, the size of the olanzapine arm), and in the Samiei row 54.6% should read 54.5% (12 of 22). Every other arm percentage fits its arm size (editors' check).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; Table 1 should be used, and the Leelahanaj row may contain a misprint.

reporting_issues.issue: Farnia's trial is dated 2013 in Table 1 (p. 4) and 2014 in the text (pp. 3, 5, 6) and the reference list (p. 8).
reporting_issues.consequence: Labelling only; same trial.

reporting_issues.issue: The methods name a local approach to inconsistency (2.8), but the five direct comparisons form a chain without a closed loop, so each indirect estimate is the sum of single-trial estimates: olanzapine vs risperidone -1.09 is olanzapine vs haloperidol (-0.49) plus haloperidol vs risperidone (-0.60), and quetiapine vs risperidone -0.86 is -0.26 plus -0.60 (editors' arithmetic from Table 2A). The paper does not say that the inconsistency check was impossible.
reporting_issues.consequence: Both significant advantages over risperidone, and three of the four over aripiprazole, depend on the single open-label haloperidol-risperidone trial (Samiei 2016, 44 participants); the abstract does not say so.

reporting_issues.issue: The network has six two-arm trials and six drugs and no closed loop, so its heterogeneity statistic has one degree of freedom (6 trials minus 5 basic comparisons), contributed entirely by the two aripiprazole–risperidone trials (Farnia 2014; Wang 2016): the global I² of 0% for main symptoms and of 72.5% for dropout (3.7; Fig. 3 legend) describe only that pair (editors' reasoning from Table 1 and Fig. 2A). The authors decline to downgrade main symptoms and dropout for inconsistency because I² was below 75% (3.9) without saying this.
reporting_issues.consequence: The 0% cannot be cited as evidence that the trials agree: consistency across the network cannot be examined at all.

design_detail: Systematic review without meta-analysis (PRISMA-guided; no protocol or registration mentioned) of the psychiatric symptom profile and the duration of methamphetamine-associated psychosis across all designs: 94 studies with 7387 participants (20 cross-sectional, 29 case-control, 10 longitudinal, 29 case reports with 49 cases, 6 laboratory studies in which methamphetamine was given to induce psychotic symptoms). Each study was reduced to symptom present or absent; persistence was the share of participants with symptoms more than one month after stopping use, summarized as unweighted medians across studies. Read: the cover sheet and all article pages of the online-first PDF (pp. 1–11, pages numbered as printed on that version); Figures 1 and 2 are images whose values are given in the text; Supplementary Tables S1 to S7 not read.
can_establish: Which psychiatric symptoms the published literature on methamphetamine-associated psychosis reports, and how often studies report them, up to March 2018; and the spread across studies of the share still psychotic after a month and of later schizophrenia diagnoses.
cannot_establish: A pooled or population rate of persistence or of transition to schizophrenia (unweighted medians of study proportions, no intervals, no appraisal of study quality); how frequent or severe any symptom is (binary coding of studies); persistence in people who are never hospitalized (no community study of duration); and whether methamphetamine causes lasting psychosis or reveals a primary psychotic illness.

sample.recruitment: PsycINFO, Medline, PubMed, Scopus and Ovid searched with a librarian to 14 March 2018, plus hand-searching of recent issues of key journals, subject reviews and reference lists: 4455 records (4451 from databases, 4 by hand), 2464 after de-duplication, 404 full texts (pp. 2–3). Included studies were published 1949 to 2018; 72% recruited hospital in- or outpatients, 11% drug-treatment services, 5% prisons, 4% community settings and 3% private practitioners (p. 4).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: peer-reviewed English-language empirical studies in humans of the profile or duration of symptoms in people whom the authors identified as having symptoms of methamphetamine-associated psychosis, who were diagnosed with it, or who had substance-induced psychosis and currently used methamphetamine or amphetamine. Excluded: reviews, commentaries, unpublished papers and book chapters; where several articles described one population only the most detailed was kept (15 excluded) (pp. 2–3).
sample.demographics: Mostly men (interquartile range of study percentages 70–90%); mean ages 29 to 37 years (interquartile range); 45% of studies reported the share with methamphetamine dependence, median 99% where reported. Substance of interest: methamphetamine in 59 studies (63%), amphetamine 15 (16%), both 8 (9%), prescription amphetamines 30 (32%) (p. 4).
sample.attrition: Longitudinal studies followed participants for 3 months to 16 years and retained 54–100% (interquartile range) (p. 4).
sample.selection_effects: Weighted to hospitalized, mostly male samples with dependence; the authors note that this may overstate negative and understate affective symptoms, and that people with milder or transient symptoms who do not seek care are missed (p. 8). English-language, published studies only.

exposure.measurement: As defined by each study: an explicit diagnosis of methamphetamine-associated or substance-induced psychosis in 65% of studies (DSM in 23, ICD in 9, both in 5, the Chinese CCMD-3 in 1), and otherwise identification of symptoms by the study's authors; standardized symptom scales in 4% of case reports and in 40% to 80% of the other designs (p. 4).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not synthesized; the authors note that many included studies did not account for frequency or duration of use (p. 8). Laboratory studies gave methamphetamine under study conditions, once or repeatedly over hours or days (p. 4).
exposure.polysubstance: Not handled; the authors list polydrug use among the factors most included studies did not adjust for (p. 8).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Persistence was counted from cessation of use as each study reported it; verification of abstinence is not described, and the authors note that no study measured duration in community samples, probably because abstinence is hard to verify there (p. 8).

comparison.controls: None for the descriptive synthesis; from case-control studies only the data on participants with methamphetamine-associated psychosis were used (p. 3).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Family history, earlier psychotic episodes and premorbid functioning are not synthesized, so persistent cases cannot be separated from primary psychoses.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable.

outcomes.instruments: Whatever each study used: BPRS (9 studies), PANSS (3), MINI (3), SANS (3), SAPS (2), Methamphetamine Experience Questionnaire (2), SCID (2), CIDI (1), or case descriptions (pp. 4–5).
outcomes.operationalization: Symptom present (reported as a prevalence, a scale score or in a case description) or absent; persistence as symptoms continuing more than one month after stopping use, the DSM-5 time frame; for case reports, time to resolution in bands (one week or less, 1–4 weeks, 1–6 months, over 6 months); for laboratory studies, the longest time to resolution (p. 4).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable to the descriptive tallies of about 30 symptoms (Figure 2, Table 1); the one significance test (Japanese versus other studies, p. 6) is uncorrected.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Eligibility: one reviewer judged all 404 full texts and a second independently judged 336 (85%), with 88% initial agreement and 42 disagreements resolved by discussion or a third reviewer (p. 3); extraction by one reviewer, the first author taking responsibility for its accuracy (p. 9).

analysis.effect_sizes: No effect sizes or intervals. Share of studies reporting each symptom: persecutory delusions 84%, auditory hallucinations 69%, visual hallucinations 65%, hostility 53%, conceptual disorganization 36%, depression 31%, flat affect 19%, other negative symptoms 6–15% (p. 5). Persistence beyond one month (27 studies): median 25%; longitudinal studies median 40% (range 14–96%); laboratory studies none (resolution within 12 hours to 7 days); Japanese studies median 44% (18–96%) against 12% (0–39%) elsewhere, t = 4.79, p = .0001; case reports 2 of 24 (8%) (p. 6). Later schizophrenia diagnosis: 33–38% after 6–7 years in two studies, 16% within 16 years in one (p. 7).
analysis.covariates: None.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned; a PRISMA checklist is in Supplementary Table S1 (not read).
analysis.selective_reporting: Duration was extracted only where a proportion with persistence could be calculated (27 of 94 studies); the median includes six laboratory studies in volunteers that observed no persistence (symptoms resolved within 12 hours to 7 days), and only 25 of the 27 studies are accounted for in the comparison by country.
analysis.power: Not applicable; the t-test (degrees of freedom not reported) compares study-level proportions from 11 Japanese and 14 other studies.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Across 27 studies with duration data, the median study reported 25% of participants still psychotic more than a month after stopping use, with a range from none (laboratory administration to volunteers) to 96%, higher in Japanese studies (median 44%) than elsewhere (12%); two cohorts found a third or more re-diagnosed with schizophrenia after 6–7 years and a Finnish register study 16% within 16 years. The symptom profile is a tally of how many studies reported each symptom.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract gives the median of 25% for persistence beyond one month without saying that it is an unweighted median of study proportions spanning 0% to 96% that includes laboratory studies that observed no persistence, and concludes that negative symptoms "are typically absent" (p. 1) from the share of studies reporting them (the abstract's results give it as under 20%, a share of studies that reads like a share of people), a binary tally that the authors themselves say cannot give prevalence (p. 9). The suggestion that persistent psychosis may be drug-precipitated schizophrenia is offered as a hypothesis needing research (p. 8). The abstract counts 20 longitudinal studies where the results count 10 (reporting issue 1).

timeline.event: Narrative review on whether amphetamine psychosis is a separate entity or a primary psychosis triggered in vulnerable people (Bramness et al., 2012), cited by this review.
Narrative review giving 16% and 17% still psychotic after 1 and 3 months of abstinence (Glasner-Edwards & Mooney, 2014).
Systematic review of risk factors for methamphetamine-associated psychosis from an overlapping author group (Arunogiri et al., 2018), cited by this review.
Narrative review of methamphetamine psychosis compared with schizophrenia (Wearne & Cornish, 2018).
This review: the first systematic review of the symptom profile, duration and course, by the authors' account (p. 7).
Meta-analysis of transition from substance-induced, brief and atypical psychoses to schizophrenia (Murrie et al., 2020); identified by the currency check of 2026-10-16, not yet read.
A meta-analysis of methamphetamine psychosis versus schizophrenia cites this review for the rarity of negative symptoms (Cohen-Laroque et al., 2024, p. 188).

replication.where_it_stands: The only systematic review of duration identified so far. Its persistence figure is a crude unweighted median and its transition figures are quoted from three studies, none appraised. It is best cited for the range of reported persistence and for the Japanese excess and the authors' diagnostic explanation of it, which the review's own figures support for at most the third of Japanese studies that used ICD-10; pooled transition rates should come from the 2020 meta-analysis and the register cohorts once read.

funding.funder: Australian Postgraduate Scholarship held by the first author (p. 9).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors report no conflicts of interest (p. 9).
funding.affiliations_note: Australian National University; National Drug and Alcohol Research Centre, University of New South Wales; St Vincent's Hospital and the University of Melbourne; Curtin University. The senior author (McKetin) is an author of several studies the review cites (McKetin et al., 2016a, 2016b, 2017); whether they are among the included studies is shown only in a supplement not read, and no procedure for appraising one's own studies is described.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective inception cohort of people presenting with methamphetamine psychosis in emergency and community settings, with urine-verified abstinence, structured diagnostic reassessment at 1, 6 and 12 months and after several years, family history and premorbid functioning recorded at entry and antipsychotic treatment documented, reporting with confidence intervals the share still psychotic and the share later diagnosed with a primary psychosis.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: A descriptive question: population (people identified with methamphetamine-associated psychosis) and outcomes (symptom profile, duration) are specified; no comparator is needed (pp. 2–3).
No protocol or registration is mentioned.
All designs from case reports to laboratory studies were included without an explanation of the choice; the descriptive question would justify it, but none is given.

Five sources searched with a librarian and an example Medline strategy given, plus hand-searching of journals, reviews and reference lists (pp. 2–3); but Ovid is a platform hosting Medline and PsycINFO rather than a separate database, and the search was limited to peer-reviewed, English-language published studies with no reason given. AMSTAR 2 gives 'partial yes' only when publication restrictions such as language are justified, so the item is not met; no grey literature or registries were searched either.

A second reviewer independently judged 85% of full texts with 88% initial agreement (p. 3), which meets AMSTAR 2's option of duplicate selection of a sample with at least 80% agreement; abstract screening is not described as duplicate.
Extraction by one reviewer; no second extractor is described (p. 9).

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Reasons for exclusion appear only as counts in the PRISMA figure; the supplements the article describes (S1 to S7) list included studies only.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Provisional: per-study characteristics are only in Supplementary Tables S3 to S7, which were not read; the article itself describes the included studies only in aggregate.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: No risk-of-bias or quality assessment of the included studies; the authors note that studies of disparate quality were aggregated without weighting (p. 9).

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Not reported.
No meta-analysis; unweighted medians of study proportions and one t-test.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: No meta-analysis.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: No study-level risk of bias was assessed, so none could be accounted for; the discussion names design-level limitations of the reviewed studies (hospital samples, self-report, no adjustment for polydrug use or medication, laboratory confinement) (p. 8).
Variation by design, country, diagnostic system, sex ratio and recruitment setting is described and discussed, including the diagnostic explanation of the Japanese excess (pp. 6, 8).
No meta-analysis.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding (a postgraduate scholarship) and the absence of conflicts are stated (p. 9).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Five critical items are not met (2: no protocol; 4: an unjustified English-language and published-only limit; 7: no list of excluded studies; 9: no appraisal of the included studies; 13: risk of bias therefore not accounted for): critically low confidence; the provisional item 8 cannot change this. The review is a careful descriptive tally and may be cited for which symptoms and what range of persistence the literature reports; its median persistence and transition figures are unappraised second-hand summaries and should not be cited as rates.

key_findings.finding: Searches to 14 March 2018 plus hand-searching gave 4455 records, 2464 screened and 404 full texts; 94 studies with 7387 participants were included: 20 cross-sectional, 29 case-control, 10 longitudinal, 29 case reports (49 cases) and 6 laboratory administration studies, published 1949 to 2018.
key_findings.locator: Method › Search strategy (pp. 2–3); Inclusion criteria (p. 3); Results › Study characteristics › Overview of studies (p. 4)
key_findings.note: The abstract gives 20 longitudinal studies; the results give 10, which with the other designs sums to 94. The counts are the text's; Figure 1 gives 2465 abstracts screened and its numbers do not add up (reporting issue 5).

key_findings.finding: 72% of studies recruited hospital in- or outpatients; samples were mostly men (interquartile range 70–90%) with mean ages of 29 to 37 years; only 65% of studies gave an explicit diagnosis of methamphetamine-associated or substance-induced psychosis (18% of case reports, none of the laboratory studies).
key_findings.locator: Results › Participant demographics; Diagnosis or identification of MAP

key_findings.finding: Share of studies reporting each symptom: persecutory delusions 84%, auditory hallucinations 69%, visual hallucinations 65%, hostility 53%, conceptual disorganization 36%, depression 31%, hyperactivity 28%, tactile hallucinations 21%, flat affect 19%, other negative symptoms 6–15%.
key_findings.locator: Results › Profile of psychiatric symptoms; Figure 2
key_findings.note: Shares of studies reporting a symptom, not shares of people; each study was coded only as symptom present or absent.

key_findings.finding: 27 studies (12 case-control, 5 cross-sectional, 4 longitudinal, 6 laboratory) gave the share of participants with psychotic symptoms more than one month after stopping use: median 25%. No laboratory study found persistence (symptoms abated within 12 hours to 7 days of the last dose); longitudinal studies reported a median of 40% (range 14–96%).

Japanese studies (11 of the 27, 41%) reported a median of 44% persisting (range 18–96%), against 12% (range 0–39%) in 14 studies from the USA, Australia, Canada, Iran and elsewhere in Asia (t = 4.79, p = .0001). Japanese studies more often used ICD-10 (35%) than DSM-IV (25%), the others mostly DSM-IV (42%, ICD-10 6%); the discussion attributes the excess to the ICD classification, under which psychosis may last up to 6 months after intoxication before a primary psychotic disorder is diagnosed.
key_findings.locator: Results › Duration of symptoms, 2nd paragraph (p. 6); Discussion › Duration of psychotic symptoms, 1st paragraph (pp. 7–8)
key_findings.note: 11 plus 14 is 25 of the 27 studies; the other two are not described. By the review's own figures only 35% of the Japanese studies used ICD-10 (25% DSM-IV), so the diagnostic explanation the discussion gives (Japanese studies typically using the ICD, p. 8) can apply to about a third of them at most; persistence by classification system is not reported.

key_findings.finding: Of 24 case reports giving duration, symptoms persisted beyond one month in 2 (8%), lasted 1–4 weeks in 14 (58%) and one week or less in 8 (printed as 36%).
key_findings.note: 8 of 24 is 33%, not 36% (editors' arithmetic); 36% would fit 8 of 22. The review calls the 24 case studies but counts their outcomes as participants (2 + 14 + 8 = 24), while its 29 case reports describe 49 cases (p. 4), so whether 24 counts reports or cases is unclear.

key_findings.finding: Four longitudinal studies tracked symptoms over time: positive symptoms fell in three and were stable in one; negative symptoms were stable in three and rose in one (Tomiyama 1990, hospitalized patients on antipsychotics, over 4 months); in a 3-month follow-up (Javadian 2016) positive symptoms rose in those who resumed methamphetamine use.
key_findings.locator: Results › Longitudinal changes in symptom profile, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Three longitudinal studies reported later schizophrenia diagnoses: 33–38% re-diagnosed after 6–7 years in two (Kittirattanapaiboon et al., 2010, 1116 people; Medhus et al., 2015, 28 people) and 16% within 16 years in a study of 825 people (Niemi-Pynttäri et al., 2013).
key_findings.locator: Results › Longitudinal changes in symptom profile, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: The review writes these sample sizes with k, its symbol for numbers of studies; they are numbers of people. The Finnish study's title describes a register of 18,478 inpatient cases of substance-induced psychosis (reference list, p. 11).

key_findings.finding: Of 104 psychiatric inpatients with amphetamine delusional disorder who did not meet criteria for schizophrenia (Iwanami et al., 1994), 27% had symptoms beyond one month and 17% beyond three months despite abstinence and antipsychotic treatment.

The authors state that many included studies did not adjust for polydrug use, frequency and duration of use or antipsychotic medication; that most recruited inpatients and may reflect more severe illness; that no study examined duration in community samples; and that binary coding cannot give prevalence and studies were not weighted for quality or size.

design_detail: Serial cross-sectional analysis (a four-page research note) of US death certificates in the CDC WONDER Multiple Cause of Death database, 1999–2023, all ages: yearly counts and crude rates per 100,000 population of overdose deaths involving methamphetamine and of those involving cocaine, stratified by sex, race and ethnicity and opioid co-involvement (fentanyl; other opioids), with Joinpoint regression giving annual percentage changes (APC) within segments and an average annual percentage change (AAPC) over the period. Drug involvement is defined by ICD-10 codes listed only in a supplement; 2023 data are provisional.
can_establish: How many US death certificates coded as overdose deaths involving methamphetamine (as the authors define it) there were each year from 1999 to 2023, their crude population rate, and when the growth in these counts sped up or slowed, overall and with or without opioids.
cannot_establish: Death rates among people who use methamphetamine (no denominator of use), that methamphetamine caused the deaths (multiple-cause coding; many deaths involve fentanyl), trends independent of changes in toxicology testing and certification practice, or age-adjusted comparisons (given only in a supplement).

sample.recruitment: Registry: all US death certificates in the CDC WONDER Multiple Cause of Death database, 1999–2023; counts below 10 are suppressed and rates based on fewer than 20 deaths are considered unreliable (p. 1946).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Overdose deaths involving methamphetamine or cocaine, identified by ICD-10 codes given in Supplement 1 (not read) (p. 1946). Because of suppression, the methamphetamine-with-fentanyl series starts in 2003 and the American Indian or Alaska Native series in 2004 (p. 1948); trends for Asian American and Native Hawaiian or Other Pacific Islander people were not assessed because of discrepancies between the preliminary and final databases (Table 1 note 3).
sample.demographics: 2023 methamphetamine-involved deaths: 25,296 men (72.57%) and 9,559 women (27.43%), mean age 45 years (SD 12); cocaine-involved: 73.36% men, mean age 47 (13) (p. 1947).
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: A complete count of certificates, but deaths whose certificates name no specific drug cannot be attributed, and the authors note possible racial misclassification on death certificates (p. 1948).

exposure.measurement: Drug involvement as coded among the multiple causes on the death certificate; the codes used for methamphetamine are not stated in the article (Supplement 1, not read), so whether the series is the broader code for psychostimulants with abuse potential cannot be checked from the text.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable.
exposure.polysubstance: Stratified by fentanyl and by other opioid co-involvement (Table 1; Figure 1); other drugs are not considered, and the paper does not say whether deaths involving both methamphetamine and cocaine are counted in both series.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: None: descriptive comparisons across years, sex, race and ethnicity and opioid co-involvement.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable (registry counts).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable.

outcomes.instruments: Death certificates coded with ICD-10 (multiple causes), from CDC WONDER; crude rates per 100,000 population; age-adjusted rates only in eTable 1 (not read) (p. 1946).
outcomes.validity_norms: Not discussed beyond racial misclassification and data suppression (p. 1948). Changes over time in toxicology testing and in how specifically certificates name drugs are not considered.
outcomes.operationalization: Overdose death involving methamphetamine: a death certificate whose multiple-cause codes include the authors' methamphetamine code(s); involvement does not mean that the drug was the cause.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; 18 Joinpoint series (2 drugs by 9 strata, Table 1).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.covariates: None (crude rates); age-adjusted Joinpoint analyses only in eTable 1, not read.
analysis.preregistration_detail: STROBE followed (p. 1946); no protocol.
analysis.selective_reporting: Yearly counts are not printed except for 1999 and 2023; the rates by opioid co-involvement and by race and ethnicity are shown only in Figure 1, without printed values.
analysis.power: Not applicable for national counts; early-year subgroup counts are suppressed.

interpretation_gap.results_show: US overdose deaths coded as involving methamphetamine rose about 64-fold in count (547 to 34,855) and 52-fold in crude rate (editors' calculation) from 1999 to 2023, fastest in 2018–2021 (37% a year), then slowed to 3.4% a year in 2021–2023 (provisional 2023 data). Deaths involving methamphetamine with fentanyl grew fastest (76% a year in 2012–2021), and those with other opioids fell in 2021–2023.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract stresses rising stimulant mortality and racial disparities and calls for harm reduction, research funding and targeted interventions (p. 1946); it does not mention that the methamphetamine increase slowed sharply after 2021. Its statement that methamphetamine-involved deaths were highest among American Indian or Alaska Native people is given as a share of their overdose deaths (44.50%); Figure 1C shows their crude rate as the highest too (about 32 per 100,000 in 2023 against about 12 for White people, read from the figure), so this statement is borne out. The discussion's statement that cocaine and methamphetamine accounted for roughly one-third of overdose deaths (p. 1948) is ambiguous: read as a combined share it is not given by the note (deaths involving both drugs are not separated); read as each drug separately, it fits 33.19% and 28.06%.

timeline.event: Analysis of the same national death records for ages 18–64, 2015–2019: deaths involving psychostimulants other than cocaine rose from 5,526 to 15,489
Hoopsick and Andrew Yockey (2023), cited here as reporting a 50-fold increase in methamphetamine-related mortality among US residents aged 15–74 from 1999 to 2021 (p. 1946); not read
This note: extends the series to 2023, all ages
CDC report on drug overdose deaths involving stimulants, January 2018–June 2024; not yet read

replication.where_it_stands: A registry description, not a test of a hypothesis: other analyses draw on the same certificates, so agreement among them is not independent replication. A check against a different data system (for example toxicology-based medical-examiner surveillance) would be the meaningful comparison.

funding.declared_conflicts: No potential conflict of interest was reported by the author(s) (p. 1949).
funding.affiliations_note: Virginia Commonwealth University (Medical Scientist Training Program; Epidemiology) and Stanford University School of Medicine (p. 1946).

what_would_settle_it: Toxicology-confirmed death surveillance with standardized testing across states and years, reporting methamphetamine separately from other psychostimulants, with age-adjusted rates and, from surveys of the same years, the number of people who use methamphetamine as a denominator.

National counts; small early subgroup counts are suppressed (p. 1946).

domains.note: One coding system for the whole period, but testing and certification practices vary by jurisdiction and over 25 years, which the note does not discuss.

Joinpoint regression with intervals is standard for such series and crude rates are justified for burden (p. 1946), but two different 2023 counts are given and two AAPCs in Table 1 appear transposed (see reporting issues).

domains.note: Registry count.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: National death-certificate counts are the standard source for this question and the trend is large, but the series is a coded proxy whose definition is not shown in the article, the latest year is provisional, and the note contains internal inconsistencies. It may be cited for the counts and crude rates of certificates coded as methamphetamine-involved overdose deaths by year and for the timing of changes in their growth, labelled as such; not for rates among people who use methamphetamine, not for cause, and not for exact 2023 figures without noting the two versions.

key_findings.finding: Data: CDC WONDER Multiple Cause of Death database; crude mortality rates per 100,000 for methamphetamine- and cocaine-involved overdose deaths, all ages, 1999–2023; drug types by ICD-10 codes listed in Supplement 1; counts below 10 suppressed and rates on fewer than 20 deaths unreliable; Joinpoint regression (version 5.2.0) with APC by segment and AAPC; age-adjusted rates only in eTable 1.

Methamphetamine-involved overdose deaths rose from 547 in 1999 to 34,855 in 2023 (25,296 men, 72.57%; 9,559 women, 27.43%; mean age 45, SD 12); the crude rate rose from 0.20 (95% CI 0.18–0.21) to 10.41 (10.30–10.52) per 100,000, AAPC 18.49% (17.67–20.17).

key_findings.note: The 2021–2023 segment, like every 2021–2023 segment in Table 1, is fitted to three yearly values (2021, 2022 and the provisional 2023), so its estimate is fragile beyond the provisional-data point (editors' reading).

key_findings.locator: Table 1, Opioid co-involvement rows (p. 1947); Results, 2nd paragraph (p. 1948)

key_findings.finding: Stimulants were involved in 7.95% of fentanyl-involved overdose deaths in 1999 (58 of 730), 10.28% in 2011 (274 of 2,666) and 56.67% in 2023 (41,583 of 73,379). No count or share of methamphetamine-involved deaths that also involved opioids is printed; Figure 1A plots their crude rates per 100,000 overall, with fentanyl and with other opioids (values not extracted), and the overlap of the two opioid series is not given.

In 2023 methamphetamine was involved in 33.19% of all overdose deaths (35,126 of 105,826) and in 44.50% of overdose deaths among American Indian or Alaska Native people (785 of 1,764); cocaine in 28.06% (29,692 of 105,826) and in 48.47% among Black people (10,936 of 22,563).
Cocaine-involved overdose deaths rose from 3,822 to 29,449 (crude rate 1.37 to 8.79 per 100,000; AAPC 8.80%, 8.18–9.95).
Figure 1 shows crude rates by opioid co-involvement and by race and ethnicity with shaded 95% intervals; the legend states that 2023 data are provisional. Values were not extracted from the figure.

Limitations named by the authors: possible racial misclassification on death certificates, a limited range of sociodemographic variables, and data suppression (methamphetamine-with-fentanyl deaths available only from 2003, American Indian or Alaska Native deaths only from 2004).

reporting_issues.issue: Two different 2023 counts are given for methamphetamine-involved deaths (34,855 in the abstract and results, p. 1947; 35,126 of 105,826 in the results, p. 1948) and for cocaine-involved deaths (29,449 and 29,692).
reporting_issues.consequence: Probably final against provisional data (Table 1 note 3 mentions both databases, and the Figure 1 legend says 2023 data are provisional); the 2023 figure should be cited with this uncertainty.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 1 the overall AAPC for women in the methamphetamine series (8.54) and for men in the cocaine series (18.61) appear transposed: recomputing each AAPC from its printed segment APCs, weighted by segment length, gives 18.61 for women (methamphetamine) and 8.54 for men (cocaine), and reproduces every other overall AAPC in the table to two decimals (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: The printed sex-specific AAPCs should not be cited; by the segments, methamphetamine-involved deaths grew about as fast in women as in men.

reporting_issues.issue: The cocaine segments for Black people are printed as 1999–2006, 2006–2021 and 2012–2023, which overlap; the printed AAPC (9.63) is reproduced only if the middle segment is 2006–2012 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor and not about methamphetamine; a typing error in the segment label.

reporting_issues.issue: The ICD-10 codes defining methamphetamine involvement are given only in a supplement, and the provisional status of 2023 data only in a figure legend.
reporting_issues.consequence: From the article alone, the series cannot be matched to other analyses of the same records, and the 2021–2023 slowdown rests partly on provisional data.

reporting_issues.issue: The discussion says cocaine and methamphetamine accounted for roughly one-third of overall overdose deaths (p. 1948), while the results give 33.19% for methamphetamine and 28.06% for cocaine separately; the sentence can be read as a combined share or as each drug separately (with nearly half, respectively, for methamphetamine among American Indian or Alaska Native people, 44.50%, and for cocaine among Black people, 48.47%).
reporting_issues.consequence: The combined share is not given (deaths involving both are not separated) and should not be cited.
