design_detail: Cross-sectional comparison of 37 adults with current DSM-IV methamphetamine dependence (not seeking treatment; tested after a mean of 6.9 days of urine-verified abstinence) and 41 healthy controls, with school transcripts obtained retrospectively as a premorbid proxy (for the methamphetamine group, only school years before self-reported first use). A regression fitted in the controls (adult cognitive composite on childhood grade point average, parental income, age and smoking status) predicted each methamphetamine participant's expected adult score; predicted and actual scores were compared with paired t-tests, overall and in three domains. Structural MRI (cortical thickness, FreeSurfer) in 31 per group; within the methamphetamine group, shortfalls from prediction were related to thickness. From the London laboratory at UCLA.
can_establish: Whether this methamphetamine group's adult test scores were lower than predicted from their pre-use school grades and from family and demographic factors, using a model built in these controls, and whether their grades before first use were already lower than the controls'.
cannot_establish: That methamphetamine caused the shortfall (other drug use, premorbid factors that grades do not capture and early-abstinence effects are not separated, and the prediction model explains about 40% of the variance in controls); whether scores lie within population norms (scores are standardized to the controls); or whether the shortfall lasts beyond the first weeks of abstinence (single assessment).

sample.recruitment: Internet and local newspaper advertisements; participants were paid for maintaining abstinence and completing procedures; not seeking treatment. 22 of the methamphetamine group took part while living on the research ward of the UCLA General Clinical Research Center and 15 as outpatients after it closed (their battery scores did not differ); all controls were outpatients (Methods and materials › Participants, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: SCID for DSM-IV Axis I. Excluded: neurological disease (for example stroke, head injury with loss of consciousness over 30 minutes), structural brain abnormality on MRI, systemic, cardiovascular or pulmonary disease, HIV infection, abnormal laboratory tests, psychotropic medication, current abuse or dependence on any substance other than methamphetamine, marijuana or nicotine, and current non-substance-induced Axis I disorders (one methamphetamine participant with current social phobia was kept). Current marijuana abuse or dependence: 4 in the methamphetamine group, 2 controls (Methods and materials › Participants, 1st paragraph). Schools were asked for all transcripts and standardized test scores from elementary through high school; how many recruited people were excluded because records could not be obtained is not reported (Measures/procedures › Academic records).
sample.demographics: Methamphetamine group vs controls: age 34.0 (SD 8.9) vs 33.7 (7.6); education 12.6 (1.7) vs 12.7 (1.4) years; estimated full-scale IQ (Wechsler Test of Adult Reading) 104.9 (8.4) vs 105.0 (9.7); men 25 of 37 vs 21 of 41; employed 10 of 37 vs 24 of 41 (p<0.01); cigarette smokers 34 of 37 vs 14 of 41 (p<0.01); highest parental education 12.9 (3.2) vs 13.9 (2.6) years; Caucasian 12 vs 13, African American 3 vs 8, Hispanic 14 vs 15, Asian or Pacific Islander 3 vs 3 (Table 1; Results › Group comparisons of demographic characteristics, 1st paragraph).
sample.attrition: Single assessment. Usable MRI for 31 of 37 and 31 of 41 (contraindications or motion) (Methods and materials › Structural MRI).
sample.selection_effects: Advertisement-recruited, paid, non-treatment-seeking people with dependence who could stay abstinent and had no current comorbid dependence other than marijuana or nicotine, no HIV and no current psychiatric disorder, against healthy controls screened for current Axis I disorders; both groups needed obtainable school records. The comparison is between relatively healthy people with dependence and controls healthier than the general population, although lifetime alcohol and marijuana use disorders were not rare among controls (9 of 41 each).

exposure.measurement: SCID diagnosis of current methamphetamine dependence; drug-use history from standard intake forms (self-report), including the average amount used on days of use; urine positive for methamphetamine at entry and negative for methamphetamine and other drugs on the days of testing and MRI (Methods and materials › Participants, 1st paragraph; Measures/procedures › Self-report measures).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Self-reported: 21.9 (SD 8.2) days of use in the past 30; 6.5 (6.0) years of heavy use (at least three times a week, or twice-weekly binges); 1.1 (0.8) g a day on days of use (Table 1). Route not reported.
exposure.polysubstance: Lifetime abuse or dependence, methamphetamine group vs controls: alcohol 26 vs 9, cocaine 12 vs 0, marijuana 21 vs 9, other drugs 9 vs 0 (all p<0.01); current marijuana abuse or dependence 4 vs 2; smokers 92% vs 34% (Table 1). Within the methamphetamine group, past diagnoses were not independently associated with battery scores (ps > 0.35), and the 6 with no past diagnosis scored non-significantly lower than the 31 with one (−0.84 vs −0.60, p = 0.30) (Results › Group comparisons, 1st paragraph); the authors state that it is difficult to disentangle effects of methamphetamine from other substance use, and that their data lack the detail to tell whether this leads to under- or overestimation (Discussion, 4th paragraph). Smoking status entered the prediction model.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Mean 6.9 days (SD 2.7; range 3–30), verified by urine tests, supervised on the ward for residential participants; withdrawal rated with the Amphetamine Cessation Symptom Assessment on each testing day (Methods and materials › Participants, 1st paragraph; Measures/procedures › Self-report measures).

comparison.controls: 41 healthy controls recruited through the same advertisements, tested as outpatients; urine negative for drugs except marijuana, with saliva tests confirming brief abstinence from marijuana and at least 3 days' self-reported abstinence from drugs (Methods and materials › Participants, 1st paragraph).
comparison.matching: Not individually matched; the groups did not differ in age, sex, education, estimated IQ, ethnicity, childhood economic class, parental education and income, or the income of the areas where they went to school (Results › Group comparisons, 1st paragraph); a grade-matched subgroup (28 per group) was analysed as a check.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Childhood grades are the premorbid proxy (methamphetamine group: years before self-reported first use only; 4.3 vs 5.2 years of grades, p > 0.10); standardized school test scores exist for a subset. Not measured: childhood attention or conduct problems, adversity, prenatal exposures, family history of substance use disorders, and any cognitive test before first use.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Lifetime alcohol abuse or dependence 9 of 41, marijuana abuse or dependence 9 of 41, current marijuana abuse or dependence 2; days of alcohol and of marijuana use in the past month similar to the methamphetamine group (Table 1).

outcomes.instruments: Battery given over two days by clinical psychology doctoral students trained by the first author, with stand-alone and embedded effort measures (all participants passed). Attention/concentration: Trail Making A, Stroop colour and word, Digit Symbol Coding, Digit Span, Continuous Performance Test, Wisconsin Card Sorting failure to maintain set, Brief Test of Attention, Spatial Capacity Delayed Response Test. Learning/memory: Selective Reminding Test, Rey Auditory Verbal Learning Test, Brief Visuospatial Memory Test-Revised. Executive function: Stroop interference, Trail Making B, verbal fluency and category switching, Wisconsin Card Sorting perseverative errors, Attention Network Task, Stop Signal Task. Composite and domain scores = means of test z-scores standardized to the control group (Measures/procedures › Cognitive battery). Structural MRI at 1.5 T, FreeSurfer 5.3 cortical thickness (Methods and materials › Structural MRI).
outcomes.validity_norms: Scores were standardized to the control group rather than to published norms, which the authors prefer so that differences between normative datasets do not add variation; the paper therefore says nothing about whether scores were in the normal range. The prediction model explained 41% of the variance of the overall composite in controls (domains 30% to 41%).
outcomes.operationalization: Deficit = actual minus predicted score, in the averaged z-score units of the control sample, where the prediction comes from the control-group regression; no impairment threshold and no classification of individuals is used.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None: four predicted-versus-actual comparisons (overall and three domains), two sensitivity analyses, correlations of the deficit scores with withdrawal and with three use variables, a group comparison of thickness and two thickness models, each at p<0.05; regional thickness correlations are given uncorrected in a supplement (not read).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported; 22 of the methamphetamine group were tested while living on a research ward.

analysis.effect_sizes: Childhood grade point average before first use 2.1 (SD 0.7) vs 2.5 (0.6), p = 0.016 (standardized difference about 0.6, editors' calculation from the rounded means and SDs); standardized school test percentile 48.7 (22.7) vs 58.5 (23.7), p = 0.178, in 24 and 19 (Table 1; Results › Group comparisons, 2nd paragraph). Raw battery scores lower in the methamphetamine group, p < 0.001; the group mean is not printed, but the two subgroup means (−0.84 in 6, −0.60 in 31) give about −0.64 in control units (editors' calculation). Control-group model: composite = −0.886 − 0.008 × age + 0.025 × parental income − 0.200 × smoking status + 0.404 × grade point average, R² 0.41, p < 0.001; applied to the methamphetamine group, predicted exceeded actual scores: d 0.61, t(36) = 3.732, p = 0.001; attention d 0.69, t(36) = 4.177, p < 0.001; memory d 0.46, t(36) = 2.805, p < 0.01; executive function not lower (printed d −0.27, t(36) = −0.169, p = 0.87). These d values equal t/√37, the mean shortfall divided by the SD of the individual shortfalls (editors' check), not differences in control-SD units. With withdrawal partialled out: d 0.54, t(36) = 3.302, p = 0.002. Standardized test scores in place of grades (24 and 19): d 1.41, t(23) = 6.888, p < 0.001. Grade-matched subgroups (28 each): d 0.71, p = 0.001. Overall and attention shortfalls correlated with grams used per day (r −0.397, p = 0.045; r −0.494, p = 0.010), not with years or frequency of use; withdrawal correlated with the overall shortfall (r −0.360, p = 0.029). Cortical thickness: no group difference (about 1% and 0.55% thinner, ns); within the methamphetamine group, memory shortfall related to whole-brain thickness (F(1,29) = 4.771, p = 0.037; left r 0.34, p = 0.060; right r 0.40, p = 0.026; n = 31). Editors' calculation from the equation and the Table 1 means (with smoking coded 1 for smokers, which reproduces a control mean of 0.00): the model's predicted mean for the methamphetamine group is about −0.30, of which grades contribute about −0.16 and smoking about −0.12; against an actual mean of about −0.64, roughly half of the group's gap from the controls is attributed by the model to the predictors and half remains as the shortfall.
analysis.covariates: Prediction model: age, parental income, childhood grade point average and current smoking status, the last included although not significant in controls because most of the methamphetamine group smoked (Results › Predictive modeling of cognition, 2nd paragraph). Education was deliberately left out because methamphetamine use can affect it (Methods and materials › Data analysis, 1st paragraph); smoking, which can also follow drug use, was kept.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration mentioned; the hypotheses (lower childhood grades; current performance below prediction; shortfalls related to thinner cortex) are stated in the Introduction.
analysis.selective_reporting: Group means for the battery and the domains are not printed (they are shown in figures and for subgroups only); regional thickness correlations are only in a supplement (not read); the number of participants in the correlations with amount of use is not stated.
analysis.power: Not reported; the authors call the control sample modest for prediction and recommend replication (Discussion, 7th paragraph). For d 0.61 in 37 people, the 95% interval is about 0.26 to 0.96 (editors' calculation), and wider still if the uncertainty of the prediction model were included.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 37 people with methamphetamine dependence tested after about a week of abstinence, school grades before first use were lower than the controls' (grade point average 2.1 vs 2.5), and adult composite scores were lower than a control-derived model predicted from grades, parental income, age and smoking (d 0.61; attention 0.69, memory 0.46; executive function no shortfall). The shortfall was larger with more grams used per day, remained after allowing for withdrawal, and the memory shortfall went with thinner cortex; the groups did not differ in cortical thickness.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says the results "support the view that chronic methamphetamine use causes a decline in cognition" and/or a failure to develop normal abilities, adding that other drug use and unidentified factors likely contribute; the limitations state that the methods did not allow a causal relationship to be shown (Discussion, 7th paragraph). Gaps: (1) the premorbid estimate is a model with R² 0.41 fitted in 41 healthy controls and including current smoking, so the unexplained shortfall can reflect anything the model leaves out that differs between people who develop dependence and healthy controls (attention or conduct problems, adversity, other drugs), not only decline; (2) testing after about a week of abstinence, with withdrawal related to the shortfall, cannot separate lasting from early-abstinence effects; (3) the paired t-tests treat each predicted score as known, ignoring the uncertainty of a model estimated in 41 people, so the p values and intervals are too optimistic; (4) lifetime alcohol, cocaine, marijuana and other drug use disorders were far more common in the methamphetamine group; (5) deficit means below the model's prediction, not impaired against norms; (6) the paired d values are called medium (0.69, 0.46) and moderate (0.54) and consistent with meta-analytic data (Discussion, 3rd and 6th paragraphs), but they divide the mean shortfall by the SD of the individual shortfalls, while meta-analytic d values are between-group differences in pooled-SD units; in the composite's own units the mean shortfall is about 0.34 (editors' calculation); (7) the discussion says confidence in the causal reading is strengthened because the groups were well matched on demographics (2nd paragraph), but demographic matching does not touch what the model leaves out (other substance use disorders, premorbid differences that grades do not capture). The abstract's other conclusion, an apparent premorbid weakness, is supported by the lower grades before first use.

timeline.event: Meta-analysis cited for medium methamphetamine–control differences (d −0.34 in language to −0.66 in learning)
Same laboratory: methamphetamine group means between the 16th and 55th percentiles of norms after about 6 days of abstinence, with a retested control group
Sibling study cited for inhibitory-control deficits shared by people with stimulant dependence and their siblings (ref. 6)
Dean, Hellemann, Sugar and London (2012), educational attainment is not a good proxy for cognitive function in methamphetamine dependence, a precedent for this prediction method (ref. 39); not read
Same group's review weighing animal, cross-sectional, twin, abstinence and dose evidence on methamphetamine-caused cognitive decline
Okita et al. (2017): cortical thickness compared in about 70% of this sample, no group difference (ref. 17); not read
This study: adult scores below a prediction from pre-use school grades

replication.where_it_stands: The only study read so far that estimates a premorbid starting point for adults with methamphetamine dependence; it suggests both a premorbid weakness and a shortfall beyond it, from one laboratory and an unreplicated method, with the shortfall measured in early abstinence. Its cognitive data had not been published before, so for cognition it is a new sample from the same laboratory as Simon et al. (2010), not an independent team; about 70% of its participants overlap with Okita et al. (2017) for cortical thickness.

funding.funder: NIH grants K23 DA027734 and R21 DA034928 (A.C.D.), P20 DA022539 and R01 DA020726 (E.D.L.), M01 RR00865 (UCLA General Clinical Research Center), UL1TR000124 (UCLA CTSI), and endowments from the Thomas P and Katherine K Pike Chair in Addiction Studies and the Marjorie M Greene Trust (E.D.L.) (Funding).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare that they have no conflict of interest (Competing interest).
funding.affiliations_note: UCLA Department of Psychiatry and Biobehavioral Sciences (Semel Institute), Brain Research Institute and Department of Molecular and Medical Pharmacology. Same laboratory as Simon et al. (2010) and the review by Dean et al. (2013), which argued that methamphetamine probably causes mild cognitive decline in at least some people; recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective cohort with cognitive testing in adolescence before any methamphetamine use (the authors mention the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development study), retested after the start of regular use and after sustained abstinence, alongside peers retested at the same intervals, with other substance use recorded throughout; meanwhile, a replication of the school-record method with a larger normative sample, prediction intervals that carry the model's uncertainty, and testing after months rather than days of abstinence.

domains.note: Other substance use disorders were far more common in the methamphetamine group and are not in the model (past diagnoses were only tested as predictors within the group); premorbid factors that grades do not capture (attention, conduct, adversity) are unmeasured; the model adjusts for grades, parental income, age and smoking and explains 41% of the variance in controls.
Dependence by SCID is reliable; amounts, duration and the date of first use (which decides which school years count) are self-reported.
Advertisement-recruited, paid volunteers and healthy controls screened for current disorders; the number excluded because school records could not be obtained is not reported.
Testing after a mean of 6.9 days of abstinence, 22 of 37 on a residential ward; withdrawal was related to the shortfall.

MRI unusable in 6 of 37 and 10 of 41; standardized school test scores for only 24 and 19; the correlations with amount of use appear to rest on about 26 people (editors' calculation, reporting issue 4).
Standard tests with effort checks, but blinding of testers to group is not reported, and scores are standardized to the controls rather than to norms.
No registered plan and several tests without correction, but the hypotheses were stated in advance and all three domains are reported, including the null for executive function.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The design is the nearest thing to a pre-use baseline that this page has, and the analysis is transparent. But the expected score comes from a model fitted in 41 healthy controls that explains about 40% of the variance and whose own uncertainty the tests ignore; the methamphetamine group differed in ways the model does not capture and had far more other substance use disorders; and testing was in the first weeks of abstinence. It may be cited for the lower pre-use school grades of this methamphetamine group and for adult scores below a grade-based prediction (overall, attention, memory), as one laboratory's estimate; not as proof of drug-caused decline, not for impairment against norms, and not for lasting effects.

key_findings.finding: 37 non-treatment-seeking adults with current methamphetamine dependence (recruited by advertisement, paid, 22 living on a research ward) and 41 healthy controls; the methamphetamine group was tested after a mean of 6.9 days of urine-verified abstinence (SD 2.7; range 3–30).
key_findings.note: The printed SD cannot be right with that range (reporting issue 1).

key_findings.finding: The groups were similar in age (34.0 vs 33.7), education (12.6 vs 12.7 years), estimated IQ (104.9 vs 105.0), sex, ethnicity, childhood economic class and parental education and income; the methamphetamine group was more often unemployed (27 of 37 vs 17 of 41) and more often smoked (34 of 37 vs 14 of 41).
key_findings.locator: Table 1; Results › Group comparisons of demographic characteristics, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Lifetime abuse or dependence, methamphetamine group vs controls: alcohol 26 vs 9, cocaine 12 vs 0, marijuana 21 vs 9, other drugs 9 vs 0 (all p<0.01); within the methamphetamine group these past diagnoses were not independently associated with battery scores (ps > 0.35).
key_findings.locator: Table 1; Methods and materials › Participants, 2nd paragraph; Results › Group comparisons of demographic characteristics, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Grade point average from school transcripts before self-reported first use: 2.1 (SD 0.7) in the methamphetamine group vs 2.5 (0.6) in controls, p = 0.016; standardized school test percentiles 48.7 vs 58.5 (24 and 19 participants), p = 0.178. Battery scores were lower in the methamphetamine group, p < 0.001.
key_findings.locator: Table 1; Results › Group comparisons of demographic characteristics, 2nd paragraph; Measures/procedures › Academic records
key_findings.note: Standardized difference in grades about 0.6 (editors' calculation from the rounded means and SDs).

key_findings.finding: In controls, grades (r 0.58), parental income (r 0.31) and age (r −0.30, trend) related to the overall composite; the model with age, parental income, grade point average and smoking status explained 41% of the variance (equation: −0.886 − 0.008 × age + 0.025 × parental income − 0.200 × smoking + 0.404 × grade point average).
key_findings.locator: Results › Predictive modeling of cognition, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Applied to the methamphetamine group, predicted overall scores were higher than actual scores: d 0.61, t(36) = 3.732, p = 0.001.
key_findings.locator: Results › Predictive modeling of cognition, 2nd paragraph; Fig. 1 legend
key_findings.note: d equals t/√37, a paired standardized difference (editors' check). Model-based decomposition (editors' calculation): predicted mean about −0.30, actual about −0.64 in control units.

key_findings.finding: By domain: attention/concentration below prediction (d 0.69, t(36) = 4.177, p < 0.001), memory below prediction (d 0.46, t(36) = 2.805, p < 0.01), executive function not below prediction (printed d −0.27, t(36) = −0.169, p = 0.87); domain models in controls had R² 0.41, 0.30 and 0.38.
key_findings.locator: Results › Predictive modeling of cognition, 3rd paragraph; Fig. 2 legend
key_findings.note: The printed d for executive function does not fit its t (reporting issue 2).

key_findings.finding: Withdrawal correlated with the overall shortfall (r −0.360, p = 0.029); with withdrawal partialled out, the shortfall remained (d 0.54, t(36) = 3.302, p = 0.002). Withdrawal was not related to the attention or memory shortfalls.
key_findings.locator: Results › Predictive modeling of cognition, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Larger overall and attention shortfalls went with more methamphetamine used per day (r −0.397, p = 0.045; r −0.494, p = 0.010); shortfalls were unrelated to years or frequency of use.
key_findings.locator: Results › Predictive modeling of cognition, 5th paragraph
key_findings.note: The n is not stated; both r and p pairs fit about 26 participants, not 37 (editors' calculation; reporting issue 4).

key_findings.finding: Checks: with standardized school test scores in place of grades (24 and 19 participants), predicted exceeded actual scores (d 1.41, t(23) = 6.888, p < 0.001); in grade-matched subgroups of 28 per group, d 0.71, p = 0.001.
key_findings.locator: Results › Predictive modeling of cognition, 6th and 7th paragraphs
key_findings.note: The grade-matched result is printed with t(36) although each subgroup had 28 people (reporting issue 3). The standardized-test model was fitted in only 19 controls (R² 0.46, p = 0.017), and the grade-matched groups did not differ on grades (p = 0.58).

key_findings.finding: Cortical thickness did not differ between the groups (about 1% and 0.55% thinner in the methamphetamine group, ns; 31 per group). Within the methamphetamine group, memory shortfall related to whole-brain thickness (F(1,29) = 4.771, p = 0.037; left hemisphere r 0.34, p = 0.060; right r 0.40, p = 0.026), with no regional pattern; the attention shortfall did not.
key_findings.locator: Results › Cortical thickness, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Fig. 3 legend

key_findings.finding: Scores were standardized to the control group, not to published norms.
key_findings.locator: Methods and materials › Measures/procedures › Cognitive battery

key_findings.finding: The authors' limitations: the methods do not show a causal relationship; grades and the other predictors explain about 40% of the variance; the control sample is modest for prediction; replication is recommended. They also state that it is difficult to disentangle effects of methamphetamine from other substance use, which could make the results an underestimate (if it preceded methamphetamine) or an overestimate (if it accompanied it), and that their data lack the detail to tell which.

reporting_issues.issue: Abstinence at testing is given as a mean of 6.9 days (SD 2.7; range 3–30) for 37 people. A single value of 30 with that mean would by itself make the SD at least about 3.9 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods and materials › Participants, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The mean, SD or range is misprinted; most participants were clearly tested within the first one to two weeks, but the exact distribution is uncertain.

reporting_issues.issue: For executive function the printed d is −0.27, but t(36) = −0.169 implies about −0.03 (every other d in the paper equals t/√n); the printed p = 0.87 fits the t.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Predictive modeling of cognition, 3rd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Executive scores were essentially as predicted, not slightly better; cite as no shortfall.

reporting_issues.issue: The grade-matched subgroup analysis (28 per group) is reported with t(36); its d of 0.71 equals 3.776/√28, which fits 28 participants (27 degrees of freedom).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Predictive modeling of cognition, 7th paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: A degrees-of-freedom misprint; the result is unchanged.

reporting_issues.issue: The number of participants in the correlations with grams used per day is not stated: r −0.397 with p 0.045 and r −0.494 with p 0.010 both fit about 26 participants, while the withdrawal correlation (r −0.360, p 0.029) fits 37 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Predictive modeling of cognition, 4th and 5th paragraphs
reporting_issues.consequence: The amount-of-use association appears to rest on about 26 of 37 people, with the missing data undescribed; it should be cited as such.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1's ethnicity counts sum to 39 of 41 controls and 32 of 37 in the methamphetamine group; the Other row is empty.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; 2 and 5 participants are unaccounted for in the ethnicity rows.

design_detail: Retrospective population cohort from linked Taiwanese administrative databases, 2007–2016: the Taiwan Illicit Drug Issue Database (TIDID: drug-abuse prevention case records, police drug-crime and penalty data, Ministry of Justice deferred-prosecution data) linked by encrypted identifier to National Health Insurance claims (NHIRD). Exposed: 74,601 adults whose first arrest for illicit use of an amphetamine-type substance (every arrest with a positive urine test; the 23 listed substances include methamphetamine, amphetamine, MDMA and MDA) fell in the period; index date = first arrest. Comparison: 298,404 insured adults with no record of illicit drug use, four per exposed person, frequency matched on index year, age and sex, with a random index month and day. People with a recorded psychosis diagnosis before the index date were excluded from both groups. Outcome: first recorded psychosis diagnosis (ICD-9-CM claims), followed to diagnosis, death or 31 December 2016. Cox models adjusted for age, sex and five comorbidity diagnoses; Kaplan–Meier cumulative incidence; strata by age, sex, comorbidity, number of arrests and rehabilitation under deferred prosecution.
can_establish: That adults arrested for amphetamine-type substance use in Taiwan had a first psychosis diagnosis recorded more often in the following years than insured adults of the same age, sex and index year with no record of illicit drug use, and how large that difference was in rates per person-year and in cumulative incidence.
cannot_establish: That amphetamine use caused the psychosis (adjustment only for age, sex and five comorbidity diagnoses, some recorded after the index date; no adjustment for other drug or alcohol use, socio-economic position, family history or other psychiatric history); a risk specific to methamphetamine (the substances are not broken down); a dose–response (the number of arrests is counted over the whole follow-up and reflects police contact); or that rehabilitation under deferred prosecution lowers risk (prosecutors offered it to about 10% judged to have promising treatment outcomes).

sample.recruitment: Registry. TIDID holds date of birth, sex, arrest records and deferred prosecution for rehabilitation treatment; National Health Insurance is a compulsory single-payer programme covering 99% of the population, and its claims form the NHIRD (Methods › Data source, 1st and 2nd paragraphs). Comparison people were drawn from beneficiaries with no record of illicit drug use who were insured in the index year of the exposed person they were matched to (Methods › Study population, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Adults aged 18 or older resident in Taiwan, followed from 1 January 2007 to 31 December 2016. Exposed: arrested for illicit use of one of 23 listed amphetamine-type substances (amphetamine, dexamphetamine, levamphetamine, methamphetamine and its racemate, levomethamphetamine, MDMA, MDA, MDEA, N-hydroxy-MDA, brolamfetamine, DOM, DOET, 2,5-dimethoxyamphetamine, 4-methoxyamphetamine, TMA, 5-methoxy-MDA, N-ethylamphetamine, N,N-dimethylamphetamine, fluoro-, chloro- and methoxymethamphetamine, lisdexamphetamine), every arrest accompanied by a positive urine test; index date = first arrest. Both groups: excluded if a psychosis diagnosis (ICD-9-CM 291.3, 291.5, 292.1, 292.11, 292.12, 293.81, 293.82, 295, 296.04–296.64 with psychotic features, 297, 297.3, 298.0, 298.1, 298.4, 298.8, 298.9, 780.1) was recorded before the index date (Methods › Study population, 1st and 2nd paragraphs). The look-back period for earlier diagnoses, whether arrests before 2007 were considered in choosing the first arrest, and the counts excluded at each step (given only in the Figure 1 flowchart, an image) are not stated in the text.
sample.demographics: Mean age 33.3 (SD 9.45) in both cohorts; 84.2% men; aged 18–29 38.2%, 30–44 49.1%, 45 or older 12.7% (identical by design). Comorbidities, amphetamine vs non-amphetamine cohort: depression 1.98% vs 0.42% (SMD 0.14), anxiety 0.91% vs 0.27% (0.08), ischaemic heart disease 1.32% vs 0.78% (0.05), cardiovascular disease 0.79% vs 0.45% (0.04), stroke 1.31% vs 0.66% (0.07) (Findings, 1st paragraph; Table 1). No data on education, income, occupation, ethnic group, alcohol or other drug use, or psychiatric history beyond these codes.
sample.attrition: Followed from the index date to a psychosis diagnosis, death or 31 December 2016: mean 4.93 (SD 2.93) years in the amphetamine cohort and 4.99 (2.93) in the comparison cohort; 367,696 and 1,487,536 person-years (Findings, 1st paragraph; Table 2). Deaths are treated as censoring and their number is not reported; loss of insurance cover, emigration and time in prison are not discussed.
sample.selection_effects: The exposed group is defined by arrest, not by use. The authors note that arrests reflect police activity and priorities, that many people who use amphetamines are never arrested (so the comparison group may include some), and that people who use more often may be more likely to be arrested (Conclusions and clinical implications, 6th paragraph). The comparison group excludes anyone with any record of illicit drug use, so it is the general insured population, not people who use other drugs; differences in other drug use, alcohol and socio-economic position are built into the comparison. The rehabilitation subgroup was chosen by prosecutors, who offered deferred prosecution to about 10% judged to have promising treatment outcomes (8th paragraph).

exposure.measurement: Administrative record of arrest for illicit amphetamine-type substance use, each arrest accompanied by a positive urine test (Methods › Study population, 1st paragraph). Exposure is fixed at the first arrest; later use is unknown. The number of arrests is counted from the index date to the end of the study, and the authors treat it as implying cumulative dose (Methods › Statistics, 1st paragraph). Rehabilitation treatment comes from the deferred-prosecution records (Methods › Study population, 3rd paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not recorded: the authors state that the database has no validated measures of dose, frequency, amount or severity of dependence (Conclusions and clinical implications, 3rd paragraph) and that periods and doses of use could not be obtained (10th paragraph). Number of arrests: one 40,880 people, two 15,026, three 7,710, four 4,413, five or more 6,572 (Table 3).
exposure.polysubstance: Not adjusted for. Other drug use by the exposed group is recorded in the same database (the comparison group is defined by having no such record) but is neither reported nor used for adjustment; alcohol use is not reported. The substances counted as amphetamine include MDMA, MDA and other ring-substituted amphetamines, and no breakdown by substance (for example the share involving methamphetamine) is given.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable (registry outcome).

comparison.controls: 298,404 insured adults with no record of illicit drug use, four per exposed person, randomly selected after frequency matching on index year, age and sex; index month and day assigned at random within the index year; those with an earlier psychosis diagnosis excluded (Methods › Study population, 1st paragraph).
comparison.matching: Frequency matched on index year, age and sex (identical distributions, Table 1). Not matched or adjusted on socio-economic status: the authors note that people who use amphetamines often have lower socio-economic status but argue, citing controversy about socio-economic status and psychosis, that omitting it might not have affected the results (Conclusions and clinical implications, 7th paragraph).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Genetic data, ethnic group, obstetric complications and childhood adversity (named by the authors as unavailable, 8th paragraph); also, not mentioned by the authors, family history of psychosis, education and psychiatric history other than the five comorbidity codes; socio-economic position was not matched (7th paragraph). Other drug use is recorded in the same database (the comparison group is defined by having no such record) but is not used for adjustment.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: None recorded by design (no record of illicit drug use); alcohol and tobacco use unknown; the authors note that some may have used amphetamines without being arrested.

outcomes.instruments: Diagnoses in National Health Insurance claims, ICD-9-CM. Outcome codes listed: 295, 296.04, 296.14, 296.24, 296.34, 296.44, 296.54, 296.64, 297, 298.0, 298.1, 298.4, 298.8, 298.9 and 780.1, following Moran et al. (2019) (Methods › Study population, 2nd paragraph).
outcomes.validity_norms: No validation of the codes in this population is reported. The authors note that rehabilitation under deferred prosecution took place in hospital psychiatric departments, which might increase the chance of a diagnosis (Conclusions and clinical implications, 8th paragraph). The comparison group's rate (0.77 per 1,000 person-years, 77 per 100,000) is 2.4 to 2.9 times the pooled incidence of psychotic disorders the authors cite (31.7 and 26.6 per 100,000 person-years) and lies between two US rates of first psychotic symptoms (46 and 86 per 100,000) (2nd paragraph; editors' arithmetic), consistent with a broad code set that includes hallucinations and affective disorders with psychotic features.
outcomes.operationalization: Psychosis = a first recorded claim with one of the listed outcome codes. The text says the definition includes other stimulant use disorders with psychosis, but the outcome code list omits the drug-induced psychosis codes (292.1, 292.11, 292.12) that are in the exclusion list (see reporting issues). How many claims, or what kind of visit, were required is not stated.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None: 14 adjusted hazard ratios (overall; three age, two sex and two comorbidity strata; five arrest categories; rehabilitation) and one trend test, each at two-sided p<0.05 (Methods › Statistics, 2nd paragraph). The authors state that the analysis was not preregistered and that the results should be considered exploratory (Methods › Data source, 2nd paragraph).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable (routinely recorded diagnoses); clinicians who recorded diagnoses may have known about drug use or arrest.

analysis.effect_sizes: First recorded psychosis: 1,722 events in 367,696 person-years (4.68 per 1,000) in the amphetamine cohort against 1,144 in 1,487,536 (0.77 per 1,000); crude HR 6.08 (95% CI 5.64–6.55); HR 5.28 (4.90–5.70) adjusted for age, sex and comorbidities (Table 2). Rate difference about 3.9 per 1,000 person-years (editors' calculation). Kaplan–Meier cumulative incidence at 10 years 3.75% against 0.63%, log-rank p<0.0001 (Findings, 2nd paragraph). Adjusted HRs by stratum: ages 18–29 5.09 (4.50–5.75), 30–44 5.33 (4.79–5.93), 45 or older 5.41 (4.29–6.82); men 4.81 (4.42–5.24), women 7.49 (6.30–8.91), from rates of 4.16 and 7.33 against 0.77 and 0.78 per 1,000; without comorbidity 6.30 (5.79–6.86), with comorbidity 2.28 (1.93–2.69), from rates of 3.91 against 0.62 and 20.02 against 7.39 per 1,000, so the rate difference is larger with comorbidity (about 12.6 against 3.3 per 1,000; editors' calculation). Number of arrests, adjusted: one 4.49 (4.09–4.93), two 5.07 (4.51–5.72), three 5.24 (4.52–6.09), four 5.53 (4.60–6.64), five or more 6.25 (5.42–7.20); p for trend 0.038 (Table 3). Rehabilitation against none, within the amphetamine cohort: 112 events in 29,884 person-years (3.75 per 1,000) against 1,610 in 337,812 (4.77); crude HR 0.74 (0.61–0.90), adjusted 0.74 (0.61–0.89) (Table 4).
analysis.covariates: Age, sex and five comorbidities (depression, anxiety, ischaemic heart disease, cardiovascular disease, stroke) diagnosed at any time during 2007–2016, not only before the index date (Methods › Study population, 3rd paragraph; Table 2 footnote †); number of arrests added in the rehabilitation model (Table 4 footnote). No adjustment for socio-economic position, alcohol or other drug use, or psychiatric history.
analysis.preregistration_detail: The authors state that the analysis was not preregistered and that the results should be considered exploratory (Methods › Data source, 2nd paragraph).
analysis.selective_reporting: One overall model with many strata and no sensitivity analyses (no lag period after the arrest, no restriction to methamphetamine, no analysis of substance-induced against other psychoses); no test of proportional hazards (the authors say a single average HR may mislead, 9th paragraph of the Conclusions); no interaction tests for the sex and comorbidity differences; the trend test is not described; the breakdown of the exposed group by substance and the counts at each selection step are not given in the text.
analysis.power: Not an issue for the main estimate (1,722 and 1,144 events); the rehabilitation comparison rests on 112 events among 7,733 people.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In linked administrative records, adults arrested for amphetamine-type substance use had a first psychosis diagnosis recorded at about six times the rate of insured adults of the same age, sex and index year with no drug record (4.68 against 0.77 per 1,000 person-years; 10-year cumulative incidence 3.75% against 0.63%), HR 5.28 after adjustment for age, sex and five comorbidity diagnoses only. The HR was larger in women and rose from 4.49 with one arrest to 6.25 with five or more; within the arrested group, the roughly 10% chosen by prosecutors for rehabilitation had a lower rate (HR 0.74).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract states that people with illicit amphetamine use were "5.28 times more likely" to experience psychosis and reports a significant decrease in risk with rehabilitation; the discussion infers "a direct effect of amphetamine" from the larger HR in people without comorbidity (Conclusions and clinical implications, 3rd paragraph) and "a preventive effect of psychotherapy" from the rehabilitation comparison (5th paragraph). Gaps: (1) the comparison group had no drug record, and other drug and alcohol use, socio-economic position and family history were not adjusted for, while the adjustment used comorbidities recorded after the index date; (2) the smaller HR with comorbidity reflects a baseline rate about twelve times higher in that stratum: the rate difference is larger with comorbidity (12.6 against 3.3 per 1,000 person-years), so it does not point to a direct effect; (3) the rehabilitation group was chosen by prosecutors for promising outcomes, the timing of treatment relative to follow-up is not described, and the treatment's content is never described although the discussion calls it psychotherapy, so the lower HR cannot be read as an effect of treatment; (4) the arrest gradient uses arrests counted over the whole follow-up, which accumulate with time observed (about 4.4 person-years per person with one arrest against 6.5 with five or more; editors' calculation) and with police contact, so it is not a dose–response, as the authors themselves concede for dose; (5) amphetamine here includes MDMA and other substances without a breakdown; (6) the larger HR in women (7.49 against 4.81) is called a greater risk of amphetamine-induced psychosis and given a hormonal explanation from animal studies (4th paragraph), although no interaction test is reported and the same paragraph offers a confounding explanation (women arrested were more disadvantaged). The authors do state that the analysis was exploratory and not preregistered, that arrest is a proxy for use, that amphetamine might precipitate rather than cause psychotic symptoms in people already vulnerable, and that confounders such as childhood adversity could not be controlled (6th to 10th paragraphs).

timeline.event: Prospective within-person study of people with methamphetamine dependence showing dose-related psychotic symptoms, cited by the authors in support of their arrest gradient (their ref. 24)
Systematic review of risk factors for methamphetamine-associated psychosis, cited by the authors for amphetamine use as the primary risk factor (their ref. 23)
Moran et al. (2019), psychosis with methylphenidate or amphetamine in patients with ADHD, the source of the outcome definition (their ref. 19); not read
Meta-analysis of mostly cross-sectional studies: amphetamine use disorder and psychosis, adjusted OR 2.4 (1.6–3.5; 4 studies)
This study: arrest-defined exposure in a national registry, HR 5.28 against people with no drug record
General-population birth cohort (New Zealand): any use in a period, OR 1.33 (1.03–1.72) after adjustment including concurrent cannabis use

replication.where_it_stands: The direction of the association is found across designs, but its size depends on the comparison and the adjustment: about 2.4 for use disorder in the meta-analysis of mostly within-sample comparisons, 1.33 in a general-population birth cohort after adjustment including cannabis, and 5.28 here against people with no drug record and minimal adjustment. This is the largest cohort read so far and the only one giving rates of new recorded diagnoses after a dated index event, but it cannot separate methamphetamine from other amphetamine-type substances, or the drug from the other circumstances of people who are arrested.

funding.funder: Supported in part by the Ministry of Science and Technology (MOST 104-3011-F-039-001), the Ministry of Health and Welfare (M05B4352), the National Health Research Institutes (NP-108-GP-05), the Ministry of Health and Welfare Clinical Trial Centre (MOHW109-TDU-B-212-114004), and China Medical University Hospital and China Medical University under the Higher Education Sprout Project of the Ministry of Education, Taiwan; the funders had no role in study design, the decision to publish or preparation of the manuscript (Footnotes › Funding).
funding.declared_conflicts: Competing interests: none (Footnotes).
funding.affiliations_note: Tsaotun Psychiatric Centre (Ministry of Health and Welfare), China Medical University School of Medicine and Graduate Institute of Biomedical Sciences, and China Medical University Hospital (Management Office for Health Data; Centre for Drug Abuse and Addiction), Taiwan. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A linkage of the same registries that identifies methamphetamine specifically, starts follow-up after a lag from the first recorded use, compares people arrested for methamphetamine with people arrested for other drugs (or with siblings), adjusts for other substance use, alcohol, socio-economic position and psychiatric contact measured before the index date, treats arrests and treatment as time-varying, and reports substance-induced and primary psychotic disorders separately.

domains.note: Adjusted only for age and sex (matched) and five comorbidity diagnoses that were recorded at any time in 2007–2016, so partly after exposure, and whose depression codes include two outcome codes (296.24, 296.34). No adjustment for other drug or alcohol use, socio-economic position, family history or earlier psychiatric contact, all expected to be strongly related both to arrest for drug use and to psychosis, against a comparison group with no record of any illicit drug use. A second reader may judge this high rather than very high; the overall would then be high.

Arrest with a positive urine test is specific for some use at the time but insensitive (most use is never detected and the comparison group may include people who use); exposure is fixed at the first arrest; 23 substances including MDMA are pooled without a breakdown; the number of arrests is counted over the whole follow-up.

Exposure is defined by arrest, which selects people with police contact and possibly heavier or more visible use; follow-up starts at the first arrest, not at the start of use, so people whose psychosis was diagnosed before their first arrest are excluded while episodes that led to an arrest and were diagnosed afterwards count as new; the look-back for earlier diagnoses is not stated.

Arrest is followed by prosecution, deferred prosecution with hospital treatment for about 10%, and possibly imprisonment (not discussed); these change both later use and contact with services, and the rehabilitation comparison is itself an intervention allocated by prosecutors.
Registry linkage appears complete, but the counts excluded at each step are only in a flowchart image, deaths (censored) are not counted, and loss of insurance cover is not addressed.

Claims diagnoses not validated in this population; the listed outcome codes omit the drug-induced psychosis codes that the text says were included; people arrested for drug use, and particularly those treated in hospital psychiatric departments under deferred prosecution, are likely to have more contact with services where a diagnosis can be recorded (the authors note this for the rehabilitation group).

Not preregistered and described as exploratory; many strata, no sensitivity analyses, and an undescribed trend test whose printed p value is reproduced by a regression on five category rates (see reporting issues).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The association is large and precisely estimated, and the design gives rates of new recorded diagnoses after a dated index event, which most of this literature lacks. But the comparison is between people arrested for drug use and insured people with no drug record, adjusted only for age, sex and five comorbidity codes partly recorded after exposure; other drug and alcohol use, socio-economic position, family history, earlier psychiatric contact and greater contact with services after arrest could each account for a large part of an HR of 5.28, and every one of these biases would make the estimate larger. It may be cited for the rates of first recorded psychosis diagnoses after an amphetamine-related arrest in Taiwan against the general insured population, and as a cohort agreeing in direction with other designs; not for the size of an effect of methamphetamine, not for a dose–response, and not for an effect of rehabilitation.

key_findings.finding: Linked Taiwanese registries, 2007–2016: 74,601 adults arrested for illicit use of an amphetamine-type substance (every arrest urine-confirmed; index date = first arrest) and 298,404 insured adults with no record of illicit drug use, four per exposed person, frequency matched on index year, age and sex; people with a psychosis diagnosis recorded before the index date excluded from both groups.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Study population, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Findings, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: The exposure covers 23 listed substances, including methamphetamine, amphetamine, dexamphetamine, MDMA, MDA, MDEA, brolamfetamine, DOM and lisdexamphetamine; no breakdown of the cohort by substance is given.

Both cohorts: mean age 33.3 (SD 9.45), 84.2% men. Comorbidities recorded during 2007–2016, amphetamine vs comparison cohort: depression 1.98% vs 0.42%, anxiety 0.91% vs 0.27%, ischaemic heart disease 1.32% vs 0.78%, cardiovascular disease 0.79% vs 0.45%, stroke 1.31% vs 0.66%. Mean follow-up 4.93 and 4.99 years (SD 2.93).
key_findings.locator: Findings, 1st paragraph; Table 1; Methods › Study population, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: First recorded psychosis diagnosis: 1,722 in 367,696 person-years (4.68 per 1,000) vs 1,144 in 1,487,536 (0.77 per 1,000); crude HR 6.08 (95% CI 5.64–6.55); HR 5.28 (4.90–5.70) adjusted for age, sex and the five comorbidities.
key_findings.note: Rate difference about 3.9 per 1,000 person-years (editors' calculation). The abstract calls the adjusted HR 5.28 times more likely; the Findings use the same phrase for the crude ratio 6.08.

key_findings.finding: Kaplan–Meier cumulative incidence of psychosis at the end of 10 years of follow-up: 3.75% in the amphetamine cohort vs 0.63% in the comparison cohort (log-rank p<0.0001).
key_findings.locator: Findings, 2nd paragraph; Figure 2 (image; values not extracted beyond the text)
key_findings.note: Kaplan–Meier estimates with death treated as censoring (the number of deaths is not reported), so they describe the risk in the absence of death rather than observed proportions, and somewhat overstate the cumulative incidence when deaths compete (editors' note).

key_findings.finding: Adjusted HRs by age: 18–29 5.09 (4.50–5.75), 30–44 5.33 (4.79–5.93), 45 or older 5.41 (4.29–6.82). By sex: men 4.81 (4.42–5.24; rates 4.16 vs 0.77 per 1,000), women 7.49 (6.30–8.91; rates 7.33 vs 0.78). No interaction test is reported.
key_findings.locator: Table 2, Age and Sex rows; Findings, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: By comorbidity: without comorbidity, rates 3.91 vs 0.62 per 1,000, adjusted HR 6.30 (5.79–6.86); with comorbidity, rates 20.02 vs 7.39 per 1,000, adjusted HR 2.28 (1.93–2.69). The authors read the larger HR without comorbidity as pointing to a direct effect of amphetamine.
key_findings.locator: Table 2, Comorbidities rows; Findings, 3rd paragraph; Conclusions and clinical implications, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: On the absolute scale the excess is larger with comorbidity: about 12.6 against 3.3 per 1,000 person-years (editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: By number of arrests (counted from the index date to the end of the study), adjusted HRs against the comparison cohort: one 4.49 (4.09–4.93; 40,880 people, 4.40 per 1,000), two 5.07 (4.51–5.72), three 5.24 (4.52–6.09), four 5.53 (4.60–6.64), five or more 6.25 (5.42–7.20; 6,572 people, 5.45 per 1,000); p for trend 0.038, printed in the incidence-rate column. The authors state they could not assert dose dependence because the database has no validated measures of dose, frequency, amount or severity.
key_findings.locator: Table 3; Findings, 4th paragraph; Methods › Statistics, 1st paragraph; Conclusions and clinical implications, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: Person-years per person rise from about 4.4 with one arrest to 6.5 with five or more (editors' calculation), so more arrests go with longer observation. A linear regression of the five category incidence rates on the number of arrests gives p = 0.038 (editors' calculation), which suggests that the printed trend test used the five rates rather than individual data.

key_findings.finding: Within the amphetamine cohort, the 7,733 people who received rehabilitation treatment during deferred prosecution had 112 psychosis diagnoses in 29,884 person-years (3.75 per 1,000) against 1,610 in 337,812 (4.77) among the 66,868 without; adjusted HR 0.74 (0.61–0.89), adjusted also for the number of arrests. Prosecutors offered deferred prosecution to about 10% of people arrested, those with promising treatment outcomes as judged by the prosecutors, and treatment took place in hospital psychiatric departments.
key_findings.locator: Table 4; Findings, 4th paragraph; Conclusions and clinical implications, 5th and 8th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The authors state that the analysis was not preregistered and that the results should be considered exploratory.

Limitations stated by the authors: amphetamine may precipitate rather than cause psychotic symptoms; arrests reflect police activity and priorities and do not capture all use (many people who use are never arrested), so the comparison group may include people who use and arrested people may use more often; severity of dependence is not documented; socio-economic status was not matched; prosecutors selected about 10% for rehabilitation; no genetic data or information on ethnic group, obstetric complications or childhood adversity; four controls per case may reduce representativeness; a single average HR may mislead; exposure could not be modelled as time-varying.
key_findings.locator: Conclusions and clinical implications, 6th to 10th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The comparison group's psychosis rate, 77 per 100,000 person-years, is described by the authors as slightly higher than published figures: pooled incidence of psychotic disorders 26.6 (international, 2002–17) and 31.7 per 100,000 person-years (England), and US rates of first psychotic symptoms of 86 (ages 15–29) and 46 per 100,000 (ages 30–59).
key_findings.note: 77 is 2.4 to 2.9 times the two pooled incidences of psychotic disorders (editors' arithmetic); slightly higher fits only the US symptom rates.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says the psychosis definition includes other stimulant use disorders with psychosis, and the exclusion list for earlier psychosis contains the drug-induced psychosis codes 292.1, 292.11 and 292.12 (with 291.3, 291.5, 293.81, 293.82 and 297.3), but the list of outcome codes that ends follow-up does not contain them.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods › Study population, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: It is unclear whether substance-induced psychotic disorders were counted as outcomes. If they were not, the outcome is schizophrenia, affective disorders with psychotic features, other nonorganic psychoses and hallucinations, and the HR does not describe drug-induced psychosis; if they were, the printed code list is incomplete.

reporting_issues.issue: Comorbidities were assigned from diagnoses made at any time during 2007–2016 (Methods › Study population, 3rd paragraph), yet Table 1 is titled as baseline factors; and the depression codes (296.20–296.24, 296.30–296.34) include 296.24 and 296.34, major depression with psychotic features, which are also outcome codes.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods › Study population, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Table 1
reporting_issues.consequence: The adjustment for, and stratification by, comorbidity partly conditions on diagnoses made after exposure and on the outcome itself; the adjusted HR and the comorbidity strata (6.30 against 2.28) cannot be read as a conventional adjustment for baseline differences.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods give the age groups as 18–35, 35–49 and 50 or older; Tables 1 and 2 use 18–29, 30–44 and 45 or older.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods › Study population, 3rd paragraph; Tables 1–2
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the tables' groups are the ones analysed.

reporting_issues.issue: The p for trend (0.038) is printed in the incidence-rate column of Table 3 and the test is not described. A regression of the five category incidence rates (4.40, 4.80, 4.81, 4.84, 5.45) on the number of arrests reproduces p = 0.038 (editors' calculation, 3 degrees of freedom), while the adjusted HRs for one arrest and for five or more have non-overlapping intervals (4.09–4.93 and 5.42–7.20). Arrests were counted from the index date to the study end date, which implies that arrests after a psychosis diagnosis were also counted (this is not stated explicitly).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Table 3; Methods › Statistics, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The trend test appears to treat five group rates as five observations; the gradient should be cited without this p value, and in any case as a gradient in arrests counted over the whole follow-up, not in amount of use.

reporting_issues.issue: The Conclusions call the rates of 77 and 468 per 100,000 persons annual cumulative incidence rates; they are the incidence rates per person-year of Table 2 (0.77 and 4.68 per 1,000 person-years). The comparison group's 77 is called slightly higher than published incidences of 26.6 and 31.7 per 100,000 person-years for psychotic disorders.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Conclusions and clinical implications, 2nd paragraph; Table 2
reporting_issues.consequence: A rate 2.4 to 2.9 times the cited incidence of psychotic disorders (editors' arithmetic) shows that the outcome is broader than psychotic disorder as usually counted; slightly higher understates the gap.

reporting_issues.issue: The same phrase, times more likely, is used for the crude rate ratio (6.08, Findings, 2nd paragraph) and for the adjusted HR (5.28, abstract).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract › Findings; Findings, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the headline figure is an adjusted hazard ratio, not a ratio of risks.

design_detail: CDC surveillance report (MMWR) with two analyses. (1) SUDORS, the State Unintentional Drug Overdose Reporting System: unintentional and undetermined-intent overdose deaths in 49 states and the District of Columbia, January 2021 to June 2024, pooled (309,274 deaths; a jurisdiction had to report at least 75% of its overdose deaths in at least one 6-month period, and four were included for only part of the period), with a drug counted as involved when the medical examiner or coroner listed it as a cause of death on the death certificate, in their report or in the postmortem toxicology report; percentages of deaths involving any stimulant, methamphetamine and cocaine, with and without opioids, and decedents' characteristics and circumstances (46 states and DC with circumstance data). (2) NVSS, the National Vital Statistics System: all US death certificates, 2018–2023 (520,525 overdose deaths), age-adjusted rates of deaths with the multiple-cause codes for cocaine (T40.5) and for psychostimulants with abuse potential (T43.6), overall and by race and ethnicity, with and without opioid codes.
can_establish: What share of overdose deaths in nearly all US states in January 2021 to June 2024 involved methamphetamine as named by medical examiners, coroners and toxicology, how many of these also involved opioids, how decedents with and without opioid involvement differed in what was recorded about them, and how national age-adjusted death rates coded as involving psychostimulants changed from 2018 to 2023.
cannot_establish: Death rates among people who use methamphetamine (no denominator of use); that methamphetamine caused each death (involvement means listed as causing or contributing); any change over time in the methamphetamine-specific SUDORS figures (one pooled period, with jurisdictions entering for different periods); or whether opioid co-use was intentional (the report infers this from drug-checking studies, not from its own data).

sample.recruitment: Registries. SUDORS: CDC funds 49 states and DC under Overdose Data to Action to report unintentional and undetermined-intent overdose deaths from death certificates, postmortem toxicology and medical examiner or coroner reports; deaths are identified by underlying-cause codes X40–X44 and Y10–Y14 and by text searches of the cause-of-death fields (Methods › Data Sources, 1st paragraph; main-text footnote †). NVSS: death certificates for all US deaths (Methods › Data Sources, 2nd paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: SUDORS: a jurisdiction had to report at least 75% of its overdose deaths in at least one 6-month period; all except California, Texas, Wisconsin and Wyoming reported for the whole period; California and Wisconsin are included for part of it, Texas and Wyoming only for January–June 2024, and North Dakota (not funded) not at all (main-text footnote †††). Circumstance analyses: 46 states and DC with circumstance data for at least 75% of deaths in at least one 6-month period (California, Idaho, North Dakota and Texas are not on the list); in those jurisdictions 93.1% of deaths had circumstance data (main-text footnotes §§§ and ¶¶¶). NVSS: underlying cause X40–X44 or Y10–Y14, with multiple-cause codes T40.5 for cocaine, T43.6 for psychostimulants with abuse potential (which the authors say primarily includes methamphetamine and other amphetamines) and T40.0–T40.4 and T40.6 for opioids (Methods › Data Sources, 2nd paragraph).
sample.demographics: Methamphetamine-involved SUDORS deaths: 72.2% male; aged 25–34 20.3%, 35–44 29.4%, 45–54 23.1%, 55–64 18.5%, 65 or older 5.1%; non-Hispanic White 74.2%, non-Hispanic Black 10.4%, Hispanic or Latino 10.2%, non-Hispanic American Indian or Alaska Native 2.5% (Table). Aged 45 or older: 64% of those without opioids against 39% of those with opioids (19,350 of 30,124 and 25,770 of 66,463 with known age; editors' calculation from the Table).
sample.attrition: Not applicable (registry counts). Missing data: age and sex under 0.1%, race and ethnicity 1.0%; circumstance variables up to 3.0% (Table footnotes ** and ¶¶).
sample.selection_effects: SUDORS covers almost every state but four of them only for part of the period and North Dakota not at all, so the pooled percentages weight jurisdictions by the periods they reported; circumstance analyses leave out four states. The authors expect stimulant-involved deaths to be undercounted, because some are certified with cardiovascular causes and get no overdose code, and because toxicology testing varies and does not routinely cover emerging stimulants (Discussion › Limitations).

exposure.measurement: SUDORS: a drug counts as involved if the medical examiner or coroner listed it as a cause of death on the death certificate, in the medical examiner or coroner report or in the postmortem toxicology report (main-text footnote §§; Table footnote *); methamphetamine is named specifically. NVSS: the multiple-cause code T43.6, psychostimulants with abuse potential, which the authors describe as primarily methamphetamine and other amphetamines, so it is not specific to methamphetamine.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable. A history of methamphetamine use was recorded for 32.9% of methamphetamine-involved decedents with circumstance data (43.8% of those without opioids, 28.1% with opioids) (Table).
exposure.polysubstance: Opioid co-involvement is the main stratifier: 68.8% of methamphetamine-involved deaths also involved opioids. 3.8% of all overdose deaths involved both methamphetamine and cocaine, and the methamphetamine and cocaine columns of the Table overlap (Table footnote *). Other co-involved drugs (alcohol, sedatives) are not reported; the only-stimulants category (14.5%) excludes deaths in which other drugs contributed (Figure 1 footnote **).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: None: descriptive comparisons between deaths with and without opioid involvement, between stimulant types, between racial and ethnic groups and across years.

outcomes.instruments: Death certificates, medical examiner and coroner reports and postmortem toxicology (SUDORS); death certificates coded with ICD-10 (NVSS); age-adjusted rates per 100,000 standardized to the 2000 US standard population (main-text footnote ¶¶).
outcomes.validity_norms: The authors name five limitations: deaths certified with cardiovascular causes in the setting of stimulant toxicity may get no overdose code and be missed; postmortem toxicology testing varies and does not routinely cover emerging stimulants (both causing underestimation); circumstance information depends on investigative reports; race and ethnicity may be misclassified; and some large states are excluded from the circumstance analyses (Discussion › Limitations).
outcomes.operationalization: Stimulant-involved death: cocaine, methamphetamine, other amphetamines, synthetic cathinones, prescription stimulants or any other central nervous system stimulant listed as causing or contributing (SUDORS; Methods › Data Sources, 1st paragraph); in NVSS, cocaine (T40.5) or psychostimulants with abuse potential (T43.6). Opioid co-involvement: an opioid also listed (SUDORS) or coded (NVSS). Prescription stimulants include amphetamine and dextroamphetamine only when methamphetamine is not detected (main-text footnote **).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable: descriptive percentages and rates are reported without statistical tests or confidence intervals.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: SUDORS, January 2021–June 2024, 309,274 overdose deaths: any stimulant 182,502 (59.0%), with opioids 133,293 (43.1%), without opioids 49,209 (15.9%); methamphetamine 96,614 (31.2%), with opioids 66,475 (21.5% of all deaths; 68.8% of methamphetamine-involved deaths), without opioids 30,139 (9.7% of all deaths; 31.2% of methamphetamine-involved deaths, editors' calculation); cocaine 92,697 (30.0%), 79.1% of them with opioids; methamphetamine and cocaine together 3.8%; prescription stimulants 1.6%, synthetic cathinones 0.7%, MDMA or MDA 0.4%; only stimulants 14.5% (Results › SUDORS, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table, Overall row; Figure 1). Methamphetamine-involved deaths with circumstance data (67,831), without against with opioids: known history of cardiovascular disease 39.3% vs 19.8%; seen in an emergency department for the fatal overdose 30.3% vs 17.4%; evidence of opioid use history 12.2% vs 41.1%; ever treated for mental health or substance use disorders 14.2% vs 24.0%; homelessness or housing instability 15.7% vs 18.9%; naloxone given 15.6% vs 27.1% (Table). NVSS age-adjusted rates per 100,000, 2018 and 2023: psychostimulants 3.9 and 10.4, cocaine 4.5 and 8.6; psychostimulants among non-Hispanic American Indian or Alaska Native people 11.0 and 32.9 and among non-Hispanic Native Hawaiian or Pacific Islander people 7.4 and 16.3; cocaine among non-Hispanic Black people 9.1 and 24.3 (Results › NVSS, 1st paragraph). Counts cited from an NCHS data brief: psychostimulant-involved deaths 2,266 in 2011 and 34,855 in 2023, cocaine-involved 4,681 and 29,449 (Introduction). No confidence intervals anywhere.
analysis.covariates: None. NVSS rates are age-adjusted; SUDORS percentages are crude.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Surveillance report; reviewed by CDC and deemed not research (Methods › Statistical Analysis, 2nd paragraph).
analysis.selective_reporting: The NVSS trends with and without opioids, overall and for White, Asian and Hispanic people, are shown only in Figure 2 and a Supplementary Figure (an image and a separate file, not read); the text says only that the largest increases in every group were in deaths also involving opioids, without figures. The SUDORS figures are pooled over 3.5 years, so no trend in the methamphetamine-specific share is given. Provisional declines in 2024 are mentioned without figures (Introduction; Discussion, 4th paragraph).
analysis.power: Not applicable (registry counts).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Methamphetamine was involved in 31.2% of overdose deaths in 49 states and DC in January 2021 to June 2024; about two-thirds of these deaths (68.8%) also involved opioids, and 30,139 (9.7% of all overdose deaths) did not. Decedents without opioids were older and more often had a recorded history of cardiovascular disease. National age-adjusted death rates coded as involving psychostimulants rose from 3.9 to 10.4 per 100,000 between 2018 and 2023, with the largest increases among American Indian or Alaska Native people and, by the text's account, in deaths also involving opioids.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The summary and most of the discussion describe the data accurately. Three statements go beyond them: (1) that drug-checking programmes rarely found opioids in stimulant products, suggesting that people who died with both had intentionally used separate products (Discussion, 4th paragraph), an inference from other studies, not from these deaths; (2) that stable survey prevalence among American Indian or Alaska Native and Black people "suggests increased drug potency or differential access" to care (Discussion, 6th paragraph), from survey tables the report does not analyse; (3) that the 38.7% with a known history of cardiovascular disease among deaths with stimulants and no opioids, against about 10% of all US adults, possibly reflects long-term stimulant use (Discussion, 2nd and 5th paragraphs): the comparison is not age-standardized, although two-thirds of these decedents were 45 or older, and history of hypertension is excluded from the decedents' figure (Table footnote ***). The recommendations (contingency management, low-barrier care, naloxone and stimulant overdose education) rest on cited guidance, not on the report's data.

timeline.event: Analysis of the same national death records for ages 18–64, 2015–2019: deaths with the code for psychostimulants other than cocaine rose from 5,526 to 15,489, more than half of the 2019 deaths with opioids

Spencer, Miniño and Garnett (2023), NCHS Data Brief 474, opioid co-involvement in deaths involving cocaine and psychostimulants, 2011–2021, cited here for the rise in stimulant deaths without opioids; not read

Analysis of the same national death records, all ages, 1999–2023: 34,855 methamphetamine-involved deaths in 2023, the same number this report gives for deaths coded as involving psychostimulants (T43.6), which suggests that the later analysis used that code (editors' inference)
This report: methamphetamine named in 31.2% of SUDORS overdose deaths, January 2021–June 2024, 68.8% of them with opioids

replication.where_it_stands: The NVSS part re-analyses the same national death records as Han et al. (2021) and Zhu et al. (2025), so its trend is not independent replication. The SUDORS part draws on a partly separate source (medical examiner, coroner and toxicology reports, naming methamphetamine specifically) and is the first source read for this page that gives the share of methamphetamine-involved overdose deaths with and without opioids, for one pooled period.

funding.funder: No funding statement; a CDC report written by staff of the Division of Overdose Prevention, National Center for Injury Prevention and Control. SUDORS is funded by CDC through the Overdose Data to Action in States programme (Methods › Data Sources, 1st paragraph; author affiliations).

funding.affiliations_note: All eight authors are CDC staff (Division of Overdose Prevention). The agency that runs the surveillance system and funds the state overdose-prevention programmes wrote the report and its recommendations; recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: Methamphetamine-specific, toxicology-based death surveillance with complete and stable jurisdiction coverage, reported year by year rather than pooled, with intervals, the counts with and without opioids for each year, and a denominator of people who use methamphetamine from surveys of the same years.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A large surveillance analysis whose definitions are stated in full. Its limits concern coverage (four states partly or not covered in SUDORS, four absent from the circumstance analyses), variable toxicology and certification, which the authors expect to undercount stimulant deaths, the non-specific T43.6 code in the trend analysis, and the absence of intervals. In the editors' reading, the undercount may fall more on deaths without opioids, since deaths certified as cardiovascular are the ones missed and decedents without opioids were older and more often had cardiovascular disease, so the share with opioids may be somewhat overstated. It may be cited for the share of methamphetamine-involved overdose deaths with and without opioids in January 2021 to June 2024, for decedents' recorded characteristics, and for the age-adjusted rates of deaths coded T43.6 in 2018 and 2023; not for rates among people who use methamphetamine, not for causes of death, and not as independent confirmation of the national death-record trend.

key_findings.finding: Data: SUDORS (49 states and DC; unintentional and undetermined-intent overdose deaths, January 2021–June 2024; a drug counted as involved when the medical examiner or coroner listed it as a cause of death on the death certificate, in their report or in the postmortem toxicology report) and NVSS (all US death certificates, 2018–2023; underlying cause X40–X44 or Y10–Y14 with multiple-cause codes T40.5 for cocaine, T43.6 for psychostimulants with abuse potential and T40.0–T40.4 and T40.6 for opioids; age-adjusted to the 2000 US standard population).

key_findings.finding: SUDORS coverage: a jurisdiction had to report at least 75% of its overdose deaths in at least one 6-month period; all but four reported for the whole period, California and Wisconsin were included for part of it, Texas and Wyoming only for January–June 2024, and North Dakota not at all. Circumstance analyses: 46 states and DC (226,698 deaths), with circumstance data for 93.1% of deaths in those jurisdictions.

key_findings.finding: Of 309,274 overdose deaths, 59.0% involved any stimulant, 31.2% methamphetamine and 30.0% cocaine; 3.8% both methamphetamine and cocaine; prescription stimulants 1.6%, synthetic cathinones 0.7%, MDMA or MDA 0.4%. 73.0% of stimulant-involved deaths co-involved opioids, including 79.1% of cocaine-involved and 68.8% of methamphetamine-involved deaths; 14.5% of deaths involved only stimulants.
key_findings.locator: Results › SUDORS: Stimulant-Involved Overdose Deaths During January 2021–June 2024, 1st paragraph; Figure 1 (image; values not extracted beyond the text)

For any stimulant, 66.5% of decedents without opioids and 44.2% of those with opioids were 45 or older. About 72% of methamphetamine-involved decedents were male.

key_findings.finding: Methamphetamine-involved deaths with circumstance data (67,831), without vs with opioids: known history of cardiovascular disease (hypertension excluded) 39.3% vs 19.8%; seen in an emergency department for the fatal overdose 30.3% vs 17.4%; evidence of opioid use history 12.2% vs 41.1%; ever treated for mental health or substance use disorders 14.2% vs 24.0%; homelessness or housing instability 15.7% vs 18.9%. Psychostimulants among non-Hispanic American Indian or Alaska Native people 11.0 and 32.9, among non-Hispanic Native Hawaiian or Pacific Islander people 7.4 and 16.3; cocaine among non-Hispanic Black people 9.1 and 24.3. Across groups, the largest increases were in deaths co-involving stimulants and opioids (no figures in the text).

Limitations named by the authors: stimulant overdose deaths certified with cardiovascular causes may lack overdose codes and be missed; postmortem toxicology varies and emerging stimulants are not tested routinely (both lead to underestimation); circumstance information depends on investigative reports; race and ethnicity may be misclassified; some large states are excluded from the circumstance analyses.

The discussion infers intentional co-use of separate stimulant and opioid products from drug-checking studies that rarely found opioids in stimulant samples, and compares the 38.7% cardiovascular history of decedents with stimulants and no opioids with about 10% of all US adults, possibly representing long-term stimulant use.
