design_detail: Within-person analysis of longitudinal panel data from the Methamphetamine Treatment Evaluation Study (MATES) cohort, Sydney and Brisbane, Australia (recruited 2006–2007, followed to 2010). 469 people with DSM-IV methamphetamine dependence at entry contributed up to four non-contiguous one-month windows: the month before the baseline interview and the months before the interviews at 3 months, 1 year and 3 years. Logistic models (Stata xtlogit) relate any methamphetamine use in a month to self-reported crime in the same month (any crime, drug dealing, property crime, fraud and violent crime), unadjusted, adjusted for time-varying age, income, unemployment and unstable housing (Model 1), and further adjusted for other substance use (Model 2); a dose analysis compares 1–15 and 16 or more days of use with none. The methods describe random-effects models with a random intercept and say that the fixed-effects option was used for the within-person effect (p. 3). The authors describe having applied the same within-person approach to psychotic symptoms and hostility (McKetin et al., 2013b and 2014, p. 2); the 2013 paper used the MATES cohort (card sc_mcketin_2013). The PDF (pp. 1–6) was read in full; Table 1 and Fig. 1 were checked on rendered pages. The online supplement (Table S1, crime items; Table S2, full models; Table S3, adjusted dose models) is not in the PDF and was not read.
can_establish: Within the same people with methamphetamine dependence, how much more often each type of self-reported crime occurred in months with methamphetamine use than in months without, with a comparison designed to remove stable personal characteristics (sex, heritable traits, personality, childhood adversity; fully so with the fixed-effects estimator the methods name, see reporting issues) and with age, income, employment, housing and other drug use adjusted for as they changed.
cannot_establish: Which came first within a month (use and crime are reported for the same four weeks, and the authors say the direction could be disputed); that methamphetamine use causes crime rather than travelling with changes over time that were not measured (entering treatment, treatment received, imprisonment, involvement in drug markets, mental state); anything about people who use methamphetamine without dependence (the authors say the findings should not be generalized to recreational use); or offending recorded by police or courts (self-report only).

sample.recruitment: MATES: 400 people entering community-based drug treatment for methamphetamine use in Sydney and Brisbane, and 101 people in Sydney who were not in treatment, recruited through needle and syringe programmes and outreach services, who screened positive for methamphetamine dependence. Recruited in 2006 and 2007; follow-up interviews from 2006 to 2010, face-to-face or by phone; volunteers reimbursed up to AUD40 per interview (p. 2). The cohort's procedures are described in an earlier paper (McKetin et al., 2012), not read.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: MATES: age 16 or over, comprehension of English, willingness to be followed up, and no methamphetamine treatment, other inpatient drug treatment or imprisonment in the month before entry, so that the baseline month reflected use outside treatment or prison (p. 2). This analysis: DSM-IV past-year methamphetamine dependence at entry on the Composite International Diagnostic Interview; 17 excluded for not meeting dependence criteria at recruitment, 14 for no methamphetamine use in any analysed month and 1 for declining the crime questions, leaving 469 aged 16–57 (p. 2).
sample.demographics: At baseline: mean age 31.6 years (SD 8.1); 74% male, 73% single, 82% unemployed; 87% born in Australia and 96% preferring English; median 10 years of schooling (range 6–12), 41% with a technical or trade qualification and 6% with a university degree; mean 13.3 years (SD 7.9) of methamphetamine use; 74% usually injected, 18% smoked and 7% used other routes; 84% had used crystalline methamphetamine in the month before entry, and 58% named it as their main form (base 31%, powder 8%) (p. 3).
sample.attrition: All 469 were interviewed at baseline; 379 (81%) at 3 months, 357 (76%) at 12 months and 315 (67%) at 3 years. Seven crime responses were missing, giving 1,518 person-months for property crime, fraud and violent crime, 1,514 for dealing and 1,513 for any crime (p. 2). How many people had at least one follow-up interview, and whether people lost to follow-up differed from those retained in use or crime, is not reported.
sample.selection_effects: A sample of people with methamphetamine dependence, most entering treatment and most injecting; the authors state the findings should not be generalized to people who use recreationally (p. 5). For most participants the baseline month is the month before entering treatment, which may be a period of heavier use and more crises than later months (editors' reasoning, not examined in the paper). A fixed-effects within-person estimate, the estimator the methods name, draws only on people whose crime status and use changed across their observed months: for violent crime at most the 22% who ever reported it (p. 3), about 103 people (editors' calculation), and the number actually contributing to each estimate is not reported. Losses at follow-up (a third by 3 years) may be related to both use and crime, for example through imprisonment (editors' reasoning).

exposure.measurement: Self-reported days of methamphetamine use in the past four weeks on the Opiate Treatment Index (OTI) at each interview, coded for the main models as any use in the month against none; route and main form also recorded (pp. 2–3). Self-reported abstinence was checked against hair toxicology in a subsample of the MATES cohort (n = 83; 6% false reports of abstinence), as reported in the cohort paper (McKetin et al., 2012) (p. 2). No biological verification in this analysis.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Frequency only. Dose analysis: 1–15 days and 16 or more days of use in the month against none (p. 3). Methamphetamine was used in 61% of observed months, and 10% of participants used at every follow-up interview; in months of use the median was 10 days (interquartile range 3–20), and injecting was the main route in 80% of them (smoking 14%, snorting or swallowing 6%) (p. 3). Mean duration of use before entry 13.3 years. Amount and purity were not measured.
exposure.polysubstance: Days of use of heroin, cocaine, ecstasy, hallucinogens, cannabis, alcohol and tobacco in the past four weeks were recorded (p. 3). In observed months: tobacco 90% (median 28 days), cannabis 58% (median 21 days), alcohol 62% (median 7 days), heroin 19% (median 4 days), cocaine 15% (median 2 days), ecstasy 16% (median 3 days), hallucinogens 3%; other drug use was more likely in months of methamphetamine use (rs 0.08–0.40, p < 0.01) (p. 3). Model 2 adjusts for alcohol and cannabis (0, 1–15, 16 or more days) and for any past-month cocaine, heroin and ecstasy use; hallucinogens (too few months) and tobacco are not among the covariates (p. 3). Adding other substance use to the adjustment reduced the odds ratios by a third to nearly two-thirds (Model 1 to Model 2, Table 1; editors' calculation).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable: months without methamphetamine use are one of the two exposure states, by self-report (6% false reports of abstinence in the hair-tested subsample of the cohort).

comparison.controls: Each participant's own months without methamphetamine use (593 person-months) against months with use (927); no external comparison group.
comparison.matching: Not applicable: the within-person comparison is designed to remove stable characteristics (fully so with the fixed-effects estimator the methods name; the abstract names a random-intercept model, see reporting issues).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Time-invariant premorbid factors (childhood neglect and trauma, personality, sex, heritable traits) are what the within-person design is meant to remove (fully so with the fixed-effects estimator the methods name; see reporting issues), which is the study's central strength, as the authors say (pp. 2, 4). Not measured or not adjusted for: changes over time such as entering treatment, treatment received during follow-up, arrest or imprisonment, involvement in drug markets and with peers involved in crime, mental state (psychotic symptoms or hostility, measured in the same cohort in other papers), and tobacco use. Age is adjusted for, which in a within-person model also absorbs a linear trend over the follow-up, but not a change specific to the baseline month (editors' reasoning).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Months without methamphetamine often involved other drugs (tobacco, cannabis, alcohol, and less often heroin, cocaine and ecstasy); Model 2 adjusts for these, except tobacco and hallucinogens, with coarse categories (any use for heroin, cocaine and ecstasy).

outcomes.instruments: OTI Crime Scale, past month: self-reported frequency (none, less than weekly, weekly, more than weekly but less than daily, daily) of property crime (break and enter, robbery without violence, shoplifting, stealing a prescription pad or a car, receiving stolen goods), dealing (selling drugs to someone), fraud (forging cheques or prescriptions, social security fraud such as cash-in-hand work, using another person's credit card) and crimes involving violence (such as violence in a robbery or assault) (p. 2). The item wording is in Table S1 of the supplement, not read.
outcomes.validity_norms: Self-report, not convictions. The authors cite the OTI development study for agreement with other self-report measures, good test-retest reliability and agreement of self-reported convictions with records (p. 5); no validation in this cohort is reported.
outcomes.operationalization: Each crime type coded as any against none in the past month; any crime means any of the four types (p. 3). Violent crime does not separate instrumental violence (for example robbery) from expressive violence (for example domestic assault), as the authors note (p. 4).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None: five outcomes, each in three models, plus a dose analysis, all at two-sided p < 0.05 (p. 3).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable: use and crime were self-reported in the same structured interview.

analysis.effect_sizes: Within-person odds ratios, months with use against months without (Table 1, p. 3). Any crime: unadjusted 13.2 (95% CI 8.5–20.6); Model 1 10.5 (6.6–16.7); Model 2 4.7 (2.8–8.0). Dealing: 18.2 (10.2–32.5), 15.8 (8.6–29.1), 5.9 (3.0–11.9). Fraud: 3.4 (2.0–5.8), 2.8 (1.6–5.0), 1.7 (0.8–3.3), p = 0.158. Property crime: 10.6 (6.3–18.0), 8.4 (4.8–14.5), 5.5 (2.8–10.8). Violent crime: 8.2 (4.2–15.9), 5.3 (2.6–10.7), 3.4 (1.5–8.0), p = 0.005. All other estimates p < 0.001. Shares of months with each crime, without against with use: any crime 104 of 593 (17%) against 515 of 927 (56%); dealing 6% against 36%; fraud 5% against 13%; property crime 7% against 30%; violent crime 19 (3%) against 113 (12%). Dose: unadjusted percentages by 0, 1–15 and 16 or more days of use in Fig. 1 (p. 4), with no values printed; editors' reading of the bars (pixel measurement on the rendered page): violent crime about 3%, 9% and 19% of months, any crime about 18%, 48% and 71%, dealing about 6%, 27% and 53%, property crime about 7%, 26% and 39%, fraud about 5%, 12% and 16%; the adjusted dose estimates are in Table S3 of the supplement, not read. Editors' calculation from Table 1: the raw shares for any crime are in a ratio of 3.2 (55.6% against 17.5%) and the raw odds ratio is 5.9, against a within-person odds ratio of 13.2; for violent crime, 3.8 and 4.2 against 8.2. Odds ratios comparing months within the same person are on a different scale from population-averaged or between-person odds ratios and are usually further from 1, so they should not be compared directly with those of other studies.
analysis.covariates: Model 1: time-varying age, net income in the past fortnight, unemployment and unstable accommodation. Model 2: Model 1 plus alcohol and cannabis (0, 1–15, 16 or more days) and any past-month cocaine, heroin and ecstasy use (Table 1 notes; p. 3). No covariate for interview wave, treatment or imprisonment.
analysis.preregistration_detail: The authors state that the analysis was exploratory and therefore not pre-registered (p. 3).
analysis.selective_reporting: The full models (Table S2), the adjusted dose models (Table S3) and the crime items (Table S1) are only in the supplement, which was not available. The number of participants contributing to each within-person estimate is not given, and which estimator produced the printed odds ratios is described ambiguously (random intercept or fixed effects; see reporting issues).
analysis.power: Not addressed formally. The authors note that few participants committed crime in months without use, which reduced robustness and widened the confidence limits, and that the dose findings rest on small numbers (p. 5). Violent crime was reported in 19 of the 593 months without use.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 469 people with methamphetamine dependence, followed over up to four one-month windows from 2006 to 2010, every type of self-reported crime was more common in months with methamphetamine use than in the same people's months without. After adjustment for age, income, employment, housing and other substance use, the odds ratios were 4.7 for any crime, 5.9 for dealing, 5.5 for property crime and 3.4 (1.5–8.0) for violent crime; fraud was no longer clearly associated (1.7, 0.8–3.3). Adding other substance use to the adjustment (Model 1 to Model 2) reduced the odds ratios by a third to nearly two-thirds (any crime 10.5 to 4.7, dealing 15.8 to 5.9, fraud 2.8 to 1.7, property crime 8.4 to 5.5, violent crime 5.3 to 3.4; editors' calculation: falls of 35% to 63%). Unadjusted percentages rose with days of use.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that use was associated with significant increases in crime beyond premorbid risk and that crime is a likely social consequence of use (p. 1). The discussion calls the data robust evidence of a large increase beyond any pre-existing risk, says the time-varying controls show that the increase could not be accounted for by other substance use or socio-economic disadvantage, and says that violent crime is not only a consequence of pre-existing risk (p. 4); the conclusion calls acquisitive and violent crime likely significant social consequences of use in people dependent on the drug (p. 5). Gaps: (1) consequence is a causal reading of a same-month association; the authors themselves say the direction could be disputed, and their argument that crime leading to more use is unlikely, given the participants' long drug histories (p. 5), is not tested by the design; (2) the within-person design is meant to remove stable confounders (fully so with the fixed-effects estimator the methods name), not changes over time: entering treatment, treatment received, imprisonment, drug-market involvement and mental state are not adjusted for, and other drugs are measured coarsely, so could not be accounted for says more than adjustment for the measured covariates shows; (3) five times more likely (p. 4) and 13.2 times more likely (p. 3) read odds ratios as risk ratios; for any crime the raw shares, 56% against 17.5%, are in a ratio of 3.2 (editors' calculation); (4) effects were dose related (abstract) rests in the article on unadjusted percentages pooled across people (Fig. 1), with the adjusted analysis only in the supplement; (5) use and crime are self-reported in the same interview; (6) the authors' own statement that the findings apply to people dependent on methamphetamine, most of whom injected, is in the limitations but not in the abstract's conclusion.

timeline.event: Within-person analysis of psychotic symptoms in the same MATES cohort, with the same four one-month windows

Within-person analysis of hostility in the MATES cohort (McKetin et al., 2014, Addiction 109, 798–806), cited on p. 2 as an earlier application of the same approach; its title, in the reference list (p. 6), asks whether methamphetamine use increases violent behaviour; not yet read
Meta-analysis by an overlapping author group, whose pooled violence estimates include the 2014 MATES hostility analysis; pooled adjusted odds ratio for violence with any amphetamine use 1.4 (0.8–2.4)
General-population birth cohort (Christchurch) sharing three authors with this study (McKetin, Boden, Foulds): adjusted odds of violence perpetration 1.60 (1.01–2.54) in periods of use
This study: within-person associations between months of methamphetamine use and self-reported crime, including violent crime (adjusted odds ratio 3.4, 1.5–8.0)

replication.where_it_stands: The within-person association between months of use and self-reported violent crime agrees in direction with the general-population birth cohort and with the within-person hostility analysis of the same cohort, but all three come from overlapping author groups and two share the MATES sample, so their agreement is not independent replication. No independent within-person study of acquisitive crime or dealing has been read for the encyclopedia; the status records the project's reading, not a search of the literature.

funding.funder: National Health and Medical Research Council (Project Grant No. 350974) and the Australian Government Department of Health and Ageing (p. 5). The role of funding source statement reads: Nothing declared (p. 5).
funding.declared_conflicts: MF and LD have received investigator-initiated untied educational grants for studies of opioid medications in Australia from Indivior, Mundipharma and Seqirus; RA has received untied educational grants from Reckitt Benckiser/Indivior and Mundipharma for studies of opioid substitution and agonist treatments in Australia; the other authors report no financial relationships with commercial interests (p. 5).
funding.affiliations_note: National Drug and Alcohol Research Centre, University of New South Wales; Christchurch Health and Development Study and Department of Psychological Medicine, University of Otago; University of Queensland; University of Adelaide; University of Newcastle (p. 1). The first author was the lead investigator on the research grant (p. 5). Three authors (McKetin, Boden, Foulds) are authors of the Christchurch birth-cohort paper, and four (McKetin, Foulds, Farrell, Degenhardt) of the 2019 meta-analysis cited in the same claim (reference list, p. 6). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: Repeated short-interval measurement (weekly diaries or momentary assessment) of methamphetamine use, intoxication, other drug use and violent and acquisitive offending in people who use methamphetamine, with biological verification of use, records-based offending outcomes, and measurement of treatment, imprisonment, income, drug spending and drug-market involvement, analysed within person, so that use can be placed before or after each offence; a comparison of people entering treatment with people not in treatment would also show how much of the association reflects the period around entering treatment.

domains.note: The within-person design is meant to remove all stable confounding, the main threat in this literature (fully so with the fixed-effects estimator the methods name; see reporting issues), and time-varying age, income, unemployment, housing and other substance use are adjusted for. Remaining concerns: changes over time that were not measured, above all the period around entering treatment (for most participants the baseline month is the month before treatment entry, when both use and crime may peak; editors' reasoning), drug-market involvement and mental state; other drugs measured coarsely; and reverse causation within the month (crime, especially dealing, can bring money or access to drugs), which the authors acknowledge (p. 5).

Self-reported days of use in the past four weeks, without biological verification in this analysis; hair testing in a subsample of the cohort found 6% false reports of abstinence. Frequency, not amount, is measured.

A sample of people with methamphetamine dependence, most entering treatment; 32 of 501 excluded (17 not dependent, 14 without use in any analysed month, 1 declining crime questions). Only people whose crime status changed contribute to a fixed-effects within-person estimate, and their number is not reported.

Most participants entered treatment at baseline; treatment received, arrest and imprisonment during follow-up are not reported or adjusted for, although they plausibly change both use and the opportunity for crime.
81%, 76% and 67% retained at 3 months, 1 year and 3 years; retained and lost participants are not compared, and missed interviews may be related to heavy use or imprisonment.

Self-reported crime in the past month, uncorroborated, collected in the same interview as self-reported use, face-to-face or by phone; willingness to disclose may vary between interviews in the same way for use and for crime, which would inflate a within-person association. The OTI crime scale was validated elsewhere.
An exploratory analysis without a protocol; the full and the adjusted dose models are only in the supplement; the estimator is described ambiguously; five outcomes in three models each.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No single domain is high, but concerns in all seven domains, several acting in the same direction (same-interview self-report, unmeasured changes around treatment entry and imprisonment, reverse causation within the month), together substantially lower confidence in the size of the adjusted associations. The design is nonetheless the strongest applied to this question in the encyclopedia's reading: comparing each person with themselves is designed to remove the premorbid differences that make cross-sectional comparisons of crime uninterpretable (fully so with the fixed-effects estimator the methods name). The study may be cited for within-person adjusted associations between months of methamphetamine use and self-reported crime, including violent crime, in people with methamphetamine dependence; not for a causal effect, not for people who use without dependence, and not for offending recorded by police or courts.

key_findings.finding: MATES cohort: 400 people entering community-based treatment for methamphetamine use in Sydney and Brisbane and 101 people in Sydney not in treatment (recruited through needle and syringe programmes and outreach) who screened positive for dependence; recruited in 2006–2007 and interviewed at baseline, 3 months, 1 year and 3 years (to 2010), face-to-face or by phone. Entry required age 16 or over, English, willingness to be followed up and no methamphetamine treatment, other inpatient drug treatment or prison in the month before entry.
key_findings.locator: Methods › 2.1. Participants and procedure, 1st paragraph (begins in the left column)

key_findings.finding: Exclusions: 17 not meeting DSM-IV methamphetamine dependence at recruitment, 14 with no methamphetamine use in any analysed month and 1 declining the crime questions, leaving 469 aged 16–57; 379 (81%) were interviewed at 3 months, 357 (76%) at 12 months and 315 (67%) at 3 years; with seven missing crime responses, 1,518 person-months were analysed for property crime, fraud and violent crime, 1,514 for dealing and 1,513 for any crime.
key_findings.note: The 1st paragraph of 2.1 says that 469 participants met DSM-IV criteria; by the exclusions listed here, 484 met them and 469 were analysed (editors' arithmetic, 501 − 17).

key_findings.finding: Measures for the past month at each interview: crime on the OTI crime scale (self-reported frequency of property crime, dealing, fraud and crimes involving violence, such as violence in a robbery or assault), coded any against none; days of methamphetamine use in the past four weeks (OTI), with route and main form; days of use of heroin, cocaine, ecstasy, hallucinogens, cannabis, alcohol and tobacco; age, net income in the past fortnight, unemployment and unstable housing. In a hair-tested subsample of the cohort (n = 83), 6% of reports of abstinence were false.
key_findings.locator: Methods › 2.1.1.1. Crime and 2.1.1.2. Substance use (p. 2, continuing on p. 3); 2.1.1.3. Age and socio-economic disadvantage (p. 3)

key_findings.finding: The analysis was exploratory and not pre-registered: logistic models (Stata xtlogit) with a random intercept per person, the fixed-effects option being used for the within-person effect; outcome any crime of each type in the past month; predictor any methamphetamine use in the past month; dose analysis 1–15 and 16 or more days against none; time-varying covariates alcohol and cannabis (0, 1–15, 16 or more days), any cocaine, heroin and ecstasy use, income, unemployment and unstable housing, and age (named in Table 1, notes a and b, and in the abstract; the list in 2.1.2 omits it); hallucinogen use too rare to include; two-sided p < 0.05.
key_findings.locator: Methods › 2.1.2. Design and statistical analysis; Table 1, notes a and b

key_findings.finding: At baseline: mean age 31.6 (SD 8.1); 74% male, 73% single, 82% unemployed, 87% born in Australia; median 10 years of schooling (range 6–12); mean 13.3 years (SD 7.9) of methamphetamine use; 74% usually injected (18% smoked, 7% other routes); 84% had used crystalline methamphetamine in the month before entry and 58% named it as their main form (base 31%, powder 8%).
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.1. Characteristics of the sample, 1st paragraph (begins in the left column)

key_findings.finding: Methamphetamine was used in 61% of observed months, and 10% of participants used at every follow-up interview; in months of use the median was 10 days (IQR 3–20) and injecting was the main route in 80% (smoking 14%, snorting or swallowing 6%). Other drugs in observed months: tobacco 90%, cannabis 58%, alcohol 62%, heroin 19%, cocaine 15%, ecstasy 16%, hallucinogens 3%; other drug use was more likely in months of methamphetamine use (rs 0.08–0.40, p < 0.01). Median net income AUD500 a fortnight (IQR 420–800); unemployed in 68% and without stable housing in 15% of months.
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.1. Characteristics of the sample, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Three-quarters of participants reported crime in at least one observed month (dealing 52%, property crime 45%, fraud 25%, violent crime 22%); 41% of all months involved crime (dealing 24%, property crime 21%, fraud 10%, violent crime 9%).
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.1. Characteristics of the sample, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Crime in months without against months with methamphetamine use: any crime 104 of 593 (17%) against 515 of 927 (56%); dealing 33 (6%) against 330 (36%); fraud 32 (5%) against 121 (13%); property crime 43 (7%) against 279 (30%); violent crime 19 (3%) against 113 (12%).
key_findings.locator: Table 1, columns for months without and with methamphetamine use
key_findings.note: 104 of 593 is 17.5% (editors' calculation), printed as 17%; the denominators (593 and 927, total 1,520) are all interview-months, not the 1,513–1,518 analysed months.

key_findings.finding: Within-person odds ratios, months with use against months without: any crime 13.2 (95% CI 8.5–20.6) unadjusted, 10.5 (6.6–16.7) in Model 1 (age, income, unemployment, unstable accommodation) and 4.7 (2.8–8.0) in Model 2 (plus other substance use); dealing 18.2 (10.2–32.5), 15.8 (8.6–29.1) and 5.9 (3.0–11.9); fraud 3.4 (2.0–5.8), 2.8 (1.6–5.0) and 1.7 (0.8–3.3), p = 0.158; property crime 10.6 (6.3–18.0), 8.4 (4.8–14.5) and 5.5 (2.8–10.8); violent crime 8.2 (4.2–15.9), 5.3 (2.6–10.7) and 3.4 (1.5–8.0), p = 0.005; all others p < 0.001.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, odds-ratio columns; Results › 3.2. Changes in crime during periods of methamphetamine use, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
key_findings.note: Each printed odds ratio sits at the geometric middle of its interval (editors' check), so no transcription errors are apparent. The Model 1 violent-crime value is printed with a stray full stop (5.3.).

key_findings.finding: In the adjusted models, heroin use was also related to dealing, property crime and fraud, and cannabis use to dealing and fraud; heavier alcohol use (16 or more days) had a non-significant association with violent crime; none of the socio-economic indicators was significantly associated with crime.
key_findings.note: These estimates are in Table S2 of the supplement, which was not read.

key_findings.finding: Crime was more common in months with 16 or more days of use than in months with fewer (Fig. 1: unadjusted percentages of months with each crime by 0, 1–15 and 16 or more days of use); the authors report that the gradient remained after adjustment for socio-economic disadvantage and other substance use (Table S3).
key_findings.note: Fig. 1 prints no values. Editors' reading of the bars (pixel measurement on the rendered page): violent crime about 3%, 9% and 19% of months; any crime about 18%, 48% and 71%; dealing about 6%, 27% and 53%; property crime about 7%, 26% and 39%; fraud about 5%, 12% and 16%. These percentages pool months across people and are not within-person estimates; Table S3 was not read.

key_findings.finding: The authors interpret the results as robust evidence of a large increase in crime beyond any pre-existing risk, say that the time-varying controls show the increase could not be accounted for by other substance use or socio-economic disadvantage, and say that violent crime among people who use methamphetamine is not only a consequence of pre-existing risk; they add that they cannot tell whether the violence was instrumental (for example robbery) or expressive (for example domestic assault).

Limitations stated by the authors: crime was self-reported, not convictions; the direction of the same-month relationship could be disputed (they think crime leading to more use unlikely, given long drug histories and dependence at entry, and the association more likely to reflect desisting from crime during abstinence); the findings apply to people dependent on methamphetamine, most of whom injected, and should not be generalized to recreational use; few participants committed crime in months without use, giving wide confidence limits, and small numbers limit the dose findings; unmeasured factors in the same months may have contributed.

The authors state that they previously applied the same within-person approach to hostility and to psychotic symptoms (McKetin et al., 2013b and 2014); the author list includes McKetin, Boden and Foulds, three of the four authors of the Christchurch birth-cohort study of violence (Foulds et al., 2020; its fourth author, Newton-Howes, is not an author of this paper), which the introduction cites.
key_findings.locator: Author list and Introduction, 1st paragraph (p. 1); Introduction, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (p. 2); reference list (p. 6)
key_findings.note: That the 2014 hostility analysis used the MATES cohort is stated by the 2019 meta-analysis (claim anchor, Results › 3.4 Violence, 4th paragraph) and that the 2013 analysis did by its own card (sc_mcketin_2013), not by this paper.

reporting_issues.issue: The estimator is described ambiguously: the abstract says the within-person odds ratios came from a random-intercept logistic model (p. 1), and the methods describe random-effects models with a random intercept but say the fixed-effects option was used for the within-person effect (p. 3). The number of participants contributing to each estimate is not reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: If a fixed-effects (conditional) logistic model was used, only people whose crime status changed contribute, for violent crime at most the 22% who ever reported it (about 103 people, editors' calculation), so the effective sample is far smaller than 469; if a random-intercept model without separating within- from between-person variation was used, the estimates are not purely within-person. Either way the printed odds ratios cannot be fully interpreted from the article.

reporting_issues.issue: The discussion says participants were five times more likely to report crime in months of use (p. 4), and the results that crime was 13.2 times more likely (Results › 3.2, 1st paragraph, p. 3); the results also say that, after adjustment, participants were five to six times more likely to report property crime and dealing and 3.4 times more likely to report violent crime (Results › 3.2, 2nd paragraph, p. 3). These are odds ratios read as risk ratios.
reporting_issues.consequence: For common outcomes the reading overstates the relative risk: for any crime the raw shares (55.6% against 17.5% of months) are in a ratio of 3.2 (editors' calculation). For violent crime, which is rarer (3% of months without use), odds ratio and risk ratio are closer (raw risk ratio 3.8, raw odds ratio 4.2; editors' calculation).

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says effects were dose related (p. 1), but the article shows the gradient only as unadjusted percentages pooled across people and months, without values or intervals (Fig. 1, p. 4); the adjusted dose analysis is only in Table S3 of the supplement.
reporting_issues.consequence: The dose-response cannot be checked or cited as an adjusted within-person result from the article itself.

reporting_issues.issue: The results text says crime was more likely in months with 16 or more days of use than for 0–15 days (p. 3), while the methods and Fig. 1 compare 1–15 and 16 or more days with no use (pp. 3–4).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the comparison actually reported is unclear from the text, and the figure shows three categories.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 percentages are computed on all 1,520 interview-months (593 without and 927 with use), not on the 1,513–1,518 months analysed (p. 2); 104 of 593 (17.5%) is printed as 17%, while Fig. 1 shows about 18% (editors' reading).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; percentages may differ from those of the analysed months by a fraction of a percentage point.

reporting_issues.issue: The first paragraph of the methods says that 469 participants met DSM-IV criteria for methamphetamine dependence, but the exclusions in the second paragraph (17 not dependent, 14 without use in any analysed month, 1 declining crime questions) show that 484 met them and 469 were analysed.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the analysed sample is 469.

reporting_issues.issue: The role of funding source statement reads Nothing declared (p. 5), while the funding section names the National Health and Medical Research Council and the Australian Government Department of Health and Ageing (p. 5).
reporting_issues.consequence: Probably means that the funders had no role; the funding itself is as given in the funding section.

reporting_issues.issue: Fig. 1's caption describes the bars as the percentage of participants reporting crime in the past month, but the bars for months without use reproduce Table 1's shares of months: by the editors' measurement against the gridlines (300 dpi) they read about 18, 6, 5, 7 and 3% for any crime, dealing, fraud, property crime and violent crime, which are the shares of the 593 months without use in Table 1 (17.5, 5.6, 5.4, 7.3 and 3.2%; printed 17, 6, 5, 7 and 3).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor: the bars are shares of person-months pooled across people, as the card and the claims read them, not shares of people; the caption's wording should not be cited for the share of people.

design_detail: Fifteen-day residential laboratory study in 7 healthy volunteers with previous stimulant experience, living in a continuously observed facility in two groups (one of four, one of three). Oral methamphetamine was given twice daily (1000 and 1800 h) on two 3-day blocks: days 4-6 and days 10-12, at 5 mg twice daily in one block and 10 mg twice daily in the other (total daily doses of 10 and 20 mg); placebo capsules were given at both times on all other days, with days 1-3 as the placebo baseline. Four participants received the smaller dose block first and three the larger. Participants were not told that methamphetamine would be given. Measures taken through each day: a 45-minute performance battery nine times, a 50-item visual analogue mood scale eleven times, a six-item drug-effects questionnaire twice (one hour after each dose), continuous bar-code recording of all food and drink, and Nightcap sleep monitors with a morning sleep questionnaire each night.
can_establish: Whether the subjective, food-intake and sleep effects of a low oral dose of methamphetamine change across three consecutive days of twice-daily dosing, and whether effects persist on the placebo days that follow, within the same people and against their own placebo baseline days.
cannot_establish: What happens at the doses, routes and binge patterns of non-medical use (only oral 5 and 10 mg twice daily were given, for three days); effects in people who use methamphetamine regularly or who are dependent (this sample reported minimal current stimulant use); and anything about plasma concentrations, which were not measured.

sample.recruitment: Healthy research volunteers at a residential laboratory of the New York State Psychiatric Institute and Columbia University; the recruitment route is not described (p. 398).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Healthy volunteers aged 23-42 who passed medical and psychological screening and were within normal weight ranges by life-insurance height and weight tables; all reported previous experience with stimulants. No further inclusion or exclusion criteria are listed (p. 398).
sample.demographics: Seven completers (four women, three men), mean age 28.9 years (SD 6.4), mean weight 71.9 kg (SD 12.8). Current use at screening: one person used cocaine twice a week, one used cannabis twice a week, five used caffeine (4-21 cups a week), four drank alcohol (2-18 drinks a week) and four smoked 2-20 cigarettes a day, with free access to cigarettes in the laboratory except 2330-0845 h (p. 398).
sample.attrition: One further man began the study and left because of difficulty sleeping after methamphetamine; the analyses are of the seven completers only. Of 105 possible sleep records, 16 (15%) were lost to monitor malfunction or sensor detachment and were replaced by multiple imputation (pp. 398-399).
sample.selection_effects: Healthy volunteers reporting minimal current stimulant use, screened for medical and psychiatric health and willing to live in a laboratory for 15 days; the authors themselves attribute the small number of positive ratings to this population, contrasting it with people who use stimulants heavily. The person whose sleep was most disturbed left the study, so the completers may under-represent sleep disruption.

exposure.measurement: Drug given in the laboratory under supervision in a private vestibule, so exposure is known by administration rather than measured; no plasma or urine concentrations were taken.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: oral methamphetamine hydrochloride (Desoxyn 5 mg tablets repackaged into opaque capsules with lactose filler), two capsules at 1000 h and two at 1800 h. In the 10 mg daily condition one active and one placebo capsule were given at each time; in the 20 mg daily condition two active capsules were given at each time. Each block ran three consecutive days (pp. 398-399).
exposure.polysubstance: Tobacco was freely available except overnight and is not quantified in the analyses; caffeine, alcohol and other drugs were not available during the residential phase. Prior use of cocaine, cannabis, alcohol and caffeine was recorded at screening but not adjusted for (pp. 398-399).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Residential confinement for the whole 15 days, with placebo baseline days 1-3 before the first active block and placebo days between blocks; no biological verification is described. Each participant had received a single 10 mg sample dose as an outpatient before admission, so the first active day was not the first exposure (pp. 398-399).

comparison.controls: The same participants on placebo: the three baseline days (days 1-3) for the active-day comparisons, and the three placebo days after each active block for the residual-effect comparisons; each active or post-drug day was compared with the corresponding baseline day (day 1 with day 1, and so on).
comparison.matching: Within-person; the order of the two dose blocks was varied (four participants had the smaller dose first, three the larger), but allocation is not described as random.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable: every comparison is within person against the same person's placebo baseline days.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable (no separate control group); tobacco use continued in both conditions.

outcomes.instruments: Fifty 100-mm visual analogue scales of mood and physical state, eleven times a day; a six-item drug-effects questionnaire (good, bad and other effects rated 0-4; liking from -4 to +4; desire to take the drug again), twice a day one hour after each dose; a 45-minute performance battery nine times a day (digit-symbol substitution, repeated acquisition, divided attention, rapid information processing, immediate and delayed digit recall); continuous food and drink recording by bar code, verified against the discarded packaging, giving total calories, macronutrients, number of eating occasions, occasion size and the interval between occasions; Nightcap eye- and body-movement monitors giving sleep efficiency, movements, non-REM sleep, REM sleep and total sleep, plus six sleep visual analogue scales and an estimate of hours slept (pp. 398-399).
outcomes.validity_norms: Standard laboratory instruments for this research group; the visual analogue scales have no external norms, and the Nightcap is a movement-based monitor rather than polysomnography.
outcomes.operationalization: Tolerance is operationalized as a significant difference from the matched placebo baseline day on day 1 of dosing that is no longer significant by day 3, not as a tested interaction between dose and day. 'Abuse liability' is inferred from the balance of positive and negative subjective ratings and from debriefing reports.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: A modified Bonferroni rule: only planned comparisons with P below 0.01 were treated as significant. With fifty visual analogue items, six drug-effects items, five sleep measures, six sleep ratings, several food-intake measures and five performance tasks, each tested on three active days and three post-drug days at two doses, the number of comparisons is far larger than the number reported (p. 399).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Participants were told only that they would receive one or more commonly prescribed medications that might feel stimulant-like, sedative-like or like nothing at all, and were debriefed at discharge; capsules were identical. The paper does not state that staff were blind, and blinding integrity was not tested (p. 398).

analysis.effect_sizes: No standardized effect sizes and almost no printed means: the subjective, food-intake and sleep results are given as F values with P values, with the values themselves shown only in Figures 1-3 and Table 1. The quantities that are printed are the reductions in total daily intake, about 1150 kcal at 10 mg a day and about 1450 kcal at 20 mg a day relative to the placebo baseline (p. 401), and an increase of about 65 minutes in the interval between eating occasions on day 1 of the larger dose. All F values have 1 and 48 degrees of freedom.
analysis.covariates: None. Repeated-measures analyses of variance with planned comparisons on area-under-the-curve values (trapezoidal), by condition (placebo baseline, each dose, and the placebo days after each dose) and day (1, 2, 3 within each condition).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or protocol is mentioned; the study was approved by the New York State Psychiatric Institute Institutional Review Board (p. 398).
analysis.selective_reporting: Performance results are dismissed in one sentence as showing no consistent effects and are not shown; the drug-effects questionnaire results are described as 'data not shown'; macronutrient and eating-occasion-size results are partly not shown; time courses and absolute values appear only in figures without printed numbers.
analysis.power: No sample-size calculation and no power statement. Seven participants, with every effect tested within person on area-under-the-curve values across three days.

interpretation_gap.results_show: At 20 mg a day, ratings of 'good drug effect' and 'high' rose above the matched placebo baseline on the first day of dosing and were no longer significantly raised by day 3, while several unpleasant ratings (dizzy, flu-like symptoms, confused, depressed, nauseated, chills, unable to concentrate, bad drug effect) became significant only on day 3; ratings of 'heart pounding' and 'trouble sleeping' were raised on all three days. At the same dose, sleep measures were disrupted on the first night only. Food intake fell by about 1150-1450 kcal a day and stayed down on all three days at both doses. The 10 mg a day condition did not differ from baseline on the positive ratings.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and discussion describe the study as providing clear evidence of tolerance to positive subjective effects and of emerging negative effects, and conclude that the abuse liability of oral methamphetamine is relatively low in this population. The results support a loss of the positive effects across three days at the larger dose, but tolerance is inferred from a significant difference on day 1 that is absent on day 3 rather than from a tested dose-by-day interaction, the number of participants is seven, and the conclusion about abuse liability rests on ratings and debriefing in volunteers reporting minimal current stimulant use, with no self-administration or choice measure. The authors themselves attribute the difference from earlier reports to the population tested.

timeline.event: Thirteen days of daily oral methamphetamine 10 mg (slow-release) in 6 men: tolerance to the heart-rate increase but not to ratings of 'high', with a single daily dose

Three days of twice-daily oral d-amphetamine (10 mg/70 kg) in a residential laboratory from the same group: tolerance to ratings of potency, liking and stimulation by day 3, without a rise in negative ratings (Kelly, Foltin & Fischman, 1991)
Pharmacokinetics before and after 13 days of daily oral methamphetamine: no change that could explain tolerance

Three administrations of oral methamphetamine 10 mg with and without alcohol over two days in a residential laboratory: heart-rate and 'good drug effect' increases diminished by the third administration

replication.where_it_stands: Loss of the positive subjective effects of low oral methamphetamine over days of repeated dosing has now been seen in two residential studies from the same laboratory (this one and Kirkpatrick et al.) and with d-amphetamine in the same setting; the one study with a single daily dose of a slow-release preparation found no such loss on ratings of 'high' but did find it for heart rate. The emergence of unpleasant effects by day 3 rests on this study alone.

funding.funder: Grant DA-03746 from the National Institute on Drug Abuse (p. 403).
funding.declared_conflicts: Not reported: the article carries no conflict-of-interest statement.
funding.affiliations_note: All authors are at the Division on Substance Abuse, New York State Psychiatric Institute and Columbia University; the same laboratory produced the d-amphetamine comparison study that the discussion leans on and the later methamphetamine-alcohol study, so these are not independent replications.

what_would_settle_it: A residential study in people who use methamphetamine regularly, with the drug given at the same time each day for a week or more by a route and dose closer to non-medical use, with plasma concentrations measured, a self-administration or choice procedure beside the ratings, and a pre-specified dose-by-day interaction test rather than day-wise comparisons against baseline.

domains.domain: Randomization process (order of the two dose blocks)
domains.note: Four participants received the smaller dose block first and three the larger, but allocation is not described as random and no sequence generation or concealment is reported.

Three placebo days separated the two active blocks, and each active day was compared with the matching baseline day; residual effects were measured and had disappeared by the second or third placebo day for most measures.

Participants were misled about the drug class and capsules were identical, but staff blinding is not stated and blinding integrity was not assessed; participants reported clear drug effects at the larger dose.
One of eight participants left because of methamphetamine-related insomnia and is not in the analyses, and 16 of 105 sleep records were imputed.

Food intake was recorded objectively and verified against discarded packaging, and sleep was measured by movement monitors; the primary outcome, however, is self-rated mood on scales whose blinding cannot be assumed.

No protocol or pre-specified primary outcome; fifty mood items and several dozen further measures tested on six days at two doses with a P<0.01 rule; performance and drug-effects-questionnaire results are not shown; and several Table 1 entries are marked at thresholds their own F values do not reach (see reporting issues).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A within-person residential design with its own placebo baseline days, continuous observation and objective food and sleep recording is a strong way to study repeated dosing, and the food-intake and sleep findings are measured rather than rated. The overall judgment is driven by the reported-result domain: there is no protocol, the number of comparisons is far larger than the number reported, the performance data are set aside in a sentence, and the significance markings in the main table do not all match the stated thresholds. The source can be cited for the direction and timing of the changes across three days of low oral dosing in healthy volunteers with little current stimulant use, and for the sustained fall in food intake; it cannot be cited for effects at non-medical doses or routes, for people who use methamphetamine regularly, or for precise effect sizes, which are not printed.

key_findings.finding: Ratings of 'good drug effect' and 'high' rose above the matched placebo baseline day only on the first day of the 20 mg-a-day condition (F(1,48)=8.0 and 15.0 respectively) and had returned to baseline levels by day 3, which the authors read as tolerance. Ratings in the 10 mg-a-day condition did not differ from baseline on either item.
key_findings.locator: Results > Subjective effects, 1st paragraph (p. 399, right column, continuing p. 400); Figure 1 (p. 400)
key_findings.note: The printed P values for these two F values are transposed: with 1 and 48 degrees of freedom, F=8.0 corresponds to P=0.007 and F=15.0 to P=0.0003, while the paper prints P<0.0003 for the first and P<0.007 for the second (editors' calculation from the F distribution).

key_findings.finding: Unpleasant ratings moved the other way across the three days. Dizziness (F(1,48)=9.8, P<0.003) and flu-like symptoms (F(1,48)=13.2, P<0.007) rose on the third day but not the first of the 20 mg-a-day condition, and ratings of being unable to concentrate, chills, confused, depressed and nauseated, and 'bad drug effect' on the drug-effects questionnaire (F=17.4), also became significant only on day 3.
key_findings.locator: Results > Subjective effects, 2nd paragraph; Figure 2; Table 1 (p. 400)

key_findings.finding: Two unpleasant effects did not fade: 'heart pounding' and 'trouble sleeping' were raised on all three days of the 20 mg-a-day condition (heart pounding F=16.4, 7.1 and 6.4 on days 1-3; trouble sleeping F=12.2, 13.2 and 8.8), and 'heart pounding' was also raised on day 3 of the 10 mg-a-day condition (F=11.9).

Total daily food intake fell by about 1150 kcal at 10 mg a day and about 1450 kcal at 20 mg a day relative to the placebo baseline, and the reduction was sustained on all three active days at both doses (F(1,48)=19.2, 44.4 and 29.9 on days 1-3 at the smaller dose; 62.7, 43.9 and 39.6 at the larger; all P<0.0001). Both doses also reduced protein, carbohydrate and fat intake, with no selective effect.
key_findings.locator: Results > Food intake, 1st paragraph and the sentence at the top of the right column; Figure 3 (p. 401)

key_findings.finding: The fall in intake came from fewer eating occasions (F=7.0 at the smaller dose day 1; F=12.1 at the larger) and from smaller occasions (F=19.1 and 11.6 on day 2), with the interval between eating occasions about 65 minutes longer on day 1 of the larger dose (F=7.9). Intake was still below baseline on the first placebo day after both doses (F=9.7 and 16.6) and on the third placebo day after the smaller dose (F=11.1).

Sleep was disrupted on the first night of the 20 mg-a-day condition only: total sleep time (F=12.5), total non-REM sleep (F=8.2) and sleep efficiency (F=8.1) fell and movements rose (F=15.4) against the matched baseline night, with matching falls in ratings of sleeping well, satisfaction with sleep, falling asleep easily and estimated hours slept, and a rise in waking often. Most of these effects were present on day 1 but not days 2 or 3, which the authors also read as tolerance, and no rebound was seen on the placebo days that followed.
key_findings.locator: Results > Sleep, whole section (p. 401, right column)

key_findings.finding: Ratings of hunger fell significantly (F=8.2 on day 2 of the smaller dose and 11.2 on day 1 of the larger), and the desire to take the drug again was significantly lower than baseline (F=11.2, day 2 of the smaller dose). Methamphetamine had no consistent effect on any performance task, and those data are not shown.
key_findings.locator: Data analysis, last paragraph (p. 399); Table 1, 'Hungry' and 'Desire to take drug again' rows (p. 400); Results > Food intake / drug-effects questionnaire paragraph (p. 401)

key_findings.finding: Most participants said at debriefing that they did not like the effects of methamphetamine and would not take it again outside the laboratory, attributing their dislike mainly to stomach upset and disturbed sleep; one of the eight people who started the study left because of difficulty sleeping after dosing.
key_findings.locator: Materials and methods > Participants, 1st paragraph (p. 398); Discussion, 1st paragraph (p. 401)

reporting_issues.issue: The P values printed for the two positive subjective ratings are transposed. With 1 and 48 degrees of freedom, F=8.0 gives P=0.007 and F=15.0 gives P=0.0003, but the Results print 'good drug effect' as F(1,48)=8.0, P<0.0003 and 'high' as F(1,48)=15.0, P<0.007 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Neither claim changes: both comparisons are significant under the paper's own P<0.01 rule. A reader quoting the smaller P value for the wrong item would misstate the strength of the test.

reporting_issues.issue: Several Table 1 entries carry significance markers their F values do not support under the stated thresholds. The table defines * as P<0.01 and ** as P<0.005, yet with 1 and 48 degrees of freedom P<0.01 requires F of about 7.19 and P<0.005 about 8.66. Entries marked * with F=6.4 (twice), 6.5, 6.6, 6.7 and 7.1 correspond to P of about 0.015, 0.014, 0.013, 0.013 and 0.010, and the entry marked ** with F=8.6 corresponds to P of about 0.005 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Six of the negative-effect entries do not meet the paper's own modified Bonferroni rule of P<0.01, including 'anxious' on day 1, 'depressed', 'nauseated', 'noises seem loud' on day 2 and 'heart pounding' on days 2 and 3 of the larger dose. Claims should rest on the entries that clear the threshold ('trouble sleeping', 'sweating', 'jittery', 'confused', 'noises seem loud' on day 3, 'bad drug effect') and say that the day-3 picture is built from many uncorrected comparisons.

reporting_issues.issue: Doses are expressed in two ways without a consistent label: the title, abstract and methods give '5, 10 mg BID', while the discussion compares '5 mg BID (total daily dose of 10 mg)' with the higher condition, and the food-intake section writes 'Five and 10 mg methamphetamine significantly reduced total caloric intake'.
reporting_issues.consequence: A reader taking the food-intake sentence at face value would record a daily dose half the size of the one given. Anything citing this study should state the dose as 5 or 10 mg twice daily.

reporting_issues.issue: Every participant received a single 10 mg oral dose of methamphetamine on an outpatient basis before admission, to check for unusual reactions and to familiarize them with the drug; this is reported in the general procedures but not mentioned where tolerance is interpreted.
reporting_issues.consequence: The 'first day' of each dosing block was not each person's first exposure, so the measured decline is a decline from the first in-laboratory day rather than from a drug-naive state.

reporting_issues.issue: Tolerance is read from a pattern of day-wise comparisons against baseline (significant on day 1, not significant on day 3) rather than from a tested interaction between day and condition, and no means or confidence intervals for the day-1 to day-3 change are printed; the values appear only in figures.
reporting_issues.consequence: The size of the decline cannot be read from the paper, and a non-significant day-3 comparison in seven people is weak evidence that the effect has gone. The finding should be reported as a loss of a detectable effect, not as a measured percentage of tolerance.

reporting_issues.issue: The data-analysis section states that there were no consistent effects of methamphetamine on task performance and that those data will not be discussed further; drug-effects-questionnaire values, macronutrient intakes and eating-occasion sizes are also reported as 'data not shown'.
reporting_issues.consequence: A reader cannot judge the performance null result, which is the one outcome this group's earlier d-amphetamine work had found sensitive, and cannot check the questionnaire findings against the visual analogue scales.

reporting_issues.issue: Sixteen of 105 sleep records (15%) were lost to equipment failure or sensor detachment and replaced by multiple imputation, and the person who left the study did so because of methamphetamine-related insomnia.
reporting_issues.consequence: The sleep analyses are of completers with imputed values, and the direction of both departures runs against finding sleep disruption.

verification.source_read: PDF pp. 397-404 (PDFs/Methamphetamine/Comer_2001_RepeatedOralMethamphetamine.pdf); text layer extracted and Table 1 and Figures 1-3 checked against the rendered pages 400-401

design_detail: Open before-and-after pharmacokinetic study in 8 men who had used amphetamines recreationally. An oral challenge dose of deuterated S-(+)-methamphetamine was given on day 1, followed by 13 days of 10 mg a day of a slow-release oral preparation of S-methamphetamine taken each morning in the laboratory, and the same challenge dose again on day 15. Two challenge dose levels were studied in separate rounds about three months apart, 0.125 and 0.250 mg/kg, with six men at each level and four taking part in both. Plasma was sampled to 48 hours, saliva to 24 hours and urine to 72 hours; concentrations of the deuterated challenge drug, the non-deuterated daily drug and their amphetamine metabolites were measured separately by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. A one-compartment model with first-order absorption and a lag time was fitted to each person's plasma curve, and day-15 parameters were subtracted from day-1 parameters within person.
can_establish: Whether the absorption, distribution, clearance, half-life and urinary excretion of a fixed oral dose of methamphetamine change after thirteen days of daily low-dose exposure, within the same men, and how large a change the study could have detected.
cannot_establish: Whether tolerance develops to any effect of methamphetamine: subjective and cardiovascular measures were taken but are reported in the companion paper, not here. It also cannot establish anything about other routes, larger doses or binge patterns, or about women, who were not studied.

sample.recruitment: Paid, informed male volunteers familiar with the recreational use of amphetamines; the recruitment route is not described (p. 857).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Men aged 19-32 in good health by medical and psychiatric history and physical examination, eating a normal diet, not currently using tobacco, prescription or over-the-counter drugs; each contracted to abstain from the recreational use of amphetamines or any other drug for two weeks before the experiment and throughout it, with daily urine screening by EMIT for cannabis, opiates, amphetamines, phencyclidine, cocaine metabolite, barbiturates, methadone, propoxyphene, ethanol, benzodiazepines and methaqualone (p. 857).
sample.demographics: Eight men, weight 73.5 kg (SD 2.9), aged 19-32. No further demographic information is given; race, education and amphetamine-use history are not reported (p. 857).
sample.attrition: No dropouts are reported, but several pharmacokinetic parameters are based on fewer than six people: the amount excreted in urine and the urinary rate constant rest on 3 or 4 of the 6 in each low-dose condition, because complete urine collection was not achieved for everyone (Table 1, p. 858).
sample.selection_effects: Healthy men, non-smokers, with recreational amphetamine experience but excluded if currently using any drug; a sample chosen for a clean pharmacokinetic measurement rather than for resembling people who use methamphetamine regularly.

exposure.measurement: Drug given in the laboratory and measured directly: splitless gas chromatography with positive chemical-ionization mass spectrometry and selected-ion monitoring quantified deuterated and non-deuterated methamphetamine and amphetamine separately, using more highly deuterated internal standards; replicate analyses over 1-25 ng/mL varied by 1-7% for methamphetamine (pp. 857-858).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: a single oral challenge capsule of deuterated S-(+)-methamphetamine hydrochloride at 0.125 or 0.250 mg/kg, swallowed with 50 mL of water, on day 1 and again on day 15; between them, 10 mg a day of a slow-release oral preparation (Desoxyn Gradumet) each morning for 13 days (p. 857).
exposure.polysubstance: Participants were not currently using tobacco, prescription or over-the-counter drugs and contracted to abstain from all other drugs; daily urine screening showed no compliance problems (pp. 857-858).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Two weeks' abstinence before the study and throughout, with daily urine screening. The day-15 challenge was given on top of residual drug from the daily dosing: non-deuterated methamphetamine averaged 6.08 ng/mL (SEM 0.94) and amphetamine 2.3 ng/mL (SEM 0.3) at the start of day 15 (pp. 857-858).

comparison.controls: The same men on day 1, before the daily dosing began; there was no placebo condition and no separate control group. The two challenge doses are also compared with each other by two-sample t test, since not everyone received both.
comparison.matching: Within-person before-and-after, with day-15 parameters subtracted from day-1 parameters for each person; the order is fixed by the design.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable for the within-person pharmacokinetic comparison.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable (no separate control group).

outcomes.instruments: Non-compartmental and one-compartment model-derived pharmacokinetic parameters: peak concentration, time to peak, the extrapolated concentration at time zero, absorption and elimination rate constants and half-lives, lag time, apparent total and renal clearance, amount excreted in urine, urinary excretion constant and the percentage of dose recovered in urine; plus saliva-to-plasma ratios. Subjective and cardiovascular measures were taken by the methods of the companion paper but are not reported here (pp. 857-858).
outcomes.validity_norms: Standard pharmacokinetic methods with a validated stereoselective assay; the model choice (one compartment with lag time) is justified against a two-compartment fit.
outcomes.operationalization: Pharmacokinetic tolerance is operationalized as a significant within-person change in a model parameter between day 1 and day 15, and its absence is quantified by a power analysis giving the detectable difference for each parameter.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None: thirteen parameters were each tested at two dose levels by a one-sample t test or a Wilcoxon signed-rank test, with a Shapiro-Wilk test used to choose between them, and the dose contrast by a two-sample t test with Satterthwaite's approximation where variances differed (p. 858).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: None: an open study with no placebo condition. The assay itself is objective and the isotope label distinguishes the challenge dose from the daily dose.

analysis.effect_sizes: Table 1 gives means with standard errors and the number contributing to each cell; Table 2 gives, for each parameter and dose, the day-1 mean with upper and lower detection limits, the observed day-15 difference as a percentage and the difference the study could have detected. The two significant changes are both at the larger challenge dose: the extrapolated zero-time concentration rose from 47.34 ng/mL (SEM 1.06) to 51.39 (SEM 0.91), about 8.5%, and the peak concentration from 37.2 ng/mL (SEM 1.3) to 41.8 (SEM 1.7), about 12.5%. Elimination half-life averaged 10.14 h (SEM 0.63) overall, with condition means of 8.46, 9.71, 11.45 and 10.93 h; the discussion gives 10.1 h (SEM 0.6) with a range of 6.4-15.1 h. The percentage of the dose excreted in urine was higher at the smaller dose than the larger (54.1% against 34.6% on day 1; 50.0% against 30.0% on day 15).
analysis.covariates: None; within-person differences and two-sample dose comparisons.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration is mentioned; the study was approved by the University of North Carolina committee for the protection of human subjects (p. 857).
analysis.selective_reporting: The subjective and cardiovascular measures collected in the same sessions are reported only in the companion paper; area under the curve appears in the power table but not in Table 1; the urine and saliva data are presented mostly as figures.
analysis.power: Unusually well handled for a study of this period: Table 2 gives, for every parameter at both doses, the difference that could have been detected with a two-sided test at 5% and 80% power. A 20% change in the elimination rate constant, peak concentration and area under the curve would have been detected (detectable differences 21.2% and 14.8%, 18.3% and 6.1%, 20.1% and 15.6%); for absorption rate, lag time, time to peak and the urinary measures the detectable differences are 29.7% to 156.5%, so those null results are uninformative.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Thirteen days of daily low-dose methamphetamine left absorption, apparent clearance, apparent metabolic clearance, renal clearance, the elimination rate constant and half-life statistically unchanged. The only significant changes were at the larger challenge dose, where the extrapolated zero-time concentration was about 8.5% higher and the peak concentration about 12.5% higher on day 15. Both changes raise, not lower, the concentration reached by a given dose.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that minor pharmacokinetic differences after subchronic treatment would act to increase plasma concentration, so that pharmacodynamic tolerance could not be explained by a change in pharmacokinetics; the conclusion repeats this for the heart-rate tolerance reported in the companion paper. This follows from the results for the parameters the study could test precisely, and the power table is printed so that a reader can see which null results are informative. The qualification the paper does not make in its abstract is that the tolerance it is explaining was measured in the same six men at only the smaller dose, in an open study, so the inference is only as strong as that finding.

timeline.event: The clinical arm of the same programme, in the six men of the low-dose round: a smaller heart-rate rise on day 15, with unchanged ratings of 'high'
Smoked and intravenous methamphetamine in 6 men: half-life 11.1-12.2 h, consistent with the 10.1 h found here for the oral route
Three days of twice-daily oral dosing with tolerance to positive subjective effects; no plasma concentrations were measured, so the pharmacokinetic question was not revisited

replication.where_it_stands: This remains the only human study of methamphetamine pharmacokinetics before and after a course of daily dosing. Its half-life estimate agrees with later studies by other routes, but the finding that daily dosing does not induce its own metabolism rests on this study alone, at one low daily dose.

funding.funder: National Institute on Drug Abuse contract 271-87-8126 (p. 856).
funding.declared_conflicts: Not reported: the article carries no conflict-of-interest statement.
funding.affiliations_note: Research Triangle Institute with the University of North Carolina Department of Psychiatry; this paper and Perez-Reyes et al. (1991) report different measures from one study in the same men, so they are not independent sources.

what_would_settle_it: A repeated-dosing study at doses and by routes closer to non-medical use, with plasma sampling long enough to measure accumulation, a placebo challenge arm, and the subjective and cardiovascular measures reported alongside the concentrations, so that the presence of tolerance and the absence of a pharmacokinetic explanation are established in the same analysis.

domains.domain: Randomization process (no randomization: fixed before-and-after order)
domains.note: Day 1 always preceded day 15, there was no placebo challenge, and the two dose rounds were run about three months apart rather than allocated.

domains.domain: Period and carryover effects (within-person before and after)
domains.note: The day-15 challenge was given on a background of steady-state drug (6.08 ng/mL, SEM 0.94) and metabolite, but the deuterium label separates the two sources analytically, and the isotopomers are shown to share the same terminal elimination rate.

Open study with no placebo, which matters little for an assay-based outcome but means nothing is blinded; daily dosing was supervised in the laboratory and urine screening showed no compliance problems.
Complete urine collection was achieved for only 3 or 4 of 6 men in several conditions, so the excretion parameters rest on subsets, and the half-life estimates come from all six.
A validated stereoselective assay with deuterated internal standards, replicate variation of 1-7% for methamphetamine, and model fits whose coefficients of variation are printed for each parameter.

No protocol, 26 uncorrected within-person tests, and area under the curve reported only in the power table; against this, the power analysis for every parameter is printed, which is the opposite of selective reporting.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The measurement is the strongest part of this study: a stereoselective isotope-label assay, per-person model fits and a printed power analysis make the null results interpretable for the parameters that were measured precisely. The design, however, is an open before-and-after comparison in six men per dose with no placebo challenge, which is why the overall judgment stays at the level of its weakest domains. The source can be cited for the absence of a change in absorption, clearance and half-life after thirteen days of low daily dosing, for the small rise in peak concentration at the larger challenge dose, and for oral pharmacokinetic values; it cannot be cited for tolerance to any effect, which it did not measure.

key_findings.finding: After thirteen days of 10 mg a day, the pharmacokinetics of the same oral challenge dose were essentially unchanged: absorption, apparent clearance, apparent metabolic clearance, renal clearance, the elimination rate constant and the elimination half-life did not differ significantly between day 1 and day 15 at either challenge dose.
key_findings.locator: Results > Pharmacokinetic Analysis, last paragraph (p. 859, right column, continuing p. 860); Discussion, 4th paragraph (p. 860, right column)

key_findings.finding: Two parameters did change, both at the larger challenge dose and both upward: the extrapolated zero-time concentration rose from 47.34 ng/mL (SEM 1.06) on day 1 to 51.39 (SEM 0.91) on day 15, about 8.5% higher, and the peak concentration from 37.2 ng/mL (SEM 1.3) to 41.8 (SEM 1.7), about 12.5% higher (p<=0.05).
key_findings.locator: Table 1, C1 and Cmax rows with footnotes b and c (p. 858); Results > Pharmacokinetic Analysis, last paragraph (p. 859)

key_findings.finding: The study states what it could have detected: Table 2 gives the detectable difference for each parameter at each dose with 80% power. A 20% change would have been detected in the elimination rate constant (detectable 21.2% at the smaller dose, 14.8% at the larger), peak concentration (18.3% and 6.1%) and area under the curve (20.1% and 15.6%), while for absorption rate, lag time and the urinary measures the detectable differences run from 29.7% to 156.5%.
key_findings.locator: Table 2, Observed Difference and Detectable Difference columns

key_findings.finding: The elimination half-life of oral S-(+)-methamphetamine averaged 10.14 h (SEM 0.63, n=24 profiles), with condition means of 8.46, 9.71, 11.45 and 10.93 h; the discussion gives 10.1 h (SEM 0.6) with a range of 6.4-15.1 h. Peak concentrations were reached about 3 hours after dosing (overall time to peak 3.13 h, SEM 0.24) after a lag of about half an hour.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, elimination t1/2, tmax and Lag time rows (p. 858); Results > Pharmacokinetic Analysis, 3rd paragraph (p. 859); Conclusion (p. 862)

key_findings.finding: Daily dosing produced measurable steady-state concentrations: at the start of day 15, before the challenge, non-deuterated methamphetamine from the daily slow-release dose averaged 6.08 ng/mL (SEM 0.94) and its amphetamine metabolite 2.3 ng/mL (SEM 0.3).
key_findings.locator: Results > Concentrations in Biological Fluids, 1st paragraph (p. 857, right column, continuing p. 858)

key_findings.finding: Renal excretion was large and dose-dependent: 54.1% of the smaller dose against 34.6% of the larger was recovered in urine on day 1 (50.0% against 30.0% on day 15), and renal clearance depended on urine pH (p=0.0001), urine flow (p=0.0001) and dose (p=0.0003). Average renal clearance, 164 mL/min, exceeded the usual glomerular filtration rate of about 125 mL/min, which the authors read as active secretion.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, % dose in urine row (p. 858); Results > Pharmacokinetic Analysis, 1st paragraph of p. 860; Discussion, 7th paragraph (p. 860, right column)

key_findings.finding: Amphetamine, the metabolite, reached much lower concentrations than the parent drug and peaked much later: 1.6 ng/mL (SEM 0.2) after the smaller dose and 4.0 (SEM 0.5) after the larger, at 11.7 h (SEM 0.8) against about 3.1 h for methamphetamine, with an area under the curve about 30% of the parent drug's; 15.1% (SEM 2.0) of the methamphetamine dose was recovered in urine as amphetamine on a molar basis.
key_findings.locator: Results > Pharmacokinetic Analysis, 2nd-4th paragraphs of p. 860 (left column)

key_findings.finding: Saliva concentrations averaged 7.76 times (SEM 0.51, 149 paired samples) those in plasma, but the relationship was loose: linear regression gave r-squared 0.498 (p<0.0001), improved only to 0.620 by adding saliva pH and the logarithms of both measures, so saliva cannot be used to predict a plasma concentration accurately.
key_findings.locator: Results > Concentrations in Biological Fluids, 2nd paragraph (p. 858); Figure 3 (p. 859); Discussion, 9th paragraph (p. 861)

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 2 the area under the curve for the smaller challenge dose on day 1 is 312 ng.hr/mL and for the larger 735, while the Discussion gives 330 and 755 for the same parameter. Neither figure appears in Table 1, which does not list area under the curve at all.
reporting_issues.consequence: Two sets of values circulate for the same quantity; the Discussion figures appear to average the day-1 and day-15 values, so the day-specific figures in Table 2 are the ones to cite.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion gives the maximum concentrations of the challenge drug as 20.0 and 39.5 ng/mL 'table 1', but Table 1 prints 19.8 (SEM 2.7) and 20.3 (SEM 3.0) for the smaller dose on days 1 and 15 and 37.2 (SEM 1.3) and 41.8 (SEM 1.7) for the larger.
reporting_issues.consequence: The quoted pair are averages of the two study days, not table entries; a reader checking them against Table 1 will not find them, and the day-15 value for the larger dose is one of the study's two significant findings, which the averaging hides.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results state that quantities of the challenge drug averaging 30-54% of the dose were excreted in urine 'together with lesser amounts of S-methamphetamine-d3 (10-23% of dose)'; the second compound must be the metabolite S-amphetamine-d3, as the following sentences and Figures 4 and 5 make clear.
reporting_issues.consequence: As printed, the sentence says the same compound was excreted in two different amounts; the 10-23% figure belongs to amphetamine.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion states that a difference of 20% in the elimination rate constant, peak concentration and area under the curve could have been detected, but Table 2 gives detectable differences of 21.2% for the elimination rate constant and 20.1% for the area under the curve at the smaller dose, both just above 20%.
reporting_issues.consequence: The claim is right for the larger dose and marginally wrong for the smaller; the per-parameter values in Table 2 should be cited rather than the rounded statement.

reporting_issues.issue: Several Table 1 cells rest on fewer participants than the others (amount excreted in urine and the urinary rate constant on 3 or 4 of 6; renal clearance on 3, 6, 6 and 4), and the table does not say why; the reason, incomplete urine collection, appears only in the Discussion.
reporting_issues.consequence: The urinary parameters are less precise than the plasma ones, and their dose comparison rests on small subsets.

reporting_issues.issue: The elimination half-life is given three ways: 10.1 hr in the abstract, an overall mean of 10.14 h (SEM 0.63) in Table 1, and 10.1 (SEM 0.6) with a range of 6.4-15.1 h in the conclusion; the Results also note that computing the half-life from the mean rate constant instead would give 9.32 h.
