reporting_issues.consequence: Not an error, but a reader should cite the table value with its standard error and note which averaging method was used.

verification.source_read: PDF pp. 856-862 (PDFs/Methamphetamine/Cook_1992_PKRepeatedDailyDosing.pdf). The embedded text layer is scrambled in reading order, so the pages were rendered at 300 dpi and read with optical character recognition; Table 1 (p. 858) and Table 2 (p. 861) were then checked cell by cell against the page images.

design_detail: Twenty-day within-participant double-blind residential laboratory study in 9 men, run in three groups of three or four. Four 5-day blocks, one per drug condition: oral methamphetamine 10 mg with a placebo drink, methamphetamine 10 mg with alcohol 0.375 g/kg, methamphetamine 10 mg with alcohol 0.75 g/kg, and a placebo capsule with alcohol 0.75 g/kg; there was no placebo-plus-placebo condition. Within each block, day 1 was a placebo baseline, active drug was given three times (morning and evening of day 2 and evening of day 3), placebo was given on the morning of day 3 and on days 4-5. Capsules were given at 0900 and 2100 h and drinks an hour later. Breath alcohol, blood pressure, heart rate, mood ratings and a five-task cognitive battery were measured repeatedly; sleep was measured each night by actigraphy and a morning questionnaire; social behaviour and cigarette use were recorded. The tolerance analysis compares the first administration (day 2 morning) with the third (day 3 evening). Dosing order was counterbalanced so that no two people had the same condition in the same block.
can_establish: How a single oral dose of methamphetamine, alcohol and their combination differ on heart rate, blood pressure, mood ratings, performance and sleep in the same men; and whether those differences are smaller by the third administration of the same combination within about 36 hours.
cannot_establish: Cross-tolerance between the two drugs in the usual sense (no condition tested one drug after a course of the other); what happens at the doses and routes of non-medical methamphetamine use; effects in people who use methamphetamine regularly, since only one of the nine reported current methamphetamine use; and whether a smaller third response is tolerance rather than an effect of time of day or of the previous night's lost sleep, a limitation the authors state.

sample.recruitment: Adults who used stimulants and alcohol, recruited by word of mouth and by newspaper and online advertisement in New York City (Methods > Participants, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: At least 21 years old, past-year use of amphetamine, methamphetamine or MDMA and current (past 30 days) alcohol use; excluded for significant medical history (cardiovascular, neurological or major psychiatric illness, other than stimulant dependence) or any condition increasing the risk of participation.
sample.demographics: Nine men (six Black, one Hispanic, two White), mean age 41.1 years (SD 3.9), 13.6 years of education (SD 1.6), body mass index 26.4 (SD 3.5). All drank alcohol currently (1-5 days a week, 3-7 drinks a day) and all used cocaine currently (1-6 days a week); two used cannabis, one used methamphetamine (3 days a week), six smoked 5-10 cigarettes a day and eight used caffeine. Three met criteria for cocaine dependence; none was seeking treatment and none met criteria for any other Axis I disorder.
sample.attrition: None reported: nine men completed the 20-day study.
sample.selection_effects: Men only, middle-aged, all drinking currently and all using cocaine currently, recruited in one city for a 20-day residential stay at $70 a day. Only one reported current methamphetamine use, which the authors name as an important limitation for the sleep findings; alcohol tolerance is likely in a sample drinking 3-7 drinks a day.

exposure.measurement: Drug given under supervision in a private vestibule and measured for alcohol by breath analyser at baseline and 0.75, 1.5, 2.25, 3, 4, 5 and 6 hours after the capsule; methamphetamine concentrations were not measured.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: oral methamphetamine hydrochloride (Desoxyn tablets repackaged in opaque capsules with lactose) at 10 mg or placebo, and a 500 mL drink containing vodka at 0.375 or 0.75 g/kg of estimated total body water, or a matched placebo drink, both topped with 1 mL of vodka and a drop of peppermint oil and matched for calories. Three active administrations per block (day 2 morning, day 2 evening, day 3 evening).
exposure.polysubstance: Alcohol is itself one of the study conditions. Tobacco was available from 0800 to 2330 h and cigarette counts were analysed; the authors report that cigarette consumption did not affect the drug results, while the combination with the larger alcohol dose raised consumption by about 4-5 cigarettes a day. No other drugs were available during the residential stay; current cocaine use by all participants and cocaine dependence in three are background characteristics, not exposures during the study.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Residential confinement for 20 days with placebo baseline and washout days in each block; no biological verification of abstinence from other drugs is described. Before enrolment each person received 10 mg methamphetamine with the largest alcohol dose on an outpatient day, so the first in-study administration was not the first exposure to the combination.

comparison.controls: Within-person: the placebo baseline day of each block, the placebo mornings and washout days, and the other three drug conditions. Methamphetamine alone and alcohol alone each serve as the comparator for the combination; there was no placebo-plus-placebo condition, which the authors justify by the study's aim and the time burden.
comparison.matching: Within-person crossover with counterbalanced dosing order across blocks, so that no two participants received the same condition in the same block.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable: every comparison is within person.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable (no separate control group); all participants used cocaine currently, which is a feature of the sample rather than a between-group difference.

outcomes.instruments: A computerized 100-mm visual analogue mood questionnaire; a drug-effect questionnaire rating good and bad effects and drug strength 0-4, desire to take the drug again, and liking from -4 to +4; a five-task cognitive battery (digit recall, digit-symbol substitution, divided attention, rapid information processing, repeated acquisition); blood pressure and heart rate; breath alcohol; Actiwatch actigraphy giving total sleep time, sleep-onset latency, sleep efficiency and wake bouts, with a morning sleep questionnaire; computer-prompted observation of social behaviour every 2.5 minutes; cigarette counts.
outcomes.validity_norms: Established laboratory instruments for this group; actigraphy is a movement-based estimate of sleep rather than polysomnography, and the mood scales have no external norms.
outcomes.operationalization: Tolerance is operationalized as a significant fall in the area under the effect-time curve from the first to the third administration of the same condition, tested as a drug condition by administration-number interaction with planned comparisons.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None at the family level: two-factor repeated-measures analyses of variance with planned between-drug and within-drug comparisons, p<0.05, with Huynh-Feldt corrections where appropriate. Tables 3, 4 and 5 report fifteen, five and fourteen outcomes respectively, each with three or four comparisons.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Double-blind for the capsule; participants were told the study concerned alcohol and an approved stimulant or sedative. Alcohol itself cannot be blinded in people who drink regularly, and ratings of 'drunk' differed sharply by condition, so blinding of the alcohol conditions cannot be assumed; blinding integrity was not tested.

analysis.effect_sizes: Effect sizes labelled d are given for every comparison alongside F values, with means and standard errors in Tables 3-5. Degrees of freedom are consistent with nine participants throughout (F 21,168 for the four-condition by eight-time-point acute analyses, F 3,24 for the tolerance analyses, F 18,144 for performance, F 12,96 for sleep and residual effects, F 12,60 for cigarettes in the six smokers). The printed d values reach 33.3 for breath alcohol and 6.7-33.3 across the alcohol comparisons, which cannot be conventional between-group standardized differences; the paper does not say how they were computed, so they should be read as within-person standardized values from the analysis-of-variance error term and not compared with Cohen's benchmarks (editors' note).
analysis.covariates: None; within-person analyses of variance with planned comparisons.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or protocol is mentioned. The study was approved by the Institutional Review Board of the New York State Psychiatric Institute.
analysis.selective_reporting: Peak cardiovascular and subjective data are said to be reported in Table 3 only 'for the sake of brevity'; several analyses are reported as 'data not shown' (cigarette comparisons between conditions); the sleep and residual tables report only the measures that reached significance.
analysis.power: No sample-size calculation and no power statement; nine men, every effect tested within person. The authors attribute some null findings to the sample and note that most participants did not use methamphetamine regularly.

interpretation_gap.results_show: At the first administration, the combination raised heart rate and ratings of 'good drug effect' more than either drug alone; methamphetamine reduced alcohol-related performance decrements and ratings of 'drunk' and 'sedated'; and the larger alcohol dose blunted methamphetamine's disruption of sleep. By the third administration, about 36 hours later, the heart-rate and 'good drug effect' advantages of the combination were significantly smaller and no longer differed from alcohol alone, while blood-pressure effects were unchanged. Residual next-day effects were few.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says that by the third administration many of these effects were significantly diminished, 'suggesting that participants developed tolerance', and the discussion repeats this while listing two alternatives in the same paragraph: the first administration was in the morning and the third in the evening, and the third followed a night of drug-disrupted sleep. The data show a smaller response at the third administration; the study design does not separate tolerance from time of day or from accumulated sleep loss, and the authors say so. The conclusion that the combination's profile explains why the drugs are used together is an interpretation, since no self-administration or choice measure was taken.

timeline.event: Single-dose intravenous methamphetamine 30 mg with oral alcohol 1 g/kg: greater heart-rate rise and euphoria than either drug alone, and less subjective intoxication, with no performance effects (Mendelson et al., 1995)
Three days of twice-daily oral methamphetamine in the same residential laboratory: tolerance to positive subjective ratings and to sleep disruption across days
Thirteen days of daily oral methamphetamine: a smaller heart-rate response to a fixed challenge afterwards

replication.where_it_stands: The acute interaction (greater heart rate and euphoria, less felt intoxication) agrees with the one earlier human study of this combination and with studies of alcohol combined with cocaine, caffeine and d-amphetamine. The loss of those effects by a third administration within 36 hours is reported here alone; the same laboratory had previously found tolerance to positive subjective effects of methamphetamine alone across three days.

funding.funder: Grant DA-03746 from the National Institute on Drug Abuse (Acknowledgments).
funding.declared_conflicts: Not reported in the PubMed Central author manuscript: no competing-interests statement appears.
funding.affiliations_note: Columbia University and the New York State Psychiatric Institute; the same laboratory and the same grant number as Comer et al. (2001), so the two studies are not independent replications of one another.

what_would_settle_it: A residential study giving the same methamphetamine-alcohol combination at the same time of day on several consecutive days, with a placebo-plus-placebo condition, sleep held constant or measured as a mediator, plasma methamphetamine concentrations, and people who use methamphetamine regularly, so that a smaller later response can be attributed to tolerance rather than to time of day or lost sleep.

domains.domain: Randomization process (counterbalanced order of the four blocks)
domains.note: Dosing order was counterbalanced so that no two participants had the same condition in the same block, but the method of allocation is not described and no period effect is reported.

Blocks were separated by placebo washout days and residual effects were measured and were small, but within a block the three administrations fall in about 36 hours and the tolerance comparison is between a morning dose and an evening dose two nights later, with the second night's sleep disturbed by the drug.

The capsule was double-blind, but alcohol at 0.75 g/kg in men who drink 3-7 drinks a day is recognizable: ratings of 'drunk' reached 44.2 under alcohol alone against 1.1 under methamphetamine alone. Blinding integrity was not assessed, and the main outcomes are self-rated.
All nine men completed the 20-day protocol and no missing data are reported.

Breath alcohol, cardiovascular measures, actigraphy and performance are objective; the tolerance outcomes that carry the conclusion are self-rated mood scales, and sleep is estimated from movement rather than polysomnography.

No protocol or pre-specified primary outcome; roughly sixty outcomes with uncorrected planned comparisons; peak data confined to a table 'for the sake of brevity'; several analyses reported as data not shown; and the significance footnotes of Tables 3 and 4 do not define all the markers used.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A 20-day within-person residential design with four conditions, counterbalanced order and objective measurement of alcohol, sleep and performance is a strong way to study a drug combination, and the degrees of freedom check out against the sample size throughout. The overall judgment is set by the blinding of the alcohol conditions and by the number of uncorrected comparisons behind the subjective findings. The source can be cited for the acute interaction between oral methamphetamine and alcohol on heart rate, mood and performance, for the attenuation of methamphetamine's sleep disruption by alcohol, and for the observation that these differences were smaller by a third administration; it cannot be cited for cross-tolerance between the drugs, for doses and routes used outside the laboratory, or for effects in people who use methamphetamine regularly.

key_findings.finding: At the first administration the combination raised heart rate more than either drug alone, and the larger alcohol dose more than the smaller (F 21,168 = 10.9-30.2, p<0.005 for all comparisons, d = 1.5-2.3). All active conditions raised heart rate above baseline; methamphetamine-containing conditions raised systolic pressure and the combinations raised diastolic pressure, while alcohol alone did not significantly raise blood pressure.
key_findings.locator: Results > Acute effects (day 2) > Cardiovascular effects, whole subsection; Figure 1

key_findings.finding: By the third administration the heart-rate advantage of the combination had shrunk: both combinations produced significantly smaller heart-rate area-under-curve values at administration 3 than at administration 1 (F 3,24 = 15.4-26.5, p<0.0001, d = 0.8-1.6), and only the larger-alcohol combination still exceeded methamphetamine alone and alcohol alone (F 3,24 = 11.3-14.5, p<0.005, d = 0.7-0.9). Blood-pressure effects were unchanged across administrations.
key_findings.locator: Results > Tolerance > Cardiovascular and BAL effects, whole subsection; Figure 4 (left panel)

key_findings.finding: The same pattern appeared in the wanted subjective effects. At administration 1 the larger-alcohol combination produced higher 'good drug effect' and lower 'drunk' ratings than alcohol alone (F 3,24 = 10.7-12.7, p<0.005, d = 0.6-0.8); by administration 3 neither differed from alcohol alone, and 'good drug effect' area-under-curve values were significantly smaller at administration 3 than at administration 1 for both combinations (F 3,24 = 12.1-14.9, p<0.005, d = 0.7-0.8).
key_findings.locator: Results > Tolerance > Subjective effects, whole subsection; Figure 4 (middle and right panels)

key_findings.finding: Table 4 gives the size of the fall for the larger-alcohol combination between the first and third administration: 'content' from 122.6 (SEM 40.3) to 72.6 (SEM 26.1), 'energetic' from 118.2 (SEM 31.5) to 70.1 (SEM 23.0), 'high' from 96.6 (SEM 27.0) to 56.0 (SEM 18.3), drug-effect-questionnaire 'good drug effect' from 4.8 (SEM 0.9) to 3.2 (SEM 0.6) and drug liking from 3.1 (SEM 1.7) to 1.1 (SEM 1.5), all significant against the same condition's first administration. Under alcohol alone, 'energetic' (112.6 to 40.0) and drug liking (3.6 to 1.3) also fell significantly.
key_findings.locator: Table 4, visual analogue scale and drug-effects-questionnaire rows

key_findings.finding: At the first administration the combination produced larger increases in 'good drug effect' than either drug alone (F 21,168 = 12.5-52.0, p<0.05, d = 1.0-2.0), while alcohol alone produced the highest ratings of 'drunk' (peak 44.2, SEM 13.5, against 13.9 for the larger-alcohol combination and 1.1 for methamphetamine alone) and of 'sedated' (34.3 against 10.6 and 3.3).
key_findings.locator: Results > Acute effects (day 2) > Subjective effects, 1st paragraph; Table 3, peak subjective-effect ratings

key_findings.finding: Methamphetamine blunted alcohol's effect on performance: alcohol alone reduced maximum tracking speed on the divided-attention task compared with every other condition (F 18,144 = 6.3-12.9, p<0.05, d = 2.4-2.7) and reduced hits on the rapid information task compared with methamphetamine alone (F 18,144 = 6.7, p<0.05, d = 1.3), while the combinations produced no such decrements. The combination with the larger alcohol dose did raise errors on the repeated-acquisition task compared with methamphetamine alone and with the smaller-alcohol combination (F 18,144 = 14.4-18.2, p<0.001, d = 1.5-1.7).
key_findings.locator: Results > Acute effects (day 2) > Cognitive/psychomotor performance effects, whole subsection; Figure 3

key_findings.finding: Alcohol softened methamphetamine's disruption of sleep. On the night of day 2, all methamphetamine conditions reduced hours slept and sleep efficiency compared with alcohol alone (F 12,96 = 11.6-30.7, p<0.005, d = 1.2-2.5), and methamphetamine alone reduced both more than the combination with the larger alcohol dose (F 12,96 = 4.6, p<0.05, d = 0.7-0.8); the same pattern appeared in estimated hours slept and ratings of sleeping well. Sleep-onset latency was 53.4 minutes (SEM 13.1) after methamphetamine alone against 20.6 (SEM 3.9) after alcohol alone, with 6.9 awakenings an hour against 3.5.
key_findings.locator: Results > Sleep effects, whole subsection; Table 5, sleep questionnaire and Actiwatch rows; Figure 5

key_findings.finding: Residual effects the next day were few: heart rate was still slightly raised on day 3 by methamphetamine alone and by the larger-alcohol combination compared with alcohol alone (F 12,96 = 7.3-19.4, p<0.01, d = 0.5-0.8), ratings of 'upset stomach' were higher and ratings of 'tired' higher after methamphetamine alone, and there were no residual effects on any cognitive or psychomotor task.
key_findings.locator: Results > Residual effects > Cardiovascular effects and Subjective effects; Results > Residual effects > Cognitive/psychomotor performance effects; Figure 6; Table 5

key_findings.finding: The combination with the larger alcohol dose increased cigarette smoking among the six smokers by about 4-5 cigarettes a day (9.5, SEM 1.4, against 14.2, SEM 1.9; F 12,60 = 24.1, p<0.05, d = 0.9) and more than every other condition, and participants spent a smaller share of their social time talking after methamphetamine alone (10.9%) than under any alcohol condition (24.8-28.5%).
key_findings.locator: Results > Acute effects (day 2) > Effects of cigarette smoking and > Effects on social interactions

reporting_issues.issue: Tables 3, 4 and 5 use four and five asterisks on several entries, but their footnotes define only one, two and three asterisks (significantly different from methamphetamine alone, from the smaller-alcohol combination and from the larger-alcohol combination; and in Table 4 from the first and third administrations of alcohol alone and the first of the combination).
reporting_issues.locator: Table 3 footnotes and rows 'Good drug effect', 'High', 'Mellow', 'Stimulated', 'Drunk'; Table 4 footnotes and row 'Content'; Table 5 footnotes and rows 'Fell asleep easily', 'Headache'
reporting_issues.consequence: The comparison that each marked entry refers to cannot be determined from the table alone; where an entry carries an undefined marker, the claim should rest on the comparisons stated in the running text instead.

reporting_issues.issue: The effect sizes printed as d reach 33.3 for breath alcohol and run from 6.7 to 33.3 across the alcohol comparisons, with values of 2.1-3.3 for heart rate against baseline; no formula is given.
reporting_issues.locator: Results > Acute effects (day 2) > Breath alcohol levels and > Cardiovascular effects
reporting_issues.consequence: These cannot be read as conventional standardized mean differences, where values above about 2 are already very large. Any claim citing this study should quote the means and standard errors in the tables rather than the d values.

reporting_issues.issue: The tolerance comparison is between the first administration, given at 0900 h on day 2, and the third, given at 2100 h on day 3; the discussion names time of day and the previous night's drug-disturbed sleep as alternative explanations, but the abstract states only that tolerance developed.
reporting_issues.locator: Methods and materials > Design; Abstract; Discussion, 3rd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: A reader taking the abstract alone would treat a morning-to-evening comparison after a disturbed night as a clean measure of tolerance. The claim should say that the response was smaller at the third administration and that the design cannot separate tolerance from time of day or sleep loss.

reporting_issues.issue: There is no placebo-plus-placebo condition, so no measurement in these men is free of both drugs apart from the baseline day of each block.
reporting_issues.locator: Methods and materials > Procedure > Drug, last paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Every reported effect of methamphetamine alone is against alcohol alone or against the block's baseline day, not against a double placebo; the size of each drug's effect cannot be separated from the other's absence in the within-day comparisons.

reporting_issues.issue: Each participant received 10 mg methamphetamine with the largest alcohol dose on an outpatient day before enrolment, to check for adverse reactions and to give them experience of the combination.
reporting_issues.consequence: The first in-study administration was not the first exposure to the combination, so any tolerance measured from it starts from an already exposed state.

reporting_issues.issue: Only one of the nine participants reported current methamphetamine use, while all nine used cocaine currently and three met criteria for cocaine dependence; the abstract describes the sample only as 'nine adult male volunteers'.
reporting_issues.locator: Methods and materials > Participants, 2nd paragraph; Table 1; Discussion, 4th paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The sample's stimulant experience is mostly with cocaine, which the authors name as a limitation for the sleep findings; results should not be transferred to people who use methamphetamine regularly.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC3220757 (author manuscript of Psychopharmacology 2011;219(1):191-204), read in the browser pane; tables 1-5 render as text and were read in full, figures 1-6 are images and no values were taken from them. Supplementary material: none offered.

design_detail: Open, uncontrolled before-and-after challenge study in 6 men who had used amphetamines recreationally. Each took 10 mg of slow-release oral methamphetamine hydrochloride (Desoxyn Gradumet) at 9 a.m. in the laboratory on 13 consecutive days (days 2-14). On day 1, before the daily dosing began, and on day 15, after it ended, each received an oral challenge dose of deuterated methamphetamine 0.125 mg/kg, so that the plasma concentrations from the challenge could be told apart from those left by the daily dosing. Heart rate, blood pressure, a 0-100 self-rating of 'high' and plasma concentrations of both forms were measured on the two challenge days, with blood sampled to 48 hours. No placebo, no randomization and no blinding are described.
can_establish: Whether the heart-rate, blood-pressure, subjective and pharmacokinetic responses to one low oral dose of methamphetamine differ after thirteen days of daily low-dose exposure, within the same six men.
cannot_establish: Whether tolerance develops to subjective effects at doses large enough to produce them (the challenge produced a mean peak 'high' below 20 out of 100) or to blood-pressure effects (peak rises were under 15 mm Hg systolic), both of which the authors state the study could not test; anything about the doses, routes or binge patterns of non-medical use; and whether the heart-rate change reflects tolerance rather than habituation to the laboratory, since there was no placebo condition and no control group.

sample.recruitment: Paid volunteers at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill; the recruitment route is not described (p. 353).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Healthy men who had previously used amphetamines for recreational purposes, selected for infrequent past use so that tolerance would have room to develop; each agreed to abstain from amphetamines and any other illegal drug for two weeks before and throughout the study, with daily urine screening. No other inclusion or exclusion criteria are listed (pp. 353-354).
sample.demographics: Six men, age 24 years (SEM 2), weight 72.6 kg (SEM 1.1), height 179 cm (SEM 3.6); lifetime use of amphetamine, dextroamphetamine or methamphetamine 8 times (SEM 3.9) (p. 353).
sample.attrition: None reported; six men are described throughout.
sample.selection_effects: Men only, healthy, with a lifetime average of about eight occasions of amphetamine use; a sample chosen for low previous exposure so that tolerance could develop, and far from the pattern of people who use methamphetamine heavily.

exposure.measurement: Drug given in the laboratory each morning and measured directly in plasma: gas chromatography-mass spectrometry with a deuterated internal standard quantified deuterated (challenge) and non-deuterated (daily-dose) methamphetamine separately, with blood drawn every 30 minutes for the first 4 hours and at 5, 6, 8, 10, 24, 28, 32 and 48 hours (pp. 354-355).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: 10 mg of a slow-release oral preparation each morning for 13 consecutive days, with oral challenge doses of deuterated methamphetamine 0.125 mg/kg on day 1 and day 15. The authors state the daily dose was chosen as a commonly used therapeutic dose that in pilot work caused no adverse effect other than falling asleep earlier than usual (pp. 353-354).
exposure.polysubstance: Participants contracted to abstain from amphetamines and any other illegal drug for two weeks before and throughout the study; daily urine samples tested by EMIT were consistently negative. Tobacco, alcohol and caffeine are not mentioned (p. 353).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Two weeks' abstinence before the study and throughout, verified by daily urine screening. On day 15 the challenge was given on top of residual drug from the daily dosing: non-deuterated methamphetamine averaged 5.03 ng/mL (SEM 1.88) before the challenge dose (pp. 353, 355).

comparison.controls: The same six men on day 1, before the daily dosing began; there was no placebo condition and no separate control group.
comparison.matching: Within-person before-and-after comparison; the order is fixed by the design (day 1 always precedes day 15), so period and order effects cannot be separated from drug effects.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable for the within-person comparison, but nothing controls for repetition: familiarity with the procedure, the room and the measurements can lower a cardiovascular response on a second occasion, and no placebo challenge was run to measure that.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable (no separate control group).

outcomes.instruments: Heart rate from a chest-electrode electrocardiogram and blood pressure from an automated portable monitor (Accutracker), analysed only at baseline and at 2.5 and 3.5 hours after dosing because psychomotor testing contaminated the other time points; a 0-100 self-rating of 'high' anchored at 100 to the highest the person had ever been on amphetamines, repeated at frequent intervals, with each rating made while the person was shown his previous rating; plasma concentrations by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. A neuropsychological battery was given but reported elsewhere (pp. 354-355).
outcomes.validity_norms: The 'high' scale is anchored to each person's own previous experience rather than to a common standard, so ratings are not comparable between people; cardiovascular measurement is objective.
outcomes.operationalization: Tolerance is operationalized as a smaller rise in heart rate over baseline on day 15 than on day 1 at the two uncontaminated time points.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None described; repeated-measures analyses of variance were run on heart rate, systolic and diastolic blood pressure, ratings of 'high' and plasma concentrations, and the report states that no other cardiovascular effect reached significance (p. 355).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: None: the study was open, with no placebo condition, and both participants and investigators knew which day was which.

analysis.effect_sizes: No effect sizes, confidence intervals or printed means for the cardiovascular outcome: the heart-rate result is given as F=8.26 with P below 0.035 in the summary and P below 0.03 in the Results, and the day-1 and day-15 rises are shown only as bars in Figure 3 (about 10 and 7 beats/min at 2.5 h and about 14 and 8 beats/min at 3.5 h, read from the figure and not printed). Peak 'high' was 16.8 (SEM 6.5) of 100 on day 1 and 10.0 (SEM 3.9) on day 15, a difference the authors report as not significant; peak plasma concentrations occurred at 3.1 h (SEM 0.3) and 2.8 h (SEM 0.4) and did not differ. Converting the standard errors with six participants gives standard deviations of about 15.9 and 9.6 for the two 'high' ratings (editors' calculation).
analysis.covariates: None; repeated-measures analyses of variance on the raw measures.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration is mentioned; the consent form was approved by the University of North Carolina committee for the protection of human subjects (p. 353).
analysis.selective_reporting: The neuropsychological battery, named in the introduction as part of the study, is deferred to a separate report; blood-pressure results are given only as the statement that systolic pressure rose over time on both days with no other significant effect; the time course of 'high' is not shown at all.
analysis.power: Not reported; no sample-size calculation. With six men and a within-person comparison the heart-rate test has F(1,5), and the authors state explicitly that the small subjective and blood-pressure responses to the challenge dose limited the chance of observing tolerance in those measures.

interpretation_gap.results_show: After thirteen days of 10 mg a day, the same challenge dose produced a smaller rise in heart rate than before (F=8.26, P<0.035 in the summary and P<0.03 in the Results), while peak ratings of 'high' (16.8 against 10.0 out of 100) and the plasma concentration-time course of the challenge dose were statistically unchanged. Steady-state concentrations of the daily drug were present on day 15 (5.03 ng/mL, SEM 1.88, before the challenge), so the smaller heart-rate response occurred despite a higher total drug concentration.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The summary and discussion conclude that tolerance to the cardioacceleratory effect was induced while disposition and subjective effects were unaltered, and that the reduction 'becomes more robust' once the residual drug is taken into account. The direction is supported, but with six men, no placebo and no blinding, and a single statistic, a smaller second response cannot be separated from habituation to a repeated laboratory procedure; the authors are careful to say that tolerance to the subjective and blood-pressure effects cannot be shown here because the responses were too small, which is a statement about power rather than evidence of no tolerance.

timeline.event: The pharmacokinetic arm of the same programme, in 8 men including these 6: no change in absorption, clearance or half-life after the 13-day regimen, so the heart-rate tolerance could not be explained by a change in disposition
Three days of twice-daily oral methamphetamine in a residential laboratory: tolerance to positive subjective ratings and to sleep disruption, with no fall in the anorectic effect
Repeated oral methamphetamine with and without alcohol: heart-rate increases diminished by the third administration over two days

replication.where_it_stands: A fall in the heart-rate response with repeated low oral dosing has been seen here and, over a much shorter interval, in the methamphetamine-alcohol study of Kirkpatrick and colleagues; the finding of unchanged subjective effects is specific to this study's single daily slow-release dose and small response, and the later twice-daily study found the opposite for ratings of 'high'.

funding.funder: National Institute on Drug Abuse contract 271-87-8126 (p. 358).
funding.declared_conflicts: Not reported: the article carries no conflict-of-interest statement.
funding.affiliations_note: University of North Carolina Department of Psychiatry with Research Triangle Institute; the same investigators published the pharmacokinetic analysis of the same participants (Cook et al., 1992), so the two papers are one study reported twice and are not independent.

what_would_settle_it: The same 13-day design with a placebo challenge arm and a randomized or counterbalanced order, in a larger sample including women, at a dose that produces a substantial subjective response, so that a smaller second response can be separated from habituation and so that tolerance to the wanted effects can actually be tested.

domains.domain: Randomization process (no randomization: fixed before-and-after order)
domains.note: Day 1 always came before day 15 and there was no placebo challenge, so the comparison is a repeated measurement in a fixed order rather than an allocated comparison.

domains.domain: Period and carryover effects (within-person before and after)
domains.note: The day-15 challenge was given on top of steady-state drug from the daily dosing (5.03 ng/mL, SEM 1.88), and familiarity with the laboratory procedure on the second occasion is not controlled; the authors argue the residual drug makes the finding stronger, but it also means the two sessions are not comparable.
Open study: participants and investigators knew the order of the sessions, and the subjective rating required each person to compare himself with his own previous rating.
All six men completed both challenge sessions; no missing data are reported.

Heart rate and blood pressure were measured by instrument, and plasma concentrations by a validated assay; only two cardiovascular time points were analysable because psychomotor testing contaminated the rest, and the 'high' scale is anchored to each person's own experience.

No protocol; the neuropsychological battery is deferred to another paper; blood-pressure and subjective time courses are not printed; and the same heart-rate test is given with two different P values in the same article.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: This is an open before-and-after study without a placebo condition, in six men, with a single significant test to support its conclusion; the direction may well be right, and the pharmacokinetic arm rules out a disposition explanation, but the design cannot separate tolerance from habituation to a repeated procedure. The source can be cited for the observation that the heart-rate rise to a fixed oral challenge was smaller after thirteen days of daily dosing, and for the pharmacokinetic and subjective measures being unchanged in this low-response setting; it cannot be cited for the absence of tolerance to subjective effects, which the authors themselves say the study could not test.

key_findings.finding: The rise in heart rate over baseline after the same oral challenge dose was significantly smaller on day 15, after thirteen days of daily methamphetamine, than on day 1 (F=8.26, P<0.03), measured at the two time points free of psychomotor-task contamination, 2.5 and 3.5 hours after dosing.
key_findings.locator: Results > Cardiovascular effects, continuing on p. 357 above the Discussion; Figure 3 (p. 357)
key_findings.note: The summary on p. 352 prints the same test as P<0.035 and the Results as P<0.03; the day-1 and day-15 rises themselves are shown only as bars in Figure 3 and are not printed anywhere.

key_findings.finding: Heart rate rose significantly over time after the challenge on both test days (F=14.24, P<0.001) and systolic blood pressure also rose on both days (F=10.6, P<0.001); no other cardiovascular measure reached significance, and baseline heart rate and blood pressures did not differ between day 1 and day 15.
key_findings.locator: Results > Cardiovascular effects, 1st paragraph (p. 355) continuing at the top of p. 357
key_findings.note: Degrees of freedom are not given for these two tests; with six men they cannot be checked against the printed P values.

key_findings.finding: Ratings of 'high' after the challenge dose were modest and did not differ significantly between test days: mean peak 16.8 (SEM 6.5) of 100 on day 1 and 10.0 (SEM 3.9) on day 15. The authors state that this small response (under 20% of the highest the men had ever felt) limited the study's ability to observe tolerance to the subjective effect.

The disposition of the challenge dose was unchanged: plasma concentration-time curves for the deuterated drug did not differ significantly between day 1 and day 15, and peak concentrations occurred at 3.1 h (SEM 0.3) and 2.8 h (SEM 0.4).
key_findings.locator: Results > Methamphetamine plasma concentrations, 1st paragraph (p. 355); Figure 1 (p. 356)

key_findings.finding: Daily dosing produced a steady state: before the day-15 challenge, non-deuterated methamphetamine averaged 5.03 ng/mL (SEM 1.88), stayed about level for the next 4 hours, then declined, and was undetectable 48 hours later. Amphetamine, the metabolite, stayed below 2 ng/mL.
key_findings.locator: Results > Methamphetamine plasma concentrations, 2nd paragraph (p. 355); Figure 2 (p. 356)

key_findings.finding: Over the thirteen days of daily dosing the men reported no 'high', no loss of appetite and no insomnia; the only effect reported was falling asleep earlier than usual, and no withdrawal symptoms or other effects were reported when dosing stopped.

Peak rises in blood pressure after the challenge were small: under 15 mm Hg systolic and under 6 mm Hg diastolic. The authors conclude that tolerance to the blood-pressure effects cannot be shown from this study.

reporting_issues.issue: The same heart-rate test is printed with two different significance levels: the summary gives F(1,5)=8.26, P<=0.035 and the Results give F=8.26, P<0.03. With 1 and 5 degrees of freedom, F=8.26 corresponds to P=0.035 (editors' calculation), so the Results value is too small.
reporting_issues.consequence: The study's single supporting statistic is reported inconsistently; the correct value, 0.035, is the one in the summary, and it is above the conventional 0.01 but below 0.05.

reporting_issues.issue: Degrees of freedom are given only for the heart-rate comparison (1,5). The two time-course tests (F=14.24 and F=10.6, both P<0.001) are printed without degrees of freedom, and with six men neither P value can be reproduced from a one-way within-person test: F(1,5)=14.24 gives P=0.013 and F(2,10)=14.24 gives P=0.0012 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: The reader cannot tell which test was run; the P<0.001 values are only reproducible if the time factor had more than two levels, which the methods (baseline, 2.5 h and 3.5 h) would allow.

reporting_issues.issue: No means, standard deviations or confidence intervals are printed for the study's main outcome. The day-1 and day-15 heart-rate rises appear only as bars with error bars in Figure 3.
reporting_issues.consequence: The size of the tolerance cannot be quoted from the paper; any figure read off the bars would be an estimate from an image and should not be cited as a measured value.

reporting_issues.issue: Because of psychomotor testing between measurements, only baseline and the 2.5-hour and 3.5-hour time points were analysed for the cardiovascular outcome, which the methods state plainly but the summary and discussion do not repeat.
reporting_issues.consequence: The heart-rate conclusion rests on two post-dose time points chosen for being free of activity, not on the whole time course, and peak cardiovascular effects may not have been captured.

reporting_issues.issue: The challenge dose is described as '10 mg of oral deuterated methamphetamine HCl' in the summary and as '0.125 mg/kg of deuterated methamphetamine HCl' in the methods; at the mean weight of 72.6 kg these correspond to about 9.1 mg, so the summary rounds a weight-adjusted dose to a fixed one.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor, but a reader comparing this challenge with the 10 mg daily dose would take them to be identical when the challenge was scaled to body weight.

reporting_issues.issue: The neuropsychological battery is named in the introduction as part of the study and its results are deferred to a separate report that is not identified.
reporting_issues.consequence: Cognitive outcomes after thirteen days of daily dosing cannot be checked against the subjective and cardiovascular findings.

verification.source_read: PDF pp. 352-358 (PDFs/Methamphetamine/PerezReyes_1991_DailyMethamphetamineClinicalEffects.pdf). The file has no text layer: pages were rendered at 300 dpi and read with optical character recognition, and every number used in this card was then checked against the page images (summary p. 352, participants p. 353, challenge dose p. 354, results p. 355, Figures 1-2 p. 356, Figure 3 and discussion p. 357).

design_detail: Two-week inpatient, double-blind, placebo-controlled, within-participant laboratory study with dose order counterbalanced across participants: 11 adults who used methamphetamine regularly by the intranasal route and were not seeking treatment each completed four two-day blocks (placebo and three active doses). Sleep was measured on the night after the dose (wrist actigraphy in 6 of 11; morning questionnaire in all 11), and next-morning plasma methamphetamine, heart rate, blood pressure, mood ratings and a psychomotor and memory battery were taken to assess 'residual' effects. Same participants as the acute-effects report Hart et al. (hart_2008).
can_establish: Within these 11 people, whether a single laboratory dose, compared with placebo, changes measured and self-rated sleep that night and mood, heart rate, blood pressure and test performance the next morning, and whether those changes depend on dose.
cannot_establish: What happens after repeated doses or binges over several days (the usual pattern the authors describe), after other routes, with street product, alongside alcohol or other drugs, or in people who are not experienced; objective sleep in the five participants whose actigraphy was lost; and whether small next-day effects on performance were missed (11 people, one morning test, no performance data shown).

sample.recruitment: Not described in this report beyond non-treatment-seeking adults studied as inpatients at the New York State Psychiatric Institute; the same participants are described in the acute-effects report (Hart et al.).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: DSM-IV current methamphetamine abuse or dependence, not seeking treatment; no other Axis I disorder; passed medical and psychiatric evaluation; normal weight range (2.1 Participants).
sample.demographics: Age 22 to 45 (mean 30.7); body mass index 24.1 (SD 4.4); methamphetamine used 3.6 (SD 1.7) days a week, mainly intranasally (nine had also smoked it, one injected). Six also used cocaine, seven alcohol, seven cannabis, and eight smoked tobacco (2.1 Participants).
sample.attrition: All 11 completed. Actigraphy data for the first five participants were lost through equipment malfunction (2.3 Sleep Monitoring).
sample.selection_effects: Experienced, non-treatment-seeking people who use mainly intranasally and agreed to a two-week inpatient study; screened free of other psychiatric disorders. Missing actigraphy was due to equipment, so it is unlikely to be related to the outcome, but it leaves objective sleep in only six people.

exposure.measurement: Doses given by the investigators under double-blind conditions in an inpatient unit; plasma methamphetamine measured the next morning.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions: single intranasal doses of 0 (lactose placebo), 12, 25 and 50 mg/70 kg methamphetamine hydrochloride (NIDA), each made up to 60 mg/70 kg with lactose and insufflated through a straw within 30 seconds; maximum single dose capped at 60 mg, so three participants over 84 kg received 41 to 48 mg/70 kg. Dose at about 10:00 on day 1 of each block; lights out at 23:00 for an 8-hour sleep period (about 13 hours after dosing); next-morning measures from about 10:00 on day 2 (about 24 hours after dosing). Blocks separated by at least 48 hours (Methods) or at least 24 hours (abstract). Next-morning plasma methamphetamine: 6.72, 13.67 and 38.08 ng/ml after the three active doses.
exposure.polysubstance: Inpatient residence from at least two days before the first session was intended to ensure washout and prevent other drug use during the study; current cocaine, alcohol, cannabis and tobacco use reported at entry (tobacco use during the study not described).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Admitted at least two days before the first session and resident throughout; no drug testing during the stay is described.

comparison.controls: Each participant's own placebo block.
comparison.matching: Within-person; dose order counterbalanced (method not described).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to the within-person comparison; habitual sleep and its baseline were not measured or reported.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable (same people).

outcomes.instruments: Actiwatch wrist actigraphy (total sleep time, awakenings; 6 participants); morning estimate of hours slept and six 100-mm visual analogue sleep items (slept well, woke early, fell asleep easily, clear-headed, woke often, satisfied); computerized visual analogue mood, drug-effect, physical-symptom and craving items; Digit-Symbol Substitution, repeated acquisition, divided attention, rapid information processing and digit recall tasks; heart rate, systolic and diastolic pressure; plasma methamphetamine.
outcomes.validity_norms: Actigraphy is a validated proxy for sleep but not polysomnography; the visual analogue items are laboratory-specific; no norms.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Residual' effects were defined by the authors as effects present once plasma levels are falling and acute effects are negligible (their time threshold is given in the exposure field); sleep disruption as shorter total sleep, more awakenings and worse ratings.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. The number of subjective items and task measures analysed is not stated (the questionnaire is described only by example); Table 1 shows 6 sleep items, 6 of the mood ratings and 4 physiological measures.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Double-blind dosing; outcomes were self-ratings, task scores and devices. Blinding integrity was not assessed, and the higher doses have noticeable acute effects.

analysis.effect_sizes: Repeated-measures ANOVA with planned comparisons against placebo (Huynh-Feldt), df 1 and 30 for the 11-person measures. Actigraphy (n = 6): total sleep 4.4 against 6.4 hours with the highest dose (p < .01; '±' values 1.03 and 1.16 unlabelled); more awakenings with the highest dose than with any other condition (p < .01). Self-estimated sleep: 7.70 (SEM 0.31) hours after placebo, 6.77 (0.56), 4.83 (0.85) and 2.84 (0.89) after the three active doses, so about 2.9 and 4.9 hours less after the two higher doses (p < .001). 'Woke often' 16.50 (6.66) against 64.80 (12.48) and 67.56 (11.52); 'slept well' 85.20 (3.82) against 49.60 (11.68) and 21.44 (7.41). Next morning after the highest dose: alert 38.09 against 55.55, content 37.36 against 53.91, friendly 43.00 against 65.00, social 40.82 against 67.09, talkative 37.36 against 58.46 (all marked p < .05 against placebo); heart rate 90.46 against 78.36 bpm, systolic 124.00 against 118.00 and diastolic 78.55 against 69.00 mm Hg. Standardized effects and confidence intervals are not reported.
analysis.covariates: None; within-person design.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or protocol is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: Only selected subjective items are tabulated; 'depressed', 'anxious' and 'I want meth' are reported in the discussion as unchanged without values; no numbers at all are given for the five performance tasks.
analysis.power: Not addressed; 11 participants, 6 for objective sleep.

interpretation_gap.results_show: After the highest dose, measured sleep that night was about 2 hours shorter with more awakenings (6 people); after the two higher doses, people reported far less and worse sleep (11 people). The next morning, after the highest dose, several positive mood ratings were lower, heart rate and blood pressure were higher and methamphetamine was still in the blood; ratings of feeling depressed or anxious or wanting methamphetamine did not change, and no effect on the performance tasks was detected.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and discussion are mostly faithful. Gaps: (1) the discussion's statement that self-reports "may dramatically overestimate" sleep disruption compares 11 people's reports with 6 people's actigraphy, and actigraphy itself is only a proxy for sleep; (2) the absence of next-day performance effects is stated without data, from one morning test in 11 people, which can show only that no large effect was found; (3) next-day mood changes are summarized as limited although five of six tabulated positive-mood ratings fell after the highest dose. The authors themselves name the single-dose design, the six actigraphy records and the single morning test as limits.

timeline.event: Hart et al., acute physiological and behavioural effects of the same doses in the same participants.
This report of next-night and next-day effects: the first controlled study of residual effects of intranasal methamphetamine, by the authors' account.

replication.where_it_stands: A single small study; no replication with polysomnography, repeated dosing or a full next-day test schedule was found in the material read. The same participants appear in hart_2008, so the two reports are one sample.

funding.funder: Not reported in the PMC author manuscript (no acknowledgements or funding section). Methamphetamine was provided by the National Institute on Drug Abuse; the paper is an NIH author manuscript (NIHMS41862).
funding.declared_conflicts: Not reported.
funding.affiliations_note: Columbia University and New York State Psychiatric Institute (Hart, Foltin, Gunderson and colleagues).

what_would_settle_it: A larger crossover study with polysomnography in every participant, single and repeated doses over consecutive days at the times people actually use, and next-day mood, performance and driving tests repeated through the day, with all outcomes pre-registered and reported.

domains.domain: Randomization process (order of the four dose conditions)
domains.note: Dose order counterbalanced; the scheme is not described.

Single doses with a washout between blocks (the abstract and Methods give different minimum gaps; exposure field); carry-over unlikely to be large, though next-morning plasma levels show the drug was still present the following day.
Double-blind with a lactose placebo, but the higher doses produce noticeable effects and blinding integrity was not checked; this matters for the self-rated sleep and mood outcomes.
Actigraphy missing for 5 of 11 through equipment failure (unlikely to depend on the outcome), leaving objective sleep in 6; other outcomes complete.
Objective actigraphy and vital signs are at low risk; the sleep and mood ratings are self-reports by participants who may have recognised the dose.
No protocol; only selected subjective items are tabulated and the performance results are reported without numbers.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Several domains raise some concerns, none high; the objective outcomes (actigraphy, heart rate, blood pressure, plasma level) carry less risk than the self-rated sleep and mood outcomes. Judged some concerns overall rather than high because the main effects are large and dose-related and the objective and subjective sleep measures point the same way. May be cited for the size and direction of next-night sleep loss and next-morning mood and cardiovascular changes after a single laboratory dose in experienced people; not for the absence of next-day cognitive effects, which rests on unreported data.

key_findings.finding: Measured sleep (actigraphy, 6 participants): after the highest dose, total sleep that night was 4.4 hours against 6.4 hours after placebo, an average reduction of 2 hours (p < .01), and awakenings were more frequent than after any other condition (p < .01); the two lower doses did not significantly change measured sleep.
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.1 Sleep, 1st paragraph; Figure 1 legend (left panels, n = 6)

key_findings.finding: Self-rated sleep (11 participants): estimated hours slept 7.70 (SEM 0.31) after placebo, 6.77 (0.56), 4.83 (0.85) and 2.84 (0.89) after the three active doses, about 2.9 and 4.9 hours less after the two higher doses (p < .001); after both higher doses people also rated falling asleep less easily, sleeping less well, waking more often and being less satisfied with their sleep, and after the highest dose feeling less clear-headed.
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.1 Sleep, 2nd paragraph; Table 1, sleep questionnaire rows

key_findings.finding: Next morning after the highest dose, ratings were lower than after placebo for alert (38.09 against 55.55), content (37.36 against 53.91), friendly (43.00 against 65.00), social (40.82 against 67.09) and talkative (37.36 against 58.46); energetic (22.80 against 35.20) is marked as different only from the lowest active dose. 'Social' was also lower after the lowest dose (50.36; F = 4.46, marked p < .05).
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.2 Subjective effects; Table 1, subjective-effect rows

key_findings.finding: Ratings of feeling depressed, feeling anxious and wanting methamphetamine were not changed by the previous day's dose (no values reported).

No significant next-day effect on the cognitive and psychomotor battery (digit-symbol substitution, repeated acquisition, divided attention, rapid information processing, immediate and delayed digit recall); no means or test statistics are reported.

The next morning, after the highest dose, heart rate was 90.46 against 78.36 bpm after placebo, systolic pressure 124.00 against 118.00 and diastolic 78.55 against 69.00 mm Hg (all p < .05), and plasma methamphetamine was still measurable after every active dose.
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.4 Physiological measures; Table 1, physiological rows

key_findings.finding: Measured and self-rated awakenings after the highest dose were correlated at r = -.89 (p < .02, n = 6); there were no significant correlations after the middle dose. The authors read the gap between about 5 fewer self-reported and 2 fewer measured hours as self-report overestimating sleep loss.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and the Methods give different minimum gaps between the dose blocks (the abstract's is half the Methods'; values in the exposure field).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract; 2.2 Design and Procedures, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The washout cannot be stated with certainty; with the shorter gap, methamphetamine from the previous block could still be measurable at the next dose, since it was measurable the morning after every active dose.

reporting_issues.issue: The correlation between measured awakenings and 'woke often' ratings after the highest dose is printed as r = -.89: a negative sign means that people with more measured awakenings reported waking less often. The text calls the measures significantly correlated without discussing the direction (n = 6, df 4).
reporting_issues.consequence: Either the sign is a typographical error or the two measures disagreed person by person; the correlation cannot be used as agreement between self-report and actigraphy.

reporting_issues.issue: Significance marks in Table 1 do not follow the F values consistently: with df 1 and 30, F = 4.33 (unmarked, twice) and F = 4.38 (marked) both correspond to p of about .045 (editors' calculation); 'energetic' after the highest dose has F = 5.33 (p about .03) but is marked only as different from the lowest dose, while the text lists it among ratings significantly decreased.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Table 1; Results › 3.2 Subjective effects
reporting_issues.consequence: Borderline effects (next-morning heart rate after the middle dose, 'energetic') cannot be classified with confidence; the main effects are far from the threshold and unaffected.

reporting_issues.issue: The discussion contrasts nearly 5 fewer self-reported hours with 2 fewer measured hours, but the self-reports come from all 11 participants and the measured hours from 6; the same-person comparison is shown only in an image (Figure 1, right panels).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Discussion, 2nd paragraph; Figure 1 legend
reporting_issues.consequence: The size of any self-report overestimate is not established; part of the gap may reflect who had actigraphy.

reporting_issues.issue: The measured total sleep values (4.4 '±' 1.03 against 6.4 '±' 1.16 hours) do not say whether the spread is an SD or an SEM; elsewhere the paper uses SEM.
reporting_issues.consequence: A standardized effect cannot be computed reliably.

reporting_issues.issue: No funding or conflict-of-interest statement appears in the PMC author manuscript.
reporting_issues.consequence: Funding cannot be stated from the source read; the published version may carry it.

verification.first_pass_by: AI (Claude, reading agent), AI reader 111 (first reader)
verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC2267907 (author manuscript; all sections and Table 1 rendered as text, reference list read; Figure 1 is an image and its values were not extracted; no acknowledgements, funding or conflict statement present)

design_detail: Open-label randomized controlled trial (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01103531) in a publicly funded residential treatment programme in Southern California, 2010 to 2013: 135 adults with methamphetamine dependence newly admitted to residential treatment were randomized (computerized urn randomization stratified by sex and severity of use) to a supervised progressive aerobic and resistance exercise programme or to an equal number of group health-education sessions. This report analyses weekly Beck Depression and Beck Anxiety Inventory totals over the programme with mixed-effects models. The same trial is reported elsewhere for methamphetamine use after discharge, fitness, heart-rate variability, dopamine receptors and craving.
can_establish: Whether, during residential treatment in early abstinence, people randomized to a supervised exercise programme reported larger falls in depression and anxiety scores over the programme than people randomized to health-education sessions.
cannot_establish: Whether exercise itself, rather than knowing one was in the exercise group, lowered self-rated symptoms (no blinding, self-report outcomes); whether effects last after the programme (follow-up data registered but not reported here); whether more exercise causes more benefit (attendance was not randomized); effects outside residential treatment, in people with major depression (excluded by the registry criteria), or in people who use methamphetamine occasionally.

sample.recruitment: Clients newly admitted to a publicly funded residential treatment programme (registry: Cri-Help, North Hollywood, California), recruited by flyers in the facility, 2010 to 2013.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Methamphetamine dependence, English proficiency, age 18 to 45 for men or 18 to 55 for women, able to attend sessions; excluded for medical impairment affecting safety, opiate dependence, or psychiatric impairment needing hospitalization or primary treatment (Procedures, 1st paragraph). The registry adds DSM-IV-TR dependence, normal vital signs and ECG, and exclusion of major depression, psychosis and bipolar illness, among others.
sample.demographics: Mean age 31.7 (SD 6.9), range 18 to 47; 29.6% women; 48.1% Latino, 41.5% non-Latino white, 4.4% African American, 3.7% Asian; 16.3% employed in the month before entry; 64.7% with high-school education; 15.9 (SD 9.9) days of methamphetamine use in the month before entry (Results › Participant characteristics).
sample.attrition: Two participants (one per group) discharged for positive drug tests and excluded from analyses. The number contributing data at the end of the programme is not given in the text (the CONSORT diagram is an image); the registry says early discharge from the facility ended study participation.
sample.selection_effects: Treatment-seeking adults in one residential programme who volunteered for an exercise trial and passed medical screening; people with major depression were excluded by the registry criteria, so the sample began with mostly minimal to mild depressive symptoms.

exposure.measurement: Randomized assignment; attendance recorded by sign-in sheets.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions: exercise three times a week for 8 weeks (24 sessions) of about 55 minutes (the abstract says 60): 5-minute warm-up, 30 minutes on a treadmill at 60% to 80% of maximum heart rate (registry: 60% to 85%), 15 minutes of weight training of the major muscle groups, 5-minute cool-down; individually supervised by an exercise physiologist, with progressive increases in treadmill speed or slope and in weights. Control: 24 group health-education sessions of 55 minutes on stress reduction, health screening, healthy relationships and sexually transmitted diseases (registry: also healthy eating, meditation, sleep hygiene, cancer screening). Participants received a $10 gift card per session attended. Questionnaires at baseline, weekly and at discharge (week 9). Attendance: exercise 17.4 (SD 7.3) sessions, health education 18.5 (SD 7.0).
exposure.polysubstance: People with opiate dependence were excluded; other substance use is not reported.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Abstinence required by the facility and checked by random urine screens at least weekly; a positive test led to discharge.

comparison.controls: Health-education sessions of equal number and length, in group format, within the same residential treatment.
comparison.matching: Randomization stratified by sex and by severity of use (18 or fewer against 19 or more days in the previous month). The text says groups did not differ at baseline, but the reported baseline anxiety means differ by 4.6 points (see reporting issues).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to the randomized comparison; baseline imbalance in anxiety is relevant.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Same facility rules for both groups.

outcomes.instruments: Beck Depression Inventory (21 items, 0 to 63) and Beck Anxiety Inventory (21 items), self-completed at the end of each week; weekly totals analysed.
outcomes.validity_norms: Standard validated self-report scales; the paper gives the usual BDI bands (0 to 13 minimal, 14 to 19 mild, 20 to 28 moderate, 29 to 63 severe).
outcomes.operationalization: Change in weekly total scores over the programme (treatment by time interaction); secondary: a three-way interaction of sessions attended, group and time.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None (two primary outcomes in this report, plus attendance analyses).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: None: the registry records masking as none (open label); outcomes were self-reported by participants who knew their group.

analysis.effect_sizes: Mixed-effects repeated-measures models, adjusted for demographics. Depression: treatment by time beta -0.63, P = 0.001; at the end of the programme BDI 2.43 (SD 4.22) with exercise against 4.82 (SD 5.71) with health education. Anxiety: beta -0.95, P = 0.001; BAI 2.18 (SD 4.94) against 5.11 (SD 7.79). Editors' calculation from these figures, assuming all randomized participants contributed: differences of 2.4 and 2.9 points, standardized about 0.48 and 0.45. Attendance by group by time: depression beta -0.61 (95% CI printed as -0.20 to -1.02), P < 0.001; anxiety -0.22 (-0.42 to -0.06), P = 0.009. No confidence intervals are given for the main treatment by time effects.
analysis.covariates: Demographics (not specified); baseline score in the attendance models.
analysis.preregistration_detail: NCT01103531, first submitted 31 March 2010 at the start of the trial. Registered primary outcome: self-reported days of methamphetamine use over the 12 weeks after discharge. 'Psychiatric symptoms' is a registered secondary outcome, measured from baseline to discharge and to 12 and 26 weeks after discharge. This paper calls depression and anxiety its two primary outcomes and reports only the programme period.
analysis.selective_reporting: The post-discharge psychiatric-symptom data registered as part of the secondary outcome are not reported here; the attendance analyses are described as secondary and not pre-specified in the registry.
analysis.power: Planned for 130 participants to give 80% power to detect a 3.5-point difference (SD 5) from baseline to the end of the programme; the observed end-of-programme differences (2.4 and 2.9 points) are smaller than that target.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Both groups' depression and anxiety scores fell steeply during residential treatment (from mild or minimal levels to near zero); the exercise group ended about 2.4 BDI and 2.9 BAI points lower than the health-education group, with significant group by time interactions. The exercise group had started with higher anxiety.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that results support a structured exercise programme "as an effective intervention" for depression and anxiety in methamphetamine abstinence, and the discussion recommends that providers encourage this kind of exercise. Gaps: (1) open-label allocation with self-reported outcomes cannot separate exercise from expectation and attention; (2) the larger fall in anxiety in a group that started 4.6 points higher is partly what regression to the mean would produce; (3) the end-of-programme differences are below the trial's own planned minimum difference; (4) the 'dose effect' rests on attendance, which participants chose; (5) the outcomes were secondary in the registry, with follow-up not reported.

timeline.event: Trial registered (NCT01103531); design paper Mooney et al. 2014 (Contemp Clin Trials 37:139-147).

This report (depression and anxiety); companion reports of the same trial: Haglund et al. 2015 (predictors of depression outcomes) and Rawson et al. 2015 (methamphetamine use after discharge, Drug Alcohol Depend 156:21-28).
Xu et al. systematic review lists this trial three times among 17 entries on exercise in methamphetamine use disorder.

replication.where_it_stands: The only randomized trial of exercise for depression and anxiety in early methamphetamine abstinence read here with numbers; other trials reported in the same direction (mostly in Chinese compulsory rehabilitation) are known only through a review without numbers (xu_2024).

funding.funder: National Institute on Drug Abuse grant R01 DA027633.
funding.declared_conflicts: None declared.
funding.affiliations_note: UCLA Integrated Substance Abuse Programs and UCLA exercise physiology (Dolezal, Cooper); the same group published several reports of this trial.

what_would_settle_it: A trial with blinded outcome assessment or objective outcomes, an attention-matched active control, analysis of the registered outcomes at the registered times including after discharge, baseline-adjusted comparisons, and a sample that includes people with clinically significant depression and people outside residential care.

domains.note: Computerized urn randomization held by a data management centre, so concealment is plausible; but baseline anxiety differed by 4.6 points (about 0.8 SD by the editors' calculation) despite the text's statement of no difference.
Open label; participants attended about three quarters of sessions in both arms; two randomized participants were excluded from analysis; the analysis set at the end of the programme is not reported.
Early discharge ended participation (registry) and the number with week-8 data is not given in the text; mixed models assume data missing at random.
Self-reported depression and anxiety by participants who knew whether they were exercising, in a trial that the exercise group may have expected to help.

Registered as a secondary outcome with longer follow-up; this report presents it as primary over the programme period only, with several analyses (interaction terms, end-of-programme means, attendance models).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: High because the outcomes are self-reports by unblinded participants; the baseline imbalance in anxiety, unreported attrition and the shift from a registered secondary outcome add further concerns. May be cited for the observed difference between groups over the programme, with these limits; not for a causal effect of exercise on mood, for durability, or for a dose-response relation.

key_findings.finding: 135 adults with methamphetamine dependence in residential treatment were randomized: 69 to exercise and 66 to health education; mean age 31.7 (SD 6.9), 29.6% women, 48.1% Latino; 15.9 (SD 9.9) days of methamphetamine use in the month before entry. Two participants (one per group) were discharged for positive drug tests and excluded.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Procedures, 2nd paragraph; Measures, 2nd paragraph; Results › Participant characteristics

key_findings.finding: Baseline scores as reported: Beck Depression Inventory 13.7 (SD 5.3) with exercise against 12.0 (SD 6.3), P = 0.21; Beck Anxiety Inventory 16.5 (SD 6.0) against 11.9 (SD 5.1), P = 0.08.
key_findings.locator: Results › Changes in depression and anxiety symptoms, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation from these means and SDs with 69 and 66 participants: anxiety t about 4.8, p < 0.0001 (standardized difference about 0.8); depression p about 0.09. See reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Depression: significant treatment by time effect (beta -0.63, P = 0.001), with BDI at the end of the programme 2.43 (SD 4.22) in the exercise group against 4.82 (SD 5.71) in the health-education group, after adjustment for demographics.
key_findings.locator: Results › Changes in depression and anxiety symptoms, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Difference 2.4 points; editors' standardized difference about 0.48 if all randomized participants contributed (week-8 numbers not reported).

key_findings.finding: Anxiety: significant treatment by time effect (beta -0.95, P = 0.001), with BAI at the end of the programme 2.18 (SD 4.94) against 5.11 (SD 7.79).
key_findings.locator: Results › Changes in depression and anxiety symptoms, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Difference 2.9 points; editors' standardized difference about 0.45.

key_findings.finding: Attendance did not differ between arms (17.4, SD 7.3, sessions with exercise against 18.5, SD 7.0, with health education); more sessions attended went with lower depression and anxiety in both arms, and more so in the exercise arm (attendance by group by time: depression beta -0.61, P < 0.001; anxiety beta -0.22, 95% CI -0.42 to -0.06, P = 0.009).
No harms or unintended effects occurred in either group during the trial.

The trial was powered for a 3.5-point difference (SD 5) between groups in depression and anxiety change; the authors' limitations are a residential treatment sample, self-report measures, stress content in the health-education sessions, and a mostly male sample (70%).

Registry record: primary outcome self-reported days of methamphetamine use over 12 weeks after discharge; secondary outcomes include psychiatric symptoms from baseline to discharge and at 12 and 26 weeks after discharge; masking none (open label); first submitted 31 March 2010.
key_findings.locator: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01103531, Study Plan › Design Details; Primary and Secondary Outcome Measures; Study Record Dates

reporting_issues.issue: The reported baseline P values do not fit the reported means and SDs: anxiety 16.5 (6.0) against 11.9 (5.1) with 69 and 66 participants gives t about 4.8, p < 0.0001 (editors' calculation), not P = 0.08; depression 13.7 (5.3) against 12.0 (6.3) gives p about 0.09, not 0.21. The text states there were no significant baseline differences.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Changes in depression and anxiety symptoms, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The exercise group probably started with clearly higher anxiety, so part of its larger fall may be regression to the mean; the anxiety result should be read as adjusted at best for demographics, not for baseline.

reporting_issues.issue: The text gives P = 0.03 for the effect of sessions attended on depression; Table 1 gives P < 0.001 for the same coefficient (-0.52, -0.83 to -0.22).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Dose effect; Table 1
reporting_issues.consequence: One of the two values is wrong; the confidence interval fits the table's value.

reporting_issues.issue: Several Table 1 P values do not match their confidence intervals (editors' calculation from interval width): baseline anxiety 0.23 (0.03 to 0.39) implies p about 0.01, printed < .001; treatment on anxiety -6.51 (-9.93 to -3.07) implies p about 0.0002, printed 0.02; sessions attended on anxiety (-0.42 to -0.16) implies p < 0.0001, printed 0.01; and the depression interaction interval is printed with its bounds reversed (-0.20, -1.02).
reporting_issues.consequence: The table's statistics cannot be taken at face value; the direction of the effects is not in doubt.

reporting_issues.issue: Depression and anxiety are called the two primary outcomes, but the registry lists self-reported methamphetamine use after discharge as the primary outcome and psychiatric symptoms as a secondary outcome with follow-up to 26 weeks after discharge, which is not reported here.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods › Measures, 1st paragraph; registry record NCT01103531
reporting_issues.consequence: Outcome switching between registration and report; the durability of any mood benefit is unknown from this paper.

reporting_issues.issue: The end-of-programme means (2.43 and 4.82; 2.18 and 5.11) are introduced in wording that could be read as change scores from baseline; read against the baselines they must be end-of-programme scores. The number of participants contributing at that time is not given.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Changes in depression and anxiety symptoms, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Standardized differences can only be approximated (editors' calculation assumes everyone randomized contributed).

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and Methods give different session lengths for the exercise programme (exposure field).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract › Methods; Methods › Intervention Condition
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the Methods describe the session in detail.
